Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddasikkhā-mūlasikkhā

The Minor Training and The Fundamental Training

Khuddasikkhā

The Minor Training

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

(Ka)

(Ka)

Ādito [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] upasampanna-sikkhitabbaṃ samātikaṃ;

Khuddasikkhaṃ pavakkhāmi, vanditvā ratanattayaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I shall explain the Minor Training: the training with its summary that should be learned from the beginning by one who has received the higher ordination.

Tatrāyaṃ mātikā –

Herein is the summary:

(Kha)

(Kha)

Pārājikā ca cattāro, garukā nava cīvaraṃ;

Rajanāni ca patto ca, thālakā ca pavāraṇā.

The four Pārājikas, the nine grave offenses, robes; dyes, the bowl, the small bowl, and the invitation.

(Ga)

(Ga)

Kālikā [V 0.0002] ca paṭiggāho, maṃsesu ca akappiyaṃ;

Nissaggiyāni pācitti, samaṇakappa bhūmiyo.

Time-bound items and their acceptance, and what is impermissible regarding meat; offenses entailing forfeiture, offenses of expiation; grounds and conduct suitable for a recluse.

(Gha)

(Gha)

Upajjhācariyavattāni, vaccappassāvaṭhānikaṃ;

Āpucchakaraṇaṃ naggo, nhānakappo avandiyo.

Duties towards preceptors and teachers, the place for feces and urine; asking permission, nakedness, the allowance for bathing, those unworthy of veneration.

(Ṅa)

(Ṅa)

Cammaṃ upāhanā ceva, anolokiyamañjanī;

Akappiyasayanāni, samānāsanikopi ca.

Hides and sandals, applying collyrium without looking; improper beds, and sharing a seat.

(Ca)

(Ca)

Asaṃvāsiko ca kammaṃ, micchājīvavivajjanā;

Vattaṃ vikappanā ceva, nissayo kāyabandhanaṃ.

The formal act making one unfit for communion, avoidance of wrong livelihood; duties, determination, dependence, and the waistband.

(Cha)

(Cha)

Pathavī [M 0.0002] ca parikkhāro, bhesajjuggahadūsanaṃ;

Vassūpanāyikā cevāvebhaṅgiyaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ.

The earth and requisites, medicine, acceptance, and spoiling; entering the rains-residence, what is not to be distributed, and miscellaneous matters.

(Ja)

(Ja)

Desanā chandadānādi, uposathappavāraṇā;

Saṃvaro suddhi santoso, caturakkhā vipassanāti.

Confession of faults, giving of consent, and so on; the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā; restraint, purity, contentment; the four protections, and insight.

1. Pārājikaniddeso

1. Exposition of the Offenses of Defeat

Pārājikā ca cattāroti –

The four Pārājikas are as follows:

1.

1.

Maggattaye anikkhittasikkho santhatasanthate;

Allokāse nimittaṃ saṃ, tilamattampi santhataṃ.

For one who has not renounced the training, when in any of the three passages there is continuous contact, even in an open space, with his own organ inserted even as much as a sesame seed.

2.

2.

Asanthatamupādiṇṇaṃ, pavesanto cutotha vā;

Pavesanaṭṭhituddhārapaviṭṭhakkhaṇasādako.

Whether it is unaroused or aroused, upon entering or withdrawing; the offense is accomplished at the moment of entering, remaining, withdrawing, or having entered.

3.

3.

Ādiyeyya [V 0.0003] hareyyāvahareyya iriyāpathaṃ;

Kopeyya ṭhānā cāveyya, saṅketaṃ vītināmaye.

He might take it, carry it away, or misappropriate it; he might change its posture, shake it, or move it from its place; he might move it beyond a designated boundary.

4.

4.

Adinnaṃ theyyacittena, bhave pārājikotha vā;

Theyyābalakusacchannaparikappāvahārako;

Bhaṇḍakālagghadesehi, paribhogettha nicchayo.

Taking what is not given with thieving intent results in an offense of defeat. Or one who takes away by theft, force, trickery, concealment, or pre-arrangement; the determination here is by the article, time, value, place, and its use.

5.

5.

Manussaviggahaṃ cicca, jīvitā vā viyojaye;

Satthahārakaṃ vāssa maraṇacetano upanikkhipe.

One might intentionally deprive a human being of life, or with murderous intent, one might find a weapon-bearer for him or place a weapon nearby.

6.

6.

Gāheyya maraṇūpāyaṃ, vadeyya maraṇe guṇaṃ;

Cuto payogā sāhatthinissaggāṇattithāvarā.

He might take up a means of death, or speak in praise of death; by direct effort, by one's own hand, by throwing, by command, or by a fixed device.

7.

7.

Iddhivijjāmayā kālavatthāvudhiriyāpathā;

Kriyāviseso okāso, cha āṇattiniyāmakā.

By means of psychic power and knowledge; time, object, weapon, posture, a specific action, and opportunity—these six are the determinants of a command.

8.

8.

Jhānādibheda nosantamattanattupanāyikaṃ;

Katvā koṭṭhāsamekekaṃ, paccuppannabhavassitaṃ.

Claiming for oneself the various distinctions of jhāna and so on, which are not actually present; making each a separate part, based on one's present state.

9.

9.

Aññāpadesarahitaṃ[M 0.0003], dīpentonadhimāniko;

Kāyena vācā viññatti-pathe ñāte cuto bhave.

Without reference to another, making it known, while not possessing the attainment; when it is understood through the avenue of intimation by body or speech, he has fallen.

10.

10.

Pārājikete cattāro, asaṃvāsā yathā pure;

Abhabbā bhikkhubhāvāya, sīsacchinnova jīvituṃ.

These four are offenses of defeat, making one unfit for communion, just as before ordination; one is incapable of the state of a bhikkhu, like one with a severed head is of living.

11.

11.

Pariyāyo ca āṇatti, tatiye dutiye pana;

Āṇattiyeva sesesu, dvayametaṃ na labbhati.

Indirect speech and command apply in the third and second offenses; in the remaining ones, this pair is not found.

12.

12.

Sevetukāmatācittaṃ[V 0.0004], magge maggappavesanaṃ;

Imaṃ methunadhammassa, āhu aṅgadvayaṃ budhā.

The intention to engage in intercourse, and the penetration of one passage by another; these two, the wise say, are the factors of the sexual act.

13.

13.

Manussasaṃ tathāsaññī, theyyacittañca vatthuno;

Garutā avahāro ca, adinnādānahetuyo.

That it belongs to another, the perception that it is so, the thieving intention for the object, its significant value, and the act of taking it away—these are the causes for taking what is not given.

14.

14.

Pāṇo mānussako pāṇa-saññitā ghātacetanā;

Payogo tena maraṇaṃ, pañcete vadhahetuyo.

A human being, the perception that it is a living being, the intention to kill, the effort made, and the resulting death—these five are the causes of killing.

15.

15.

Asantatā attani pāpamicchatā-

Yārocanā tassa manussajātitā;

Nāññāpadeso ca tadeva jānanaṃ,

Pañcettha aṅgāni asantadīpane.

The non-existence of the quality in oneself, a declaration with wicked intent, the listener being human, no reference to another, and the listener's understanding—these are the five factors in declaring what is not real.

16.

16.

Asādhāraṇā cattāro, bhikkhunīnamabhabbakā;

Ekādasa ca vibbhantā, bhikkhunī mudupiṭṭhiko.

Four are not held in common, making bhikkhunīs unfit; and eleven for a corrupt bhikkhunī, and for a weak-minded one.

17.

17.

Lambī mukhena gaṇhanto, aṅgajātaṃ parassa ca;

Tatthevābhinisīdanto, cattāro anulomikā.

Taking with the mouth the hanging organ of another, and sitting down right upon the private part—these four are compliant offenses.

18.

18.

Magge maggappavesanā, methunassa idhāgatā;

Cattāroti catubbīsa, samodhānā parājikāti.

The penetration of one passage by another has been stated here for sexual intercourse; the four offenses, becoming twenty-four by combination, are the offenses of defeat.

2. Saṅghādisesaniddeso

2. Exposition of the Saṅghādisesa Offenses

Garukā [M 0.0004] navāti –

The nine grave offenses are as follows:

19.

19.

Mocetukāmatā sukka-ssupakkamma vimocayaṃ;

Aññatra supinantena, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

With the desire to emit semen, making an effort to emit it, except in a dream, a recluse thereby commits a grave offense.

20.

20.

Itthisaññī [V 0.0005] manussitthiṃ, kāyasaṃsaggarāgavā;

Samphusanto upakkamma, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

Perceiving a human female as such, and lustful for bodily contact, by making an effort to touch her, a recluse commits a grave offense.

21.

21.

Tathā suṇantiṃ viññuñca, maggaṃ vārabbha methunaṃ;

Duṭṭhullavācārāgena, obhāsetvā garuṃ phuse.

Likewise, to a discerning woman who is listening, speaking with lust and coarse words that allude to the passages connected with intercourse; having addressed her thus, he commits a grave offense.

22.

22.

Vatvāttakāmupaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇaṃ methunarāgino;

Vācā methunayuttena, garuṃ methunayācane.

Speaking in praise of attending to one's own lusts to a person with sexual passion, with speech connected to intercourse, is a grave offense of solicitation.

23.

23.

Paṭiggahetvā sandesaṃ, itthiyā purisassa vā;

Vīmaṃsitvā haraṃ paccā, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

Accepting a message from a woman for a man or from a man for a woman, and carrying it back and forth as a go-between, a recluse thereby commits a grave offense.

24.

24.

Saṃyācitaparikkhāraṃ, katvādesitavatthukaṃ;

Kuṭiṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ, attuddesaṃ garuṃ phuse.

Building for his own sake a hut with materials obtained by asking, if it is on a site not designated by the Sangha or exceeds the proper measure, he commits a grave offense.

25.

25.

Mahallakaṃ vihāraṃ vā, katvādesitavatthukaṃ;

Attano vasanatthāya, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

Or, for the sake of his own dwelling, having a large monastery built on a site not designated by the Sangha, a recluse commits a grave offense.

26.

26.

Amūlakena codento, codāpentova vatthunā;

Antimena ca cāvetuṃ, suṇamānaṃ garuṃ phuse.

Accusing or causing another to accuse a bhikkhu of a final offense with a groundless charge, in order to dislodge him from the holy life, is a grave offense.

27.

27.

Aññassa kiriyaṃ disvā, tena lesena codayaṃ;

Vatthunā antimenāññaṃ, cāvetuṃ garukaṃ phuse.

Having seen some other action, using it as a pretext to accuse another bhikkhu of a final offense in order to dislodge him, one commits a grave offense.

28.

28.

Chādeti jānamāpannaṃ, parivaseyya tāvatā;

Careyya saṅghe mānattaṃ, parivuttho cha rattiyo.

If he knowingly conceals an offense he has committed, he should live on probation for as long as he concealed it. Having completed probation, he should undergo the six-night mānatta penance in the Sangha.

Ciṇṇamānattamabbheyya, taṃ saṅgho vīsatīgaṇo.

When he has completed the mānatta penance, a Sangha with a quorum of twenty bhikkhus should reinstate him.

29.

29.

Āpattinukkhittamanantarāya [M 0.0005][V 0.0006]

Pahuttatāyo tathasaññitā ca;

Chādetukāmo atha chādanāti,

Channā dasaṅgehyaruṇuggamamhīti.

The offense, its not being set aside, the absence of an obstacle, the competence of a confessor, and the perception of it as such; the desire to conceal, and then the act of concealment—by ten factors is the offense concealed at the rising of the sun.

3. Cīvaraniddeso

3. Exposition of Robes

Cīvaranti –

Regarding robes:

30.

30.

Khomakoseyyakappāsa-sāṇabhaṅgāni kambalaṃ;

Kappiyāni chaḷetāni, sānulomāni jātito.

Linen, silk, cotton, hemp, canvas, and wool—these six are allowable, being naturally suitable.

31.

31.

Dukūlañceva paṭṭuṇṇa-paṭaṃ somāracīnajaṃ;

Iddhijaṃ devadinnañca, tassa tassānulomikaṃ.

Fine linen, silk cloth, woolen cloth, Somāra and Chinese fabric, that produced by psychic power, and that which is divinely given, are suitable for each respective person.

32.

32.

Ticīvaraṃ parikkhāra-coḷaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ;

Adhiṭṭhe na vikappeyya, mukhapuñchananisīdanaṃ.

The triple robe, accessory cloth, rains-garment, face-wiping cloth, and sitting cloth: one should determine these, not relinquish them.

33.

33.

Paccattharaṇakaṃ kaṇḍu-cchādimettha ticīvaraṃ;

Na vaseyya vinekāhaṃ, cātumāsaṃ nisīdanaṃ.

The groundsheet, the itch-covering, and the triple robe here: one should not be without them for a single day; the sitting cloth, for four months.

34.

34.

“Imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃdhiṭṭhāmi”, saṅghāṭimiccadhiṭṭhaye;

Ahatthapāsametanti, sesesupi ayaṃ nayo.

‘I determine this outer robe,’ one should thus determine the outer robe. ‘This is beyond arm’s reach.’ This is the method for the remaining items.

35.

35.

Adhiṭṭhahanto saṅghāṭi-ppabhutiṃ pubbacīvaraṃ;

Paccuddharitvādhiṭṭheyya, pattādhiṭṭhahane tathā.

When determining a robe, beginning with the outer robe, one should first withdraw the determination from a former one; likewise when determining a bowl.

36.

36.

Etaṃ [V 0.0007] imaṃ va saṅghāṭiṃ, saṃse paccuddharāmiti;

Evaṃ sabbāni nāmena, vatvā paccuddhare vidū.

‘I withdraw this very outer robe’—thus should the wise one withdraw all things by naming them.

37.

37.

Saṅghāṭi pacchimantena, dīghaso muṭṭhipañcako;

Uttamantena sugata-cīvarūnāpi vaṭṭati.

The outer robe, at its lower edge, should be five fists in length; at its upper edge, it is permissible for it to be less than the Sugata’s robe.

38.

38.

Muṭṭhittikañca tiriyaṃ, tathā ekaṃsikassapi;

Antaravāsako cāpi, dīghaso muṭṭhipañcako;

Aḍḍhateyyo dvihattho vā, tiriyantena vaṭṭati.

Three fists widthwise, and likewise for the single-shouldered robe; the inner robe also, lengthwise five fists; two and a half or two cubits are permissible widthwise.

39.

39.

Nisīdanassa [M 0.0006] dīghena, vidatthi dve visālato;

Diyaḍḍhaṃ dasā vidatthi, sugatassa vidatthiyā.

For the sitting cloth, the length is two spans, the width one and a half spans, and the border one span, according to the Sugata’s span.

40.

40.

Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādikassa, tiriyaṃ dve vidatthiyo;

Dīghantato catassova, sugatassa vidatthiyā.

For the itch-covering cloth, the width is two spans and the length is four, by the Sugata’s span.

41.

41.

Vassikasāṭikāyāpi, dīghaso cha vidatthiyo;

Tiriyaṃ aḍḍhateyyāva, sugatassa vidatthiyā.

For the rains-bathing cloth also, the length is six spans and the width two and a half, by the Sugata’s span.

42.

42.

Ettha chedanapācitti, karontassa taduttari;

Paccattharaṇa mukhacoḷā, ākaṅkhitappamāṇikā.

For one who makes it larger than that, there is a pācittiya offense requiring it to be cut down; the underlay and face-cloth may be of any desired size.

43.

43.

Parikkhāracoḷe gaṇanā, pamāṇaṃ vā na dīpitaṃ;

Tathā vatvā adhiṭṭheyya, thavikādiṃ vikappiyaṃ.

For an accessory cloth, no number or size is specified. Thus, one should determine it; a bag and so forth should be made allowable by sharing.

44.

44.

Ahatāhatakappānaṃ, saṅghāṭi diguṇā siyā;

Ekacciyottarāsaṅgo, tathā antaravāsako.

For new and worn cloth, the outer robe should be double-layered; the upper robe is single-layered, and likewise the inner robe.

45.

45.

Utuddhaṭāna [V 0.0008] dussānaṃ, saṅghāṭi ca catugguṇā;

Bhaveyyuṃ diguṇā sesā, paṃsukūle yathāruci.

For cloths taken from a heap, the outer robe should be four-layered; the rest should be double-layered. For rag-robes, it is as one wishes.

46.

46.

Tīsu dve vāpi ekaṃ vā, chinditabbaṃ pahoti yaṃ;

Sabbesu appahontesu, anvādhimādiyeyya vā;

Acchinnañca anādiṇṇaṃ, na dhāreyya ticīvaraṃ.

In three places, or two, or even one, whatever is suitable should be marked; if the cloth is not sufficient in all places, one may add a patch. One should not wear a triple robe that is unmarked.

47.

47.

Gāme nivesane uddo-sitapāsādahammiye;

Nāvāṭṭamāḷaārāme, satthakhettakhale dume.

In a village, a dwelling, a storied mansion, a palace; in a boat, a watchtower, a hall, a monastery; in a caravan, a field, a threshing floor, or a tree.

48.

48.

Ajjhokāse vihāre vā, nikkhipitvā ticīvaraṃ;

Bhikkhusammutiyāññatra, vippavatthuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Having put aside the triple robe in the open or in a dwelling, it is not allowable to dwell separated from it, except by an agreement of the bhikkhus.

49.

49.

Rogavassānapariyantā, kaṇḍucchādikasāṭikā;

Tato paraṃ vikappeyya, sesā apariyantikā.

The itch-covering cloth and the rains-bathing cloth are limited to periods of illness and the rainy season, respectively. Beyond that time, one should make them allowable by sharing. The remaining items are not limited.

50.

50.

Paccattharaṇa [M 0.0007] parikkhāra-mukhapuñchanacoḷakaṃ;

Dasaṃ pyarattanādiṇṇakappaṃ labbhaṃ nisīdanaṃ.

The underlay, the accessory cloth, the face-wiping cloth, and the sitting cloth are allowable. An extra robe is also allowable for up to ten days, even if unmarked.

51.

51.

Adasaṃ rajitaṃyeva, sesacīvarapañcakaṃ;

Kappatādiṇṇakappaṃva, sadasaṃva nisīdanaṃ.

The remaining five robes, without a border and dyed, are allowable. The sitting cloth with a border is also allowable, even if not formally determined.

52.

52.

Anadhiṭṭhitanissaṭṭhaṃ, kappetvā paribhuñjaye;

Hatthadīghaṃ tatopaḍḍha-vitthārañca vikappiyaṃ.

One may use a robe that is undetermined and not given up, after making it allowable. A piece of cloth a cubit long and half a cubit wide must be made allowable by sharing.

53.

53.

Ticīvarassa bhikkhussa, sabbametaṃ pakāsitaṃ;

Parikkhāracoḷiyo sabbaṃ, tathā vatvā adhiṭṭhati.

All this has been declared for a bhikkhu with the triple robe; all accessory cloths, having said so, he determines.

54.

54.

Acchedavissajjanagāhavibbhamā[V 0.0009],

Paccuddharo māraṇaliṅgasikkhā;

Sabbesvadhiṭṭhānaviyogakāraṇā,

Vinividdhachiddañca ticīvarassa.

Robbery, giving away, seizing, disrobing, withdrawal of determination, death, change of gender, and giving up the training—all these are causes for the cessation of determination, as is a hole pierced through the triple robe.

55.

55.

Kusavākaphalakāni, kambalaṃ kesavālajaṃ;

Thullaccayaṃ dhārayatolūkapakkhājinakkhipe.

For one who wears garments of kusa-grass, bark-fibre, or wood, or a blanket made of human or animal hair, there is a grave offense; likewise for one who wears an owl’s wing or a hide.

56.

56.

Kadalerakakkadusse, potthake cāpi dukkaṭaṃ;

Sabbanīlakamañjeṭṭha-pītalohitakaṇhake.

For wearing cloth of banana-fibre or eraka-grass, or for a bag, there is an offense of wrong-doing; all pure blue, crimson, yellow, red, and black dyes are forbidden.

57.

57.

Mahāraṅgamahānāma-raṅgaratte tirīṭake;

Acchinnadīghadasake, phalapupphadase tathā;

Kañcuke veṭhane sabbaṃ, labhaticchinnacīvaroti.

A tirīṭaka garment dyed with primary colors or with famous dyes; a robe with uncut or long fringes, or with fruit- or flower-patterned fringes; all jackets and head-wraps—all these are considered uncut robes.

4. Rajananiddeso

4. Explanation of Dyes

Rajanāni cāti –

Dyes, namely—

58.

58.

Mūlakkhandhatacapatta-phalapupphappabhedato;

Rajanā chappakārāni, anuññātāni satthunā.

From roots, trunks, bark, leaves, fruits, and flowers—six kinds of dyes are permitted by the Teacher.

59.

59.

Mūle [M 0.0008] haliddiṃ khandhe ca, mañjeṭṭha tuṅgahārake;

Alliṃ nīlañca pattesu, tace loddañca kaṇḍulaṃ;

Kusumbhaṃ kiṃsukaṃ pupphe, sabbaṃ labbhaṃ vivajjiyāti.

Turmeric from roots; madder and tuṅgahāraka from trunks; alli and indigo from leaves; lodda and kaṇḍula from bark; safflower and flame-of-the-forest from flowers—all are obtainable, but the bright colors should be avoided.

5. Pattaniddeso

5. Explanation of the Bowl

Patto [V 0.0010] cāti –

The bowl, namely—

60.

60.

Ayopatto bhūmipatto, jātiyā kappiyā duve;

Ukkaṭṭho majjhimo ceva, omako ca pamāṇato.

An iron bowl, a clay bowl—these two are allowable by nature; superior, medium, and inferior by size.

61.

61.

Ukkaṭṭho magadhe nāḷi-dvayataṇḍulasādhitaṃ;

Gaṇhāti odanaṃ sūpaṃ, byañjanañca tadūpiyaṃ.

The superior bowl holds cooked rice prepared with two nāḷis of Magadhan rice, along with suitable soup and curry.

62.

62.

Majjhimo tassupaḍḍhova, tatopaḍḍhova omako;

Ukkaṭṭhato ca ukkaṭṭho, apatto omakomako.

The medium is half of that, and the inferior is half of that again; a bowl superior to the superior, or inferior to the inferior, is not a bowl.

63.

63.

Atirekapatto dhāreyyo, dasāhaparamaṃ sako;

Kappo nissaggiyo hoti, tasmiṃ kāletināmite.

An extra bowl may be kept as one's own for a maximum of ten days; it becomes subject to forfeiture when that time is exceeded.

64.

64.

Acchedadānagāhehi, vibbhamā maraṇuddhaṭā;

Liṅgasikkhāhi chiddena, pattādhiṭṭhānamujjhati.

By being taken by force, by giving it away, by its being seized; through madness, by being carried off by death; by abandoning the monastic signs or the training, the determination of the bowl is relinquished.

65.

65.

Pattaṃ na paṭisāmeyya, sodakaṃ na ca otape;

Uṇhe na nidahe bhumyā, na ṭhape no ca laggaye.

One should not put the bowl away improperly, nor place it in the sun while it is wet; one should not set it on the ground in the heat, nor place it carelessly, nor hang it up.

66.

66.

Miḍḍhante paribhaṇḍante, aṅke vā ātapattake;

Pādesu mañcapīṭhe vā, ṭhapetuṃ na ca kappati.

It is not allowable to place the bowl in a latrine, in a storeroom, on one's lap, or on a sunshade; nor on one's feet, a bed, or a stool.

67.

67.

Na nīhareyya ucchiṭṭho-dakañca calakaṭṭhikaṃ;

Pattena pattahattho vā, kavāṭaṃ na paṇāmaye.

One should not carry out leftover water or a waste receptacle with the bowl; nor, holding the bowl, should one push open a door with it.

68.

68.

Bhūmiādhārake [V 0.0011] dārudaṇḍādhāre susajjite;

Duve patte ṭhapeyyekaṃ, nikkujjitvāna bhūmiyaṃ.

On a ground-stand or on a well-prepared wooden stand, one may place two bowls; or one may place a single bowl inverted on the ground.

69.

69.

Dārurūpiyasovaṇṇa-maṇiveḷuriyāmayā[M 0.0009];

Kaṃsakācatipusīsaphalikātambalohajā.

Made of wood, silver, gold, gems, or beryl; of bronze, glass, tin, lead, crystal, copper, or metal.

70.

70.

Chavasīsamayo cāpi, ghaṭītumbakaṭāhajā;

Pattā akappiyā sabbe, vuttā dukkaṭavatthukāti.

And also those made of a skull, a water pot, a gourd, or a pan; all such bowls are unallowable, and are said to be the basis for a dukkaṭa offense.

6. Thālakaniddeso

6. Exposition on Cups

Thālakā cāti –

And as to cups:

71.

71.

Kappiyā thālakā tisso, tambāyomattikāmayā;

Dārusovaṇṇarajatamaṇiveḷuriyāmayā.

Three kinds of cups are allowable: those made of copper, iron, and clay. Those made of wood, gold, silver, gems, and beryl are not.

72.

72.

Akappā phalikākācakaṃsajā gihisantakā;

Saṅghikā kappiyā tumbaghaṭijā tāvakālikāti.

Unallowable are those made of crystal, glass, or bronze, and those belonging to householders. Those belonging to the Sangha are allowable, as are those made from a gourd or a water pot for temporary use.

7. Pavāraṇāniddeso

7. Exposition on Indicating Satisfaction

Pavāraṇāti –

As to indicating satisfaction:

73.

73.

Yenīriyāpathenāyaṃ, bhuñjamāno pavārito;

Tato aññena bhuñjeyya, pācittinatirittakaṃ.

If a bhikkhu, having indicated he is satisfied while eating, should then eat further food that has not been made a leftover, he commits a pācittiya offense.

74.

74.

Asanaṃ bhojanañceva, abhihāro samīpatā;

Kāyavācāpaṭikkhepo, pañcaaṅgā pavāraṇā.

Being seated, the food, the offering, proximity, and refusal by body or speech: these are the five factors of indicating satisfaction.

75.

75.

Odano [V 0.0012] sattu kummāso, maccho maṃsañca bhojanaṃ;

Sāli vīhi yavo kaṅgu, kudrūsavaragodhumā;

Sattannamesaṃ dhaññānaṃ, odano bhojjayāgu ca.

Staple food consists of cooked rice, meal, barley-cakes, fish, and meat. The seven kinds of grain are fine rice, paddy, barley, millet, kudrūsa, vara, and wheat; from these are made cooked rice and edible gruel.

76.

76.

Sāmākāditiṇaṃ kudrūsake varakacorako;

Varake sāliyañceva, nīvāro saṅgahaṃ gato.

Grasses such as sāmāka are included under kudrūsaka, varaka, and coraka. Under varaka and fine rice, wild rice is also included.

77.

77.

Bhaṭṭhadhaññamayo sattu, kummāso yavasambhavo;

Maṃso ca kappiyo vutto, maccho udakasambhavo.

Meal is made from roasted grain; barley-cake originates from barley. Meat is said to be allowable, and fish is what originates from water.

78.

78.

Bhuñjanto [M 0.0010] bhojanaṃ kappa-makappaṃ vā nisedhayaṃ;

Pavāreyyābhihaṭaṃ kappaṃ, tannāmena imanti vā.

While eating, one may refuse food, whether it is allowable or not. One should indicate satisfaction regarding allowable food that has been offered, either by mentioning its name or by saying, 'This.'

79.

79.

Lājā taṃsattubhattāni, goraso suddhakhajjako;

Taṇḍulā bhaṭṭhapiṭṭhañca, puthukā veḷuādinaṃ.

Roasted grain, dishes made with meal, milk products, and pure hard foods; uncooked rice, roasted flour, flattened rice, bamboo shoots, and so on.

80.

80.

Bhattaṃ vuttāvasesānaṃ, rasayāgu rasopi ca;

Suddhayāguphalādīni, na janenti pavāraṇaṃ.

The remaining foods that have been mentioned, savory gruel, broth, plain gruel, fruits, and so on, do not occasion an indication of satisfaction.

81.

81.

Pavāritena vuṭṭhāya, abhuttena ca bhojanaṃ;

Atirittaṃ na kātabbaṃ, yena yaṃ vā pure kataṃ.

One who has indicated satisfaction and risen from his seat may not eat food unless it has been made a leftover by another bhikkhu who is still eating.

82.

82.

Kappiyaṃ gahitañcevu-ccāritaṃ hatthapāsagaṃ;

Atirittaṃ karontevaṃ, “alameta”nti bhāsatu.

When making into a leftover allowable food that has been taken up and is within arm's reach, one should say: 'This is enough.'

83.

83.

Na karenupasampanna-hatthagaṃ pesayitvāpi;

Kāretuṃ labbhate sabbo, bhuñjituṃ tamakārakoti.

One should not have it done through the hand of one not fully ordained, even by sending them. It is permissible for anyone who did not make it a leftover to eat all of it.

8. Kālikaniddeso

8. Exposition on Time-Limited Requisites

Kālikā [V 0.0013] cāti –

And as to time-limited requisites:

84.

84.

Paṭiggahitā cattāro, kālikā yāvakālikaṃ;

Yāmakālikaṃ sattāha-kālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

The accepted time-limited items are four: that for the morning, that for a day and a night, that for seven days, and that for a lifetime.

85.

85.

Piṭṭhaṃ mūlaṃ phalaṃ khajjaṃ, goraso dhaññabhojanaṃ;

Yāgusūpappabhutayo, hontete yāvakālikā.

Flour, roots, fruits, hard food, milk products, and grain-based staple food; gruel, soups, and the like—these are items for the morning.

86.

86.

Madhumuddikasālūka-cocamocambajambujaṃ;

Phārusaṃ naggisantattaṃ, pānakaṃ yāmakālikaṃ.

Drinks made from madhuka fruit, grapes, lotus root, banana, plantain, mango, rose-apple, and phārusaka fruit are for a day and a night.

87.

87.

Sānulomāni dhaññāni, ṭhapetvā phalajo raso;

Madhūkapupphamaññatra, sabbo puppharasopi ca.

Juice from fruit is allowed, excluding that from secondary grains; and all flower juice, except for that from the madhuka flower.

88.

88.

Sabbapattaraso ceva, ṭhapetvā pakkaḍākajaṃ;

Sītodamadditodicca-pāko vā yāmakāliko.

All leaf juice is also allowed, except that from cooked ḍāka leaves. Sugarcane juice, whether pressed with cold water or cooked, is for a day and a night.

89.

89.

Sappinonītatelāni[M 0.0011], madhuphāṇitameva ca;

Sattāhakālikā sappi, yesaṃ maṃsamavāritaṃ.

Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses are items for seven days. Ghee is for those for whom meat is not forbidden.

90.

90.

Telaṃ tilavaseraṇḍa-madhusāsapasambhavaṃ;

Khuddābhamaramadhukari-makkhikāhi kataṃ madhu;

Rasādiucchuvikati, pakkāpakkā ca phāṇitaṃ.

Oil is that which comes from sesame, tallow, castor beans, madhuka seeds, or mustard seeds. Honey is that made by small bees, large bees, honey-making bees, or flies. Molasses is a product of sugarcane juice and so on, whether cooked or uncooked.

91.

91.

Savatthupakkā sāmaṃ vā, vasā kāle amānusā;

Aññesaṃ na pace vatthuṃ, yāvakālikavatthunaṃ.

Fat from non-human creatures, cooked with its own substance or by oneself at the proper time, is allowable. One should not cook the substance of yāvakālika items for others.

92.

92.

Haliddiṃ [V 0.0014] siṅgiverañca, vacattaṃ lasuṇaṃ vacā;

Usīraṃ bhaddamuttañcātivisā kaṭurohiṇī;

Pañcamūlādikañcāpi, mūlaṃ taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Turmeric, ginger, orris root, garlic, sweet flag, vetiver, bhaddamutta, ativisā, and kaṭurohiṇī; the five medicinal roots and others—these roots are for a lifetime.

93.

93.

Biḷaṅgaṃ maricaṃ goṭṭha-phalaṃ pipphali rājikā;

Tiphaleraṇḍakādīnaṃ, phalaṃ taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Vidanga, black pepper, goṭṭha fruit, long pepper, and mustard; the fruits of the three myrobalans, the castor-oil plant, and others—these fruits are for a lifetime.

94.

94.

Kappāsanimbakuṭajapaṭolasulasādinaṃ;

Sūpeyyapaṇṇaṃ vajjetvā, paṇṇaṃ taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

The leaves of the cotton plant, neem, kurchi, pointed gourd, tulasi, and so on—excluding leaves suitable for curry—are for a lifetime.

95.

95.

Ṭhapetvā ucchuniyyāsaṃ,

Sarasaṃ ucchujaṃ tacaṃ;

Niyyāso ca taco sabbo,

Loṇaṃ lohaṃ silā tathā.

Excluding sugarcane sap and juicy sugarcane bark, all other saps and barks are for a lifetime, as are salt, metal, and minerals.

96.

96.

Suddhasitthañca sevālo, yañca kiñci sujhāpitaṃ;

Vikaṭādippabhedañca, ñātabbaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Pure beeswax and moss, whatever has been thoroughly burnt, and the various kinds of processed substances should be known as being for a lifetime.

97.

97.

Mūlaṃ sāraṃ taco pheggu, paṇṇaṃ pupphaṃ phalaṃ latā;

Āhārattha masādhentaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Roots, heartwood, bark, sapwood, leaves, flowers, fruits, and creepers—so long as they are not prepared for the purpose of food—are all for a lifetime.

98.

98.

Sabbakālikasambhogo, kāle sabbassa kappati;

Sati paccaye vikāle, kappate kālikattayaṃ.

The partaking of all time-limited items is allowable for everyone at the proper time. When there is a reason, at the wrong time, the three other kinds of time-limited items are allowable.

99.

99.

Kālayāmamatikkantā[M 0.0012], pācittiṃ janayantubho;

Janayanti ubhopete, antovutthañca sannidhiṃ.

Transgressing the time limits for morning-items and day-and-night-items generates a pācittiya. Both of these also generate offenses for what has remained indoors and for storing.

100.

100.

Sattāhakālike [V 0.0015] satta, ahāni atināmite;

Pācitti pāḷināruḷhe, sappiādimhi dukkaṭaṃ.

In the case of seven-day items, when seven days are exceeded, there is a pācittiya for what is mentioned in the Pāḷi; for ghee and so on, there is a dukkaṭa.

101.

101.

Nissaṭṭhaladdhaṃ makkheyya, naṅgaṃ najjhohareyya ca;

Vikappentassa sattāhe, sāmaṇerassadhiṭṭhato;

Makkhanādiñca nāpatti, aññassa dadatopi ca.

Having received back what was forfeited, one may smear it but should not consume it. When assigning it to a novice within seven days, or from a novice's determination, there is no offense in smearing it and so on, or in giving it to another.

102.

102.

Yāvakālikaādīni, saṃsaṭṭhāni sahattanā;

Gāhāpayanti sabbhāvaṃ, tasmā evamudīritaṃ.

When yāvakālika items and so on are mixed together, they take on the nature of the most restrictive. Therefore, it is declared as follows.

103.

103.

Pure paṭiggahitañca, sattāhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ;

Sesakālikasammissaṃ, pācitti paribhuñjato.

For one who consumes a seven-day or lifetime item received beforehand that has been mixed with another time-limited item, there is a pācittiya.

104.

104.

Yāvakālikasammissaṃ, itaraṃ kālikattayaṃ;

Paṭiggahitaṃ tadahu, tadaheva ca bhuñjaye.

When the other three kinds of time-limited items are mixed with a yāvakālika item, having been received on that day, one should consume it on that very day.

105.

105.

Yāmakālikasammissaṃ, sesamevaṃ vijāniyaṃ;

Sattāhakālikamissañca, sattāhaṃ kappatetaranti.

It should be understood similarly for the remaining items when mixed with a day-and-night item. And when the other kind is mixed with a seven-day item, it is allowable for seven days.

9. Paṭiggāhaniddeso

9. Exposition on Receiving

Paṭiggāhoti –

Receiving is—

106.

106.

Dātukāmābhihāro ca, hatthapāseraṇakkhamaṃ;

Tidhā dente dvidhā gāho, pañcaṅgevaṃ paṭiggaho.

The intention to give, the bringing near, and the object being within hand's reach—threefold on the part of the giver; twofold in the taking—thus, receiving has five factors.

107.

107.

Asaṃhāriye tatthajāte, sukhume ciñcaādinaṃ;

Paṇṇe vāsayhabhāre ca, paṭiggāho na rūhati.

In what is not movable, in things born there, in subtle things like tamarind and so on, on a leaf, or in an unbearable burden, receiving is not established.

108.

108.

Sikkhāmaraṇaliṅgehi, anapekkhavisaggato;

Acchedānupasampanna-dānā gāhopasammati.

Acceptance is nullified by giving up the training, by death, by changing the characteristic marks, by abandoning without regard, by non-severance, and by the giving of one not fully ordained.

109.

109.

Appaṭiggahitaṃ [M 0.0013][V 0.0016] sabbaṃ, pācitti paribhuñjato;

Suddhañca nātibahalaṃ, kappate udakaṃ tathā.

For one who consumes anything that is unaccepted, there is a pācittiya. Likewise, water that is pure and not too thick is allowable.

110.

110.

Aṅgalaggamavicchinnaṃ, dantakkhikaṇṇagūthakaṃ;

Loṇassukheḷasiṅghāṇi-semhamuttakarīsakaṃ.

What is attached to the body and not separated from it: waste from the teeth, eyes, and ears; salty tears, spittle, snot, phlegm, urine, and feces.

111.

111.

Gūthamattikamuttāni, chārikañca tathāvidhe;

Sāmaṃ gahetvā seveyya, asante kappakārake.

Feces, clay, urine, and ash of a similar kind—one may take and use these oneself when an attendant is not available.

112.

112.

Durūpaciṇṇe rajokiṇṇe, athuggahappaṭiggahe;

Antovutthe sayaṃpakke, antopakke ca dukkaṭanti.

Regarding that which is difficult to place, covered with dust, or difficult to take up and receive; if stored inside, self-cooked, or cooked inside—it is an offense of wrong-doing.

10. Akappiyamaṃsaniddeso

10. The Section on Unallowable Meat

Maṃsesu ca akappiyanti –

And regarding meats, these are unallowable—

113.

113.

Manussahatthiassānaṃ, maṃsaṃ sunakhadīpinaṃ;

Sīhabyagghataracchānaṃ, acchassa uragassa ca.

The flesh of humans, elephants, horses, dogs, leopards, lions, tigers, hyenas, bears, and snakes.

114.

114.

Uddissakatamaṃsañca, yañca appaṭivekkhitaṃ;

Thullaccayaṃ manussānaṃ, maṃse sesesu dukkaṭaṃ.

Meat specifically prepared for a monastic, and that which is not properly inspected—regarding the flesh of humans, it is a grave offense; for the remaining meats, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

115.

115.

Aṭṭhīpi lohitaṃ cammaṃ, lomamesaṃ na kappati;

Sacittakaṃva uddissa-kataṃ sesā acittakāti.

The bones, blood, skin, and hair of these are not allowable. That which has consciousness is like that which is specifically prepared; the remainder is without consciousness.

11. Nissaggiyaniddeso

11. The Section on Forfeitable Items

Nissaggiyānīti [V 0.0017] –

The forfeitable items are—

116.

116.

Arūpiyaṃ rūpiyena, rūpiyaṃ itarena ca;

Rūpiyaṃ parivatteyya, nissaggi idha rūpiyaṃ.

Exchanging a non-monetary item for money, money for another item, or money for money—in such a case, the money is to be forfeited.

117.

117.

Kahāpaṇo sajjhu siṅgī, vohārūpagamāsakaṃ;

Vatthamuttādi itaraṃ, kappaṃ dukkaṭavatthu ca.

A kahāpaṇa, silver, gold, a coin used in trade, a māsaka; cloth, pearls, and other items—exchanging these, whether for an allowable item or not, is grounds for an offense of wrong-doing.

118.

118.

“Imaṃ [M 0.0014] gahetvā bhutvā vā, imaṃ dehi karānaya;

Demi vā”ti samāpanne, nissaggi kayavikkaye.

“Having taken this, or having consumed this, give this; or bring this; or I will give”—when a transaction is thus concluded, there is forfeiture in buying and selling.

119.

119.

Attano aññato lābhaṃ, saṅghassaññassa vā nataṃ;

Pariṇāmeyya nissaggi, pācitti cāpi dukkaṭaṃ.

If one should divert to oneself a gain intended for the Sangha or for another, it is to be forfeited; and there is also a pācittiya offense and an offense of wrong-doing.

120.

120.

Anissajjitvā nissaggiṃ, paribhuñje na deyya vā;

Nissaṭṭhaṃ sakasaññāya, dukkaṭaṃ aññathetaranti.

Should one use or not give away a forfeitable item without having forfeited it, it is an offense. To perceive a forfeited item as one's own is an offense of wrong-doing; otherwise, it is another offense.

12. Pācittiyaniddeso

12. The Section on Pācittiya Offenses

Pācittīti –

The pācittiya offenses are—

121.

121.

Musāvādomasāvāde, pesuññaharaṇe tathā;

Padasodhammasāgāre, ujjhāpanakakhīyane.

In false speech, contemptuous speech, and likewise in slander; in teaching the Dhamma word-by-word, in finding fault, and in belittling.

122.

122.

Talasattianādarakukkuccuppādanesu ca;

Gāmappavesanāpucchā, bhojane ca paramparā.

In striking with the palm, in disrespect, and in causing remorse; in the rule concerning informing before entering a village, and in eating in succession.

123.

123.

Anuddharitvā [V 0.0018] gamane, seyyaṃ senāsanāni vā;

Itthiyāddhānagamane, ekekāya nisīdane.

In going without having put away a bed or lodging; in traveling along a road with a woman; in sitting down alone with a woman.

124.

124.

Bhīsāpanākoṭanaaññavāde,

Vihesaduṭṭhullapakāsachāde;

Hāsodake nicchubhane vihārā,

Pācitti vuttānupakhajjasayaneti.

In frightening, striking, and prevarication; in vexing, in disclosing or concealing a grave offense; in playing in water, in evicting from a monastery—these are stated as pācittiya offenses, along with sleeping by encroaching.

13. Samaṇakappaniddeso

13. The Section on What is Allowable for a Recluse

Samaṇakappāti –

What is allowable for a recluse is—

125.

125.

Bhūtagāmasamārambhe, pācitti katakappiyaṃ;

Nakhena vāggisatthehi, bhave samaṇakappiyaṃ.

In damaging living plants, there is a pācittiya offense, unless it has been made allowable. By one's nail, by fire, or by a knife, it becomes allowable for a recluse.

126.

126.

Sa mūlakhandhabījagga-phaḷubījappabhāvito;

Ārambhe dukkaṭaṃ bījaṃ, bhūtagāmaviyojitaṃ.

Regarding that which is propagated from roots, stems, cuttings, joints, and seeds—for a seed separated from a living plant, there is an offense of wrong-doing in damaging it.

127.

127.

Nibbaṭṭabījaṃ [M 0.0015] nobīja-makatañcāpi kappati;

Kaṭāhabaddhabījāni, bahiddhā vāpi kāraye.

A plant grown from a cutting, a seedless plant, and also that which is not made allowable by oneself is permissible. As for seeds bound in a pot, one may have them made allowable outside.

128.

128.

Ekābaddhesu bījesu, bhājane vāpi bhūmiyaṃ;

Kate ca kappiyekasmiṃ, sabbesveva kataṃ bhave.

When seeds are bound together, or are in a pot or on the ground, if one is made allowable, it is as if all have been made so.

129.

129.

Nikkhitte kappiyaṃ katvā, mūlapaṇṇāni jāyaruṃ;

Kappiyaṃ puna kāreyya, bhūtagāmo hi so tadā.

If, after something has been put down and made allowable, roots and leaves should sprout, one should make it allowable again, for it is then a living plant.

130.

130.

Sapaṇṇo [V 0.0019] vā apaṇṇo vā, sevālodakasambhavo;

Cetiyādīsu sevālo, nibbaṭṭadvattipattako;

Bhūtagāmova bījampi, mūlapaṇṇe viniggate.

That which is born of moss or water, whether with leaves or without; moss on shrines and the like; a sprout that has put forth two or three leaves; and also a seed from which roots and leaves have emerged—these are considered living plants.

131.

131.

Ghaṭādipiṭṭhe sevālo, makuḷaṃ ahichattakaṃ;

Dukkaṭasseva vatthūni, phullamabyavahārikaṃ.

Moss on the surface of pots and the like, a bud, a mushroom; these are grounds for an offense of wrong-doing, as is a blossomed flower that is not for use.

132.

132.

Lākhāniyyāsachattāni, allarukkhe vikopiya;

Gaṇhato tattha pācitti, chindato vāpi akkharaṃ.

For one who takes lac, resin, or fungi, thereby damaging a living tree, there is a pācittiya offense; or for one who carves even a single letter.

133.

133.

Pīḷetuṃ nāḷikerādiṃ, dārumakkaṭakādinā;

Chindituṃ gaṇṭhikaṃ kātuṃ, tiṇādiṃ na ca kappati.

It is not allowable to press a coconut or the like with a wooden press or similar tool; nor to cut, to tie a knot, or to bundle grass and the like.

134.

134.

Bhūtagāmaṃ va bījaṃ vā, chinda bhindocināhi vā;

Phālehi vijjha paca vā, niyametvā na bhāsaye.

Regarding a living plant or a seed, whether one cuts, splits, or plucks it; or splits, pierces, or cooks it—one should not speak, having made a specific instruction.

135.

135.

Imaṃ karohi kappiyaṃ, imaṃ gaṇhedamāhara;

Imaṃ dehi imaṃ sodhehevaṃ vaṭṭati bhāsitunti.

"Make this allowable," "Take this," "Bring this," "Give this," "Clean this"—such speech is permissible.

14. Bhūminiddeso

14. The Exposition on Grounds

Bhūmiyoti –

On grounds—

136.

136.

Sammutussāvanantā ca, gonisādī gahāpati;

Kappiyā bhūmiyo yāsu, vutthaṃ pakkañca kappati.

Designated by proclamation, a cow-pen, a householder's dwelling—these are allowable grounds where dwelling and cooking are permissible.

137.

137.

Vāsatthāya [M 0.0016] kate gehe, saṅghike vekasantake;

Kappiyā kuṭi laddhabbā, sahaseyyappahonake.

For dwelling purposes, in a house built for the Saṅgha, or in a private dwelling, an allowable hut should be obtained, sufficient for a shared sleeping space.

138.

138.

Gehe [V 0.0020] saṅghassa vekassa, karamānevamīrayaṃ;

Paṭhamiṭṭhakathambhādiṃ, ṭhapeyyussāvanantikā;

“Kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti.

While constructing a dwelling for the Saṅgha or for an individual, one should first place a brick, pillar, or the like near the site for making the announcement, saying, "We make an allowable hut, we make an allowable hut."

139.

139.

Yebhuyyenāparikkhitto, ārāmo sakalopi vā;

Vuccate “gonisādī”ti, sammutī saṅghasammatā.

A monastery that is mostly unenclosed, or even the entire monastery, is called a "cow-pen"; this is a designation agreed upon by the Saṅgha.

140.

140.

Bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā aññehi, dinno tesaṃva santako;

Atthāya kappakuṭiyā, geho gahapatī mato.

Given by others, excluding a monk, it belongs to them. A householder's house is considered for the purpose of an allowable hut.

141.

141.

Akappakuṭiyā vutthasappiādīhi missitaṃ;

Vajeyya antovutthattaṃ, purimaṃ kālikadvayaṃ.

One should avoid having stayed overnight in an unallowable hut, and also the first two kinds of time-limited items, such as ghee and the like, stored overnight.

142.

142.

Teheva bhikkhunā pakkaṃ, kappate yāvajīvikaṃ;

Nirāmisaṃva sattāhaṃ, sāmise sāmapākatā.

Cooked by that same bhikkhu, it is permissible for life; non-flesh for seven days; with flesh, if it is self-prepared.

143.

143.

Ussāvanantikā yehi, thambhādīhi adhiṭṭhitā;

Tesuyevāpanītesu, tadaññesupi tiṭṭhati.

The designation established near the proclamation site by pillars and the like remains valid by means of other markers, even when those original ones are removed.

144.

144.

Sabbesu apanītesu, bhave jahitavatthukā;

Gonisādī parikkhitte, sesā chadanavibbhamāti.

When all markers are removed, the designation becomes one with an abandoned basis. A cow-pen is enclosed; the rest are errors regarding covering.

15. Upajjhācariyavattaniddeso

15. Exposition on the Observances toward Preceptors and Teachers

Upajjhācariyavattānīti –

The observances toward preceptors and teachers are—

145.

145.

Nissāyupajjhācariye, vasamāno supesalo;

Dantakaṭṭhāsanaṃ toyaṃ, yāguṃ kāle dade sadā.

Living in dependence on a preceptor or teacher, being well-behaved, one should always offer a tooth-stick, a seat, water, and rice gruel at the proper time.

146.

146.

Patte vattaṃ care gāma-ppavese gamanāgame;

Āsane pādapīṭhe ca, kathalopāhanacīvare.

One should observe the duties regarding the bowl, on entering the village and on going and coming; regarding a seat and footstool, discourse, sandals, and robes.

147.

147.

Paribhojanīyapānīya-vaccappassāvaṭhānisu[V 0.0021];

Vihārasodhane vattaṃ, puna paññāpane tathā.

In regard to food and drink, and places for defecation and urination; the observance in cleaning the monastery, and likewise in setting it in order again.

148.

148.

Na [M 0.0017] papphoṭeyya sodhento, paṭivāte ca saṅgaṇe;

Vihāraṃ bhikkhu pānīya-sāmantā sayanāsanaṃ.

While cleaning, one should not shake things out, nor sweep up rubbish against the wind. A monk should clean the monastery, the area around the drinking water, and the bedding and seating.

149.

149.

Nhāne nhātassa kātabbe, raṅgapāke ca dhovane;

Sibbane cīvare theve, rajanto na vaje ṭhite.

One should assist when a senior is bathing, and in boiling dye and washing robes. When sewing or storing robes, or while dyeing, one should not leave while the elder is standing.

150.

150.

Ekaccassa anāpucchā, pattaṃ vā cīvarāni vā;

Na dadeyya na gaṇheyya, parikkhārañca kiñcanaṃ.

Without asking him, one should not give or take his bowl or robes, or any requisite whatsoever.

151.

151.

Ekaccaṃ pacchato kātuṃ, gantuṃ vā tassa pacchato;

Piṇḍapātañca ninnetuṃ, nīharāpetumattano.

Without asking, one should not make another his attendant, nor walk behind him, nor take out his alms-bowl, nor have one's own requisites carried by him.

152.

152.

Kiccayaṃ parikammaṃ vā, kesacchedañca attano;

Kārāpetuṃ va kātuṃ vā, anāpucchā na vaṭṭati.

To perform a task or make preparations, or to cut one's own hair—to have it done or to do it oneself—is not proper without first asking.

153.

153.

Gāmaṃ susānaṃ nissīmaṃ, disaṃ vā gantumicchato;

Attano kiccayaṃ vāpi, anāpucchā na vaṭṭati.

For one wishing to go to a village, a charnel ground, outside the boundary, or to another region, or even for one's own business—it is not proper without first asking.

154.

154.

Uppannaṃ aratiṃ diṭṭhiṃ, kukkuccaṃ vā vinodaye;

Kareyya vāpi ussukkaṃ, saṅghāyattesu kammasu.

If discontent, wrong view, or remorse has arisen in him, one should dispel it; or one should make an effort on his behalf in matters pertaining to the Saṅgha.

155.

155.

Gilānesu upaṭṭheyya, vuṭṭhānaṃ nesamāgame;

Vattabhedena sabbattha, anādarena dukkaṭanti.

One should attend on them when they are sick, until their recovery. In all these cases, breaking the observances through disrespect is an offense of wrong-doing.

16. Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikaniddeso

16. Exposition on the Places for Defecation and Urination

Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikanti [V 0.0022] –

Regarding the places for defecation and urination—

156.

156.

Na kareyya yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, vaccaṃ yātānupubbiyā;

Vaccapassāvakuṭiyo, nhānatitthañca labbhati.

One should not defecate out of turn, but in successive order according to seniority; latrines for defecation and urination, and bathing places, are to be used.

157.

157.

Paviseyyubbhajitvā no, sahasā paviseyya ca;

Ukkāsitvāvubbhajeyya, pādukāsveva saṇṭhito.

One should enter having hitched up one's robe; one should not enter hastily. Having cleared one's throat, one should stand firmly on the foot-rests.

158.

158.

Na [M 0.0018] kare nitthunaṃ vaccaṃ, dantakaṭṭhañca khādayaṃ;

Vaccapassāvadoṇīnaṃ, na kareyyubhayaṃ bahi.

One should not groan while defecating or while chewing a tooth-stick; one should not defecate or urinate outside of the receptacles.

159.

159.

Kūpe kaṭṭhaṃ na pāteyya, kheḷaṃ passāvadoṇiyā;

Nāvalekheyya pharuse-nuhatañcāpi dhovaye.

One should not drop the cleaning-stick into the latrine pit, nor spit into the urine pot. One should not scrape oneself with a rough object, and one should wash oneself when soiled.

160.

160.

Na nikkhameyya sahasā-vubbhajitvā na nikkhame;

Capu capu nācameyya, uklāpañca visodhayeti.

One should not depart hastily; one should not depart having hitched up one's robe. One should not make 'capu capu' sounds when rinsing the mouth, and one should clean the spittoon.

17. Āpucchakaraṇaniddeso

17. Exposition on Asking for Permission

Āpucchakaraṇanti –

Regarding asking for permission—

161.

161.

Anajjhiṭṭhova therena, pātimokkhaṃ na uddise;

Dhammaṃ na kathaye pañhaṃ, na pucche na ca vissaje.

Without being invited by an elder, one should not recite the Pātimokkha, teach the Dhamma, ask a question, or answer one.

162.

162.

Āpucchitvā kathentassa, puna vuḍḍhatarāgame;

Puna āpucchanaṃ natthi, bhattagge cānumodato.

For one who is speaking after having asked permission, there is no need to ask again if a more senior monk arrives, nor when giving the blessing at a meal.

163.

163.

Vasanto [V 0.0023] ca anāpucchā, vuḍḍhenekavihārake;

Na sajjhāyeyya uddesaṃ, paripucchañca no dade.

When dwelling with an elder in the same monastery, one should not, without his permission, make a recitation, give a passage for recitation, or ask questions about it.

164.

164.

Dhammaṃ na bhāsaye dīpaṃ, na kare na ca vijjhape;

Vātapānaṃ kavāṭaṃ vā, vivareyya thakeyya ca.

One should not teach the Dhamma, nor light or extinguish a lamp, nor open or shut a window or a door.

165.

165.

Caṅkame caṅkamantopi, vuḍḍhena parivattaye;

Yena vuḍḍho sa saṅghāṭi-kaṇṇenenaṃ na ghaṭṭayeti.

While walking on a meditation path, one should make way for an elder, so that one does not brush against him with the corner of one's outer robe.

18. Nagganiddeso

18. Exposition on Nakedness

Naggoti –

Regarding nakedness—

166.

166.

Naggo maggaṃ vaje bhuñje, pive khāde na sāyaye;

Na gaṇhe na dade neva, vande vandāpayeyya vā.

Naked, one should not walk on a road, nor eat, drink, chew, or taste. One should neither take nor give, nor pay homage nor have others pay homage to oneself.

167.

167.

Parikammaṃ na kāreyya, na kare paṭichādisu;

Parikamme duve vattha-cchādi sabbattha kappiyāti.

One should not do any work, nor should one do so even in a concealed place. For any work, two garments for covering are allowable everywhere.

19. Nhānakappaniddeso

19. Exposition on Proper Conduct in Bathing

Nhānakappoti [M 0.0019] –

Regarding proper conduct in bathing—

168.

168.

Na ca nhāyeyya therānaṃ, puratopari vā tathā;

Dadeyya otarantānaṃ, maggamuttaramānako.

One should not bathe in front of or upstream from the elders. One who is coming out of the water should give way to those who are entering.

169.

169.

Kuṭṭatthambhataruṭṭāne, nhāyamāno na ghaṃsaye;

Kāyaṃ gandhabbahatthena, kuruvindakasuttiyā.

While bathing, one should not rub oneself against a wall, a post, or a tree trunk. One may rub the body with a bath-scraper or a string of kuruvinda beads.

170.

170.

Mallakenāññamaññaṃ [V 0.0024] vā, sarīrena na ghaṃsaye;

Kapāliṭṭhakakhaṇḍāni, vatthavaṭṭi ca vaṭṭati.

One should not rub one's body against another's, either with a bathing-glove or with one's body. Broken potsherds, pieces of brick, and a roll of cloth are allowable.

171.

171.

Sabbesaṃ puthupāṇī cā-kallassākatamallakaṃ;

Pāsāṇapheṇakathalā, kappanti pādaghaṃsaneti.

A broad-bladed scraper is allowable for all, and a simple bathing-glove for the sick. Pumice stone and gravel are allowable for rubbing the feet.

20. Avandiyaniddeso

20. Exposition on Those Unworthy of Veneration

Avandiyoti –

Those unworthy of veneration are—

172.

172.

Ukkhittānupasampanna-nānāsaṃvāsaitthiyo;

Navo ca garukaṭṭho ca, paṇḍako ca avandiyāti.

The suspended, the unordained, those of a different communion, and women; a novice, one under a heavy penalty, and a paṇḍaka—these are unworthy of veneration.

21. Cammaniddeso

21. Exposition on Hides

Cammanti –

Regarding hides—

173.

173.

Migājeḷakacammāni, kappanti paribhuñjituṃ;

Rohiteṇipasadā ca, kuruṅgā migajātikā.

The hides of deer, goats, and rams are allowable to use, as are those of red deer, black-buck, spotted deer, and other species of antelope and deer.

174.

174.

Anuññātattayā aññaṃ, cammaṃ dukkaṭavatthukaṃ;

Thavikopāhane cammaṃ, sabbaṃ kappatimānusanti.

To use any hide other than those permitted is an offense of wrong-doing. For bags and footwear, all non-human hide is allowable, they say.

22. Upāhananiddeso

22. Exposition on Footwear

Upāhanā cevāti –

Regarding footwear—

175.

175.

Majjhadese na kappanti, gaṇaṅgaṇūpāhanā navā;

Sabbassa kappantārāme, sabbatthākallakassa ca.

In the Middle Country, new multi-strapped sandals are not allowable. They are allowable for all in a monastery, and everywhere for the sick.

176.

176.

Sabbanīlakaodātapītalohitakaṇhakā[V 0.0025][M 0.0020];

Mahāraṅgamahānāma-raṅgarattā cupāhanā.

Footwear that is entirely blue, white, yellow, red, or black, or dyed with expensive or renowned dyes, is not allowable.

177.

177.

Sabbamañjeṭṭhikā citrā, nīlapītādivaddhikā;

Tittirapattikā meṇḍa-ajavisāṇavaddhikā.

Footwear dyed entirely with madder, multi-colored, with blue, yellow, etc., straps; or with partridge-feather patterns, or with ram's horn or goat's horn adornments, is not allowable.

178.

178.

Khallabaddhā puṭabaddhā, tūlapuṇṇā cupāhanā;

Pāliguṇṭhimakā mora-piñchena parisibbitā.

Footwear tied with straps or wrappings, or stuffed with cotton; or with a fringe around the edge stitched with peacock feathers, is not allowable.

179.

179.

Vicchikāḷikatā sīhabyagghuddājinadīpinaṃ;

Majjārakāḷakolūkacammehi ca parikkhaṭā;

Pādukā saṅkamanīyā, koci dhāreyya dukkaṭaṃ.

Footwear adorned with scorpion-tail ornaments, or made with the skins of lions, tigers, otters, or leopards, or adorned with the hides of cats or owls—should anyone wear such, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

180.

180.

Nīlādivaṇṇaṃ sakalaṃ, puñchitvā vekadesakaṃ;

Upāhanā vaḷañjeyya, hāretvā khallakādikanti.

Having wiped off all the color, such as blue, or a part of it, and having removed the straps and other adornments, one may use the footwear.

23. Anolokiyaniddeso

23. Exposition on Not Looking

Anolokiyanti –

'Not looking' means:

181.

181.

Sāratto itthiyā yoniṃ, mukhaṃ vā bhikkhadāyiyā;

Parassa pattamujjhānasaññī vā attano mukhaṃ;

Ādāsodakapatte vā, olokeyyassa dukkaṭanti.

To look lustfully at a woman's genital organ or at the face of a female alms-giver; or to look at another's bowl with the intention of finding fault, or at one's own face in a mirror or a bowl of water—for one who does so, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

24. Añjanīniddeso

24. Exposition on Eye-Ointment

Añjanīti [V 0.0026] –

'Eye-ointment' means:

182.

182.

Vaṭṭāṭṭhasoḷasaṃsā vā, maṭṭhā vaṭṭati añjanī;

Tissopi mūle gīvāyaṃ, lekhā ekāva bandhituṃ.

A round eye-ointment container with eight or sixteen compartments is allowable, or a polished one. It is also permissible to apply a single line at the base of the neck, as was the case for Tissa.

183.

183.

Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ mālādikammaṃ makaradantakaṃ;

Gomuttakaḍḍhacandādi-vikāraṃ nettha vaṭṭati.

Any kind of figure, work such as garlands, the makara-tooth pattern, or decorations such as the cow-urine pattern and the half-moon pattern, are not allowable in this case.

184.

184.

Labbhekavaṇṇasuttena, sibbituṃ thavikā tathā;

Sipāṭi kuñcikākoso, salākāpi acittakā.

It is allowable to sew a bag with thread of a single color. Likewise, a sheath, a key case, and an applicator stick are allowable, if they are undecorated.

185.

185.

Saṅkhanābhivisāṇaṭṭhi-naḷadantamayā [M 0.0021] tathā;

Phalakaṭṭhamayā veḷu-lākhālohamayāpi ca.

Likewise, those made of conch shell, horn, bone, reed, or ivory; and also those made of wood, bamboo, lac, or metal.

186.

186.

Añjaniyo salākāyo, dhūmanettā ca labbhare;

Tathā satthakadaṇḍāni, natthudānā ca tammayāti.

Eye-ointment containers, applicator sticks, and inhalation tubes are allowable. Likewise, handles for lancets and snuff boxes made of those materials are also allowable.

25. Akappiyasayananiddeso

25. Exposition on Unallowable Beds and Seats

Akappiyasayanānīti –

'Unallowable beds and seats' means:

187.

187.

Āsandī tūlī pallaṅko, paṭikaṃ gonacittakaṃ;

Paṭalī vikatī udda-lomī ekantalomikā.

A high chair, a cotton mattress, a divan, a white woolen coverlet, a long-fleeced colorful coverlet, a coverlet embroidered with flowers, a coverlet with figures, a coverlet with fleece on both sides, and a coverlet with fleece on one side.

188.

188.

Kuttaṃ koseyyaṃ kaṭṭissaṃ, hatthiassarathattharā;

Jinappaveṇikadalī-migappavaraattharā.

A large woolen carpet, a silk coverlet, a woolen carpet embroidered with gems, spreads for elephants, horses, or chariots, a spread made of antelope skins sewn together, and a choice spread made of the hide of the kadalī deer.

189.

189.

Salohitavitānañcu-bhatorattūpadhānakaṃ[V 0.0027];

Akappiyāni etāni, dukkaṭaṃ paribhuñjato.

And a bed with a red canopy and red pillows at both ends. These are unallowable; for one who uses them, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

190.

190.

Āsandādittayā sese, labbhate gihisantake;

Dhammāsane ca bhattagge, ghare cāpi nisīdituṃ;

Bhūmattharaṇasaṅkhepe, sayituñcāpi kappati.

Except for the first three—the high chair, divan, and long-fleeced rug—it is allowable to use the remaining ones if they belong to a householder. It is also permissible to sit upon them on a Dhamma-seat, in a refectory, or in a house. And it is allowable to lie down on a simple ground-covering.

191.

191.

Caturaṃsapīṭhā sattaṅgā, pañcaṅgā uccapādakā;

Tūlonaddhā ghareyeva, mañcapīṭhā nisīdituṃ.

Square stools, stools with seven parts, stools with five parts, those with high legs, and those stuffed with cotton—it is for sitting on such couches and stools only in a house.

192.

192.

Coḷavākuṇṇapaṇṇānaṃ, tiṇānañceva pūritā;

Cīvaracchaviyo pañca, bhisī sabbattha kappiyā.

A cushion filled with rags, bark-fibers, wool, leaves, or grass is allowable everywhere, as are the five kinds of robe-cloth covers.

193.

193.

Tūlattayaṃ bhisigabbho, lomāni migapakkhinaṃ;

Bimbohane anuññātaṃ, tūlavajjā masūrake.

The three kinds of cotton, cushion stuffing, the fur of beasts, and the feathers of birds are permitted for a pillow. For a bolster, these are permitted, except for cotton.

194.

194.

Manussalomamuṇṇāyaṃ, paṇṇe pupphaṃ tamālakaṃ;

Suddhaṃ na āsanañceva, labbhamappaṭivekkhitanti.

Human hair, wool, leaves, flowers, or tamāla leaves are not allowable. A clean seat is not to be used if it has not been inspected.

26. Samānāsanikaniddeso

26. Exposition on Sharing a Seat

Samānāsanikopi [M 0.0022] cāti –

And also 'sharing a seat' means:

195.

195.

Tivassantarānuññātaṃ, bhikkhūnamekamāsanaṃ;

Sattavassativassehi, pañcavasso nisīdituṃ.

It is allowed for monks within three years of each other's seniority to share one seat. A monk of five years' seniority may sit with one of seven years' or three years' seniority.

196.

196.

Ṭhapetvā paṇḍakaṃ itthiṃ, ubhatobyañjanaṃ muni;

Dīghāsane anuññāsi, sabbeheva nisīdituṃ.

Excluding a paṇḍaka, a woman, and a person with both male and female characteristics, the Sage allowed all monks to sit together on a long seat.

197.

197.

Antaṃ [V 0.0028] dīghāsanaṃ tiṇṇaṃ, yaṃ pahoti nisīdituṃ;

Mañcake vāpi pīṭhe vā, dvinnaṃ labbhaṃ nisīditunti.

A long seat is one that is sufficient for three to sit on. On a couch or a stool, it is allowable for two to sit.

27. Asaṃvāsikaniddeso

27. Exposition on Those Unfit for Communion

Asaṃvāsiko cāti –

'One unfit for communion' means:

198.

198.

Ukkhittonupasampanno, bhikkhunī chinnamūlako;

Nānāsaṃvāsanissīma-ṭṭhitavehāyasaṇṭhitā;

Ekādasa abhabbā ca, asaṃvāsāti dīpitāti.

One who is suspended, one not fully ordained, a nun, one whose roots are cut; one of a different communion, one standing outside the boundary, one 'suspended in the air'; and the eleven incapable persons—these are declared to be unfit for communion.

28. Kammaniddeso

28. Exposition on Formal Acts

Kammañcāti –

'A formal act' means:

199.

199.

Vaggena adhammakammaṃ, samaggena adhammikaṃ;

Vaggena dhammakammañca, samaggena ca dhammikaṃ;

Catutthaṃyevānuññātaṃ, sesakammesu dukkaṭaṃ.

An act against the Dhamma by an incomplete assembly; an act against the Dhamma by a complete assembly; an act in accordance with the Dhamma by an incomplete assembly; and an act in accordance with the Dhamma by a complete assembly. Only the fourth is allowed; for participating in the other acts, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

200.

200.

Catuvaggo pañcavaggo, dasavīsativaggiko;

Tirekavīsativaggo, pañca saṅghā vibhāvitā.

A group of four, a group of five, a group of ten, a group of twenty, and a group of more than twenty—thus five kinds of Sangha are distinguished.

201.

201.

Catuvaggettha abbhānu-pasampadāpavāraṇā;

Pañcavaggo ca abbhānaṃ, majjhadesupasampadaṃ.

A group of four is for rehabilitation, higher ordination, and pavāraṇā; a group of five is for rehabilitation and higher ordination in the Middle Country.

202.

202.

Dasavaggo [M 0.0023] ca abbhānaṃ, ṭhapetvā sabbakammiko;

Itaro sabbakammesu, kammappattoti dīpito.

A group of ten is for rehabilitation, and a group of twenty is for all formal acts. Any other group is declared as fit for all formal acts.

203.

203.

Catuvaggena [V 0.0029] kattabbe, cattāro pakatattakā;

Kammappattā pare chandā-rahā sesepyayaṃ nayo.

For an act to be done by a group of four, there must be four monks of normal status fit for the act, while others are eligible to give consent. This same method applies to the remaining groups.

204.

204.

Catuvaggādikattabbaṃ, asaṃvāsakammāraha;

Garukaṭṭhesvaññataraṃ, katvāna gaṇapūrakaṃ;

Parivāsādikaṃ kammaṃ, kataṃ kuppañca dukkaṭaṃ.

If, in a formal act requiring a group of four or more, a monk who is unfit for communion is used to complete the quorum for one or another of the serious procedures, such as imposing probation, the act is invalid and entails an offense of wrong-doing.

205.

205.

Adhammakammaṃ vāreyya, antarāye duve tayo;

Diṭṭhāvimekodhiṭṭhānaṃ, vārenteva tatodhikā.

One should prevent an unlawful act, even if there are two or three obstacles. Having seen the fault, one should prevent it with resolve, and even more so if there are more obstacles.

206.

206.

Kammārahā asaṃvāsā, khittacittadukhaṭṭitā;

Etesaṃ saṅghamajjhamhi, paṭikkhepo na ruhati.

An objection raised in the midst of the Sangha by those who are unfit for the act, unfit for communion, insane, or afflicted by severe pain is not valid.

207.

207.

Pakatattekasīmaṭṭha-samasaṃvāsabhikkhuno;

Ārocentassantamaso-nantarassāpi rūhati.

An objection from a monk in good standing, who dwells within the same boundary and is in communion, is valid, even if he only informs the monk next to him.

208.

208.

Kopetuṃ dhammikaṃ kammaṃ, paṭikkoseyya sammukhā;

Tirokkhā kāyasāmaggiṃ, chandaṃ no deyya dukkaṭanti.

To protest against a lawful act in order to invalidate it, whether in person or from outside the assembly, or to withhold one's consent from a physically complete assembly, is an offense of wrong-doing.

29. Micchājīvavivajjanāniddeso

29. Exposition on the Avoidance of Wrong Livelihood

Micchājīvavivajjanāti –

'Avoidance of wrong livelihood' means:

209.

209.

Dāruṃ veḷuṃ phalaṃ pupphaṃ, cuṇṇaṃ nhānamukhodakaṃ;

Mattikādantakaṭṭhādiṃ, na dade kulasaṅgahā.

One should not give wood, bamboo, fruit, flowers, aromatic powder, bathing powder, water for washing the face, clay, tooth-sticks, and so on, for the sake of ingratiating oneself with families.

210.

210.

Pāribhaṭakatāmugga-sūpyatāvatthuvijjayā;

Paheṇadūtakammena, jaṅghapesaniyena vā.

By acting as a retainer, by sycophancy, by practicing the science of building sites, by acting as a go-between or messenger, or by running errands.

211.

211.

Anuppadānappaṭipiṇḍa-vejjakammena [V 0.0030][M 0.0024] vā pana;

Nāññena vāpi sambuddhappaṭikuṭṭhena jīvaye.

One should not make a living by giving things in anticipation of a return, by bartering, or by practicing medicine, nor by any other means condemned by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

212.

212.

Viññattinesanābhūtullapanākuhanādihi;

Kuladūsādinuppannapaccaye parivajjayeti.

One should avoid requisites obtained by means of hinting, scheming, flattery, hypocrisy, and so on, and by other ways of corrupting families.

30. Vattaniddeso

30. The Exposition on Observances

Vattanti –

On observances—

213.

213.

Āgantuko na ārāmaṃ, pavise saupāhano;

Sachattoguṇṭhito sīse, karitvā vāpi cīvaraṃ.

A guest should not enter the monastery wearing sandals, with a parasol, with his head covered, or with the robe draped over his head.

214.

214.

Pānīyena na dhoveyya, pāde vuḍḍhatarepi ca;

Āvāsikebhivādeyya, puccheyya sayanāsanaṃ.

He should not wash even elder monks' feet with drinking water; he should greet the resident monks and inquire about lodging and bedding.

215.

215.

Gamiko paṭisāmetvā, dārumattikabhaṇḍakaṃ;

Vihārañca thaketvāna, āpuccha sayanāsanaṃ.

A departing monk, having put away the wooden and clay utensils and having locked up the monastery, should take leave of his lodging and bedding.

216.

216.

Āpucchitabbe asati, saṃgopetvāna sādhukaṃ;

Pakkameyyaññathā tassa, pakkantuṃ na ca kappati.

If there is no one from whom to take leave, he should carefully put it away; otherwise, it is not permissible for him to depart.

217.

217.

Āvāsiko paññāpeyya, vuḍḍhāgantussa āsanaṃ;

Upanikkhipe pādoda-ppabhutiṃ pattacīvaraṃ.

A resident should prepare a seat for an elder guest; he should set out foot water and the like, and place down his bowl and robe.

218.

218.

Paccuggantvāna gaṇheyya, pānīyena ca pucchaye;

Āgantukebhivādeyya, paññape sayanāsanaṃ.

He should go out to meet him and take his bowl, and ask about drinking water; he should greet the newcomer, and provide lodging and bedding.

219.

219.

Ajjhāvutthamavutthaṃ [V 0.0031] vā, gocarāgocaraṃ vade;

Vaccapassāvaṭhānāni, katikaṃ sekkhasammutiṃ.

He should inform him about what is inhabited or uninhabited, the proper and improper alms range, the places for urination and defecation, and the established training rules.

220.

220.

Pavesanikkhame kālaṃ, paribhojiyapāniyaṃ;

Nisinnova navakassa, etaṃ sabbaṃ samuddiseti.

The time for entering and leaving, and water for consumption; while seated, he explains all this to the newcomer.

31. Vikappanāniddeso

31. The Exposition on Allocation

Vikappanā [M 0.0025] cevāti –

Regarding allocation—

221.

221.

Sammukhā parammukhāti, duve vuttā vikappanā;

Sammukhāya vikappento, byattassekassa santike;

“Imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ, vikappemī”ti bhāsaye.

"Face-to-face or in absence"—these two kinds of allocation are stated. When allocating face-to-face, one should speak in the presence of a competent bhikkhu: "I allocate this robe to you."

222.

222.

Ettāvatā nidhetuṃva, kappatī na ca kappati;

Paribhogādikaṃ tena, appaccuddhaṭabhāvato.

By this much, it is permissible to put it away, but it is not permissible for him to use it and so on, because it has not been taken back.

223. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti –

223. "Use what belongs to me, give it away, or do with it as is appropriate."

Tena paccuddhaṭeyeva, paribhogādi kappati.

Only when it has been taken back by him is use and so on permissible.

224.

224.

Aparā sammukhāvekā, bhikkhussekassa santike;

Gahetvā nāmamekassa, pañcannaṃ sahadhamminaṃ.

Another kind of face-to-face allocation is in the presence of one bhikkhu, taking the name of one of the five co-religionists.

225. “Imaṃ cīvaraṃ tissassa bhikkhuno, tissāya bhikkhuniyā, tissassa sāmaṇerassa, tissāya sāmaṇeriyā, tissāya sikkhamānāya vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ.

225. One should say: "I allocate this robe to the bhikkhu Tissa, the bhikkhunī Tissā, the sāmaṇera Tissa, the sāmaṇerī Tissā, or the sikkhamānā Tissā."

Tena bhikkhunā “tissassa bhikkhuno, tissāya bhikkhuniyā, tissassa sāmaṇerassa[V 0.0032], tissāya sāmaṇeriyā, tissāya sikkhamānāya santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vattabbaṃ.

That bhikkhu should say: "Use what belongs to the bhikkhu Tissa, the bhikkhunī Tissā, the sāmaṇera Tissa, the sāmaṇerī Tissā, or the sikkhamānā Tissā; give it away, or do with it as is appropriate."

226.

226.

Parammukhāvikappane-kassantikevamīraye;

“Imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti.

In an allocation in absence, one should speak thus in the presence of one bhikkhu: "I give this robe to you for the purpose of allocation."

227. Tena vattabbo “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā”ti. Itarena cevaṃ vattabbaṃ “tisso bhikkhū”ti vā [M 0.0026] “tissā bhikkhunī”ti vā “tisso sāmaṇero”ti vā “tissā sāmaṇerī”ti vā “tissā sikkhamānā”ti vā.

227. He should be asked by that bhikkhu, "Who is your friend or acquaintance?" The other should reply thus: "The bhikkhu Tissa," or "The bhikkhunī Tissā," or "The sāmaṇera Tissa," or "The sāmaṇerī Tissā," or "The sikkhamānā Tissā."

Puna tena “ahaṃ tissassa tissāya vā dammī”ti vikappetvā teneva “tissassa bhikkhuno, tissāya bhikkhuniyā, tissassa sāmaṇerassa, tissāya sāmaṇeriyā, tissāya sikkhamānāya santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti paccuddharitabbaṃ.

Then, having allocated it by saying, "I give this to Tissa or to Tissā," that same bhikkhu should have it taken back with the statement: "Use what belongs to the bhikkhu Tissa, the bhikkhunī Tissā, the sāmaṇera Tissa, the sāmaṇerī Tissā, or the sikkhamānā Tissā; give it away, or do with it as is appropriate."

228.

228.

Dūrasantikattekattabahubhāvaṃ vijāniya;

“Etaṃ ima”nti “etāni, imānī”tettha yojaye.

Having recognized the state of being far or near, singular or plural, one should apply 'this' and 'these' in this context.

229.

229.

Dasāhaṃ māsamekaṃ vā, pañca vā kathinatthate;

Pāripūratthamūnassa, paccāsā sati māsakaṃ;

Nuppādayati nissaggiṃ, nādhiṭṭhitavikappitanti.

When the Kathina has been spread, for ten days, or one month, or five months, if there is an expectation for a month for the completion of a deficient robe, it does not become subject to forfeiture, nor is it determined or allocated.

32. Nissayaniddeso

32. The Exposition on Dependence

Nissayoti –

Regarding dependence—

230.

230.

Byattassa pañcavassassa, natthi nissaya kāriyaṃ;

Yāvajīvampi abyatto, nissitoyeva jīvati.

For a competent one of five years' standing, there is no need for dependence; but an incompetent one lives in dependence even for a lifetime.

231.

231.

Ekaṃsaṃ [V 0.0033] cīvaraṃ katvā, paggaṇhitvāna añjaliṃ;

Ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā, vade yāvatatīyakaṃ;

“Ācariyo me, bhante, hohi,

Āyasmato nissāya vacchāmī”ti.

Having arranged the robe over one shoulder, raising the hands in añjali, and sitting in a squatting position, one should say up to three times: "Venerable sir, be my teacher. I will live in dependence on the Venerable One."

232.

232.

Pakkante pakkhasaṅkante, vibbhante vāpi nissayo;

Maraṇāṇattupajjhāya-samodhānehi sammati.

Dependence ceases when the teacher has departed, gone over to another side, or disrobed; it also ceases through death, by an order, or by agreement with the preceptor.

233.

233.

Nissāya [M 0.0027] na vaselajjiṃ, apubbaṃ ṭhānamāgato;

Āgame catupañcāhaṃ, ñātuṃ bhikkhusabhāgataṃ.

Having come to a place not visited before, one should not take up dependence for four or five days upon arrival, in order to get to know the common character of the bhikkhus.

234.

234.

Addhikassa gilānassa, gilānupaṭṭhakassa ca;

Yācitassa araññe vā, sallakkhantena phāsukaṃ;

Sabhāge dāyakesante, vasituṃ tāva labbhatīti.

For a traveler, a sick person, and one attending the sick, or for one who has been invited, or when in the forest, discerning what is suitable, it is permissible to stay for a while in a shared lodging in the presence of a supporter.

33. Kāyabandhananiddeso

33. The Exposition on the Body-Band

Kāyabandhananti –

Regarding the body-band—

235.

235.

Akāyabandhano gāmaṃ, dukkaṭaṃ paviseyya ce;

Bandheyya yattha sarati, tatthevāsatiyā gato.

If one without a body-band should enter a village, it is a wrongdoing. Having gone there due to lack of mindfulness, he should bind it wherever he remembers.

236.

236.

Paṭṭikā sūkarantanti, duvidhaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ;

Dussapaṭṭo ca rajju ca, ekā tadanulomikā.

A strip and a boar's intestine are the two kinds of body-bands. A cloth strip and a rope; the first is in conformity with that.

237.

237.

Macchakaṇṭakakhajjūrī-pattā maṭṭhā ca paṭṭikā;

Labbhā dasā catassopi, ante diguṇasuttakaṃ.

Strips made of fish-bones, date palm leaves, and smooth strips are permissible. A width of ten or four fingers is allowable, with a double-threaded cord at the end.

238.

238.

Mālādiṃ [V 0.0034] kakkaṭacchādiṃ, dassetvā guṇasuttaka;

Koṭṭitā kuñjaracchādiṃ, paṭṭikā na ca kappati.

A strip like a garland, with a crab-eye design, displaying a string of beads, or a hammered one with an elephant-eye design—such a strip is not permissible.

239.

239.

Ghaṭakaṃ makaramukhādiṃ, na kappanti dasāmukhe;

Ubhante ghaṭakā lekhā, vidhe aññañca cittakaṃ.

Pot-shapes, makara-faces, and the like are not permissible on the fringed ends. At both ends, pot-shapes, lines, and other designs are permissible in a certain manner.

240.

240.

Deḍḍubhakañca murajaṃ, maddavīṇaṃ kalābukaṃ;

Na kappanti dasāsu dve, majjhimāyeva kappare.

Deḍḍubhaka, muraja, maddavīṇa, and kalābuka designs are not permissible on the two fringed ends; only those in the middle are permissible.

241.

241.

Veḷudantavisāṇaṭṭhikaṭṭhalākhāphalāmayā;

Saṅkhanābhimayā suttanaḷalohamayāpi ca;

Vidhā kappanti kappiyā, gaṇṭhiyo cāpi tammayāti.

Made of bamboo, ivory, horn, bone, wood, lac, or fruit; conch-shell, mother-of-pearl, thread, reed, or metal as well—these kinds are permissible, and knots made of them as well.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāraṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The first recitation section is concluded.

34. Pathavīniddeso

34. Exposition on Earth

Pathavī cāti –

And 'earth' is:

242.

242.

Jātājātāti [M 0.0028] duvidhā, suddhamattikapaṃsukā;

Jātādaḍḍhā ca pathavī, bahumattikapaṃsukā;

Cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhapaṃsumattikarāsi ca.

It is of two kinds, arisen and unarisen. The unarisen is pure clay and dust. The arisen is burnt earth, abundant clay and dust, and a heap of dust and clay rained on for more than four months.

243.

243.

Suddhasakkharapāsāṇamarumbakathalavālukā;

Daḍḍhā ca bhūmi yebhuyyasakkharādimahīpi ca;

Dutiyā vuttarāsi ca, cātumāsomavaṭṭhako.

Pure gravel, stones, sandy soil, hard ground, and sand; also burnt earth, and earth that is mostly gravel and the like; and the second kind of heap mentioned, rained on for less than four months.

244.

244.

Dve [V 0.0035] bhāgā tīsu bhāgesu, mattikā yassa bhūmiyā;

Yebhuyyamattikā esā, sesesupi ayaṃ nayo.

That earth of which two parts out of three are clay, this is 'mostly clay.' This same method applies to the rest.

245.

245.

Pācitti khaṇane jāte, jātasaññissa dukkaṭaṃ;

Dveḷhassājātasaññissa, nāpattāṇāpane tathā.

There is a pācittiya for digging what is arisen. When digging what is unarisen, there is a dukkaṭa for one who perceives it as arisen. For one who is in doubt or perceives it as unarisen, there is no offense, and similarly when one gives an order.

246.

246.

Pahāre pahārāpatti, khaṇamānassa attanā;

Ekāyāṇattiyā ekā, nānāṇattīsu vācaso.

When digging by oneself, there is an offense for every stroke. For a single command, there is one offense; for different commands, an offense for each utterance.

247.

247.

“Imaṃ ṭhānamimaṃ kandamidha vāpiṃ khaṇettha ca;

Jālehaggi”nti vā vattuṃ, niyametvā na vaṭṭati.

It is not allowable to specify, saying: 'Dig this place, this pit, or dig a pond here,' or 'Light a fire.'

248.

248.

“Thambhassimassāvāṭaṃ vā, mattikaṃ jāna māhara;

Karohi kappiyañce”ti, vacanaṃ vaṭṭatedisaṃ.

Such speech as this is allowable: 'For the hole for this post, know that clay is needed. Do not bring it; make it allowable.'

249.

249.

Asambaddhaṃ pathaviyā, sukkhakaddamaādikaṃ;

Kopetuṃ tanukaṃ labbhamussiñcanīyakaddamaṃ.

It is allowable to break up a thin piece of dry mud and the like that is not connected to the earth, but not mud that is moist enough to be sprinkled.

250.

250.

Gaṇḍuppādaṃ upacikāmattikaṃ mūsikukkiraṃ;

Cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhaṃ, leḍḍādiñca na kopaye.

One should not damage earthworm castings, termite mound clay, rat-diggings, molehills, a heap rained on for more than four months, or lumps of clay and the like.

251.

251.

Patite vāpiādīnaṃ, kūle udakasantike;

Pāsāṇe ca raje lagge, patite navasoṇḍiyā.

When something has fallen on the bank of a pond or the like near the water; when it clings to a stone or to dust; when it has fallen into a fresh rock-pool;

252.

252.

Vammike [M 0.0029] mattikākuṭṭe, abbhokāsuṭṭhite tathā;

Yebhuyyakathalaṭṭhāne, tiṭṭhatiṭṭhakakuṭṭako.

on an anthill or a clay mound, or similarly, having arisen in an open space; in a place that is mostly hard ground, a heap of things standing firmly.

253.

253.

Thambhādiṃ [V 0.0036] gaṇhituṃ bhūmiṃ, sañcāletvā vikopayaṃ;

Dhārāya bhindituṃ bhūmiṃ, kātuṃ vā visamaṃ samaṃ.

To take earth for a post and so on, shaking and damaging it; to break the earth with a current of water, or to make the uneven even;

254.

254.

Sammuñjanīhi ghaṃsituṃ, kaṇṭakādiṃ pavesituṃ;

Dassessāmīti bhindanto, bhūmiṃ caṅkamituṃ padaṃ.

to rub it with brooms, to insert thorns and the like into it; breaking the ground while saying, 'I will show you'; to make a walking path on the ground with one's feet;

255.

255.

Ghaṃsituṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ, kaṇḍurogī taṭādisu;

Hatthaṃ vā dhovituṃ bhūmiṃ, ghaṃsituṃ na ca kappati.

It is not allowable for one with an itching disease to rub his limbs and joints on a riverbank or the like, nor to wash one's hands by rubbing them on the ground.

256.

256.

Thambhādiujukuddhāro, pāsāṇādipavaṭṭanaṃ;

Sākhādikaḍḍhanaṃ rukkhalatācchedanaphālanaṃ.

To pull up a post or the like to straighten it; to roll away stones and the like; to pull branches and the like; to cut and split trees and creepers;

257.

257.

Seko passāvaādīnaṃ, suddhacittassa vaṭṭati;

Allahatthaṃ ṭhapetvāna, rajaggāho ca bhūmiyā.

The discharge of urine and the like is allowable for one with a pure mind, but not placing a wet hand on the ground or taking up dust from it.

258.

258.

Aggissa anupādāne, kapāle iṭṭhakāya vā;

Pātetuṃ labbhate aggiṃ, bhūmiyaṃ vāvase satīti.

When there is no fuel for a fire, it is allowable to drop the fire on a potsherd or a brick, or on the ground if there is a layer of covering.

35. Parikkhāraniddeso

35. Exposition on Requisites

Parikkhāroti –

As to requisites:

259.

259.

Pañcavaṇṇehi suttehi, anto bahi ca sibbituṃ;

Girikūṭaḍḍhacandādiṃ, chatte paṇṇe ca chindituṃ.

To sew inside and out with five-colored threads; to cut designs of mountain-peaks, half-moons, and so on, on an umbrella or a leaf;

260.

260.

Ghaṭakaṃ vāḷarūpaṃ vā, daṇḍe lekhā na vaṭṭati;

Vaṭṭatī daṇḍabundamhi, ahicchattakasādisaṃ.

A pot-shaped design, an animal-shaped design, or writing on a staff is not allowable. It is allowable on the knob of a staff if it is like a mushroom.

261.

261.

Sibbituṃ [V 0.0037] ekavaṇṇena, pañjaraṃ vā vinandhituṃ;

Thiratthaṃ vaṭṭatī chatte, daṇḍe lekhāva bandhituṃ.

To sew with a single color or to weave a lattice-work design for the sake of firmness is allowable on an umbrella; also to bind writing onto a staff.

262.

262.

Ante [M 0.0030] paṭṭamukhe vāpi, veṇi saṅkhalikāpi vā;

Sūcivikāramaññaṃ vā, cīvare na ca kappati;

Kappabinduvikārampi, pāḷikaṇṇikaādikaṃ.

On the border or the fringe of a robe, a braid, a chain-pattern, or other needlework is not allowable; nor is a decorative marking-spot or border designs such as the 'earring' pattern.

263.

263.

Gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭāpi, catukkoṇāva agghiyaṃ;

Muggaro kakkaṭacchādi-vikāraṃ nettha vaṭṭati.

Knots, loops, bands, a square fringe, a hammer-shaped design, a crab's-eye design, and similar decorations are not allowable here.

264.

264.

Koṇasuttā ca pīḷakā, duviññeyyāva kappare;

Gandhaṃ telaṃ va lākhaṃ vā, rajane na ca pakkhipe.

Corner-threads and raised patterns, if they are difficult to discern, are allowable. One should not add perfume, oil, or lacquer to dye.

265.

265.

Rattaṃ saṅkhena maṇinā, ghaṭṭeyyaññena vā na ca;

Ghaṃseyya doṇiyaṃ katvā, pahāre na ca muṭṭhinā.

One should not burnish a dyed robe with a shell, a gem, or anything similar; nor should one rub it after placing it in a trough, nor strike it with the fist.

266.

266.

Kaṇṇakoṇakasuttāni, ratte chindeyya cīvare;

Lekhā na vaṭṭatī dhamma-karaṇe chattavaṭṭiyaṃ.

One may cut the threads at the corners and edges of a dyed robe. Writing is not allowable on a manuscript or on the ring of an umbrella.

267.

267.

Lekhaṃ ṭhapetvā maṇikā, pīḷakā kuñcikāya ca;

Pipphale ca pariccheda-lekhā daṇḍamhi vaṭṭati.

A dividing line is allowable on a staff. Setting aside the general prohibition on decoration, it is also allowable on beads, on a pīḷakā, on a key, and on a pipphala-shaped object.

268.

268.

Mālādyaraṇiyaṃ patta-maṇḍale bhittikamma ca;

Heṭṭhā lekhādvayaṃ uddhaṃ, ahicchattakasādisaṃ.

Garland-work and the like, leaf-circles, and wall-work are allowable. This may consist of two lines below and one above, resembling a mushroom.

269.

269.

Hitvā kattarayaṭṭhimhi, sūcisaṇḍāsakepi ca;

Yaṃ kiñci girikūṭādi-vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati.
