Except on a walking stick, a needle, or tweezers, any kind of polished color-work such as mountain-peak designs is not allowable.

270.

270.

Bimbohane [V 0.0038] bhisimañca-pīṭhādisayanāsane;

Sammuñjanimhi saṅkāra-chaḍḍane raṅgabhājane.

On a pillow, a mattress, a couch, a chair, and other seats and beds; on a broom, on a rubbish-receptacle, and on a dye-pot;

271.

271.

Pānīyabhājane pāda-pīṭhe kathalikāya ca;

Pattādhārapidhānesu, tālavaṇṭe ca bījane;

Yaṃ kiñci mālākammādi-vaṇṇamaṭṭhamavāritaṃ.

on a water-pot, on a foot-stool, and on a kettle; on bowl-stands and lids, on a palm-leaf fan and a whisk-fan—on these, any kind of polished color-work such as garland-work is not forbidden.

272.

272.

Senāsane pana dvārakavāṭādippabhedane;

Sovaṇṇamayanuññātaṃ, vaṇṇamaṭṭhamhi kā kathā.

But in a lodging, with regard to its different parts such as doors and door-panels, golden ornamentation is allowed. What then needs to be said about polished color-work?

273.

273.

Visāṇanāḷilābvādippabhede [M 0.0031] telabhājane;

Pumitthirūparahitaṃ, vaṇṇamaṭṭhamavāritanti.

On oil-containers of different kinds, such as those made of horn, tube, or gourd, polished color-work is not forbidden, provided it is devoid of male and female figures.

36. Bhesajjaniddeso

36. The Exposition on Medicines

Bhesajjanti –

Medicines:

274.

274.

Janassa kātuṃ bhesajjaṃ, dātuṃ vattuṃ na labbhati;

Bhikkhācariyaviññatti, sakehi sahadhamminaṃ.

To make medicine for the laity, to give it, or to speak of it is not permissible; a request by a monk is for one's own companions in the Dhamma.

275.

275.

Pitūnaṃ tadupaṭṭhākabhikkhunissitabhaṇḍunaṃ;

Labbhaṃ bhesajjakaraṇaṃ, veyyāvaccakarassa ca.

For one's parents, for the monks who attend upon them, for dependent relatives, and for one who performs a service, the preparation of medicine is allowable.

276.

276.

Mahācūḷapitāmātābhātābhaginiādinaṃ;

Tesaṃ sakenattaniye, dātabbaṃ tāvakālikaṃ.

To one's grandfather, uncle, mother, brother, sister, and so on, what is one's own property may be given to them for temporary use.

277.

277.

Kuladūsanaviññatti, bhesajjakaraṇādi hi;

Mātāpitūhi sambandhañātakesu na rūhati.

Indeed, a request that corrupts a family, such as making medicine and so on, does not apply in the case of one's parents and connected relatives.

278.

278.

Piṇḍapāto [V 0.0039] anāmaṭṭho, mātādīnamavārito;

Channaṃ dāmarikacorassa, dātumissariyassa ca.

It is not forbidden to give unappropriated almsfood to one's mother and others, but it should not be given to the six unsuitable persons, to a violent person or a thief, or to one in authority.

279.

279.

Tesaṃ suttodakeheva, parittaṃ kayirā nattano;

Bhaṇitabbaṃ bhaṇāpente, parittaṃ sāsanogadhaṃ.

For them, one should not perform a protective chant of one's own making with consecrated thread and water; one should recite, or have someone recite, a protective chant that is grounded in the Teaching.

280.

280.

Sīlaṃ dhammaṃ parittaṃ vā, āgantvā detu bhāsatu;

Dātuṃ vattuñca labbhati, gantvā kenaci pesitoti.

Let them come and give or speak on virtue, the Dhamma, or a protective chant. It is permissible for a monk to go and give or speak when sent by someone.

37. Uggahaniddeso

37. The Exposition on Acquisition

Uggahoti –

Acquisition:

281.

281.

Kammacetiyasaṅghañña-puggalatthaṃ gaṇassa ca;

Dasabhedampi ratanaṃ, uggaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who acquires any of the ten kinds of valuables for the sake of a construction project, a shrine, the Sangha, another individual, or a group, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

282.

282.

Nissaggi [M 0.0032] tesu attatthaṃ, dvīsu sesesu dukkaṭaṃ;

Anāmasitvā vutte tu, gaṇaṃ saṅghañca puggalaṃ.

Among these, if it is for one's own use, it entails forfeiture; for the other cases, it is an offense of wrong-doing. This is so unless it is said without specifying whether it is for a group, the Sangha, or an individual.

283.

283.

“Cetyassa navakammassa, dammī”ti na paṭikkhipe;

Vade kappiyakārānaṃ, “vadantevamime” iti.

When it is said, 'I will give for the new construction of the shrine,' one should not refuse it. One should tell the stewards: 'These people are saying this.'

284.

284.

Khettaṃ vatthuṃ taḷākaṃ vā, dente dāsapasvādikaṃ;

Paṭikkhipitvā gaṇheyya, kappiyena kamena ca;

Khettādīni vihārassa, vutte dammīti vaṭṭati.

When they give a field, a building site, a reservoir, or slaves, cattle, and so on, one should first refuse and then accept it through an allowable procedure. When it is said, 'I will give fields and so on for the monastery,' it is permissible.

285.

285.

Navamātikakedāra-taḷākakiriyānave;

Mattikuddharaṇaṃ bandho, thirakāro ca āḷiyā.

In the new or old construction of water channels, fields, and reservoirs: the digging of soil, the building of a dam, and the strengthening of an embankment.

286.

286.

Tirekabhāgagahaṇaṃ[V 0.0040], kedāre anave nave;

Aparicchannabhāge ca, sasse “dethettake” iti;

Kahāpaṇuṭṭhāpanañca, sabbesampi akappiyaṃ.

Taking a share of the produce from a field, whether old or new; saying, 'Give this much!' from an undivided portion of the crop; and fixing a price in coins—all this is unallowable.

287.

287.

Avatvā kasa vappiccādettikāya ca bhūmiyā;

Patiṭṭhāpeti bhūmiṃ vā, bhāgo deyyoti ettako.

Without having said, 'Plow, sow,' etc., concerning the land, one establishes ownership of the land or says, 'This much is the share to be given.'

288.

288.

Bhūmibhāge kataṃ sassaṃ, ettake gaṇhathettakaṃ;

Gaṇhanatthaṃ vadantevaṃ, pamāṇaṃ daṇḍarajjubhi.

Regarding the crop produced on a plot of land, saying, 'Take this much, this much is the portion,' and for the purpose of taking it, measuring with a rod and rope is unallowable.

289.

289.

Minane rakkhaṇe ṭhatvā, khale taṃnīharāpane;

Koṭṭhādipaṭisāmane, tassevetamakappiyaṃ.

To stand by during measuring and guarding, at the threshing floor during the removal of straw, and during the repair of a granary and so on—this is unallowable for him.

290.

290.

Paṭisāmeyya pācitti, yaṃ kiñci gihisantakaṃ;

Bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena, sacepi pitusantakaṃ.

Should one repair anything belonging to a householder, it is an offense entailing expiation. This is so even if it belongs to one's father and is done with the resources of the monastery's storekeeper.

291.

291.

Pitūnaṃ kappiyaṃ vatthuṃ, avassaṃ paṭisāmiyaṃ;

Attano santakaṃ katvā, labbhate paṭisāmituṃ.

An allowable article belonging to one's parents that must be repaired may be repaired only after one has made it one's own property.

292.

292.

Dehīti paṭisāmetvā, vutte cāpi paṭikkhipe;

Pātetvāna gate labbhaṃ, palibodhoti gopituṃ.

If, having taken something into custody with the promise, 'I will give it back,' one then refuses when asked; or if something is dropped by one who has departed, it is permissible to guard it as an impediment.

293.

293.

Kammaṃ [M 0.0033] karonto ārāme, sakaṃ vaḍḍhakiādayo;

Parikkhārañca sayana-bhaṇḍaṃ vā rājavallabhā.

While work is being done in the monastery, one's own carpenters and so on, or royal favorites, may ask for requisites or bedding and furniture.

294.

294.

Dehīti paṭisāmetvā, vadanti yadi chandato;

Na kareyya bhayā ṭhānaṃ, guttaṃ dassetu vaṭṭati.

If, after one has taken something into custody, they say 'Give it' out of desire, one should not act out of fear. It is proper to show that it is guarded.

295.

295.

Balakkārena [V 0.0041] pātetvā, gatesu paṭisāmituṃ;

Bhikkhuṃ manussā saṅkanti, naṭṭhe vatthumhi tādise.

People are suspicious of a monk when such an item is lost, thinking he caused it to be dropped by force and then took it into his care after they had gone.

296.

296.

Vihārāvasathassanto, ratanaṃ ratnasammataṃ;

Nikkhipeyya gahetvāna, maggeraññepi tādise;

Sāmikānāgamaṃ ñatvā, patirūpaṃ karīyatīti.

If within a monastery or rest house, or similarly on a road or in the wilderness, one finds a jewel or what is considered a jewel, one should pick it up and put it aside. Having ascertained that the owner will not return, one should deal with it in a suitable way.

38. Kuladūsananiddeso

38. The Exposition on Corrupting Families

Dūsananti –

Corrupting:

297.

297.

Pupphaṃ veḷuṃ phalaṃ cuṇṇaṃ, dantakaṭṭhañca mattikaṃ;

Saṅgahaṇatthaṃ dadato, kuladūsanadukkaṭaṃ.

For a monk who gives flowers, bamboo, fruit, powder, a tooth-stick, or clay for the purpose of gaining favor, it is an offense of wrong-doing involving the corruption of families.

298.

298.

Thullaccayaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ, issarenettha saṅghikaṃ;

Dentassa dukkaṭādīni, theyyā saṅghañña santakaṃ.

For one who gives a heavy article belonging to the Sangha to an authority, it is a grave offense. Giving what belongs to the Sangha or to another is theft; other such giving entails offenses of wrong-doing and so on.

299.

299.

Kulasaṅgahā ropetuṃ, ropāpetuñca sabbathā;

Phalapupphūpagaṃ rukkhaṃ, jaggituñca na vaṭṭati.

For the sake of gaining favor with a family, it is not permissible in any way to plant, have planted, or tend a tree that bears fruit and flowers.

300.

300.

Nimittobhāsato kappavohārapariyāyato;

Attano paribhogatthaṃ, ropanādīni labbhare.

By means of hints, allusions, conventional speech, and indirect talk, it is allowable to have planting and so on done for the sake of one's own use.

301.

301.

Vuttāva vejjikā jaṅghapesane gihikammasu;

Ṭhapetvā pitaro bhaṇḍuṃ, veyyāvaccakaraṃ sakaṃ.

As has been said regarding medical practice, acting as a messenger, and performing household duties, these are unallowable except in the case of one's parents, kinsmen, and one's own attendant.

302.

302.

Dukkaṭaṃ padavārena, haraṇe dūtasāsanaṃ;

Sāsanaṃ aggahetvāpi, paṭhamaṃ vadato puna.

In carrying a messenger's message, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every step. This applies even if one has not accepted the message, for one who speaks first and then again.

303.

303.

Uppannapaccayā [V 0.0042][M 0.0034] evaṃ, pañcannampi akappiyā;

Abhūtārocanārūpa-saṃvohāruggahādisā.

Thus, due to conditions that have arisen, five things are also unallowable: making a false accusation, improper dealings, forceful acquisition, and so on.

304.

304.

Harāpetvā haritvāpi, pitūnaṃ sesañātinaṃ;

Pattānaṃ vatthupūjatthaṃ, dātuṃ pupphāni labbhati;

Maṇḍanatthañca liṅgādi-pūjatthañca na labbhati.

Having carried them or caused them to be carried, it is permissible to give flowers to one's parents and other relatives for the purpose of honoring the bowl and robe. But it is not permissible to give them for the purpose of adornment or for the worship of emblems and the like.

305.

305.

Tathā phalaṃ gilānānaṃ, sampattissariyassa ca;

Paribbayavihīnānaṃ, dātuṃ saparasantakaṃ.

Likewise, it is permissible to give fruit to the sick, to a visitor of rank, and to those destitute of provisions, whether it is one's own property or another's.

306.

306.

Bhājente phalapupphamhi, deyyaṃ pattassa kassaci;

Sammatenāpaloketvā, dātabbamitarena tu.

When distributing fruit and flowers, they should be given into someone's bowl. But having announced it and gained consent, it should be given by another.

307.

307.

Vihāre vā paricchijja, katvāna katikaṃ tato;

Deyyaṃ yathāparicchedaṃ, gilānassetarassa vā;

Yācamānassa katikaṃ, vatvā rukkhāva dassiyā.

Or in the monastery, having marked a boundary and made an agreement, a share should be given according to the boundary to a sick person or to another. To one who asks, one should state the agreement and show the trees.

308.

308.

Sirīsakasavādīnaṃ, cuṇṇe sese ca nicchayo;

Yathāvuttanayo eva, paṇṇampettha pavesayeti.

The decision concerning Sirīsa powder, astringents, and the like, and what remains, is exactly according to the method already stated. A leaf should be inserted here.

39. Vassūpanāyikaniddeso

39. Exposition on Entering the Rains-Residence

Vassūpanāyikā cevāti –

As to 'entering the rains-residence'—

309.

309.

Purimikā pacchimikā, duve vassūpanāyikā;

Tatthālayapariggāho, vacībhedo ca ediso.

The earlier and the later are the two enterings upon the rains; therein, the taking up of a dwelling with attachment and such a verbal distinction are involved.

310.

310.

“Imasmiṃ [V 0.0043] vihāre imaṃ, temāsaṃ vassaṃ upemi;

Idha vassaṃ upemī”ti, cittuppādettha ālayo.

‘In this monastery I enter upon the rains for this three-month period; I enter upon the rains here’—the arising of such a thought is attachment.

311.

311.

Nopetukāmo āvāsaṃ, tadahūtikkameyya vā;

Bhaveyya dukkaṭāpatti, jānaṃ vānupagacchato.

If one does not wish to go to the dwelling, or if one lets that day pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who, knowing, does not go.

312.

312.

Dutiyaṃ [M 0.0035] upagaccheyya, chinnavassonupāgato;

Na pakkameyya temāsaṃ, avasitvāna cārikaṃ.

One whose rains-residence is broken should go to a second one; having settled, one should not depart on tour for the three-month period.

313.

313.

Mātāpitūnamatthāya, pañcannaṃ sahadhamminaṃ;

Gilānatadupaṭṭhāka-bhattamesissamosadhaṃ.

For the sake of one's mother and father, for the five kinds of companions in the Dhamma, for a sick person or their attendant, or to seek food or medicine.

314.

314.

Pucchissāmi upaṭṭhissaṃ, gantvānabhirataṃ ahaṃ;

Vūpakāsissaṃ kukkuccaṃ, diṭṭhiṃ garukamādikaṃ.

‘Having gone, I will ask, I will attend; being discontented, I will dispel my remorse, or a wrong view, or a serious matter, and so on.’

315.

315.

Karissaṃ vāpi kāressaṃ, vinodanaṃ vivecanaṃ;

Vuṭṭhānaṃ vāpi ussukkaṃ, gantumiccevamādinā;

Labbhaṃ sattāhakiccena, pahitāpahitepi vā.

‘I will do it or have it done for the sake of dispelling discontent or for seclusion; or I will make an effort to depart.’ With such reasons as these, leave is allowable for a seven-day duty, whether one is sent or not.

316.

316.

Saṅghakamme vaje dhamma-ssavanatthaṃ nimantito;

Garūhi pahito vāpi, garūnaṃ vāpi passituṃ.

One may go for a formal act of the Sangha, if invited to hear the Dhamma, if sent by one's teachers, or to see one's teachers.

317.

317.

Na bhaṇḍadhovanuddesa-ñātupaṭṭhākadassane;

Labbhaṃ na pāpuṇeyyajje-vāgamissantudūrago.

Leave is not allowable for washing requisites, for recitation, or for seeing relatives or supporters. One who is going far away and would not be able to return on the same day cannot obtain it.

318.

318.

Sesañātīhi pahite, bhikkhunissitakena ca;

Upāsakopāsikāhi, niddisitvāva pesite.

When sent by other relatives, or by one dependent on a bhikkhunī, or by male and female lay followers, having been sent after a purpose has been specified.

319.

319.

Vassacchede [V 0.0044] anāpatti, antarāye satattano;

Saṅghasāmaggiyā vā no, chinnavasso pavāraye.

There is no offense in breaking the rains-residence if there is a personal danger, or if there is no harmony in the Sangha. One whose rains-residence is broken may still perform the Pavāraṇā.

320.

320.

Ajjhokāse ca rukkhassa, susire viṭapepi vā;

Chavakuṭichattacāṭī-sūpagantuṃ na vaṭṭati.

It is not proper to enter upon the rains-residence in the open air, in the hollow of a tree, or on a branch, nor in a corpse-hut, under an umbrella, or in a large pot.

321.

321.

Asenāsanikenāpi, upagantuṃ na labbhati;

Pavāretuñca labbhati, nāvāsatthavajūpagoti.

It is not allowable for one without a fixed dwelling to enter upon the rains-residence, but it is allowable for such a one to perform the Pavāraṇā, provided they do not resort to an improper dwelling.

40. Avebhaṅgiyaniddeso

40. Exposition on Indivisible Items

Avebhaṅgiyanti –

As to 'indivisible items'—

322.

322.

Ārāmārāmavatthūni, vihāro tassa vatthu ca;

Mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bibbo-hanādisayanāsanaṃ.

A monastery park and its land, a dwelling and its site; a bed, a chair, a cushion, a bolster, and other such bedding and seating.

323.

323.

Lohakumbhī [M 0.0036] kaṭāho ca,

Lohabhāṇakavārako;

Kuṭhārī vāsi pharasu,

Kuddālo ca nikhādanaṃ.

A metal pot and a cauldron, a metal vessel and a water pot; an axe, an adze, a hatchet, a spade, and a pickaxe.

324.

324.

Valli veḷu tiṇaṃ paṇṇaṃ, muñjapabbajamattikā;

Dārumattikabhaṇḍāni, pañcete avibhājiyā.

Creepers, bamboo, grass, leaves, muñja and babbaja grass, and clay; wooden and earthenware articles—these five kinds of things are indivisible.

325.

325.

Thullaccayaṃ bhājayato, bhājitāpi abhājitā;

Garubhaṇḍāni vuccanti, etevissajjiyāni ca.

For one who divides them, there is a grave offense, whether they have been divided or not. These are called heavy articles, and they are also not to be disposed of.

326.

326.

Valliḍḍhabāhumattāpi[V 0.0045], veḷu aṭṭhaṅgulāyato;

Tiṇādi muṭṭhimattampi, paṇṇaṃ ekampi mattikā.

A creeper of the thickness of half an upper arm, bamboo eight finger-breadths long, a handful of grass and the like, even a single leaf, and clay.

327.

327.

Pākatā pañcavaṇṇā vā, sudhākaṅguṭṭha ādikā;

Tālapakkappamāṇāpi, dinnā vā tatthajātakā.

Clay, whether natural or of five colors, or plaster, red arsenic, and the like, even of the size of a ripe palm fruit, whether it was given or originated there.

328.

328.

Rakkhitā saṅghikā rajju-yottādīpi abhājiyā;

Niṭṭhite bhājiyā kamme, saṅghike cetiyassa vā.

Ropes, yokes, and the like belonging to the Sangha are to be guarded and are indivisible. When the work—whether for the Sangha or for a shrine—is finished, they may be divided.

329.

329.

Pattādi bhikkhusāruppaṃ, tathā vippakatākataṃ;

Bhājiyaṃ lohabhaṇḍesu, vārakaṃ pādagaṇhakaṃ.

Among metal articles, the following are divisible: bowls and other items suitable for a bhikkhu, as well as unfinished and finished work; a water-strainer and a foot-scraper.

330.

330.

Veḷumhi bhājiyā tela-nāḷi kattaradaṇḍako;

Chattadaṇḍasalākāyo, tathopāhanadaṇḍako.

Among bamboo items, the following are divisible: an oil tube, a handle for a cutting tool, an umbrella shaft and its ribs, and likewise a shoe-form.

331.

331.

Anuññātavāsidaṇḍo, karaṇḍo pādagaṇhako;

Araṇañjanisiṅgādi, bhikkhūpakaraṇaṃ tathā.

An allowed handle for an adze, a casket, a foot-scraper; a fire-stick, collyrium, a horn, and other such requisites for a bhikkhu are likewise divisible.

332.

332.

Tacchitāniṭṭhitaṃ dārubhaṇḍaṃ dantañca bhājiyaṃ;

Bhikkhūpakaraṇe pādaghaṭako mattikāmayo.

Worked and unfinished wooden articles and ivory are divisible. Among a bhikkhu's requisites, an earthenware foot-washer is divisible.

333.

333.

Bhājiyaṃ kappiyaṃ cammaṃ, eḷacammamabhājiyaṃ;

Garunā garubhaṇḍañca, thāvaraṃ thāvarena ca.

Allowable leather is divisible, but ram's hide is indivisible. Heavy articles may be exchanged for heavy articles, and immovable property for immovable property.

334.

334.

Thāvaraṃ [M 0.0037] parivatteyya, tathā katvā ca bhuñjatu;

Vallādiṃ phātikammena, gaṇhe sesamabhājiyanti.

One may exchange immovable property, and having done so, may make use of it. One may acquire creepers and the like by means of a transaction for the Sangha's benefit. The remainder is indivisible.

41. Pakiṇṇakaniddeso

41. Exposition on Miscellaneous Matters

Pakiṇṇakanti [V 0.0046] –

As to 'miscellaneous matters'—

335.

335.

Sadvārabandhane ṭhāne, sodukkhalakapāsake;

Sayantena divā dvāraṃ, bandheyya parivaṭṭakaṃ.

In a place with a door-fastening that has a faulty latch, one who is lying down during the day should fasten the door with the bolt.

336.

336.

Sante viññumhi purise, ābhogo cāpi kappati;

Savase taṃ vinākāraṃ, sayanto dukkaṭaṃ phuse.

If a discerning person is present, it is proper to give attention to this. But if one is alone, lying down without doing so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.

337.

337.

Ratanānitthirūpāni, dhaññamitthipasādhanaṃ;

Tūriyāvudhabhaṇḍāni, āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who touches gems, images of women, grain, women's ornaments, musical instruments, or weapons, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

338.

338.

Sitthatelodatelehi, phaṇahatthaphaṇehi vā;

Kocchenavāpi yo kese, osaṇṭheyyassa dukkaṭaṃ.

Whoever arranges their hair with perfumed oil or other oils, or with a hand-comb or a comb, or with a brush, commits an offense of wrong-doing.

339.

339.

Nekapāvuraṇā ekattharaṇā vā tuvaṭṭayuṃ;

Tathekamañce bhuñjeyyuṃ, ekasmiṃ vāpi bhājane.

Two bhikkhus should not lie down together sharing one outer robe or one covering; likewise, they should not eat on one bed or from a single vessel.

340.

340.

Caturaṅgulato ūnamadhikaṭṭhaṅgulaṃ tathā;

Dantakaṭṭhaṃ na khādeyya, lasuṇaṃ na akallako.

One should not chew a tooth-stick that is less than four finger-breadths or more than eight finger-breadths long. One who is not sick should not eat garlic.

341.

341.

Hīnukkaṭṭhehi ukkaṭṭhaṃ, hīnaṃ vā jātiādihi;

Ujuṃ vāññāpadesena, vade dubbhāsitaṃ davā.

To speak disparagingly of the superior or the inferior based on birth and so on, whether directly or with a pretext, or to speak maliciously, is an offense of wrong speech.

342.

342.

Dīghe nakhe ca kese ca, nāsalome na dhāraye;

Na labbhaṃ vīsatimaṭṭhaṃ, sambādhe lomahāraṇaṃ.

One should not maintain long fingernails, long hair, or long nose-hairs. It is not allowable to be massaged in a confined space, nor to have hair removed there.

343.

343.

Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ na bādheyya, saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃva saṅghikaṃ;

Adhotaallapādehi, nakkame sayanāsanaṃ;

Sudhotapādakaṃ vāpi, tatheva saupāhano.

One should not disrupt the seating according to seniority, nor what is designated by or belongs to the Sangha. One should not step on bedding or seating with unwashed and wet feet, nor likewise while wearing sandals, even with well-washed feet.

344.

344.

Saṅghāṭiyā [V 0.0047][M 0.0038] na pallatthe, bhittādiṃ na apassaye;

Parikammakataṃ sante, udake no na ācame.

One should not sit cross-legged while wearing the outer robe. One should not lean against a wall or the like. When water has been prepared for use, one should not rinse one's mouth with it.

345.

345.

Akappiyasamādāne, davā silāpavijjhane;

Desanāya sabhāgāya, āvikamme ca dukkaṭaṃ.

In undertaking what is improper, in jesting, in splitting a rock, in teaching an unsuitable person, and in disclosing another's offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

346.

346.

Paṭissavavisaṃvāde, suddhacittassa dukkaṭaṃ;

Paṭissavakkhaṇe eva, pācitti itarassa tu.

In breaking a promise, for one with a pure intention there is an offense of wrong-doing; but for the other, there is a pācittiya offense at the very moment of making the promise.

347.

347.

Na rukkhamabhirūheyya, sati kicceva porisaṃ;

Āpadāsu yathākāmaṃ, kappatī abhirūhituṃ.

One should not climb a tree higher than a man's height, except when there is a reason. In times of danger, it is allowable to climb as one wishes.

348.

348.

Vināddhānaṃ vajantassa, dukkaṭaṃ parisāvanaṃ;

Yācamānassa addhāne, adadantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For one going on a journey, to be without a water-strainer is an offense of wrong-doing. For one on a journey who is asked for one, not giving it is an offense of wrong-doing.

349.

349.

Thullaccayaṃ phuse aṅgajātacchedena dukkaṭaṃ;

Ābādhappaccayāññatra, sesaṅge attaghātane.

By cutting off one's own male organ, one incurs a grave offense. In attempting suicide by harming other limbs, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing, except for the reason of illness.

350.

350.

Cittapotthakarūpāni, na kare na ca kāraye;

Na vuṭṭhāpeyya bhuñjantaṃ, ārāmāraññagehasu.

One should not make or cause to be made paintings, books, or images. One should not make a person who is eating get up, whether in a monastery, a forest, or a house.

351.

351.

Yānāni pumayuttāni, sivikaṃ hatthavaṭṭakaṃ;

Pāṭaṅkiñca gilānassa, kappatī abhirūhituṃ.

It is allowable for a sick person to mount vehicles yoked with men, a palanquin, a hand-litter, and a stretcher.

352.

352.

Buddhaṃ dhammañca saṅghañca, ārabbha karaṇe davaṃ;

Dukkaṭaṃ parisaṃ vāpi, aññassa upalāḷane.

Making a joke concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Sangha is an offense of wrong-doing; likewise in flattering an assembly or another person.

353.

353.

Kāyaṃ [V 0.0048] ūruṃ nimittaṃ vā, bhikkhunīnaṃ na dassaye;

Vivaritvā na siñceyya, tā kaddamudakādinā.

One should not show one's body, thigh, or private part to bhikkhunīs. Having uncovered oneself, one should not sprinkle them with muddy water or the like.

354.

354.

Na gaṇhato ca ovādaṃ, na paccāharatopi ca;

Bālaṃ gilānaṃ gamiyaṃ, vajjayitvāna dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who does not receive advice, or for one who does not report back, it is an offense of wrong-doing, excepting a fool, a sick person, or one about to depart.

355.

355.

Lokāyataṃ na vāceyya, palitaṃ na ca gāhaye;

Peḷāyapi na bhuñjeyya, na kīḷe kiñci kīḷitaṃ.

One should not teach worldly lore, nor have grey hairs pulled out. One should not eat from a basket, nor should one play any kind of game.

356.

356.

Pārupe [M 0.0039] na nivāseyya, gihipārutanivāsanaṃ;

Saṃvelliyaṃ nivāseyya, dāyaṃ nālimpayeyya vā.

One should not drape or wear robes in the manner of householders. One should wear the lower robe wrapped around. One should not anoint oneself with forest produce.

357.

357.

Vaḍḍhiṃ payojaye yāce, noññātakappavārite;

Attano paribhogatthaṃ, dinnamaññassa no dade;

Aggaṃ gahetvā bhutvā vā, katipāhaṃ puno dade.

One should not engage in usury nor ask for it, unless invited by relatives. What is given for one's own use, one should not give to another. Having taken the best part or having used it for some days, one should give it back.

358.

358.

Uddissa yācane rakkhaṃ, ñatvāñatvā va daṇḍinaṃ;

Gīvāssa daṇḍite daṇḍo, sayaṃ daṇḍāpane pana;

Daṇḍassa agghabhedena, ñeyyā pārājikādikā.

If, in asking for protection for someone, one causes another to be punished, whether knowingly or not; if one causes the punishment oneself, then according to the value of the fine, offenses beginning with pārājika are to be understood.

359.

359.

Harantesu parikkhāraṃ, “coro coro”ti bhāsite;

Anatthāyesaṃ gaṇhante, daṇḍaṃ gīvāssa tattakaṃ.

When requisites are being carried away, and one says, ‘A thief! A thief!’, causing them to be seized for their harm, one is liable for a corresponding fine.

360.

360.

Vighāsuccārasaṅkāra-muttaṃ chaḍḍeyya dukkaṭaṃ;

Bahi pākārakuṭṭānaṃ, vaḷañje nāvalokiya;

Harite vāpi vīhādi-nāḷikerādiropime.

It is an offense of wrong-doing to discard leftover food, feces, urine, or rubbish on green grass, or in a place where paddy, coconuts, and the like are planted. One should dispose of them outside the monastery wall, without looking at the latrine.

361.

361.

Yojāpetuṃ [V 0.0049] payojetuṃ, payuttāni ca passituṃ;

Na labbhaṃ dhammayuttampi, naccaṃ gītañca vāditaṃ;

“Upahāraṃ karomā”ti, vutte vā sampaṭicchituṃ.

It is not allowable to arrange, to cause to be arranged, or to go to see dancing, singing, and music, even if connected with the Dhamma. Nor is it allowable to accept when it is said, ‘Let us make an offering.’

362.

362.

Rājāgāraṃ pokkharaṇiṃ, uyyānaṃ cittagārakaṃ;

Kīḷatthaṃ gacchato daṭṭhuṃ, ārāmaṃ dukkaṭaṃ kataṃ.

For one who goes for the sake of amusement to see a royal palace, a lotus pond, a park, a picture gallery, or a pleasure grove, an offense of wrong-doing is committed.

363.

363.

Nave na paṭibāheyyā-sanenuṇhe na cīvaraṃ;

Nidaheyya khamāpeyya, garunā ca paṇāmito.

One should not obstruct a novice. One should not warm a robe on a seat; one should put it down. Having been dismissed by a senior, one should ask for forgiveness.

364.

364.

Akkosane parammukhā, āpattīhi ca sattahi;

Bhikkhuṃ upāsakaṃ vāpi, aññeneva ca dukkaṭaṃ.

In abusing a bhikkhu or a male lay follower behind their back with reference to the seven classes of offenses, or in any other way, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

365.

365.

Na labbhaṃ vinipātetuṃ, saddhādeyyañca cīvaraṃ;

Labbhaṃ pitūnaṃ sesānaṃ, ñātīnampi na labbhati.

It is not allowable to spoil a robe given in faith. It is allowable to give it to one's parents, but it is not allowable for other relatives.

366.

366.

Vassaṃvutthoññatoññatra[M 0.0040], bhāgaṃ gaṇheyya dukkaṭaṃ;

Paṭideyya naṭṭhe jiṇṇe, gīvā no deyya codito;

Dhuranikkhepato tesaṃ, hoti bhaṇḍagghakāriyo.

For one who has spent the rains-residence in one place to take a share from another place is an offense of wrong-doing. If the item is lost or worn out, one must repay its value. When requested, one should not refuse. From their laying down of the charge, one becomes responsible for the value of the goods.

367.

367.

Na santaruttaro gāmaṃ, kallo vā saupāhano;

Paviseyya na dhāreyya, cāmarīmakasabījaniṃ.

A healthy bhikkhu should not enter a village wearing both his upper and lower robes, nor with sandals on. He should not carry a chowrie-whisk or a fly-whisk.

368.

368.

Agilāno na chindeyya, kese kattariyā bahi;

Ārāmato na dhāreyya, chattaṃ labbhati guttiyā.

One who is not sick should not cut one's hair with scissors outside the monastery. One should not carry an umbrella, though it is allowed for protection.

369.

369.

Gāheyya nubhatokājaṃ, ekantarikakājakaṃ;

Sīsakkhandhakaṭibhārā, hattholambo ca labbhati.

One should not carry a load with a pole on both shoulders, but one may carry it on one shoulder. It is allowable to carry burdens on the head, shoulder, or hip, or hanging from the hand.

370.

370.

Āpattiyā [V 0.0050] anokāsa-kataṃ codeyya dukkaṭaṃ;

Suddhassa ca avatthusmiṃ, tathā okāsakāraṇe.

To accuse another of an offense without having been given leave is an offense of wrong-doing; likewise to accuse a pure one without grounds, or to do so after creating an opportunity.

371.

371.

Aṭṭhaṅgulādhikaṃ mañcapaṭipādaṃ na dhāraye;

Pakataṅgulena sattānaṃ, mañcaṃ vā uccapādakaṃ.

One should not use a bed or a chair with legs longer than eight standard finger-breadths. One should not use a high-legged bed or chair.

372.

372.

Mūgabbatādiṃ gaṇheyya, dukkaṭaṃ titthiyabbataṃ;

Khurabhaṇḍaṃ parihare, tathā nhāpitapubbako.

To undertake vows of the sectarians, such as the vow of silence, is an offense of wrong-doing. One who was formerly a barber may carry a case of razors.

373.

373.

Yaṃ kiñci yācituṃ hatthakammaṃ tadanusārato;

Laddhaṃ gahetuṃ nikkammamayācitvāpi kappati;

Kāretumāharāpetuṃ, yaṃ kiñciparasantakaṃ.

It is allowable to request any manual labor and accordingly take what is obtained, even without asking; and to have anything belonging to another done or brought.

374.

374.

Gihīnaṃ gopake dente, gahetuṃ deti yattakaṃ;

Labbhaṃ yathāparicchedaṃ, saṅghacetiyasantake.

When laypeople give to the guardian, he gives as much as is to be taken; what is obtainable from the property of the Sangha or a shrine is according to the specified limit.

375.

375.

Dvīhāpajjeyya āpattiṃ, kāyavācāhi vā chahi;

Alajjiññāṇakukkuccapakatattā satiplavā;

Akappiye vā kappiye, kappākappiyasaññitā.

One might commit an offense in two ways, through body and speech, or in six ways: through shamelessness, ignorance, scrupulousness, being of a certain nature, a lapse of mindfulness, or by perceiving what is improper as proper or what is proper as improper.

376.

376.

Alajjiññāṇatāpattiṃ[M 0.0041], kāyavācāhi chādaye;

Liṅge saṅghe gaṇekasmiṃ, catudhāpattivuṭṭhiti.

One might conceal with body and speech an offense born of shamelessness and ignorance. Rehabilitation from an offense is fourfold: by the sign, before the Sangha, a group, or a single individual.

377.

377.

Parikathobhāsaviññatti, na labbhā paccayadvaye;

Viññattiyeva tatiye, sese sabbampi labbhati.

Allusion, intimation, and a request are not allowable in two conditions; only a request is allowable in the third; in the remaining cases, everything is allowable.

378.

378.

Na rūhataccaye dānaṃ, pañcannaṃ sahadhamminaṃ;

Saṅghasseva ca taṃ hoti, gihīnaṃ pana rūhati.

A gift for the five kinds of fellow monastics does not accrue to them upon their death; that gift belongs only to the Sangha. For laypeople, however, it does accrue.

379.

379.

Bhikkhu [V 0.0051] vā sāmaṇero vā, kālaṃ kayirāthūpassaye;

Bhikkhusaṅghova dāyajjo, tattha sesepyayaṃnayo.

Should a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera die in his residence, the Sangha of bhikkhus is the heir; this same principle applies to the others.

380.

380.

Purimassevimaṃ dinnaṃ, dehi netvāsukassati;

Pacchimasseva dammīti, dinnaṃ ñatvā imaṃ vidhiṃ;

Gaṇhe vissāsagāhaṃ vādhiṭṭhe matakacīvaraṃ.

Knowing this procedure for what has been given—'This was given to the first one; take it and give it to so-and-so,' or 'I give it to the last one'—one may take the robe of the deceased by trust or determine it.

381.

381.

Lohabhaṇḍe paharaṇiṃ, dārubhaṇḍe ca dārujaṃ;

Pattaṃ pādukapallaṅkaṃ, āsandiṃ mattikāmaye;

Ṭhapetvā kappati sabbaṃ, katakaṃ kumbhakārikanti.

A striker for a metal vessel, and a wooden one for a wooden vessel; a bowl, footwear, a couch, a chair made of clay—setting aside what is made by a potter, all this is allowable.

42. Desanāniddeso

42. Exposition of Confession

Desanāti –

Confession is:

382.

382.

Cāgo yo bhikkhubhāvassa, sā pārājikadesanā;

Yathāvuttena vuṭṭhānaṃ, garukāpattidesanā.

The abandonment of the state of a bhikkhu is the 'confession' for a pārājika offense. Rehabilitation according to the prescribed procedure is the confession for a serious offense.

383.

383.

Ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā, paggaṇhitvāna añjaliṃ;

Thullaccayādiṃ deseyya, evamekassa santike.

Having sat down in the squatting position and raised his hands in añjali, one should confess a thullaccaya offense and so on in the presence of a single monk.

384. “Ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ thullaccayāpattiṃ āpajjiṃ, taṃ tumhamūle paṭidesemī”ti vatvā tena “passasi, āvuso, taṃ āpatti”nti vutte “āma, bhante, passāmī”ti vatvā puna tena “āyatiṃ, āvuso, saṃvareyyāsī”ti vutte “sādhu suṭṭhu, bhante, saṃvarissāmī”ti [M 0.0042] vattabbaṃ. “Ahaṃ, bhante, dve thullaccayāpattiyo āpajjiṃ, ahaṃ bhante sambahulā thullaccayāpattiyo āpajjiṃ, tā tumhamūle paṭidesemī”ti vattabbaṃ.

384. "Venerable sir, I have committed one thullaccaya offense; I confess it in your presence." Having said this, when told by the other, "Friend, do you see that offense?" one should say, "Yes, venerable sir, I see it." Then, when told by him, "In the future, friend, you should be restrained," one should say, "Very well, venerable sir, I will be well restrained." It should be said: "Venerable sir, I have committed two thullaccaya offenses... venerable sir, I have committed many thullaccaya offenses; I confess them in your presence."

Nissaggiyesu pana “idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ dasāhātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ āyasmato [V 0.0052] nissajjāmī”ti. “Imāni me, bhante, cīvarāni…pe… etaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ…pe… etāni me, bhante, cīvarāni dasāhātikkantāni nissaggiyāni, etānāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmī”ti.

In the case of offenses requiring forfeiture, one says: "Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been kept beyond ten days, is to be forfeited. I relinquish it to the venerable one." "Venerable sir, these robes of mine...pe... that robe of mine...pe... those robes of mine, having been kept beyond ten days, are to be forfeited. I relinquish them to the venerable one."

385.

385.

Nissajjitvāna deseyya, āpattiṃ tena bhikkhunā;

Paṭiggahetvā āpattiṃ, deyyaṃ nissaṭṭhacīvaraṃ.

Having relinquished the robe, one should confess the offense. After that monk has accepted the confession, the relinquished robe should be given back.

“Imaṃ, imāni, etaṃ, etāni cīvarāni āyasmato dammī”ti.

"I give this (these, that, those) robe(s) to the venerable one."

386. (Ka) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ rattivippavutthaṃ aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā nissaggiyaṃ.

386. "(Ka) Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been kept apart overnight without the bhikkhus' permission, is to be forfeited."

(Kha) idaṃ me, bhante, akālacīvaraṃ māsātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Kha) Venerable sir, this unseasonal robe, kept beyond a month, is to be forfeited."

(Ga) idaṃ me, bhante, purāṇacīvaraṃ aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā dhovāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ga) Venerable sir, this old robe of mine, which I had washed by a bhikkhunī not related to me, is to be forfeited."

(Gha) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato paṭiggahitaṃ aññatra pārivattakā nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Gha) Venerable sir, this robe, which I received from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī without an exchange, is to be forfeited."

(Ṅa) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ aññatra samayā viññāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ṅa) Venerable sir, this robe of mine, which I requested from an unrelated householder at an improper time, is to be forfeited."

(Ca) idaṃ [M 0.0043] me, bhante, cīvaraṃ aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ tatuttari viññāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ca) Venerable sir, this robe of mine, which I requested from an unrelated householder in excess of the proper limit, is to be forfeited."

(Cha) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavārito aññātakaṃ gahapatikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Cha) Venerable sir, this robe of mine is to be forfeited, as I approached an unrelated householder by whom I was not invited and made a specification for it."

(Ja) idaṃ [V 0.0053] me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavārito aññātake gahapatike upasaṅkamitvā vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ja) Venerable sir, this robe of mine is to be forfeited, as I approached unrelated householders by whom I was not invited and made a specification for it."

(Jha) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ atirekatikkhattuṃ codanāya atirekachakkhattuṃ ṭhānena abhinipphāditaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Jha) Venerable sir, this robe of mine is to be forfeited, which was produced by prompting more than three times and by standing by more than six times."

(Ña) idaṃ me, bhante, kosiyamissakaṃ santhataṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ña) Venerable sir, this felt cloth mixed with silk, which I had made, is to be forfeited."

(Ṭa) idaṃ me, bhante, suddhakāḷakānaṃ eḷakalomānaṃ santhataṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ṭa) Venerable sir, this felt cloth made entirely of pure black sheep's wool, which I had made, is to be forfeited."

(Ṭha) idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ anādiyitvā tulaṃ odātānaṃ tulaṃ gocariyānaṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ṭha) Venerable sir, this felt cloth is to be forfeited, which I had made without including a measure of white wool and a measure of brown wool."

(Ḍa) idaṃ me, bhante, santhataṃ ūnakachabbassāni kārāpitaṃ aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ḍa) Venerable sir, this felt cloth, made less than six years after the old one and without the bhikkhus' permission, is to be forfeited."

(Ḍha) idaṃ me, bhante, nisīdanasanthataṃ anādiyitvā purāṇasanthatassa sāmantā sugatavidatthiṃ kārāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

"(Ḍha) Venerable sir, this sitting-rug is to be forfeited, which I had made without incorporating a piece from the old rug's border of a Buddha-span in size."

(Ṇa) imāni me, bhante, eḷakalomāni tiyojanaparamaṃ atikkāmitāni nissaggiyāni.

Venerable sir, this sheep's wool of mine, having been carried beyond the three-yojana limit, is to be forfeited.

(Ta) imāni [M 0.0044] me, bhante, eḷakalomāni aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā dhovāpitāni nissaggiyāni.

Venerable sir, this sheep's wool of mine, having been washed by a bhikkhunī who is not a relative, is to be forfeited.

(Tha) ahaṃ, bhante, rūpiyaṃ paṭiggahesiṃ, idaṃ me, bhante, nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmi.

Venerable sir, I accepted gold and silver. This, venerable sir, is to be forfeited. I relinquish this to the Sangha.

(Da) ahaṃ[V 0.0054], bhante, nānappakārakaṃ rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ samāpajjiṃ, idaṃ me, bhante, nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmīti.

Venerable sir, I engaged in various kinds of transactions involving gold and silver. This, venerable sir, is to be forfeited. I relinquish this to the Sangha.

387.

387.

Nissajjitvāna āpattiṃ, deseyyātha gihiṃ vade;

“Jānāhima”nti iminā, so vadeyyāharāmi kiṃ.

Having relinquished the object of the offense, one should confess. One should then tell a layperson: 'Know this.' He might say: 'What shall I bring?'

388.

388.

Avatvāmanti telādiṃ, vade bhikkhūna kappiyaṃ;

Yaṃ āharati so tena, parivattetvāna kappiyaṃ.

Without mentioning 'oil' and so on, one should state what is allowable for bhikkhus. Whatever he brings, having been obtained in exchange for that, is allowable.

389.

389.

Labbhaṃ ṭhapetvā dvepete, sesehi paribhuñjituṃ;

Tato aññena laddhopi, bhāgo tesaṃ na kappati.

Except for these two, it is allowable for the others to use it. Even if a share is obtained from that by another, it is not allowable for them.

390.

390.

Rukkhacchāyāpyantamaso, tannibbattā na kappati;

Nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭiladdhampi, ādito santhatattayaṃ.

Even so much as the shade of a tree produced from that is not allowable. The three kinds of felt cloths, from the beginning, are not allowable even if relinquished and received back.

391.

391.

No ce labhetha evaṃ so, imaṃ chaḍḍehi saṃsiyo;

Evampi bhikkhu chaḍḍeyya, no ce labhetha sammato.

If he does not obtain an agent in this way, he should abandon that forfeited item, being in suspense. Even so, a bhikkhu should abandon it if he does not find an authorized person.

392.

392.

Etāni dutiyo patto, saṅghe sesāni labbhare;

Saṅghekasmiṃ gaṇe vattuṃ, labbhaṃ bhāsantarenapi.

These offenses concerning the bowl, and the second one, and the remaining ones are to be dealt with in the Sangha. It is allowable to state them before the Sangha, a group, or a single bhikkhu, even in another language.

393. (Ka) ahaṃ, bhante, nānappakārakaṃ kayavikkayaṃ samāpajjiṃ, idaṃ me, bhante, nissaggiyaṃ.

393. Venerable sir, I engaged in various kinds of buying and selling. This, venerable sir, is to be forfeited.

(Kha) ayaṃ [M 0.0045] me, bhante, patto dasāhātikkanto nissaggiyo.

Venerable sir, this bowl of mine, having been kept beyond ten days, is to be forfeited.

(Ga) ayaṃ me, bhante, patto ūnapañcabandhanena pattena cetāpito nissaggiyo, imāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmīti.

Venerable sir, this bowl of mine, which I had exchanged for a bowl with fewer than five mends, is to be forfeited. I relinquish it to the Sangha.

394.

394.

Nissajjitvāna [V 0.0055] deseyya, āpattiṃ pattagāhakaṃ;

Sammannitvāna saṅghassa, pattantaṃ tassa dāpaye.

Having relinquished it, one should confess the offense to the bhikkhu who receives the bowl. Having been authorized by the Sangha, one should have the last bowl in the storeroom given to him.

395. (Ka) idaṃ me, bhante, bhesajjaṃ sattāhātikkantaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

395. Venerable sir, this medicine of mine, having been kept beyond seven days, is to be forfeited.

(Kha) idaṃ me, bhante, vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ atirekamāse sese gimhāne pariyiṭṭhaṃ, atirekaḍḍhamāse sese gimhāne katvā paridahitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this rains-bathing cloth of mine was sought when more than a month of the hot season remained, and having had it made and worn when more than half a month remained, it is to be forfeited.

(Ga) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ bhikkhussa sāmaṃ datvā acchinnaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this robe, which I took back after having given it to a bhikkhu myself, is to be forfeited.

(Gha) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ sāmaṃ suttaṃ viññāpetvā tantavāyehi vāyāpitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this robe, which was woven by weavers after I myself requested the thread, is to be forfeited.

(Ṅa) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ pubbe appavārito aññātakassa gahapatikassa tantavāye upasaṅkamitvā vikappaṃ āpannaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this robe of mine is to be forfeited, as, not having been invited beforehand, I approached the weavers of an unrelated householder and made a specification for it.

(Ca) idaṃ me, bhante, accekacīvaraṃ cīvarakālasamayaṃ atikkāmitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this urgent robe of mine, kept beyond the robe-season, is to be forfeited.

(Cha) idaṃ me, bhante, cīvaraṃ atirekachārattaṃ vippavutthaṃ aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā nissaggiyaṃ.

Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been kept apart from me for more than six nights without a bhikkhu's authorization, is to be forfeited.

(Ja) idaṃ me, bhante, jānaṃ saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ pariṇataṃ attano pariṇāmitaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ āyasmato nissajjāmīti.

Venerable sir, knowing that this gain was designated for the Sangha, I diverted it to myself. It is to be forfeited. I relinquish it to the venerable one.

396. Sesaṃ [M 0.0046] sabbaṃ yathāyogaṃ, ādimhi viya yojaye.

396. All the rest should be applied as is suitable, as at the beginning.

397. (Ka) ahaṃ[V 0.0056], bhante, ekaṃ pācittiyāpattiṃ āpajjiṃ. Dve sambahulā pācittiyāpattiyo āpajjiṃ.

397. Venerable sir, I have committed one pācittiya offense. I have committed two... many pācittiya offenses.

(Kha) gārayhaṃ, bhante, dhammaṃ āpajjiṃ asappāyaṃ pāṭidesanīyaṃ, taṃ paṭidesemīti. Tena “passasi, āvuso, taṃ dhamma”nti vattabbaṃ.

Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable act that should be acknowledged. I acknowledge it." He should be told: "Friend, do you see that act?"

(Ga) ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ dukkaṭāpattiṃ āpajjiṃ. Dve sambahulā dukkaṭāpattiyo āpajjiṃ.

Venerable sir, I have committed one dukkaṭa offense. I have committed two... many dukkaṭa offenses.

(Gha) ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ dubbhāsitāpattiṃ āpajjiṃ. Dve sambahulā dubbhāsitāpattiyo āpajjiṃ. Tā tumhamūle paṭidesemīti.

Venerable sir, I have committed one dubbhāsita offense. I have committed two... many dubbhāsita offenses. I confess them in your presence.

(Ṅa) “ahaṃ, bhante, dve nānāvatthukā thullaccayāpattiyo āpajjiṃ. Sambahulā nānāvatthukā thullaccayāpattiyo āpajjiṃ, tā tumhamūle paṭidesemī”ti vatvā tena “passasi, āvuso, tā āpattiyo”ti vutte “āma, bhante, passāmī”ti vatvā puna tena “āyatiṃ, āvuso, saṃvareyyāsī”ti vutte “sādhu suṭṭhu, bhante, saṃvarissāmī”ti vattabbaṃ.

“Venerable sir, I have committed two grave offenses on different grounds. I have committed a number of grave offenses on different grounds. I confess them in your presence.” When he is told, “Friend, do you see those offenses?” one should reply, “Yes, venerable sir, I see them.” Then, when he is told, “Friend, you should restrain yourself in the future,” one should reply, “Very well, venerable sir, I will restrain myself.”

398.

398.

Adesanāgāminiyaṃ, anāpattiñca desitaṃ;

Nānā saṃvāsanissīmaṭṭhitānaṃ catupañcahi;

Manasā pakatattānaṃ, nānekāti na desayeti.

One does not confess an offense that does not require it, nor what has been declared a non-offense. One does not confess to four or five bhikkhus of different communions or standing outside the boundary. One does not confess to a normal bhikkhu by mind alone, nor to more than one at a time.

43. Chandadānaniddeso

43. The Exposition on the Giving of Consent

Chandadānādīti –

Regarding the giving of consent and so forth—

399.

399.

Bheriṃ ghaṇṭiṃ patāḷetvā, kammappatte samāgate;

Saṅghe hareyya chandaṃ vā, pārisuddhiṃ pavāraṇaṃ.

Having sounded the drum or the bell, when the time for the formal act has arrived, one should convey to the Sangha one’s consent, purity, or invitation.

400.

400.

Ekaṃ [V 0.0057][M 0.0047] bhikkhuṃ upaggamma, nisīditvā ukkuṭikaṃ;

Añjaliṃ paggaṇhitvāna, dade chandaṃ vicakkhaṇo.

Having approached a single bhikkhu and sat down in the squatting position, having raised his hands in reverential salutation, the discerning one should give his consent.

401. (Ka) “chandaṃ dammi, chandaṃ me hara, chandaṃ me ārocehī”ti vattabbaṃ.

401. One should say: “I give my consent, convey my consent, announce my consent.”

(Kha) pārisuddhiṃ dentena “pārisuddhiṃ dammi, pārisuddhiṃ me hara, pārisuddhiṃ me ārocehī”ti vattabbaṃ.

When giving one's purity, one should say: “I give my purity, convey my purity, announce my purity.”

402.

402.

Pārisuddhippadānena, sampādeti uposathaṃ;

Saṅghassa attano cāpi, sesakammaṃ vibādhati.

By giving one’s purity, one accomplishes the Uposatha; but for the Sangha and for oneself, it obstructs other formal acts.

403.

403.

Chandadānena saṅghassa, dvayaṃ sādheti nattano;

Tasmā chandaṃ dadantena, dātabbā pārisuddhipi.

By giving consent, one accomplishes a twofold matter for the Sangha, but not for oneself. Therefore, when giving consent, one’s purity should also be given.

404.

404.

Hareyyeko bahūnampi, paramparā na hāraye;

Paramparāhaṭā chanda-pārisuddhi na gacchati.

One bhikkhu may convey the consent of many, but he should not have it conveyed in succession. Consent and purity conveyed in succession are not valid.

405. Sabbūpacāraṃ katvāna, evaṃ deyyā pavāraṇā. “Pavāraṇaṃ dammi, pavāraṇaṃ me hara, pavāraṇaṃ me ārocehi, mamatthāya pavārehī”ti.

405. Having performed all the preliminary procedures, the invitation should be given thus: “I give the invitation, convey my invitation, announce my invitation, invite on my behalf.”

406. Ārocetvātha so saṅghaṃ, pavāreyyevamāgato. “Itthannāmo, bhante, saṅghaṃ pavāreti diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu taṃ saṅgho anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissatī”ti.

406. Then the one who has come, having informed the Sangha, should invite thus: “Venerable sirs, the bhikkhu so-and-so invites the Sangha on the grounds of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. Let the Sangha speak to him out of compassion. If he sees a fault, he will make amends.”

407.

407.

Gahetvā pārisuddhiṃ vā, chandaṃ vāpi pavāraṇaṃ;

Hārako saṅghamappatvā, vibbhameyya mareyya vā.

Having taken the purity, or the consent, or the invitation, the carrier, without reaching the Sangha, might disrobe or die.

408.

408.

Sāmaṇerādibhāvaṃ [V 0.0058] vā,

Paṭijāneyya nāhaṭā;

Patvā saṅghaṃ tathā heyya,

Āhaṭā hoti hārako.

Or he might acknowledge being a novice or the like; or declare it has not been conveyed; or having reached the Sangha, he might abandon it. The carrier is one who has successfully conveyed it.

409.

409.

Saṅghappatto [M 0.0048] pamatto vā, sutto nārocayeyya vā;

Anāpattiva sañcicca, nārocentassa dukkaṭanti.

Having reached the Sangha, if he does not announce it because he is heedless or asleep, there is no offense. But for one who intentionally does not announce it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

44. Uposathaniddeso

44. The Exposition on the Uposatha

Uposathoti –

Regarding the Uposatha—

410.

410.

Duve uposathā cātu-ddaso pannaraso iti;

Suttuddesamadhiṭṭhāna-pārisuddhivasā tayo.

There are two Uposatha days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth. There are three kinds by way of recitation of the Pātimokkha, determination, and purity.

411.

411.

Suttuddesova saṅghassa, adhiṭṭhānauposatho;

Puggalasseva sesānaṃ, pārisuddhiuposatho.

The recitation of the Pātimokkha is for the Sangha. The Uposatha of determination is for an individual alone. For the remaining ones, there is the Uposatha of purity.

412.

412.

Pubbakicce ca karaṇe, pattakalle samānite;

Suttaṃ uddisati saṅgho, pañcadhā so vibhāvito.

When the preliminary duties and proceedings are done, and the time is deemed fit, the Sangha recites the Pātimokkha. This is explained in five ways.

413.

413.

Vināntarāyaṃ saṅkhepe-nuddeso vinivārito;

“Therova issaro dvīsu, uddesesvettha tīsu vā;

Visadesū”ti vuttattā, avattantepi vaṭṭati.

Recitation in brief when there is no obstacle is forbidden. Because it is said, “The senior bhikkhu is the authority in this matter concerning two or three recitations, or the detailed ones,” it is allowable even when not explicitly stated.

414.

414.

Āgaccheyyuṃ yadi samā, uddisante va thokikā;

Uddiṭṭhaṃ yaṃ suuddiṭṭhaṃ, sotabbamavasesakaṃ.

If, while the recitation is in progress, an equal or smaller number of bhikkhus arrive, what has been recited is well-recited. They should listen to the remainder.

415.

415.

Uddiṭṭhamatte [V 0.0059] sakalā-yekaccāyuṭṭhitāya vā;

Pārisuddhiṃ kareyyesaṃ, santike bahukātha ce;

Katvā sabbavikappesu, pubbakiccaṃ punuddise.

If, just as the whole Pātimokkha or a part of it has been recited, a larger group of bhikkhus arrives nearby, one should take their declaration of purity. In all such cases, one should perform the preliminary duties again and recite from the beginning.

416.

416.

Pannarasovāsikānaṃ, itarānaṃ sacetaro;

Samānetarenuvattantu, purimānaṃ sacedhikā;

Purimā anuvattantu, tesaṃ sesepyayaṃ nayo.

Regarding those observing the fifteenth-day Uposatha and those observing another day: if the latter group is smaller or equal in number, they should conform to the former. If the former group is smaller, they should conform to the latter. This is the principle in all such cases.

417.

417.

Pāṭipadovāsikānaṃ, itarānaṃ uposatho;

Samathokānaṃ sāmaggiṃ, mūlaṭṭhā dentu kāmato.

Regarding those observing the Uposatha on the first day of the fortnight and others: if the groups are equal or small, let the resident bhikkhus willingly establish unity.

418.

418.

Bahi gantvāna kātabbo, no ce denti uposatho;

Deyyānicchāya sāmaggī, bahūsu bahi vā vaje.

If they do not grant unity, the Uposatha should be done after going outside the boundary. Unity should not be given unwillingly. If there are many, one should go outside.

419.

419.

Pāṭipadegantukānaṃ[M 0.0049], evameva ayaṃ nayo;

Sāveyya suttaṃ sañcicca, assāventassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For visiting bhikkhus on the first day of the fortnight, this is the very same principle. One should have the Pātimokkha recited; for one who intentionally does not have it recited, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

420.

420.

Sammajjituṃ padīpetuṃ, paññāpetuṃ dakāsanaṃ;

Na kareyya tathā kallo, mahātherena pesito.

To sweep, to light a lamp, to set out water and seats: a competent bhikkhu sent by a senior bhikkhu should not do this.

421. Sammajjitvā padīpetvā, paṭṭhapetvā dakāsanaṃ. Gaṇañattiṃ ṭhapetvevaṃ, kattabbo tīhuposatho. “Suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajjuposatho pannaraso, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kareyyāmā”ti.

421. Having swept, lit the lamp, and set out water and seats, the Uposatha for three persons should be performed thus. One should state the motion: “Let the venerable sirs listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If it is the proper time for the venerable sirs, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purity.”

422. Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, nisīditvā ukkuṭikaṃ,. Therena añjaliṃ tevaṃ, paggayha samudīriyā. “Parisuddho [V 0.0060] ahaṃ āvuso, parisuddhoti maṃ dhārethā”ti, vade yāvatatīyakaṃ.

422. Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and sat down in the squatting position, a senior bhikkhu should raise his hands in reverential salutation to a junior bhikkhu and declare up to three times: “I am pure, friend; remember me as pure.”

423. Samattapubbārambhena, te navenevamīriyā. “Parisuddho ahaṃ bhante, parisuddhoti maṃ dhārethā”ti, vade yāvatatīyakaṃ.

423. Then the junior bhikkhu should declare thus up to three times: “I am pure, venerable sir; remember me as pure.”

424. Dvīsu therena kattabbaṃ, katvevamīriyo navo. “Parisuddho ahaṃ āvuso, parisuddhoti maṃ dhārehī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbo.

424. In a group of two, the senior bhikkhu should speak first, and then the junior. The senior says three times: “I am pure, friend; remember me as pure.”

425.

425.

Navena thero tikkhattuṃ, evamassa udīriyo;

“Parisuddho ahaṃ bhante, parisuddhoti maṃ dhārethā”ti.

The senior bhikkhu should be addressed thus three times by the junior bhikkhu: ‘I am pure, venerable sir; may you remember me as pure.’”

426. Pubbakiccaṃ [M 0.0050] samāpetvā, adhiṭṭheyyevamekako. “Ajja me uposatho pannarasoti vā cātuddasoti vā adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vattabbaṃ, no cedhiṭṭheyya dukkaṭaṃ.

426. Having completed the preliminary duties, one who is alone should make a determination thus: “I determine that today is my Uposatha, the fifteenth,” or “...the fourteenth.” If he does not make this determination, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.

427.

427.

Yattha vasanti cattāro, tayo vā yadi vā duve;

Pārisuddhiṃ haritvāna, ekekassitarītare;

Taṃ taṃ uposathaṃ kayiruṃ, siyā āpatti dukkaṭaṃ.

Where four bhikkhus reside, or three, or two, should they perform that Uposatha by conveying their purity to one another, there would be an offense of wrong-doing.

428.

428.

Vagge samagge vaggoti, saññino vimatissa vā;

Dukkaṭaṃ karoto bhedā-dhippāyena thullaccayaṃ;

Vagge samaggenāpatti, samaggo iti saññino.

If one performs the Uposatha in a united group while perceiving it as divided, or being in doubt, one commits an offense of wrong-doing. If one does so with the intention to cause a schism, one commits a grave offense. If one performs it in a united group while perceiving it as united, there is no offense.

429.

429.

Ukkhittassa [V 0.0061] gahaṭṭhassa, sesānaṃ sahadhamminaṃ;

Pārājikassābhabbassa, sikkhānikkhittakassa ca.

With one who is suspended, a householder, the remaining co-religionists of other sects, one who has committed a pārājika offense, one who is incapable, and one who has given up the training;

430.

430.

Nisinnaparisāyañca, sabhāgāpattiko tathā;

Chandena parivutthena, pātimokkhaṃ na uddise.

And in a seated assembly where there is one with a similar unconfessed offense, or with one who is living apart due to favoritism—one should not recite the Pātimokkha.

431.

431.

Adesayitvānāpannaṃ, nāvikatvāna vematiṃ;

Nuposathepi vā kātuṃ, posatho na ca kappati.

Without having confessed an offense, and without having dispelled one's doubt, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha.

432.

432.

Aṭṭhitoposathāvāsā, na vaje tadahū vinā;

Antarāyaṃ va saṅghaṃ vā-dhiṭṭhātuṃ sīmameva vāti.

One not dwelling in the residence where the Uposatha is held should not go away on that day without determining an obstacle, or the Sangha, or the boundary.

45. Pavāraṇāniddeso

45. Exposition on the Pavāraṇā

Pavāraṇāti –

Pavāraṇā is:

433.

433.

Dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ catunnañca, aññamaññappavāraṇā;

Ekassa ca adhiṭṭhānaṃ, sesā saṅghappavāraṇā.

For two, three, or four, there is mutual invitation; for one, there is a determination; for the rest, there is the Sangha's invitation.

434.

434.

Pubbakicce ca karaṇe, pattakalle samānite;

Ṭhapetvā ñattiṃ saṅghena, kattabbevaṃ pavāraṇā.

When the preliminary duties have been done and the proper time has arrived, the Pavāraṇā should be performed thus by the Sangha, having presented the motion.

“Suṇātu [M 0.0051] me bhante saṅgho, ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho pavāreyyā”ti.

“Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. Today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth. If the time is right for the Sangha, let the Sangha perform the Pavāraṇā.”

435.

435.

Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, nisīditvā ukkuṭikaṃ;

Therena añjaliṃ saṅgho, paggayha samudīriyo.

Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and sat squatting, the most senior bhikkhu, raising his joined hands, should address the Sangha.

436. “Saṅghaṃ, āvuso, pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto [V 0.0062] anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi, āvuso, saṅghaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

436. “Friends, I invite the Sangha by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, friends, I invite the Sangha by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

437.

437.

Pavārentesu theresu, nisajjukkuṭikaṃ navo;

Pavāreti sayaṃ yāva, ukkuṭikova acchatu.

While the senior bhikkhus are performing the invitation, the junior bhikkhu, seated in the squatting posture, should remain so until he himself performs the invitation.

438. Pubbārambhaṃ samāpetvā, navo saṅghamudīraye.

438. When the senior bhikkhus have finished, the junior bhikkhu should address the Sangha.

439. “Saṅghaṃ, bhante, pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi, bhante, saṅghaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

439. “Venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

440.

440.

Dānena dhammasākacchā, kalahehi ca rattiyā;

Tevācikāya okāse-sati khepitabhāvato;

Antarāye dasavidhe, ñattiṃ vatvānurūpato.

When, due to giving, Dhamma discussion, or quarrels, the night has been spent, and thus the opportunity for the three-fold invitation is lost; or in the case of the ten kinds of obstacles, one should state the motion appropriately.

441. “Suṇātu me bhante saṅgho, manussehi dānaṃ dentehi, dvīhi bhikkhūhi dhammaṃ sākacchantehi, kalahaṃ karontehi yebhuyyena ratti khepitā. Sace saṅgho [M 0.0052] tevācikaṃ pavāressati, appavāritova saṅgho bhavissati, athāyaṃ ratti vibhāyissati. Ayaṃ rājantarāyo, ayaṃ corantarāyo, ayaṃ agyantarāyo, ayaṃ udakantarāyo, ayaṃ manussantarāyo, ayaṃ amanussantarāyo, ayaṃ vāḷantarāyo, ayaṃ sarīsapantarāyo, ayaṃ jīvitantarāyo, ayaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo. Sace saṅgho tevācikaṃ pavāressati, appavāritova saṅgho bhavissati, athāyaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo bhavissati. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho dvevācikaṃ, ekavācikaṃ, samānavassikaṃ pavāreyyā”ti.

441. “Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. The night has been mostly spent while people were giving gifts, while bhikkhus were discussing the Dhamma, or while they were quarreling. If the Sangha performs the invitation with three statements, the Sangha will remain without having performed the invitation as this night comes to an end. There is danger from kings, danger from thieves, danger from fire, danger from water, danger from human beings, danger from non-human beings, danger from beasts of prey, danger from creeping things, danger to life, danger to the holy life. If the Sangha performs the invitation with three statements, the Sangha will remain without having performed the invitation, and this will become a danger to the holy life. If the time is right for the Sangha, let the Sangha perform the invitation with two statements, with one statement, or by common seniority.”

442.

442.

Pavāreyyānurūpena[V 0.0063], yathāṭhapitañattiyā;

Āgaccheyyuṃ yadi samā, ādikā cettha āhare.

They should perform the invitation in the appropriate way, according to the motion that was established. If others of equal seniority should arrive, the original ones should include them.

443. Evaṃ ticatuvaggo ca, ñattiṃ vatvā pavāraye. “Suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pavāreyyāmā”ti.

443. Thus a group of three or four, having stated the motion, should perform the invitation. “Let the venerable ones hear me. Today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth. If the time is right for the venerable ones, let us perform the mutual invitation.”

444.

444.

Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, nisīditvā ukkuṭikaṃ;

Therena añjaliṃ tevaṃ, paggayha samudīriyā.

Having arranged their robes over one shoulder and sat squatting, they should be addressed thus by the most senior among them, who has raised his joined hands in reverence.

445. “Ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmante pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmantā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmante pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmantā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

445. “Friends, I invite the venerable ones by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, friends, I invite the venerable ones by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

Navenāpi [M 0.0053] “ahaṃ, bhante, āyasmante pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmantā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi ahaṃ, bhante, āyasmante pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmantā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

And the junior bhikkhu says: “Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

446. Dvīsu therena kattabbaṃ, navo katvevamīriyo.

446. In a group of two, the senior bhikkhu should act first; then the junior bhikkhu should speak thus.

447. “Ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmantaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu maṃ āyasmā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmantaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu maṃ āyasmā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

447. “Friend, I invite the venerable one by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable one speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, friend, I invite the venerable one by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable one speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

Navenāpi [V 0.0064] “ahaṃ, bhante, āyasmantaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu maṃ āyasmā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmi. Dutiyampi…pe… tatiyampi ahaṃ, bhante, āyasmantaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu maṃ āyasmā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti.

And the junior bhikkhu says: “Venerable sir, I invite the venerable one by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable one speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends. For a second time… For a third time, venerable sir, I invite the venerable one by what has been seen, by what has been heard, or by what is suspected. Let the venerable one speak to me out of compassion. Seeing it, I will make amends.”

448. Pubbakiccaṃ samāpetvā, adhiṭṭheyyevamekako. “Ajja me pavāraṇā cātuddasīti vā pannarasīti vā adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vattabbaṃ.

448. Having completed the preliminary duties, one who is alone should make a determination thus: “I determine that today, the fourteenth (or: the fifteenth), is my Pavāraṇā.”

449.

449.

Yasmiṃ vasanti vā pañca, cattāro vā tayo duve;

Pavāraṇaṃ haritvāna, ekekassitarītare.

Where five, or four, or three, or two reside, they should perform the Pavāraṇā by offering the invitation to one another.

450.

450.

Taṃ [M 0.0054] taṃ pavāraṇaṃ kayiruṃ,

Siyā āpatti dukkaṭaṃ;

Sesā uposathe vuttā,

Gāthāyo cettha āhare.

They should perform their respective Pavāraṇā; not to do so would be an offense of wrong-doing. The remaining verses that are stated for the Uposatha should be recited here as well.

451.

451.

Pavāriteva saṅghamhi, pārisuddhiuposathaṃ;

Kareyya chinnavasso vā, avuttho vānupagato.

When the Sangha has performed the Pavāraṇā, a bhikkhu who has broken the rains-residence, or has not completed it, or is absent, should perform the Uposatha of purity.

452.

452.

Cātumāsiniyā cāpi, kate saṅghenuposathe;

Vutthavassā pavāreyyuṃ, sace appatarā siyunti.

And also on the four-monthly day, after the Sangha has performed the Uposatha, those who have completed the rains-residence should perform the Pavāraṇā, if they are fewer in number.

46. Saṃvaraniddeso

46. The Exposition of Restraint

Saṃvaroti –

Restraint is:

453.

453.

Cakkhusotādibhedehi, rūpasaddādigocare;

Abhijjhādomanassādi-ppavattiṃ vinivāraye.

Through the divisions of the eye, ear, and so forth, in the sphere of forms, sounds, and so forth, one should prevent the arising of covetousness, displeasure, and the like.

454.

454.

Niggaṇheyya [V 0.0065] sakaṃ cittaṃ, kiṭṭhādiṃ viya duppasuṃ;

Satimā sampajāno ca, care sabbiriyāpatheti.

One should restrain one's own mind, like a difficult beast from a cornfield; mindful and clearly comprehending, one should fare in every posture.

47. Suddhiniddeso

47. The Exposition of Purity

Suddhīti –

Purity is:

455.

455.

Desanā saṃvaro eṭṭhipaccavekkhaṇa bhedato;

Suddhī catubbidhā pātimokkhasaṃvarasammataṃ;

Desanāya visuddhattā, desanāsuddhi vuccati.

Purity is fourfold by way of confession, restraint, seeking, and reflection; it is acknowledged as the restraint of the Pātimokkha. Because of purity through confession, it is called the purity of confession.

456.

456.

“Na punevaṃ karissa”nti, cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvarā;

Vutto saṃvarasuddhīti, sujjhatindriyasaṃvaro.

Through restraint by mental determination, 'I will not do so again,' is called the purity of restraint; the restraint of the senses is purified.

457.

457.

Pahāyānesanaṃ dhammenuppādentassa eṭṭhiyā;

Suddhattā eṭṭhisuddhīti, vuttamājīvanissitaṃ.

For one who, having abandoned improper seeking, generates requisites righteously, because of purity in seeking, it is called the purity of seeking, which is based on livelihood.

458.

458.

Yoniso [M 0.0055] paṭisaṅkhāya, cīvaraṃ paṭisevati;

Evamādiyathāvutta-paccavekkhaṇasujjhanā;

Paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti, vuttaṃ paccayanissitanti.

‘Wisely reflecting, one uses the robe’; through purification by reflection on this and so forth as stated, it is called the purity of reflection, which is based on the requisites.

48. Santosaniddeso

48. The Exposition of Contentment

Santosoti –

Contentment is:

459.

459.

Appena anavajjena, santuṭṭho sulabhena ca;

Mattaññū subharo hutvā, care saddhammagāravo.

Content with little that is blameless and easily obtained, knowing moderation, being easy to support, one should fare with reverence for the true Dhamma.

460.

460.

Atītaṃ [V 0.0066] nānusocanto, nappajappamanāgataṃ;

Paccuppannena yāpento, santuṭṭhoti pavuccatīti.

Not lamenting the past, not yearning for the future, sustaining oneself with the present, one is said to be content.

49. Caturārakkhaniddeso

49. The Exposition of the Four Protections

Caturakkhāti –

The four protections are:

461.

461.

Buddhānussati mettā ca, asubhaṃ maraṇassati;

Ārakattādinārahaṃ, sammā sāmañca buddhato.

Recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, the foul, and mindfulness of death; on account of being a protection and so forth, it is worthy, and rightly the recluseship from the Buddha.

462.

462.

Sammāsambuddhaiti vānussati yā punappunaṃ;

Navabhede bhagavato, buddhānussati sā guṇe.

That recollection, 'He is a Perfectly Enlightened One,' which is practiced again and again regarding the ninefold virtues of the Blessed One, is the recollection of the Buddha.

463.

463.

Sīmaṭṭhasaṅghe sīmaṭṭhadevatāsu ca issare;

Jane gocaragāmamhi, tatthupādāya mānuse.

Towards the Sangha within the boundary, the deities within the boundary, and rulers; towards the people in the alms-resort village, including the humans there—

464.

464.

Sabbasattesu sukhitā, hontāverātiādinā;

Paricchijja paricchijja, bhāvanā mettabhāvanā.

By means of 'May all beings be happy, free from animosity,' and so forth, delimiting again and again, this cultivation is the cultivation of loving-kindness.

465.

465.

Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānaokāsa-disato paricchedato;

Vavatthapetvā kesādi-koṭṭhāse anupubbato.

Having determined the parts such as hair of the head in due order, by way of color, shape, location, direction, and delimitation.

466.

466.

Nātisīghañca saṇikaṃ, vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhayaṃ;

Paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamma, muñcantassānupubbato.

Neither too fast nor too slow, warding off distraction; having gone beyond the concept, for one who is gradually releasing.

467.

467.

Vaṇṇaāsayasaṇṭhāna-gandhokāsehi [M 0.0056] bhāvanā;

Paṭikkūlāti koṭṭhāse, uddhumātādivatthusu;

Gahetvā asubhākāraṃ, pavattā bhāvanāsubhaṃ.

The cultivation regarding the parts of the body as repulsive, and regarding objects such as the bloated, is by means of color, basis, shape, smell, and location. Having grasped the aspect of foulness, the cultivation of the foul proceeds.

468.

468.

“Maraṇaṃ [V 0.0067] me bhavissati, jīvitaṃ ucchijjissati;

Maraṇaṃ maraṇaṃ vā”ti, bhāvayitvāna yoniso.

“Death will befall me, my life will be cut off; death, death”—having cultivated thus wisely,

469.

469.

Vadhakassevupaṭṭhānā, sampattīnaṃ vipattito;

Upasaṃharato kāyabahusādhāraṇā tathā.

By its appearance as an executioner, by the perishing of success, by comparison, and likewise by the body being common to many.

470.

470.

Āyudubbalato kālavavatthānassabhāvato;

Addhānassa paricchedā, bhāvanā maraṇassatīti.

From the frailty of the life-force, from the uncertainty of the time, and from the limitation of the life-span, is the cultivation of mindfulness of death.

50. Vipassanāniddeso

50. The Exposition of Insight

Vipassanāti –

Insight is:

471.

471.

Nāmarūpaṃ pariggayha, tato tassa ca paccayaṃ;

Hutvā abhāvatoniccā, udayabbayapīḷanā.

Having comprehended name-and-form, and then its conditions, one sees impermanence in their passing into non-existence after having been, and the oppression of rise and fall.

472.

472.

Dukkhā avasavattittā, anattāti tilakkhaṇaṃ;

Āropetvāna saṅkhāre, sammasanto punappunaṃ;

Pāpuṇeyyānupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayanti.

As suffering, as not subject to control, as not-self—these three characteristics are applied to formations. Reflecting again and again, one gradually reaches the destruction of all fetters.

Nigamanakathā

Conclusion

473.

473.

Adhisīlādhicittānaṃ, adhipaññāya sikkhanā;

Bhikkhukiccamato khuddasikkhāyaṃ samudāhaṭā.

The training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom—therefore, the duties of a monk are fully declared in the Minor Training.

474.

474.

Mahato kittisaddassa, yassa lokavicārino;

Parissamo na sambhoti, mālutasseva niccaso.

Great is the fame of him, the investigator of the world; for him, weariness does not arise, just like for the ceaseless wind.

475.

475.

Tena [M 0.0057][V 0.0068] dhammasirīkena, tambapaṇṇiyaketunā;

Therena racitā dhammavinayaññupasaṃsitā.

By that Elder Dhammasiri, the banner of Tambapaṇṇi, was this composed, praised by those who know the Dhamma and Vinaya.

476.

476.

Ettāvatāyaṃ niṭṭhānaṃ, khuddasikkhā upāgatā;

Pañcamattehi gāthānaṃ, satehi parimāṇatoti.

Thus far the Minor Training has come to its conclusion, with a measure of about five hundred verses.

Khuddasikkhā niṭṭhitā.

The Minor Training is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddasikkhā-purāṇaṭīkā

The Minor Training—Ancient Commentary

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Yo [V 0.0069][M 0.0059] ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, viditvā dukkhitaṃ janaṃ;

Tathāpi nāvabujjhantamanukampāya codito.

He who, having known for a long, long time the suffering people who were not awakening, was yet impelled by compassion,

Bodhāya paṇidhiṃ katvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ;

Tassa pāde namassitvā, dhammaṃ saṅghañca sādhukaṃ.

Having made a resolution for enlightenment, he attained the supreme enlightenment; having paid homage at his feet, and well to the Dhamma and the Sangha,

Pubbācariyapādesu, ṭhapetvā sīsamattano;

Therena dhammasirinā, thirasīlena yā katā.

Having placed my own head at the feet of the ancient teachers; [concerning that which] was composed by the Elder Dhammasiri, firm in virtue,

“Ādito [V 0.0070] upasampannasikkhitabba”ntiādinā;

Khuddasikkhā samāsena, tassā atthavinicchayaṃ.

[I will write] a determination of the meaning of the concise Minor Training, which begins with, “From the beginning, the training for the ordained should be undertaken,” and so on.

Likhissāmi hitatthāya, ādikammikabhikkhunaṃ;

Tattha yuttaṃ gahetabbamayuttaṃ tujjhitabbakanti;

I will write for the benefit of the newly-ordained monks. Therein, what is fitting should be adopted, and what is unfitting should be discarded.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

(Ka) etthāha – katamā khuddasikkhā, kathaṃ sikkhitabbā, kasmā sikkhitabbā, ke sikkhanti, ke sikkhitasikkhāti? Vuccate – adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāvasena tisso sikkhā, ganthavasenettha saṅkhipitvā vuttattā taddīpano gantho “khuddasikkhā”ti [M 0.0060] vuccati, atha vā “khuddaṃ anelakaṃ madhupaṭala”ntiādīni viya sikkhākāmānaṃ madhuratāya khuddā ca tā sikkhā cāti khuddasikkhā, atha vā “khuddaputtamhi samaṇa posa ma”ntiādīsu viya bahuvidhattāpi khuddā ca tā sikkhitabbato sikkhā cāti khuddasikkhā. Adhisīlasikkhā panettha cārittavārittavasena duvidhampi sīlaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamānena tappaṭipakkhe kilese tadaṅgappahānavasena pajahantena sikkhitabbā, adhicittasikkhā pana yathāvuttesu ārammaṇesu abhiyogakaraṇavasena jhānappaṭipakkhānaṃ nīvaraṇagaṇānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kurumānena sikkhitabbā, adhipaññāsikkhā pana yathānurūpaṃ samucchedavasena sānusaye kilese samucchindantena sikkhitabbā.

Here it is said: What is the Minor Training? How should it be trained? Why should it be trained? Who trains? Who are those whose training is completed? It is said: There are three trainings—higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Because it is stated concisely in this book, the book which illuminates it is called the “Minor Training.” Alternatively, just as in “minor, pure, like a honeycomb,” and so on, due to its sweetness for those desiring the training, it is both minor and a training—thus it is the Minor Training. Or, as in “monk, support me, a minor son,” and so on, though of many varieties, it is minor, and because it is to be trained in, it is a training—thus it is the Minor Training. Herein, the training in higher virtue should be undertaken by one who practices both kinds of virtue—that of conduct and that of restraint—as instructed, abandoning the opposing defilements by way of temporary suppression. The training in higher mind, however, should be undertaken by one who, by applying effort to the aforesaid objects, accomplishes the abandonment by suppression of the group of hindrances which are the opponents of jhāna. The training in higher wisdom, however, should be undertaken by one who, as is suitable, eradicates the defilements together with their underlying tendencies by way of cutting them off.

Kasmā sikkhitabbāti ettha –

Why should one train? In this connection:

Jātiādīhi dukkhehi, anekehi upaddutaṃ;

Khandhalokaṃ jahitvāna, pattuṃ khemaṃ puraṃ sivaṃ.

To abandon the world of aggregates, harassed by many sufferings such as birth and so on, in order to attain the safe, auspicious city.

Kalyāṇaputhujjanena saha satta sekkhā sikkhanti. Arahanto sikkhitasikkhā.

The virtuous worldling trains along with the seven trainees. The Arahants are those whose training is completed.

Ye [V 0.0071] vītamohā munipuṅgavassa;

Sissesu aggā muninā pasatthā;

Te tīsu sikkhāsu samattasikkhā;

Tato pare kena samattasikkhāti.

Those who are rid of delusion, chief among the disciples of the foremost Sage, praised by the Sage—they are completely trained in the three trainings. Who beyond them is completely trained?

Āditoti ettha ādimhiyevāti attho, ādito paṭṭhāyāti vā. Upasampannena ca upasampannāya ca sikkhitabbaṃ upasampannasikkhitabbaṃ. Saha mātikāya samātikaṃ. Pubbe vuttappakāraṃ khuddasikkhaṃ pavakkhāmi ādarena, pakārena vā vakkhāmi ratanattayaṃ vanditvāti attho. Apica thero āditoti vacanena saddhāpabbajitānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ ālasiyadosena appaṭipajjantānaṃ aññāṇadosena aññathā paṭipajjantānaṃ [M 0.0061] saṃvegaṃ janeti. Kathaṃ? Atidullabhaṃ khaṇasamavāyaṃ paṭilabhitvā taṅkhaṇaṃ na kusītena vā niratthakakathāpasutena vā vītināmetabbaṃ, kiṃ kātabbaṃ? Ādito paṭṭhāya nirantarameva tīsu sikkhāsu ādaro janetabboti. Etthāha – kiṃ taṃ ratanattayaṃ nāma, yaṃ vanditvā thero khuddasikkhaṃ pavakkhatīti? Vuccate – buddharatanaṃ dhammaratanaṃ saṅgharatananti imāni tīṇi ratanāni. Tāni hi ratijananaṭṭhena “ratanānī”ti vuccanti. Apica –
