Herein, 'Ādito' ('From the beginning') means 'in the very beginning,' or 'starting from the beginning.' That which should be trained in by an ordained man and by an ordained woman is 'the training for the ordained.' That which is together with the matrix is 'samātikaṃ.' The meaning is: 'Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I will explain with reverence, or I will explain in detail, the Minor Training of the aforesaid type.' Furthermore, the Elder, with the word 'from the beginning,' generates a sense of urgency in the sons of good family who have gone forth in faith but who, due to the fault of laziness, do not practice, or who, due to the fault of ignorance, practice otherwise. How? Having obtained the extremely rare conjunction of opportune conditions, that moment should not be passed by one who is lazy or given to useless talk. What should be done? From the very beginning, reverence for the three trainings should be continuously generated. Here it is said: What is this so-called Triple Gem, which the Elder venerates before explaining the Minor Training? It is said: the Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Sangha-gem—these are the three gems. For they are called 'gems' in the sense of generating delight. Furthermore:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (dī. nī. aṭṭha. 2.33; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.223; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50; udā. aṭṭha. 45) –

“Esteemed and of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold, fit for the enjoyment of the noblest beings—for these reasons it is called a gem.”

Imissā gāthāya vasena ratanattho veditabbo.

By means of this verse, the meaning of 'gem' should be understood.

Mātikāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Matrix

(Kha-ja) idāni “samātika”nti vuttattā mātikaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “pārājikā ca cattāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Sabbasikkhānaṃ pana mūlabhūtattā adhisīlasikkhāva paṭhamaṃ vuttā. “Sīle patiṭṭhāyā”ti (suṃ. ni. 1.1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) hi [V 0.0072] vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi mahāsāvajjattā, mūlacchejjavasena pavattanato ca sabbapaṭhamaṃ jānitabbāti pārājikāva paṭhamaṃ vuttāti. Idāni yathānikkhittāni mātikāpadāni paṭipāṭiyā vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “pārājikā ca cattāro”ti paṭhamapadaṃ uddhaṭaṃ, tassāyamattho – pārājikāti parājitā parājayamāpannā, sikkhāpadaṃ atikkamitvā teneva āpattiṃ āpajjitvā, tāya vā parājayamāpāditānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, te pana cattāroti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, because 'with the matrix' was said, in order to first show the matrix, the passage beginning, 'and the four pārājikas,' is commenced. And since it is the root of all trainings, the training in higher virtue is stated first. For it is said, 'Established in virtue…' Therein also, because they are of great faultiness and because they proceed by way of cutting off the root, the pārājikas should be known first of all; thus the pārājikas are stated first. Now, in order to explain in detail and in order the terms of the matrix as they have been laid down, the first term, 'and the four pārājikas,' is taken up. This is its meaning: 'pārājikā' means defeated, having met with defeat. It is a designation for those who, having transgressed a training rule and thereby incurred an offense, have been brought to defeat by it. And it is said that they are four.

1. Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pārājika Offenses

1-2. Idāni [M 0.0062] te dassetuṃ “maggattaye”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha manussāmanussatiracchānagatānaṃ vasena tisso itthiyo, tayo ubhatobyañjanakā, tayo paṇḍakā, tayo purisāti pārājikavatthubhūtānaṃ nimittānaṃ nissayā dvādasamattā honti, tesaṃ vaccamaggappassāvamaggamukhamaggavasena tayo maggā. Tattha manussitthiyā tayo, amanussitthiyā tayo, tiracchānagatitthiyā tayoti nava, tathā manussaubhatobyañjanakādīnaṃ. Manussapaṇḍakādīnaṃ pana vaccamaggamukhamaggavasena dve dve katvā cha, tathā manussapurisādīnanti sabbesaṃ vasena tiṃsa maggā honti. Te sabbe pariggahetvā idha “maggattaye”ti vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ maggattayeti attho. Anikkhittasikkhoti bhikkhubhāvato cavitukāmatācittena yathālakkhaṇaṃ apaccakkhātasikkhoti attho. Santhatasanthateti vatthādīsu yena kenaci santhate vā asanthate vā. Allokāseti maggattayassa pakativātena asamphuṭṭhappadese. Nimittanti aṅgajātaṃ. Saṃsanthataṃ vā asanthataṃ vāti attano aṅgajātaṃ vatthādīnaṃ aññatarena paṭicchannaṃ vā appaṭicchannaṃ vā. Upādiṇṇanti anaṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ. Vuttappakāre maggattaye pavesanto cuto pārājikoti sambandho. Naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ pana pīḷakaṃ vā cammakhilaṃ vā lomaṃ vā pavesantassa dukkaṭaṃ, manussānaṃ pana jīvamānakasarīre akkhināsākaṇṇacchiddavatthikosesu satthakādīhi katavaṇe vā methunarāgena tilabījamattampi aṅgajātaṃ pavesantassa thullaccayaṃ, avasesasarīresu upakacchakādīsu ca dukkaṭaṃ. Tiracchānagatānaṃ hatthiassagoṇagadrabhaoṭṭhamahiṃsādīnaṃ nāsāya thullaccayaṃ, tathā tesaṃ vatthikosesu. Sabbesampi tiracchānagatānaṃ akkhikaṇṇavaṇesu dukkaṭaṃ, tathā tesaṃ avasesasarīresupi.

Now, to explain them, the exposition is begun with 'in the three paths,' etc. Herein, by way of humans, non-humans, and animals, there are three kinds of women, three kinds of hermaphrodites, three kinds of eunuchs, and three kinds of men—thus there are twelve supports for the 'sign' which is the basis for a pārājika offense. Their paths are three: the path of excrement, the path of urine, and the path of the mouth. Among these, there are three for a human woman, three for a non-human woman, and three for an animal woman, making nine; similarly for human hermaphrodites and so on. For human eunuchs and so on, there are two each—the path of excrement and the path of the mouth—making six; the same applies to human men and so on. Thus, in total for all of them, there are thirty paths. Having included all these, it is said here 'in the three paths'; this is the meaning of 'in the three paths.' 'One who has not given up the training' means one who has not formally renounced the training in the prescribed manner, with a mind desiring to fall away from the state of a bhikkhu. 'Covered or uncovered' means covered or uncovered by some kind of cloth, etc. 'In an open space' means in a place of the three paths not touched by the natural wind. 'The sign' means the sexual organ. 'Covered or uncovered' means one's own sexual organ being covered or uncovered by some kind of cloth, etc. 'Clung-to' means not deprived of bodily sensitivity. The connection is this: one who inserts it into the three paths in the way described is fallen, defeated. However, for one who inserts what is deprived of bodily sensitivity—such as a boil, a callus, or a hair—there is an offense of wrong-doing. For humans, if one, with sexual lust, inserts the sexual organ even to the extent of a sesame seed into the eye socket, nasal passage, ear hole, or bladder sheath of a living body, or into a wound made by a knife or the like, there is a grave offense. In the case of other parts of the body, such as the armpits, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For animals—such as elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, camels, and buffaloes—inserting it into the nose is a grave offense, and likewise into their bladder sheaths. For all animals, inserting it into the eyes, ears, or a wound is an offense of wrong-doing, and likewise for the remaining parts of their bodies.

Idāni [M 0.0063] pavesanaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ attupakkameneva hoti, bhikkhupaccatthikādīnaṃ pana vasena [V 0.0073] parūpakkamenāpi hoti, tatthāpi sevanacitte sati pārājiko hotīti dassanatthaṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – yo bhikkhu pavesanapaviṭṭhaṭhitauddhāraṇakkhaṇesu sādiyati, tasmiṃ khaṇe sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti, sopi pārājiko hoti. Yo pana bhikkhu sabbaso asādiyanto āsīvisamukhaṃ aṅgārakāsuñca paviṭṭhaṃ viya maññati, so nipparādho hoti. Ettha ṭhitaṃ nāma sukkavissaṭṭhisamayappavatti.

Now, insertion does not occur only through one's own effort but also through the effort of another, such as an adversary of the bhikkhu. To show that even in that case one commits a pārājika offense if there is a mind set on indulgence, the phrase 'or else,' etc., is stated. This is its meaning: a bhikkhu who consents at the moments of insertion, entry, remaining, or withdrawal, and at that moment establishes a mind set on indulgence, he too commits a pārājika offense. But a bhikkhu who does not consent at all, who regards it as like entering the mouth of a venomous snake or a pit of live coals, is without offense. Here, 'remaining' means the process at the time of the emission of semen.

Paṭhamaṃ.

The First.

3-4. Idāni dutiyaṃ dassetuṃ “ādiyeyyā”tiādimāha. “Ādiyeyyā”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ “adinnaṃ theyyacittena bhave pārājiko”ti iminā sambandho. Ādiyeyyāti ārāmādiṃ abhiyuñjitvā yo bhikkhu gaṇheyya, so bhave pārājikoti attho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Hareyyāti vetanena vā mittabhāvena vā aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto puna theyyacitte uppanne “sīse bhāraṃ theyyacitto āmasatī”tiādinā gaṇheyyāti attho. Avahareyyāti “upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ ‘dehi me bhaṇḍa’nti vuccamāno ‘nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”tiādinā avahareyya. Iriyāpathaṃ kopeyyāti “sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ nessāmī”ti teneva purisena taṃ netuṃ tassa gamanapathaṃ vāretvā aññena maggena taṃ santajjetvā neti, evaṃ nentassa tassa purisassa paṭhamapāde thullaccayaṃ, dutiyapāduddhāre pārājikaṃ. “Thalaṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto āmasatī”tiādinā ṭhānā cāveyya. Parikappitaṭṭhānaṃ vā suṅkaghātaṃ vā atikkāmento saṅketaṃ vītināmeyya. Yaṃ kiñci parapariggahitaṃ sassāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ tehi sāmikehi kāyena vā vācāya vā na dinnanti adinnaṃ.

Now, to explain the second, he says, 'should take,' etc. The words beginning with 'should take' are connected with this: 'taking what is not given with a thieving mind, one commits a pārājika offense.' 'Should take' means: a bhikkhu who, having laid claim to a monastery or the like, should take it, he commits a pārājika offense. So too in the remaining cases. 'Should carry away' means: while carrying another's goods for wages or out of friendship, when a thieving mind arises again, he should take it in the way described as 'with a thieving mind, he touches the load on his head.' 'Should steal' means: when goods have been deposited nearby and he is told, 'Give me the goods,' he should steal them by saying, 'I did not take them,' and so on. 'Should change its course' means: intending 'I will lead away the carrier along with the goods,' he blocks that person's path and, intimidating him, leads him by another route. For the one leading thus, there is a grave offense with the first step, and a pārājika offense upon lifting the second foot. 'Should move from its place' means he should move it from its place in the way described as 'with a thieving mind, he touches the goods lying on the ground.' One who crosses a designated place or a customs post violates the agreement. Whatever goods are taken possession of by another, having an owner, which have not been given by those owners by body or by speech, are 'what is not given.'

Idāni [M 0.0064] na imināva ākārena avahārako pārājiko hoti, aññathāpi hotīti dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Theyyāvahārako ca balāvahārako ca kusāvahārako ca paṭicchannāvahārako ca parikappāvahārako ca bhave pārājikoti sambandho. Tattha theyyāvahāro nāma sandhicchedādīhi vā kaṃsakūṭamānakūṭatulākūṭādīhi vā vañcetvā gahaṇaṃ. Pasayhāvahāro balāvahāro. Kusasaṅkamanaṃ katvā parakoṭṭhāsaggahaṇaṃ kusāvahāro. Parabhaṇḍaṃ paṃsuādinā paṭicchādetvā sāmikesu apassitvā gatesu paccāgantvā gahaṇaṃ paṭicchannāvahāro. Parikappāvahāro pana duvidho bhaṇḍokāsavasena. Tattha “sāṭako ce, gaṇhissāmi, suttañce, na gaṇhissāmī”ti bhaṇḍaṃ parikappetvā andhakāre pasibbakaṃ gaṇhāti. Tattha ce sāṭako hoti, uddhāreyeva [V 0.0074] pārājikaṃ. Sace suttaṃ hoti, rakkhati, puna “sutta”nti ñatvāpi “yaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ gahetabba”nti uggaṇhanto uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ, ayaṃ bhaṇḍaparikappo. Okāsaparikappo gabbhadvārappamukhavihārādīnaṃ vasena paricchedaṃ karoti “sace maṃ etthantare passanti, dassāmi, no ce passanti, gaṇhitvā gacchāmī”ti, tassa taṃ parikappitaparicchedaṃ atikkamantassa padavārena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ, ayaṃ okāsaparikappo.

Now, it is not only in this way that a thief commits a pārājika offense; he does so in other ways too. To show this, the phrase 'or else,' etc., is stated. The connection is: a thief by stealth, a thief by force, a thief by a ruse, a thief by concealment, and a thief by a stratagem commit a pārājika offense. Herein, theft by stealth is taking by deception, by means of house-breaking and the like, or by false bronze coins, false measures, false scales, and so on. Theft by force is taking by overpowering. Theft by a ruse is taking another's share by manipulating the lots. Theft by concealment is covering another's goods with dust or the like and, when the owners have gone out of sight, returning to take them. Theft by a stratagem, however, is of two kinds: by way of the goods and by way of the place. Here, the stratagem concerning goods is when one thinks, 'If it is a cloth, I will take it; if it is thread, I will not take it,' and then takes a bag while groping in the dark. If it contains a cloth, he commits a pārājika offense as soon as he lifts it. If it is thread, he protects himself. But later, even knowing it is thread, if he thinks, 'Whatever is obtained should be taken,' and takes it, he commits a pārājika offense as soon as he lifts it. This is the stratagem concerning goods. The stratagem concerning place is when one sets a boundary by way of a storeroom doorway, the entrance to a monastery, or the like, thinking, 'If they see me within this area, I will give it back; if they do not see me, I will take it and go.' For him, when he crosses that designated boundary, the pārājika offense should be understood to occur with each step. This is the stratagem concerning place.

Idāni imasmiṃ adinnādāne vinicchayanayaṃ dassetuṃ “bhaṇḍakālagghadesehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etthāti adinnādāne. Nicchayoti vinicchayo kātabboti attho. Tattha kenaci bhikkhunā “mayā idaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacittena gahita”nti vutte vinayadharena sahasāva taṃ āpattiṃ anāropetvā tassa bhaṇḍassa sāmikaassāmikabhāvaṃ upaparikkhitvā yadi sassāmikaṃ, tassa bhaṇḍassa agghavasena āpattiyā kāretabbo. Sace nirālayakāle gahitaṃ[M 0.0065], pārājikena na kāretabbo, ayaṃ bhaṇḍavasena vinicchayo.

Now, to show the method of judgment in this case of taking what is not given, the phrase 'by the goods, time, value, and place,' etc., is stated. 'Herein' means in the case of taking what is not given. 'Judgment' means a decision should be made; this is the meaning. In this regard, if some bhikkhu says, 'I took such-and-such an item with a thieving mind,' the Vinaya expert should not hastily charge him with an offense without first investigating whether the item has an owner or not. If it has an owner, the offense should be determined according to the value of the item. If it was taken at a time when it was abandoned, it should not be treated as a pārājika offense. This is the judgment by way of the goods.

Kāloti avahārakālo. Tadeva hi bhaṇḍaṃ kadāci mahagghaṃ hoti, kadāci appagghaṃ, tasmā yasmiṃ kāle avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃ kāle yo tassa aggho, tena agghena āpattiyā kāretabbo, ayaṃ kālavasena vinicchayo.

'Time' is the time of the theft. For the same goods are sometimes of great value, sometimes of little value. Therefore, at whatever time they were stolen, the offense should be determined by the value they had at that time. This is the judgment by way of time.

Agghoti bhaṇḍaggho. Navabhaṇḍassa hi yo aggho, so pacchā parihāyati, tasmā sabbadā bhaṇḍaṃ pakatiagghavaseneva na kāretabbaṃ, ayaṃ agghavasena vinicchayo. Desoti avahāradeso. Bhaṇḍuṭṭhānadese hi bhaṇḍaṃ appagghaṃ hoti, aññattha mahagghaṃ, tasmā yasmiṃ dese bhaṇḍaṃ avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva dese agghena kāretabbo, ayaṃ desavasena vinicchayo.

'Value' is the value of the goods. For the value of new goods later diminishes; therefore, the valuation should not always be made simply according to the standard value of the goods. This is the judgment by way of value. 'Place' is the place of the theft. For in the place where goods originate, they are of little value, but elsewhere of great value. Therefore, in whatever place the goods were stolen, the valuation should be made according to the value in that very place. This is the judgment by way of place.

Paribhogenapi sāṭakādikassa bhaṇḍassa aggho parihāyati, tasmā tassa paribhogavasena parihīnāparihīnabhāvo upaparikkhitabbo, ayaṃ paribhogavasena vinicchayo.

The value of goods such as cloth also diminishes through use. Therefore, its state of being worn out or not worn out should be investigated by way of its use. This is the judgment by way of use.

Dutiyaṃ.

The Second.

5. Idāni tatiyaṃ dassetuṃ “manussaviggaha”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha manussaviggahanti paṭisandhiviññāṇena [V 0.0075] saddhiṃ uppannaṃ kalalarūpaṃ ādiṃ katvā pakatiyā vīsativassasatāyukassa sattassa yāva maraṇakālā etthantare anupubbena vuddhippatto attabhāvo, eso manussaviggaho nāma, evarūpaṃ manussaviggahanti attho. Ciccāti vadhakacetanāvasena sañcetetvā pakappetvā abhivitaritvā vītikkamoti attho. Jīvitā vā viyojayeti vuttappakāraṃ manussaviggahaṃ [M 0.0066] kalalakālepi tāpanamaddanehi vā bhesajjasampadānena vā tato vā uddhampi tadanurūpena upakkamena santativikopanavasena yo jīvitā viyojeyya, so cuto bhaveti sambandho. Kiñca bhiyyo – “satthahārakaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha haratīti hārakaṃ, kiṃ harati? Jīvitaṃ, haritabbanti vā hārakaṃ, upanikkhipitabbanti attho, satthañca taṃ hārakañcāti satthahārakaṃ. Assāti manussaviggahassa. Yathā manussaviggaho icchiticchitakkhaṇe taṃ asiādisatthaṃ paṭilabhati, tathā sayaṃ maraṇacetano maraṇādhippāyo hutvā upanikkhipeyya. Sopi cuto bhaveti attho. Etena thāvarappayogaṃ dasseti.

5. Now, to show the third, the passage beginning with “a human individual existence” is introduced. Herein, “a human individual existence” means the individual existence that has developed in stages, starting from the embryonic form that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, up to the time of death for a being whose natural lifespan is one hundred and twenty years. This is called “a human individual existence”; the meaning is “such a human individual existence.” “Intentionally” means having transgressed after having willed, contrived, and exerted oneself with a murderous intention. “Or should deprive of life”: the connection is that whoever deprives a human individual existence of the kind described of life—even at the embryonic stage by heating or crushing, or by administering medicine, or thereafter by a suitable means that disrupts the life-continuum—he falls away. Furthermore, it is said: “or one who provides a weapon.” Herein, `hāraka` is one who takes away. What does he take away? Life. Or `hāraka` means what is to be brought, that is, what is to be placed near. `Satthahāraka` is a weapon and a provider thereof. “Of this” means of the human individual existence. Just as the human individual existence, at the desired moment, obtains that sword or other weapon, so one with a murderous intention, aiming for death, might place it nearby. The meaning is that he too falls away. By this, he shows the use of a fixed contrivance.

6-7. Idāni “maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”tiādividhiṃ dassetuṃ “gāheyya maraṇūpāyaṃ, vadeyya maraṇe guṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha “satthaṃ vā āhara, visaṃ vā khāda, rajjuyā vā ubbandhitvā kālaṃ karohī”tiādinā nayena maraṇatthāya upāyaṃ gāheyya. Maraṇasaṃvaṇṇanā panettha bahuvidhā “kāyena saṃvaṇṇeti, vācāya kāyavācāya dūtena lekhāya vā saṃvaṇṇetī”ti vuttattā. Tattha kāyena saṃvaṇṇeti nāma kāyena viññāpeti. “Yo papāte papatanādīni katvā marati, so dhanaṃ vā labhati, yasaṃ vā labhati, saggaṃ vā gacchatī”tiādinā nayena saṃvaṇṇeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā koci “marissāmī”ti dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ uppādeti, thullaccayaṃ. Marati ce, pārājikaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Dūtena saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana dūtassa sāsanaṃ ārocāpeti “evaṃ ārocehī”ti, “yo evaṃ marati, so dhanaṃ vā labhatī”ti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Lekhāya saṃvaṇṇeti nāma giripabbatapurāṇādilekhaṃ likhati, “yo evaṃ maratī”tiādi vuttanayameva. Etthāpi yo maraṇūpāyaṃ vā gāheyya, maraṇe vā guṇaṃ vadeyya, so cuto bhaveti sambandho.

Now, to show the method beginning with “or one might praise death,” it is said: “One might incite another to take up a means of death, or speak of the benefit in death.” Herein, one might incite another to take up a means for death in such ways as: “Bring a weapon, eat poison, or hang yourself with a rope and die.” The praise of death here is manifold, as it is said: “One praises by body, by speech, by both body and speech, by a messenger, or by writing.” Herein, “one praises by body” means one makes it known with the body. One praises in such ways as: “Whoever dies by doing things like throwing oneself from a cliff gains wealth, or gains fame, or goes to heaven.” This entails an offense of wrong-doing. If, having heard his words, someone arouses a painful feeling with the thought, “I will die,” it is a grave offense. If he dies, it is a pārājika. So too in the remaining cases. In praising by a messenger, one has the messenger announce the message, “Announce thus,” and everything is the same as before: “Whoever dies in this way gains wealth….” “One praises by writing” means one writes an inscription on a mountain, hill, ancient ruin, etc., in the way already stated: “Whoever dies in this way….” Here too, the connection is that whoever incites another to take up a means of death or speaks of the benefit in death, he falls away.

Idāni [M 0.0067] pana imassa manussaviggahassa chabbidhe payoge dassetuṃ “payogā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Sāhatthikanissaggikaāṇattikathāvaraiddhimayavijjāmayānaṃ vasena tassa manussaviggahassa chappayogāti adhippāyo. Tattha sāhatthikoti sayaṃ mārentassa kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena [V 0.0076] vā paharaṇaṃ. Nissaggikoti dūre ṭhitaṃ māretukāmassa kāyādīhi ususattiyantapāsāṇādīnaṃ nissajjanaṃ. Āṇattikoti “asukaṃ nāma mārehī”ti aññaṃ āṇāpentassa āṇāpanaṃ. Thāvaroti opātakkhaṇanaṃ, apassenasaṃvidhānaṃ, asiādīnaṃ upanikkhipanaṃ, taḷākādīsu visasampayojanaṃ, rūpūpahāroti evamādi. Kammavipākajāya iddhiyā payojanaṃ iddhipayogaṃ. Māraṇatthāya vijjānaṃ parijappanaṃ vijjāmayoti.

Now, to show the six kinds of means of attack on this human individual existence, the section beginning with “means of attack” is introduced. The intention is that there are six means of attack on this human individual existence, namely: by one’s own hand, by missile, by command, by a fixed contrivance, by psychic power, and by a spell. Herein, “by one’s own hand” is the striking by one who is himself killing, with his body or with something connected to his body. “By missile” is the releasing of arrows, spears, projectiles, stones, etc., by one standing at a distance who desires to kill. “By command” is the ordering of another, saying, “Kill so-and-so.” “By a fixed contrivance” includes digging a pitfall, arranging a trap, placing a sword or other weapon nearby, applying poison in a pond, offering a deceptive sight, and so on. The means of psychic power is the use of psychic power born of the result of kamma. “By a spell” is the muttering of spells for the purpose of killing.

Idāni imesu chasu payogesu āṇattiyaṃ saṅketavisaṅketataṃ dassetuṃ “kālavatthāvudhiriyāpathā”tiādimāha. Tattha kāloti pubbaṇhasāyanhādikālo ca yobbanathāvariyādikālopi ca. Imesu yaṃ kiñci kālaṃ niyametvā “imasmiṃ nāma kāle mārehī”ti āṇatto sace tasmiṃyeva kāle māreti, āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Sace niyamitakālato pure vā pacchā vā māreti, āṇāpako muccati. Vatthūti māretabbo puggalo. Sace āṇatto tameva māreti, āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Atha aññaṃ māreti, āṇāpako muccati. Evaṃ sesesupi vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Āvudhanti asiādi. Iriyāpathoti māretabbassa gamanaṃ vā nisajjā vāti evamādiko. Kiriyāvisesoti vijjhanaṃ vā chedanaṃ vā bhedanaṃ vā sūlāropanaṃ vāti evamādiko. Okāsoti gāmo vā vanaṃ vā gehaṃ vāti evamādiko. Imesu yathā [M 0.0068] yathā vadhako āṇatto, tathā tathā kate āṇāpakassa āpatti, aññathā kate visaṅketo hoti. Āṇattiyaṃ pana ayaṃ viseso “adhiṭṭhāyāti adhiṭṭhahitvā āṇāpeti ‘evaṃ vijjha, evaṃ pahara, evaṃ ghātehī”ti vuttāya pāḷiyā labbhatīti ñātabbo.

Now, to show concord and discord in a command regarding these six means of attack, he says, “time, object, weapon, posture,” etc. Herein, “time” is the time of day, such as morning or evening, and also the time of life, such as youth or old age. Among these, if having specified a certain time, one gives the command, “Kill at this particular time,” and if the one commanded kills at that very time, it is a pārājika offense for the one who gave the command at the moment of command. If he kills before or after the specified time, the one who gave the command is absolved. “Object” is the person to be killed. If the one commanded kills that very person, it is a pārājika offense for the one who gave the command at the moment of command. But if he kills another, the one who gave the command is absolved. The decision should be understood in the same way for the remaining cases according to the method stated. “Weapon” is a sword, etc. “Posture” is that of the one to be killed, such as walking or sitting. “Specific action” is piercing, or cutting, or breaking, or impaling. “Place” is a village, or a forest, or a house. In these cases, when the killer acts exactly as commanded, the one who gave the command incurs the offense; when he acts otherwise, it is a discord. Regarding a command, however, this special point should be known: it is obtained from the Pāḷi which says, 'Having specified (adhiṭṭhāya), he commands: “Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus.”'

Tatiyaṃ.

The Third.

8-9. Idāni catutthaṃ dassetuṃ “jhānādibheda”ntiādimāha. Tassattho – “jhānaṃ vimokkho samādhi samāpatti ñāṇadassanaṃ maggabhāvanā phalasacchikiriyā kilesappahānaṃ vinīvaraṇatā cittassa suññāgāre abhiratī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ attani natthitāya nosantaṃ “mayi atthī”ti attani vā taṃ “ahaṃ ettha sandissāmī”ti attānaṃ vā tattha upanetvā dīpento cuto bhave. Koṭṭhāsaṃ vāti ettha “jhānalābhī, vimokkhalābhī, samādhilābhī, samāpattilābhīmhī”ti evamādinā nayena koṭṭhāsato vāti attho. Ekekaṃ vāti “paṭhamassa [V 0.0077] jhānassa lābhī, dutiyassa jhānassa lābhīmhī”ti evamādinā nayena ekekaṃ vāti attho. “Atītabhave sotāpannomhī”ti vadato atītabhavaṃ sandhāya kathitattā pārājikaṃ natthi, tasmā “paccuppannabhavassita”nti vuttaṃ, tassa paccuppannabhavanissitaṃ katvāti attho. Aññāpadesarahitanti “yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī”tiādinā nayena aññāpadesaṃ vināti attho. Evaṃ dīpento hi thullaccayamāpajjati. Dīpentoti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjiṃ, samāpajjāmi, samāpanno, paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhīmhi, vasīmhi, sacchikataṃ assā”ti evamādinā nayena dīpentoti attho. “Adhigato”ti māno adhimāno, so yassa natthi, so anadhimāniko. Kena evaṃ dīpentoti ce? Taṃ dassetuṃ “kāyena vācā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0069], kāyena vā vācāya vā tadubhayena vāti attho. Viññattipatheti yattha ṭhito manussajātiko gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā tassa vacanaṃ pakatisotena sutvā samanantarameva “imaṃ nāma esa vadatī”ti jānāti, tattha ṭhatvā dīpento cuto bhave, na devabrahmādīsu aññatarena ñāteti attho.

Now, to show the fourth, he says, “the divisions of jhāna,” etc. Its meaning is: one who, regarding a superior human state—spoken of as “jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandonment of defilements, the mind’s freedom from hindrances, delight in a secluded dwelling”—which is non-existent in himself, makes it known by presenting it as “it exists in me,” or by presenting himself in that connection as “I am seen therein,” would be fallen. “Or a portion”: the meaning here is by way of portions, in such ways as, “I am an obtainer of jhāna, an obtainer of liberation, an obtainer of concentration, an obtainer of attainment.” “Or one by one”: the meaning is one by one, in such ways as, “I am an obtainer of the first jhāna, an obtainer of the second jhāna.” For one who says, “In a past existence I was a stream-enterer,” since it is spoken with reference to a past existence, there is no pārājika. Therefore, it is said, “based on the present existence,” the meaning being, having made it based on the present existence. “Without an indirect reference” means without an indirect reference in such ways as, “The bhikkhu who lives in your monastery is an obtainer of the first jhāna.” For one who makes it known thus incurs a grave offense. “Making it known” means making it known in such ways as: “I have attained the first jhāna; I am attaining it; I am one who has attained it; I am an obtainer of the first jhāna; I am a master of it; it has been realized by me.” `Adhimāna` is the conceit, “I have attained.” One who does not have this is one without such conceit. If it is asked, “By what does one make it known?” to show this, it is said, “by body, speech,” etc., meaning by body, or by speech, or by both. “In the range of communication” means: standing in a place where a human being, whether a householder or one gone forth, having heard his words with a normal ear, knows immediately, “He is saying such-and-such”—one who makes it known while standing there would be fallen. The meaning is that it is not so if it is known by some deva, brahmā, or other non-human.

Catutthaṃ.

Fourth.

10. Idāni catunnampi sādhāraṇavinicchayaṃ vattuṃ “pārājikete cattāro”tiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepo – cattāropi ete pārājikā “ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatā”ti evaṃ vuttasaṃvāsassa abhabbatāya asaṃvāsā, yathāpure pubbe gihikāle ca anupasampannakāle ca asaṃvāsikā, evaṃ pacchā pārājikaṃ āpannāpi asaṃvāsāti. Kiñca bhiyyo – abhabbā bhikkhubhāvāya puna tena attabhāvena upasampadāya avatthutāya upasampannā bhavitumpi abhabbāti attho. Kiṃ viyāti ce? Sīsacchinnova jīvituṃ, yathāpi sīsacchinno tena attabhāvena puna jīvituṃ abhabbo, evamime cattāroti adhippāyo.

10. Now, to state the general ruling for all four, he says, “These four are pārājikas,” etc. Herein, this is the summary: all these four pārājikas are causes for non-communion because of unfitness for the communion described as “having a common formal act, a common recitation, and equal training.” Just as formerly, during their time as householders and before their higher ordination, they were not in communion, so too, after having committed a pārājika offense, they are not in communion. Furthermore, they are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu; the meaning is that because the basis for higher ordination is absent, they are incapable of becoming ordained again in that same individual existence. If it is asked, “Like what?” Like one whose head has been cut off is incapable of living. The intention is that just as one whose head has been cut off is incapable of living again in that same individual existence, so too are these four.

11. Idāni imesu catūsu pārājikesu ye pariyāyāṇattīhi sambhavanti, te dassetuṃ “pariyāyo cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pariyāyoti maraṇādhippāyassa kāyapayogo vā vacīpayogo vā. Tasmā “yo īdise muhutte satthaṃ vā āharitvā visaṃ vā khāditvā sobbhādīsu vā papatitvā marati, so dhanaṃ vā labhati, yasaṃ vā labhatī”tiādinā nayena maraṇaṃ abhinandanto “idaṃ sutvā yo koci maratū”ti yo pariyāyena vadati, taṃ sutvā sace [V 0.0078] koci tathā marati, pārājikaṃ. Niyamitena pana yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasseva maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Āṇatti [M 0.0070] pana vuttatthāyeva. Tatiye manussaviggahapārājike labbhatīti sambandho. Dutiye pana adinnādāne āṇatti eva labbhati, na pariyāyoti attho. Kasmā naṃ pariyāyena nāpajjatīti? Yathā manussaviggahe “maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti vuttaṃ, tathā idha adinnādāne “vaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti avuttattā. Sesesūti paṭhamacatutthesu pariyāyāṇattidvayaṃ na labbhatīti attho.

11. Now, to show which cases of indirect speech and command are possible in these four pārājikas, the words beginning 'and by indirect speech' were stated. Here, 'indirect speech' means bodily or verbal exertion with the intention of causing death. Therefore, if someone, extolling death, speaks indirectly, saying, 'Whoever dies at such a moment by bringing a weapon, or by consuming poison, or by falling into a pit, etc., will obtain wealth or fame,' with the thought, 'Let someone die on hearing this,' and if someone, having heard this, dies in that way, it is a pārājika. But if it was spoken with reference to a specific person, it is a pārājika only on that person's death. A command, however, is just as has been explained. The connection is that this is found in the third pārājika, that on killing a human being. But in the second, that on taking what is not given, only a command is found, not indirect speech; this is the meaning. Why does one not fall into an offense by indirect speech? Because, just as in the case of killing a human being it is said 'or one might praise the beauty of death,' so here in the case of taking what is not given, it is not said 'or one might praise the beauty [of it].' 'In the remaining ones' means that in the first and fourth, the pair of indirect speech and command is not found.

12. Idāni catūsupi yathāsambhavaṃ aṅgabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “sevetukāmatācitta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha methunadhammassāti methunadhammapārājikassa. Budhāti vinayadharā.

12. Now, to show the analysis of the factors for each of the four as they are possible, the passage beginning 'the thought of wishing to engage' was stated. Here, 'of the act of intercourse' means of the pārājika on the act of intercourse. 'The wise' means the Vinaya-experts.

13. Manussasanti manussasantakatā. Etena petatiracchānagatapariggahesu anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Tathāsaññīti manussasantakavasena parapariggahitasaññīti attho. Vatthuno garutāti pañcamāsakaṃ vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā tadagghanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vā hotīti attho. Avahāro cāti pañcavīsatiyā avahāresu yena kenaci avahāro hotīti attho. Adinnādānahetuyoti adinnādānapārājikassa etāni pañca aṅgānīti adhippāyo.

13. 'Belonging to a human' means being the property of a human. By this it is shown that there is no offense in taking what is possessed by ghosts or animals. 'Perceiving it as such' means perceiving it as possessed by another on account of its being human property. 'The object being of value' means that it is an article worth five māsakas, or more than five māsakas, or goods of that value. 'And the taking away' means that there is a taking away by any of the twenty-five kinds of taking away. 'For the reason of taking what is not given' means that these five are the factors of the pārājika on taking what is not given; this is the intention.

14. Pāṇo mānussakoti manussajātikapāṇo. Tasmiṃ pāṇe pāṇasaññitā. Ghātacetanāti vadhakacetanā. Payogoti taṃsamuṭṭhito sāhatthikādīnaṃ channaṃ payogānaṃ aññatarapayogo. Tena payogena maraṇaṃ. Pañcete vadhahetuyoti manussaviggahapārājikassa pañca aṅgānīti attho.

14. 'A human living being' means a living being of the human species. Perception of it as a living being in regard to that living being. 'Intention to kill' means the volition to kill. 'An effort' means one or another of the six kinds of effort—such as by one's own hand, etc.—arisen from that intention. Death by means of that effort. 'These five are for the reason of killing' means that these are the five factors of the pārājika on killing a human being.

15. Asantatāti uttarimanussadhammassa attani asantatā cāti attho. Pāpamicchatāyārocanāti iminā yo kevalaṃ [M 0.0071] pāpamicchataṃ vinā mandattā momūhattā bhaṇati, tassa anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Tassāti yassa āroceti, tassa manussajātitā ca. “Yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu arahā”tiādinā (pari. 160, 336) nāññāpadeso ca. Tadevāti tadā eva taṅkhaṇeyeva jānanaṃ. Asantadīpaneti uttarimanussadhammārocanapārājiketi attho.

15. 'Its not being present' means the non-presence of a superhuman state in oneself. 'Declaring it out of evil desire': by this it is shown that there is no offense for one who speaks merely out of stupidity or bewilderment, without evil desire. 'Of that one' means that the one to whom one declares it is of the human species. And not by indirect reference, as in the example, 'The bhikkhu who dwells in your monastery is an arahant,' etc. 'At that very time' means knowing it at that very moment, at that instant. 'In the declaration of what is not present' means in the pārājika on declaring a superhuman state.

16. Idāni [V 0.0079] “pārājikā ca cattāro”ti ettha ca-saddena saṅgahitehi saddhiṃ samodhānetvā dassetuṃ “asādhāraṇā cattāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā vajjappaṭicchādikā ukkhittānuvattikā aṭṭhavatthukāti ime cattāro bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūhi asādhāraṇā nāma. Etāsu ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā nāma yā kāyasaṃsaggarāgena avassutā teneva rāgena avassutassa manussapurisassa akkhakānaṃ adho, jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ kapparānañca upari yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena āmasanādiṃ sādiyati, tassā adhivacanaṃ. Yā pana bhikkhunī aññissā bhikkhuniyā pārājikasaṅkhātaṃ vajjaṃ jānaṃ paṭicchādeti, sā vajjappaṭicchādikā nāma. Samaggena pana saṅghena ukkhittaṃ bhikkhuṃ yā bhikkhunī yaṃdiṭṭhiko so hoti, tassā diṭṭhiyā gahaṇavasena anuvattati, sā ukkhittānuvattikā nāma. Yā pana kāyasaṃsaggarāgena tintā tathāvidhasseva purisassa hatthaggahaṇaṃ vā saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ vā sādiyati, kāyasaṃsaggasaṅkhātassa asaddhammassa paṭisevanatthāya purisassa hatthapāse santiṭṭhati vā, tattha ṭhatvā sallapati vā, saṅketaṃ vā gacchati, purisassa āgamanaṃ vā sādiyati, kenaci vā paṭicchannokāsaṃ pavisati, hatthapāse ṭhatvā kāyaṃ upasaṃharati, ayaṃ aṭṭhavatthukā nāmāti veditabbā.

16. Now, to show the connection with those included by the word 'and' in the phrase 'and the four pārājikas,' the words beginning 'the four that are not shared' were stated. Here, the four that are not shared by bhikkhus with bhikkhunīs are: ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā, vajjappaṭicchādikā, ukkhittānuvattikā, and aṭṭhavatthukā. Among these, ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā is the designation for a bhikkhunī who, infatuated with lust for bodily contact, consents to being touched, etc., by any part of the body of a human male who is similarly infatuated, below the collarbones and above the knees and elbows. A bhikkhunī who, knowing of another bhikkhunī's fault reckoned as a pārājika, conceals it, is called vajjappaṭicchādikā. A bhikkhunī who follows a bhikkhu suspended by a united Sangha, by way of adopting whatever view he holds, is called ukkhittānuvattikā. A bhikkhunī who, steeped in lust for bodily contact, consents to a man of the same kind taking her hand or taking the corner of her outer robe; or stands within arm's reach of a man for the purpose of engaging in the unwholesome act of bodily contact; or converses while standing there; or goes to an appointed place; or consents to a man's approach; or enters a concealed place with someone; or brings her body close while standing within arm's reach—this is to be understood as the aṭṭhavatthukā.

Abhabbakā [M 0.0072] ekādasāti ettha paṇḍako theyyasaṃvāsako titthiyapakkantako tiracchānagato mātughātako pitughātako arahantaghātako bhikkhunidūsako saṅghabhedako lohituppādako ubhatobyañjanakoti ime ekādasa abhabbapuggalā nāma. Vibbhantā bhikkhunīti yadā bhikkhunī vibbhamitukāmā hutvā setavatthaṃ vā kāsāyameva vā gihinivāsanākārena nivāseti, tadā pārājikamāpannā nāma hoti, puna upasampadaṃ na labhati, sā ca pārājikāti attho. Mudupiṭṭhiko nāma kataparikammāya mudukāya piṭṭhiyā samannāgato. So ettāvatā na pārājiko, atha kho yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhamaggavaccamaggesu aññataraṃ paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti.

Herein, 'the eleven incapable persons': a eunuch, one who has entered the Sangha by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a killer of an arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic of the Sangha, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, and a hermaphrodite—these eleven are called incapable persons. 'A bhikkhunī who has apostatized': when a bhikkhunī, wishing to apostatize, dresses in white clothes or even in ochre robes in the manner of a laywoman, she is then said to have fallen into a pārājika offense, she cannot receive ordination again, and she is a pārājika; this is the meaning. 'One with a soft back' is one endowed with a soft back on which a procedure has been performed. He is not a pārājika on that account. But when, oppressed by discontent, he inserts his own sexual organ into one of his own passages—the mouth or the anus—then he becomes a pārājika.

17-18. Lambīti aṅgajātassa dīghattā evaṃ vutto. Sopi yadā anabhiratiyā pīḷito attano aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhe vā vaccamagge vā paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti. Mukhena gaṇhantoti ettha yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa suttassa vā pamattassa vā aṅgajātaṃ attano mukhena gaṇhāti, so cāti attho. Tatthevāti parassa aṅgajātevāti attho[V 0.0080]. Yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa aṅgajātaṃ kammaniyaṃ disvā attano vaccamaggena tassa upari nisīdati, taṃ attano vaccamaggaṃ paveseti, so cāti attho. Ete cattāro anulomikā methunassāti sambandho. Kathamiti ce? Magge maggappavesanasadisatāya, na ubhinnaṃ rāgavasena sadisabhāvūpagatānaṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattisadisatāya. Idhāgatā cattāroti methunadhammādivasena pārājikā cattāro cāti evaṃ samodhānato catuvīsati pārājikāti attho.

17-18. 'The long one' (Lambī): he is so called because of the length of his sexual organ. When he too, oppressed by discontent, inserts his own sexual organ into his own mouth or anus, he becomes a pārājika. 'One who takes with the mouth': this means one who, oppressed by discontent, takes into his mouth the sexual organ of another who is asleep or heedless. 'In that very place' means in the other's sexual organ. And this means: one who, oppressed by discontent, seeing another's sexual organ to be serviceable, sits down upon it with his own anus and makes it enter his own anus. The connection is that these four are conformable to sexual intercourse. How so? Because of the similarity to an orifice entering an orifice, not because of the similarity to the coming together in a couple of two people who have reached a similar state through lust. 'The four that have come here' means the four pārājikas by way of the act of intercourse, etc., and thus by this combination there are twenty-four pārājikas; this is the meaning.

Etthāha [M 0.0073] – mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakā tatiyapārājikaṃ āpannā, bhikkhunidūsako lambīādayo cattāro paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannāyevāti katvā kuto catuvīsatīti? Adhippāyo panettha atthi, mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idha anupasampannāyeva adhippetā, lambīādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā ekena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ appaṭisevinopi honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttāti. Pārājikavinicchayo.

Here one might say: 'Since matricides, patricides, and killers of arahants have fallen into the third pārājika, and the violator of a bhikkhunī and the four beginning with the 'long one' have fallen into the first pārājika, how can there be twenty-four?' There is an intention here. For the four beginning with the matricide are here intended as being unordained. Although the four beginning with the 'long one' are included in the first pārājika, they are mentioned separately because in one way they are also non-partakers of the act of intercourse. The Exposition of the Pārājikas.

Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Pārājikas is completed.

2. Saṅghādisesaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Saṅghādisesas

19. Idāni saṅghādisesaṃ pakāsetuṃ “garukā navā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Garukāti saṅghādisesā idha adhippetā, aññattha pana pārājikāpi saṅgayhanti. Kasmā “terasā”ti avatvā “navā”ti vuttanti ce? Vītikkamakkhaṇeyeva āpajjitabbattā paṭhamāpattikā vuttā, yāvatatiyakā pana cattāro saṅghādisesā saṅghāyattattā cirena āpajjantīti na vuttā. Tattha mocetukāmatāti mocetukāmatāyāti attho “alajjitā”tiādīsu viya. Iminā pana nayena mocanassādo muccanassādo muttassādo methunassādo phassassādo kaṇḍūvanassādo dassanassādo nisajjanassādo vācassādo gehasitapemaṃ vanabhaṅgiyanti ekādasa assādā vuttā, tesu ekaṃyeva mocanassādaṃ gahetvā sesā paṭikkhittā honti.

19. Now, to expound the Saṅghādisesa, the section beginning with “grave, nine,” and so forth, has been commenced. “Grave” here refers to the Saṅghādisesa offenses; elsewhere, however, even Pārājika offenses are included. Why is it said “nine” instead of “thirteen”? Because the first offenses are those that are incurred at the very moment of transgression; however, the four Saṅghādisesa offenses that require up to three admonitions are incurred slowly, since they depend on the Saṅgha, and thus are not mentioned here. Here, “desiring release” means “with the desire for release,” just as in cases such as “shameless,” and so forth. By this method, eleven pleasures are mentioned: the pleasure of releasing, the pleasure of being released, the pleasure of the released, the pleasure of sexual intercourse, the pleasure of touch, the pleasure of scratching, the pleasure of seeing, the pleasure of sitting, the pleasure of speech, household-based affection, and forest-breaking. Among these, only the pleasure of releasing is taken, while the rest are rejected.

Tesaṃ assādānaṃ vasena evaṃ vinicchayo veditabbo – mocetuṃ assādo mocanassādo. Mocanassādacetanāya [V 0.0081] nimitte upakkamati, muccati, saṅghādiseso. Na muccati [M 0.0074] ce, thullaccayaṃ. Muccanassāde sace attano dhammatāya muccamānaṃ assādeti, na upakkamati, anāpatti. Sace muccamānaṃ assādento upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādisesova. Attano dhammatāya mutte assādo muttassādo. Etthāpi upakkamassa natthitāya anāpatti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Methunassādena itthiṃ gaṇhantassa muttepi anāpatti, ayaṃ methunassādo. Phassassādo duvidho ajjhattiko bāhiro cāti. Tattha ajjhattike tāva attano nimittaṃ “thaddhaṃ mudukanti jānissāmī”ti vā lolabhāvena vā kīḷāpayato sace muccati, anāpatti. Bāhiraphassassāde kāyasaṃsaggarāgena mātugāmaṃ phusato āliṅgato ca mutte anāpatti. Kaṇḍūvanassāde daddukacchādīnaṃ vasena khajjamānaṃ nimittaṃ kaṇḍūvanassādena kaṇḍūvato muttepi anāpatti. Dassanassāde mātugāmassa anokāsaṃ upanijjhāyato muttepi anāpatti. Nisajjanassāde mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisinnassa muttepi anāpatti. Vācāya assādo vācassādo. Tena assādena mātugāmaṃ methunappaṭisaṃyuttāhi vācāhi obhāsantassa muttepi anāpatti. Gehasitapeme mātādīnaṃ mātādipemena āliṅganādiṃ karontassa muttepi anāpatti. Vanabhaṅge ca santhavakaraṇatthāya itthiyā pesitaṃ pupphādivanabhaṅgasaññitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ “itthannāmāya nāma idaṃ me pesita”nti assādena āmasantassa muttepi anāpatti. Etesu pana mocanassādavaseneva upakkamantassa āpatti, sesānaṃ vasena anāpattīti veditabbaṃ.

The determination should be understood thus in terms of these pleasures: the pleasure in releasing is the pleasure of release. With the intention of the pleasure of release, one makes an effort regarding the organ; if one is released, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. If one is not released, it is a thullaccaya offense. In the pleasure of being released, if one enjoys the release that occurs by its own nature and does not make an effort, there is no offense. If, while enjoying the release, one makes an effort and releases, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. The pleasure in what has been released by its own nature is the pleasure of the released. Here too, because there is no effort, there is no offense. So it is in all cases. For one who takes a woman with the pleasure of sexual intercourse, even if there is a release, there is no offense; this is the pleasure of sexual intercourse. The pleasure of contact is twofold: internal and external. Therein, regarding the internal, if one releases while playing with one's own organ, thinking, 'I will know if it is stiff or soft,' or out of wantonness, there is no offense. In the external pleasure of contact, for one who touches or embraces a woman with lust for bodily contact, if there is a release, there is no offense. In the pleasure of scratching, for one who scratches the organ due to ringworm, scabies, and so on, with the pleasure of scratching, even if there is a release, there is no offense. In the pleasure of seeing, for one who intently gazes at a woman's private parts, even if there is a release, there is no offense. In the pleasure of sitting, for one sitting in seclusion with a woman, even if there is a release, there is no offense. The pleasure in speech is the pleasure of speech. With that pleasure, for one who addresses a woman with words connected to sexual intercourse, even if there is a release, there is no offense. In household-based affection, for one who embraces, etc., one's mother and others with motherly affection, even if there is a release, there is no offense. And in 'breaking a branch,' for one who, with pleasure, touches a gift of flowers and so forth, known as 'breaking a branch,' sent by a woman for the purpose of establishing intimacy, thinking, 'This was sent to me by such-and-such a woman,' even if there is a release, there is no offense. However, among these, an offense is incurred only by one who makes an effort motivated by the pleasure of release; it should be understood that in the other cases, there is no offense.

Sukkassāti “nīlaṃ pītakaṃ lohitakaṃ odātaṃ takkavaṇṇaṃ dakavaṇṇaṃ telavaṇṇaṃ khīravaṇṇaṃ dadhivaṇṇaṃ sappivaṇṇa”nti (pārā. 237) evaṃ āgatesu dasasu vaṇṇesu yassa kassaci sukkassāti adhippāyo[M 0.0075]. Upakkammāti “ajjhattarūpe moceti, bahiddhārūpe moceti, ajjhattabahiddhārūpe moceti, ākāse kaṭiṃ kampento mocetī”ti (pārā. 237) evaṃ vuttesu catūsu upāyesu aññatarena upāyena “rāgūpatthambhe moceti, vaccūpatthambhe moceti, passāvūpatthambhe moceti, vātūpatthambhe moceti, uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhūpatthambhe mocetī”ti evaṃ vuttesu pañcasu kālesu kismiñci kāle aṅgajāte kammaniyaṃ patte “ārogyatthāya moceti, sukhatthāya moceti, bhesajjatthāya, dānatthāya, puññatthāya, yaññatthāya, saggatthāya, bījatthāya, vīmaṃsatthāya, davatthāya mocetī”ti (pārā. 237) evaṃ vuttesu dasasu adhippāyesu yena kenaci adhippāyena hatthādīsu yena kenaci upakkamitvāti attho. Vimocayanti antamaso yaṃ ekā khuddakamakkhikā piveyya, tattakampi mocentoti attho. Aññatra supinantenāti yā supinante [V 0.0082] sukkavissaṭṭhi hoti, taṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Samaṇoti yo koci upasampanno. Garukanti saṅghādisesaṃ. Phuseti āpajjeyyāti attho.

'Of semen' means semen of any of the ten colors that have been mentioned: 'blue, yellow, red, white, the color of buttermilk, the color of water, the color of oil, the color of milk, the color of curds, the color of ghee' (Pārā. 237); this is the intention. 'By making an effort' means: by any one of the four methods that have been mentioned—'one releases in an internal form, one releases in an external form, one releases in an internal-and-external form, one releases while shaking the hips in the air' (Pārā. 237)—at any of the five times that have been mentioned—'one releases due to the pressure of lust, one releases due to the pressure of feces, one releases due to the pressure of urine, one releases due to the pressure of wind, one releases due to the pressure from the bite of a crawling creature'—when the sexual organ has become ready for action, with any of the ten intentions that have been mentioned—'one releases for the sake of health, for the sake of pleasure, for the sake of medicine, for the sake of a gift, for the sake of merit, for the sake of a sacrifice, for the sake of heaven, for the sake of seed, for the sake of testing, for the sake of sport' (Pārā. 237)—having made an effort by any means such as with the hand; this is the meaning. 'They release' means: they release even an amount that a small fly could drink; this is the meaning. 'Except in a dream' means: excluding that emission of semen which occurs in a dream; this is the meaning. 'A recluse' means any who is fully ordained. 'A grave offense' means a Saṅghādisesa. 'Touches' means one would incur; this is the meaning.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The first training rule on the emission of semen.

20. Idāni kāyasaṃsaggaṃ dīpetuṃ “itthisaññī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha itthisaññīti tadahujātāyapi manussitthiyā itthisaññīyeva hutvāti attho. Sace tattha vematiko vā paṇḍakapurisatiracchānagatasaññī vā hoti, thullaccayaṃ, tathā itthiyā kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhāmasane ca kāyappaṭibaddhena kāyāmasane ca yakkhīpetīpaṇḍakānaṃ kāyena kāyāmasane ca. Purisatiracchānagatitthīnaṃ pana kāyena kāyāmasanepi dukkaṭaṃ, tathā yakkhīādīnaṃ kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhādīsu [M 0.0076] ca. Matitthiyā pana thullaccayaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgavāti iminā mātupemādiṃ mokkhādhippāyañca paṭikkhipati. Samphusantoti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena upakkamma antamaso lomenapi manussitthiṃ samphusantoti atthasambandho. Iminā yo itthiyā āliṅgatopi kāyena na vāyamati, kevalaṃ phassaṃyeva anubhavati, tassa anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hoti.

20. Now, to clarify bodily contact, the passage beginning 'perceiving her to be a woman' is introduced. Therein, 'perceiving her to be a woman' means perceiving as a woman even a human female born that very day; this is the meaning. If one is uncertain, or perceives her as a eunuch, a male, or an animal, it is a thullaccaya offense. Likewise, it is a thullaccaya offense for touching a woman's body with one's body, for touching something connected to her body with one's body, for touching her body with something connected to one's body, and for touching the body of a female spirit, a female hungry ghost, or a eunuch with one's body. However, for touching the body of a male or female animal with one's body, it is a dukkaṭa offense; and likewise for touching the body of a female spirit, etc., with something connected to one's body, and so on. For a deceased woman, it is a thullaccaya offense. By the phrase 'with lust for bodily contact,' affection for one's mother and so on, as well as the intention for liberation, are excluded. 'Touching' means that, having made an effort out of lust for bodily contact, one touches a human woman, even with a single hair; this is the connection of the meaning. By this it is shown that there is no offense for one who, though being embraced by a woman, does not exert his body but merely experiences the contact.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The second training rule on bodily contact.

21. Idāni duṭṭhullavācaṃ pakāsetuṃ “tathā suṇanti”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tathāti itthisaññī. Manussitthiṃ suṇantinti sambandho. Suṇantinti iminā paṭibalāyapi itthiyā aviññattipathe ṭhitāya dūtena vā paṇṇena vā ārocentassa duṭṭhullavācāpattina hotīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Viññuñcāti iminā yā mahallikāpi bālāpi eḷamūgāpi asaddhammappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ na jānāti, sā idha nādhippetāti dasseti. Vaccamaggapassāvamaggānaṃ vasena maggaṃ vā methunaṃ vā ārabbhāti sambandho. Duṭṭhullavācāya rāgo duṭṭhullavācārāgo, tena duṭṭhullavācārāgena. Taṃ assādento obhāsetvā duruttavacanaṃ vatvā garukaṃ phuseti attho.

21. Now, to illuminate coarse speech, the passage beginning 'in such a way that she hears' is introduced. Therein, 'in such a way' means perceiving her to be a woman. The connection is 'to a human woman who hears.' By 'who hears,' it is shown that an offense of coarse speech is not incurred by one who informs a woman, even a capable one, by messenger or by letter, when she is beyond the range of direct communication. By 'and intelligent,' it is shown that a woman who does not understand speech connected with the unseemly act—be she elderly, a child, or a deaf-mute—is not intended here. The connection is: concerning the 'path'—meaning the path of feces and the path of urine—or concerning sexual intercourse. Lust for coarse speech is 'lust-for-coarse-speech'; with that lust for coarse speech, enjoying it, one addresses her, speaks a lewd word, and 'touches' a grave offense; this is the meaning.

Kathaṃ dve magge ārabbha pasaṃsati garahati? Tattha pasaṃsāyapi tāva “itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti vadati, na tāvasīsaṃ eti. “Tava vaccamaggo ca passāvamaggo ca subho susaṇṭhāno dassanīyo, īdisena nāma itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti [V 0.0083] vadati, sīsaṃ eti, saṅghādiseso hotīti attho. Garahaṇe pana “sikharaṇīsi, sambhinnāsi, ubhatobyañjanāsī”ti imāni tīṇi suddhāniyeva sīsaṃ enti vaccamaggapassāvamaggānaṃ niyatavacanattā accoḷārikattā ca. Aññāni pana “animittāsi, nimittamattāsī”tiādīni [M 0.0077] maggānaṃ aniyatavacanattā methunena ghaṭetvā vuttāni eva sīsaṃ enti. Methunappaṭisaṃyutte “dehi me, arahasi me dātu”ntiādīhi pana sīsaṃ na eti, “methunadhammaṃ dehī”tiādinā methunadhamme ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso. Itthiyā vaccamaggapassāvamagge ṭhapetvā adhakkhakaṃ ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ ādissa vaṇṇādibhaṇane thullaccayaṃ, tathā yakkhīpetīpaṇḍakesu vaccamaggapassāvamagge methunepi. Imesaṃ pana yakkhīādīnaṃ adhakkhakādike vuttappakāre padese duṃkkaṭaṃ, tathā itthiyādīnaṃ ubbhakkhake adhojāṇumaṇḍale kāyappaṭibaddhe cāti.

How does one praise or disparage concerning the two paths? Therein, regarding praise, if one says, 'You are endowed with the marks of a woman, with auspicious marks,' this does not yet reach the head of the offense. But if one says, 'Your path of feces and path of urine are beautiful, well-formed, and lovely; you are endowed with such marks of a woman, with such auspicious marks,' it reaches the head, meaning it becomes a Saṅghādisesa offense. Regarding disparagement, these three terms—'you are a sikharaṇī,' 'you are deformed,' 'you are a hermaphrodite'—in and of themselves reach the head, because they are specific terms for the path of feces and the path of urine, and because of their extreme coarseness. But other terms, such as 'you are without a sign,' 'you are merely a sign,' and so on, because they are not specific terms for the paths, only reach the head when spoken in connection with sexual intercourse. Regarding speech connected to sexual intercourse, phrases like 'Give to me,' 'You ought to give to me,' and so on, do not reach the head of the offense; a Saṅghādisesa is incurred only when it is connected to the act of intercourse, such as by saying, 'Give me the act of intercourse.' For a woman, speaking of the qualities of any part below the collarbone and above the kneecap, excluding the path of feces and the path of urine, is a thullaccaya offense. The same applies to a female spirit, a female hungry ghost, or a eunuch, regarding their path of feces, path of urine, and sexual intercourse. For these beings—female spirits and so on—to speak of the aforementioned regions below the collarbone is a dukkaṭa offense; likewise, for women and so on, to speak of the region above the collarbone, below the kneecap, or of things connected to the body, is also a dukkaṭa offense.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The third training rule on coarse speech.

22. Idāni attakāmapāricariyaṃ dassetuṃ “vatvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vatvāti duṭṭhullobhāsane vuttappakāraṃ itthiṃ itthisaññīyeva hutvā vatvāti attho. Attakāmupaṭṭhānavaṇṇanti ettha methunadhammasaṅkhātena kāmena upaṭṭhānaṃ kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ, attano atthāya kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ, attanā vā kāmitaṃ icchitanti attakāmaṃ, sayaṃ methunarāgavasena patthitanti attho, attakāmañca taṃ upaṭṭhānañcāti attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ, tassa vaṇṇo attakāmupaṭṭhānavaṇṇo, taṃ attakāmupaṭṭhānavaṇṇaṃ. “Etadaggaṃ, bhagini, pāricariyānaṃ yā mādisaṃ sīlavantaṃ kalyāṇadhammaṃ brahmacāriṃ etena dhammena paricareyyā”ti evaṃ vatvāti sambandho. Methunarāginoti iminā gilānapaccayādīhi upaṭṭhānassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇato anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Vācā methunayuttenāti ettha methunayutteneva vācāya methunayācane garukaṃ hoti, na aññathāti adhippāyo.

22. Now, to show the service for one's own gratification, the phrase 'having said' and so forth is stated. Here, 'having said' means having spoken to a woman, perceiving her as a woman, in the manner of coarse speech as previously described. Regarding 'the praise of service for one's own gratification': Here, service through the act of sexual intercourse is called 'service of desire.' Service of desire for one's own sake is 'service for one's own gratification.' Alternatively, 'one's own gratification' means that which is desired or wished for by oneself—that is, desired by oneself out of sexual lust. And that which is both for one's own gratification and a service is 'service for one's own gratification'; the praise of that is 'the praise of service for one's own gratification.' The connection is to be made thus: 'Sister, this is the foremost of services: that one should attend to someone like me—virtuous, of good character, and practicing celibacy—with this act.' By this phrase 'with sexual lust,' it is indicated that there is no offense in praising service such as attending with requisites for the sick. Regarding 'speech connected with sexual intercourse': the intention here is that the offense is serious only with speech connected with requesting sexual intercourse, and not otherwise.

Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadaṃ catutthaṃ.

The fourth training rule on service for one's own gratification.

23. Idāni [M 0.0078] sañcarittaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭiggahetvā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭiggahetvāti itthiyā vā purisena vā ubhinnaṃ mātādīhi vā “bhante, itthannāmaṃ itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti vutto tesaṃ vacanaṃ “sādhū”ti vā “hotū”ti vā “bhaṇāmī”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena vacībhedaṃ katvā, sīsakampanādīhi vā sampaṭicchitvāti attho. Sandesanti ettha [V 0.0084] pana itthī dasavidhā māturakkhitā piturakkhitā mātāpiturakkhitā bhāturakkhitā bhaginirakkhitā ñātirakkhitā gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā sārakkhā saparidaṇḍāti. Dasa bhariyāyo dhanakkītā chandavāsinī bhogavāsinī paṭavāsinī odapattakinī obhaṭacumbaṭakā dāsī ca bhariyā ca kammakārī ca bhariyā ca dhajāhaṭā muhuttikā cāti.

23. Now, to illustrate acting as a go-between, the passage beginning with 'having accepted' and so forth is commenced. Here, 'having accepted' means that when a woman or a man, or the mothers and so on of both, say, 'Venerable, tell this woman or man such and such,' and one responds with any verbal expression such as 'good,' 'very well,' or 'I will say it,' or by accepting with a nod of the head and so on, thus making a verbal utterance by any means, that is the meaning of having accepted. Regarding 'message' here, a woman is of ten kinds: one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by both parents, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her lineage, one protected by the Dhamma, one under her own protection, and one subject to punishment. There are also ten kinds of wives: one bought with wealth, one living by consent, one living for material support, one living for clothing, one acquired by the water-pot ceremony, one acquired by removing the head-pad, a slave who is also a wife, a servant who is also a wife, one captured in war, and a temporary wife.

Tāsu māturakkhitā bhikkhuṃ pahiṇati “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ brūhi ‘homi itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā…pe… muhuttikā cā”ti, ayaṃ itthiyā sandeso nāma. Sace māturakkhitāya mātāpitābhātābhaginiādayo bhikkhuṃ pahiṇanti “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ brūhi ‘hotu itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā…pe… muhuttikā cā”ti, ayampi itthiyā sandesoyeva nāma. Evaṃ piturakkhitādīsupi nayo netabbo. Puriso bhikkhuṃ pahiṇati “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ māturakkhitaṃ brūhi…pe… saparidaṇḍaṃ brūhi ‘hotu kira itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā…pe… muhuttikā cā”ti, ayaṃ purisassa sandeso nāma. Sace purisassa mātāpitābhātābhaginiādayo bhikkhuṃ pahiṇanti “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ māturakkhitaṃ brūhi…pe… saparidaṇḍaṃ brūhi ‘hotu itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā…pe… muhuttikā cā”ti, ayampi purisassa sandesoyeva nāma, āṇāpananti attho.

Among these, a mother-protected woman sends a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir, and tell so-and-so, “I will be so-and-so’s wife, whether bought with wealth… or temporarily.”' This is called the woman’s message. If the mother, father, brother, sister, or others of a mother-protected woman send a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir, and tell so-and-so, “Let her be so-and-so’s wife, whether bought with wealth… or temporarily.”' This too is called the woman’s message. The same method should be applied in the cases of father-protected women and so on. A man sends a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir, and tell so-and-so, the mother-protected one… or the one subject to punishment, “Let her be so-and-so’s wife, whether bought with wealth… or temporarily.”' This is called the man’s message. If the mother, father, brother, sister, or others of a man send a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir, and tell so-and-so, the mother-protected one… or the one subject to punishment, “Let her be so-and-so’s wife, whether bought with wealth… or temporarily.”' This too is called the man’s message—the meaning is a command.

Vīmaṃsitvāti [M 0.0079] ettha vuttappakārena sāsanaṃ gahetvā tassā itthiyā vā purisassa vā tesaṃ avassārocanakānaṃ mātāpitābhātābhaginiādīnaṃ vā ārocetvāti attho. Haranti yattha pahito, tattha gantvā tassā itthiyā vā purisassa vā āroceti, sā itthī vā puriso vā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchatu vā, mā vā, lajjāya vā tuṇhī hotu, puna āgantvā tassā itthiyā vā purisassa vā haranto garukaṃ phuseti sambandho. Ettāvatā “paṭiggaṇhati vīmaṃsati paccāharatī”ti vuttaṃ aṅgattayaṃ sampāditaṃ hoti. Imāya tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso, ito yehi kehici dvīhi aṅgehi thullaccayaṃ, ekena dukkaṭaṃ. Yakkhīpetīpaṇḍakesu aṅgattayenapi thullaccayameva, ekena vā dvīhi vā dukkaṭanti.

Regarding 'having investigated': having taken the message in the manner stated, the meaning is that one informs that woman or man, or their parents, brothers, sisters, and so on, who must be informed. Having gone where one was sent, one informs that woman or man. Whether that woman or man accepts it with 'Good,' or not, or remains silent out of shame, upon returning and delivering the reply on behalf of that woman or man, one commits a serious offense; this is the connection. By this much, the threefold factor stated as 'accepts, investigates, brings back' is accomplished. With the fulfillment of these three factors, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. With any two of these factors, it is a thullaccaya offense; with one, a dukkaṭa offense. In the case of female yakkhas, female petas, and paṇḍakas, even with all three factors it is only a thullaccaya offense; with one or two factors, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The fifth training rule on acting as a go-between.

24. Idāni kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ āvi kātuṃ “saṃyācitaparikkhāra”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ [V 0.0085] saṅkhepattho – “vāsiṃ detha, pharasuṃ dethā”tiādinā sayaṃ pavattitayācanāya gahitaparikkhāraṃ saṃyācitaparikkhāraṃ padabhājane vuttanayena saṅghaṃ tikkhattuṃ yācitvā laddhabhikkhūhi vā saṅgheneva vā tattha gantvā sārambhānārambhasaparikkamanāparikkamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā adesitavatthukaṃ “kuṭi nāma ullittā vā hoti avalittā vā ullittāvalittā vā”ti (pārā. 349) evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ kuṭiṃ. “Tatridaṃ pamāṇaṃ, dīghaso dvādasa vidatthiyo sugatavidatthiyā, tiriyaṃ sattantarā”ti (pārā. 348) evaṃ vuttapamāṇātikkantaṃ, “mayhaṃ vāsāgāraṃ esā”ti evaṃ attā uddeso etissāti attuddesā, taṃ attuddesaṃ katvā garuṃ saṅghādisesaṃ phuseti sambandho. Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo – adesitavatthukaṃ [M 0.0080] pamāṇātikkantaṃ kunthakipillikādīnaṃ āsaye katattā sārambhaṃ dvīhi balībaddehi yuttena sakaṭena gantuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya aparikkamanaṃ ullittādibhedaṃ kuṭiṃ attano vasanatthāya karonto vā kārāpento vā “idāni niṭṭhānaṃ gamissatī”ti paṭhamapiṇḍadāne thullaccayaṃ, dutiyapiṇḍadānena lepe ghaṭite dve ca saṅghādisese dve ca dukkaṭāni, sace desitavatthukāyeva vā pamāṇātikkantāyeva vā hoti, ekaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ dve ca dukkaṭāni āpajjatīti.

24. Now, to clarify the training rule on hut-making, the passage beginning with 'requisites obtained by requesting' and so forth is commenced. Here is the summary of its meaning: 'Give an adze, give an axe,' and so on—requisites obtained through such self-initiated requests are called 'requisites obtained by requesting.' As explained in the word analysis, after requesting the Sangha three times and obtaining permission through bhikkhus or the Sangha itself, one goes there and determines whether the site has living beings or not, and whether it is accessible or not. Without the site having been designated, a hut is defined as 'plastered or unplastered, or plastered and unplastered.' If it exceeds the prescribed measurement—'Here, the measurement is twelve spans in length according to the Sugata’s span, seven spans in width within'—and if one makes it for one's own use, saying, 'This is my dwelling,' then by doing so, one commits a serious saṅghādisesa offense; this is the connection. Here is the judgment in this matter: If one builds or has built a hut for one's own use—without the site having been designated, exceeding the measurement, on a site with living beings as it is a habitat for insects and ants, inaccessible such that it cannot be reached by a cart yoked with two strong bulls, and of the plastered, etc., type—then at the first application of a lump of material, thinking 'now it will be completed,' one commits a thullaccaya offense. At the second application of a lump, when the plaster is applied, two saṅghādisesa offenses and two dukkaṭa offenses are incurred. If it is either without a designated site only, or exceeding the measurement only, one incurs one saṅghādisesa and two dukkaṭa offenses.

Kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth training rule on hut-making.

25. Idāni vihārakārasikkhāpadaṃ dassetuṃ “mahallaka”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mahallakanti sassāmikabhāvena saṃyācitakuṭito mahantabhāvo etassa atthi, yasmā vā vatthuṃ desāpetvā pamāṇātikkamenāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā pamāṇamahantatāyapi mahallako, taṃ mahallakaṃ vihāraṃ vā katvāti attho. Ettha pana adesitavatthukabhāvena eko saṅghādiseso, sesaṃ anantarasadisameva. Idha ca tattha ca vāsāgāraṃ ṭhapetvā uposathāgāraṃ vā jantāgharaṃ vā aggisālaṃ vā bhavissatīti evamādinā nayena karontassa anāpatti.

25. Now, to explain the training rule on building a monastery, the passage beginning with 'large' and so forth is commenced. Here, 'large' means that it is of a greater status than a hut built by requesting, as it is built with a donor; or, because it is permissible to build it even exceeding the prescribed dimensions after having the site designated, it is therefore also 'large' due to its great size. The meaning is: having built that large monastery. However, here, there is one saṅghādisesa offense due to the site being undesignated; the remainder is similar to the immediately preceding rule. And in both this rule and that one, there is no offense for one who builds, excluding a dwelling, an Uposatha hall, a steam bath, or a fire hall, with such an intention.

Vihārakārasikkhāpadaṃ sattamaṃ.

The seventh training rule on building a monastery.

26. Idāni amūlakasikkhāpadaṃ pakāsetuṃ “amūlakenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha amūlakenāti yaṃ codakena cuditakamhi puggale adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, idaṃ etesaṃ dassanasavanaparisaṅkāsaṅkhātānaṃ mūlānaṃ abhāvato amūlakaṃ, tena amūlakena vatthunāti sambandho. Tattha [V 0.0086] adiṭṭhaṃ nāma attano pasādacakkhunā vā dibbacakkhunā vā adiṭṭhaṃ. Asutaṃ [M 0.0081] nāma tatheva kenaci vuccamānaṃ na sutaṃ. Aparisaṅkitaṃ nāma cittena aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ pana diṭṭhasutamutavasena tividhaṃ. Tattha bhikkhuñca mātugāmañca tathārūpe ṭhāne disvā “addhā imehi kata”nti vā “karissantī”ti vā parisaṅkati, idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma. Andhakāre paṭicchannokāse vā bhikkhussa ca mātugāmassa ca vacanaṃ sutvā dutiyassa atthibhāvaṃ ajānanto pubbe vuttanayena parisaṅkati, idaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma. Dhuttehi itthīhi saddhiṃ paccantavihāresu pupphagandhasurādīhi anubhavitvā gataṭṭhānaṃ disvā “kena nu kho idaṃ kata”nti vīmaṃsanto tatra kenaci bhikkhunā gandhādīhi pūjā katā hoti, bhesajjatthāya ariṭṭhaṃ vā pītaṃ, so tassa gandhaṃ ghāyitvā “ayaṃ so bhavissatī”ti parisaṅkati, idaṃ mutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma. Evaṃ tividhāya parisaṅkāya abhāvena aparisaṅkitanti attho.

26. Now, to expound the groundless training rule, the passage beginning with 'groundlessly' and so forth is commenced. Herein, 'groundlessly' means, with regard to a person who has been accused by an accuser, something unseen, unheard, or unsuspected. This is called groundless because it lacks these roots, namely seeing, hearing, and suspicion; that is the connection to the groundless matter. Herein, 'unseen' means not seen with one’s own physical eye or divine eye. 'Unheard' means not heard being said by anyone. 'Unsuspected' means not suspected by the mind. This suspicion, however, is threefold, based on what is seen, heard, or sensed. Herein, seeing a bhikkhu and a woman in such a place, one suspects, 'Surely they have done this' or 'They will do it'—this is called suspicion based on seeing. Hearing the voices of a bhikkhu and a woman in darkness or in a concealed place, and not knowing of the presence of a second person, one suspects in the manner previously stated—this is called suspicion based on hearing. Seeing a place in border monasteries where wanton women have gone after enjoying flowers, perfumes, liquor, and so on, and wondering, 'Who has done this?'—if a bhikkhu has made offerings with perfumes and so on, or has drunk ariṭṭha for medicinal purposes, and someone, smelling the scent, suspects, 'This must be him'—this is called suspicion based on sensing. Thus, 'unsuspected' means the absence of these three kinds of suspicion.

Codentoti “pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosi, assamaṇosi, asakyaputtiyosī”tiādīhi vacanehi sayaṃ codentoti attho. Evaṃ codentassa vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso. Codāpento vāti attanā tassa samīpe ṭhatvā aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetvā codāpento tassa āṇattassa vācāya vācāya garuṃ phuseti attho. Atha sopi cāvanādhippāyena “mayāpi diṭṭhaṃ atthī”tiādinā nayena codeti, dvinnampi vācāya āpatti. Vatthunā antimena cāti bhikkhuno anurūpesu ekūnavīsatiyā pārājikesu aññatarenāti attho. Cāvetunti brahmacariyā cāvetuṃ, yo suddhaṃ vā asuddhaṃ vā katūpasampadaṃ puggalaṃ suddhadiṭṭhiko samāno cāvanādhippāyena codeti vā codāpeti vā, tassa saṅghādisesoti adhippāyo. Suṇamānanti iminā parammukhā dūtena vā paṇṇena vā codeti. Codentassa [M 0.0082] na ruhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Parammukhā pana sattahi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

'Accusing' means oneself accusing with words such as, 'You have committed a pārājika offense, you are no ascetic, you are no son of the Sakyan.' For each utterance when thus accusing, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. 'Or causing another to accuse' means standing near him and ordering another bhikkhu to accuse; for each utterance of the one ordered, he incurs a grave offense. Then, if that one also accuses with the intention of expulsion, saying, for instance, 'I too have seen it,' an offense is incurred for each utterance of both. And 'with the final matter' means with any one of the nineteen pārājika offenses appropriate for a bhikkhu. 'To expel' means to expel from the holy life. The intention is that if someone, being pure in view, accuses or causes another to accuse a person who has received a pure or impure ordination with the intention of expulsion, it is a saṅghādisesa. By the implication of the accused 'hearing', it is shown that if one accuses in absence, through a messenger or a letter, the offense does not arise for the accuser. However, for speaking in absence concerning the seven classes of offenses, there is a dukkaṭa.

Amūlakasikkhāpadaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The eighth, the groundless training rule.

27. Idāni aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadaṃ dassetuṃ “aññassa kiriya”ntiādimāha. Tattha aññassa kiriyanti aññassa khattiyādijātikassa pārājikassa vītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ kiriyaṃ disvāti sambandho. Tena lesenāti “dasa lesā jātileso nāmaleso gottaleso liṅgaleso āpattileso pattaleso cīvaraleso upajjhāyaleso ācariyaleso senāsanaleso”ti (pārā. 394) evaṃ [V 0.0087] vuttesu dasasu lesesu yo tasmiṃ puggale dissati, tena lesena tadaññaṃ puggalaṃ brahmacariyā cāvetuṃ antimavatthunā codento garukaṃ phuseti attho. Tattha aññampi vatthuṃ lissati silissati vohāramatteneva īsakaṃ allīyatīti leso, jātiyeva leso jātileso. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Lesena codento kathaṃ codeti? Añño khattiyajātiko iminā codakena pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto diṭṭho hoti, so aññaṃ attano veriṃ khattiyajātikaṃ bhikkhuṃ passitvā taṃ khattiyajātilesaṃ gahetvā evaṃ codeti “khattiyo mayā diṭṭho pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto, tvampi khattiyo pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosī”ti vā “so tvaṃ khattiyo, nāñño, pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī”ti vā codeti. Evaṃ nāmalesādayopi veditabbā.

27. Now, to present the training rule concerning a partial matter, the passage beginning with 'another's act' is stated. Herein, 'another's act' is connected thus: having seen an act, designated as a transgression of a pārājika, committed by another person, for instance, of the khattiya caste. 'By that pretext' means: among the ten pretexts stated thus, 'There are ten pretexts: pretext of birth, pretext of name, pretext of clan, pretext of gender, pretext of offense, pretext of bowl, pretext of robe, pretext of preceptor, pretext of teacher, pretext of dwelling' (Pārā. 394), by whichever pretext is seen in that person, accusing another person with the ultimate matter with the intent to expel him from the holy life, means that he incurs a grave offense. Herein, a pretext (lesa) is so called because another matter clings (lissati), adheres (silissati), or is slightly connected (īsakaṃ allīyati) merely by verbal convention. Birth itself is the pretext, hence 'pretext of birth'. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. How does one accuse by a pretext? Another person of the khattiya caste is seen by this accuser committing a pārājika offense. Then, seeing another bhikkhu of the khattiya caste who is his enemy, he seizes upon that pretext of khattiya birth and accuses him thus: 'A khattiya was seen by me committing a pārājika offense; you too are a khattiya, you have committed a pārājika offense,' or 'It is you who are that khattiya, not another; you have committed a pārājika offense.' In the same way, the pretexts of name and so on should be understood.

Aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadaṃ navamaṃ.

The ninth, the training rule on a partial matter.

28. Ettāvatā [M 0.0083] “garukā navā”ti uddiṭṭhe vitthārato dassetvā idāni tesu āpannesu paṭipajjanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “chādeti jānamāpanna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassāyaṃ piṇḍattho – yo bhikkhu “ayaṃ itthannāmā āpattī”ti āpattivasena vā “idaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti evaṃ vatthuvasena vā jānamāpannaṃ āpattiṃ yāva chādeti, tāva tena bhikkhunā akāmā parivāso vasitabboti. Careyyāti mānattaṃ samādāya vaseyya. Kittakaṃ divasanti ce? Cha rattiyo. Mānattavāso pana saṅgheyeva, na gaṇe, na puggale, tena vuttaṃ “saṅghe”ti. Parivutthoti “tayo kho upāli pārivāsikassa bhikkhuno ratticchedā sahavāso vippavāso anārocanā”ti (cūḷava. 83) evaṃ vuttaṃ ratticchedaṃ akatvā parivutthoti attho. Tattha sahavāsoti pakatattena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekacchanne udakapātaṭṭhānabbhantare vāso. Vippavāso nāma aññaṃ pakatattaṃ bhikkhuṃ vinā vāso. Anārocanāti āgantukādīnaṃ anārocanā. Etesu tīsu ekenāpi ratticchedo hoti eva. Ettha pana upacārasīmagatānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ, na bahi ṭhitānaṃ, bahi ṭhitānampi sace saddaṃ suṇāti, passati, dūraṃ vā gantvā ārocetabbameva, anārocentassa ratticchedo ceva vattabhede dukkaṭañca hoti. Ajānantasseva upacārasīmaṃ pavisitvā gacchanti ce, ratticchedova hoti, na vattabhedo.

28. Having thus explained in detail the nine serious offenses that were specified, now, to show the procedure to be followed when one has committed them, the passage beginning 'he conceals, knowing he has committed an offense' is stated. The summary of this is: for as long as a bhikkhu conceals an offense, knowing it either as an offense, thinking, 'This is an offense of such-and-such a name,' or as a matter, thinking, 'This is not allowable for bhikkhus,' for that long must that bhikkhu unwillingly undergo probation (parivāsa). 'He should practice' means he should undertake and live the penance (mānatta). If it is asked, 'For how many days?' For six nights. The residence for the penance, however, is only in a Saṅgha, not in a group, nor with an individual; hence it is said 'in a Saṅgha.'
