'Having completed probation' means having completed it without a break in the nights, as it is said: 'Upāli, there are three breaks in the nights for a probationary bhikkhu: co-residence, separation, and non-reporting' (Cūḷavagga 83). Herein, 'co-residence' means living with a bhikkhu in good standing under one roof or within the boundary of a water-splash. 'Separation' means living without another bhikkhu in good standing. 'Non-reporting' means not reporting to visiting bhikkhus and so on. A break in the nights occurs through even one of these three. Here, one must report to those who have entered the precincts of the boundary, not to those standing outside. Even for those standing outside, if one can hear their voice or see them, one must go some distance and report. For one who does not report, there is a break in the nights and also a dukkaṭa for a breach of duties. If they enter the precincts of the boundary without one's knowledge and then depart, there is only a break in the nights, not a breach of duties.

Ciṇṇamānattanti “cattāro kho, upāli, mānattacārikassa bhikkhuno ratticchedā sahavāso [V 0.0088] vippavāso anārocanā ūne gaṇe caraṇa”nti (cūḷava. 92) evaṃ vuttaṃ ratticchedaṃ akatvā ciṇṇamānattaṃ pariniṭṭhitamānattanti attho. Ettha pana sahavāsādayo parivāse vuttappakārā eva. “Ūne gaṇe caraṇa”nti ettha gaṇo cattāro vā atirekā vā bhikkhū, tasmā [M 0.0084] sacepi tīhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ vasati, ratticchedo hotiyeva, “sace pana tena tesaṃ atthibhāvaṃ disvā ārocite pakkamanti, ūne gaṇe caraṇadoso na hotī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 97) aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ kira. Abbheyyāti taṃ bhikkhuṃ vīsatigaṇo saṅgho abbheyya sampaṭiccheyya, abbhānakammavasena osāreyyāti attho. Sace ekenapi ūno vīsatigaṇo bhikkhusaṅgho taṃ bhikkhuṃ abbheyya, so ca bhikkhu na abbhito, te ca bhikkhū gārayhā, dukkaṭaṃ āpajjantīti attho.

'Having completed the penance' means having completed the penance without a break in the nights, as it is said: 'Upāli, there are four breaks in the nights for a bhikkhu practicing the penance: co-residence, separation, non-reporting, and practicing in an incomplete group' (Cūḷavagga 92); it means the penance is finished. Here, co-residence and so on are of the same kind as described for probation. Regarding 'practicing in an incomplete group,' a group here is four or more bhikkhus. Therefore, if one lives with only three bhikkhus, it is indeed a break in the nights. It is said in the commentaries: 'But if, having seen their presence and reported, they depart, there is no fault of practicing in an incomplete group' (Cūḷavagga-aṭṭhakathā 97). 'Should recall' means a Saṅgha of twenty bhikkhus should recall that bhikkhu, should accept him back; it means they should reinstate him by means of the act of recall. If a Saṅgha of bhikkhus even one short of twenty should recall that bhikkhu, that bhikkhu is not recalled, and those bhikkhus are blameworthy and incur a dukkaṭa; this is the meaning.

29. Idāni yathā chāditā āpatti channā hoti, taṃ pakāraṃ dassetuṃ “āpattī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ padayojanā – āpattitā ca anukkhittatā ca anantarāyatā ca pahuttatā ca āpattinukkhittaanantarāyapahuttatāyo, etāsu catūsu tathāsaññitā ca chādetukāmo hutvā chādanā cāti evaṃ dasahaṅgehi aruṇuggamamhi channā hotīti. Ettha pana āpattiādīsu catūsu āpattisaññitā ca anukkhittasaññitā ca anantarāyasaññitā ca pahuttasaññitā cāti evaṃ saññāvasena yojetvā aṭṭhaṅgāni gahetabbāni, chādetukāmoti idamekaṃ, chādanāti idamekanti evaṃ dasa.

29. Now, to show how a covered offense becomes concealed, the passage beginning 'an offense' is stated. Herein, this is the arrangement of terms: the fact of it being an offense, not being suspended, having no obstacles, and being capable. In regard to these four, there is the corresponding perception, the desire to conceal, and the act of concealment—thus, with these ten factors, it becomes concealed at the rising of the dawn. Here, however, regarding the four beginning with 'offense,' by combining them with perception—namely, perception of it as an offense, perception of it as not suspended, perception of it as having no obstacles, and perception of it as capable—eight factors should be understood. The desire to conceal is one, and the act of concealment is one; thus there are ten.

Etesu pana ādito paṭṭhāya ayaṃ vinicchayo – “āpatti ca hoti āpattisaññī cā”ti ettha yaṃ āpanno, sā terasannaṃ aññatarā hoti, sopi ca tattha garukāpattisaññīyeva hutvā jānanto chādeti, channā hoti. Sace tattha anāpattisaññī vā aññāpattisaññī vā vematiko vā hoti, acchannāva hoti. Tividhaṃ pana ukkhepanīyakammaṃ, tena akato anukkhitto. So [M 0.0085] ce pakatattasaññī hutvā chādeti, channā hoti. Sace apakatattasaññī chādeti, acchannā hoti. Apakatattena pana pakatattasaññināpi apakatattasaññināpi chāditaṃ acchāditameva hotīti. Anantarāyikoti yassa dasasu rājacoraaggiudakamanussāmanussavāḷasarīsapajīvitabrahmacariyantarāyesupi ekopi natthi, so ce anantarāyikasaññī hutvā chādeti, channā hoti. Sace so andhakārabhīruko anantarāye eva vāḷādiantarāyasaññī hutvā chādeti, acchannāva hoti. Pahūti yo sakkoti sabhāgabhikkhuno samīpaṃ gantuñceva ārocituñca[V 0.0089], so ce pahusaññī hutvā chādeti, channā hoti. Yo pana apahu hutvā pahusaññī, pahu vā apahusaññī hutvā chādeti, acchannāva hotīti.

Regarding these, the analysis, beginning from the first, is as follows: In the case of 'there is an offense, and one is aware of it as an offense,' whatever offense one has committed, it is one of the thirteen. If that person, aware of it as a grave offense, knowingly conceals it, then it is concealed. If one is unaware of it as an offense, or aware of it as a different offense, or is in doubt, then it remains unconcealed. The act of suspension is threefold; one who has not been subjected to it is not suspended. If such a one, perceiving oneself as a monk in good standing, conceals it, then it is concealed. If one with the perception of not being a monk in good standing conceals it, it remains unconcealed. However, if one who is not a monk in good standing conceals it, whether perceiving oneself as in good standing or not, it remains unconcealed. 'Free from obstacles' refers to one for whom there is not even one among the ten obstacles: from kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild beasts, reptiles, danger to life, or danger to the holy life. If such a one, aware of being free from obstacles, conceals it, then it is concealed. But if one, being fearful of darkness, perceives an obstacle such as a wild beast even when there is no real obstacle, and conceals it, then it remains unconcealed. 'Capable' refers to one who is able to go to a fellow monk and inform them. If such a one, aware of being capable, conceals it, then it is concealed. But if one who is incapable but perceives oneself as capable, or who is capable but perceives oneself as incapable, conceals it, then it remains unconcealed.

Aruṇuggamamhīti ettha purebhattaṃ vā āpattiṃ āpanno hoti pacchābhattaṃ vā, yāva aruṇaṃ na uggacchati, tāva ārocetabbā. Sace pana aruṇabbhantare satakkhattumpi chādetukāmatā uppajjati, acchannāva hoti. Ārocento pana sabhāgasaṅghādisesaṃ āpannassa ārocetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace āroceti, āpatti pana āvikatā hoti, ārocanapaccayā pana aññaṃ dukkaṭaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Iminā aññampi vatthusabhāgāpattiṃ ārocetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dīpito hoti. Ārocentena pana “ahaṃ tava santike ekaṃ āpattiṃ āvi karomī”ti vā “ācikkhāmī”ti vā “ārocemī”ti vā “ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpannabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti vā “ekaṃ garukāpattiṃ āvi karomī”ti vā ādinā nayena vattabbaṃ, ettāvatā acchannāva hoti. Sace “lahukāpattiṃ ārocemī”ti vadati, channāva hotīti. Saṅghādisesavinicchayo.

Regarding 'at the rising of the dawn': whether one has committed an offense before the meal or after the meal, it should be disclosed before the dawn has risen. But if, before the dawn has risen, the desire to conceal it arises even a hundred times, it remains unconcealed. However, when disclosing, it is not proper to disclose to one who has fallen into a Saṅghādisesa offense of the same kind. If one does disclose it to such a person, the offense becomes revealed, but on account of that disclosure one incurs another offense of wrong-doing. By this it is shown that it is not proper to disclose any other offense with a similar basis. When disclosing, one should say in this way: 'I am revealing an offense in your presence,' or 'I am declaring it,' or 'I am announcing it,' or 'Know that I have committed an offense,' or 'I am revealing a grave offense,' and so on. By this much, it remains unconcealed. But if one says, 'I am disclosing a light offense,' it becomes concealed. This is the determination on the Saṅghādisesa.

Saṅghādisesaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the exposition on the Saṅghādisesa.

3. Cīvaraniddesavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Exposition on Robes

30. Evaṃ [M 0.0086] garuke sikkhitabbākāraṃ dassetvā idāni cīvaresu dassetuṃ “cīvara”nti uddhaṭaṃ. Tattha jātito cha cīvarāni (mahāva. 339; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.462-463; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā), tāni kānīti ce, taṃ dassetuṃ “khomā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha khomaṃ nāma khomavākasuttehi kataṃ vatthaṃ. Sāṇaṃ nāma sāṇavākehi kataṃ vatthaṃ. Bhaṅgaṃ nāma khomasuttādīhi pañcahi missetvā kataṃ vatthaṃ. Pāṭekkaṃ vākamayameva vāti vadanti. Kambalaṃ nāma manussalomaṃ vāḷalomaṃ ṭhapetvā lomehi vāyitvā kataṃ vatthaṃ. Chaḷetānīti cha etāni. Saha anulomehīti sānulomāni. Jātito pana kappiyāni cha cīvarānīti vuttaṃ hoti.

30. Having thus shown the manner in which one should train in regard to the grave offenses, now, to explain about robes, the term 'robe' is cited. In this connection, by origin there are six kinds of robes. If it is asked what they are, to show this, the passage beginning 'linen' is stated. Herein, 'linen' (khoma) is cloth made from threads of flax bark. 'Hemp' (sāṇa) is cloth made from threads of hemp bark. 'Mixed cloth' (bhaṅga) is cloth made by mixing five kinds of thread, including linen thread. Some say that each of the former is made purely of bark-fiber. 'Woolen cloth' (kambala) is cloth woven from wool, excluding human hair and the hair of wild beasts. 'These six' (chaḷetāni) means these six. 'Together with the allowable kinds' (saha anulomehi) is sānulomāni. Thus it is said that by origin there are six kinds of allowable robes.

31. Idāni [V 0.0090] tesaṃ anulomāni dassetuṃ “dukūla”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 305) dukūlaṃ sāṇassa anulomaṃ vākamayattā. Paṭṭuṇṇanti paṭṭuṇṇadese pāṇakehi sañjātavatthaṃ. Somāradese, cīnadese jātaṃ somāracīnajaṃ paṭanti sambandho. Imāni tīṇipi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhijanti ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ. Taṃ pana khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hoti. Kapparukkhehi nibbattaṃ jāliniyā devakaññāya anuruddhattherassa dinnavatthādikaṃ devadinnaṃ. Tampi khomādīhi nibbattavatthasadisattā channampi anulomaṃ hotiyeva kappāsikassa vā, iddhijampi tatheva veditabbaṃ. Tassa tassāti khomādikassa. Anulomikanti anurūpaṃ.

31. Now, to show their allowable counterparts, the passage beginning 'dukūla' is stated. Herein, dukūla is an allowable counterpart of hemp because it is made of bark-fiber. Paṭṭuṇṇa is cloth produced by creatures in the Paṭṭuṇṇa country. What is produced in the Somāra country and the Cīna country is read as somāracīnaja; this is the connection. These three are allowable counterparts of silk because they are made of thread produced by creatures. Iddhija is a robe produced by the spiritual power of merit of the 'Come, bhikkhu' monks. But that is one of the kinds such as linen. Cloth produced by wishing-trees, such as that given by the celestial maiden Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha, is 'divinely given.' That too, being similar to cloth produced from linen and so on, is an allowable counterpart for all six, or for cotton. The magically created robe should be understood in the same way. 'Of each of these' (tassa tassa) refers to linen and so on. 'Allowable counterpart' (anulomika) means suitable.

32-33. Evaṃ jātito sānulomāni cha cīvarāni dassetvā idāni tesu adhiṭṭhānādikaṃ vidhānaṃ dassetuṃ “ticīvara”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kathinasikakhāpadavaṇṇanā; mahāva. 358) dhiṭṭhānato pubbe ticīvaraṃ nāma [M 0.0087] pāṭekkaṃ natthi saṅghāṭiādippahonakassa paccattharaṇādivasenāpi adhiṭṭhātuṃ anuññātattā. Tasmā “ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭheyya na vikappeyyā”ti ettha “imaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti evaṃ nāme gahite “adhiṭṭhāna”micceva vattabbaṃ, “vikappemī”ti pana na vattabbanti adhippāyo. Evaṃ sesesupi. Mukhapuñchanañca nisīdanañca mukhapuñchananisīdanaṃ. Kaṇḍucchādinti kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ adhiṭṭheyya, na vikappeyyāti sambandho. Etthāti imesu navasu cīvaresu. Ticīvaranti ticīvarādhiṭṭhānanayena adhiṭṭhitaticīvaraṃ. Vinā aladdhasammutiko bhikkhu avippavāsasammutialaddhaṭṭhāne ekāhampi hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā na vaseyyāti attho. “Na bhikkhave cātumāsaṃ nisīdanena vippavasitabbaṃ, yo vippavaseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti khuddakakkhandhake (cūḷava. 263) vuttattā cātumāsaṃ nisīdanaṃ vinā na vaseyyāti attho.

32-33. Having thus shown the six robes with their allowable counterparts by way of origin, now, to show the procedure for their determination and so on, the passage beginning 'the triple robe' is stated. Herein, before determination, there is no 'triple robe' as such, since it is permitted to determine what is sufficient for an outer robe, etc., also as a groundsheet, etc. Therefore, in the statement 'One should determine the triple robe, one should not make it common property,' the meaning is that when the name has been taken, as in 'this outer robe,' one should just say 'I determine it,' but one should not say 'I make it common property.' The same applies to the others. Mukhapuñchananisīdanaṃ is a face-towel and a sitting cloth. Kaṇḍucchādi means one should determine a scab-covering cloth, not make it common property; this is the connection. 'Herein' (etthā) refers to among these nine robes. 'Triple robe' (ticīvara) means the triple robe that has been determined by the method of determining the triple robe. The meaning is that a bhikkhu who has not received the permission for being away from his robes should not dwell for even a single day having left his triple robe out of his hand's reach in a place where he has not received that permission. Because it is said in the Khuddakakkhandhaka: 'Bhikkhus, one should not be separated from the sitting cloth for four months. Whoever should be separated from it commits an offense of wrong-doing,' the meaning is that one should not dwell without a sitting cloth for four months.

34. Idāni adhiṭṭhānavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “imaṃ saṅghāṭi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha miccadhiṭṭhayeti iti adhiṭṭhaye, “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti evaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhayeti attho. Ahatthapāsametanti dūre ṭhitaṃ pana ṭhapitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā sace ekaṃ, “eta”nti, bahūni ce, “etānī”ti vatvā adhiṭṭhayeti atthasambandho. Sesesupi ayaṃ nayoti yathā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ “imaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ, imaṃ kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti evaṃ attano nāmeneva vatvā sammukhāpi parammukhāpi vuttanayena adhiṭṭhātabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

34. Now, to show the method of determination, the passage beginning 'this outer robe' is stated. Herein, 'one should determine' means that one determines the outer robe thus: 'I determine this outer robe.' Regarding what is not within hand's reach: if it is placed at a distance, having noted the place where it is put, if it is one, one should determine it by saying 'that,' or if there are many, by saying 'those'; this is the connection of meaning. This is the method for the others too. Just as it is said, 'I determine this outer robe,' so too it is said that one should determine by stating its own name, as in 'I determine this upper robe,' 'I determine this scab-covering cloth,' whether in one's presence or absence, in the way that has been explained.

35. Idāni [V 0.0091] sace pubbe adhiṭṭhitaṃ ticīvaraṃ nisīdanaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ kaṇḍuppaṭicchādīti imesu chasu cīvaresu aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ atthi, puna tathāvidhaṃ cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā pariharituṃ icchantena “dve pana na vaṭṭantī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttattā pubbe adhiṭṭhitaṃ paccuddharitvā [M 0.0088] adhiṭṭhātabbanti dassetuṃ “adhiṭṭhahanto”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ uttānameva. Pattādhiṭṭhahane tathāti “imaṃ pattaṃ, etaṃ patta”nti evaṃ nāmamattameva viseso. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti attho.

35. Now, if among these six robes—the triple robe, the sitting cloth, the rains-bathing cloth, and the scab-covering cloth—one has a previously determined robe, and wishing to determine and use another such robe, then because it is said, 'but two are not allowable,' the previously determined one should be relinquished and the new one determined. To show this, the passage beginning 'while determining' was stated, which is self-evident. In the determination of a bowl it is the same; the only difference is the name, thus: 'this bowl,' 'that bowl.' The meaning is that the rest is just the same.

36. Etaṃ imaṃ va saṅghāṭiṃ saṃseti ettha sace antogabbhe vā sāmantavihāre vā hoti, ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā, sace hatthapāse hoti, “imaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti tesaṃ tesaṃ nāmavasena vācā bhinditabbāti attho. Paccuddhārepi eseva nayo. Ettha pana “dve cīvarassa adhiṭṭhānā kāyena vā adhiṭṭheti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭhetī”ti (pari. 322) vuttattā saṅghāṭiādikaṃ hatthena gahetvā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādinā nayena cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena aphusantassa na vaṭṭati. Vācāya adhiṭṭhahantena vacībhedaṃ katvāva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Tathā pattepi. Vidūti paṇḍito.

36. Explaining 'that' or 'this' outer robe: if it is in an inner chamber or in a nearby monastery, having noted the place where it is put, the speech should be broken by saying, 'I determine that outer robe.' The meaning is that if it is within hand's reach, the speech should be broken by saying 'this outer robe,' according to the name of each item. This same method applies also to relinquishment. Herein, because it is said: 'There are two determinations of a robe: one determines by body or one determines by speech,' one should determine by body by taking the outer robe, etc., in hand, making a bodily gesture while paying attention with the mind in the manner of 'I determine this outer robe.' It is not allowable for one who does not touch it with some part of the body. One determining by speech must determine it only after making a verbal declaration. The same applies to the bowl. Vidū means a wise person.

37-8. Idāni tesaṃ pamāṇaparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ “saṅghāṭi pacchimantenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dīghato muṭṭhipañcakato (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) paṭṭhāya “tatridaṃ sugatassa sugatacīvarappamāṇaṃ, dīghaso nava vidatthiyo sugatavidatthiyā, tiriyaṃ cha vidatthiyo”ti (pāci. 548) evaṃ vuttasugatacīvarūnāpi vaṭṭati. Tiriyaṃ pana muṭṭhittikaṃ. Ca-saddena atirekampi vaṭṭatīti attho. Uttarāsaṅgassapi etadeva pamāṇanti taṃ dassetuṃ “tathā ekaṃsikassāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Antaravāsakassa pana “pārupanenapi hi sakkā nābhiṃ paṭicchādetu”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) aṭṭhakathāvacanato “dvihattho vā”ti vuttaṃ.

37-38. Now, to show the delimitation of their measurements, the passage beginning 'the outer robe with its minimum hem' is stated. Herein, starting from five fists in length, even one smaller than the Sugata's robe is allowable, which is stated thus: 'Herein, this is the measurement of the Sugata's robe: nine Sugata-spans in length by the Sugata-span, and six spans in width.' In width, however, it is three fists. The meaning is that by the word 'and' (ca), an excess is also allowable. To show that the upper robe has this same measurement, it is said: 'Similarly for the single-shoulder robe.' As for the inner robe, however, because of the commentary statement, 'For it is possible to cover the navel even when just draping it,' 'or two cubits' is said.

39. Nisīdanassa [M 0.0089] dīghenāti ettha (pāci. 531 ādayo; pāci. aṭṭha. 531; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nisīdanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nisīdananti santhatasadisaṃ santharitvā ekasmiṃ ante vuttappamāṇena dvīsu ṭhānesu phāletvā katāhi tīhi dasāhi yuttassa parikkhārassetaṃ nāmaṃ.

39. Regarding 'by length of the sitting cloth': herein, 'sitting cloth' is the name for that requisite similar to a felt rug which, having been spread out, is furnished with three borders made by splitting it in two places at one end according to the stated measurement.

40. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi [V 0.0092] (pāci. 538; mahāva. 354; pāci. aṭṭha. 537; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kaṇḍuppaṭicchādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nāma yassa adhonābhiubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ kaṇḍu vā piḷakā vā assāvo vā thullakacchu vā ābādho, tassa paṭicchādanatthāya anuññātaṃ cīvaraṃ. Gāthāyo suviññeyyāva.

40. A 'scab-covering cloth' is the name for a robe permitted for the purpose of covering for one who has an affliction—an itch, a boil, a discharge, or a thick scab—in the region below the navel and above the circle of the knees. The verses are very easy to understand.

41. Aḍḍhateyyāvāti (pāci. 544) ettha tato uddhaṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho.

41. Regarding 'up to two and a half': the meaning here is that more than that is not allowable.

42. Etthāti saṅghāṭito paṭṭhāya yāva vassikasāṭikā, tāva dassitacīvaresūti attho. Taduttarinti tato tesaṃ cīvarānaṃ vuttappamāṇato uttariṃ karontassa chedanapācitti hotīti pāṭhaseso, taṃ atirekaṃ chinditvā puna pācittiyaṃ desetabbanti attho. Paccattharaṇamukhacoḷāti ettha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāva mahantaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ ākaṅkhati, tāva mahantaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 353) vuttattā paccattharaṇassa pamāṇaparicchedo natthi,. Mukhapuñchanacoḷassa pana ukkaṭṭhavasena vā antimavasena vā pamāṇaparicchedo na vutto, tasmā tampi appamāṇikaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “ākaṅkhitappamāṇikā”ti, icchitappamāṇikāti attho. Yāva ekaṃ dhovīyati, tāva aññaṃ paribhogatthāya icchitabbanti dvepi vaṭṭanti.

42. Here, this means from the outer robe up to the rains-bathing cloth; such is the meaning in regard to the robes that have been shown. 'Beyond that' means that for one who makes those robes exceeding the stated measurement, there is an offense of expiation entailing cutting; this is the remainder of the text. The meaning is that having cut the excess, one should confess the offense of expiation again. Regarding 'bedspread and face-wiping cloth,' because it is said, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a bedspread to be made as large as one wishes,' there is no fixed measurement for a bedspread. As for the face-wiping cloth, however, no fixed measurement is stated, either as a maximum or a minimum. Therefore, it too is without a fixed measurement. Hence it is said, 'of a size as one wishes'; the meaning is, of a desired size. While one is being washed, another may be desired for use; thus both are allowable.

43. Na [M 0.0090] dīpitanti kattha na dīpitaṃ? Aṭṭhakathāsu. Kasmāti ce? “Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhūnaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti ticīvaraṃ, attho ca hoti parissāvanehipi thavikāhipi. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, parikkhāracoḷaka”nti (mahāva. 357) bahūnaṃ pattathavikaparissāvanādīnaṃ saṅgahavasena vuttattā pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhanti. Yasmā pana bhagavatā “yaṃ yaṃ labbhati, taṃ taṃ iminā vidhānena adhiṭṭhahitvā puna yena yena parissāvanādinā attho hoti, taṃ taṃ katvā gaṇhantū”ti anukampāya anuññātaṃ, tasmā vikappanupagapacchimacīvarappamāṇaṃ thavikampi paṭaparissāvanampi bahūnipi ekato katvā “imāni cīvarāni parikkhāracoḷāni adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vatvā adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Tasmā vuttaṃ “tathā vatvā”ti, “parikkhāracoḷa”nti vatvāti attho. Vikappiyanti vikappanupagaṃ.

43. 'Not explained'—where is it not explained? In the commentaries. If it is asked why: because it was said, 'At that time the bhikkhus had a complete set of three robes, and there was also a need for water-strainers and bags. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, a requisite-cloth”', and since many things such as bowl-bags, water-strainers, etc., were spoken of collectively, there is no individual introductory story for each. Moreover, because the Blessed One, out of compassion, has allowed, 'Whatever one gets, having determined it by this method, then whatever water-strainer, etc., is needed, one may make it and take it,' therefore, a bag the size of the smallest robe subject to sharing, a cloth water-strainer, or many such things together, may indeed be determined by saying, 'I determine these cloths as requisite-cloths.' Thus it is said, 'having said so,' which means, having said 'requisite-cloth.' 'To be shared' means subject to sharing.

44. Ahatakappānanti (mahāva. 348) ekavāraṃ dhovitakānaṃ.

44. 'Treated as new' refers to cloths that have been washed once.

45. Utuddhaṭānanti [V 0.0093] ututo dīghakālato uddhaṭānaṃ, katavatthakiccānaṃ pilotikānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesāti uttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakā. Paṃsu viya kucchitabhāvaṃ paṭikkūlabhāvaṃ ulati gacchatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, coḷakhaṇḍānametaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmiṃ paṃsukūle yathārucīti attho. Kasmāti ce? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ dussānaṃ ahatakappānaṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ ekacciyaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekacciyaṃ antaravāsakaṃ, utuddhaṭānaṃ dussānaṃ catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ diguṇaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ diguṇaṃ antaravāsakaṃ, paṃsukūle yāvadatthaṃ, pāpaṇike ussāho karaṇīyo”ti vuttattā, tasmā susānādīsu patitapaṃsukūle ca antarāpaṇe patitapilotikacīvare ca paṭaparicchedo natthi, paṭasatampi vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ.

45. 'Removed from season' means removed for a long time from its season; this means rags that have served their purpose as cloth. 'The rest' means the upper robe and the inner robe. 'Rag-heap cloth' (paṃsukūla) is so called because, like dust (paṃsu), it goes (ulati) to a despised, repulsive state; this is a name for scraps of cloth. The meaning is 'as much as one wishes from the rag-heap cloth.' If it is asked why, it is because it is said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, for new cloths treated as new, a double-layered outer robe, a single-layered upper robe, and a single-layered inner robe; for cloths removed from season, a quadruple-layered outer robe, a double-layered upper robe, and a double-layered inner robe; from rag-heap cloth, as much as is needed; one should be diligent at the shop.' Therefore, for rag-heap cloth fallen in cemeteries and so on, and for rag-cloth fallen in the marketplace, there is no limit on the pieces; even a hundred pieces are allowable. Thus it is established.

46. Idāni [M 0.0091] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, chinnakaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ chinnakaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ chinnakaṃ antaravāsaka”nti (mahāva. 345) vatvā puna “tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno ticīvare kayiramāne sabbaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve chinnakāni ekaṃ acchinnakanti. Dve chinnakāni ekaṃ acchinnakaṃ nappahoti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve acchinnakāni ekaṃ chinnakanti. Ekaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahoti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anvādhikampi āropetuṃ. Na ca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ acchinnakaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 360) evaṃ vuttavidhānaṃ dassetuṃ “tīsū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tassa attho – tīsu cīvaresu yaṃ chinditvā sibbituṃ sabbapacchimappamāṇaṃ pahoti, taṃ chinditabbaṃ. Sabbesu pana appahontesu anvādhikaṃ ādiyeyyāti. Tattha anvādhi nāma anuvātaṃ viya saṃharitvā cīvarassa upari saṅghāṭiākārena āropetabbaṃ. Āgantukapattantipi vadanti. Idaṃ pana appahonake anuññātaṃ. Sace pahoti, na vaṭṭanti, chinditabbameva. Anādiṇṇanti anāropitaṃ anvādhikaṃ. Na dhāreyyāti ticīvarādhiṭṭhānavasena adhiṭṭhahitvā na dhāretabbanti adhippāyo.

46. Now, after saying, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a cut outer robe, a cut upper robe, and a cut inner robe' (Mahāvagga 345), it was said further: 'Now at that time, when a certain bhikkhu was having his three robes made, all the cut pieces were not sufficient. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, two cut robes and one uncut one.” Two cut robes and one uncut one were not sufficient. “I allow, bhikkhus, two uncut robes and one cut one.” One cut robe was not sufficient. “I allow, bhikkhus, to apply an extra piece. But, bhikkhus, a completely uncut set of robes should not be worn. Whoever should wear one, commits an offense of wrong-doing”' (Mahāvagga 360). To explain the rule thus stated, the passage beginning 'In the three...' was introduced. Its meaning is: of the three robes, whichever is sufficient to be cut and sewn to the very last measure, that one should be cut. But when all are insufficient, one may take an extra piece. Here, an 'extra piece' is to be gathered like a screen and applied over the robe in the manner of an outer robe. Some also call it a 'guest-cloth.' This, however, is allowed when there is an insufficiency. If there is sufficiency, it is not allowable; it must be cut. 'Not taken' means an extra piece not applied. 'Should not wear' means that one should not determine it and wear it as one of the three robes; this is the intention.

47-8. Idāni udositasikkhāpadanayaṃ dassetuṃ “gāme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha pana sace gāmo (pārā. 478; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.477-478; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ekassa rañño vā bhojakassa vā vasena ekakulassa hoti, pākārādinā parikkhittattā ekūpacāro ca, evarūpe gāme cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā tasmiṃ gāme yathārucitaṭṭhāne [V 0.0094] vasituṃ labbhati. Sace so gāmo aparikkhitto, yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ ghare vasitabbaṃ, tassa vā gharassa samantato hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ.

47-48. Now, to explain the method of the training rule on being separated from a robe, the passage beginning 'in a village' is stated. Here, if a village is under the authority of a single king or chieftain, belongs to a single family, and is enclosed by a wall or the like, having a single precinct, in such a village, having deposited a robe, one is permitted to dwell in any preferred place within that village. If that village is unenclosed, one must dwell in the house where the robe was deposited, or one must not go beyond hand-reach all around that house.

Sace [M 0.0092] so gāmo vesālikusinārādayo viya nānārājūnaṃ vā bhojakānaṃ vā hoti, vuttappakārena parikkhitto ca, evarūpe gāme yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ ghare vā vatthabbaṃ. Yassā vīthiyā taṃ gharaṃ hoti, tassā vīthiyā tassa gharassa sammukhāṭṭhāne sabhāye vā nagaradvāre vā vatthabbaṃ, tesaṃ sabhāyadvārānaṃ hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhitto, yasmiṃ ghare nikkhittaṃ, tattha vā tassa hatthapāse vā vatthabbaṃ.

If that village, like Vesālī, Kusinārā, and so on, is under various kings or chieftains, and is enclosed in the way described, in such a village one should dwell either in the house where the robe was deposited, or, on whatever street that house is, one should dwell on that street in a place opposite that house, or in an assembly hall, or at a city gate, or one must not go beyond the hand-reach of those assembly halls and gates. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the house where it was deposited or within its hand-reach.

Nivesanādayo hammiyapariyosānā gāmaparikkhepato bahi sanniviṭṭhāti veditabbā. Itarathā tesaṃ gāmaggahaṇeneva gahitattā gāmassa ekakulanānākulaekūpacāranānūpacāratāvaseneva vinicchayo vattabbo siyā. Nivesanādīnaṃ vaseneva pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 478 ādayo) attho vibhatto, na gāmavasena. Udositavinicchaye ayaṃ nayo vuttoyeva.

'Dwellings' and so on, ending with 'mansions,' should be understood as being established outside the village enclosure. Otherwise, since they would be included by the very term 'village,' the decision would have to be made solely on the basis of whether the village belongs to a single family or multiple families, and has a single precinct or multiple precincts. In the Pāli text (Pārā. 478 ff.), the meaning is analyzed on the basis of dwellings and so on, not on the basis of the village. This method has already been stated in the 'Decision on Being Separated from a Robe'.

Nivesaneti ettha sace ekakulassa nivesanaṃ hoti parikkhittañca, antonivesane cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antonivesane vatthabbaṃ. Aparikkhittañce hoti, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthabbaṃ, tassa gabbhassa hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa hoti parikkhittañca, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ gabbhe vatthabbaṃ, sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇadvāramūle vā tesaṃ gabbhadvāramūle vā tesaṃ gabbhadvāramūlānaṃ vā hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ. Aparikkhittañce hoti, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ gabbhe vatthabbaṃ, hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ.

Here, in the case of a 'dwelling': if it is the dwelling of a single family and is enclosed, having deposited the robe inside the dwelling, one should dwell inside the dwelling. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the inner chamber where the robe was deposited, or one must not go beyond the hand-reach of that inner chamber. If it belongs to multiple families and is enclosed, one should dwell in the inner chamber where the robe was deposited, or at the common doorway for all, or at the doorway of their inner chambers, or one must not go beyond the hand-reach of the doorways of their inner chambers. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the inner chamber where the robe was deposited, or one must not go beyond its hand-reach.

Udositoti yānādīnaṃ bhaṇḍānaṃ sālā. Pāsādoti dīghapāsādo. Hammiyanti muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Nāvā [M 0.0093] pana thalaṃ āropetvā nikkhittāpi hoti, samudde ṭhitāpi. Sace ekakulassa nāvā hoti, antonāvāya cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antonāvāya vatthabbaṃ. Nānākulassa nāvā hoti nānāgabbhā nānāovarakā, yasmiṃ ovarake cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthabbaṃ, cīvarassa hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ.

'Shed' means a hall for vehicles, goods, and so on. 'Storeyed building' means a long storeyed building. 'Mansion' means a storeyed building with a flat roof. A boat, furthermore, may be one that has been drawn up onto land and deposited there, or one that is standing in the sea. If a boat belongs to a single family, having deposited the robe inside the boat, one should dwell inside the boat. If a boat belongs to multiple families, having various inner chambers and various cabins, one should dwell in the cabin where the robe was deposited, or one must not go beyond the hand-reach of the robe.

Aṭṭoti [V 0.0095] paṭirājādīnaṃ paṭibāhanatthaṃ iṭṭhakāhi kato bahalabhittiko catupañcabhūmiko patissayaviseso. Māḷoti ekakūṭasaṅgahito caturassapāsādo. Imesu pana udositādīsu māḷapariyosānesu nivesane vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Nivesananti pana udositādīnaṃ vasena akatāya patissayavikatiyā adhivacanaṃ.

'Watchtower' is a particular kind of lodging with thick walls made of bricks, four or five storeys high, for the purpose of repelling enemy kings and so on. 'Pavilion' is a square storeyed building with a single gabled roof. In these cases—from sheds to pavilions—the decision should be understood according to the method explained for a 'dwelling.' 'Dwelling,' however, is a designation for a type of lodging that is not a modification made in the manner of sheds and so on.

Ārāmo nāma pupphārāmaphalārāmādiko. Sace ekakulassa ārāmo hoti parikkhitto ca, antoārāme cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antoārāme vatthabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhitto, cīvarassa hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa ārāmo hoti parikkhitto ca, dvāramūle vā vatthabbaṃ, dvāramūlassa hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ. Aparikkhitto ce, cīvarassa hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ.

A park means a flower park, a fruit park, and so on. If the park belongs to a single family and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the park, one should stay inside the park. If it is unenclosed, one should not go beyond the hand-reach of the robe. If the park belongs to many families and is enclosed, one should stay at the gate, or one should not go beyond the hand-reach of the gate. If it is unenclosed, one should not go beyond the hand-reach of the robe.

Sattho nāma jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthānamaññataro. Sace ekakulassa sattho hoti, satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā purato vā pacchato vā sattabbhantarā na vijahitabbā, passato abbhantaraṃ na vijahitabbaṃ. Abbhantaraṃ nāma aṭṭhavīsatihatthaṃ hoti. Sace gacchanto sattho sakaṭe vā bhagge, goṇe vā naṭṭhe antarā chijjati, yasmiṃ koṭṭhāse cīvaraṃ nikkhipitabbaṃ, tattha vasitabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa hoti[M 0.0094], satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā cīvarassa hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ.

A caravan means either a caravan on foot or a caravan of carts. If the caravan belongs to a single family, having placed the robe in the caravan, one should not go beyond seven abbhantaras in front or behind, nor beyond one abbhantara to the side. An abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits. If, while the caravan is traveling, it is broken up in the middle because a cart is broken or an ox is lost, one should stay in that section where the robe was placed. If it belongs to many families, having placed the robe in the caravan, one should not abandon the hand's-reach of the robe.

Khettakhalesu ārāme vuttasadisova vinicchayo. Dumeti rukkhamūle. Sace ekakulassa rukkhamūlaṃ hoti, yaṃ majjhanhikakāle samantā chāyā pharati, tasmiṃ ṭhāne aviraḷe padese tassa chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsassa anto eva nikkhipitabbaṃ. Sace viraḷasākhassa pana rukkhassa ātapena phuṭṭhokāse ṭhapeti, aruṇuggamane sace so bhikkhu tassa hatthapāse na hoti, aññasmiṃ vā ṭhāne tassa chāyāyapi hoti, nissaggiyaṃ hotiyeva. Nānākulassa ce hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ.

For fields and threshing floors, the ruling is the same as that stated for a park. 'At a tree' means at the foot of a tree. If the foot of the tree belongs to a single family, the robe should be placed right inside the space touched by its shade, in a place where the shade that spreads all around at midday is dense. But if one places it under a tree with sparse branches, in a place touched by the sun, and at sunrise that bhikkhu is not within hand's-reach of it, or is in another place even though it is within its shade, it definitely becomes subject to forfeiture. If it belongs to many families, one should not abandon the hand's-reach of the robe.

Ajjhokāse pana viñjhāṭavīādīsu araññesupi samuddamajjhe macchabandhānaṃ agamanapathesu dīpakesupi cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā tato samantā sattabbhantare padese yattha katthaci vasitabbaṃ. Sace sattabbhantarato kesaggamattampi atikkamitvā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapeti, nissaggiyaṃ hoti.

But in the open air—in wildernesses such as the Vindhya forest, in the middle of the sea, on the routes of fishermen, or on small islands—having placed the robe, one may dwell anywhere in a place within seven abbhantaras all around it. If one lets the dawn rise having gone beyond the seven abbhantaras by even a hair's breadth, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

Ettha [V 0.0096] pana pāḷiyaṃ “gāmo ekūpacāro nānūpacāro”tiādinā (pārā. 477) avisesena mātikaṃ nikkhipitvāpi gāmanivesanaudositakhettadhaññakaraṇaārāmavihārānaṃ ekūpacāranānūpacāratā “gāmo ekūpacāro nāma ekakulassa gāmo hoti parikkhitto ca aparikkhitto cā”tiādinā (pārā. 478) parikkhittāparikkhittavasena vibhattā. Aṭṭamāḷapāsādahammiyanāvāsattharukkhamūlaajjhokāsānampi evaṃ avatvā “ekakulassa aṭṭo hoti, nānākulassa aṭṭo hotī”tiādinā (pārā. 484) nayena ekakulanānākulavasena ca ante “ajjhokāso ekūpacāro nāma agāmake araññe samantā sattabbhantarā ekūpacāro, tato paraṃ nānūpacāro”ti (pārā. 494) ca evaṃ ekūpacāranānūpacāratā vibhattā. Tasmā gāmādīsu [M 0.0095] parikkhittaṃ ekūpacāraṃ, aparikkhittaṃ nānūpacāranti ca aṭṭādīsu yaṃ ekakulassa, taṃ ekūpacāraṃ nānākulassa nānūpacāranti ca gahetabbaṃ. Ajjhokāsapade vuttanayena gahetabbaṃ.

Here, in the Pāli text, although the matrix is laid down without distinction with the words 'a village is of single-precinct, of multiple-precincts,' etc. (Pārā. 477), the single-precinct and multiple-precinct nature of villages, settlements, abandoned sites, fields, threshing floors, parks, and monasteries is distinguished based on whether they are enclosed or unenclosed, with the words 'A village of single-precinct means a village belonging to a single family, whether enclosed or unenclosed,' etc. (Pārā. 478). For watchtowers, halls, mansions, storied buildings, boats, caravans, the foot of a tree, and the open air, without stating it in this way, their single-precinct and multiple-precinct nature is distinguished based on whether they belong to a single family or many families, by the method beginning 'A watchtower belongs to a single family, a watchtower belongs to many families,' etc. (Pārā. 484); and at the end, 'The open air is of single-precinct means that in a village-less wilderness, the area within seven abbhantaras all around is of single-precinct; beyond that, it is of multiple-precincts' (Pārā. 494). Therefore, in the case of villages and the like, what is enclosed is to be taken as of single-precinct, and what is unenclosed as of multiple-precincts. And in the case of watchtowers and the like, what belongs to a single family is to be taken as of single-precinct, and what belongs to many families as of multiple-precincts. In the case of the open air, it should be taken according to the method stated.

Bhikkhusammutiyāññatrāti yaṃ gilānassa bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamituṃ asakkontassa ñattidutiyena kammena avippavāsasammuti dīyati, taṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Laddhasammutikassa pana yāva rogo na vūpasammati, tasmiṃ vūpasante añño vā kuppati, anāpattiyeva.

'Except by the bhikkhus' consent' means: excepting the consent for non-separation that is given by a formal act preceded by a motion to a sick bhikkhu who is unable to take his robe and depart. For one who has obtained this consent, there is no offense as long as the illness has not subsided, or if another illness arises when that one has subsided.

49. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ yāva ābādhā adhiṭṭhātuṃ, tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ. Vassikasāṭikaṃ vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ, tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vuttattā rogapariyantā kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi, vassānapariyantā vassikasāṭikāti attho. Sesāti ticīvarādayo kālavasena apariyantikāti attho.

49. Because it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I allow the determination of an itch-covering cloth for as long as the illness lasts; after that it should be shared. I allow the determination of a rains-cloth for the four months of the rains; after that it should be shared' (Mahāvagga 358), the meaning is that the itch-covering cloth is limited by the illness, and the rains-cloth is limited by the rains-retreat. 'The rest' means that the three robes and so on are not limited by time.

50. Paccattharaṇādittayaṃ sadasampi adasampi rattampi arattampi ādiṇṇakappampi anādiṇṇakappampi labbhatīti attho. Nisīdananti nisīdanañca rattaṃ anādiṇṇakappañca labbhatīti adhippāyo. Paccattharaṇaparikkhāramukhapuñchanacoḷāni pana nīlampi pītakampi lohitakampi pupphadasādikampi vaṭṭanti, tasmā “sadasampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evarūpaṃ pana nivāsetuṃ vā pārupituṃ vā na vaṭṭati, kevalaṃ paccattharaṇādivasena adhiṭṭhānamattaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

50. The meaning is that the three items beginning with the ground-covering may be obtained whether disfigured or not disfigured, dyed or undyed, with a determination-mark applied or without one. 'Sitting cloth': the intention is that a sitting cloth that is dyed and without a determination-mark applied may be obtained. However, ground-coverings, requisite-cloths, and face-wiping cloths may be blue, yellow, red, or have a flower-patterned border, etc.; therefore it was said 'whether disfigured or not,' etc. But it is not allowable to wear such a cloth as a lower garment or to drape it over as an upper garment; it is only allowable to make a determination of it for use as a ground-covering, etc.

51. Ticīvaraṃ [V 0.0097] kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi vassikasāṭikāti idaṃ pana sesacīvarapañcakaṃ adasaṃ rajitaṃyeva kappati, tañca ādiṇṇakappamevāti attho. Sadasaṃva nisīdananti idaṃ pana pubbe “sadasampī”ti ettha vuttattā adasampi nisīdanaṃ vaṭṭatīti sammohanivāraṇatthaṃ vuttanti vadanti.

51. But these five remaining robes—the three robes, the itch-covering cloth, and the rains-cloth—are allowable only when not disfigured and dyed, and also only with a determination-mark applied; this is the meaning. 'A sitting cloth only if disfigured'—this, they say, was said to prevent the confusion that an undisfigured sitting cloth is also allowable, which might be inferred from the previous statement 'even if disfigured.'

52. Anadhiṭṭhitanti [M 0.0096] ticīvarādivasena anadhiṭṭhitaṃ. Anissaṭṭhaṃ nāma aññesaṃ avissajjitaṃ, taṃ pana vikappetvā paribhuñjitabbanti attho.

52. 'Undetermined' means not determined as one of the three robes, etc. 'Unrelinquished' means not given up to others. The meaning is that it should be used after having been shared.

Idāni vikappanupagassa pamāṇaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena dassetuṃ “hatthadīgha”ntiādimāha. Tattha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āyāmena aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena caturaṅgulavitthataṃ pacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vuttattā dīghato ekahatthaṃ puthulato upaḍḍhahatthaṃ vikappetabbanti adhippāyo.

Now, to show the minimum size of a cloth fit for sharing, he said: 'a cubit long,' etc. In this connection, because it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I allow a cloth that is at least eight Sugata-fingerbreadths in length and four fingerbreadths in width to be shared' (Mahāvagga 358), the intention is that a cloth one cubit long and half a cubit wide should be shared.

53. Ticīvarassāti vinayaticīvarassa, na dhutaṅgaticīvarassa. Tassa pana imesu navasu cīvarattayameva labbhati, na aññaṃ labbhati. Sabbametanti sabbaṃ adhiṭṭhānavidhānañca pariharaṇavidhānañcāti attho. Parikkhāracoḷiyo sabbanti ticīvarādikaṃ navavidhampi cīvaraṃ. Tathā vatvāti “parikkhāracoḷa”nti vatvā. Adhiṭṭhatīti adhiṭṭhāti. Kiṃ pana ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatīti? Āma vaṭṭati, “parikkhāracoḷaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhametanti ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Udositasikkhāpade pana ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā pariharantassa parihāro vutto”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) vuttaṃ, tasmā ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhahantena paccuddharitvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ.

53. 'Of the three robes' means of the three robes of the Vinaya, not of the three robes of the ascetic practice. For such a one, among these nine, only the set of three robes is allowed, not any other. 'All this' means the entire procedure of determination and the procedure of use. 'All the requisite-cloths' means all nine kinds of robes, beginning with the three robes. 'Having said thus' means having said 'requisite-cloth.' 'Determines' means one determines. But is it allowable to determine the three robes as a 'requisite-cloth'? Yes, it is allowable. It is said in the commentary: 'It is called "requisite-cloth" because it is an individual means of storage. Thus it is allowable to determine the three robes as a "requisite-cloth" and use them. However, in the training rule on abandoned sites, the way of using the three robes after determining them is stated' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.469). Therefore, one who is determining the three robes as a 'requisite-cloth' must first rescind the previous determination and then determine it anew.

54. Idāni etesaṃ adhiṭṭhānavijahanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “acchedavissajjanagāhavibbhamā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha acchedoti corādīhi acchindanaṃ. Vissajjananti aññesaṃ dānaṃ. Kathaṃ pana dinnaṃ, kathaṃ gahitaṃ sudinnaṃ suggahitañca hotīti? Sace “idaṃ tuyhaṃ demi dadāmi dajjāmi oṇojemi pariccajāmi nissajjāmi vissajjāmī”ti vā “itthannāmassa demi…pe… vissajjāmī”ti [M 0.0097] vā vadati, sammukhāpi parammukhāpi dinnaṃyeva hoti. “Tuyhaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti [V 0.0098] vutte “mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti vadati, sudinnaṃ suggahitañca. “Tava santakaṃ karohi, tava santakaṃ hotu, tava santakaṃ karissatī”ti vutte “mamasantakaṃ karomi, mama santakaṃ hotu, mama santakaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati, duddinnaṃ duggahitañca. Sace pana “tava santakaṃ karohī”ti vutte “sādhu, bhante, mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ.

54. Now, to show the ways of abandoning the determination of these, it is said: 'taking by force, giving away, taking, and disrobing,' etc. Here, 'taking by force' means its being taken away by thieves and others. 'Giving away' means giving to others. But how is something given and how is it taken so that it is well-given and well-taken? If one says: 'I give this to you, I present it, I will give it, I dedicate it, I renounce it, I release it, I give it away,' or 'I give... I give it away to so-and-so,' it is properly given whether face-to-face or not. If, when one says, 'Take this for yourself,' the other says, 'I take it for myself,' it is well-given and well-taken. If, when one says, 'Make it your property; let it be your property; it will be your property,' the other says, 'I make it my property; let it be my property; I will make it my property,' it is ill-given and ill-taken. But if, when one says, 'Make it your property,' the other takes it, saying, 'Good, venerable sir, I take it for myself,' it is well-taken.

Gāhoti vissāsaggāho (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.131). So pana evaṃ veditabbo – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa vissāsaṃ gahetuṃ. Sandiṭṭho ca hoti, sambhatto ca, ālapito ca, jīvati ca, jānāti ca ‘gahite me attamano bhavissatī’”ti (mahāva. 356). Tattha sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamattakamitto. Sambhattoti daḷhamitto. Ālapitoti “mama santakaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gaṇheyyāsi, āpucchitvā gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti vutto. Jīvatīti anuṭṭhānaseyyāya sayitopi yāva jīvitindriyupacchedaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Gahite ca attamanoti gahite ca tuṭṭhacitto. Evarūpassa santakaṃ “gahite me attamano bhavissatī”ti jānantena gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anavasesapariyādānavasena cetāni pañca aṅgāni vuttāni, vissāsaggāho pana tīhi aṅgehi ruhati. Kathaṃ? Sandiṭṭho jīvati gahite attamano, sambhatto jīvati gahite attamano, ālapito jīvati gahite attamanoti evaṃ.

By 'gāho' is meant taking on trust (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.131). This should be understood as follows: "Monks, I allow taking on trust from one endowed with five factors. He is seen, he is intimate, he has been spoken to, he is alive, and he knows, 'He will be pleased if it is taken.'" (Mahāva. 356). Here, 'seen' means a friend merely seen. 'Intimate' means a firm friend. 'Spoken to' means one who has been told: 'Whatever of mine you wish, you may take it; there is no need to ask permission before taking.' 'Alive' means that even if he is lying in a state of inactivity, he does not reach the cessation of the life faculty. 'Pleased if taken' means that he is pleased in mind when something is taken. It is permissible for one who knows 'he will be pleased if it is taken' to take what belongs to such a person. These five factors are stated in the sense of not leaving anything out, but taking on trust is established through three factors. How? One who is seen, alive, and pleased if taken; one who is intimate, alive, and pleased if taken; one who has been spoken to, alive, and pleased if taken—thus it is.

Yo pana jīvati, na ca gahite attamano hoti, tassa santakaṃ vissāsabhāvena gahitampi puna dātabbaṃ. Dadantena matakadhanaṃ tāva ye tassa dhane issarā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā, tesaṃ dātabbaṃ. Yo pana paṭhamaṃyeva “suṭṭhu [M 0.0098] kataṃ tayā mama santakaṃ gaṇhantenā”ti vacībhedena vā cittuppādamattena vā anumoditvā pacchā kenaci kāraṇena kupito, so paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yopi adātukāmo, cittena pana adhivāseti, na kiñci vadati, sopi puna paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yo pana “mayā tumhākaṃ santakaṃ gahita”nti vā “paribhutta”nti vā vutte nādhivāseti, “paṭidehī”ti bhaṇati, so paccāharāpetuṃ labhati.

However, if one is alive but not pleased with what was taken, even if it was taken on trust, what belongs to him should be given back. When giving the wealth of a deceased person, it should first be given to those who have authority over his wealth, whether householders or renunciants. But if someone initially approves, either by verbal expression or merely by a mental thought, saying, "You did well by taking what is mine," and later becomes angry for some reason, he is not permitted to reclaim it. Even if one is unwilling to give but consents in mind, saying nothing, he is not permitted to reclaim it. However, if someone, when told, "I took what is yours" or "I used what is yours," does not consent and says, "Give it back," he is permitted to reclaim it.

Vibbhamāti iminā bhikkhuniyāyeva adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ gahitaṃ hoti. Sā pana yadā vibbhamati, tadā assamaṇī hoti. Bhikkhu pana vibbhamantopi yāva sikkhaṃ na paccakkhāti, tāva bhikkhuyevāti adhiṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatīti. Liṅgasikkhāti liṅgaparivattanañca sikkhāpaccakkhānañcāti [V 0.0099] attho. Sabbesūti navasu cīvaresu. Adhiṭṭhānaviyogakāraṇāti adhiṭṭhānavijahanakāraṇā, imesu aññatarena adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti attho.

By 'vibbhamati' (disrobing) is meant the relinquishment of determination by a bhikkhunī only. However, when she disrobes, she becomes a non-recluse. But even if a bhikkhu disrobes, as long as he does not renounce the training, he remains a bhikkhu; thus, he does not relinquish his determination. 'Training in the outward sign' means both the change of outward sign and the renunciation of the training. 'Among all' refers to all nine robes. 'Causes for the separation from determination' means causes for the relinquishment of determination; the meaning is that one relinquishes determination by any one of these.

Kiñca bhiyyo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) – ticīvarassa pana vinibbiddhachiddañca adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ karotīti attho. Tattha saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgānaṃ dīghantato vidatthippamāṇassa tiriyantato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhapiṭṭhippamāṇakaṃ chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati. Antaravāsakassa dīghantato vidatthippamāṇasseva tiriyantato caturaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, parato pana na bhindati. Tasmā chidde jāte ticīvaraṃ atirekacīvaraṃ hoti, sūcikammaṃ katvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Itaresaṃ pana chiddena vijahanaṃ nāma natthi. Yo pana ticīvarepi dubbalaṭṭhāne paṭhamaṃ aggaḷaṃ datvā pacchā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā apaneti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati. Maṇḍalaparivattanepi eseva nayo. Yo pana [M 0.0099] ubho koṭiyo majjhe karonto sace paṭhamaṃ chinditvā pacchā ghaṭeti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati, atha ghaṭetvā chindati, na vijahati. Rajakehi dhovāpetvā setakaṃ karontassāpi na vijahati eva.

Furthermore (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.469) – the meaning is that a hole that pierces through the three robes causes the relinquishment of determination. There, for the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) and upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), a hole the size of the back of a little finger's nail, within a portion that is a span in length and eight fingers in width, violates the determination. For the inner robe (antaravāsaka), a hole within a portion that is a span in length and four fingers in width violates the determination, but beyond that area, it does not. Therefore, when a hole occurs, the three robes become an extra robe; it must be sewn and then redetermined. For other robes, however, there is no relinquishment due to a hole. But if one first applies a patch to a weak spot in the three robes and later cuts away the weakened part, the determination is not violated. The same principle applies to turning the robe around. If one brings both edges to the middle—if one first cuts and then joins, the determination is relinquished; but if one joins and then cuts, it is not relinquished. Even when having it washed by launderers and whitened, the determination is not relinquished.

55. Idāni akappiyacīvarāni dassetuṃ “kusavākaphalakānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kusacīraṃ (mahāva. 371; mahāva. aṭṭha. ) nāma kuse ganthetvā katacīvaraṃ. Vākacīraṃ nāma tāpasānaṃ vakkalaṃ. Phalakacīraṃ nāma phalakāni sibbitvā katacīvaraṃ. Kesakambalanti kesehi tantaṃ vāyitvā katakambalaṃ. Vālakambalanti camaravālehi vāyitvā katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhanti ulūkasakuṇassa pakkhehi katanivāsanaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti salomaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinamigacammaṃ. Imesu sattasu vatthesu yaṃ kiñci dhārayato thullaccayanti attho. Yathā imesu thullaccayaṃ, tathā akkanāḷaṃ nivāsentassa. Akkanāḷaṃ nāma akkadaṇḍe vākādīhi ganthetvā katacīvaraṃ. “Na bhikkhave akkanāḷaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ, yo nivāseyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (mahāva. 371) hi vuttaṃ.

55. Now, to show the unallowable robes, the section beginning 'kusavākaphalakāni' (robes of kusa grass, bark, and planks) has been commenced. Here, a 'kusa-robe' (Mahāva. 371; Mahāva. Aṭṭha.) means a robe made by tying kusa grass together. A 'bark-robe' means the bark garment of ascetics. A 'plank-robe' means a robe made by sewing planks together. A 'hair-blanket' means a blanket made by weaving threads from hair. A 'tail-hair blanket' means a blanket made by weaving from the tail-hairs of a yak. An 'owl-wing' garment means a lower garment made from the wings of an owl. An 'antelope-hide' means the hide of an antelope with its hair and hooves. The meaning is that whoever wears any of these seven cloths incurs a grave offense. Just as a grave offense is incurred by wearing these, so too by wearing an 'akkanāḷa'. An 'akkanāḷa' means a robe made by tying stalks of the akka plant with bark, etc. For it was said: "Monks, an akkanāḷa should not be worn; whoever wears it commits a grave offense" (Mahāva. 371).

56. Kadalerakakkadusse potthake cāpīti ettha kadalierakaakkamakacivākehi katāni vatthāni evaṃ vuttānīti veditabbāni. Etesu potthakoyeva pāḷiyaṃ āgato, itarāni taggatikattā aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittāni. Imesu catūsupi dukkaṭameva. “Na bhikkhave naggiyaṃ [V 0.0100] titthiyasamādānaṃ samādiyitabbaṃ, yo samādiyeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (mahāva. 370) vuttattā naggiyampi na kappati eva. Sabbameva nīlakaṃ sabbanīlakaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Ettha nīlaṃ umāpupphavaṇṇaṃ hoti[M 0.0100]. Mañjeṭṭhakaṃ mañjeṭṭhakavaṇṇameva. Pītakaṃ kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Lohitakaṃ jayasumanapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Kaṇhakaṃ addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇaṃ.

56. Here, by 'kadalierakakkadusse potthake cāpi' (and also in cloths of plantain fiber, eraka grass, and kakkha, and in bark-cloth), it should be understood that cloths made from plantain fiber, eraka grass, akka, and makaci bark are thus stated. Among these, only the 'potthaka' (bark-cloth) is mentioned in the Pāli text; the others are rejected in the commentaries because they fall into that category. For all four of these, only a minor offense (dukkaṭa) is incurred. Since it was said: "Monks, the practice of nudity, an ascetic observance, should not be undertaken; whoever undertakes it commits a grave offense" (Mahāva. 370), therefore even nudity is not allowable. All 'blue' means completely blue. The same applies to the rest. Here, 'blue' is the color of the umā flower. 'Mañjeṭṭhaka' is exactly the color of the mañjeṭṭhaka flower. 'Pītaka' (yellow) is the color of the kaṇikāra flower. 'Lohitaka' (red) is the color of the jayasumana flower. 'Kaṇhaka' (black) is the color of the addāriṭṭhaka flower.

57. Mahāraṅgaṃ nāma satapadipiṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Mahānāmaṃ nāma rattasambhinnavaṇṇaṃ hoti. Padumapupphavaṇṇantipi vuttaṃ, mandarattanti attho. Tirīṭaketi rukkhatace. Acchinnadīghadasaketi sabbaso acchinnadasake ca majjhe chinnadasake cāti attho. Aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā katadasaṃ phaladasaṃ nāma. Ketakapupphādipupphasadisāhi dasāhi yuttaṃ pupphadasaṃ nāma. Etesupi “potthake cāpī”ti ettha vuttaapi-saddena dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Tathāti yathā etesu kadalidussādīsu pupphadasāvasānesu dukkaṭaṃ, tathā kañcukaveṭhanesupi yaṃ kiñci dhārentassa dukkaṭanti attho.

57. 'Mahāraṅga' (great dye) is the color of the back of a centipede. 'Mahānāma' (great name) is a color mixed with red. It is also said to be the color of a lotus flower, meaning deep red. 'Tirīṭaka' refers to tree bark. 'Acchinnadīghadasaka' (long uncut fringes) means both entirely uncut fringes and fringes cut in the middle. Fringes made by sewing them together are called 'phaladasa' (fruit fringes). Fringes adorned with fringes similar to ketaka flowers and other flowers are called 'pupphadasa' (flower fringes). In these cases too, a minor offense (dukkata) should be understood by the word 'api' (also) mentioned in 'potthake cāpi' (and also book covers). Similarly, just as there is a minor offense (dukkata) in the case of kadali cloth and other cloths ending in flower fringes, so too is there a minor offense for anyone wearing any kind of bodice or wrapping.

Etesu pana ayaṃ vinicchayo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 372) – sabbanīlakādīni rajanāni vametvā puna rajitvā dhāretabbāni, na sakkā ce vametuṃ, paccattharaṇādīni vā kāretabbāni, tipaṭṭacīvarassa majjhe vā dātabbāni. Acchinnadasakādīni dasā chinditvā dhāretabbāni. Kañcukaṃ vijaṭetvā rajitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Veṭhanepi eseva nayo. Tirīṭakaṃ pādapuñchanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sabbanti imaṃ vuttappakāraṃ kusacīrādikaṃ akappiyacīvaraṃ acchinnacīvaro labhatīti attho. Vuttampi cetaṃ parivāre.

In this regard, the following decision is made (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 372): All cloths dyed with blue dye and the like should be discharged of the dye and dyed again before being worn. If they cannot be discharged of the dye, they should be made into coverings or the like, or they should be placed in the middle of a triple robe. Fringes that are uncut or the like should be worn after cutting off the fringes. A bodice should be unstitched, dyed, and then used. The same principle applies to wrappings. A tirīṭaka should be made into a foot-wiper. By 'all' is meant that a bhikkhu whose robe has been taken may receive this type of unallowable robe, such as a kusa-robe, etc. And this is also stated in the Parivāra.

“Akappakataṃ nāpi rajanāya rattaṃ,

Tena nivattho yena kāmaṃ vajeyya;

Na cassa hoti āpatti,

So ca dhammo sugatena desito;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 481);

"Not made according to rule, nor dyed with a proper dye,

With which one is clothed and goes as one pleases—

There is no offense in this,

And this is the Dhamma taught by the Sugata;

This question was pondered by the skilled." (Pari. 481)

Ayañhi [M 0.0101] pañho acchinnacīvarabhikkhuṃ sandhāya vutto, tasmā hi yaṃ kiñci akappiyacīvaraṃ nivāsetvā vā pārupitvā vā acchinnacīvarakena aññaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Ettha pana “idha pana, bhikkhave, manussā nissīmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cīvaraṃ denti ‘imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa [V 0.0101] demā’ti, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sādituṃ, na tāva taṃ gaṇanūpagaṃ, yāva na hatthaṃ gacchatī”ti (mahāva. 259) vuttattā yāva āharitvā taṃ na dinnaṃ, “tumhākaṃ, bhante, cīvaraṃ uppanna”nti pahiṇitvā vā nārocitaṃ, tāva gaṇanaṃ na upeti, anadhiṭṭhitaṃ vaṭṭati. Pattepi eseva nayo. Ānetvā dinne vā ārocite vā parihāro natthi, dasāhaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Cīvaravinicchayo.

This question was spoken with reference to a bhikkhu whose robe has been taken. Therefore, a bhikkhu whose robe has been taken, having worn or covered himself with any unallowable robe, should seek another. Here, however, since it was said (Mahāva. 259): "Monks, when people give robes to bhikkhus who have gone beyond the boundary, saying, 'We give this robe to so-and-so,' I allow you, monks, to accept it. It does not yet count as part of the reckoning until it reaches the hand"—therefore, until it is brought and given, or until the message 'Venerable, a robe has arisen for you' is sent and announced, it does not count as part of the reckoning; it is allowable as undetermined. The same principle applies to bowls. Once it has been brought and given or announced, there is no remedy; it must be determined within ten days. The Decision on Robes.

Cīvaraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Robes is concluded.

4. Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of Dyes

58. Idāni tesaṃ cīvarānaṃ rajanavidhānaṃ dassetuṃ “rajanāni cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cha rajanāni mūlarajanaṃ khandharajanaṃ tacarajanaṃ pattarajanaṃ puppharajanaṃ phalarajana”nti (mahāva. 344) evaṃ bhagavatā anuññātattā “chappakārāni anuññātāni satthunā”ti vuttaṃ.

58. Now, to show the method of dyeing those robes, it is said, "and dyes." Here, because the Blessed One has permitted, "I allow, monks, six dyes: root dye, stem dye, bark dye, leaf dye, flower dye, and fruit dye" (Mahāva. 344), thus it is said, "Six kinds are permitted by the Teacher."

59. Tattha mūleti mūlarajaneti attho. Haliddiṃ vivajjiya sabbaṃ labbhanti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tuṅgahārako nāma eko sakaṇṭakarukkho, tassa haritālavaṇṇaṃ khandharajanaṃ hoti. Gihiparibhuttaṃ pana allipattena ekavāraṃ rajituṃ vaṭṭati. Phalarajane akappiyaṃ nāma natthi, sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti. Rajanavinicchayo.

59. Here, “root” means root dye. With the exception of turmeric, all are permissible—this is the connection. The same applies to the rest. “Tuṅgahāraka” is the name of a thorny tree; its stem dye is orpiment-colored. However, if it has been used by laypeople, it is permissible to dye with it once using allipa leaves. In fruit dye, there is nothing impermissible—all are permissible. The Decision on Dyes.

Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Dyes is concluded.

5. Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Exposition of Bowls

60. Idāni [M 0.0102][V 0.0102] bhājanavikatiṃ dassetuṃ “patto cā”ti uddhaṭaṃ. Ettha pana paṭhamagāthā suviññeyyā.

60. Now, to show the variety of bowls, "and a bowl" is stated. Here, however, the first verse is easily understood.

61. Dutiye “magadhanāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhita”nti vattabbe vibhattilopaṃ akatvā gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ “magadhe nāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhita”nti vuttaṃ, pacitanti attho. Ettha (pārā. 602; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.602; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) magadhanāḷi nāma aḍḍhaterasapalaṃ gaṇhāti. Odananti ettha sabbappakārasampannaṃ avassāvitodanaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Odanassa catutthabhāgappamāṇaṃ nātighanaṃ nātitanukaṃ hatthahāriyamuggasūpañca ālopassa ālopassa anurūpaṃ yāva carimakālopappahonakaṃ macchamaṃsādibyañjanañca yo patto gaṇhāti, so ukkaṭṭho nāmāti attho. Sappitelatakkarasakañjikādīni pana gaṇanūpagāni na honti, tāni hi odanagatikāneva honti, neva hāpetuṃ, na vaḍḍhetuṃ sakkonti. Evametaṃ sabbaṃ pakkhittaṃ sace pattassa heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, suttena vā hīrena vā chindantassa suttassa vā hīrassa vā heṭṭhimantaṃ phusati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamitvā thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti, antogatameva hoti, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho nāma patto.

61. In the second verse, where it should be stated as the compound 'magadhanāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhita' (prepared with two Magadha measures of rice), for the sake of ease in poetic composition, the case ending was not elided, and it is said as 'magadhe nāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhita' (in Magadha, prepared with two measures of rice), meaning 'cooked.' Here, a Magadha measure is said to hold twelve and a half palas. 'Cooked rice' here refers to fully prepared, unstrained rice. The bowl that holds this cooked rice, along with mung bean soup amounting to a quarter of the rice—neither too thick nor too thin, and able to be eaten by hand—as well as fish, meat, and other curries suitable for each morsel up to the very last, is called the 'superior' bowl. Items like ghee, oil, buttermilk, and sour gruel, however, are not counted separately, as they are considered part of the rice and cannot be decreased or increased. If all this, when put into the bowl, reaches the lower rim, and when cut with a thread or horsehair, the thread or hair touches the lower edge, this is called the 'superior' bowl. If it forms a mound above the rim, it is called the 'superior-inferior' bowl. If it does not reach the rim but remains within, this is called the 'most superior' bowl.

62. “Majjhimo nāma patto nāḷikodanaṃ gaṇhātī”ti vuttattā “majjhimo tassupaḍḍho vā”ti vuttaṃ. Etthāpi vuttappakārena majjhimo majjhimomako majjhimukkaṭṭhoti pattattikaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Omako nāma patto patthodanaṃ gaṇhātī”ti (pārā. 602) vacanato “tatopaḍḍho”ti vuttaṃ. Magadhanāḷiyā upaḍḍhanāḷikodanañca tadūpiyaṃ sūpaṃ byañjanañca gaṇhāti, so [M 0.0103] omako nāma. Idhāpi omako omakomako omakukkaṭṭhoti pattattikaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imesu pana navasu pattesu ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho ca omakomako ca apatto. Etesu adhiṭṭhātabbakiccaṃ natthi, sesā satta pattā adhiṭṭhātabbā, vikappetabbā cāti attho.

62. Since it is said that a "middling bowl holds one nāḷi measure of rice," it is also stated that "the middling [holds] half of that [amount of rice]." Here too, the three types of bowls—middling, middling-inferior, and middling-superior—should be understood in the manner already stated. Based on the statement that "an inferior bowl holds one pattha measure of rice," it is said, '[holds] half of that [amount of rice].' An inferior bowl holds half a nāḷi measure of rice according to the Magadha nāḷi, along with a corresponding soup and curry. Here too, the three types—inferior, inferior-inferior, and inferior-superior—should be understood. Among these nine bowls, the 'most superior' and the 'most inferior' are not proper bowls. There is no function of formal determination for these; the remaining seven bowls are to be formally determined and assigned—this is the meaning.

63. Atirekapattoti (pārā. 601) anadhiṭṭhito avikappito. Sakoti sasantako. Kappoti kappiyo. Ayamevettha saṅkhepo – yo patto kākaṇikamattassāpi mūlassa dātabbassa natthitāya [V 0.0103] sako. Ayopatto pañcahi pākehi mattikāpatto dvīhi pākehi pakkattā kappo. So dasāhaparamaṃ kālaṃ anadhiṭṭhito avikappito dhāreyyoti.

63. An "extra bowl" (atirekapatta) refers to one that has not been determined or assigned. "Owned" (sako) means it is possessed. "Permitted" (kappo) means it is suitable. The summary here is this: a bowl is considered "owned" if, due to a lack of value even the worth of a kākaṇī-coin, there is no obligation to give it away. An iron bowl is "permitted" after being fired five times, and an earthen bowl after two firings. Such a bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days without being determined or assigned.

64. Acchedādayo cīvare vuttappabhedāyeva. Chiddenāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.608; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ettha yassa pattassa mukhavaṭṭito heṭṭhā dvaṅgulappadese yena chiddena kaṅgusitthaṃ nikkhamati, tattakena chiddena bhijjati. Tasmiṃ pana ayacuṇṇādīhi paṭipākatike kate dasāhabbhantare puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Pattādhiṭṭhānamujjhatīti patto adhiṭṭhānaṃ ujjhati.

64. The terms like "accheda" (severance) are of the same kinds as stated for the robe. "Chiddena" (by a hole) here refers to a bowl where, from the rim down to a two-finger breadth, a hole allows kaṅgu grains to seep out. The bowl is considered broken by that extent of damage. However, if it is repaired with iron powder or other materials prepared accordingly, it must be re-established within ten days. The phrase "pattādhiṭṭhānamujjhati" means the bowl relinquishes its established status.

65. Idāni pariharaṇavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “pattaṃ na paṭisāmeyya sodaka”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Sodakaṃ (cūḷava. 254) pattaṃ na paṭisāmeyya, ātape ca sodakaṃ pattaṃ na otapeti adhippāyo. Na nidaheti nirudakaṃ katvāpi atikālaṃ na nidaheti adhippāyo. Bhumyāti bhūmiyaṃ. Na ṭhapeti taṭṭikācammakhaṇḍādīsu yena kenaci anatthatāya paṃsusakkharamissāya bhūmiyā na ṭhapeyyāti attho. No ca laggayeti etthapi nāgadantādīsu (cūḷava. 254) yattha katthaci laggantassa dukkaṭameva.

65. Now, to explain the method for handling the bowl, the instruction begins: "One should not store a bowl with water," etc. "Sodakaṃ" (with water) means one should not store a bowl with water, nor should one expose a bowl with water to the sun—this is the intended meaning. "Na nidaheti" means one should not put it away; even after making it dry, one should not put it away for too long. "Bhumyā" means on the ground. "Na ṭhapeti" means one should not place it on mats, pieces of leather, and so on, nor on the ground mixed with dust or gravel, which would be for its harm—this is the meaning. "No ca laggayeti" here also means one should not hang it on pegs, etc.; for one who hangs it anywhere, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

66. Miḍḍhanteti (cūḷava. 254; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 254) [M 0.0104] miḍḍhapariyante. Sace pana parivattetvā tattheva patiṭṭhāti, evarūpāya vitthiṇṇāya miḍḍhiyā abbhantaraparicchede ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, na pariyante. Paribhaṇḍanteti bāhirapasse katāya tanukamiḍḍhiyā anteti attho. Aṅke vāti (cūḷava. 254) dvinnaṃ ūrūnaṃ majjhe. Ettha pana aṃsabaddhake aṃsakūṭe laggetvā aṅke ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, na itarathā. Ātapattaketi chatte. Ettha bhattapūropi aṃsakūṭe laggitapattopi ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

66. "Miḍḍhante" (at the edge of a bed) means at the edge of the bed-frame. But if one turns the bowl over and places it there, it is permissible to place it within the inner boundary of a wide bed-frame, but not at the edge. "Paribhaṇḍante" means at the end of a thin bed-frame made on the outer side—this is the meaning. "Aṅke vā" means on the lap, that is, between the two thighs. Here, it is permissible to place the bowl on the lap after having attached it by its strap to the shoulder, but not otherwise. "Ātapattake" means on a sunshade. Here, it is not permissible to place there even a bowl filled with food or a bowl attached to the shoulder.

67. Ucchiṭṭhodakaṃ (cūḷava. 255; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 255) nāma mukhavikkhālanodakaṃ, taṃ patte niṭṭhubhitvā pattena na nīhareyyāti attho. Calakañca aṭṭhikañca calakaṭṭhikaṃ. Etesu yaṃ kiñci pattena nīharantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Pattaṃ paṭiggahaṃ katvā hatthaṃ dhovitumpi na labhati. Hatthadhovitavatthadhovitaudakampi patte ākiritvā nīharituṃ na vaṭṭati. Anucchiṭṭhapattaṃ ucchiṭṭhahatthena gahetumpi na vaṭṭati. Hatthaṃ pana bahi dhovitvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Macchamaṃsaphalāphalādīni khādanto yaṃ mukhena luñcitvā luñcitvā khādati, taṃ vā tesaṃ aṭṭhiādikaṃ [V 0.0104] vā mukhato nīhaṭaṃ puna akhāditukāmo chaḍḍetukāmo patte ṭhapetuṃ na labhati. Siṅgiveranāḷikerakhaṇḍādīni khādantehi ḍaṃsitvā ḍaṃsitvā puna ṭhapetuṃ labhati. “Na bhikkhave pattahatthena kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetabbaṃ, yo paṇāmeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vuttattā yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena pattaṃ gahetvā ṭhito yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetuṃ na labhati, tasmā “pattahatthovā”ti vuttaṃ. Aṃsakūṭe laggitvā ṭhitassa vaṭṭati.

67. Ucchiṭṭhodaka refers to water used for rinsing the mouth; the meaning is that after spitting it into the bowl, one should not carry it out with the bowl. Calakaṭṭhikaṃ means a movable bone and a bone. For anyone who carries out any of these with the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing. One is not allowed to use the bowl as a receptacle for washing one's hands. It is not permissible to pour water from washing hands or clothes into the bowl and carry it out. It is not permissible to handle a bowl that is not soiled with leftovers with a hand that has touched leftovers. However, it is permissible to handle it after washing one's hands outside. When eating fish, meat, fruits, or the like, one is not allowed to place in the bowl what has been chewed and taken from the mouth, or its bones and so on, if one does not intend to eat it again and wishes to discard it. But when eating ginger, pieces of coconut, and so on, one is allowed to bite them and then place them back. Since it is said, "Bhikkhus, a door should not be pushed open with the hand holding a bowl. Whoever should push it open commits an offense of wrong-doing" (Cūḷavagga 255), one who is standing holding a bowl with any part of the body is not allowed to push open a door with any part of the body; this is why it was said, "with the hand holding a bowl." It is permissible for one whose bowl is attached to the shoulder.

68. Bhūmiādhāraketi ettha dantavallivettavākādīhi kate valayādhārake. Dārudaṇḍādhāreti ekadārunā kataādhārake [M 0.0105] ca bahūhi daṇḍehi kataādhārake cāti attho. Tidaṇḍe na vaṭṭati. Etesu pana susajjitesu ekaṃ pattaṃ ṭhapetvāva tassupari ekaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, tayo pana na vaṭṭanti. Ekaṃ nikkujjitvāva bhūmiyanti ettha bhūmiyaṃ kaṭasārakādīsu aññataraṃ pattharitvā tassupari nikkujjitvā vā ukkujjitvā vā ekaṃ ṭhapeyya, dve ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Dve pana ṭhapentena upari ṭhapitapattaṃ ekena passena bhūmiyaṃ phusāpetvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

68. Here, bhūmiādhārake refers to a support-ring made of materials such as ivory, creeper, rattan, or bark. Dārudaṇḍādhārake means a support made of a single piece of wood, or a support made of many sticks. A three-legged stand is not permissible. However, on these well-arranged supports, it is permissible to place one bowl and then another on top of it, but three are not permissible. "One overturned on the ground" here means that one should spread something like a mat or other material on the ground and place one bowl upon it, either overturned or upright; it is not permissible to place two—this is the intended meaning. However, some say that when placing two bowls, it is permissible to place the upper bowl so that one side touches the ground.

69-70. Idāni akappiyapatte dassetuṃ “dārurūpiyasovaṇṇā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha maṇiveḷuriyāmayāti (cūḷava. 252; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 252) maṇīti indanīlakabarakatādi. Sace gahaṭṭhā bhattagge suvaṇṇarūpiyataṭṭakādīsu sūpabyañjanaṃ katvā upanāmenti, āmasitumpi na vaṭṭati. Ghaṭikaṭāhajā (cūḷava. 255; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 255) ca tumbakaṭāhajā ca ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā. Ettha tumbakaṭāhajānāma alābu. Pattavinicchayo.

69-70. Now, to explain unallowable bowls, the passage beginning with "wooden, silver, or gold" was introduced. Therein, maṇiveḷuriyāmayāti (made of gems and beryl): maṇi means gems such as sapphire and emerald. If householders, at mealtime, prepare soup and curry in gold or silver dishes and offer them, it is not permissible even to touch them. Ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā refers to those made from clay pots (ghaṭikaṭāhajā) and those made from gourd pots (tumbakaṭāhajā). Here, tumbakaṭāhajā means a bottle gourd. The Determination Concerning Bowls.

Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Bowls is concluded.

6. Thālakaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Exposition of Dishes

71-2. Idāni thālakesu kappiyākappiyavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “thālakā cā”ti padaṃ uddhaṭaṃ. Tattha [V 0.0105] akappāti dārumayādayo thālakā akappiyāti attho. Phalikathālakādayo (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 252) gihisantakā vā saṅghasantakā vā kappiyā. Ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā (cūḷava. 255) tāvakālikā, tāsu bhuñjitvā chaḍḍetabbā, na pariharitabbāti adhippāyo. Thālakavinicchayo.

71-72. Now, to show the rule of what is allowable and unallowable concerning dishes, the phrase "thālakā ca" is cited. Here, akappā means that dishes made of wood and so on are unallowable. Dishes made of crystal and so on, whether belonging to householders or to the Saṅgha, are allowable. Those made from clay pots and gourd pots are for temporary use; the meaning is that having eaten from them, they should be discarded, not kept for use. The Determination Concerning Dishes.

Thālakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Dishes is concluded.

7. Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Invitation

73. Idāni [M 0.0106] pavāraṇāvidhiṃ dassetuṃ “pavāraṇā”ti (pāci. 238-239; pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) padaṃ uddhaṭaṃ. Tattha iriyāpathenāti ṭhānagamanasayananisajjānaṃ aññatarena iriyāpathenāti attho. Tato iriyāpathato aññena iriyāpathena anatirittakaṃ paribhuñjeyya ce, pācittiyanti attho. Pācittinatirittakanti pācitti anatirittakaṃ.

73. Now, to show the procedure for the invitation (pavāraṇā), the word "pavāraṇā" is cited. Here, "by way of posture" means by any of the postures of standing, walking, lying down, or sitting. The meaning is that if one then consumes what is not a leftover from that posture by means of another posture, it is a pācittiya offense. Pācittinatirittakaṃ means a pācittiya offense for what is not a leftover.

74. Idāni yehi aṅgehi pavāraṇā hoti, tāni aṅgāni dassetuṃ “asana”ntiādimāha. Tattha asananti etena avippakatabhojanatā vuttā, bhuñjamāno ca so puggalo hotīti attho. Bhojanañcevāti yaṃ bhuñjanto pavāreti, taṃ odano kummāso sattu maccho maṃsanti imesu aññataraṃ hotīti attho. Abhihāroti dāyako tassa taṃ bhattaṃ kāyena abhiharatīti attho, vācābhihāro pana na gahetabbo. Samīpatāti dāyako pavāraṇappahonakabhojanaṃ gahetvā aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇe okāse hotīti attho. Kāyavācāpaṭikkhepoti hatthapāse ṭhitena abhihaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhipeyyāti attho.
