Ettha pana sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, ānisadassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya, sace ṭhito, paṇhiantato paṭṭhāya, sace nipanno, yena passena nipanno, tassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya dāyakassāpi tathāvidhassa ṭhapetvā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ tassa āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa vasena paricchedo kātabbo. Pañca aṅgā pavāraṇāti “asanaṃ paññāyati, bhojanaṃ paññāyati, hatthapāse ṭhito abhiharati, paṭikkhepo [M 0.0107] paññāyatī”ti (pāci. 239; pari. 428) [V 0.0106] pāḷiyaṃ vuttehi imehi pañcahi aṅgehi pavāraṇā hotīti attho.

74. Now, to show the factors by which the invitation occurs, he says "asana" and so on. Here, by "asana" (eating) is meant that the meal is not yet finished, and that person is eating—this is the meaning. "Bhojanañceva" (and the food) means that what one is eating when one makes the invitation is one of these: cooked rice, gruel, flour, fish, or meat—this is the meaning. "Abhihāro" (offering) means the donor physically offers that meal—this is the meaning; a verbal offering, however, is not to be taken. "Samīpatā" (proximity) means the donor, having taken food sufficient for the invitation, is within a distance of two and a half handspans—this is the meaning. "Kāyavācāpaṭikkhepo" (rejection by body or speech) means that one should reject the almsfood offered by one standing within arm's reach either physically or verbally—this is the meaning. Here, if a bhikkhu is seated, the measurement begins from the edge of his sitting place; if standing, from the end of his heel; if lying down, from the edge of the side on which he is lying. For the donor as well, excluding his outstretched hand, the boundary should be determined based on whichever part of him is closest. "Pañca aṅgā pavāraṇā" (the invitation has five factors) means that the invitation occurs by these five factors stated in the Pāli: "Eating is apparent, food is apparent, one standing within arm's reach offers it, rejection is apparent"—this is the meaning.

75. Idāni etesu pañcasu bhojanaṃ dassetuṃ “odano”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idāni odanādayo imehi nibbattāti dassetuṃ “sālī”tiādimāha. Tattha setarattakāḷabhedā sabbāpi kaṅgujātiyo kaṅgūti gahetabbā. Kāḷasetā kudrūsavarakā. Imesaṃ sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ odano ca bhojjayāgu ca odano nāmāti attho.

75. Now, to show 'food' among these five factors, "cooked rice" and so on was stated. Next, to indicate that cooked rice and the like are produced from these, he says 'sāli' and so on. Here, all kinds of millet, distinguished by white, red, and black varieties, should be taken as 'kaṅgu'. Kudrūsa and varaka are the black and white kinds. Of these seven kinds of grain, both cooked rice and edible gruel are called 'cooked rice'—this is the meaning.

76. Sāmākāditiṇaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) kudrūsake saṅgahaṃ gatanti attho. Varakacorako varake saṅgahaṃ gato, sāliyañceva nīvāro saṅgahaṃ gato setattāti vadanti. Imesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ sānulomānaṃ sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ taṇḍule gahetvā “yāguṃ pacissāmā”ti vā “bhattaṃ pacissāmā”ti vā yaṃ kiñci sandhāya pacanti, sace uṇhaṃ vā sītalaṃ vā bhuñjantānaṃ bhojanakāle gahitagahitaṭṭhāne odhi paññāyati, ayaṃ odano nāma, pavāraṇaṃ janeti. Yopi pāyāso vā ambilayāgu vā uddhanato otāritamattā abbhuṇhā āvijjhitvā pivituṃ sakkā, gahitokāsepi odhiṃ na dasseti, ayaṃ pavāraṇaṃ na janeti. Usumāya pana vigatāya ghanabhāvaṃ gacchati, odhi paññāyati, puna pavāraṇaṃ janeti, pubbe tanukabhāvo na rakkhati. Bhatte pana udakakañjikakhīrādīni ākiritvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadanti, kiñcāpi tanukā hoti, pavāraṇaṃ janetiyeva tasmiṃ yāguyā natthibhāvato. Sace pana pakkuthitesu udakādīsu pakkhipitvā pacitvā denti, yāgusaṅgahameva gacchati.

76. 'Sāmāka grass' and so on (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 238-239) are included under kudrūsa—this is the meaning. Varaka and coraka are included under varaka. They say that cultivated rice and wild rice are included together due to their whiteness. When taking the grains of these seven kinds of grain, described as such and in their proper order, and cooking them with the intention of making gruel or cooked rice, if, while eating it hot or cold, a distinct boundary is discernible at the place where it is taken, this is called 'cooked rice' and generates an invitation. Even if it is a sweet gruel or sour gruel, if it can be drunk after being taken down from the stove, still hot, and stirred, and does not show a distinct boundary even where taken, this does not generate an invitation. However, when the heat has dissipated, it becomes thick, a distinct boundary becomes discernible, and it again generates an invitation; its previous thinness is not maintained. But if water, rice-water, milk, and so on are poured into cooked rice and they say, "Take the gruel," even if it is thin, it still generates an invitation because the state of gruel is not present in it. If, however, they put it into boiling water and so on, cook it, and then give it, it is simply classified as gruel.

77. Bhaṭṭhadhaññamayoti [M 0.0108] sattavidhānipi dhaññāni gahetvā kharapākabhajjitānaṃ tesaṃ taṇḍule koṭṭetvā katacuṇṇakuṇḍakāni sattu nāma. Samapākabhajjitānaṃ pana ātapasukkhānaṃ vā taṇḍulānaṃ cuṇṇakuṇḍakāni sattusaṅkhyaṃ na gacchanti. Yavasambhavoti aññehi pana muggādīhi katakummāso na pavāretīti adhippāyo. Udakasambhavoti iminā kakkaṭakasippikasambukādayopi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Sace yāgupānakāle ekasmiṃ bhājane ṭhapetvā macchamaṃsaṃ vā khādanti, te ce akhādanto aññaṃ pavāraṇappahonakaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Khāditepi sace mukhe avasiṭṭhaṃ natthi, tadā paṭikkhipantopi na pavāretiyeva. Sace [V 0.0107] patte avasiṭṭhaṃ atthi, mukhe natthi, tañce akhāditukāmo hoti, aññattha vā gantvā khāditukāmo, tasmiṃ khaṇe paṭikkhipantopi na pavāretiyeva.

77. 'Bhaṭṭhadhaññamaya' means that taking all seven kinds of grain, roasting them until hard, pounding their grains, and making them into coarse or fine flour is called 'sattu'. But the coarse or fine flour of grains roasted to a medium degree or dried in the sun does not fall into the category of 'sattu'. 'Yavasambhava' means that porridge made from other things like mung beans and so on does not generate an invitation—this is the intended meaning. 'Udakasambhava' means that by this, crabs, shellfish, conches, and so on are also included. If, while drinking gruel, one eats fish or meat placed in the same bowl, and if, not having eaten it, one rejects another offering sufficient for invitation, one does not generate an invitation. Even if it was eaten, if nothing remains in the mouth, then even if one rejects it, one does not generate an invitation. If something remains in the bowl but nothing is in the mouth, and one does not want to eat it or wants to go elsewhere to eat it, then even if one rejects it at that moment, one does not generate an invitation.

78. Bhojananti (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) pañcasu bhojanesu yaṃ kiñci bhojanaṃ. Kappiyaṃ vā akappiyaṃ vā bhuñjantoti sambandho. Nisedhayanti kāyenābhihaṭaṃ aṅgulicalanādinā vā bhamukavikārena vā kuddhabhāvena olokena vā paṭikkhipanto kāyena vā “ala”nti vā “na gaṇhāmī”ti vā “mā ākirā”ti vā “apagacchā”ti vā ādinā nayena paṭikkhipanto vācāya vā nisedhayantoti attho. Kappanti kappiyabhojanameva paṭikkhipanto so pavāreti, akappiyamaṃsaṃ vā bhojanaṃ vā paṭikkhipanto na pavāreti. Kasmā? Tassa paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā. Sace kappiyabhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno akappiyaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kasmā? Tassa paṭikkhipitabbato. Idāni missakanayaṃ dassetuṃ “tannāmenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ piṇḍattho – tannāmena vā imanti vā abhihaṭaṃ [M 0.0109] kappiyaṃ nisedhayaṃ pavāreyyāti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo pana macchamaṃsamissaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā; pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) yāguṃ byañjanaṃ vā āharitvā “macchaṃ gaṇhatha, maṃsaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Sace “yāguṃ gaṇhatha, rasabyañjanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā na hoti. Kasmā? Tassāpi atthitāya. Sace “imaṃ gaṇhathā”ti savatthukaṃ katvā deti, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Bhattamissakepi eseva nayo. Sace aññassa abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāraṇā natthiyeva.

78. 'Bhojana' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 238-239) refers to any food among the five kinds of food. The connection is with one who is eating, whether it is allowable or unallowable. 'Nisedhayanti' means rejecting what is offered. One rejects by body—by moving a finger and so on, by a frown, or by an angry look—or by speech, by saying 'Enough,' or 'I do not take it,' or 'Do not pour it,' or 'Go away,' and so on; this is the meaning. He generates an invitation by rejecting only allowable food; but by rejecting unallowable meat or food, he does not generate an invitation. Why? Because it stands in the place of what should be rejected. If, while eating allowable food, one rejects unallowable food, one does not generate an invitation. Why? Because it should be rejected. Now, to show the mixed case, 'by that name' and so on is stated. Here, the condensed meaning is: one should generate an invitation by rejecting allowable food offered by that name or as 'this'. What is meant? If someone brings gruel or curry mixed with fish or meat and says, 'Take the fish, take the meat,' then for one who rejects that, an invitation occurs. If they say, 'Take the gruel, take the seasoned curry,' then for one who rejects that, an invitation does not occur. Why? Because that also exists. If they give it with a clear indication, saying, 'Take this,' then for one who rejects that, an invitation occurs. The same method applies to mixed rice. If one rejects what is offered to another, there is no invitation at all.

79-80. Idāni pavāraṇaṃ ajanente dassetuṃ “lājā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha lājā taṃsattubhattānīti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) lājā ca lājehi katasattubhattāni cāti attho. Macchamaṃsapūvesu pana pavāraṇā hoti, tasmā “suddhakhajjako”ti vuttaṃ. Bhaṭṭhapiṭṭhanti pubbe āmakaṃ pacchā bhajjitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Veḷuādīnaṃ vuttāvasesānaṃ bhattanti sambandho. Rasayāgu raso pakkayāgu. Maṃsādīhi amissitā suddhayāgu. Puthukāmayaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci pavāraṇaṃ na janeti.

Now, to show what does not generate an invitation, 'lājā' and so on is stated. Here, 'lājā taṃsattubhattāni' (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule) means parched grains and food made from flour of parched grains; this is the meaning. However, an invitation occurs with fish, meat, and cakes; therefore, 'suddhakhajjako' is stated. 'Bhaṭṭhapiṭṭha' means that what was previously raw is afterwards roasted; this is what is meant. The connection for the remaining items mentioned, such as bamboo shoots and so on, is as 'food'. 'Rasayāgu' is flavored gruel; 'pakkayāgu' is cooked gruel. 'Suddhayāgu' is pure gruel, unmixed with meat and so on. But whatever is made of flattened rice does not generate an invitation.

81. Vuṭṭhāyāti (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) āsanā uṭṭhāya atirittaṃ na kātabbanti [V 0.0108] sambandho. Sace pavāretvā āsanā na vuṭṭhāti bhikkhu, tassāpi atirittaṃ kātuṃ labhati. Abhuttena ca bhojananti yena pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ antamaso kusaggenāpi na bhuttaṃ, tenāpi atirittaṃ na kātabbanti attho. Yena pana aruṇuggamepi bhuttaṃ hoti, so ce apavārito āsanā vuṭṭhitopi majjhanhikasamayepi puna kiñci abhutvāpi kātuṃ labhati. Yena yaṃ vā [M 0.0110] pure katanti yena yaṃ vā pubbe kataṃ, tena tampi pacchā na kātabbaṃ. Aññena pana taṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

81. The connection for 'Vuṭṭhāyāti' (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 238-239) is that having arisen from the seat, an excess should not be made. If a bhikkhu, having indicated satisfaction, does not rise from his seat, he is also allowed to make an excess. And 'abhūttena ca bhojanan'ti means that by one who has not eaten any of the five kinds of food, not even to the extent of a kusa-grass tip, an excess should not be made; this is the meaning. However, one who has eaten even at dawn, if he is not satisfied and has risen from his seat, is allowed to make an excess even at midday without having eaten anything again. 'Yena yaṃ vā pure katan'ti means that whatever was done previously by someone, that same thing should not be done afterwards by that person. But they say that it is allowable for another person to do it.

82. Yaṃ phalaṃ vā kandamūlaṃ vā pañcahi samaṇakappehi katakappiyaṃ aññampi kappiyabhojanaṃ vā kappiyamaṃsaṃ vā, idaṃ kappiyaṃ nāma, vuttappakāraviparītaṃ akappiyaṃ nāma, tasmiṃ atirittakaraṇaṃ na ruhati, yañca paṭiggahetvā na gahitaṃ, tasmimpi na ruhati, tena vuttaṃ “kappiyaṃ gahitañcevā”ti. Uccāritanti kappiyaṃ kāretuṃ āgatena bhikkhunā īsakampi ukkhittaṃ vā apanamitaṃ vāti attho. Hatthapāsato bahi ṭhitaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, tena vuttaṃ “hatthapāsaga”nti. Atirittaṃ karontevanti atirittaṃ karonto “alametaṃ sabba”nti vacībhedaṃ katvā evaṃ bhāsatūti attho. “Alametaṃ sabba”nti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ kira āciṇṇo. Vinayadharā kira pana “sakiṃ eva vattabba”nti vadanti. Alametaṃ sabbanti idampi vo adhikaṃ, ito aññaṃ na lacchasīti attho.

82. Whatever fruit or root, made allowable according to the five monastic allowances, or any other allowable food or allowable meat—this is called “allowable” (kappiya). What is contrary to the stated kind is called “unallowable” (akappiya). Making an excess of that is not valid, nor is it valid for what has been received but not taken. Therefore it is said, “allowable and taken.” 'Uccārita' means lifted or removed even slightly by the bhikkhu who has come to make it an excess; this is the meaning. It is not allowable to do this to something that is outside arm’s reach; therefore it is said, “within arm’s reach.” 'Atirittaṃ karonteva' means that when making an excess, one should speak thus, making a verbal declaration: “This is enough for all.” “Alametaṃ sabbaṃ” should be said three times; this is indeed the customary practice. However, Vinaya experts say it should be said only once. “Alametaṃ sabbaṃ” also means, “This is extra for you; you will not get more than this.”

83. Anupasampannahatthaganti kappiyaṃ karontena pana anupasampannassa hatthe ṭhitaṃyeva na kātabbaṃ, taṃ pana aññena bhikkhunā paṭiggahāpetvā tassa hatthe ṭhitaṃ atirittaṃ katvā anupasampannassa dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Attanā āgantvā aññassa hatthe ca pesayitvāpi kāretuṃ labbhateti attho. Taṃ pana atirittakārakaṃ ṭhapetvā añño sabbo pavāritopi appavāritopi bhuñjituṃ labhatīti attho. Sace pavārito paribhuñjati, yathā akatena missaṃ na hoti, tathā mukhañca hatthañca suddhaṃ katvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Gilānassa bhuttāvasesampi tassa “ajja vā sve vā khādissatī”ti āhaṭampi anatirittakataṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Pavāraṇāvinicchayo.

83. “Anupasampannahatthaga” means that when making something allowable, it should not be made while it is in the hands of one who is not fully ordained. However, it is allowable to have it received by another bhikkhu, and then, having made that which is in his hands leftover, to give it to the unordained person. It also means that one is allowed to have it made by coming oneself, or by sending it through another’s hands. However, apart from the one who made it leftover, everyone else, whether having been satisfied or not, is allowed to eat it. If one who has been satisfied consumes it, one should eat it after cleaning the mouth and hands, so that it does not mix with what has not been made leftover. Even what remains after a sick person has eaten, if brought with the thought “He will eat it today or tomorrow,” it is allowable to eat it without having been made leftover. This is the Judgment on the Invitation (Pavāraṇā).

Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Invitation is concluded.

8. Kālikaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Exposition of Time-Limited Items

84. Idāni [M 0.0111][V 0.0109] ye te cattāro kālikā muninā vuttā “yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvika”nti, te dassetuṃ “kālikā cā”ti padaṃ uddhaṭaṃ. Tattha (pāci. 254-256; pāci. aṭṭha. 253-256) katame te kālikāti ce, te dassetuṃ “yāvakālika”ntiādimāha. Tesu aruṇuggamanato yāva ṭhitamajjhanhikā bhuñjitabbato yāvakālikaṃ. Aruṇuggamanato yāva yāmāvasānā pipāsāya sati pipāsacchedanatthaṃ pātabbato yāmo kālo assāti yāmakālikaṃ. Tena upasametabbe ābādhe sati yāva sattāhā paribhuñjitabbato sattāhakālikaṃ. Ābādhe sati yāvajīvaṃ pariharitvā bhuñjitabbato yāvajīvikaṃ.

84. Now, to explain the four kinds of time-limited items declared by the Sage—namely, “for a limited time” (yāvakālika), “for a watch” (yāmakālika), “for seven days” (sattāhakālika), and “for life” (yāvajīvika)—the term “kālikā” has been introduced. Herein (Pāc. 254-256; Pāc. Aṭṭha. 253-256), what are these time-limited items? To explain them, it begins with “yāvakālika,” and so on. Among these, “yāvakālika” refers to what is to be consumed from the rising of dawn until midday. “Yāmakālika” refers to that which may be drunk from the rising of dawn until the end of the watch, when there is thirst, for the purpose of quenching it. “Sattāhakālika” refers to what is to be consumed for up to seven days when there is an illness that needs to be alleviated by it. “Yāvajīvika” refers to what is to be kept and consumed for life when there is an illness.

85. Tesu yāvakālikaṃ dassetuṃ “piṭṭhaṃ mūlaṃ phalaṃ khajja”ntiādimāha. Ettha (pāci. 248-250; pāci. aṭṭha. 248-249) piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ nāma sattannaṃ tāva dhaññānaṃ dhaññānulomānaṃ aparaṇṇānañca piṭṭhaṃ panasapiṭṭhaṃ labujapiṭṭhaṃ ambāṭakapiṭṭhaṃ sālapiṭṭhaṃ dhotakatālapiṭṭhaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhañcāti evamādīni tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthañca bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakāni piṭṭhāni yāvakālikāni. Imināva lakkhaṇena mūlakhādanīyādīsupi yāvakālikalakkhaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, ativitthārabhayena saṃkhittaṃ. Goraso nāma khīradadhitakkaraso. Dhaññabhojananti sānulomāni sattadhaññāni ca pañcavidhabhojanañcāti attho. Yāgusūpappabhutayoti ettha pabhuti-saddena kandakhādanīyaṃ muḷālakhādanīyaṃ matthakakhādanīyaṃ khandhakhādanīyaṃ tacakhādanīyaṃ pattakhādanīyaṃ pupphakhādanīyaṃ aṭṭhikhādanīyaṃ niyyāsakhādanīyanti imāni saṅgahitānīti veditabbāni.

85. To explain “yāvakālika” (for a limited time), it begins with “flour, roots, fruits, edibles,” and so on. Here (Pāc. 248-250; Pāc. Aṭṭha. 248-249), “flour edibles” means the flour of the seven grains, grains similar to them, and other non-grains, such as jackfruit flour, breadfruit flour, hog plum flour, sal flour, young palmyra flour, milk vine flour, etc. In various regions, these flours, which are widespread for human consumption and eating as customary food, are “yāvakālika.” By this same characteristic, the characteristic of “yāvakālika” should be understood in root edibles, etc., but it is stated concisely due to fear of excessive detail. “Milk produce” means milk, curds, and buttermilk. “Grain food” means the seven grains with their derivatives and the five kinds of staple food. “Gruel, soup, and so on”—here, by the word “so on,” it should be understood that these are included: tuber edibles, stalk edibles, shoot edibles, stem edibles, bark edibles, leaf edibles, flower edibles, seed edibles, and resin edibles.

Tatridaṃ [M 0.0112] mukhamattanidassanaṃ – bhisasaṅkhāto padumapuṇḍarīkakando piṇḍālumasālukaādayo vallikando āluvakando tālakandoti evamādi kandakhādanīyaṃ. Padumamuḷālādayo muḷālakhādanīyaṃ. Tālahintālakuntālaketakanāḷikerapūgarukkhakhajjūrīādīnaṃ kaḷīrasaṅkhātā matthakā matthakakhādanīyaṃ. Ucchukhandho nīluppalarattuppalakumudasogandhikānaṃ pupphadaṇḍakānīti evamādi khandhakhādanīyaṃ. Tacakhādanīyaṃ ucchutaco eva eko yāvakāliko, sopi saraso. Mūlakaṃ khārako caccu tambuko taṇḍuleyyakoti evamādi pattakhādanīyaṃ. Mūlakapupphaṃ khārakapupphaṃ [V 0.0110] caccupupphaṃ tambukapupphanti evamādi pupphakhādanīyaṃ, asokapupphaṃ pana yāvajīvikaṃ. Labujapanasaṭṭhiādi aṭṭhikhādanīyaṃ. Niyyāsakhādanīye yāvakālikaṃ natthi. Ete vuttappakārā yāvakālikā hontīti attho.

Here is a mere illustrative example: The bulb of the lotus and white lotus, known as bhisa; root-tubers like yams and taro; creeper tubers, yam tubers, palmyra palm tubers, and so on—these are “tuber edibles.” Lotus stalks and so on are “stalk edibles.” The tender shoots (kaḷīra) of palmyra, wild date palm, kuntāla, screwpine, coconut, areca palm, date palm, etc., are “shoot edibles.” Sugarcane stalks, the flower stalks of blue lotus, red lotus, white lotus, and fragrant water lilies, and so on—these are “stem edibles.” Among “bark edibles,” only sugarcane bark is “yāvakālika” (for a limited time), and that too, if it has juice. Radish, mustard greens, caccu, tambuka, amaranth, and so on—these are “leaf edibles.” The flowers of radish, mustard greens, caccu, tambuka, and so on—these are “flower edibles”; but the flower of the ashoka tree is “yāvajīvika” (for life). Jackfruit seeds, breadfruit seeds, and so on are “seed edibles.” There is no “yāvakālika” (for a limited time) among “resin edibles.” The meaning is that these, of the types mentioned, are “yāvakālika.”

86. Idāni “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭha pānāni ambapānaṃ jambupānaṃ cocapānaṃ mocapānaṃ madhukapānaṃ muddikapānaṃ sālūkapānaṃ phārusakapāna”nti (mahāva. 300) evaṃ vuttaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ pānakaṃ yāmakālikaṃ nāmāti dassetuṃ “madhū”tiādimāha. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 300) madhujaṃ muddikajaṃ sālūkajaṃ cocajaṃ mocajaṃ ambujaṃ jambujañcāti evamattho gahetabbo. Ettha madhujaṃ nāma madhukānaṃ jātirasena kataṃ, taṃ pana udakasambhinnameva vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Muddikapānaṃ nāma muddikā udake madditvā parissāvetvā gahitaṃ. Sālūkapānaṃ nāma rattuppalanīluppalādīnaṃ kiñjakkharehi kataṃ. Sesāni pākaṭāneva. Ettha pana sace sayaṃ etāni yāvakālikavatthūni paṭiggahetvā udake madditvā ātape ādiccapākena pacitvā parissāvetvā pānakaṃ karoti, taṃ purebhattameva kappati. Sace anupasampannena kataṃ labhati, tadahupurebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena [M 0.0113] yāva aruṇuggamanā vaṭṭati. Imāni aṭṭha pānāni sītānipi ādiccapākānipi vaṭṭanti, aggipākāni pana na vaṭṭanti, tasmā “naggisantatta”nti vuttaṃ.

86. Now, to show that the eight kinds of drinks thus stated are called “yāmakālika” (for a watch), as it is said: “I allow, bhikkhus, eight drinks: mango drink, rose-apple drink, plantain drink, banana drink, madhuka drink, grape drink, water lily drink, and phārusaka drink” (Mahāvagga 300), the text begins with “madhu,” and so on. Here (Mahāvagga Aṭṭha. 300), the meaning to be understood is that which is from madhuka, from grapes, from water lily, from plantain, from banana, from mango, and from rose-apple. Here, “madhuka drink” means that which is made from the natural juice of madhuka trees, and it is allowable only when mixed with water; pure juice is not allowable. “Grape drink” means grapes or raisins crushed in water, strained, and taken. “Water lily drink” means that which is made from the stamens of red and blue water lilies, etc. The others are well-known. Here, however, if one takes these “yāvakālika” substances oneself, crushes them in water, cooks them by the sun’s heat, strains them, and makes a drink, it is allowable only before the meal. If one obtains it made by an unordained person, it is allowable even with solid food on that day before the meal; after the meal, it is allowable for consumption without solid food until dawn. These eight drinks are allowable whether cold or sun-cooked, but they are not allowable if cooked by fire; therefore it is said, “not heated by fire.”

87. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ phalarasaṃ ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasa”nti (mahāva. 300) vuttattā dhaññaphalaraso pana na vaṭṭati, tena vuttaṃ “sānulomāni dhaññāni ṭhapetvā”ti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ puppharasaṃ ṭhapetvā madhukapuppharasa”nti vuttattā madhukapuppharaso ādiccapāko vā hotu aggipāko vā, pacchābhattaṃ na vaṭṭati, tena vuttaṃ “madhukapupphamaññatrā”ti.

87. As it is stated: “I allow, bhikkhus, all fruit juice except the juice of grain-fruit” (Mahāvagga 300), the juice of grain-fruit is not allowable; therefore it is said, “except for grains with their derivatives.” As it is stated: “I allow, bhikkhus, all flower juice except madhuka flower juice,” madhuka flower juice, whether sun-cooked or fire-cooked, is not allowable after the meal; therefore it is said, “except madhuka flowers.”

88. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ pattarasaṃ ṭhapetvā ḍākarasa”nti vuttattā udakena pakkānampi yāvakālikapattānaṃ raso purebhattameva vaṭṭati, sītodakena madditānaṃ raso yāmakālikaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “ṭhapetvā pakkaḍākaja”nti. Yāvajīvikapaṇṇassa udakena pakkassa raso yāvajīviko hoti.

88. As it is stated: “Bhikkhus, I allow all leaf juices except for ḍāka juice,” the juice of “yāvakālika” leaves cooked with water is allowable only before the meal. The juice of those crushed with cold water is “yāmakālika” (for a watch). Therefore, it is said, “except for that from cooked ḍāka.” The juice of “yāvajīvika” leaves cooked with water is “yāvajīvika” (for life).

89. Idāni [V 0.0111] sattāhakālike dassetuṃ “sappī”tiādimāha. Ettha (mahāva. 260) pana –

89. Now, to explain “sattāhakālika” (for seven days), it says “ghee,” and so on. Here, however (Mahāvagga 260):

“Sappinonītatelāni, madhuphāṇitameva ca;

Sattāhakālikā sappi, yesaṃ maṃsamavārita”nti. –

“Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses; these are ‘sattāhakālika’. Ghee is for those for whom meat is not forbidden.”

Pāṭho gahetabbo. Evaṃ pana gahite vasā telaggahaṇena gahitāva hoti “telaṃ nāma tilatelaṃ sāsapatelaṃ madhukatelaṃ eraṇḍatelaṃ vasātela”nti (pārā. 623; pāci. 260) evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vitthāritattā. Evaṃ pana aggahetvā vasā ca “madhuphāṇita”nti pāṭhe gahite yāvakālikabhūtā vasā sattāhakālikāti āpajjeyya, “yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṃ [M 0.0114] bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisāyanīyāni bhesajjāni, seyyathidaṃ – sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇita”nti (pārā. 622) evaṃ pañceva bhagavatā sattāhakālikabhesajjāni anuññātāni, tato uttari chaṭṭhassa sattāhakālikabhesajjassa atthitāpi āpajjati, bhesajjakkhandhakepi bhagavatā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasaṃ kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ sattāhakālikavasena vasaṃ ananujānitvā tato nibbattatelameva anuññātaṃ, tasmā “madhuphāṇitameva cā”ti pāṭhe aggahite pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca virujjhati. Therena pana uttaravihāravāsīnaṃ khuddasikkhāya āgatanayena vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ pana –

The reading should be adopted. When thus adopted, fat is already included by the mention of oil: “Oil means sesame oil, mustard oil, mahua oil, castor oil, and fat-oil” (Pārā. 623; Pāci. 260) because this is elaborated in the Pāli. However, if this is not adopted, and the reading is taken as 'fat, honey, and molasses', then fat, which is a lifetime requisite, would become a seven-day requisite. “Those medicines that are suitable for sick bhikkhus, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses” (Pārā. 622). Thus, only these five seven-day medicines were permitted by the Blessed One. Beyond these, the existence of a sixth seven-day medicine would arise. And in the chapter on medicines, the Blessed One said: “Monks, I allow fats as medicines—bear fat, fish fat, alligator fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—when received at the proper time, prepared at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, to be consumed with the use of oil” (Mahāva. 262). Thus, fat itself was not permitted as a seven-day requisite; only the oil derived from it was permitted. Therefore, if the reading “and honey and molasses only” is not adopted, it contradicts both the Pāli and the commentaries. However, this was stated by the Elder of the Uttaravihāravāsins according to the method found in the Khuddasikkhā. For them, however—

“Sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ, madhu phāṇitapañcamaṃ;

Acchamacchavasādi ca, honti sattāhakālikā”ti. –

“Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses as the fifth; and bear fat, fish fat, etc., these are allowable for seven days.”

Evamāgataṃ. Amhākaṃ pana visuṃ sattāhakālike āgataṭṭhānaṃ natthīti vadanti, upaparikkhitabbaṃ.

Thus it has come. But they say, “For us, there is no place where it is mentioned separately as a seven-day requisite.” This should be investigated.

Idāni tesu sappiṃ dassetuṃ “yesaṃ maṃsapavārita”nti vuttaṃ. “Sappināma gosappi vā ajikāsappi vā mahiṃ sasappi vā. Yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappi, navanītaṃ nāma tesaṃyeva navanīta”nti (pārā. 623; pāci. 260) pāḷiyaṃ vuttattā navanītaṃ pana gahitanti na vitthāritaṃ[V 0.0112], sappi pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ tadahu purebhattaṃ sāmisampinirāmisampi vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sattāhātikkame sace ekabhājane ṭhapitaṃ, ekaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Sace bahūsu, vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyapācittiyāni. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Sappi tāpentassa sāmaṃpāko na hoti, “navanītaṃ pana tāpentassa hi sāmaṃpāko na hoti, sāmaṃpakkena pana [M 0.0115] tena saddhiṃ āmisaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti ca “sace anupasampanno purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitanavanītena sappiṃ katvā deti, purebhattaṃ sāmisaṃ vaṭṭati. Sace sayaṃ karoti, sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭatī”ti ca samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.622) navanītamhiyeva sāmaṃpākatā vuttā, na sappimhi. Yaṃ pana kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ vuttaṃ “nibbattitasappi vā navanītaṃ vā pacituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti, “taṃ pana tadahu purebhattampi sāmisaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ca, tattha yāvakālikavatthunā asammissaṃ sudhotaṃ navanītaṃ sandhāya “pacituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sayaṃpacitasattāhakālikena saddhiṃ yadi āmisaṃ bhuñjati, taṃ āmisaṃ sayaṃpakkasattāhakālikena missitaṃ attano yāvakālikabhāvaṃ sattāhakālikena gaṇhāpeti, tathā ca sati yāvakālikaṃ apakkampi sayaṃpakkabhāvaṃ upagacchatīti “sāmisaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā sayaṃpakkasattāhakālikavasātelaṃ sayaṃbhajjitasāsapādiyāvajīvikavatthūnaṃ telañca sāmisaṃ tadahu purebhattampi na vaṭṭati, tathā navanītasappīti veditabbaṃ. Vakkhati ca ācariyo –

Now, to explain ghee among these, it is said: “For those whose meat is permitted.” “Ghee means cow’s ghee, or goat’s ghee, or buffalo’s ghee. For those whose meat is allowable, their ghee is allowable, and fresh butter means their fresh butter” (Pārā. 623; Pāci. 260). Since it is stated in the Pāli, fresh butter is included, but it is not elaborated upon. However, ghee received before the meal is allowable on that very day before the meal, whether mixed with meat or unmixed. From after the meal onwards, it should be consumed unmixed with meat for seven days. If it exceeds seven days and is stored in a single container, there is one offense of forfeiture. If in many, there are offenses of forfeiture and expiation according to the number of items. Ghee received after the meal is only allowable unmixed with meat for seven days. Heating ghee does not constitute self-cooking. “But heating fresh butter does not constitute self-cooking, and meat is not allowable with that which is self-cooked.” And, “If an unordained person makes ghee from fresh butter received before the meal and gives it, it is allowable with meat before the meal. If one makes it oneself, it is only allowable unmixed with meat for seven days.” In the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.622), self-cooking is mentioned only in regard to fresh butter, not ghee. However, what is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, “Ghee or fresh butter that has been produced is allowable to cook,” and “but it is not allowable to consume it mixed with meat, even before the meal on that day,” (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) there “allowable to cook” refers to pure, well-clarified fresh butter that is unmixed with any temporary requisite. If one eats meat with a self-cooked seven-day requisite, that meat, being mixed with the self-cooked seven-day requisite, has its temporary nature taken over by the seven-day requisite; and in that case, the temporary requisite, though not cooked by oneself, attains the state of being self-cooked. Therefore it is said, “It is not allowable to consume it with meat.” Just as self-cooked seven-day requisite fat-oil, and oil from self-fried mustard seeds etc., which are lifetime requisites, are not allowable with meat even on that very day before the meal, so too fresh butter and ghee should be understood. And the teacher will state—

“Yāvakālikaādīni, saṃsaṭṭhāni sahattanā. Gāhāpayanti sabbhāva”nti ca,

“Temporary things and so on, when mixed, cause the other to assume their own nature.”

“Teheva bhikkhunā pakkaṃ, kappate yāvajīvikaṃ;

Nirāmisañca sattāhaṃ, sāmise sāmapākatā”ti ca.

“With those things, what is cooked by a bhikkhu is allowable: a lifetime requisite, and a seven-day requisite unmixed with meat; with meat, it is self-cooked.”

Yā pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ navanītamhi sāmaṃpākatā vuttā, sā takkādisammissaṃ adhotanavanītaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā viññūnaṃ samantapāsādikāpi kaṅkhāvitaraṇīpi samenti, taṃ navanītaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ācariyā vadanti. Idameva yuttaṃ. Yadi sappimhi sāmaṃpākatā hoti, avassaṃyeva samantapāsādikāyaṃ [M 0.0116] vucceyya, tattha pana “sappi tāva purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ, tadahu purebhattaṃ sāmisampi nirāmisampi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.622) hi [V 0.0113] vuttaṃ, na pacanavidhānaṃ. Manussasappinavanītānaṃ, aññesampi hatthiassādīnaṃ akappiyamaṃsasappinavanītānaṃ sattāhātikkame dukkaṭaṃ. Kiṃ pana taṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti? Āma vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Paṭikkhepābhāvā ca sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu anuññātattā ca. “Yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappi, navanīta”nti (pārā. 623) idaṃ pana nissaggiyavatthuṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ vāraṇatthāya.

What is mentioned in the Samantapāsādikā regarding the self-cooking of fresh butter refers to unclarified fresh butter mixed with whey, etc. Therefore, the wise say that both the Samantapāsādikā and the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī are in agreement, stating that it refers to that kind of fresh butter. This alone is appropriate. If self-cooking were to apply to ghee, it would certainly be mentioned in the Samantapāsādikā. However, there it is said, “Ghee received before the meal is allowable to consume on that very day before the meal, whether mixed with meat or unmixed,” but it does not mention a cooking method. For human ghee and fresh butter, and also for the ghee and fresh butter from the meat of elephants, horses, and other animals whose meat is not allowable, if kept beyond seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing. But is it permissible to consume it? Yes, it is permissible. Why? Because there is no prohibition, and it is allowed in all the commentaries. The statement, “For those whose meat is allowable, their ghee and fresh butter are allowable,” is made to indicate the subject of forfeiture, not to prohibit others.

90. Idāni telaṃ dassetuṃ “telaṃ tilavaseraṇḍamadhusāsapasambhava”ntiādimāha. Ettha tilādīhi sambhavaṃ nibbattaṃ telanti sambandho. Ettha (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.100) pana purebhattaṃ tile paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya savatthukappaṭiggahitattā anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Eraṇḍamadhukasāsapaṭṭhīni paṭiggahetvā sace tāni bhajjitvā telaṃ karoti, tadahu purebhattampi sāmisaṃ na vaṭṭati, sāmaṃpākatā hoti. Sace abhajjitvā karoti, tadahu purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, paribhuñjitabbavatthūnaṃ yāvajīvikattā savatthukappaṭiggahaṇe doso natthīti. Telaggahaṇatthāya eraṇḍakaṭṭhiādīni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ atikkāmayato dukkaṭaṃ. Tathā pāḷiyaṃ anāgatāni adassitāni kosambakakusumbhādīnaṃ telāni.

90. Now, to explain oil, he said: “Oil is derived from sesame, fat, castor, madhuka, and mustard.” Here, the connection is that oil is produced from sesame and the like. In this context (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.100), if sesame is received before the meal and oil is made from it, that oil is allowable even with meat before the meal, but from after the meal onwards, because it was received with the substance, it is not to be consumed. If oil is made from sesame received after the meal, it is not to be consumed, but it may be used for anointing the head, etc. If castor, madhuka, or mustard seeds are received and one fries them to make oil, then even before the meal on that day, it is not allowable with meat; it becomes self-cooked. If one makes it without frying them, then before the meal on that day, it is allowable even with meat, but from after the meal onwards, it is only allowable unmixed with meat, as there is no fault in receiving the substance itself, since the items for use are allowable for life. If castor seeds, etc., are received for the purpose of extracting oil and one allows seven days to pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Similarly, the oils of kosambaka, kusumbha, etc., which are not mentioned or shown in the Pāli, are included.

Idāni madhuvikatiṃ dassetuṃ “khuddābhamaramadhukari-makkhikāhi kata”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) khuddāti khuddamakkhikā. Bhamarāti mahābhamaramakkhikā[M 0.0117]. Daṇḍakesu madhukarā madhukarimakkhikā nāma. Etāhi tīhi makkhikāhi kataṃ madhu nāmāti attho. “Madhu nāma makkhikāmadhū”ti pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 623; pāci. 260) vuttattā aññehi tumbaṭakādīhi kataṃ sattāhakālikaṃ na hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Now, to explain the varieties of honey, it is said: “Made by small bees, bumblebees, and honey-making bees.” Herein, “small” means small bees. “Bumblebees” means large bumblebees. “Honey-making bees” are those found in tree hollows. The meaning is that honey is that which is made by these three types of bees. Since it is stated in the Pāli, “Honey means bee-honey,” it should be understood that what is made by others, such as tumbaṭakas, is not allowable for seven days.

Idāni phāṇitaṃ dassetuṃ “rasādiucchuvikati, pakkāpakkā ca phāṇita”nti āha. Pakkā ca apakkā ca rasādiucchuvikati phāṇitanti attho. Madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaṃ vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Tassa sattāhātikkame dukkaṭaṃ. Ciñcaphāṇitañca ambaphāṇitañca yāvakālikameva.

Now, to explain molasses, it is said: “Molasses is a modification of sugarcane juice, etc., whether cooked or uncooked.” The meaning is that molasses is a modification of sugarcane juice, etc., whether cooked or uncooked. Madhuka-flower molasses is allowable with a savory component before the meal, but from after the meal onwards, it is allowable only without a savory component for seven days. If it exceeds seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Tamarind molasses and mango molasses are only allowable for the proper time (until noon).

91. Idāni [V 0.0114] etesu vasātelassa odissa anuññātattā taṃ visuṃ uddharitvā dassetuṃ “savatthupakkā sāmaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Sattavidhañhi (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) odissaṃ nāma byādhodissaṃ puggalodissaṃ kālodissaṃ samayodissaṃ desodissaṃ vasodissaṃ bhesajjodissanti.

91. Now, since fat-oil is permitted under specific circumstances, he stated, extracting it separately to explain, “whether cooked with its substance or by oneself,” etc. For there are seven kinds of specific circumstances: specific to illness, specific to persons, specific to time, specific to occasions, specific to place, specific to fat, and specific to medicine.

Tattha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, amanussikābādhe āmakamaṃsaṃ āmakalohita”nti (mahāva. 264) vuttaṃ, idaṃ byādhodissaṃ nāma. Ettha pana kālepi vikālepi kappiyākappiyamaṃsalohitaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, romanthakassa romanthana”nti (cūḷava. 273) evaṃ anuññātaṃ puggalodissaṃ nāma. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cattāri mahāvikaṭāni dātuṃ gūthaṃ muttaṃ chārikaṃ mattika”nti (mahāva. 268) evaṃ sappadaṭṭhakāle appaṭiggahitakaṃ anuññātaṃ kālodissaṃ nāma. Gaṇabhojanādi samayodissaṃ nāma. Gaṇaṅgaṇūpāhanāni desodissaṃ nāma. Vasodissaṃ nāma “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ [M 0.0118] vasānāmena anuññātaṃ. Taṃ ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ kappiyākappiyavasānaṃ telaṃ taṃtadatthikānaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhesajjodissaṃ nāma “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni pañca bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 261) evaṃ bhesajjanāmena vuttāni sappiādīni pañca.

Herein, the statement, "I allow, monks, raw flesh and raw blood for illnesses caused by non-humans," is called illness-specific. In this case, at the proper time or the wrong time, both allowable and unallowable flesh and blood are permissible. "I allow, monks, the cud of a ruminant," thus allowed, is called person-specific. "I allow, monks, to give the four great repellents—dung, urine, ashes, and clay," thus, what has not been formally received being allowed at the time of a snakebite, is called time-specific. Group meals, etc., are occasion-specific. Footwear for groups is place-specific. Fat-specific is stated as, "I allow, monks, fats as medicines," thus allowed by the name of fat. Except for human fat, oil from all fats, whether allowable or unallowable, may be consumed as an oil preparation by those in need of it. Medicine-specific is stated as, "I allow, monks, those five medicines," referring to the five, such as ghee, etc., mentioned by the name of medicine.

Yathā pana khīradadhiādīhi pakkatelaṃ pacchābhattaṃ na vaṭṭati, na evamidaṃ. Idaṃ pana telaṃ savatthukapakkampi vaṭṭati, taṃ dassetuṃ “savatthupakkā sāmaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Vasaṃ oloketvā “savatthupakkā”ti vuttaṃ. Sāmaṃ pakkā vāti attho. Yathā savatthukappaṭiggahitattā sāmaṃpakkattā dadhiādīhi pakkatelaṃ attanā kataṃ purebhattampi na vaṭṭati, na evamidaṃ. Idaṃ pana attanā savatthukapakkampi purebhattampi pacchābhattampi vaṭṭatīti attho. Ettha pana kāraṇūpacārena vasātelaṃ “vasā”ti vuttaṃ.

Just as oil prepared with milk, curds, etc., is not permissible after the meal, this is not so. But this oil is permissible even when cooked with its substance; to show this, the phrase ‘cooked with its substance or by oneself’ is stated. With reference to the fat, ‘cooked with its substance’ is stated. The meaning is ‘or cooked by oneself.’ Just as oil prepared with curds, etc., made by oneself, is not permissible even before the meal because it is received with its substance and cooked by oneself, this is not so. But the meaning is that this oil, even if cooked by oneself with its substance, is permissible both before and after the meal. Here, by a figurative expression of cause for effect, oil from fat is called ‘fat’.

Kāleti purebhattakāle parehi vā attanā vā pakkāti attho. Pacchābhattaṃ pana pacituṃ na vaṭṭati “kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭha”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā. Tasmā “kāle”ti vuttaṃ. Yo pana vikāle paṭiggahetvā vikāle pacitvā vikāle parissāvetvā paribhuñjati, so tīṇi dukkaṭāni āpajjati.

‘At the proper time’ means cooked before the meal, whether by others or by oneself. However, it is not permissible to cook after the meal, as it is said: “Received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time.” Therefore, ‘at the proper time’ is stated. But whoever receives at the wrong time, cooks at the wrong time, filters at the wrong time, and consumes it, incurs three offenses of wrong-doing.

Amānusāti [V 0.0115] ettha (mahāva. 262) pana acchavasādīnaṃ anuññātattā ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasā anuññātāti veditabbā. Maṃsesu hi manussahatthimaṃsādīni dasa maṃsāni paṭikkhittāni, vasā pana ekā manussavasā eva.

Here, regarding ‘non-human,’ it should be understood that because the fat of bears and other animals is permitted, the fat of all unallowable meats is permitted, except for human fat. For among meats, ten types, such as human flesh and elephant flesh, are prohibited, but as for fat, only human fat is prohibited.

Anupasampannena (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) katanibbaṭṭitavasātelaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ [M 0.0119] nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Yaṃ panettha sukhumarajasadisaṃ maṃsaṃ vā nhāru vā aṭṭhi vā lohitaṃ vā, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Sace sayaṃ karoti, purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā pacitvā parissāvetvā sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Nirāmisaparibhogañhi sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 262). Aññesanti sappiādīnaṃ. Vatthunti yāvakālikabhūtaṃ vatthuṃ. Yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ vatthuṃ na paceti sambandho.

Fat-oil prepared and rendered by one who is not fully ordained, if received before the meal, is permissible before the meal even with a savory component. From after the meal onward, it is permissible only without a savory component for seven days. In this case, any fine substance resembling dust—such as flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—is considered negligible. If one prepares it oneself, having received it before the meal, it must be cooked, strained, and consumed only without a savory component for seven days. For it is with reference to consuming it without a savory component that this was said: “What is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time may be consumed as an oil preparation.” ‘Of others’ refers to ghee, etc. ‘Substance’ means a substance that is allowable only until noon. The connection is that one does not cook the substance of items allowable only until noon.

92. Idāni yāvajīvikavikatiṃ dassetuṃ “haliddī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāyamanuttānapadattho (mahāva. 263; pāci. aṭṭha. 248-249) – pañcamūlādikañcāpīti ettha dvipañcamūlena saddhiṃ aññānipi taggatikāni mūlabhesajjāni gahitānīti ñātabbaṃ.

92. Now, to explain the life-long allowable derivative, “turmeric” and so on are mentioned. Herein is the meaning of the non-obvious word: in the phrase “and also the five roots, etc.,” it should be understood that along with the two five-root sets, other root-medicines of a similar nature are also included.

93-5. Biḷaṅgādīni phalabhesajjāni. Tattha (mahāva. 263) goṭṭhaphalanti madanaphalanti vadanti. Kappāsādīnaṃ paṇṇanti sambandho. Ime pana vuttappakārā mūlabhesajjaphalabhesajjapaṇṇabhesajjavasena vuttā sabbe kappiyā. Imesaṃ pupphaphalapaṇṇamūlā sabbepi kappiyā yāvajīvikāyeva. Ṭhapetvā ucchuniyyāsaṃ sabbo ca niyyāso sarasañca ucchujaṃ tacaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbo ca tacoti sambandho.

93-5. Bilanga and other fruit medicines. Herein, they say “goṭṭhaphala” is “madanaphala.” The connection is ‘leaves of cotton, etc.’ These mentioned types—spoken of as root medicines, fruit medicines, and leaf medicines—are all allowable. All of their flowers, fruits, leaves, and roots are allowable for a lifetime. The connection is: except for sugarcane sap, all saps are allowable; and except for fresh sugarcane bark, all barks are allowable.

96. Madhunā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) amakkhitaṃ suddhasitthañca. Madhumakkhitaṃ pana sattāhakālikameva. Yañca kiñcīti odanaṃ maṃsaṃ aṭṭhiādīnīti attho.

96. And pure beeswax, unmixed with honey. However, that which is mixed with honey is only allowable for seven days. And 'whatever else' means such things as rice, meat, bones, and so on; this is the meaning.

97. “Yāni vā panaññānipi atthi neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ[V 0.0116], asati [M 0.0120] paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vuttattā “āhāratthamasādhentaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ yāvajīvika”nti vuttaṃ.

97. Because it is said: “Moreover, whatever other things there are that do not serve the purpose of food among edibles, nor serve the purpose of food among comestibles, having received them, one may keep them for life. When there is a reason, one may use them; for one who uses them when there is no reason, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” therefore it is said: “Whatever does not accomplish the purpose of nourishment, all that is allowable for life.”

98. Sabbassāti gilānassāpi agilānassapīti attho. Kālikattayanti yāvakālikaṃ vajjetvā avasesaṃ sati paccaye vikāle kappatīti attho.

98. ‘For all’ means for both the sick and the not sick. ‘The three time-categories’ means that, excepting what is allowable only until noon, the remainder is permissible at the wrong time when there is a reason.

99. Janayantubhoti janayanti ubho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yāvakālikayāmakālikasaṅkhātā ubho kālikā attano kālamatikkamitvā paribhuttā pācittiṃ janayantīti attho. Kiñca bhiyyo (mahāva. 274; mahāva. aṭṭha. 274; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) – ubhopi panete akappiyakuṭiyaṃ vuttā antovutthaṃ dukkaṭañca, punadivase paribhuñjato sannidhiṃ pācittiyañca janayantīti attho.

99. Both generate. What is said is this: both time-limited allowances, designated as 'for the day' and 'for a watch,' generate a pācittiya offense when consumed after their permitted time has elapsed. This is the meaning. Moreover, both of these, as stated in the section on an improper dwelling, generate a dukkaṭa offense for having been kept inside, and a pācittiya offense for storing up for one who consumes it on the following day. This is the meaning.

100. Anāruḷheti pāḷiyaṃ anāgate manussasappiādimhīti attho.

100. In the Pāli, 'anāruḷha' means 'not included in human ghee, etc.' This is the meaning.

101. Nissaṭṭhaladdhanti (pārā. 624) vinayakammaṃ katvā puna laddhanti attho. Vikappentassa sattāheti sattāhabbhantare sāmaṇerassa “idaṃ sappiṃ tela”ntiādinā nayena nāmaṃ gahetvā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vā “itthannāmassa vikappemī”ti vā sammukhāpi vā parammukhāpi vā vikappentassa anāpattīti sambandho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “anāpatti antosattāhe adhiṭṭheti, vissajjeti, nassati, vinassati, ḍayhati, acchinditvā gaṇhanti, vissāsaṃ gaṇhantī”ti (pārā. 625) ettakameva vuttaṃ, “vikappemī”ti idaṃ pana natthi. Kiñcāpi natthi, atha kho “anadhiṭṭhite adhiṭṭhitasaññī nissaggiyaṃ [M 0.0121] pācittiyaṃ, avikappite vikappitasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti (pārā. 624) āpattivāre āgatattā therena dassitaṃ. Taṃ dassentenāpi sace upasampannassa vikappeti, attano eva santakaṃ hoti, paṭiggahaṇampi na vijahati, tasmā upasampannavasena adassetvā anupasampannavasena dassitaṃ. Tassa hi vikappite paṭiggahaṇampi vijahati, āpattipi na hotīti. Adhiṭṭhatoti abbhañjanādīni adhiṭṭhahantassa anāpattīti attho. Sace pana sattāhabbhantare nirapekkho hutvā anupasampannassa pariccajati, pariccattattā anāpatti, itarassa ca appaṭiggahitattā ubhinnampi kāyikaparibhogo vaṭṭati. Anissaggiyattā pana bāhiraparibhogena vaṭṭati. “Tāni paṭiggahetvā [V 0.0117] sattāhaparamaṃ sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbānī”ti (pārā. 623) evaṃ niyametvā anuññātattā vuttaṃ “aññassa dadatopi ca anāpattī”ti.

101. 'Nissaṭṭhaladdhanti' (Pārā. 624) means that after performing a disciplinary act (vinayakamma), it is regained. This is the meaning. For one who assigns it within seven days—whether he assigns it face-to-face or indirectly to a novice by naming it, such as saying, 'This is ghee, this is oil,' and then declaring, 'I assign this to you,' or 'I assign this to so-and-so'—there is no offense. This is the connection. In the Pāli text, however, it is only stated: 'There is no offense if, within seven days, one determines it, disposes of it, it is lost, destroyed, burned, taken by force, or if trust is placed in it' (Pārā. 625). The phrase 'I assign it' is not found there. Although it is not mentioned, because the offense section states, 'For one who perceives an undetermined item as determined, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense; for one who perceives an unassigned item as assigned, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense' (Pārā. 624), the elder has explained it. In explaining it, if one assigns it to a fully ordained monk, it remains his own property, and he does not relinquish the acceptance. Therefore, it is explained in terms of an unordained person, not a fully ordained one. For if it is assigned to him, the acceptance is relinquished, and there is no offense. 'Adhiṭṭhatoti' means there is no offense for one who determines items like ointment, etc. This is the meaning. However, if within seven days one becomes indifferent and relinquishes it to an unordained person, there is no offense because it has been relinquished. And since the other has not accepted it, physical use is permissible for both. Because it is not subject to forfeiture, external use is permissible. Since it is permitted by rule—'Having received them, they are to be consumed after being stored for a maximum of seven days' (Pārā. 623)—it is said, 'There is no offense even if given to another.'

102. Sabbhāvanti attano sabhāvaṃ. Yasmā gāhāpayanti, tasmā evamudīritanti vuttanti attho. Idāni vakkhamānaṃ sandhāya “eva”nti vuttaṃ.

102. 'Sabhāvaṃ' means one's own nature. Because they cause others to grasp, it is therefore said 'thus spoken.' This is the meaning. Now, referring to what is about to be said, 'thus' is stated.

103-5. Sattāhaṃ yāvajīvikanti (mahāva. 305; mahāva. aṭṭha. kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) sattāhakālikañca yāvajīvikañcāti attho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Sattāhakālikayāvajīvikadvayaṃ sesakālikasammissaṃ sambhinnarasaṃ katvā paribhuñjato sannidhipācitti hotīti udīritanti. Tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ tadahevāti attho. Sesanti sattāhakālikayāvajīvikadvayaṃ. Itaranti yāvajīvikaṃ. Pure paṭiggahitaṃ vā hotu, tadahu vā paṭiggahitaṃ, yāvajīvikaṃ sattāhakālikena sattāhaṃ kappatīti veditabbaṃ. “Yāvakālikena, bhikkhave, yāmakālikaṃ, sattāhakālikaṃ, yāvajīvikaṃ tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ kāle kappati, no vikāle. Yāmakālikena, bhikkhave, sattāhakālikaṃ, yāvajīvikaṃ [M 0.0122] tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ yāme kappati, yāmātikkante na kappati. Sattāhakālikena, bhikkhave, yāvajīvikaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati, sattāhātikkante na kappatī”ti hi bhesajjakkhandhake (mahāva. 305) vuttaṃ. Ettha pana “tadahu paṭiggahita”nti visesavacanassa natthitāya pure paṭiggahitampi vaṭṭatīti siddhanti. Kālikavinicchayo.

103-5. 'Sattāhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ' means both 'for seven days' and 'for life.' This is the meaning. What is said? It is declared that for one who consumes the two—that which is allowable for seven days and that which is allowable for life—mixed with the other time-limited items, making a mixed concoction, there is a pācittiya offense for storing up. 'Tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ' means 'received on that very day.' This is the meaning. 'Sesa' refers to the two: that which is allowable for seven days and that which is allowable for life. 'Itara' refers to that which is allowable for life. Whether received earlier or on that very day, it should be understood that a lifetime item, when with a seven-day item, is allowable for seven days. For it is stated in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 305): 'Bhikkhus, a yāmakālika item, a sattāhakālika item, and a yāvajīvika item, if received on that day with a yāvakālika item, are allowable at the proper time, not at the improper time. Bhikkhus, a sattāhakālika item and a yāvajīvika item, if received on that day with a yāmakālika item, are allowable during the watch; after the watch, they are not allowable. Bhikkhus, a yāvajīvika item, if received with a sattāhakālika item, is allowable for seven days; after seven days, it is not allowable.' Here, however, since there is no specifying statement 'received on that day,' it is established that even what was received earlier is permissible. The determination regarding time allowances.

Kālikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of time allowances is completed.

9. Paṭiggāhaniddesavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Exposition of Acceptance

106. Idāni “paṭiggāho”ti padaṃ vitthāretuṃ “dātukāmābhihāro cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha dātukāmassa abhihāro dātukāmābhihāro. Etena aññassa patte pakkhipituṃ ālulentassa phusitāni uṭṭhahitvā aññassa patte sace patanti, paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhatīti dīpitaṃ [V 0.0118] hoti. Eraṇakkhamanti thāmamajjhimena purisena ukkhipanakkhamaṃ, tato mahante paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhati. Tidhā denteti kāyakāyappaṭibaddhanissaggiyānaṃ vasena tidhā dente. Tassa bhikkhuno kāyakāyappaṭibaddhehi dvidhā gāhoti attho. Pañcaṅgo evaṃ pañcaṅgevaṃ. Dātukāmābhihāro ekaṃ, hatthapāso ekaṃ, eraṇakkhamatā ekaṃ, devamanussatiracchānagatesu ekena tidhā dānamekaṃ, dvidhā gāho ekanti evaṃ pañcaṅgāni honti.

106. Now, to elaborate on the word 'acceptance,' the passage beginning 'the offering by one who desires to give' is commenced. Therein, 'the offering by one who desires to give' is the offering from one who wishes to give. By this it is shown that if, while one is stirring something to place it in another’s bowl, it splashes up and falls into another’s bowl, this does not constitute acceptance. 'Eraṇakkhamaṃ' means capable of being lifted by a man of moderate strength; for anything greater than that, acceptance does not occur. 'When giving in three ways' means giving in three ways: by body, by what is connected to the body, or by relinquishing. For that bhikkhu, the taking is twofold: by the body or by what is connected to the body. This is the meaning. 'Five-factored' is thus. The five factors are thus: 1. The offering by one who desires to give is one factor. 2. Being within hand-reach is one factor. 3. Being capable of being lifted is one factor. 4. The giving in three ways by one among gods, humans, or animals is one factor. 5. The twofold taking is one factor. Thus, there are five factors.

107. Idāni yena kāyappaṭibaddhena paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhati, taṃ dassetuṃ “asaṃhāriye”tiādimāha. Khāṇuke (pāci. aṭṭha. 265) bandhitvā [M 0.0123] ṭhapitamañcādimhi vā phalake vā pāsāṇe vā asaṃhāriye na ruhatīti attho. Tatthajāte paduminipaṇṇe vā kiṃsukapaṇṇādimhi vā na vaṭṭati, sukhume ciñcaādīnaṃ paṇṇe vā na ruhati, yañca majjhimapuriso sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti, tasmiṃ asayhabhāre ca paṭiggaho na ruhatīti attho.

107. Now, to show by what thing connected to the body acceptance does not occur, the passage beginning 'on what is unmovable' is stated. The meaning is that acceptance does not occur on an unmovable bench, plank, or stone that is tied to a stump and fixed. It is not allowable on a lotus leaf, a kiṃsuka leaf, or the like, that grew in that place. Nor does it occur on delicate leaves such as those of the tamarind. And acceptance does not occur for an unbearable weight, which a person of moderate strength is unable to support. This is the meaning.

108. Idāni paṭiggahaṇavijahanaṃ dassetuṃ “sikkhāmaraṇaliṅgehī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – sikkhāpaccakkhānena ca maraṇena ca liṅgaparivattanena ca “na taṃ dāni paribhuñjissāmī”ti vā “na puna paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjissāmī”ti vā evaṃ anapekkhavissajjanena ca corādīhi vā acchedā ca anupasampannassa dānā ca gāho paṭiggāho upasammati vijahatīti. Bhikkhuniyā pana sikkhāpaccakkhānassa abhāvā vibbhamanena ca vijahatīti gahetabbaṃ.

108. Now, to show the abandonment of acceptance, the passage beginning 'through training, death, and signs' is commenced. Herein, this is the condensed meaning: the grasping, the acceptance, ceases and is abandoned through the renunciation of training, through death, or through the change of signs; through indifferent relinquishment, such as by saying, 'I will not enjoy that now' or 'I will not accept and enjoy that again'; through being taken away by thieves, etc.; or through giving to one who is not fully ordained. For a bhikkhunī, however, since there is no renunciation of training, it should be understood that abandonment occurs through going astray.

109-110

109-110

. Idāni paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ dassetuṃ “appaṭiggahitaṃ sabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dantaponasikkhāpada) – catukālikapariyāpannaṃ antamaso rajareṇumpi appaṭiggahetvā sabbaṃ paribhuñjato pācitti. Idāni appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ dassetuṃ “suddhañca nātibahala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha suddhañcāti aññesaṃ rasena asammissaṃ. Himodakasamuddodakādīsu paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Loṇañca assu ca loṇassu. Ettha loṇaṃ nāma sarīre uṭṭhitaṃ. Etāni pana sabbāni avicchinnāneva kappanti, netarāni.

Now, to show the rule regarding what is to be consumed after acceptance, the passage beginning 'all unaccepted' is stated. Its meaning is: for consuming anything included among the four time-limited items, even as little as a speck of dust, without having accepted it, there is a pācittiya offense. Now, to show what may be consumed without acceptance, the passage beginning 'pure and not too thick' is stated. Therein, 'pure' means unmixed with the flavor of anything else. For snow water, seawater, and the like, there is no act of acceptance required. Salt and tears. Here, 'salt' means that which arises on the body. All these, however, are allowable only when they are from an uninterrupted source, not otherwise.

111. Idāni anaṅgalaggānipi dassetuṃ “gūthamattikamuttānī”tiādimāha. Tathāvidheti tathāvidhe kāle, sappadaṭṭhakāleti attho. Aññesaṃ pana appaṭiggahitaṃ anaṅgalaggaṃ na vaṭṭati. Kasmā[V 0.0119]? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ karonto [M 0.0124] paṭiggaṇhāti, sveva paṭiggaho kato, na puna paṭiggahetabbo”ti (mahāva. 268) vuttattā.

111. Now, in order to show even things unrelated to a plow, he says, “dung, clay, and urine,” and so forth. “At such a time” (tathāvidheti) means at such a time, that is, at the time of a snakebite. For others, however, an unaccepted item unrelated to a plow is not allowable. Why? Because it is stated: “Bhikkhus, I allow that if one accepts something while doing (the work), that acceptance is thereby made; it should not be accepted again” (Mahāvagga 268).

112. Durūpaciṇṇeti dupparāmaṭṭhe phalikarukkhavalliādiṃ cālentassa vā āmisabharitabhājanaṃ appaṭiggahitaṃ parāmasantassa vā durūpaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho. Rajokiṇṇeti bhikkhāya carantassa patte patitarajaṃ appaṭiggahetvā puna bhikkhaṃ gaṇhato vinayadukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho. Athuggahappaṭiggaheti atha uggahappaṭiggahe, attanā eva uggahetvā gahiteti attho. Akappiyakuṭiyaṃ antovutthe ca yattha katthaci bhikkhunā sayaṃpakke ca attanā vā parena vā akappiyakuṭiyaṃ antopakke cāti sabbattha dukkaṭanti adhippāyo. Paṭiggāhavinicchayo.

112. “Durūpaciṇṇa” means that a dukkaṭa offense for improper handling is incurred when one shakes something difficult to handle, such as a crystal, a tree, or a creeper, or when one touches an unaccepted container filled with food. “Rajokiṇṇa” means that a disciplinary dukkaṭa offense is incurred when a bhikkhu, while walking for alms, takes more alms without first accepting the dust that has fallen into his bowl. “Athuggahappaṭiggahe” means then, in the case of taking and accepting, that is, taking it up and accepting it oneself. The intention is that in all cases—whether staying inside an unsuitable dwelling, or anywhere a bhikkhu cooks food himself, or food is cooked by oneself or another inside an unsuitable dwelling—it is a dukkaṭa offense. The Determination Regarding Acceptance.

Paṭiggāhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of acceptance is completed.

10. Akappiyamaṃsaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Exposition of Unallowable Meat

113. Idāni maṃsesu paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassetuṃ “maṃsesu ca akappiya”nti uddhaṭaṃ. Akappiyamaṃsamhi dassite kappiyamaṃsaṃ dassitameva hoti pārisesanayena. Uragassa cāti ettha sabbopi urago na kappati.

113. Now, to show the proper conduct regarding meats, the statement ‘and unallowable among meats’ has been cited. When unallowable meat is shown, allowable meat is also shown by implication. And regarding a snake: here, every kind of snake is unallowable.

114. Ettāvatā jātivasena dasavidhampi akappiyamaṃsaṃ dassetvā idāni kappiyamaṃsesupi akappiyavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “uddissakatamaṃsañca, yañca appaṭivekkhita”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha pañcasu sahadhammikesu yassa kassaci yaṃ kiñci uddissa kataṃ uddissakataṃ nāma, taṃ pana jānitvā paribhuñjituṃ sabbesampi na vaṭṭati, ajānantānaṃ anāpatti. Macchesupi eseva nayo. Appaṭivekkhitanti [M 0.0125] anupaparikkhitaṃ, anāpucchitanti attho. “Na bhikkhave appaṭivekkhitvā maṃsaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ, yo paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 281) [V 0.0120] vuttaṃ. Macchesu pana āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi akappiyamacchānaṃ natthitāyāti vadanti. Idāni etesu āpattibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “thullaccaya”ntiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) uttānameva.

114. Having thus shown the ten kinds of unallowable meat by way of species, now, to explain the method that makes even allowable meat unallowable, it is said: ‘and meat prepared for a specific person, and that which is not inspected.’ Herein, ‘meat prepared for a specific person’ refers to anything prepared with a specific individual in mind among the five kinds of fellow practitioners. Knowing this, it is not allowable for anyone to consume it; for those who are unaware, there is no offense. This same principle applies to fish. ‘Not inspected’ means not examined; the meaning is not inquired about. It is said: ‘Bhikkhus, meat should not be consumed without inspection. Whoever consumes it commits a dukkaṭa offense’ (Mahāvagga 281). However, regarding fish, some say there is no need to inquire, as there are no unallowable kinds of fish. Now, to explain the classification of offenses in these cases, he says, ‘a grave offense,’ and so forth. All this is evident (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Sannidhikāraka Training Rule).

115. Idāni na kevalaṃ imesaṃ manussādīnaṃ maṃsameva akappiyaṃ, aṭṭhiādīnipi akappiyānīti dassetuṃ “aṭṭhīpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha 281) lomampesanti lomampi esaṃ akappiyamaṃsavatthūnanti attho. Sacittakaṃ vāti etesu pana uddissakatameva sacittakaṃ, sesā acittakāti. Akappiyamaṃsavinicchayo.

115. Now, to show that not only the flesh of these humans and others is unallowable, but also their bones and so forth are unallowable, it is said: ‘even bones,’ and so forth. Herein (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 281), ‘lomampesanti’ means that even their hair is among these unallowable meat-items. ‘Or with consciousness’ (sacittakaṃ vā) means that among these, only what is prepared for a specific person is with consciousness; the rest are without consciousness. The Determination of Unallowable Meat.

Akappiyamaṃsaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of unallowable meat is concluded.

11. Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nissaggiya Rules

116-7. Idāni accoḷārikānaṃ vasena dassetuṃ “arūpiya”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Aññathāpi yutti pariyesitabbā. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho (pārā. 591; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.589; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. jātarupasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) – yo rūpiyena arūpiyañca parivatteyya, yo ca itarena ca arūpiyena rūpiyaṃ parivatteyya, tassa nissaggiyaṃ hotīti.

Now, to explain by way of very gross examples, the terms ‘non-monetary item’ and so on are introduced. Otherwise, a fitting explanation should be sought. Here is the condensed meaning (Pārājika 591; Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.589; Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Jātarūpa Training Rule): Whoever exchanges a monetary item for a non-monetary item, or exchanges a non-monetary item for a monetary item, it is subject to forfeiture.

Idāni rūpiyañca arūpiyañca dassetuṃ “idha rūpiya”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Ettha (pārā. 589; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. jātarupasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) sajjhu siṅgīti sajjhūti rajataṃ. Siṅgīti suvaṇṇaṃ. Tambalohādīhi vā dārūhi vā paṇṇehi vā lākhāya vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā vā asamuṭṭhāpetvā vā kataṃ cammabījamayampiyaṃ yaṃ [M 0.0126] dese vohāraṃ gacchati, idaṃ vohārūpagamāsakaṃ nāma. Idamidha rūpiyanti adhippetaṃ. Vatthādi ca muttādi ca vatthamuttādi. Itaranti arūpiyaṃ kappiyavatthuñca dukkaṭavatthuñca. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Vatthaṃ suttaṃ phālo paṭako kappāso anekappakāraṃ aparaṇṇaṃ sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitādibhesajjañcāti idaṃ kappiyavatthu nāma. Muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkhosilā pavāḷaṃ lohitaṅgo masāragallaṃ satta dhaññāni dāsī dāso khettaṃ vatthu pupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti idaṃ dukkaṭavatthu nāma, tadubhayaṃ arūpiyaṃ nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, to explain monetary and non-monetary items, the terms ‘here, a monetary item’ and so on are introduced. Here (Pārājika 589; Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Jātarūpa Training Rule), ‘sajjhu siṅgī’ means ‘sajjhu’ is silver, and ‘siṅgī’ is gold. Alternatively, items made from copper, bronze, and so forth, or from wood, or leaves, or lac, whether a form has been produced or not, including those made of leather or seeds, which circulate as currency in a region—this is called ‘currency in common use’ (vohārūpagamāsaka). This is what is intended here as a monetary item. ‘Cloth, etc., and pearls, etc.’ becomes ‘cloth, pearls, etc.’ ‘Other’ refers to a non-monetary item, which can be both an allowable item and an item entailing a dukkaṭa offense. What is meant? Allowable items include cloth, thread, ploughshares, mats, cotton, various kinds of pulses, ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, and medicines, etc.—these are called allowable items. Pearls, gems, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, rubies, cat’s-eye, the seven kinds of grain, female slaves, male slaves, fields, building sites, flower gardens, fruit orchards, etc.—these are called items entailing a dukkaṭa offense. It is said that both of these are called non-monetary items.

118. Ettāvatā rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ dassetvā idāni kayavikkayaṃ dassetuṃ “imaṃ gahetvā”tiādimāha[V 0.0121]. Tattha imanti taṇḍulādikaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā vā odanādiṃ bhutvā vā “imaṃ vatthādikaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ dehi, imaṃ rajanapacanādikaṃ kara, rajanakaṭṭhādimā naya, imaṃ vā tava demi, tvaṃ pana imañca imañca āhara, kara, dehī”ti evaṃ kayavikkaye samāpanne nissaggīti sambandho.

118. Having thus explained transactions involving monetary items, now, to explain buying and selling, he says, ‘taking this,’ and so forth. Here, ‘this’ refers to taking allowable goods such as uncooked rice, or eating cooked rice, and then saying, ‘Give me these allowable goods such as cloth,’ or ‘Do this dyeing, cooking, etc.,’ or ‘Bring this dye-wood, etc.,’ or ‘I give you this, and in return you bring, do, and give me this and that’—when buying and selling is thus engaged in, it is subject to forfeiture. This is the connection.

119. Idāni pariṇāmavasena āpattibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “attano”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ piṇḍattho (pārā. 659; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.658; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) – saṅghassa vā aññassa vā nataṃ pariṇataṃ lābhaṃ labhitabbaṃ cīvarādipaccayaṃ attano vā aññassa vā pariṇāmeyya, nissaggiyaādīni hontīti. Kathaṃ? Yo pana mātusantakampi saṅghassa pariṇataṃ attano pariṇāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ. Aññassa puggalassa pariṇāmeti, suddhikapācittiyaṃ. Aññassa saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā pariṇāmeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Yo pana aññapuggalassa vā cetiyassa vā pariṇataṃ attano vā aññapuggalassa vā saṅghassa vā aññacetiyassa vā pariṇāmeti, tassāpi dukkaṭamevāti.

119. Now, to explain the classification of offenses by way of diversion, the phrase ‘for oneself’ and so on is introduced. Here is the summary (Pārājika 659; Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.658; Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Pariṇata Training Rule): If one should divert for oneself or for another a gain or a requisite such as robes that is to be received, which has been dedicated to or has accrued to the Sangha or to another, it becomes a nissaggiya offense, and so forth. How? If one diverts for oneself what has accrued to the Sangha, even if it belongs to one’s mother, it is a nissaggiya offense. If one diverts it for another individual, it is a pācittiya offense alone. If one diverts it for another Sangha or a cetiya, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If one diverts what has accrued to another individual or a cetiya, for oneself, another individual, another Sangha, or another cetiya, it is also a dukkaṭa offense for him.

120. Yo [M 0.0127] pana nissaggiṃ nissajjitabbaṃ anissajjitvā vinayakammaṃ akatvā paribhuñjeyya, tassa dukkaṭaṃ. Yo vā parena vinayakammatthāya nissaṭṭhaṃ sakasaññāya na dadeyya, tassāpi dukkaṭaṃ. Aññathetaranti ettha aññathāti theyyasaññāya sace na dadeyya, itaraṃ tassa agghavasena pārājikañca thullaccayañca dukkaṭañca hotīti attho. Nissaggiyavinicchayo.

120. If one uses a nissaggiya item that should be forfeited, without having forfeited it and without having performed the disciplinary procedure, it is a dukkaṭa offense for him. Or if one, with the perception of it being one’s own, does not give back what was forfeited by another for the purpose of a disciplinary procedure, it is also a dukkaṭa offense for him. Here, ‘otherwise, the other’ means: if one does not give it back, but with the perception of theft, then the other offenses apply; that is, depending on its value, it is a pārājika offense, a thullaccaya offense, or a dukkaṭa offense—this is the meaning. The Determination of Nissaggiya.

Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Nissaggiya rules is concluded.

12. Pācittiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pācittiya Rules

121. Idāni pācittiyāni dassetuṃ “pācittī”ti mātikāpadaṃ uddharitvā “musāvādomasāvāde, pesuññaharaṇe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha musāvāde ca omasavāde ca pesuññaharaṇe ca pācitti vuttāti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Ettha pana “adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, amutaṃ[V 0.0122], aviññātaṃ, diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ, mutaṃ, viññāta”nti (pāci. 3; pāci. aṭṭha. 3) pubbepi “musā bhaṇissāmī”ti cetetvā vacanakkhaṇeva “musā bhaṇāmī”ti jānitvā jānantasseva musābhaṇane pācitti nāma āpatti hotīti attho. Yassa bhaṇati, so taṃ na suṇāti, āpatti na hoti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

121. Now, to set forth the pācittiya offenses, the mātikā phrase "pācittiya" is extracted, followed by "false speech, abusive speech, tale-bearing," and so forth. Here, the connection is that pācittiya is stated in regard to false speech, abusive speech, and tale-bearing. The same applies to the rest. Here, however, regarding "unseen, unheard, unfelt, unknown, seen, heard, felt, known" (Pāci. 3; Pāci. Aṭṭha. 3), the meaning is that even if one previously intends, "I will speak falsely," and at the very moment of speaking knows, "I am speaking falsely," the offense called pācittiya arises when one knowingly speaks falsely. If the person one speaks to does not hear it, there is no offense (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

“Omasavādo nāma dasahi ākārehi omasati jātiyāpi nāmenapi gottenapi kammenapi sippenapi ābādhenapi liṅgenapi kilesenapi āpattiyāpi akkosenapī”ti (pāci. 15) evaṃ vuttehi dasahi ākārehi upasampannaṃ yo khuṃseti vambheti, ayaṃ omasati nāma, tassa pācittīti [M 0.0128] attho. Parammukhā bhaṇantassa dukkaṭaṃ, tathā pāḷiyaṃ anāgatehi “coro”ti vā “gaṇṭhibhedako”ti vā ādīhi bhaṇantassa. “Santi idhekacce khattiyā brāhmaṇā caṇḍālā”tiādinā pariyāyena bhaṇantassa ca anupasampannaṃ bhaṇantassa ca sabbatthapi dukkaṭameva.

"Insulting speech is defined in ten ways: by birth, by name, by clan, by occupation, by craft, by illness, by physical characteristic, by defilements, by offenses, or by abuse." (Pācittiya 15) Thus, whoever humiliates or disparages an ordained person in these ten ways—this is called 'insulting speech', and for him there is a pācittiya offense. For one who speaks behind one's back, it is a dukkaṭa offense; similarly, for one who speaks using terms not mentioned in the Pāḷi text, such as 'thief' or 'knot-breaker,' and so forth. For one who speaks indirectly by saying, "There are some here—khattiyas, brahmins, caṇḍālas," and so forth, and for one who speaks to an unordained person, in all such cases it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Piyakamyatāya vā bhedādhippāyena vā upasampannaṃ jātiādīhi omasantassa upasampannassa vacanaṃ sutvā tassa upasaṃharaṇaṃ pesuññaharaṇaṃ nāma. Etthāpi pariyāyavacanena ca anupasampannassa upasaṃharaṇena ca dukkaṭameva.

Out of affection or with the intention of causing division, hearing the words of an ordained person who disparages another ordained person by birth and so on, and then reporting those words to that disparaged person is called tale-bearing. Here too, by means of indirect speech and by reporting such matters to one who is not ordained, it is only a dukkaṭa offense.

Padasodhammoti ettha “dhammo nāma buddhabhāsito sāvakabhāsito isibhāsito devatābhāsito atthūpasaṃhito dhammūpasaṃhito”ti (pāci. 46) evaṃ vuttaṃ saṅgītittayamāruḷhaṃ tipiṭakadhammaṃ padaanupadaanvakkharaanubyañjanavasena bhikkhuñca bhikkhuniñca ṭhapetvā anupasampannaṃ ekato vācentassa pācitti hotīti attho.

Here, regarding 'Dhamma word by word', the meaning is that for a bhikkhu who causes an unordained person (i.e., anyone other than a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī) to recite together the Tipiṭaka Dhamma—which has been stated thus: "spoken by the Buddha, by a disciple, by a sage, by a deity, connected with meaning, connected with the Dhamma" (Pāci. 46), and has been included in the three recitations—word by word, line by line, syllable by syllable, and consonant by consonant, a pācittiya offense arises.

Sāgāreti yaṃ pana sabbantimena pariyāyena diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhena pākārādinā parikkhittattā sabbaparicchinnañca yena kenaci vitānādinā antamaso vatthenapi channattā sabbacchannañca senāsanaṃ, tathārūpe senāsane ekūpacāraṭṭhāne anupasampannena saha vasantassa catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya nipajjanagaṇanāya ca anupasampannagaṇanāya ca devasikaṃ pācitti hotīti attho.

Moreover, the meaning is that a dwelling that is entirely enclosed by a wall or the like, one and a half cubits high at a minimum, and is thus entirely defined, and is entirely covered by any kind of roofing, even just a cloth—if a bhikkhu lives together with an unordained person in such a lodging, in a single precinct, starting from the fourth day, a pācittiya offense arises daily, counting each sleeping arrangement and each unordained person.

Ujjhāpanakakhiyyaneti ettha yo upasampannaṃ saṅghena sammataṃ senāsanapaññāpakaṃ vā bhattuddesakaṃ [V 0.0123] vā yāgubhājakaṃ vā phalabhājakaṃ vā khajjabhājakaṃ vā appamattakavissajjakaṃ vā maṅkukattukāmo chandena “itthannāmo senāsanaṃ paññāpeti, bhattāni ca uddisatī”ti vā vadanto aññaṃ [M 0.0129] upasampannaṃ ujjhāpeti tena avajānāpeti, yo pana tatheva vadanto upasampannassa santike tassa ayasaṃ pakāsento khīyati, tasmiṃ ujjhāpanake ca khīyanake ca pācittidvayanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, regarding "causing complaint and complaining," it should be understood that there are two pācittiya offenses: whoever, wishing to disparage an ordained person appointed by the Saṅgha as an assigner of lodgings, a distributor of food, a distributor of gruel, a distributor of fruit, a distributor of snacks, or a distributor of small items, and with such intention says, "So-and-so assigns lodgings, and distributes food," thereby causing another ordained one to complain about him and despise him; and whoever, speaking in the same way, complains in the presence of an ordained person, revealing his dishonor. In that causing of complaint and in that complaining, there are these two pācittiya offenses.

122. Talasattianādara-kukkuccuppādanesu cāti ettha yo bhikkhu upasampannassa paharaṇākāraṃ dassento kāyaṃ vā kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ vā uccāreti, tassa pācittiyaṃ. Sace viraddho pahāraṃ deti, appaharitukāmatāya dukkaṭaṃ, tathā anupasampannesupi dukkaṭameva.

122. Here, regarding raising a hand to strike, disrespect, and causing anxiety: if a bhikkhu, showing a gesture of striking towards an ordained person, raises his body or anything connected to his body, he incurs a pācittiya offense. If he fails in his restraint and strikes, but without the intention to strike, it is a dukkaṭa offense. The same applies towards those who are not fully ordained—it is also a dukkaṭa offense.

Upasampannena paññattena vuccamāno taṃ asikkhitukāmatāya vā tassa vacanaṃ asotukāmatāya vā yo anādariyaṃ karoti, tassa anādarakaraṇe pācittiyanti attho. Apaññattena vuccamānassa ca anupasampannena paññattena vā apaññattena vā vuccamānassa dukkaṭaṃ.

The meaning is that when a bhikkhu is spoken to by an appointed ordained person, if he shows disrespect due to a desire not to train or a desire not to listen to his words, the act of disrespect is a pācittiya offense. If he is spoken to by one who is not appointed, or if he is spoken to by an unordained person, whether appointed or not, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Upasampannassa “ūnavīsativasso maññe tvaṃ upasampanno, vikāle maññe tayā bhutta”ntiādinā nayena sañcicca kukkuccaṃ uppādentassa pācittiyaṃ. Anupasampannassa uppādane dukkaṭaṃ.

If a monk intentionally causes anxiety to one who is fully ordained by saying, "I think you were ordained when under twenty years of age," or "I think you ate at the wrong time," and so on, he commits a pācittiya offense. If he causes anxiety to one who is not fully ordained, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Gāmappavesanāpucchāti ettha pana majjhanhikātikkamanato paṭṭhāya yāva aruṇuggamanā vikālo nāma, etthantare sace sambahulā kenaci kammena gāmaṃ pavisanti, “vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchāmā”ti sabbehipi aññamaññaṃ āpucchitabbaṃ.
