Sace anāpucchā parikkhittassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa upacāraṃ atikkamanti, paṭhamapāde dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapāduddhāre pācittiyaṃ. Āpadāsu anāpatti.

Here, regarding taking leave to enter a village: from the passing of midday until sunrise is considered the improper time. During this interval, if several monks enter a village for some business, they must all take leave of one another, saying, "We take leave for entering the village at the improper time." If, without taking leave, they cross the boundary of an enclosed village or the vicinity of an unenclosed one, it is a dukkaṭa offense for the first foot and a pācittiya offense for lifting the second foot. There is no offense in emergencies.

Bhojane ca paramparāti paramparabhojane ca pācittiyanti attho. Ettha pana pañcasu bhojanesu aññataraṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā [M 0.0130] “odanena vā sattunā vā kummāsena vā maṃsena vā macchena vā nimantemī”tiādinā nayena, yena kenaci vevacanena vā akappiyanimantanāya nimantitassa [V 0.0124] yena yena paṭhamaṃ nimantito, tassa tassa bhojanaṃ ṭhapetvā uppaṭipāṭiyā, avikappetvā vā paṭhamanimantanaṃ parassa parassa kulassa pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ paribhuñjantassa paramparabhojane pācitti hoti. Gilānacīvaradānacīvarakālasamayesu anāpatti, tathā pañca bhojanāni ṭhapetvā sabbattha.

And regarding eating in succession: The meaning is that eating in succession is a pācittiya offense. Here, for one who has been invited with an invitation that is not exempt—that is, by naming one of the five foods, such as "I invite you with rice, or with flour, or with barley gruel, or with meat, or with fish," or by any other expression—if he consumes any of the five foods at another household in succession, without having set aside the food from the first invitation or made a stipulation regarding it, it is a pācittiya offense for eating in succession. There is no offense during times of illness, robe-giving, or the robe-making season. Similarly, there is no offense for any foods apart from the five staple foods.

123. Anuddharitvā gamane seyyanti ettha dasavidhā seyyā bhisi cimilikā uttarattharaṇaṃ bhūmattharaṇaṃ taṭṭikā cammakhaṇḍo nisīdanaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāroti. Etesu yaṃ kiñci saṅghike vihāre guttasenāsane attano vassaggena gahitaṃ attanā vā santharitvā, anupasampannena vā santharāpetvā taṃ divasaṃ gamikavasena pakkamanto neva sayaṃ uddhareyya na aññaṃ uddharāpeyya, yathā upacikādīhi na khajjeyya, evaṃ na ṭhapeyya, aññena vā na uddharāpeyya, patirūpaṃ bhikkhuṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā ārāmikameva vā anāpucchā vā gaccheyya, tassa parikkhittassa vihārassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa dve leḍḍupāte atikkamantassa pācittiyaṃ. Maṇḍaparukkhamūlādiaguttasenāsane santharitvā gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ, tathā mañcapīṭhabhisikocchakesu, guttasenāsanepi dukkaṭameva.

123. Here, regarding 'leaving bedding without putting it away': there are ten kinds of bedding: a mattress, a felt rug, a coverlet, a ground covering, a reed mat, a piece of leather, a sitting cloth, a bolster, a grass spread, and a leaf spread. Among these, whatever bedding in a Saṅgha-owned dwelling, in a guarded lodging, taken according to one’s seniority for the rains, or spread out by oneself, or having had it spread out by one who is not fully ordained—if, intending to travel, one departs that day, and neither puts it away himself nor has another put it away, and does not place it in such a way that it will not be eaten by termites or the like, or goes without informing a suitable bhikkhu, novice, or monastery worker—if he goes beyond the boundary of an enclosed dwelling, or beyond two stone-throws of an unenclosed dwelling, he incurs a pācittiya offense. If one spreads bedding in an unguarded lodging such as a pavilion or at the foot of a tree and then leaves, it is a dukkaṭa offense. Similarly, for beds, benches, mattresses, and cushions, even in a guarded lodging, it is only a dukkaṭa offense.

Senāsanāni vāti ettha anuddharitvā gamaneti sambandho. Ettha pana mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi kocchakanti catubbidhampi senāsanaṃ vassānahemantānaṃ aṭṭhasu māsesu ajjhokāse vā ovassakamaṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vā sayaṃ santharitvā vā anupasampannena santharāpetvā vā taṃ anuddharitvā vā anuddharāpetvā vā tassa senāsanassa dvinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ atikkamane pācittiyaṃ. Sammuñjanīyādi sesaparikkhāresu dukkaṭaṃ.

Here, regarding 'lodgings': the connection is with 'leaving without taking it up'. In this context, a bed, a bench, a cushion, or a mat—these four types of lodgings—having been spread out by oneself or having been caused to be spread out by an unordained person during the eight months of the rainy and winter seasons, either in the open air, under a shelter exposed to rain, or at the foot of a tree; if one goes beyond two pebble-throws from that lodging without taking it up or having it taken up, it is an offense of expiation. For the remaining requisites, such as a broom, it is an offense of wrong conduct.

Itthiyāddhānagamaneti [M 0.0131] ettha mātugāmena “gacchāma bhagini, gacchāma ayyā”ti evaṃ saṃvidahitvā “ajja vā sve vā parasuve vā”ti niyamitakālaṃ visaṅketaṃ akatvā dvāravisaṅketaṃ maggavisaṅketaṃ katvāpi gacchato gāmantare gāmantare pācittiyaṃ. Agāmake araññe addhayojane addhayojane āpatti.

Here, regarding 'traveling on a journey with a woman': for one who goes, having made an arrangement with a woman, saying, 'Let us go, sister; let us go, lady,' even having made an arrangement about the gate or the path without fixing a time such as 'today, or tomorrow, or the day after,' there is an offense of expiation for each village-interval. In an area without villages or in a forest, there is an offense for every half-yojana.

Ekekāya nisīdaneti ettha eko ekāya itthiyā nisīdaneti attho.

Here, regarding 'sitting down one with one': the meaning is that one man sits down with one woman.

124. Bhiṃsāpaneti [V 0.0125] ettha upasampanno upasampannaṃ bhiṃsāpetukāmo corakantāravāḷakantārādīni ācikkhati, bhayānakaṃ vā rūpasaddādiṃ dasseti, so bhāyatu vā mā vā, tassa payoge payoge pācittiyaṃ. Anupasampanne dukkaṭaṃ.

124. Here, regarding 'frightening': a fully ordained bhikkhu who wishes to frighten another fully ordained bhikkhu points out dangers such as a wilderness infested with robbers or a wilderness infested with wild beasts, or he shows something terrifying like frightening sights or sounds. Whether the other bhikkhu becomes afraid or not, for each attempt, there is an offense of expiation. If the act is directed toward one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong conduct.

Ākoṭaneti pahāradāne. Upasampanno upasampannassa anattamano hutvā sace uppalapattenapi pahāraṃ deti, pācittiyaṃ. Anupasampannassa gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā itthiyā vā purisassa vā antamaso tiracchānagatassāpi pahāraṃ deti, dukkaṭameva.

Striking means giving a blow. If a fully ordained person, being displeased with another fully ordained person, gives a blow even with a lotus leaf, it is an offense of expiation. If he gives a blow to an unordained person—whether a householder or a renunciant, a woman or a man, or even to an animal—it is only an offense of wrong conduct.

Anācāraṃ ācaritvā saṅghamajjhe āpattiyā vā vatthunā vā anuyuñjiyamāno taṃ akathetukāmo “ko āpanno, kiṃ āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno”tiādinā nayena aññehi vacanehi taṃ vacanaṃ paṭicchādento so aññaṃ vadati, ayaṃ aññavādako, tasmiṃ aññavādake ca kañci vītikkamaṃ disvā “āvuso, idaṃ nāma tayā kata”nti vutte taṃ na kathetukāmo tuṇhībhūtova saṅghaṃ vihesatīti saṅghavihesako, tasmiṃ vihesake ca pācitti hotīti attho. Idha pana ñattidutiyena kammena aññavādake ca vihesake [M 0.0132] ca āropite puna aññaṃ bhaṇantassa, vihesantassa pācitti. Anāropite dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ.

Having acted improperly, when interrogated in the midst of the Saṅgha concerning an offense or its basis, and wishing not to disclose it, he conceals that matter with other words such as, 'Who has offended? What is the offense? In what is the offense?'—this is an evasive speaker. And when, in the case of such an evasive speaker, someone sees any transgression and says, 'Friend, this was done by you,' but he, wishing not to disclose it, remains silent and thus vexes the Saṅgha—this is a vexer of the Saṅgha. And for such a vexer, an offense of expiation occurs—this is the meaning. Here, however, when one who has been charged by a formal motion and second announcement with evasive speech or vexing speaks evasively again or vexes, an offense of expiation occurs. If not charged, it should be understood as an offense of wrong conduct.

Duṭṭhullapakāsachādeti ettha kiñcāpi “duṭṭhullā nāma āpatti cattāri ca pārājikāni terasa ca saṅghādisesā”ti (pāci. 399) vuttā, tathāpi idha saṅghādisesāva adhippetā. Tasmā saṅghasammutiṃ vinā bhikkhussa duṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ “ayaṃ asuciṃ mocetvā saṅghādisesaṃ āpanno”tiādinā nayena vatthunā saddhiṃ āpattiṃ ghaṭetvā bhikkhuñca bhikkhuniñca ṭhapetvā yassa kassaci anupasampannassa ārocentassa pācittiyaṃ. Thullaccayādiaduṭṭhullārocane dukkaṭaṃ. Duṭṭhullacchādanepi saṅghādisesova adhippeto. Yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhussa duṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ sayaṃ vā jānitvā aññesaṃ vā sutvā “imaṃ jānitvā codessanti sāressanti maṅkuṃ karissanti, nārocissāmī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, tassa pācittiyaṃ. Dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā pacchā ārocitepi na rakkhati eva.

Regarding 'revealing and concealing a grave offense': here, although it is stated, 'Grave offenses are the four offenses of defeat and the thirteen offenses requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha' (Pāc. 399), nevertheless, in this context only the offenses requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha are intended. Therefore, for one who, without the Saṅgha's consent, reveals a grave offense of a bhikkhu to any unordained person (excluding a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī), connecting the offense with its basis in a manner such as, 'This one, having discharged semen, has committed an offense requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha,' it is an offense of expiation. For revealing a non-grave offense, such as a grave transgression, it is an offense of wrong conduct. In the case of concealing a grave offense too, only an offense requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha is intended. If a bhikkhu, knowing of a grave offense of another bhikkhu himself or having heard of it from others, lays down the burden, thinking, 'If they know this, they will accuse him, remind him, or make him feel ashamed; I will not reveal it,' for him it is an offense of expiation. Even if he reveals it later after having laid down the burden, he is not protected.

Hāsodaketi aṅgulipatodakena hāso ca udake hāso cāti evamattho veditabbo. Upasampanno upasampannaṃ hasādhippāyo kāyena kāyaṃ āmasati, āpatti pācittiyassa, ko pana vādo [V 0.0126] upakacchakādīsu ghaṭṭane. Anupasampanne dukkaṭaṃ, tathā bhikkhussa kāyappaṭibaddhāmasane ca nissaggiyena kāyappaṭibaddhāmasane ca. Ettha bhikkhunīpi anupasampannaṭṭhāne ṭhitā. Udake hasanadhammo nāma uparigopphake udake kīḷādhippāyassa nimmujjanaummujjanaplavanādikaṃ. Idha hāso nāma kīḷā vuccati.

Regarding 'play in water': the meaning should be understood as 'play by tickling with the fingers' and 'play in water'. If a fully ordained person, with the intention of playing, touches the body of another fully ordained person with his own body, it is an offense of expiation; what then to say of rubbing in the armpits and so on? With an unordained person, it is an offense of wrong conduct; likewise for touching something attached to a bhikkhu's body, and for touching something attached to the body that is an item entailing forfeiture. Here, a bhikkhunī is also considered to be in the position of an unordained person. The practice of playing in water means diving, surfacing, floating, and so on in water above the ankles with the intention of playing. Here, 'hāsa' is called play.

Nicchubhane vihārāti saṅghikā vihārā nikkaḍḍhaneti attho. Ettha pana yo kuddho hutvā upasampannaṃ hatthādīsu gahetvā vā “nikkhamā”ti vatvā vā yattakāni dvārāni [M 0.0133] ekena payogena atikkāmeti, tattha dvāragaṇanāya āpattiṃ aggahetvā payogassa ekattā ekā eva gahetabbā. Sace nānāpayogehi atikkāmeti, tattha dvāragaṇanāya gahetabbaṃ. Tassa parikkhāranikkaḍḍhane dukkaṭaṃ, tathā anupasampanne, tassa parikkhāranikkaḍḍhane ca. Alajjiādīsu pana anāpatti.

Regarding 'expelling from a dwelling': the meaning is expelling from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha. Here, if one, being angry, seizes a fully ordained person by the hand or other limbs, or says, 'Get out,' and makes him pass through however many doors with a single effort, then an offense should not be counted for each door; due to the single effort, only one offense should be counted. If one makes him pass through with multiple efforts, then an offense should be counted for each door. For throwing out his requisites, it is an offense of wrong conduct; likewise for an unordained person, and for throwing out his requisites. However, in the case of a shameless person and so on, there is no offense.

Anupakhajja sayaneti saṅghike vihāre “vuḍḍho”ti vā “gilāno”ti vā “saṅghena dinno”ti vā jānitvā mañcassa vā pīṭhassa vā pavisantassa vā nikkhamantassa vā upacāre seyyaṃ santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā “yassa sambādho bhavissati, so pakkamissatī”ti adhippāyena abhinisīdantassa ca abhinipajjantassa ca payogagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pācittiyavinicchayo.

Regarding 'lying down having encroached': in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing that a couch or a chair is for an elder, or for the sick, or has been given by the Saṅgha, for one who, in the access-space of someone entering or leaving that couch or chair, spreads out a bed or has one spread out with the intention, 'Whoever is inconvenienced will depart,' an offense of expiation should be understood for each act of sitting down or lying down. This is the determination of the offense of expiation.

Pācittiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Pācittiyas is concluded.

13. Samaṇakappaniddesavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Exposition of What is Allowable for Ascetics

125. Bhūtānaṃ jātānaṃ nibbattānaṃ gāmo bhūtagāmo (pāci. 91; pāci. aṭṭha. 91; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). Samārambhoti chedanaphālanapacanādi, tasmiṃ bhūtagāmasamārambhe bhūtagāmasamārambhahetu pācitti hotīti attho. Katakappiyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana samaṇakappiyaṃ bhaveti sambandho. Samaṇānaṃ kappiyaṃ samaṇakappiyaṃ[V 0.0127]. Idāni yena kataṃ kappiyaṃ samaṇakappiyaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “nakhena vā”tiādimāha. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ, aggiparijitaṃ satthaparijitaṃ nakhaparijitaṃ abījaṃ nibbaṭṭabījaññeva pañcama”nti (cūḷava. 250) hi vuttaṃ.

125. A habitat of beings that are born, that have come into existence, that have been produced, is `bhūtagāma` (plant life). `Samārambha` means destruction, such as cutting, splitting, or cooking; in such destruction of plant life, on account of the destruction of plant life, an offense of expiation occurs—this is the meaning. As for 'made allowable,' the connection is that it becomes allowable for ascetics. What is allowable for ascetics is `samaṇakappiyaṃ`. Now, to show by what means something made allowable becomes allowable for ascetics, it says, 'with a nail, etc.' For it is said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, the partaking of fruit made allowable for ascetics in five ways: damaged by fire, damaged by a knife, damaged by a fingernail, being without seed, and fifthly, having had its seeds removed' (Cūḷavagga 250).

126. Idāni [M 0.0134] taṃ bhūtagāmaṃ dassetuṃ “samūlā”tiādimāha. Tattha (pāci. 91; pāci. aṭṭha. 91) sa-iti so bhūtagāmo nāmāti attho, mūlabījādīhi pañcahi bījehi pabhāvito hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha mūlabījaṃ nāma haliddisiṅgiverādi. Khandhabījaṃ nāma assattho nigrodhoti evamādi. Aggabījaṃ nāma ajjukaphaṇijjakādi. Phaḷubījaṃ nāma ucchuveḷunaḷādi. “Bījabījaṃ nāma pubbaṇṇaṃ aparaṇṇaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi bīje jāyanti bīje sañjāyanti, etaṃ bījabījaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni “bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 195; ma. ni. 1.293, 411; 2.11; a. ni. 10.99; pu. pa. 179) vuttattā dhammānulomena āgataṃ bījagāmasamārambhaṃ dassetuṃ “ārambhe dukkaṭa”ntiādimāha. Tasmā etaṃ paṭhamaṃ “kappiyaṃ karohī”ti bhūtagāmaparimocanaṃ kāretvā bījagāmaparimocanatthaṃ puna kappiyaṃ kāretabbaṃ.

126. Now, to show that living plant life, he begins with 'with roots,' etc. Herein, `sa` means that this is called living plant life; it is said to be propagated by five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, etc. Among these, root-seeds refer to things like turmeric and ginger. Stem-seeds refer to trees like the pipal and banyan, and so on. Shoot-seeds are plants like `ajjuka` and `phaṇijjaka`. Joint-seeds are sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds. 'Seed-seeds are early grain and later grain, or whatever other things there are that are born from seeds and originate from seeds—this is called seed-seed,' it is said. Now, because it is said, 'He refrains from damaging plant-life and seed-life' (Dī. Ni. 1.10, 195; Ma. Ni. 1.293, 411; 2.11; Aṅ. Ni. 10.99; Pu. Pa. 179), to show the damaging of seed-life which is dealt with according to the Dhamma, he begins with 'in the undertaking, a `dukkaṭa` offense,' etc. Therefore, first, one should have the release of plant-life done by saying, 'Make it allowable,' and then, for the release of seed-life, one must again have it made allowable.

127. Nibbaṭṭabījaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 92; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhutagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nāma ambapanasādi. Nobījaṃ nāma taruṇambaphalādi, etaṃ pana sabbaṃ akappiyampi vaṭṭatīti attho. Kaṭāhabaddhabījāni kapitthaphalādīni. Bahiddhā vāpi kārayeti kapālepi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, sace ekābaddhānīti attho. Kaṭāhamuttaṃ pana bhinditvā kāretabbaṃ.

127. 'Viable seeds' (`nibbaṭṭabīja`) refer to things like mangoes and jackfruit. 'Non-seeds' (`nobīja`) are young fruits like unripe mangoes; the meaning is that all these are allowable even if not made allowable. 'Seeds bound in a husk' (`kaṭāhabaddhabījāni`) are fruits like wood apples. It is permissible to have them prepared even outside, such as on a potsherd, if they are bound together—this is the meaning. However, what is free from the husk should be broken before having it prepared.

128. Bhājane vā bhūmiyaṃ vā ekābaddhesu bījesu ekasmiṃ bīje kappiye kate sabbesveva kataṃ bhaveti attho. Yathā ca bīje, evaṃ rukkhasahassaṃ vā ucchusahassaṃ vā chinditvā ekābaddhe katepi vinicchayo veditabbo.

128. Whether in a vessel or on the ground, when one seed among connected seeds is made allowable, the meaning is that it is done for all of them. And just as with seeds, so also the determination should be understood in the case of a thousand trees or a thousand sugarcane stalks that have been cut and made into a single bundle.

129. Kappiyaṃ katvā nikkhitte bījagāme puna mūlapaṇṇāni sace jāyaruṃ, puna kappiyaṃ kāreyyāti attho. Tadāti mūle ca aṅkure ca jāteti attho.

129. If, after making seed-life allowable and setting it aside, roots or leaves should sprout again, one should make it allowable once more—this is the meaning. 'Then' means when roots and sprouts have appeared—this is the meaning.

130. Udakasambhavoti [V 0.0128][M 0.0135] udakajāto. Cetiyādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena gehappamukhapākāravedikādīsu nibbattā gahitā. Nibbattadvattipattako bhūtagāmova, anibbattako aggabīje saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Bījampi yāva mūlaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā na nikkhamati, tāva bījagāmova, mūle ca nikkhante paṇṇe ca harite jāte bhūtagāmova hotīti attho.

130. 'Water-born' means born of water. 'At shrines, etc.'—here, the word 'etc.' includes those that have arisen in places like house entrances, compound walls, and railings. What has sprouted, having two or three leaves, is living plant life; what has not sprouted is included under shoot-seeds. Even a seed, as long as a root or leaf has not emerged, is still seed-life; but the meaning is that once the root has emerged and the leaf has become green, it becomes living plant life.

131. Makuḷanti aphullaṃ. Ahichattakaṃ nāma rukkhe jātaṃ ahichattakaṃ.

131. 'Bud' means unopened blossom. '`Ahichattaka`' refers to the `ahichattaka` mushroom that grows on trees.

132. Allarukkhe gaṇhatoti sambandho. Tatthāti allarukkhe chindato vāpīti sambandho.

132. 'Taking hold of a sapling' is the connection. 'There'—the connection is with 'when cutting a sapling' or 'at a pond'.

134. “Imaṃ rukkhaṃ, imaṃ lataṃ, imaṃ kandaṃ chinda, bhindā”tiādinā nayena niyametvā bhāsituṃ na vaṭṭati. “Idaṃ, eta”nti avatvā kevalaṃ “rukkhaṃ chindā”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 92; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhūtagāmahikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nayena vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Samaṇakappavinicchayo.

134. 'Cut this tree, cut this creeper, cut this root,' and so on—it is not permissible to speak in such a way by specifying. Without saying 'this' or 'that,' it is permissible to say simply, 'Cut the tree,' and so on (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 92; Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). This is the determination of what is allowable for a recluse.

Samaṇakappaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of What is Allowable for a Recluse is concluded.

14. Bhūminiddesavaṇṇanā

14. The Commentary on the Exposition of Grounds

136. Idāni “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catasso kappiyabhūmiyo ussāvanantikaṃ gonisādikaṃ gahapatiṃ sammuti”nti (mahāva. 295) evaṃ vuttā catasso kappiyabhūmiyo dassetuṃ “sammutussāvanantā cā”tiādimāha. Yāsūti kappiyabhūmīsu (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā).

136. Now, to show the four allowable grounds that were spoken of thus, 'I allow, monks, four allowable grounds: that established by announcement, that of a cattle-pen, that of a householder, and that by designation' (Mahāvagga 295), he begins with the words 'By designation and by announcement…' and so on. `Yāsu` means 'in which allowable grounds' (Kaṅkhāvitaranī-aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Training Rule on Storing).

137. Idāni [M 0.0136] yattha kappiyakuṭi icchitabbā, taṃ dassetuṃ “vāsatthāyā”tiādimāha. Vāsatthāyāti iminā koṭṭhāgārabhattasālācetiyagharasammuñjanīmāḷakādi yaṃ yaṃ aññampi vāsatthāya [V 0.0129] karīyati, tattha tattha kappiyakuṭikaraṇakiccaṃ natthīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Bhojanasālā pana senāsanameva, tasmā tattha kātabbā evāti vadanti. Saṅghikevekasantaketi ettha ekasantako upasampannasantakova veditabbo.

137. Now, to indicate where an allowable hut may be desired, he begins with 'for dwelling purposes.' By this phrase, it is shown that there is no need to make an allowable hut in places such as storerooms, meal halls, shrine halls, sweeping terraces, or any other such place not made for dwelling. However, some say that a meal hall is indeed a lodging, so one should be made there. In the phrase 'belonging to the Sangha or to an individual,' 'belonging to an individual' should be understood as belonging to a fully ordained monk.

138. Idāni kattabbākāraṃ dassetuṃ “gehe”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅghassa vā ekassa vā gehe vihāre kariyamāne evaṃ īrayaṃ “kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vā “kappiyakuṭi kappiyakuṭī”ti vā vadanto paṭhamiṭṭhakatthambhādiṃ ṭhapeyya, evaṃ katā ussāvanantikā nāma, evaṃ udāharitavacanantikāti attho.

138. Now, to show the way it should be done, he begins with 'in a house…' and so on. There, when a dwelling or monastery belonging to the Sangha or to an individual is being built, one should place the first brick, post, or the like while declaring, 'We are making an allowable hut, we are making an allowable hut,' or 'Allowable hut, allowable hut.' A hut made in this way is called 'one established by announcement,' which means one established by an uttered statement.

139. Yebhuyyena vā aparikkhitto, sakalopi vā aparikkhitto ārāmo “gonisādī”ti vuccatīti sambandho. Ettha pana senāsanesu parikkhittesupi ārāme aparikkhitte kappiyakuṭikaraṇakiccaṃ natthi. Sammutiṃ karontehi kataṃ pariyositaṃ “imaṃ vihāraṃ aḍḍhayogaṃ pāsādaṃ hammiyaṃ guhaṃ tiṇakuṭikaṃ maṇḍapa”nti tesaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā tassā kuṭiyā hatthapāse vā ṭhatvā, tassā anto vā pavisitvā vuttanayeneva ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammannitabbaṃ.

139. The connection is that a monastery that is mostly unenclosed, or entirely unenclosed, is called a 'cattle-pen' (`gonisādī`). In this case, even if the lodgings are enclosed, as long as the monastery park is unenclosed, there is no need to make an allowable hut. When making the designation for a completed structure, one should take its name—'this monastery, this gabled building, this mansion, this storied building, this cave, this grass hut, or this pavilion'—and, while standing within arm's reach of that hut or having entered it, one should formally designate it by means of a motion with one announcement, in the way already described.

140. “Bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā aññehī”ti vacanato sesasahadhammikehipi devamanussehipi aññehi kappiyakuṭiyā atthāya dinno vā tesaṃ santako vā geho “gahapatī”ti mato ñātoti attho, saṅghasantakañca bhikkhusantakañca ṭhapetvā sabbesaṃ geho gahapatīti adhippāyo.

140. According to the phrase 'by others, excluding a bhikkhu,' a dwelling that is given for the purpose of an allowable hut, or one that belongs to other co-religionists such as devas and human beings, is considered and known as 'a householder's dwelling.' This is the meaning. The intention is that, excluding a dwelling belonging to the Sangha or to a bhikkhu, any dwelling belonging to others is considered 'a householder's dwelling.'

141. Sappiādīhi [M 0.0137] missitanti sappiādīhi pañcahi ca haliddisiṅgiverādiyāvajīvikena cāti attho. Vajeyya antovutthattanti ettha yāvakālikayāmakālikasaṅkhātaṃ purimakālikadvayaṃ saṅghikaṃ vā bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā santakaṃ sayaṃ kappiyakuṭiyā vutthampi itarehi akappiyakuṭiyā vutthehi missitaṃ antovutthabhāvaṃ āgaccheyyāti attho.

141. 'Mixed with ghee, etc.' means mixed with the five medicines beginning with ghee, and with life-long medicines such as turmeric, ginger, and so on. As for 'it would become dwelt inside,' the meaning is this: here, the first two kinds of time-limited items, known as those for the proper time (`yāvakālika`) and those for a watch (`yāmakālika`), belonging to the Sangha, a bhikkhu, or a bhikkhunī, even if kept by oneself in an allowable hut, become 'dwelt inside' if they are mixed with other such items that have been kept in a non-allowable hut.

142. Tehevāti akappiyakuṭiyaṃ vutthasappitelādīhi. Sāmapākatanti sāmaṃpakkabhāvaṃ gacchatīti attho.

142. 'With those very things' means with ghee, oil, and so on, that have been kept in a non-allowable hut. 'It becomes self-cooked' means it attains the state of being cooked by itself; this is the meaning.

143-4. Imā [V 0.0130] pana kappiyakuṭiyo yadā jahitavatthukā honti, taṃ dassetuṃ “ussāvanantikā”tiādimāha. Sace thambhe vā bhittipāde vā parivattenti, yo yo ṭhito, tattha tattha patiṭṭhāti, etenupāyena sabbesu parivattesupi na vijahitavatthukāva hotīti attho. Parikkhitte gonisādi vijahitavatthukā. Sesā chadanavibbhamāti chadanavināsā jahitavatthukā hontīti adhippāyo. Bhūmivinicchayo.

143-144. Now, to show when these allowable huts become ones with an abandoned basis, he begins with 'The one established by announcement…' and so on. If they move it on its posts or on the base of its walls, it is established wherever it is placed. By this means, even if it is moved about in every way, it does not become one with an abandoned basis; this is the meaning. When a cattle-pen is enclosed, it becomes one with an abandoned basis. As for the others, the phrase 'by the destruction of the roof' means that they become ones with an abandoned basis through the destruction of the roof; this is the intention. The Determination of Grounds.

Bhūminiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Grounds is concluded.

15. Upajjhācariyavattaniddesavaṇṇanā

15. The Commentary on the Exposition of Duties towards Preceptors and Teachers

145. Upajjhācariyeti ettha (mahāva. 64, 67, 74, 78-79; cūḷava. 375, 377; 379-382; mahāva. aṭṭha. 64, 67, 75, 76, 77) ācariyo nāma nissayācariyo pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo dhammācariyoti catubbidho. Etesu hi nissayantevāsikena yāva ācariyaṃ nissāya vasati, tāva sabbamācariyavattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Pabbajjāupasampadādhammantevāsikehi pana nissayamuttakehipi ādito [M 0.0138] paṭṭhāya yāva cīvararajanaṃ, tāva vattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Anāpucchitvā pattadānādimhi pana etesaṃ anāpatti. Etesu ca pabbajjantevāsiko ca upasampadantevāsiko ca ācariyassa yāvajīvaṃ bhāro, nissayantevāsiko ca dhammantevāsiko ca yāva samīpe vasati, tāvadeva. Suṭṭhu piyasīlo supesalo, sikkhākāmoti attho. Dantakaṭṭhaṃ dentena ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā mahantaṃ majjhimaṃ khuddakanti tīṇi dantakaṭṭhāni upanetabbāni. Tesu yaṃ tīṇi divasāni gaṇhāti, taṃ sallakkhetvā catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya tādisaṃyeva sammā ubhohi hatthehi dātabbaṃ. Sace yaṃ vā taṃ vā gaṇhāti, yathāladdhaṃ upanetabbaṃ. Toyanti sītañca uṇhañca udakaṃ upanetvā yaṃ tīṇi divasāni vaḷañjeti, catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya tādisaṃ upanetabbaṃ. Sace dvepi vaḷañjeti, duvidhampi upanetabbaṃ. Sace yāgu hoti, bhājanaṃ dhovitvā upanetabbaṃ.

145. Here, in 'preceptor and teacher,' a teacher is of four kinds: the dependence teacher, the going-forth teacher, the higher-ordination teacher, and the Dhamma teacher. Among these, a dependence-pupil must perform all the duties toward a teacher for as long as he lives in dependence on him. But pupils of the going-forth, higher ordination, and the Dhamma, even when freed from dependence, must perform the duties from the beginning until the dyeing of the robe. However, for them there is no offense in such things as giving away a bowl without having asked. Among these, the going-forth pupil and the higher-ordination pupil are a life-long charge for the teacher, whereas the dependence-pupil and the Dhamma-pupil are so only for as long as they live nearby. 'Very amiable and of pleasant conduct' means desirous of the training. When giving a tooth-stick, one should arrange one's upper robe over one shoulder and offer three tooth-sticks: a large one, a medium one, and a small one. One should note which one he takes for three days, and from the fourth day onwards, one should properly offer one of that same kind with both hands. If he takes any one of them, one should offer whatever is available. As to water, one should offer both cold and hot water. Whichever he uses for three days, from the fourth day onwards one should offer that kind. If he uses both, both kinds should be offered. If there is gruel, the bowl should be washed and offered.

146. Patte vattaṃ careti “yāguṃ pītassa udakaṃ datvā bhājanaṃ paṭiggahetvā nīcaṃ katvā [V 0.0131] sādhukaṃ aparighaṃsantena dhovitvā paṭisāmetabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ patte vattaṃ careti attho. Gāmappavese vattaṃ careti evaṃ sabbattha. “Sace upajjhāyo vā ācariyo vā gāmaṃ pavisitukāmo hoti, nivāsanaṃ dātabbaṃ, paṭinivāsanaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ dātabbaṃ, saguṇaṃ katvā saṅghāṭiyo dātabbā, dhovitvā patto sodako dātabbo”ti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) idaṃ gāmappavesane vattaṃ nāma. “Sace upajjhāyo vā ācariyo vā pacchāsamaṇaṃ ākaṅkhati, timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādentena parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā saguṇaṃ katvā saṅghāṭiyo pārupitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvā dhovitvā pattaṃ gahetvā upajjhāyassa vā ācariyassa vā pacchāsamaṇena hotabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) [M 0.0139] nayena vuttaṃ gamane vattaṃ nāma. “Nivattantena paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā āsanaṃ paññāpetabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) nayena vuttaṃ āgame vattaṃ nāma. “Upajjhāyamhi vuṭṭhite āsanaṃ uddharitabbaṃ, pādodakaṃ pādapīṭhaṃ pādakathalikaṃ paṭisāmetabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) evaṃ vuttaṃ āsanādīsu vattaṃ nāma. Upāhanāya vattaṃ nāma “upāhanā puñchitabbā, upāhanā puñchantena paṭhamaṃ sukkhena coḷakena puñchitabbā, pacchā allenā”tiādinā (cūḷava. 357, 359) vuttaṃ. Cīvare vattaṃ nāma “sace cīvaraṃ sinnaṃ hoti, muhuttaṃ uṇhe otāpetabbaṃ, na ca uṇhe cīvaraṃ nidahitabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ.

146. One should perform the duty regarding the bowl; the meaning is that one should perform the duty regarding the bowl as stated: 'Having given water to him after he has drunk gruel, one should take the bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scraping it, and put it away.' One should perform the duty when entering a village, and so in all cases. The duty when entering a village is this: 'If the preceptor or teacher wishes to enter a village, the under-robe should be given, the used under-robe should be received, the waistband should be given, the outer robes should be given folded, and the bowl, having been washed, should be given with water in it.' The duty when going is as stated in the passage beginning: 'If the preceptor or teacher desires an attendant monk, one should dress with the under-robe covering the three circles and worn evenly, tie the waistband, put on the folded outer robes, fasten the clasp, wash the bowl, take it, and become the attendant monk for the preceptor or teacher.' The duty on arrival is as stated in the passage beginning: 'When returning, one should come back first and prepare the seat.' The duty regarding the seat and so on is as stated: 'When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be cleared away; the foot-water, footstool, and foot-wiper should be put away.' The duty regarding sandals is as stated in the passage beginning: 'Sandals should be wiped. When wiping sandals, one should first wipe them with a dry cloth, then with a wet one.' The duty regarding the robe is as stated in the passage beginning: 'If the robe is damp, it should be aired in the sun for a moment, but a robe should not be left in the heat.'

147. Paribhojanīyapānīya-vaccappassāvaṭhānisūti ettha sace pānīyaṃ na hoti, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sace paribhojanīyaṃ na hoti, paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sace vaccakuṭi uklāpā hoti, vaccakuṭi sammajjitabbā. Tathā passāvaṭṭhāne evaṃ vattaṃ caritabbanti attho. “Vihāraṃ sodhentena paṭhamaṃ pattacīvaraṃ nīharitvā ekamantaṃ nikkhipitabba”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ vihārasodhane vattaṃ nāma. “Bhūmattharaṇaṃ otāpetvā sodhetvā papphoṭetvā atiharitvā yathāpaññattaṃ paññāpetabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ puna paññāpane vattaṃ nāma.

147. Here, regarding water for washing, water for drinking, the latrine, and the urinal: if there is no drinking water, drinking water should be provided. If there is no water for washing, water for washing should be provided. If the latrine is soiled, the latrine should be swept. The meaning is that one should perform the duty similarly at the urinal. The duty in cleaning the dwelling is as stated in the passage beginning: 'When cleaning the dwelling, one should first take out the bowl and robes and put them in a certain place.' The duty in relaying things is as stated in the passage beginning: 'The floor covering should be aired, cleaned, shaken out, brought back, and laid out as it was before.'

148. Idāni vihāraṃ sodhentena evaṃ sodhetabbanti taṃ dassetuṃ “na papphoṭeyyā”tiādimāha[V 0.0132]. Tassattho – vihāraṃ sodhento bhikkhu bhūmattharaṇādisayanāsanaṃ paṭivāte vā paṅgaṇe vā pānīyasāmantā vā na papphoṭeyyāti. Paṅgaṇeti bahūnaṃ sannipāte ṭhāne.

148. Now, to show how one cleaning a dwelling should clean it, he begins with 'One should not shake it out…' and so on. The meaning is this: a monk cleaning the dwelling should not shake out floor coverings, bedding, seats, and the like upwind, in a courtyard, or near the water. 'In a courtyard' means in a place where many people assemble.

149. Nhāneti [M 0.0140] “sace upajjhāyo nahāyitukāmo hoti, nahānaṃ paṭiyādetabbaṃ. Sace sītena attho hoti, sītaṃ paṭiyādetabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66; cūḷava. 376) vuttaṃ nahāne vattaṃ nāma, “upajjhāyassa gattato udakaṃ sammajjitabbaṃ, nivāsanaṃ dātabba”ntiādinā (mahāva. 66; cūḷava. 376) vuttaṃ nahātassa kātabbaṃ nāma. Raṅgapāketi “sace upajjhāyassa ācariyassa rajanaṃ pacitabbaṃ hoti, saddhivihārikena antevāsikena pacitabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ. Dhovaneti “sace upajjhāyassa ācariyassa cīvaraṃ dhovitabbaṃ hoti, saddhivihārikena antevāsikena dhovitabbaṃ, ussukkaṃ vā kātabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ. Sibbaneti “sace upajjhāyena ācariyena cīvaraṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, saddhivihārikena antevāsikena kātabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) vuttaṃ. Cīvare theve ṭhite rajanto na vaje na pakkameyyāti attho. “Cīvaraṃ rajantena sādhukaṃ samparivattakaṃ samparivattakaṃ rajitabbaṃ, na ca acchinne theve pakkamitabba”nti (mahāva. 66, 78; cūḷava. 376, 380) hi vuttaṃ.

149. Regarding bathing: the duty concerning bathing is as stated in the passage beginning: "If the preceptor wishes to bathe, bathing should be prepared. If cold water is needed, cold water should be prepared." What should be done after the bathing is as stated in the passage beginning: "Water should be wiped from the preceptor’s body, and a lower robe should be given." Regarding preparing dye: it is stated, "If dye needs to be prepared for the preceptor or teacher, the co-resident pupil or pupil should prepare it." Regarding washing: it is stated, "If the preceptor's or teacher’s robe needs to be washed, the co-resident pupil or pupil should wash it, or make an effort to have it washed." Regarding sewing: it is stated, "If the preceptor or teacher needs a robe made, the co-resident pupil or pupil should make it." The meaning is that while dyeing a robe on the frame, one should not go away or leave. For it is said: "When dyeing a robe, it should be thoroughly turned and repeatedly dyed, and one should not leave before the dripping has ceased."

150. Ekaccassāti ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ visabhāgassa anatthakāmassa veripuggalassa. Anāpucchāti ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ anārocetvā. Kiñcananti yaṃ kiñci.

150. 'For some'—meaning for a person who is discordant with, wishes harm to, or is an enemy of one's teachers and preceptors. 'Without asking'—meaning without informing one's teachers and preceptors. 'Anything'—meaning whatever it may be.

151-2. Tassāti ekaccassa. Ninnetunti nīharituṃ. Kiccayaṃ parikammaṃ vāti veyyāvaccaṃ vā piṭṭhiparikammādiparikammaṃ vā attanā tassa kātuṃ vā tena attano kārāpetuṃ vāti evamattho veditabbo.

151-2. 'Tassa' means 'of that one' (i.e., of some particular person). 'Ninnetuṃ' means to remove. 'Kiccayaṃ parikammaṃ vā' refers to a service or preparatory work, such as back-rubbing or other tasks, either doing it oneself for that person or having that person do it for oneself—this is the meaning to be understood.

153. Sace ācariyupajjhāyā aññattha gatā honti, pariveṇaṃ gantvā apassantehi gāmaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Gāmaṃ pavisanto sace passati, āpucchitabbamevāti vadanti. “Upajjhāyaṃ [M 0.0141] anāpucchā na disā pakkamitabbā”ti (mahāva. 66, cūḷava. 376) hi vuttaṃ. Attano kiccayaṃ nāma antovihārepi attano pattapacanacīvarakammakesacchedanādi.

153. If teachers or preceptors have gone elsewhere, it is permissible to enter the village after going to their residence and not seeing them. If one sees them while entering the village, it is said that one must indeed ask permission. For it is said: 'One should not depart in any direction without informing the preceptor.' One's own duties, even within the monastery, are such things as cooking for one's bowl, robe-work, hair-cutting, and so on.

154. Saṅghāyattakammāni [V 0.0133] nāma parivāsamānattaabbhānatajjanīyaniyassapabbājanīyapaṭisāraṇīyaukkhepanādayo.

154. Actions dependent on the Saṅgha are, namely: parivāsa, mānatta, abbhāna, tajjanīya, niyassa, pabbājanīya, paṭisāraṇīya, ukkhepanā, and others.

155. Vuṭṭhānaṃ nesamāgameti “sace upajjhāyo vā ācariyo vā gilāno hoti, yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabba”nti (mahāva. 66; cūḷava. 376) hi vuttaṃ. Upajjhācariyavattavinicchayo.

155. 'Vuṭṭhānaṃ nesamāgameti' means that if the preceptor or teacher is ill, one should attend to them for life and await their recovery, as it is said: 'If the preceptor or teacher is ill, one should attend to them for life and await their recovery.' This concludes the analysis of the duties toward preceptors and teachers.

Upajjhācariyavattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the duties towards preceptors and teachers is concluded.

16. Vaccappassāvaṭṭhānikaniddesavaṇṇanā

16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Section Concerning Defecation and Urination

156. Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ na kareyya vaccanti sambandho. Yathānupubbiyā labbhatīti sambandho. Imesu pana tīsu ṭhānesu yo yo paṭhamaṃ āgacchati vuḍḍho vā navo vā, so so āgatapaṭipāṭiyā kātuñca nahāyituñca labbhatīti adhippāyo.

156. The connection is that one should not use the toilet according to seniority. The connection is that it is obtained according to sequence. But in these three situations, whoever arrives first—whether senior or junior—obtains the opportunity to use the toilet and to bathe in the order of arrival; this is the intended meaning.

157. Ubbhajitvāti (cūḷava. 373, 374) nivāsanaṃ dūratova ukkhipitvā no paviseyya. Sahasā ca no paviseyyāti sambandho. “Bahi ṭhitena ukkāsitabba”nti ca “sādhukaṃ ataramānena vaccakuṭi pavisitabbā”ti ca vuttattā ukkāsitvāva ataramāno paviseyyāti attho. “Na ubbhajitvā pavisitabbā, vaccapādukāya ṭhitena ubbhajitabba”nti (cūḷava. 374) vacanato “ubbhajeyya pādukāsveva saṇṭhito”ti vuttaṃ.

157. 'Ubbhajitvā' means one should not enter having lifted one's lower garment from a distance. And the connection is that one should not enter hastily. Since it is said, 'One standing outside should cough,' and, 'One should enter the toilet carefully, without haste,' the meaning is that one should enter without haste only after having coughed. Because it is said, 'One should not enter after lifting the robe; one should lift it while standing on the toilet sandals,' it is stated: 'One should lift the robe only while standing on the sandals.'

158. Na [M 0.0142] kareyya ubhayaṃ na kareyyubhayaṃ.

158. 'Na kareyya ubhayaṃ' means one should not do both.

159. Kūpeti (cūḷava. 374) vaccakūpe. Kaṭṭhanti avalekhanakaṭṭhaṃ. Passāvadoṇiyā kheḷaṃ na kātabbanti attho. Nāvalekheyya pharusenāti phālitakaṭṭhena vā kharena vā gaṇṭhikena vā [V 0.0134] kaṇṭakena vā susirena vā pūtinā vā nāvalekhitabbanti attho. Uhatañcāpīti gūthamakkhitampi dhovaye attanā vā parena vā katanti adhippāyo.

159. 'Kūpe' means in the toilet pit. 'Kaṭṭhaṃ' means the cleaning stick. The meaning is that one should not spit into the urinal vessel. 'Nāvalekheyya pharusena' means one should not scrape with a split stick, a hard one, a knotty one, a thorny one, a hollow one, or a rotten one. 'Uhatañcāpi' means one should wash even what is smeared with excrement, whether done by oneself or by another—this is the intended meaning.

160. Ubbhajitvā na nikkhameti ettha “vaccapādukāya ṭhitena paṭicchādetabba”nti (cūḷava. 374) hi vuttaṃ, puna “ācamanapādukāyaṃ ṭhitena ubbhajitabba”nti (cūḷava. 374) ca vuttaṃ. “Capu capū”ti saddaṃ katvā nācameyyāti attho. Vaccappassāvaṭṭhānikavinicchayo.

160. Regarding 'having lifted it, one should not go out,' here it is said, 'One should cover oneself while standing on the toilet sandals,' and again, 'One should lift it while standing on the rinsing sandals.' The meaning is that one should not rinse while making the sound 'capu capu.' The analysis concerning the place for defecation and urination is concluded.

Vaccappassāvaṭṭhānikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the section concerning defecation and urination is concluded.

17. Āpucchakaraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

17. Commentary on the Exposition of Asking Permission

161. Therenāti saṅghattherena.

161. 'By the elder' means by the elder of the Saṅgha.

162. Tattha tattha sannipatitānaṃ sabbesaṃ vuḍḍho vuḍḍhataro, tasmiṃ vuḍḍhatarāgame puna āpucchanaṃ natthi. Bhattagge cānumodatoti ettha dānapatinā yācitena daharena vuḍḍhena anāpucchitvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

162. Among all those assembled here and there, the eldest is the most senior. When that most senior one is present, there is no further asking of permission. Regarding 'and giving thanks at the meal-hall,' some say that it is permissible for a junior monk, if requested by the donor, to speak without asking permission from the elder.

163. Ekavihāraketi ekovarake vuḍḍhena vasanto anāpucchā na sajjhāyeyyāti attho. Uddesaṃ paripucchañca no dadeti uddesaṃ vā paripucchaṃ vā no dadeyya.

163. 'In a single dwelling' means that one living with an elder in a single cell should not recite without asking permission. 'He does not give a recitation or an inquiry' means he should not give a recitation or an inquiry.

164. Na [M 0.0143] vivareyya na thakeyya cāti sambandho. Dvāraṃ nāma mahāvaḷañjaṃ, tattha āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi.

164. 'He should not open and he should not close' is the connection. A 'door' means the main entrance; there, the duty of asking permission does not apply.

165. Vuḍḍhena caṅkame caṅkamantopi yena vuḍḍho, tena parivattayeti sambandho. Āpucchakaraṇavinicchayo.

165. 'Even while pacing on a walking path with an elder, one should turn towards the elder'; this is the connection. The analysis of asking permission.

Āpucchakaraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Asking Permission is finished.

18. Nagganiddesavaṇṇanā

18. Commentary on the Exposition on Nakedness

166. “Na [V 0.0135] tveva naggena āgantabbaṃ, yo āgaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 517) vuttattā (cūḷava. 261;) “naggo maggaṃ na vaje”ti vuttaṃ.

166. Because it is said, 'One should certainly not come naked; should one come so, it is an offense of wrong-doing,' it is stated: 'A naked person should not go on the road.'

167. Paṭicchādisūti “tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū jantāgharepi udakepi parikammaṃ kātuṃ kukkuccāyanti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso paṭicchādiyo jantāgharappaṭicchādiṃ udakappaṭicchādiṃ vatthappaṭicchādi”nti evaṃ vuttāsu tīsu paṭicchādīsūti attho. Duveti etāsu tīsu paṭicchādīsu udakajantāgharappaṭicchādiyo parikamme kappantīti adhippāyo. Vatthacchādīti vatthappaṭicchādi. Sabbatthāti khādanīyasāyanīyādīsu sabbakammesu kappiyāti attho. Naggavinicchayo.

167. 'With coverings': this means among the three coverings spoken of thus: 'Now at that time, bhikkhus were scrupulous about doing work in the steam bath and in the water. I allow, O bhikkhus, three coverings: a steam-bath covering, a water-covering, and a cloth-covering.' 'Two': the meaning is that among these three coverings, the water-covering and the steam-bath covering are allowable for work. 'Cloth-covering' means the cloth-covering. 'In all cases' means it is allowable in all actions, such as with edibles, savories, and so on. The analysis of nakedness.

Nagganiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Nakedness is finished.

19. Nhānakappaniddesavaṇṇanā

19. Commentary on the Exposition of What is Allowable in Bathing

168. Puratoti (cūḷava. 372) therānaṃ purato upari vā na ca nhāyeyyāti attho.

168. 'In front of': the meaning is that one should not bathe in front of or upstream from the elders.

169-171. Kuṭṭatthambhataruṭṭāneti [M 0.0144] ettha (cūḷava. 243; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 243) kuṭṭe vā thambhe vā tarumhi vā aṭṭānaphalake vā kāyaṃ na ghaṃsayeti attho. Gandhabbahattho nāma makkaṭahatthasadiso dāruādimayo. Kuruvindakasuttiyāti kuruvindasuttiyā. Mallakena vā aññamaññaṃ vā. “Na bhikkhave viggayha parikammaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 243) evaṃ vuttaṃ viggahaparikammaṃ sandhāya “aññamaññaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ.

169-171. 'Against a wall, pillar, tree, or watchtower': here the meaning is that one should not rub one’s body against a wall, a pillar, a tree, or a plank of a watchtower. A 'gandhabba-hand' is the name for an implement made of wood or the like that resembles a monkey’s hand. 'By a string with kuruvinda powder' means by a string with kuruvinda powder. 'Or with a bath-gourd or with one another': the words 'or with one another' are stated with reference to contentious scrubbing, concerning which it was said: 'Bhikkhus, one should not have scrubbing done contentiously. Whoever should have it done incurs an offense of wrong-doing.'

Idāni kappiyāni dassetuṃ “kapāliṭṭhakakhaṇḍānī”tiādimāha. Sabbesaṃ vaṭṭatīti sambandho[V 0.0136]. Gilānassapi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 243) agilānassapi imāni kapāliṭṭhakakhaṇḍādīni kāyaghaṃsane vaṭṭanti. Puthupāṇīti (cūḷava. 244) hatthaparikammaṃ vuccati. Tasmā sabbesaṃ hatthena piṭṭhiparikammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Akatamallakaṃ nāma ekadāṭhimaṃ paricchinditvā kataṃ. Pāsāṇādayo pādaghaṃsane eva kappiyā. Nhānakappavinicchayo.

Now, to show what is allowable, he said, 'Potsherds and pieces of brick,' etc. The connection is: 'It is allowable for all.' For both the sick and the not-sick, these potsherds, pieces of brick, and so on are allowable for rubbing the body. 'With the flat of the hand' is said to mean work done with the hand. Therefore, it is allowable for all to perform back-scrubbing with the hand. An 'unfashioned bath-gourd' is one made by cutting a single pomegranate. Stones and so on are allowable only for rubbing the feet. The analysis of what is allowable in bathing.

Nhānakappaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of What is Allowable in Bathing is finished.

20. Avandiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

20. Commentary on the Exposition of Those Unworthy of Veneration

172. “Nānāsaṃvāsako vuḍḍhataro adhammavādī avandiyo”ti (cūḷava. 312; pari. 467) evaṃ vuttattā laddhinānāsaṃvāsako idha nānāsaṃvāsako. Pārivāsiyamūlāyapaṭikassanārahamānattārahamānattacāriabbhānārahā garukaṭṭhāti idha gahitā. Ime pana aññamaññaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanādīni labhanti, pakatattena avandanīyāti adhippāyo. Avandanīyavinicchayo.

172. Because it is said, 'A more senior bhikkhu of a different communion who is a speaker of non-Dhamma is unworthy of veneration,' here 'one of a different communion' means one of a different communion by view. Here are included those on probation, those deserving to be sent back to the beginning, those deserving mānatta, those undergoing mānatta, and those deserving rehabilitation, because they are undergoing a grave procedure. These, however, receive veneration and so on from one another according to seniority, but the meaning is that they are unworthy of veneration by a regular bhikkhu. The analysis of those unworthy of veneration.

Avandiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Those Unworthy of Veneration is finished.

21. Cammaniddesavaṇṇanā

21. Commentary on the Exposition of Hides

173. Idāni [M 0.0145] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu cammāni attharaṇāni eḷakacammaṃ ajacammaṃ migacamma”nti (mahāva. 259) evaṃ vuttacammāni dassetuṃ “migājeḷakacammānī”tiādimāha. Paribhuñjitunti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 262) mañcādīsu yattha katthaci attharitvā nipajjituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā vaṭṭantīti attho. Rohiteṇīpasadā ca kuruṅgā ca ca-saddena aññepi vāḷamigā migamātukādayopi migajātikā evāti adhippāyo.

173. Now, to show the hides spoken of thus: “I allow, O bhikkhus, in all the border districts, hides for spreading—a sheep’s hide, a goat’s hide, a deer’s hide,” he said, “hides of deer, goats, and sheep,” and so on. “To use”: the meaning is that it is allowable to spread them anywhere on a bed, etc., and to lie down or sit. The red deer, the doe, the spotted deer, and the antelope, and by the word “and,” other predatory beasts, mother-deer, and so on are to be understood as just species of deer; this is the intended meaning.

174. Anuññātattayā aññanti –

174. Other than the three that are permitted—

“Makkaṭo [V 0.0137] kāḷasīho ca, sarabho kadalīmigo;

Ye ca vāḷamigā keci, tesaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. –

“The hide of the monkey, the black lion, the sarabha, the plantain deer, and whatever other predatory beasts there are, is not allowable.”

Ettha vāḷamigaggahaṇena vuttāvasesā antamaso gomahiṃsādayo gahitāti veditabbā. Thavikāti upāhanakosakasatthakosakakuñcikakosakāti veditabbā, na pattatthavikādayo. Cammavinicchayo.

Here, by the inclusion of “predatory beasts,” it should be understood that the remaining unmentioned animals, down to cattle, buffaloes, and so on, are included. “Bags” should be understood as a shoe-bag, a weapon-sheath, and a key-pouch, not bowl-bags and so on. The Decision on Hides.

Cammaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Hides is finished.

22. Upāhananiddesavaṇṇanā

22. Commentary on the Exposition on Footwear

175. Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanāti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 245) catupaṭalato paṭṭhāya vuccati, na ekadvitipaṭalato paṭṭhāya “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ekapalāsikaṃ upāhanaṃ, na bhikkhave diguṇā upāhanā dhāretabbā, na tiguṇā upāhanā dhāretabbā, na guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 245) vuttattā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, omukkaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ, na [M 0.0146] bhikkhave navā guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 247) vuttattā “navā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāpi majjhimadese gilānopi navaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ na labhati, ekavārampi aññehi paribhuttaṃ omukkaupāhanasaṅkhātaṃ labhati, paccantimesu janapadesu gilāno navampi labhatīti veditabbaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu guṇaṅguṇūpāhana”nti (mahāva. 259) avisesena vuttattā.

175. “Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 245) is said to refer to footwear from four layers upwards, not from one or two layers, because it is stated: “I allow, O bhikkhus, single-layered footwear. O bhikkhus, double-layered footwear should not be worn, triple-layered footwear should not be worn, nor should multi-layered footwear be worn. Whoever wears them commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāva. 245). And because it is stated: “I allow, O bhikkhus, worn-out multi-layered footwear. O bhikkhus, new multi-layered footwear should not be worn. Whoever wears them commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāva. 247), the word “new” is mentioned. Everywhere in the Middle Country, even a sick person does not obtain new multi-layered footwear; he obtains what has been used even once by others, known as worn-out footwear. In the border regions, however, a sick person can obtain new ones, as it should be understood, because it is stated without distinction: “I allow, O bhikkhus, multi-layered footwear in all border regions” (Mahāva. 259).

Sabbassāti gilānassāpi agilānassāpīti attho. Majjhimadesepi paccantimadesepi ārāme ārāmūpacāre gilānassāpi agilānassāpi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ajjhārāme upāhanaṃ dhāretu”nti (mahāva. 249) vuttattā kappiyanti attho. Sabbatthāti ārāmepi gāmepi. Akallakassāti gilānassa. Ettha pana majjhimadese gilānassa guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā paribhuttāva ārāmepi gāmepi vaṭṭati, paccantimadese aparibhuttāpi. Majjhimadesepi paccantimadesepi bhagavatā gilānasseva upāhanā anuññātā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yassa pādā vā dukkhā, pādā vā phalitā, pādakhilo vā ābādho, upāhanaṃ dhāretu”nti (mahāva. 249) ca [V 0.0138] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānena bhikkhunā saupāhanena gāmaṃ pavisitu”nti (mahāva. 256) vuttattā ca. Majjhimadese ca gilāno navaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ dhāretuṃ yadi labhati, kathaṃ padesapaññatti hotīti? Sabbattha pana bhagavatā gilānasseva upāhanā anuññātā, tasmā majjhimadese gilāno navaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ labhatīti gahetabbanti vadanti.

“For all” (sabbassa) means for both the sick and the healthy. In the Middle Country and in the border regions, in the monastery and its vicinity, it is permissible for both the sick and the healthy, because it is stated: “I allow, O bhikkhus, the wearing of footwear within the monastery” (Mahāva. 249). “Everywhere” (sabbattha) means both in the monastery and in the village. “For one who is unfit” (akallakassa) refers to the sick. Here, however, in the Middle Country, for a sick person, used multi-layered footwear is suitable both in the monastery and in the village; in the border regions, even unused ones are suitable. In both the Middle Country and the border regions, the Blessed One allowed footwear only for the sick, because it is stated: “I allow, O bhikkhus, for one whose feet are painful, or whose feet are cracked, or who has a foot ailment, to wear footwear” (Mahāva. 249), and “I allow, O bhikkhus, a sick bhikkhu to enter the village wearing footwear” (Mahāva. 256). If in the Middle Country a sick person obtains new multi-layered footwear to wear, how does the regional regulation apply? However, everywhere, footwear was allowed by the Blessed One only for the sick; therefore, they say it should be understood that in the Middle Country, a sick person obtains new multi-layered footwear.

176-9. Sabbāva nīlakā (mahāva. 246; mahāva. aṭṭha. 246) sabbanīlakā. Esa nayo sabbattha odātakādīsupi. Odātaṃ pana neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 0.0147] paṭikkhittaṃ, anulomavasena pana idha paṭikkhittanti veditabbaṃ. Mahāraṅgarattā satapadipiṭṭhivaṇṇā. Mahānāmaraṅgarattā mandarattā. Mañjeṭṭhikā kaṇaverapupphavaṇṇā. Pupphalatādīhi vicittā citrā. Nīlapītādivaddhikāti ettha ādi-saddena odātalohitamañjeṭṭhikamahāraṅgamahānāmaraṅgarattādivasena vaddhikā gahitā. Sīhabyagghuddājinadīpīnaṃ cammehi cāti sambandho. Kocīti gilānopi agilānopi.

176-9. “All are blue” (Mahāva. 246; Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 246) means completely blue. This principle applies everywhere, even to white and so forth. However, white is prohibited neither in the Pāḷi nor in the commentaries; rather, it should be understood as prohibited here by way of implication. “Deep red” (mahāraṅgarattā) is the color of a centipede's back. “Great Nāma-colored red” (mahānāmaraṅgarattā) is pale red. “Madder” (mañjeṭṭhikā) is the color of the oleander flower. “Variegated” (vicittā) means adorned with floral designs and so forth. In “with borders of blue, yellow, and so on” (nīlapītādivaddhikā), by the word “and so on” are included borders of white, red, madder, deep red, great Nāma-colored red, and so on. The connection is “and with the hides of lions, tigers, otters, and leopards.” “Anyone” (koci) refers to both the sick and the not-sick.

180. Sakalaṃ vā ekadesakaṃ vā rajanaṃ coḷena (mahāva. aṭṭha. 246) puñchitvā vaḷañjeyyāti attho. Khallakādikaṃ pana sabbaṃ hāritvā vaḷañjetabbaṃ. Upāhanavinicchayo.

180. The meaning is that one should wipe off the dye, either entirely or partially, with a cloth (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 246) and then use it. However, all colored parts and so forth should be removed before use. The Decision on Footwear.

Upāhananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Footwear is concluded.

23. Anolokiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

23. Commentary on the Exposition on Not Looking

181. Itthiyāti tadahujātāyapi dārikāya. Ādāse (cūḷava. 247) vā udakapatte vā attano mukhaṃ avalokeyya, assa dukkaṭanti sambandho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā ādāse vā udakapatte vā mukhanimittaṃ oloketu”nti (cūḷava. 247) vuttattāvaṇādīni vā “jiṇṇo nu khomhi, no vā”ti evaṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ vā oloketuṃ vaṭṭati. Anolokiyavinicchayo.

181. “A woman” (itthiyā) means even a girl born on that very day. If one looks at one's own face in a mirror (Cūḷava. 247) or a water vessel, it is an offense of wrong-doing—this is the connection. Because it is stated: “I allow, O bhikkhus, on account of illness, to look at the facial features in a mirror or a water vessel” (Cūḷava. 247), it is permissible to examine one's complexion and so forth, or one's signs of aging, thinking, “Am I old or not?” The Decision on Not Looking.

Anolokiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Not Looking is concluded.

24. Añjanīniddesavaṇṇanā

24. Commentary on the Exposition on Eye-Salve Containers

182. Vaṭṭā [M 0.0148][V 0.0139] vā aṭṭhasoḷasaṃsā vā maṭṭhā pupphalatādīhi acittakā añjanī vaṭṭatīti attho. Tissopi vaṭṭanti, ekāya vā dvīsu vā kathā eva natthīti adhippāyo. Lekhāti vaṭṭalekhā. Bandhitunti pidhānakabandhanatthaṃ.

182. The meaning is that an eye-salve container that is round or has eight or sixteen sides, smooth, and not adorned with floral designs and so forth, is permissible. Even three are permissible; the intention is that there is no question about one or two. “Lekhā” means a circular line. “Bandhituṃ” means for the purpose of fastening a lid.

183. Rūpanti sakuṇarūpādi. Yadi ca edisaṃ aññehi kataṃ labhati, ghaṃsitvā vā chinditvā vā yathā vā na paññāyati, tathā suttena veṭhetvā vaḷañjetabbaṃ.

183. “Forms” (rūpa) means shapes of birds and so forth. If one obtains such a thing made by others, it should be rubbed or cut so that it is no longer recognizable, or it should be wrapped with thread and used.

184. Thavikāti añjanithavikā. Añjanisalākāpi labbhatīti sambandho.

184. “Thavikā” means an eye-salve pouch. The connection is that an eye-salve stick is also obtained.

185-6. Aṭṭhīti (mahāva. 266; mahāva. aṭṭha. 264) manussaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṭṭhi. Visāṇadantesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Āmalakakakkādīhi katā phalamayā. Tammayāti idha vutteheva nibbattā. Añjanīvinicchayo.

185-6. By “bones” (Mahāva. 266; Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 264) is meant the remaining bones, excluding human bones. There is nothing impermissible regarding horns and tusks. Those made from myrobalan, kakkaka, and so forth are fruit-based. By “made of them” (tammayā) here is meant those produced from the things mentioned here. The Decision on Eye-Salve Containers.

Añjanīniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Eye-Salve Containers is concluded.

25. Akappiyasayananiddesavaṇṇanā

25. Commentary on the Exposition of Unsuitable Couches

187-9. “Uccako āsandiko uppanno hoti, anujānāmi bhikkhave uccakampi āsandika”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato mañcassa upaḍḍhabhāgappamāṇena ekatobhāgena dīghampi sugataṅgulena atirekaṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ idha āsandīti adhippetaṃ, caturaṃsāsandiko pana pamāṇātikkantakopi vaṭṭati. Tūlīti [M 0.0149] pakatitūlikā. Pallaṅkonāma āharimehi vāḷehi katoti vutto. Tattheva “sīharūpādiṃ dassetvā kato pana vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Paṭikanti setattharaṇaṃ. Gonacittakanti ettha caturaṅgulādhikalomo kojavo “gonako”ti vuccati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kojava”nti (mahāva. 337) cīvarakkhandhake vuttattā caturaṅgulalomakaṃ pakatikojavaṃ vaṭṭati. Ratanacittaṃ cittakaṃ na vaṭṭati. Paṭalīti ghanapuppharattaattharaṇaṃ[V 0.0140]. Vikatīti sīhabyagghādirūpavicitto uṇṇāmayattharaṇako. Uddalomīti ekatouggatapupphaṃ. Ekantalomikāti ubhatouggatapupphaṃ.

187-9. According to the statement, “A high seat has come into being; I allow, monks, a high seat as well” (Cv V.297), here a seat (`āsandī`) is intended to be one that is long on one side by half the measure of a bed, with legs exceeding eight Sugata-fingerbreadths. However, a square seat, even if exceeding the measure, is allowable. A `tūlī` means an ordinary cushion. A couch (`pallaṅka`) is said to be made with imported animal hair. There, it is also said: “But if made displaying lion-shapes, etc., it is allowable.” `Paṭika` is a white spread. Regarding a woolen rug with designs (`gonacittaka`), here a `kojava` with fleece exceeding four fingerbreadths is called a `gonaka`. Since it is said in the Robes Section, “I allow, monks, a `kojava`” (Mv VIII.337), a natural `kojava` with a four-fingerbreadth fleece is allowable. A jewel-embroidered rug (`cittaka`) is not allowable. `Paṭalikā` is a thick covering dyed with a dense floral pattern. `Vikati` is a woolen covering variegated with figures of lions, tigers, etc. `Uddalomī` is one with a raised pattern on one side. `Ekantalomikā` is one with a raised pattern on both sides.

Kuttanti soḷasannaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ ṭhatvā naccanayoggaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Koseyyanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyasuttamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ. Kaṭṭissanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ. Koseyyañca kaṭṭissañca ratanaparisibbitāneva na vaṭṭanti, suddhāni vaṭṭanti. Hatthiassarathattharā tesaṃ upari attharaṇakaattharaṇāva. Ajinappaveṇīti ajinacammehi mañcappamāṇena sibbitvā katā paveṇī, tena ca kadalīmigacammaṃ setavatthassa upari pattharitvā sibbitvā kataṃ pavarappaccattharaṇaṃ kadalīmigappavarappaccattharaṇaṃ, tena ca atthataṃ ajinappaveṇīkadalīmigappavarappaccattharaṇatthataṃ.

`Kuttaka` is a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand and dance upon. `Koseyya` is a coverlet made of silk thread and interwoven with jewels. `Kaṭṭissa` is a coverlet made of silk `kaṭṭissa` cloth, interwoven with jewels. `Koseyya` and `kaṭṭissa` coverlets interwoven with jewels are not allowable; plain ones are allowable. Elephant, horse, and chariot coverings are spreads for placing on top of them. `Ajinappaveṇī` is a series of antelope hides sewn together to the size of a bed; and over that, a fine antelope hide sewn onto a white cloth spread, forming an excellent coverlet called `kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa`. Thus, it is spread with the `ajinappaveṇī` and the `kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa`.

Setavitānampi heṭṭhā akappiyappaccattharaṇe sati na vaṭṭati, kappiyappaccattharaṇe sati vaṭṭati, rattavitānassa heṭṭhā kappiyappaccattharaṇe satipi na vaṭṭati eva. Sīsūpadhānaṃ pādūpadhānanti mañcassa ubhatolohitakaṃ upadhānaṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana ekameva upadhānaṃ hoti, ubhosu antesu rattaṃ vā padumavaṇṇaṃ vā cittaṃ vā, sace pamāṇayuttaṃ, vaṭṭati, mahāupadhānaṃ pana paṭikkhittaṃ.

Under a white canopy, if there is an unsuitable spread beneath, it is not allowable; if there is a suitable spread beneath, it is allowable. Under a red canopy, even with a suitable spread beneath, it is still not allowable. Regarding a head-cushion and a foot-cushion: a cushion for a bed that is red at both ends is not allowable. But a single cushion that is red, lotus-colored, or patterned at both ends is allowable if it is of the proper size; a large cushion, however, is prohibited.

190. Āsandādittayāti [M 0.0150] āsandī tūlī pallaṅkoti idaṃ tayaṃ nāmaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā tīṇi āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ tūlikaṃ sesakaṃ gihivikaṭaṃ abhinisīdituṃ, na tveva abhinipajjitu”nti (cūḷava. 314) hi vuttaṃ. Sese gihisantake nisīdituṃ labbhatīti attho. Yadi dhammāsane saṅghikampi gonakādiṃ bhikkhūhi anāṇattā ārāmikādayo sayameva paññapenti ceva nīharanti ca, etaṃ gihivikaṭanīhāraṃ nāma, iminā gihivikaṭanīhārena vaṭṭati. Bhattaggaṃ nāma vihāre eva dānaṭṭhānaṃ.

190. `Āsandādittaya` means these three: a high seat (`āsandī`), a cushion (`tūlī`), and a couch (`pallaṅka`). For it has been said: “I allow, monks, except for these three—a high seat, a couch, and a cushion—to use the remaining household furnishings for sitting, but certainly not for lying down” (Cv VI.314). The meaning is that it is permissible to sit on the remaining items belonging to householders. If, on the Dhamma seat, monastery attendants and others, uninstructed by the monks, on their own accord arrange and remove even Saṅgha property such as woolen rugs, this is called ‘treating as household furnishings,’ and in this way it is allowable. `Bhattagga` means the place for giving food within the monastery.

191. Catunnaṃ pādānaṃ, tīsu passesu apassayānañca vasena sattaṅgo. Ekapassena yutto pañcaṅgo. Ime pana sattaṅgapañcaṅgā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uccakampi sattaṅga”nti (cūḷava. 294) vuttattā pamāṇātikkantāpi vaṭṭanti. Tena vuttaṃ “uccapādakā”ti. Tūlonaddhā mañcapīṭhā ghareyeva nisīdituṃ kappantīti sambandho.

191. A 'seven-limbed' item has four legs and three supports (a back-rest and two arm-rests). A 'five-limbed' item has one support (a back-rest). But these seven-limbed and five-limbed items, because it is said, “I allow, monks, even a high seven-limbed one” (Cv V.294), are allowable even if they exceed the standard size. Therefore they are called 'high-legged.' The connection is that beds and chairs stuffed with cotton are suitable for sitting on only inside a house.

192. Cīvaracchaviyoti [V 0.0141] channaṃ cīvarānaṃ, channaṃ anulomacīvarānañca aññataracīvaracchaviyoti attho. Sabbatthāti mañcepi pīṭhepi bhattaggepi antaragharepīti attho. Imāsaṃ pana bhisīnaṃ pamāṇaparicchedopi natthi, mañcapīṭhādīnaṃ vasena anurūpaṃ sallakkhetvā pamāṇaṃ kātabbaṃ.

192. `Cīvaracchavi` means having the color of one of the six robes or the six allowable robes. `Sabbattha` means: on a bed, on a chair, in the refectory, or inside a house. For these sitting-cloths, however, there is no fixed size limit; an appropriate size should be determined and made based on the bed, chair, and so on.

193. “Tūlikā uppannā hoti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vijaṭetvā bimbohanaṃ kātuṃ, tīṇi tūlāni rukkhatūlaṃ latātūlaṃ poṭakitūla”nti (cūḷava. 297) vuttattā tūlattayañca (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. tūlonandasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) bimbohane [M 0.0151] vaṭṭati. Imehi tīhi tūlehi sabbesaṃ rukkhalatātiṇānaṃ tūlaṃ anuññātanti veditabbaṃ. Bhisiyaṃ pana kiñci tūlaṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhisigabbhoti bhisiyā vuttaṃ coḷādipañcakaṃ bimbohane anuññātanti sambandho. Migapakkhinanti sīhādīnaṃ sabbacatuppadānaṃ haṃsamorādīnaṃ sabbapakkhīnaṃ lomāni kappanti. Masūrake anuññātanti sambandho.

193. Since it is said, “A mattress has come into being. I allow, monks, to card it and make a pillow; there are three kinds of kapok: tree-kapok, creeper-kapok, and grass-kapok” (Cv V.297), these three kinds of kapok are allowable for a pillow. By this it should be understood that kapok from all trees, creepers, and grasses is allowed. For a sitting-cloth (`bhisi`), however, no kapok at all is allowable. The connection is that the five kinds of filling beginning with cloth scraps, which are specified for a sitting-cloth, are also allowed for a pillow. `Migapakkhīnaṃ` means that the hair of all quadrupeds such as lions and the feathers of all birds such as geese and peacocks are suitable. The connection is that they are allowed for a `masūraka` pillow.

194. Idāni bhisiyaṃ kappiyākappiyaṃ dassetuṃ “manussaloma”ntiādimāha. Uṇṇāyanti (cūḷava. 297; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) uṇṇābhisiyaṃ manussalomaṃ na labbhatīti attho. Uṇṇābhisiyampi manussalomaṃ ṭhapetvā yesaṃ kesañci pakkhicatuppadānaṃ lomaṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. Paṇṇeti paṇṇabhisiyañca pupphañca suddhaṃ tamālapattañca na labbhaṃ, avasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci paṇṇaṃ labbhatīti attho. Tamālapattakampi aññehi missaṃ vaṭṭatīti. Coḷavākatiṇesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Āsanañceva appaṭivekkhitaṃ na labbhanti āsanasāmaññato pasaṅgena vuttaṃ. Akappiyasayanavinicchayo.

194. Now, to show what is suitable and unsuitable for a sitting-cloth, the text begins with “human hair.” `Uṇṇāya` means that for a woolen sitting-cloth, human hair is not to be used. The meaning is that for a woolen sitting-cloth, excepting human hair, the hair of any birds or quadrupeds is allowable. `Paṇṇe` means that for a leaf sitting-cloth, flowers and pure tamāla leaves are not to be used, but any other kind of leaf may be used. Even tamāla leaves are allowable when mixed with other things. Among cloth-scraps, bark-fibers, and grasses, there is nothing unsuitable. A seat that has not been inspected is not to be used; this is said in passing, as a general statement about seats. The Analysis of Unsuitable Couches.

Akappiyasayananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Unsuitable Couches is finished.

26. Samānāsanikaniddesavaṇṇanā

26. Commentary on the Exposition of Sharing the Same Seat

195. Tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ antaraṃ tivassantaraṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tivassantarena saha [V 0.0142] nisīditu”nti (cūḷava. 320) hi vuttaṃ. Yo dvīhi vassehi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) vuḍḍho vā navo vā, so tivassantaro nāma.

195. An interval of three years is a 'tivassantara'. For it is said: “Monks, I allow you to sit together with one who is within a three-year interval” (Cv VI.320). One who is two years senior or junior is called a 'tivassantara'.

196. Munīti buddhamuni. Sabbehevāti anupasampannehipi.

196. ‘The sage’ means the Buddha, the sage. ‘With all’ means even with those who are not ordained.

197. Antanti [M 0.0152] pacchimaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pahoti, ettakaṃ pacchimaṃ dīghāsana”nti (cūḷava. 320) vuttattā yaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pahoti, etaṃ saṃhārimaṃ vā hotu asaṃhārimaṃ vā, tathārūpesu phalakakhaṇḍesupi nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Dvinnanti dvinnaṃ samānāsanikānaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, duvaggassa mañcaṃ duvaggassa pīṭha”nti (cuḷava. 320) vuttattā dve samānāsanikā saha nisīdituṃ labhanti. Aññehi asamānāsanikehi, anupasampannādīhi vā dve hutvāpi nisīdituṃ na labhanti. Samānāsanikavinicchayo.

197. ‘The end’ means the maximum. Since it is said: “Monks, I allow a long seat that is sufficient for three; that is the maximum” (Cv VI.320), it is permissible to sit on what is sufficient for three, whether it is movable or immovable, even on such pieces of a plank. ‘For two’ means for two who share the same seat. Since it is said: “Monks, I allow a couch for two, a chair for two” (Cv VI.320), two who share the same seat are allowed to sit together. Others who do not share the same seat, or the unordained and so on, are not allowed to sit together even if they are two. The decision on sharing the same seat.

Samānāsanikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of sharing the same seat is concluded.

27. Asaṃvāsikaniddesavaṇṇanā

27. Commentary on the Exposition of One Unfit for Communion

198. Ukkhittoti āpattiyā adassane, appaṭikamme, pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge vā ukkhittakoti tividhopi idha ukkhitto gahito. Anupasampannoti iminā sikkhamānasāmaṇerasāmaṇerīsikkhāpaccakkhātakā gahitāti veditabbā. Chinnamūlako nāma antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannako. Nānāsaṃvāsoti laddhinānāsaṃvāsako. “Nānāsīmāya ṭhitacatuttho kammaṃ kareyya, iddhiyā vehāse ṭhitacatuttho kammaṃ kareyya, akammaṃ na ca karaṇīya”nti hi vuttattā imepi “asaṃvāsikā”ti vuttā. Etesu pana ukkhittakehi saddhiṃ uposathādīni karonto pācittiyaṃ āpajjati. Nissīmaṭṭhavehāsaṭṭhehi karontassa kammaṃ kuppati, dukkaṭañca hoti, itarehi dukkaṭaṃ. Asaṃvāsikavinicchayo.

198. ‘Suspended’ means one suspended for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for it, or for not relinquishing a bad view; here all three types of suspended persons are included. By ‘unordained’ it should be understood that probationers, male novices, female novices, and those who have given up the training are included. ‘One with roots cut off’ means one who has committed a terminal offense. ‘Of different communion’ means one of a different communion in doctrine. For since it is said: ‘If a fourth person standing in a different boundary should perform a formal act, or if a fourth person standing in the air by psychic power should perform a formal act, it is an invalid act and should not be done,’ therefore these too are called ‘unfit for communion.’ But among these, one who performs the Uposatha and other acts with suspended persons incurs a pācittiya offense. For one performing it with those standing outside the boundary or in the air, the formal act is invalid and there is an offense of wrong-doing. With the others, there is an offense of wrong-doing. The decision on those unfit for communion.

Asaṃvāsikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of those unfit for communion is concluded.

28. Kammaniddesavaṇṇanā

28. Commentary on the Exposition of Formal Acts

199. Adhammakammanti [M 0.0153][V 0.0143] ettha kathaṃ adhammakammaṃ hotīti ce? Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “katamañca, bhikkhave, adhammakammaṃ? Ñattidutiye ce, bhikkhave, kamme ekāya ñattiyā kammaṃ karoti, na ca kammavācaṃ anussāveti, adhammakammaṃ. Dvīhi ñattīhi kammaṃ karoti, na ca kammavācaṃ anussāveti, adhammakammaṃ. Ekāya kammavācāya kammaṃ karoti, na ca ñattiṃ ṭhapeti, adhammakammaṃ. Dvīhi kammavācāhi kammaṃ karoti, na ca ñattiṃ ṭhapeti, adhammakamma”nti (mahāva. 387). Iminā nayena sesakammesupi vuttappakārena akatvā aññathā karaṇaṃ adhammakammanti veditabbaṃ.

199. Herein, regarding 'an unlawful formal act,' if it is asked how it is an unlawful formal act, this has been said by the Blessed One: “And what, bhikkhus, is an unlawful formal act? Bhikkhus, if in a formal act done with a motion as the second step, one performs the act with one motion but does not have the proclamation recited, it is an unlawful formal act. If one performs the act with two motions but does not have the proclamation recited, it is an unlawful formal act. If one performs the act with one proclamation but does not propose a motion, it is an unlawful formal act. If one performs the act with two proclamations but does not propose a motion, it is an unlawful formal act” (Mahāvagga 387). By this method, it should be understood that in the remaining formal acts too, performing them otherwise than in the stated manner is an unlawful formal act.

Vaggenāti vaggena saṅghena. Kathañca vaggaṃ hotīti ce? Yāvatikā ca bhikkhū kammappattā, te anāgatā honti, chandārahānaṃ chando anāhaṭo hoti, sammukhībhūtā paṭikkosanti, vaggakammanti imesu yena kenaci ekenapi aṅgena vaggaṃ hoti.

‘By a faction’ means by a factional Sangha. And if it is asked how it becomes factional: when the bhikkhus who are qualified for the formal act have not come; when the consent of those who are entitled to give consent has not been brought; or when those who are present object—through any one of these factors, it becomes a factional formal act.

Samaggenāti samaggena saṅghena. Kathaṃ samaggaṃ hotīti ce? Yāvatikā ca bhikkhū kammappattā, te āgatā honti, chandārahānaṃ chando āhaṭo hoti, sammukhībhūtā nappaṭikkosanti, samaggakammanti evaṃ.

‘By a united Sangha’ means by a united Sangha. And if it is asked how it is united: when the bhikkhus who are qualified for the formal act have come; when the consent of those who are entitled to give consent has been brought; and when those who are present do not object—thus it is a united formal act.

Catutthanti samaggena dhammikaṃ. Ettāvatā “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kammāni, adhammena vaggakammaṃ, adhammena samaggakammaṃ, dhammena vaggakammaṃ, dhammena samaggakamma”nti (mahāva. 384) evaṃ vuttāni cattāri kammāni pariggahitāni hontīti veditabbāni.

‘The fourth’ is a lawful act by a united Sangha. By this much it should be understood that the four formal acts spoken of thus—“Bhikkhus, there are these four formal acts: a formal act that is unlawful and factional, a formal act that is unlawful and united, a formal act that is lawful and factional, and a formal act that is lawful and united” (Mahāvagga 384)—are included.

200-202. Dasavaggiko (mahāva. 388; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) vīsativaggiko ca dasavīsativaggiko. Abbhānopasampadāppavāraṇā ṭhapetvā sabbakammesu kammappattoti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Itaroti vīsativaggo ca atirekavīsativaggo ca.

200-202. A group of ten (Mahāvagga 388; Kaṅkhāvitaranī-aṭṭhakathā, Nidānavaṇṇanā), a group of twenty, and what pertains to groups of ten and twenty. The connection is: qualified for the formal act in all formal acts except for rehabilitation, higher ordination, and the invitation ceremony. So too in the remaining cases. ‘The other’ means a group of twenty and a group of more than twenty.

203. Idāni [M 0.0154] kammappatte ca chandārahe ca dassetuṃ “catuvaggenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha (pari. 488, 497; pari. 487-488) pakatattā nāma ye pārājikaukkhittaladdhinānāsaṃvāsakā [V 0.0144] na honti. Pareti ekasīmaṭṭhā pakatattā bhikkhū. Yadi pakatattā bhikkhūpi aññataraṃ gāmasīmaṃ vā nadīsamuddajātassarakhaṇḍasīmāsu vā aññataraṃ pavisitvā ṭhitā honti, neva kammappattā, na chandārahā. Na hi tesaṃ chando vā pārisuddhi vā āgacchati aññasīmāyaṃ ṭhitattā. Sesepīti pañcavaggādikaraṇīyepīti attho.

203. Now, to show those qualified for the formal act and those entitled to give consent, ‘by a group of four,’ etc., is said. Therein (Pari. 488, 497; Pari. 487-488), ‘regular bhikkhus’ are those who are not subject to a pārājika offense, suspended, or of a different communion in doctrine. ‘Others’ means regular bhikkhus standing within the same boundary. If even regular bhikkhus enter and stand in another village boundary or in one of the boundaries of a river, sea, natural lake, or a partial boundary, they are neither qualified for the formal act nor entitled to give consent. For because they are standing in another boundary, their consent or their purity does not arrive. ‘In the remaining cases’ means in those acts to be done by a group of five, etc.

204. Asaṃvāsagaṇapūraṃ vā katvā kataṃ kammaṃ kuppañca hoti, kārakānañca dukkaṭanti attho. “Yassa saṅgho kammaṃ karoti, taṃcatuttho kammaṃ kareyya, akammaṃ na ca karaṇīya”nti (mahāva. 389) vuttattā “kammārahagaṇapūraṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni parivāsādikammānaṃyeva parisato vipattiṃ dassetuṃ “garukaṭṭhagaṇapūraṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi anikkhittavattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nikkhittavatto pana sabbattha gaṇapūrako hoti eva.
