204. The meaning is: a formal act done by completing the quorum with one unfit for communion is invalid, and for the doers there is an offense of wrong-doing. Since it is said: “The Sangha performs a formal act for someone; he being the fourth, it should perform the formal act. It is an invalid act and should not be done” (Mahāvagga 389), the phrase ‘or completing the quorum with the subject of the act’ is stated. Now, to show the defect of the assembly precisely for formal acts such as probation, ‘or completing the quorum with one subject to a grave offense’ is said. That too is said in reference to one who has not laid down his observance. But one who has laid down his observance is always a quorum-filler everywhere.

205. Vāreyyāti paṭikkhipeyya. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, adhammakamme kayiramāne paṭikkositu”nti (mahāva. 154) hi vuttaṃ. Antarāye satīti attho. “Adhammakammaṃ idaṃ, na metaṃ khamatī”ti evaṃ dve tayo aññamaññaṃ diṭṭhiṃ āvi kareyyunti attho. Yadi eko hoti, “na metaṃ khamatī”ti evaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ kareyyāti attho. Ettāvatā ete nirāpattikā honti, antarāyā ca muccanti, kammaṃ pana adhammattā kuppameva. Vārenteva tatodhikāti ettha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catūhi pañcahi paṭikkosituṃ, dvīhi tīhi diṭṭhiṃ āvi kātuṃ, ekena adhiṭṭhātuṃ, “na metaṃ khamatī”ti (mahāva. 154) vuttattā cattāro vā pañca vā vārenti evāti attho.

205. ‘Should prevent’ means should reject. For it is said: “I allow, bhikkhus, to object when an unlawful formal act is being performed” (Mahāvagga 154). The meaning is: when there is an obstacle. The meaning is: two or three should thus make their view known to each other: “This is an unlawful formal act; this is not agreeable to me.” The meaning is: if there is one, he should make a determination thus: “This is not agreeable to me.” By this much they are without offense and are freed from the obstacle, but the formal act, being unlawful, is indeed invalid. Herein, regarding ‘those who prevent are more than that,’ the meaning is: since it is said, “I allow, bhikkhus, four or five to object, two or three to make their view known, and for one to make a determination, ‘This is not agreeable to me’” (Mahāvagga 154), four or five indeed prevent.

206. Idāni [M 0.0155] yehi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti, te dassetuṃ “kammārahā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khittacitta-ggahaṇena ummattakopi gahitova. Etesanti ye vuttappakārā, tesaṃ paṭikkhepo na ruhatīti attho.

206. Now, to show those by whom it is rejected, ‘qualified for the formal act,’ etc., is said. Therein, by the inclusion of ‘one whose mind is deranged,’ one who is insane is also included. ‘Of these’ means the meaning is that the rejection by those of the type mentioned does not hold.

207. Idāni yassa paṭikkhepo ruhati, taṃ dassetuṃ “pakatattekasīmaṭṭha-samasaṃvāsabhikkhuno”ti vuttaṃ. Tassattho (mahāva. 394) – evarūpassa bhikkhuno paṭikkosanā antamaso ānantarassāpi ārocentassa ruhatīti. “Bhikkhussa, bhikkhave[V 0.0145], pakatattassa samānasaṃvāsikassa samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitassa antamaso ānantarikassapi bhikkhuno viññāpentassa saṅghamajjhe paṭikkosanā ruhatī”ti (mahāva. 394) vuttaṃ.

207. Now, to show one whose rejection holds, it is said: ‘of a bhikkhu who is regular, standing in the same boundary, and of the same communion.’ Its meaning is (Mahāvagga 394): the objection of such a bhikkhu holds even if he informs the one immediately next to him. It is said: “Bhikkhus, the objection of a bhikkhu who is regular, of the same communion, and standing in the same boundary holds even if he makes it known in the midst of the Sangha to the bhikkhu immediately next to him” (Mahāvagga 394).

208. Sammukhā yadi paṭikkoseyyāti attho. Tirokkhāti parammukhā. Kāyasāmaggiṃ vā chandaṃ vā no dadeyya, dukkaṭanti attho. Kammavinicchayo.

208. The meaning is: if he should object in person. ‘Behind the screen’ means out of sight. The meaning is: if he does not give his bodily presence or his consent, there is an offense of wrong-doing. The decision on formal acts.

Kammaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of formal acts is concluded.

29. Micchājīvavivajjanāniddesavaṇṇanā

29. Commentary on the Exposition of Avoiding Wrong Livelihood

209. Cuṇṇanti sirīsacuṇṇādikanti attho. Mattikāti pakatimattikā vā pañcavaṇṇā vā suddhā kuṅkuṭṭhaādikā vā. Kulasaṅgahāti etehi saṅgahitānaṃ santike lābhāsāya kulasaṅgahatthanti attho. Ettha pana imehi saṅgahitānaṃ santike “kiñci labhissāmī”ti saṅghikaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā dātuṃ na vaṭṭati eva. Iminā pana nayena laddhaṃ pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na vaṭṭati, micchājīvañca hoti.

209. ‘Powder’ means powder, such as acacia powder, etc. ‘Clay’ means natural clay, or five-colored clay, or pure red arsenic, etc. ‘Gathering families’ means for the purpose of gaining offerings from those gathered by these means, that is, for the purpose of gathering families. But here, it is not proper to give to those in whose vicinity one has gathered, thinking, “I will receive something,” whether it is something belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual. Moreover, what is obtained by this method is not proper for the five kinds of co-religionists, and it constitutes wrong livelihood.

210-211. Lābhāsāya [M 0.0156] dāyakānaṃ dārake ukkhipitvā paribhaṭabhāvo pāribhaṭakatā, tāya pāribhaṭakatāya na jīvayeti sambandho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Khettādīsu pesitassa gamanaṃ paheṇakammaṃ. Sāsanappaṭisāsanaharaṇaṃ dūtakammaṃ. Pesitassa gehato gehagamanaṃ jaṅghapesaniyaṃ. Lābhāsāya lañjadānamanuppadānaṃ. Aññena vāpīti aṅgavijjādinā.

210-211. Raising donors’ children for the sake of gain is servile conduct (pāribhaṭakatā); the connection is that one should not make a living through such servile conduct. The same method applies to the rest. Sending someone to fields and so forth is the act of sending (paheṇakamma). Delivering messages or counter-messages is the act of a messenger (dūtakamma). Going from house to house when sent is leg-work (jaṅghapesaniya). Giving a bribe for the sake of gain is giving in pursuit (anuppadāna). ‘Or by other means’ refers to divination and so forth.

212. Viññattīti (pārā. 515 ādayo; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.515 ādayo) aññātakaviññatti. Anesanāti pubbe vuttena pupphadānādinā paccayesanā. Kuhanādīhīti (vibha. 861; vibha. aṭṭha. 861; mahāni. 87) kuhanā lapanā nemittakatā nippesikatā [V 0.0146] lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāti imehi pañcahi vatthūhīti attho. Micchājīvavinicchayo.

212. ‘Viññatti’ (Pārā. 515 ff.; Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.515 ff.) means a request made to the unacquainted. ‘Anesanā’ means seeking requisites by means of giving flowers and so forth, as previously mentioned. ‘By deceit, etc.’ (Vibha. 861; Vibha. Aṭṭha. 861; Mahāni. 87) means by these five things: deceit (kuhanā), boasting (lapanā), hinting (nemittakatā), disparaging (nippesikatā), and seeking gain with gain (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā). The determination of wrong livelihood.

Micchājīvavivajjanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on avoiding wrong livelihood is concluded.

30. Vattaniddesavaṇṇanā

30. Explanation of the Exposition on Duties

213. Idāni āgantukavattādīni dassetuṃ “vatta”nti mātikāpadaṃ uddhaṭaṃ. Parikkhittassa (cūḷava. 356 ādayo; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 357 ādayo) vihārassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa dvīhi leḍḍupātehi paricchinnaṭṭhānaṃ patvā upāhanaṃ omuñcitvā nīcaṃ katvā papphoṭetvā upāhanaṃ daṇḍakena gahetvā chattaṃ apanāmetvā sīsaṃ vivaritvā sīse cīvaraṃ khandhe karitvā sādhukaṃ ataramānena ārāmo pavisitabboti attho.

213. Now, to explain the duties for incoming monks and others, the heading ‘vatta’ is introduced. For an enclosed monastery (Cūḷavagga 356 ff.; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 357 ff.), one should reach the monastery enclosure. For an unenclosed monastery, one should reach the area defined by two clod throws, remove one’s sandals, hold them low, tap them together, pick up the sandals with a stick, put away the umbrella, uncover the head, place the robe on one's shoulder, and enter the monastery carefully without hurrying—this is the meaning.

214. Puccheyya [M 0.0157] sayanāsananti “katamaṃ me senāsanaṃ pāpuṇāti, kiṃ ajjhāvutthaṃ vā anajjhāvutthaṃ vā”ti evaṃ pucchitabbanti attho.

214. ‘One should ask about lodging’ means one should inquire thus: “Which lodging is available to me? Is it occupied or unoccupied?” This is the meaning.

215-6. Mañcapīṭhādidārubhaṇḍañca (cūḷava. 360; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 360) rajanabhājanādimattikābhaṇḍañca. Āpucchāti bhikkhussa vā sāmaṇerassa vā ārāmikassa vā “āvuso imaṃ jaggāhī”ti ārocetvāti attho. Aññathāti evaṃ akatvāti attho.

215-216. Wooden goods such as beds and stools (Cūḷavagga 360; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 360) and earthenware such as dye pots and other vessels. ‘Āpucchā’ means informing a monk, novice, or monastery attendant, saying, “Friend, please look after this”—this is the meaning. ‘Otherwise’ means not doing so—this is the meaning.

217-8. Vuḍḍhāgantukassāti ettha (cūḷava. 358 ādayo; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 359 ādayo) dūratova disvā yadi “vuḍḍho”ti jānāti, tasmiṃ anāgate eva āsanapaññāpanādivattaṃ kātabbanti attho. Pādodappabhutinti pādodakaṃ pādapīṭhaṃ pādakathalikaṃ upanikkhipitabbanti attho. Pānīyena āpucchantena sace sakiṃ ānītaṃ pānīyaṃ sabbaṃ pivati, punapi āpucchitabbo eva. Paññapeti “etaṃ tumhākaṃ senāsanaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti evaṃ ācikkhitabbanti attho.

217-218. Regarding ‘for an elderly incoming monk’ (Cūḷavagga 358 ff.; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 359 ff.), if one recognizes from afar that he is elderly, duties such as preparing a seat should be done even before he arrives—this is the meaning. ‘Beginning with foot water’ means providing foot water, a footstool, and a foot-scraper—this is the meaning. When inquiring with drinking water, if all the water brought at once is drunk, one should ask again. ‘Assigns’ means explaining, “This lodging is available to you”—this is the meaning.

219-20. “Bhikkhācāragāmo [V 0.0147] ito dūre”ti vā “santike”ti vā “kālasseva piṇḍāya caritabba”nti vā “upaṭṭhāke caritabba”nti vā gocaro ācikkhitabbo. Agocaroti micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ vā gāmo, paricchinnabhikkhako vā gāmo, yattha ekassa vā dvinnaṃ vā bhikkhā dīyati, so ācikkhitabboti attho. Katikanti saṅghassa katikaṭṭhānaṃ. “Imaṃ kālaṃ pavisitabbaṃ, imaṃ kālaṃ nikkhamitabba”nti evaṃ pavesananikkhamanakālaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Kesuci ṭhānesu amanussā vā vāḷā vā honti, tasmā evaṃ ācikkhitabbameva. Nisinnovāti idaṃ āpattiabhāvamattadīpakaṃ, uṭṭhahitvāpi sabbaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭateva. Vattavinicchayo.

219-220. The alms-resort should be indicated, saying, “The alms-round village is far from here,” or “is near,” or “one should go for alms early,” or “one should go to the supporters.” ‘Out of bounds’ refers to a village of those with wrong views or a village with limited alms-food where alms are given to only one or two monks; this is what should be indicated. ‘Agreement’ refers to the Saṅgha’s place of agreement. The times for entering and leaving should be indicated, saying, “One should enter at this time and leave at this time.” In some places, there may be non-humans or wild animals; therefore, this should be indicated. ‘Even sitting down’ here merely indicates the absence of an offense; even having stood up, it is still proper to do everything. The determination of duties.

Vattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on duties is concluded.

31. Vikappanāniddesavaṇṇanā

31. Explanation of the Exposition on Assignment

221. Sammukhāyāti [M 0.0158] (pāci. 374; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. vikappanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) sammukhe ṭhitassāti attho. Byattassāti vikappanavidhānaṃ paccuddharaṇādividhānañca jānantassa. Abyatto pana “iminā mayhaṃ dinna”nti gahetvāpi gaccheyyāti attho. Ekassāti ekassa bhikkhussa.

221. ‘Sammukhāyā’ (Pāc. 374; Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.469; Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Vikappanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) means ‘of one standing face-to-face’. ‘Byattassa’ refers to one who knows the procedure of assignment and the procedure for retracting it, and so forth. An incompetent one, however, might take it thinking, ‘This was given to me,’ and go away—this is the meaning. ‘Ekassa’ means of one monk.

222. Nidhetuṃvāti nidhetuṃ eva, nissaggiyaṃ na hotīti attho. Paribhuñjituṃ vā vissajjetuṃ vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vā na vaṭṭatīti attho.

222. ‘Nidhetuṃvā’ means simply to store it away; it does not become subject to forfeiture—this is the meaning. It is not allowable to use, relinquish, or resolve upon it—this is the meaning.

224-5. Aparā sammukhā vāti sammukhā vikappanā evāti attho. Imā dve vikappanā attanā eva vikappetvā parena paccuddharāpitattā sammukhā vikappanā evāti vuttā.

224-225. ‘Aparā sammukhā vā’ means it is indeed a face-to-face assignment. These two assignments are called face-to-face assignments because they are assigned by oneself and then retracted by another.

227. Mittoti daḷhamitto. Sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamatto nātidaḷhamitto. “Itarena ca pubbe vuttanayena ‘tisso bhikkhū’ti vā ‘tissā bhikkhunī’ti vā vattabbaṃ. Puna tena ‘ahaṃ tissassa [V 0.0148] bhikkhuno, tissāya bhikkhuniyā vā dammī’ti vikappetvā teneva ‘tissassa bhikkhuno, tissāya bhikkhuniyā santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī’ti paccuddharitabba”nti evaṃ pāṭho gahetabbo.

227. ‘Mitto’ means a firm friend. ‘Sandiṭṭho’ means merely an acquaintance, not a very firm friend. ‘Alternatively, in accordance with the method previously stated, one should say “three monks” or “three nuns.” Then, having assigned it by saying, “I give this to the monk Tissa or the nun Tissā,” it should be taken back by saying, “Use, give away, or manage as is suitable whatever belongs to the monk Tissa or the nun Tissā.”’ This is how the passage should be understood.

228. Dūrasantikattekatta-bahubhāvaṃ vijāniyāti ettha dūrattañca santikattañca ekattañca bahubhāvañca vijānitvāti attho.

228. ‘Dūrasantikattekatta-bahubhāvaṃ vijāniyā’ here means that one should discern distance and proximity, singularity and multiplicity.

229. “Dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti (pārā. 462) vuttattā “dasāhaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. “Cīvarakālasamayo nāma anatthate kathine vassānassa pacchimo māso, atthate kathine [M 0.0159] pañca māsā”ti (pārā. 649) vuttattā “māsamekaṃ vā pañca vā”ti vuttaṃ, māsaṃ vā ekaṃ pañca vā māseti attho. “Bhikkhuno paneva akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya, ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Paṭiggahetvā khippameva kāretabbaṃ. No cassa pāripūri, māsaparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā taṃ cīvaraṃ nikkhipitabbaṃ ūnassa pāripūriyā satiyā paccāsāyā”ti (pārā. 499) vuttattā “paccāsā sati māsaka”nti vuttaṃ. Nuppādayatīti anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ nissaggiṃ na janayatīti attho. Vikappanāvinicchayo.

229. Because it is stated, ‘An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days’ (Pārā. 462), ‘or for ten days’ is said. Because it is stated, ‘The robe season is the last month of the rains if the Kathina has not been spread, or five months if the Kathina has been spread’ (Pārā. 649), ‘one month or five’ is said, meaning one month or five months. Because it is stated, ‘If, moreover, a monk should obtain out-of-season robe-cloth, he may accept it if he wishes. Having accepted it, he should quickly have it made. If it is not complete, that monk may keep that robe-cloth for a maximum of one month, if there is hope for the completion of what is lacking’ (Pārā. 499), ‘if there is hope, for a month’ is said. ‘Nuppādayatī’ means that being undetermined and unassigned, it does not give rise to an item to be forfeited—this is the meaning. The determination of assignment.

Vikappanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on assignment is concluded.

32. Nissayaniddesavaṇṇanā

32. The Commentary on the Exposition of Dependence

230. Byattassāti ettha kittāvatā byatto hotīti ce? Nissayamuccanakena pana sabbantimena dhammaparicchedena atthato ca byañjanato ca dve mātikā paguṇā vācuggatā kātabbā, pakkhadivasesu dhammassāvanatthāya suttantato cattāro bhāṇavārā, sampattānaṃ parisānaṃ parikathanatthāya andhakavindamahārāhulovādadhammakkhandhasadiso eko kathāmaggo, saṅghabhattamaṅgalāmaṅgalesu anumodanatthāya tisso anumodanā, uposathappavāraṇādivijānanatthaṃ kammākammavinicchayo[V 0.0149], samaṇadhammakaraṇatthaṃ samādhivasena vā vipassanāvasena vā arahattapariyosānaṃ ekaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ettakaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Ettāvatā byatto nāma hoti cātudiso, itarathā abyatto.

230. Herein, regarding 'of a competent one' (byattassāti): if it is asked to what extent one is competent, then by means of the final section of the teaching on release from dependence, two matrices (mātikā), proficient in both meaning and phrasing, must be mastered orally; for hearing the Dhamma on observance days, four recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) from the Suttas; for addressing assembled gatherings, one line of discourse similar to the Andhakavinda Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, or a section of the Dhammakkhandha; for giving thanks at Sangha meals and on auspicious and inauspicious occasions, three thanksgiving discourses (anumodanā); for understanding the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so on, the determination of what is and is not a valid formal act (kammākammavinicchayo); for fulfilling the duties of a recluse, one meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) culminating in arahantship, either by way of concentration (samādhi) or by way of insight (vipassanā)—this much must be learned. To this extent one is called competent (byatto) and versatile (cātudiso); otherwise, one is incompetent (abyatto).

231. Idāni nissayaggahaṇākāraṃ dassetuṃ “ekaṃsa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha (mahāva. 103) āyasmatoti āyasmantaṃ.

231. Now, to show the way of taking dependence, the passage beginning 'arranging the upper robe over one shoulder' (ekaṃsaṃ) is stated. Here, āyasmatoti is a contraction for āyasmantaṃ (to the venerable one).

232. Idāni [M 0.0160] paṭippassaddhividhānaṃ dassetuṃ “pakkante”tiādi vuttaṃ, “pañcimā, bhikkhave, nissayappaṭippassaddhiyo upajjhāyamhā. Upajjhāyo pakkanto vā hoti vibbhanto vā kālakato vā pakkhasaṅkanto vā āṇattiyeva pañcamī”ti (mahāva. 83), “chayimā, bhikkhave, nissayappaṭippassaddhiyo ācariyamhā. Ācariyo pakkanto vā hoti vibbhanto vā kālakato vā pakkhasaṅkanto vā āṇattiyeva pañcamī, upajjhāyena vā samodhānagato hotī”ti idaṃ pana ubhayaṃ idha dassitaṃ. Sace ācariyupajjhāyā sāmantavihāresupi aparikkhittesu leḍḍupātadvayabbhantare vasanti, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Parikkhittesupi na paṭippassambhatīti eke. Ācariyā pana na icchanti. Kasmāti ce? Nissayaggahaṇappaṭippassaddhīnaṃ upacārasīmāya paricchinnattā. Leḍḍupātena upacārasīmāparicchedo pana aparikkhittesu eva labbhati, na parikkhittesu. Tasmā ācariyānaṃ vinicchayeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

232. Now, to explain the methods for relinquishing dependence, the passage beginning 'when departed' (`pakkante`) is stated: 'Bhikkhus, there are five ways of relinquishing dependence on a preceptor: the preceptor has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has changed his affiliation; the fifth is by formal declaration.' And: 'Bhikkhus, there are six ways of relinquishing dependence on a teacher: the teacher has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has changed his affiliation; the fifth is by formal declaration; or, sixth, the student has been reunited with his preceptor.' Both of these are shown here. If the teacher and preceptor reside in a neighboring monastery that is not enclosed, within the range of two clod-throws, dependence is not relinquished. Some say it is not relinquished even in an enclosed area, but the teachers do not accept this. Why? Because the taking and relinquishing of dependence are delimited by the boundary of proximity. The delimitation of the boundary of proximity by a clod-throw applies only to unenclosed areas, not to enclosed ones. Therefore, one should abide by the decision of the teachers.

Pakkanteti ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 83) sace ācariyo antevāsikaṃ anāmantetvāva upacārasīmaṃ atikkamati, nissayo paṭippassambhati. Sace upacārasīmaṃ anatikkamitvāva nivattati, na paṭippassambhati. Ācariyaṃ anāmantetvā antevāsikassa gamanepi eseva nayo. Sace ācariyo katthaci gantukāmo antevāsikaṃ āpucchati, antevāsikopi “sādhu sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, taṅkhaṇe eva paṭippassambhati. Evaṃ ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā antevāsikassa gamanepi. Dvīsupi antovihāreyeva ṭhitesu ācariyo vā antevāsikaṃ, antevāsiko vā ācariyaṃ anāpucchitvāva sace dve leḍḍupāte atikkamati, paṭippassambhati. Pakkhasaṅkante vā vibbhante vā kālakate vā taṅkhaṇeyeva paṭippassambhati[M 0.0161]. Āṇatti nāma nissayappaṇāmanā. Dassanasavanavasena duvidhaṃ samodhānaṃ.

Here, regarding 'departed' (`pakkante`): if the teacher crosses the boundary of proximity without taking leave of the pupil, the dependence is dissolved. If he turns back without crossing the boundary of proximity, it is not dissolved. The same rule applies if the pupil departs without taking leave of the teacher. If the teacher, wishing to go somewhere, takes leave of the pupil, and the pupil responds, 'Good, good,' then at that very moment, the dependence is dissolved. The same applies when the pupil takes leave of the teacher and departs. If, while both are staying within the monastery, either the teacher or the pupil goes beyond the distance of two clod-throws without taking leave of the other, the dependence is dissolved. If one defects to another sect, disrobes, or dies, the dependence is dissolved at that very moment. `Āṇatti` is the formal renunciation of dependence. The reuniting (`samodhāna`) is twofold: by way of seeing and by way of hearing.

233. Alajjinti [V 0.0150] ettha –

233. Herein, regarding 'a shameless one' (`alajjī`):

“Sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjati;

Āpattiṃ parigūhati;

Agatigamanañca gacchati;

Ediso vuccati alajjipuggalo”ti. (pari. 359) –

“He deliberately commits an offense; he conceals an offense; and he follows a wrong course of action. Such a one is called a shameless person.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ. “Na bhikkhave alajjinaṃ nissāya vatthabbaṃ. Yo vaseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 120) hi vuttaṃ.

Thus it is said. For it has been stated: “Bhikkhus, one should not live in dependence on a shameless person. Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.”

234. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, addhānamaggappaṭipannena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vatthu”nti (mahāva. 121) vuttattā “addhikassā”ti vuttaṃ. Gilānupaṭṭhākassa ca yācitassāti sambandho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānupaṭṭhākena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena yāciyamānena anissitena vatthu”nti (mahāva. 121) hi vuttaṃ. Sallakkhentena phāsukanti phāsuvihāraṃ sallakkhentena. Idaṃ pana parihāraṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 121) sotāpannādiariyasāvako vā thāmagatasamathavipassanālābhī vā bālaputhujjano vā na labhati. Yassa kho pana samathavipassanā taruṇā hoti, na thāmagatā, ayaṃ labhati. Asante nissayadāyake “yadā paṭirūpo nissayadāyako āgacchissati, tadā tassa nissāya vasissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā yāva āsāḷhīpuṇṇamā, tāva vasituṃ labhati. Sace pana āsāḷhīmāse nissayadāyakaṃ na labhati, yattha atthi, tattha gantabbaṃ. Antovasse pana anissitena vatthuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sabhāge [M 0.0162] dāyake asante vasituṃ labbhatīti sabbapadesu yojanā kātabbā. Nissayavinicchayo.

234. Because it is said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a bhikkhu traveling on a long journey who cannot find a preceptor for dependence to dwell without dependence,” the words “for a traveler” are stated. And the connection is made to “a caregiver of the sick, when he is requested.” For it is said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a bhikkhu who is a caregiver of the sick and cannot find a preceptor for dependence, when requested, to dwell without dependence.” “One who considers what is suitable” (`sallakkhentena phāsukaṃ`) means one who considers a suitable dwelling. However, this exemption is not obtained by a noble disciple such as a stream-enterer, nor by one who has attained strong serenity and insight, nor by an ordinary fool. But one whose serenity and insight are still young, not yet strong, obtains it. If there is no one to give dependence, one may dwell until the full moon of Āsāḷha after making this reflection: “When a suitable preceptor for dependence arrives, I will live in dependence on him.” But if one does not find a preceptor for dependence by the month of Āsāḷha, one must go where one is available. However, it is not proper to dwell without dependence during the rains-residence. The principle that one is allowed to dwell without a dependence-giver if a suitable one is not available should be applied in all these cases. The Determination of Dependence.

Nissayaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Dependence is finished.

33. Kāyabandhananiddesavaṇṇanā

33. Commentary on the Exposition of the Waistband

235. Akāyabandhanoti [V 0.0151] kāyabandhanaṃ abandhitvāti attho. Tato paṭṭhāya cīvaraṃ pārupitabbaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya eva kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitabbaṃ. “Na bhikkhave akāyabandhanena gāmo pavisitabbo. Yo paviseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 278) hi vuttaṃ. Tatthevāsatiyā gatoti asatiyā gato yattha sarati, tattheva bandhitabbaṃ. Saritvā pana yāva na bandhati, tāva piṇḍāya carituṃ na vaṭṭati. Yadi antogāme sarati, kāyabandhane sati ekamante ṭhatvā bandhitabbaṃ, asati ce nikkhamitvā bandhitvā puna piṇḍāya pavisitabbanti vadanti.

235. “Not having a waistband” means not having fastened the waistband. From then on, the robe should be put on, and from then on the waistband should be fastened. For it was said: “Bhikkhus, one should not enter a village without a waistband. Whoever should enter commits an offense of wrong-doing.” “There, having gone unmindfully” means: having gone unmindfully, wherever one remembers, it should be fastened right there. But having remembered, so long as one does not fasten it, it is not proper to go for alms. If one remembers inside the village, if a waistband is available, one should stand to one side and fasten it; if not, they say, one should go out, fasten it, and then enter again for alms.

236. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve kāyabandhanāni paṭṭikaṃ sūkarantaka”nti (cūḷava. 278) vuttattā “duvidha”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha sūkarantaṃ nāma kuñcikākosakā viya ante susiraṃ katvā koṭṭitaṃ. Rajju ca ekāti ekavaṭṭā rajju ca. Tadanulomikāti tesaṃ dvinnaṃ anulomikā.

236. “I allow, bhikkhus, two kinds of waistbands: a flat one and one with pig’s-intestine ends.” Because this was said, the word ‘twofold’ is stated. Here, the ‘pig’s-intestine’ one is made hollow at the end like a key-sheath and is studded. And ‘a single rope’ means a single-stranded rope. “Suitable for them” means suitable for those two.

237. Macchakaṇḍakakhajjurī-pattā maṭṭhā ca paṭṭikāti ettha (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 278) ete macchakaṇṭakādayo maṭṭhā vikārarahitā paṭṭikā ca tadantogadhāti adhippāyo. Labbhā dasā catassoti ekāya vā dvīsu vā tīsu vā kathā eva natthīti adhippāyo, tato paraṃ na vaṭṭati. Antesūti ubhosu antesu. Guṇasuttakanti diguṇasuttakaṃ.

237. “A fish-bone one, a date-palm leaf one, a smoothed one, and a flat band”: here, the meaning is that these—the fish-bone one and so on, the smoothed one without embellishment, and the flat band—are included therein. “Four fringes are allowable”: the meaning is that there is no question about one, two, or three; beyond that is not proper. “At the ends” means at both ends. “A thread of strands” means a twofold thread.

239. Makaramukhādinti [M 0.0163] ādi-saddena deḍḍubhasīsaṃ gahitaṃ. Ubhanteti ubhosu antesu. Kassāti? Vidhassa. Ghaṭakāti ghaṭakato. Lekhāti lekhāya. Ghaṭakato ca lekhāya ca aññaṃ cittakaṃ na kappatīti attho.

239. “With makara-faces, etc.”: by the word “etc.” the head of a water-snake is included. “At both ends” means at the two ends. “Of what?” Of the type. “A small pot” means from a small pot design. “A line” means by a line. The meaning is that no other decoration is allowable apart from that of a small pot and a line.

240. Deḍḍubhakanti (cūḷava. 278; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 278) udakasappasirasadisaṃ. Murajanti bahurajjuke ekato saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekāya rajjuyā paliveṭhetvā katarajju. Maddavīṇanti pāmaṅgasadisaṃ. Kalābukanti anekavaṭṭaṃ. Etāni pana sabbāni na kappanti. Dasāsu dve majjhimāti murajaṃ maddavīṇanti dve majjhimā eva. Kappareti kappantīti attho.

240. “A water-snake head” is like the head of a water snake. “A tabor” is a cord made by drawing many strings together and wrapping them with a single string. “A soft lute” is like a girdle. “A bundle” means with many strands. But all these are not allowable. “The two middle ones among the fringes”: the tabor and the soft lute are the two middle ones. “Are allowable” has the meaning “they are allowable.”

241. Gaṇṭhiyo [V 0.0152] cāpīti (cūḷava. 279) cīvaragaṇṭhiyopi. Veḷuādimayā kappantīti pasaṅgena vuttaṃ. Kāyabandhanavinicchayo.

241. “And knots too” refers also to the knots of the robe. “Made of bamboo, etc., are allowable” is said in this connection. The determination concerning the waistband.

Kāyabandhananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Waistband is finished.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāraṃ.

The First Recitation Section.

34. Pathavīniddesavaṇṇanā

34. Commentary on the Exposition of Earth

242. Jātā (pāci. 86; pāci. aṭṭha. 86-88; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ajātāti duvidhā pathavīti attho. Idāni tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “suddhamattikapaṃsukā”tiādimāha. Tattha suddhamattikapaṃsukā ca adaḍḍhā ca bahumattikapaṃsukā ca cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhapaṃsumattikarāsi ca jātapathavīti sambandho. Ettha pana adaḍḍhāti uddhanapacanakumbhakārāvāpabhājanapacanādivasena tathā tathā adaḍḍhā. Ayaṃ pana visuṃ natthi, suddhapaṃsuādīsu aññatarāva veditabbā. Suddhapaṃsu suddhamattikā [M 0.0164] yebhuyyenapaṃsu yebhuyyenamattikā atirekacātumāsādhikovaṭṭhamattikāpaṃsupuñjā ca adaḍḍhā cāti ayaṃ sabbāpi jātapathavīti veditabbā.

242. “Produced” (Pc 10) and “unproduced”: the meaning is that earth is twofold. Now, to show both of these, it says, “pure clay and dust,” etc. Here, the connection is: pure clay and dust, unfired, abundant clay and dust, and a heap of dust and clay that has stood for more than four months is “produced earth.” Here, “unfired” means not fired in such ways as in an oven, a kiln, a potter’s furnace, or for baking vessels. This, however, is not something separate but should be understood as one of pure dust and so on. Pure dust, pure clay, what is mostly dust, what is mostly clay, a pile of clay and dust that has stood for more than four months, and what is unfired—all this should be understood as “produced earth.”

243. Dutiyāti ajātapathavīti attho. Vuttarāsīti mattikarāsi ca paṃsurāsi ca cātumāsomavaṭṭhako ajātapathavīti attho.

243. “The second” means unproduced earth. “The aforesaid heap” means: a heap of clay and a heap of dust that has stood for less than four months is unproduced earth.

244. Idāni yebhuyyenamattikā yebhuyyenapaṃsukā yebhuyyenasakkharāti evaṃ vuttāsu kittāvatā yebhuyyatā hotīti taṃ dassetuṃ “dve bhāgā”tiādimāha. Tattha tīsu bhāgesu dve bhāgā mattikā yassā bhūmiyā, esā yebhuyyamattikāti sambandho. Upaḍḍhapaṃsuādayopi kappiyā eva akappiyabhāgassa anatirekato. “Yebhuyyenamattikā yebhuyyenapaṃsukā”ti (pāci. 86) hi vuttaṃ, na “upaḍḍhamattikā, upaḍḍhapaṃsukā”ti. Sesesupīti yebhuyyapaṃsukādīsupi.

244. Now, when it is said, “mostly clay,” “mostly dust,” and “mostly gravel,” to show how much constitutes “mostly,” it says, “two parts,” etc. Here, the connection is: ground of which two out of three parts are clay is “mostly clay.” Even half dust and so on are allowable, because the unallowable portion is not in excess. For it is said, “mostly clay, mostly dust” (Pc 10), not “half clay, half dust.” “In the remaining cases too” means in the cases of mostly dust and so on.

245. Jātasaññissa [V 0.0153] pācittīti sambandho. Dveḷhassa vimatissa dukkaṭaṃ. Jāte ajātasaññissa anāpatti.

245. The connection is: for one who perceives it as produced, there is a pācittiya offense. For one who is doubtful or uncertain, there is a dukkaṭa offense. When it is produced, for one who perceives it as unproduced, there is no offense.

246. Ekāyāṇattiyā ekāti sace sakiṃ āṇatto divasampi khaṇati, āṇāpakassa ekā evāti attho. Vācasoti vācāya vācāyāti attho.

246. “One for one command”: the meaning is that if, having been commanded once, one digs for a whole day, it is just one offense for the one who gave the command. “For each utterance” means for each and every utterance.

247. Ettha “jālehi aggi”nti vā vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Aniyametvā pana “pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇa, pathaviṃ khaṇa, vāpiṃ khaṇa, āvāṭaṃ khaṇa, kandaṃ khaṇā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

247. Here, it is not proper to say, “Light a fire.” But it is proper to say without specifying: “Dig a pond, dig the earth, dig a reservoir, dig a pit, dig a yam.”

248. Edisanti ettha aññampi evarūpaṃ kappiyavohāravacanaṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

248. “Such”: here the intention is that other such allowable conventional expressions are also proper.

249. Kopetuṃ [M 0.0165] labbhanti sambandho, ghaṭādīhi gahetuṃ sakkuṇeyyakaṃ ussiñcanīyakaddamaṃ.

249. The connection is that it is allowable to disturb mud that can be taken up with a pot and is able to be bailed out.

251-2. Udakasantike patiteti sambandho. Udake patitaṃ pana sabbakālaṃ kappiyameva, tasmā akappiyaṃ dassetuṃ “udakasantike”ti vuttaṃ. Pāsāṇe lagge raje ca navasoṇḍiyā patite raje cāti sambandho. Abbhokāsuṭṭhite vammike ca mattikākuṭṭe cāti attho, tathā etepi sabbe cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhā na kopetabbāti attho.

The connection is with what has fallen near water. But what has fallen into water is always allowable; therefore, to show what is unallowable, it is said, “near water.” The connection is with dust attached to a stone and with dust fallen on a new strip of cloth. The meaning is also with an anthill that has arisen in the open and with a clay wall; likewise, the meaning is that all these, having stood for more than four months, should not be disturbed.

253-5. Bhūmiṃ vikopayaṃ thambhādiṃ gaṇhituṃ na ca kappatīti sambandho. Dhārāyāti passāvadhārāya. Padaṃ dassessāmīti sambandho.

The connection is that it is not allowable to take a pillar and so on while disturbing the ground. “By a stream” means by a stream of urine. The connection is with “I will show my footstep.”

257. Sekoti siñcanaṃ. Bhūmiyā allahatthaṃ ṭhapetvāti sambandho.

257. “Sprinkling” means moistening. The connection is with placing a wet hand on the ground.

258. Avase satīti hatthadāhādīsu āpadāsūti attho. Pathavīvinicchayo.

258. “When there is an occasion” means in calamities such as burning one’s hand. The determination concerning earth.

Pathavīniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of earth is finished.

35. Parikkhāraniddesavaṇṇanā

35. Commentary on the Section on Requisites

259-260. Girikūṭanti [V 0.0154] makaradantakaṃ. Sibbituñca chindituñca na vaṭṭatīti sabbattha yojanā. Daṇḍeti chattadaṇḍe.

259-260. 'Girikūṭa' means a makara-tooth pattern. The phrase 'it is not allowable to sew or to cut' is to be applied everywhere. 'Daṇḍa' means the staff of an umbrella.

261. Sibbituṃ vā pañjaraṃ vinandhituṃ vā thiratthaṃ chatte bandhituṃ daṇḍe lekhā vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Sace vuttappakāraṃ akappiyachattaṃ [M 0.0166] labhati, ghaṭakampi vāḷarūpampi chinditvā dhāretabbaṃ, lekhāpi ghaṃsetvā apanetabbā, suttakena vā daṇḍo veṭhetabbo.

261. The connection is that it is allowable to make marks on the staff for sewing, for weaving a frame, or for tying it firmly to the umbrella. If one obtains an unallowable umbrella of the kind described, both the finial and the animal figure should be cut off and set aside. The writing, too, should be scraped off and removed, or the staff should be wrapped with a thread.

262. Anuvātaṃ sandhāya “ante vā”ti vuttaṃ. Dvinnaṃ paṭṭānaṃ saṅghaṭitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya “paṭṭamukhe vāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Varakasīsākārena sibbanaṃ sandhāya “veṇikā”ti ca satapadākārena sibbanaṃ sandhāya “saṅkhalikāpi vā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Satapadisadisaṃ aññaṃ vā sūcivikāraṃ na kappati, pakatisūcikammameva vaṭṭatīti attho. Pāḷikaṇṇikaādikaṃ cīvare na ca kappatīti sambandho.

262. 'At the end' is said with reference to the leeward side. 'Or at the edge of the strip' is said with reference to the place where two strips are joined. 'Braided' is said with reference to sewing in the shape of a varaka-bean head, and 'or chain-like' is said with reference to sewing in the shape of a centipede. Other fancy needlework similar to the centipede stitch is not allowable; only plain needlework is allowable—this is the meaning. The connection is that borders such as the pāḷikaṇṇika are not allowable on a robe.

263-4. Catukoṇāva (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) kappareti sambandho. Agghikanti agghiyaṃ cetiyasadisaṃ. Etthāti gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭe. Koṇasuttā ca pīḷakāti na kevalaṃ catukoṇā gaṇṭhikapāsakapaṭṭāva kappanti, atha kho duviññeyyā koṇasuttapīḷakā ca kappareti attho. Gandhaṃ telaṃ vāti gandhaṃ vā telaṃ vā.

263-4. The connection is that four-cornered ones are allowable (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85). 'Agghika' means a valuable object similar to a cetiya. 'Here' means on the strip with the knot and loop. Regarding 'corner-threads and pads,' the meaning is that not only are four-cornered strips with a knot and loop allowable, but also corner-threads and pads that are difficult to discern. 'Perfume, oil' means perfume or oil.

265. Rattanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) rajitaṃ. Aññena vāti muggarādinā vā. Katvāti ṭhapetvā. Pahāre na ca muṭṭhināti muṭṭhinā na pahāreyyāti attho.

265. 'Dyed' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85) means colored. 'Or with another' means with a club or the like. 'Having done' means having set down. 'And one should not strike with the fist' means one should not strike with the fist—this is the meaning.

266-7. Chattavaṭṭiyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) lekhaṃ ṭhapetvā dhammakaraṇe lekhā na vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Kuñcikāya ca pipphale ca maṇikā ca pīḷakā ca na vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Tattha maṇikāti ekā eva vaṭṭamaṇikā. Pīḷakā muttarājisadisā bahū.

266-7. The connection is that on an umbrella-handle (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85), writing is not allowable, with the exception of a mark for a legal instrument. The connection is that keys, long peppers, beads, and fasteners are not allowable. Therein, 'maṇikā' is a single round bead. 'Pīḷakā' are many, resembling a string of pearls.

268-9. Mālādyaraṇiyanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) araṇiyaṃ mālādi vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭatīti [V 0.0155] sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha. Tipusīsamaye pattamaṇḍale bhittikammañca na vaṭṭatīti attho. Hitvāti ṭhapetvā. Sūcisaṇḍāsako (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) [M 0.0167] nāma sūciṃ ḍaṃsāpetvā ghaṃsituṃ kato dārumayo. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, makaradantakaṃ chinditu”nti (cūḷava. 253) vuttattā pattamaṇḍale makaradantakaṃ vaṭṭati, aññaṃ bhittikammādivikārameva na vaṭṭati, tasmā girikūṭaṃ pattamaṇḍale ṭhapetvā avasese na vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ.

268-9. Regarding 'garlands, etc., in the wilderness' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85), the connection is that garlands and so on for the sake of decoration are not allowable in a wilderness dwelling. So too everywhere. The meaning is that bowl-polishing with tin and lead and wall-painting are not allowable. 'Hitvā' means 'having excluded.' 'Sūcisaṇḍāsaka' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85) is a wooden instrument made for rubbing a needle after having it gripped. Because it is said, 'Monks, I allow the cutting of a makara-tooth pattern' (Cūḷavagga 253), the makara-tooth pattern is allowable in bowl-polishing, but other fancy work such as wall-painting is not allowable. Therefore, it should be understood that, with the exception of the 'mountain-peak' pattern in bowl-polishing, the rest is not allowable.

272. Senāsaneti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) pāsādādisenāsaneti attho.

272. 'Senāsana' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85) means a lodging such as a mansion—this is the meaning.

273. Pumitthirūparahitanti purisarūpaitthirūparahitanti attho. Parikkhāravinicchayo.

273. 'Pumitthirūparahita' means devoid of male and female figures—this is the meaning. The Decision on Requisites.

Parikkhāraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section on Requisites is finished.

36. Bhesajjaniddesavaṇṇanā

36. Commentary on the Section on Medicines

274-5. Sahadhamminaṃ labbhaṃ bhesajjakaraṇanti sambandho. Na kevalaṃ pañcannaṃ sahadhammikānaṃyeva bhikkhācariyaviññattisakehi bhesajjakaraṇaṃ labbhati, atha kho aparesampi pañcannaṃ labbhati, te dassento “pitūna”ntiādimāha. Pitūnanti mātāpitūnanti attho. Ye mātāpitaro jagganti upaṭṭhahanti, te tadupaṭṭhākā nāma. Bhikkhuṃ eva nissāya jīvanto bhikkhunissitako nāma. Pabbajjāpekkho “bhaṇḍū”ti vuccati.

274-5. The connection is that the preparation of medicine for one's companions in the Dhamma is allowable. The preparation of medicine is allowable not only for the five companions in the Dhamma by means of the alms-round and by intimation from their own relatives, but it is also allowable for five others. To show these, he said, 'for fathers,' etc. 'For fathers' means for mother and father—this is the meaning. Those who look after and attend on their parents are called 'their attendants.' One who lives depending solely on a bhikkhu is called a 'bhikkhu-dependent.' One who is expecting to go forth is called a 'bhaṇḍu'.

276. Aparesampi dasannaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, te dassetuṃ “mahācūḷapitā”tiādimāha. Ettha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-187) pana mahāpitā cūḷapitā mahāmātā cūḷamātā mahābhātā cūḷabhātā mahābhaginī cūḷabhaginīti imehi aṭṭhahi ādi-saddena pitubhaginiñca [M 0.0168] mātubhātikañca gahetvā dasa. Etesaṃ pana sakena bhesajjena kātabbaṃ. Attaniye ca asatīti pāṭhaseso.

276. It is also allowable to prepare medicine for ten others. To show these, it is said, 'elder and younger father,' and so on. Here (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.185-187), there are these eight: elder paternal uncle, younger paternal uncle, elder maternal aunt, younger maternal aunt, elder brother, younger brother, elder sister, and younger sister; by including 'father's sister' and 'mother's brother' with the word 'etc.', there are ten. For these, however, it should be done with one's own medicine. The rest of the passage is: 'and when one's own is not available'.

277. Na kevalañca etesaṃ dasannaṃ, imehi sambandhānaṃ puttanattādīnaṃ yāvasattamā kulaparivaṭṭā [V 0.0156] kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti dassanatthaṃ “kuladūsanā”tiādimāha. Aññopi (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.285-287) yo āgantuko vā coro vā yuddhaparājito vā issaro ñātakehi pariccatto vā gamiyamanusso vā gilāno hutvā vihāraṃ pavisati, sabbesampi apaccāsīsantena bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ.

277. To show that it is allowable to prepare it not only for these ten, but also for their relatives—children, grandchildren, and so on, up to the seventh family generation—it is said, 'corrupting of the family,' and so on. Also (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.285-287), for any other person—be it a newcomer, a thief, one defeated in battle, a lord abandoned by his relatives, or a traveler—who enters the monastery sick, medicine should be prepared for all of them by one who does not expect anything in return.

278. Mātā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-187) pitā tadupaṭṭhāko bhikkhunissitako paṇḍupalāso veyyāvaccakaroti imesaṃ channaṃ anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāto avāritoti attho. Kiñca bhiyyo – dāmarikacorassa ca issariyassa ca dātumavāritoti attho.

278. The meaning is that for these six (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.185-187)—mother, father, their attendant, a bhikkhu-dependent, a 'yellow-leaf' (one preparing to go forth), and a servant—untouched almsfood is not forbidden. What is more, the meaning is that it is not forbidden to give to a violent thief and to a lord.

279. Tesanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-187) gahaṭṭhānaṃ. Sāsanogadhanti ratanaparittaāṭānāṭiyaparittādiparittaṃ bhaṇitabbanti attho.

279. 'For them' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.185-187) means for the householders. 'Immersed in the Teaching' means that protective chants such as the Ratana Paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and other parittas are to be recited—this is the meaning.

280. “Āgantvā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-187) sīlaṃ detu, dhammañca parittañca bhāsatū”ti kenaci pesitoti sambandho. Dātuṃ vattunti sīlaṃ dātuṃ, dhammañca parittañca vattuṃ labbhatīti attho. Bhesajjavinicchayo.

280. The connection is that one has been sent by someone with the message: 'Having come (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.185-187), let him give the precepts and speak on the Dhamma and the protective chants.' 'To give and to speak' means it is allowable to give the precepts and to speak on the Dhamma and the protective chants—this is the meaning. The Decision on Medicines.

Bhesajjaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Medicines is finished.

37. Uggahaniddesavaṇṇanā

37. Commentary on the Exposition of Acceptance

281. Dasabhedampīti [M 0.0169] sace kenaci heṭṭhā dassitaṃ dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ ānetvā “idaṃ saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā navakammassa vā aññapuggalassa vā suttantikagaṇassa vā dammī”ti vutte “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchantassa dukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho.

281. The meaning is that if someone brings one of the ten kinds of valuables mentioned below and says, 'I give this to the Sangha, or to a shrine, or for new construction work, or to another individual, or to a group of Suttantikas,' one who consents by saying, 'Good,' commits an offense of wrong-doing.

282-3. Tesu dasavidhesu ratanesūti attho. Dvīsūti rajatajātarūpesu. Gaṇasaṅghapuggale (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-539) anāmasitvā “idaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ cetiyassa dammi, navakammassa [V 0.0157] dammī”ti vutte na paṭikkhipeti attho. Kiṃ kātabbanti ce? Taṃ dassetuṃ “vade”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Ime evaṃ vadantī”ti kappiyakārānaṃ ācikkhitabbanti attho.

282-3. Among these ten kinds of valuables: This means among the two—silver and gold. If, without addressing a group, the Sangha, or an individual (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.538-539), someone says, 'I give this gold and silver to the shrine or for new construction work,' and one does not reject it, what should be done? To show this, the words 'one should say,' etc., were stated. The meaning is that the stewards should be informed: 'These people are saying thus.'

284. Na kevalaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādikameva, aññampi khettavatthādikaṃ akappiyaṃ na sampaṭicchitabbanti taṃ dassetuṃ “khettaṃ vatthu”ntiādimāha. Dāsapasuādikaṃ dāsapasvādikaṃ. Sace hi koci “mayhaṃ sassasampādakaṃ mahātaḷākaṃ atthi, taṃ saṅghassa dammī”ti vadati, tañce saṅgho sampaṭicchati. Paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpattiyeva. Evaṃ sesesupi.

284. Not only gold, silver, and so on, but other unallowable things such as fields and land should also not be consented to. To show this, it is said, 'field, land,' etc. 'Slaves, livestock, etc.' means slaves, livestock, and so on. For if someone says, 'I have a great reservoir that yields a harvest; I give it to the Sangha,' and the Sangha consents to it, there is an offense both in accepting it and in using it. The same applies to the other cases.

Kappiyena kamena gaṇheyyāti sambandho. “Khettaṃ dammī”ti vutte “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitvā “ito cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vā “catupaccayaparibhogatthāya dammī”ti vā vadati ce, gahetabbaṃ. Vatthumhipi eseva nayo. “Taḷākaṃ dammī”ti vutte paṭikkhipitvā “cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vā “saṅgho udakaṃ paribhuñjissati, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissatī”ti vā ādinā nayena vutte sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. “Dāsaṃ dammī”ti vutte paṭikkhipitvā “ārāmikaṃ, veyyāvaccakaraṃ, kappiyakārakaṃ dammī”ti [M 0.0170] vutte sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. “Gomahiṃsaajeḷakādayo dammī”ti vutte paṭikkhipitvā “pañcagorasaparibhogatthāyā”ti vutte sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Edisaṃ gahaṇaṃ sandhāya “paṭikkhipitvā gaṇheyyā”ti vuttaṃ.

One should take it by an allowable procedure—this is the connection. When someone says, 'I give a field,' and it is rejected with the words, 'It is not allowable,' if the person then says, 'Enjoy the four requisites from this,' or 'I give it for the purpose of enjoying the four requisites,' it should be taken. The same principle applies to a plot of land. When someone says, 'I give a pond,' and it is rejected, if it is then said, 'Enjoy the four requisites,' or 'The Sangha will use the water and wash their belongings,' and so on, it should be consented to. When someone says, 'I give a slave,' and it is rejected, if it is then said, 'I give a monastery attendant, a servant, or one who makes things allowable,' it should be consented to. When someone says, 'I give cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and the like,' and it is rejected, if it is then said, 'For the purpose of enjoying the five products of the cow,' it should be consented to. With reference to such taking, it was said, 'One should take it after having rejected it.'

285-6. Navamātikakedārataḷākakiriyā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.238-239) ca anave pubbe kappiyavohārena paṭikkhipitvā gahitataḷāke mattikuddharaṇañca bhinnaṭṭhāne pāḷibandho ca dubbalaṭṭhāne āḷiyā thirakāro ca anave kedāre purāṇabhāgato atirekabhāgaggahaṇañca nave kedāre aparicchinnabhāge “sasse detha ettake”ti kahāpaṇuṭṭhāpanañcāpīti idaṃ sabbaṃ bhikkhussa kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace karoti, evamādikaṃ sabbesampi akappiyanti attho.

285-6. The making of a new watercourse, field, or reservoir (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.238-239); and, in the case of a reservoir that is not new but was accepted after having been previously rejected through an allowable transaction, removing earth from it; and building a dike in a broken spot; and reinforcing the embankment in a weak spot; and, in a field that is not new, taking an extra share beyond the old share; and also, in a new field, in an undivided portion, setting a price in kahāpaṇas, saying, 'Give so much of the crop'—it is not allowable for a bhikkhu to do any of this. If he does, the meaning is that all such actions are unallowable.

287-9. Idāni taṃyeva akappiyaṃ dassetuṃ “avatvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.238-239) – yo pana “kasa, vappa” iccādikaṃ avatvā “ettikāya bhūmiyā ettako bhāgo deyyo”ti bhūmiṃ vā patiṭṭhāpeti, “ettake bhūmibhāge sassaṃ kataṃ, ettakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti kassake vadante pamāṇagaṇhanatthaṃ daṇḍarajjubhi minati, khale ṭhatvā rakkhaṇādīni karoti, tasseva akappiyanti.

287-9. Now, to show that very unallowable action, the words 'without saying,' etc., were stated. Its meaning is (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.238-239): One who, without saying 'plow, sow,' etc., establishes a claim on the land by saying, 'From this much land, this much of a share should be given'; or who, when the farmers say, 'On this much of a portion of land, this much crop has been made; take this much,' measures with sticks and ropes for the purpose of taking a measured portion; or who stands on the threshing floor and performs guarding and other such duties—for that one, it is unallowable.

290. Bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena [V 0.0158] pitusantakampi sace paṭisāmeyya, pācittiyanti attho.

290. The meaning is that if one should appropriate, in the manner of a storekeeper, even what belongs to one's father, it is an offense entailing expiation.

291-2. Pitūnanti mātāpitūnaṃ. Sāṭakādikappiyaṃ vatthuṃ. “Paṭisāmetvā dehī”ti vutteti sambandho. Pātetvāna gate yasmā ajjhārāmasikkhāpadavasena (pāci. 505-506) palibodho, tasmā gopituṃ labbhanti attho.

291-2. 'Of the fathers' means of the mother and father. An allowable item such as a cloth. The connection is with the words, 'Having put it away, give it.' Because when one has gone away after spreading it out, there is an impediment on account of the training rule concerning what is inside the monastery (Pācittiya 505-506), therefore it is permissible to safeguard it. This is the meaning.

293-4. Sakaṃ [M 0.0171] vāsiādiparikkhāranti attho. Idaṃ ṭhānaṃ guttanti dassetabbaṃ. “Ettha ṭhapethā”ti pana na vattabbaṃ.

293-4. The meaning is: one's own requisites such as an adze, etc. This place should be pointed out as being secure. However, one should not say, 'Place it here.'

295. Ettha “añño koci na pavisati, bhikkhūhi vā sāmaṇerehi vā gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti saṅkantīti attho. Vatthumhīti alaṅkārādivatthumhīti attho. Tādiseti yādise vatthumhi naṭṭhe āsaṅkā hoti, tādise vatthumhi naṭṭheti sambandho.

295. Here, the meaning of 'one suspects' is: 'No one else enters; it must have been taken by the bhikkhus or the novices.' The meaning of 'in the object' is in an object of adornment and so on. The word 'such' is connected thus: when an object of such a kind is lost, that is, an object of a kind that arouses suspicion when it is lost.

296. Idāni asaṅkitabbaṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “vihārāvasathassanto”tiādimāha. Vihārassa ca gharassa cāti attho. Ratananti dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ. Ratnasammatanti sāṭakaveṭhanādikaṃ. Gahetvānāti kappiyakārake asati attanāpi gahetvāna nikkhipeyyāti attho. Maggeraññepīti maggepi araññepi. Tādiseti “bhikkhūhi gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti āsaṅkitabbaṭṭhāne. Patirūpaṃ karīyatīti magge vā araññe vā tādisaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ passitvā maggā okkamma nisīditabbaṃ, sāmikesu āgatesu taṃ ṭhānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace sāmike na passati, ratanasammataṃ paṃsukūlaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ratanañce hoti, tuṇhībhūtena gantabbanti attho. Ayaṃ maggāraññakesu paṭipatti. Vihārāvasathānaṃ pana anto tādisaṃ disvā bhaṇḍakaṃ muñcitvā “ettha ettakā kahāpaṇā”tiādinā nayena rūpena vā lañchanāya vā pilotikāya vā saññāṇaṃ katvā nikkhipitabbaṃ, tato pakkamantena patirūpānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Uggahavinicchayo.

296. Now, to indicate a place where one should not be suspected, the words 'inside a monastery or a rest house,' etc., were stated. The meaning is: of a monastery and of a house. 'Valuable' means the ten kinds of valuables. 'Considered as valuable' means items like a cloth, a wrapping, and so on. 'Having taken': The meaning is that if there is no steward, one may take it oneself and put it aside. 'On a road or in the wilderness' means on a path or in a forest. 'Such': In a place where one might be suspected, thinking, 'It must have been taken by the bhikkhus.' 'One should do what is proper': This means that upon seeing such an item on a road or in the wilderness, one should step off the path and sit down. When the owners arrive, that place should be pointed out to them. If one does not see the owners, an item considered valuable should be taken as a dust-heap item. If it is a true valuable, the meaning is that one should depart in silence. This is the procedure in the case of roads and wilderness areas. However, inside a monastery or a rest house, upon seeing such an item, one should untie it and, having made a sign—by stating, 'Here are so many kahāpaṇas,' or by its shape, or by a mark, or by a piece of cloth—one should put it aside. Then, upon departing, one should inform suitable bhikkhus. This is the decision on taking up.

Uggahaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Acceptance is finished.

38. Kuladūsananiddesavaṇṇanā

38. The Commentary on the Exposition of Corrupting Families

297. “Kulāni [M 0.0172][V 0.0159] dūseti pupphena vā phalena vā cuṇṇena vā mattikāya vā dantakaṭṭhena vā veḷuyā vā vejjikāya vā jaṅghapesaniyena vā”ti (pārā. 437) vuttattā tāni aṭṭha vatthūni dassetuṃ “puppha”ntiādimāha. Imāya micchāpaṭipattiyā kulānaṃ aññesu sīlavantesu pasādaṃ dūseti vināsetīti kuladūsanaṃ dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Taṃ pana attano santake ca parasantake ca veditabbaṃ.

297. “One corrupts families with flowers, or fruit, or powder, or clay, or tooth-sticks, or bamboo, or by medical practice, or by acting as a messenger on foot,” as stated (Pārā. 437). To show those eight items, the text begins “flowers,” and so on. By this wrong practice, one spoils and destroys the confidence of families in other virtuous ones; thus, one incurs an offense of wrong doing for corrupting families. This, however, should be understood as applying to both one's own property and that of others.

298. Idāni imesu vatthūsu na kevalaṃ kuladūsanadukkaṭameva āpajjati, thullaccayādīnipi āpajjatīti dassetuṃ “thullaccaya”ntiādimāha. Saṅghikaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ issarena dentassa thullaccayanti sambandho. Senāsanatthāya niyamitaṃ pana pupphādi garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Saṅghassa vā aññassa vā santakaṃ theyyacittena dentassa dukkaṭādīni hontīti pāṭhaseso, tassa bhaṇḍassa agghavasena dukkaṭathullaccayapārājikāni hontīti attho.

298. Now, to show that in regard to these items one incurs not only an offense of wrong doing for corrupting families but also grave offenses and others, he says, “a grave offense,” and so on. The connection is that for one who gives away heavy communal property on one's own authority, there is a grave offense. However, items such as flowers designated for the purpose of lodgings are heavy property. The remainder of the text is: for one who gives away property belonging to the Sangha or to another with a thieving mind, there are offenses of wrong doing and others. The meaning is that depending on the value of that property, offenses of wrong doing, grave offenses, or defeat occur.

299-300. Sabbathāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.431) kappiyavohāraakappiyavohārapariyāyaobhāsanimittakammādīhi na vaṭṭatīti attho. Vatiādīni katvā jaggituñca. Attano paribhogatthanti phalaparibhogatthaṃ. Ropanādīnīti ropāpanādīni. Ādi-saddena siñcāpanaocināpanādīni gahitāni. Kuddālakhaṇittivāsipharasuudakabhājanādīni āharitvā samīpe ṭhapanavasena nimittato ca kuddālakhaṇittādīni ca mālāvacche ca gahetvā ṭhite “sāmaṇerādayo disvā ‘thero kārāpetukāmo’ti āgantvā karontī”ti saññāya obhāsato ca “imaṃ rukkhaṃ jāna, imaṃ āvāṭaṃ jānā”tiādikappiyavohārato [M 0.0173] ca “paṇḍitena mālāvacchādayo ropāpetabbā, na cirasseva upakārāya saṃvattantī”tiādipariyāyato ca ropanādīni labbhareti sambandho.

299-300. “Sabbathāti” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.431) means that it is not allowable by way of permissible speech, circumlocution, hinting, signs, acts, etc.; and also guarding them after having made fences and so on. “For one's own enjoyment” means for the purpose of enjoying the fruit. “Ropanādīni” means having things planted, etc. By the word “ādi” are included having things irrigated, having things harvested, etc. The connection is that planting and so on are obtained: by a sign, by bringing tools like hoes, spades, adzes, axes, water pots, etc., and placing them nearby; by a hint, by taking hoes, spades, etc., and standing in the flower gardens with the thought, “Novices and others will see this, think, ‘The elder wants to have it done,’ and come and do it”; by permissible speech such as, “Know this tree, know this pit”; and by circumlocution such as, “A wise person should have flower gardens and so on planted; they will soon become beneficial.”

301-2. Idāni aṭṭhasu vatthūsu avasesāni dve vatthūni dassetuṃ “vuttāva vejjikā jaṅghapesane”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha vejjikā pubbe vuttāva, idāni jaṅghapesanādivinicchayaṃ vakkhāmīti attho. Pitaroti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.436-437) mātāpitaro. Bhaṇḍunti pabbajjāpekkhaṃ. Bhikkhussa sakaṃ veyyāvaccakarañcāti ete ṭhapetvā kasivāṇijjādigihikammesu dūtasāsanaṃ haraṇe [V 0.0160] dukkaṭanti attho. Paṭhamaṃ sāsanaṃ aggahetvā puna taṃ disvā vā tassa santikaṃ gantvā vā vadatopi dukkaṭamevāti attho. Sāsanaṃ aggahetvā āgatānaṃ pana “bhante, tasmiṃ gāme itthannāmassa kā pavattī”ti pucchiyamāne kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pucchitapañhe doso natthi.

301-302. Now, to show the two remaining items among the eight, it is said, “Medical practice has been explained; now acting as a messenger.” Therein, medical practice has been explained before; the meaning is, “Now I will explain the determination regarding acting as a messenger, etc.” “Pitaro” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.436-437) means mother and father. “Bhaṇḍu” means one who desires ordination. The meaning is that, with the exception of one's parents, one who desires ordination, and one's own attendant, for a bhikkhu to carry a message or commission concerning lay activities such as agriculture and trade is an offense of wrong doing. The meaning is that even for one who at first does not accept the message, but later, on seeing that person or going to them, speaks of it, there is still an offense of wrong doing. However, if those who have come without accepting a message are asked, “Venerable sir, what is the news of so-and-so in that village?” it is allowable to speak. There is no fault in answering a question that has been asked.

303. Evaṃ kuladūsanena uppannapaccayā. “Pañcannampī”ti vuttattā anupasampannena katampi edisaṃ na vaṭṭati eva micchājīvattā. Ātumāvatthu (mahāva. 303) cettha nidassanaṃ. Kiṃ viyāti ce, taṃ dassetuṃ “abhūtārocanārūpa-sabyohāruggahādisā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha uggahādisāti etehi uppannapaccayasadisāti attho.

303. Thus are requisites that have arisen through corrupting families. Because it is said, “For the five also,” such a thing done even by one who is not fully ordained is not allowable, as it is wrong livelihood. The story of Ātumā (Mahāva. 303) is an example here. If it is asked, “Like what?” to show that, it is said, they are “similar to those from making a false claim, from an unsuitable transaction, from acquisition, etc.” Therein, “from acquisition, etc.” means they are similar to requisites that have arisen from these.

304. Idāni pupphādīni kesaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭanti, kesaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭantīti taṃ dassetuṃ “harāpetvā”tiādimāha. Pitūnaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.436-437) dātuṃ labbhatīti sambandho. Sesañātīnaṃ pattānaṃ eva. Liṅganti sivaliṅgaṃ.

304. Now, to show to whom it is allowable to give flowers, etc., and to whom it is not allowable, he says, “having had them brought,” etc. The connection is that it is permissible to give to one's parents (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.436-437). To other relatives, only if they are suitable recipients. “Liṅga” means a Śiva liṅga.

305. Tathā [M 0.0174] phalanti phalampi mātāpitūnaṃ haritvāpi harāpetvāpi dātuṃ labbhatīti attho. Na kevalaṃ mātāpitūnaṃyeva, aññesampi dātuṃ labbhatīti dassetuṃ “gilānāna”ntiādimāha. Saparasantakanti ettha paroti attano vissāsaññātako eva adhippeto.

305. Similarly, “fruit”: the meaning is that it is permissible to give fruit to one's parents, either by taking it oneself or by having it taken. To show that it is permissible to give not only to one's parents but also to others, he says, “to the sick,” etc. In the phrase “one's own and another's property,” “another” here is intended to mean only an acquaintance whom one trusts.

306. Bhājenteti saṅghassa phalapupphamhi bhājiyamāne sammatena deyyanti sambandho. Itarena asammatena apaloketvā dātabbanti attho.

306. “When distributing”: the connection is that when the Sangha's fruit and flowers are being distributed, they should be given by an appointed person. The meaning is that another person who is not appointed should give them only after announcing it to the Sangha.

307. Paricchijjāti āgatānaṃ dātabbanti phalavasena vā rukkhavasena vā paricchinditvāti attho. Itarassāti issarādikassa. Katikaṃ vatvāti “imasmiṃ rukkhe ettakāni phalāni labbhantī”ti evaṃ vatvā.

307. “Having demarcated”: the meaning is having demarcated, either by the kind of fruit or by the tree, what is to be given to those who have come. “For another” means for the owner and so on. “Having made an agreement” means saying, “From this tree, this many fruits are to be obtained.”

308. Seseti mattikādantakaṭṭhaveḷumhi (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.436-437). Yathāvuttanayo evāti ettha attano ca parassa ca santakaṃ kulasaṅgahatthāya dadato dukkaṭantiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva [V 0.0161] vinicchayo veditabboti attho. Paṇṇampīti kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ paṇṇadānaṃ na vuttaṃ, tathāpi kuladūsane pavesayeti attho. Kuladūsanavinicchayo.

308. “The rest” refers to clay, tooth-sticks, and bamboo (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.436-437). The meaning of “the method is as stated” is that the determination should be understood according to the method stated below, beginning with: “there is an offense of wrong doing for one who gives one's own or another's property for the sake of winning over a family.” “Leaves also”: the meaning is that although the giving of leaves is not mentioned in the Pāli Canon, it is nevertheless included under corrupting families. The determination on corrupting families.

Kuladūsananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Corrupting Families is finished.

39. Vassūpanāyikaniddesavaṇṇanā

39. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Rains-Residence

309-310. Idāni vassūpagamanaṃ dassetuṃ “purimikā”tiādimāha. Tattha purimikā pacchimikā (mahāva. 184; mahāva. aṭṭha. 185) ceti dve vassūpanāyikāti attho. Ālayapariggāho vā vacībhedo vā [M 0.0175] vassūpanāyikāti pāṭhaseso. Idāni vattabbaṃ sandhāya “ediso”ti vuttaṃ. “Idha vassaṃ vasissāmī”ti cittuppādettha ālayo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 203). Ālayapariggāho pana vaje vā satthe vā nāvāya vā vassaṃ upagantukāmassa tattha senāsanaṃ alabhantassa labbhati, satthādīsu pana vassaṃ upagantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti katvā. Yadi satthādīsu kavāṭabandhaṃ senāsanaṃ labbhati, tattha upagantabbaṃ. Upagacchantena ca “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ. Vihāre pana vacībhedo vā kātabbo. Sace “idha vassaṃ vasissāmī”ti ālayo atthi, asatiyā pana vassaṃ na upeti, chinnavasso na hoti, pavāretuñca labhati eva.

309–310. Now, to show the undertaking of the rains-residence, the text begins with “the earlier,” and so on. Here, “the earlier” and “the later” (Mahāvagga 184; Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 185) mean the two undertakings of the rains-residence. The rest of the text is: “Grasping by attachment or a verbal declaration is the undertaking of the rains-residence.” With reference to what is to be said now, it is stated, “such as this.” “I will reside for the rains here”—the arising of this thought is attachment (ālaya) (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 203). However, grasping by attachment applies to one who, wishing to undertake the rains in a cattle-pen, a caravan, or a boat, does not obtain a lodging there; for it is not proper to undertake the rains in a caravan and so on. If lodging with a closed door can be obtained in a caravan and so on, one should undertake it there. And when undertaking it, one should say three times, “I undertake the rains here.” But in a monastery, a verbal declaration should be made. If there is the attachment, “I will reside for the rains here,” but one does not undertake the rains due to mindlessness, one’s rains-residence is not broken, and one is indeed permitted to perform the Pavāraṇā.

311. Nopetukāmo āvāsaṃ, tadahūtikkameyya vāti pāṭhe (mahāva. 186) atikkamantassa āvāsaṃ tadahu vassūpanāyikātipi attho. Āvāsaṃ atikkameyya vāti sambandho. Jānaṃ vānupagacchatoti ettha vihāre nisīditvāpi anupagacchato dukkaṭāpatti hotīti adhippāyo.

311. In the passage, “Not wishing to undertake the rains in a dwelling, or one might pass beyond it on that day” (Mahāvagga 186), a meaning is also that for one passing beyond the dwelling on that day, it is an undertaking of the rains-residence. The connection is “one might pass beyond the dwelling.” In “Or knowing, one does not undertake it,” the intention is that even while sitting in the monastery, for one who does not undertake the rains, there is an offense of wrongdoing.

312. Chinnavasso (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 208) vā kenaci antarāyena paṭhamaṃ anupagato (mahāva. 185-186) vā dutiyaṃ upagaccheyyāti sambandho. Temāsanti purimaṃ vā temāsaṃ pacchimaṃ vā temāsaṃ. “Na bhikkhave vassaṃ upagantvā purimaṃ vā pacchimaṃ vā temāsaṃ [V 0.0162] avasitvā cārikā pakkamitabbā. Yo pakkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 185) hi vuttaṃ.

312. The connection is that one whose rains-residence is broken (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 208), or one who did not undertake the first residence because of some obstacle (Mahāvagga 185–186), may undertake the second. “The three-month period” means either the earlier three-month period or the later three-month period. For it is said: “Bhikkhus, having undertaken the rains-residence, one should not set out on tour without having completed either the earlier or the later three-month period. Whoever should set out commits an offense of wrongdoing” (Mahāvagga 185).

313-5. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sattannaṃ sattāhakaraṇīyena appahitepi gantuṃ, pageva pahite, ‘bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā sikkhamānāya sāmaṇerassa sāmaṇeriyā mātuyā ca pitussa ca, gilānabhattaṃ vā pariyesissāmi, gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ vā pariyesissāmi, gilānabhesajjaṃ [M 0.0176] vā pariyesissāmi, pucchissāmi vā upaṭṭhahissāmi vā’ti sattāhaṃ sannivatto kātabbo”ti (mahāva. 198) vuttattā “mātāpitūnamatthāya…pe… upaṭṭhissa”nti vuttaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepo – “mātādīnaṃ gilānabhattaṃ vā tadupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ vā gilānānaṃ osadhaṃ vā esissaṃ pariyesissa”nti vā “te gilāne gantvā pucchissāmī”ti vā “upaṭṭhissa”nti vā pahitepi appahitepi sattāhakiccena gantuṃ labhati.

313–315. Because it is said: “Bhikkhus, I allow you to go for a matter to be settled within seven days, even when not sent, let alone when sent, thinking: ‘I will search for food for a sick bhikkhu, a sick bhikkhunī, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, or for my mother and father; or I will search for food for the attendant of the sick; or I will search for medicine for the sick; or I will inquire after them or attend to them.’ A return must be made within seven days” (Mahāvagga 198), it is therefore said, “for the sake of mother and father… or attend to them.” Here is the summary: One is permitted to go on a seven-day business, whether sent or not sent, thinking: “I will search for food for a sick mother and so on, or food for their attendant, or medicine for the sick,” or “Having gone, I will inquire after the sick,” or “I will attend to them.”

Idāni sahadhammike eva sandhāya “anabhirata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Visabhāgarūpaṃ disvā anabhirati, tato vūpakāsissaṃ, taṃ gahetvā aññattha gamissa”nti adhippāyena gantumpi labbhatīti attho. Kukkuccaṃ vinodanañca diṭṭhiṃ vivecanañca ahaṃ vā kareyyaṃ aññehi vā kāreyyanti sambandho. Parivāsamānattaādīhi vuṭṭhānaṃ vā garukā. Ādi-saddena sace saṅghena kammaṃ kataṃ hoti, tassa paṭippassaddhiyā anussāvanakaraṇādīsu ussukkaṃ kareyyanti gantuṃ labbhatīti attho. Sattāhakiccenāti sattāhakaraṇīyena.

Now, with reference only to co-religionists, it is said, “discontented,” and so on. The meaning is that one is also permitted to go with the intention: “Having seen a disagreeable sight, he has become discontented; therefore I will withdraw from it; I will take him and go elsewhere.” The connection is: “I might dispel his remorse and make him relinquish his wrong view, or I might have others do so.” Or for rehabilitation from serious offenses by means of probation, penance, and so on. By the word “and so on,” the meaning is that if a formal act has been carried out by the Saṅgha, one is permitted to go to make an effort in matters such as announcing its revocation. “For a seven-day business” means for a matter to be settled within seven days.

316. Dhammasavanatthaṃ nimantito evaṃ vajeti attho. Garū nāma ācariyupajjhāyā, tehi bhaṇḍadhovanakiccena pahitassa gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti attho.

316. The meaning is that one should go when invited for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. “Respected ones” means teachers and preceptors; the meaning is that it is proper for one sent by them on the business of washing the requisites to go.

317. Na bhaṇḍadhovana…pe… dassaneti ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 199) etesupi na vajeti sambandho. Labbhanti ettha “ajjeva āgamissa”nti adūrago yadi na pāpuṇeyya, labbhanti sambandho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? “Ajjeva āgamissāmī”ti sāmantavihāraṃ gantvā puna āgacchantassa antarāmagge sace aruṇuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, vassacchedopi [M 0.0177] na hoti, ratticchedena dukkaṭampi nāpajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

317. Here, in the passage “not for washing requisites… up to … for seeing” (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 199), the connection is that one should not go for these reasons either. Here, regarding “it is permissible”: if one who is not going far, thinking “I will return today,” should not arrive back before dawn, it is permissible—this is the connection. What is said? It is said that if, thinking “I will return today,” one goes to a nearby monastery and dawn breaks while one is on the way back, there is no breach of the rains-residence, nor does one incur an offense of wrongdoing for breaking the night.

318. Sesañātihīti [V 0.0163] bhātubhaginīādīhi. Bhikkhunissitakena ca pahiteti sambandho. Niddisitvāti “āgacchantu bhadantā, icchāmi dānañca dātuṃ dhammañca sotuṃ bhikkhuñca passitu”ntiādinā yaṃ kiñci niddisitvāva pesite gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Kevalaṃ “āgacchantu bhikkhū, icchāmi bhikkhūnaṃ āgamana”nti evaṃ aniddisitvā vutte gantuṃ na labbhatīti attho.

318. “By other relatives” means by brothers, sisters, and so on. The connection is “and when sent by one dependent on a bhikkhunī.” “Having specified”: it is proper to go only when sent after one has specified something, such as: “Let the venerable sirs come; I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see a bhikkhu.” The meaning is that it is not permissible to go when it is said without specifying, merely: “Let the bhikkhus come; I wish for the bhikkhus’ arrival.”

319. Accharāye satattanoti dasavidhesu antarāyesu ekasmimpi antarāye attano satīti attho. Saṅghasāmaggiyā vā vassacchede anāpattīti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ “idha pana, bhikkhave, vassūpagato bhikkhu passati sambahule bhikkhū saṅghabhedāya parakkamante. Tatra ce bhikkhuno evaṃ hoti, ‘garuko kho saṅghabhedo vutto bhagavatā. Mā mayi sammukhībhūte saṅgho bhijjī’ti pakkamitabbaṃ, anāpatti vassacchedassā”ti (mahāva. 202). Evaṃ chinnavasso no pavārayeti attho.

319. The phrase `accharāye satattano` means: when any one of the ten kinds of obstacles is present for oneself. Or, the meaning is that there is no offense for a breach of the rains-residence for the sake of the Saṅgha’s harmony. For this was said: “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has undertaken the rains-residence sees many bhikkhus striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. If it occurs to that bhikkhu, ‘Schism in the Saṅgha has been declared a grave matter by the Blessed One. Let the Saṅgha not be split in my presence,’ he may depart; there is no offense for the breach of the rains-residence” (Mahāvagga 202). The meaning is that one whose rains-residence is broken in this way should not perform the Pavāraṇā.

320. Rukkhassa susireti ettha (mahāva. 204; mahāva. aṭṭha. 203) pana suddhe rukkhasusire eva na vaṭṭati, mahantassa pana susirassa anto padaracchadanaṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā pavisanadvāraṃ yojetvā upagantuṃ vaṭṭati. Rukkhassa viṭapeti etthāpi suddhaviṭapamatte na vaṭṭati, mahāviṭape pana aṭṭakaṃ bandhitvā vuttanayena kuṭikaṃ katvā upagantuṃ vaṭṭati. Chavakuṭi nāma pāsāṇakuṭikanti vadanti. Tīsu passesu pāsāṇe ussāpetvā upari pāsāṇena paṭicchannā.

320. Here, regarding “in a hollow of a tree” (Mahāvagga 204; Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 203), it is not proper in a mere tree hollow. However, inside a large hollow, it is proper to undertake the rains after making a hut with a roof of wooden planks, having fixed an entrance door. Here too, regarding “on a branch of a tree,” it is not proper on a mere branch. But on a large branch, it is proper to undertake the rains after constructing a platform and making a hut in the aforesaid manner. They say a `chavakuṭi` is a stone hut. It is covered on top with a stone after raising up stones on three sides.

321. Nāvādīsu [M 0.0178] pana upagato pavāretuñca labbhatīti sambandho. Vassūpanāyikavinicchayo.

321. But one who has undertaken the rains on a boat and so on is also permitted to perform the Pavāraṇā—this is the connection. The Analysis of Undertaking the Rains-Residence.

Vassūpanāyikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition on the Rains-Residence is finished.

40. Avebhaṅgiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

40. Commentary on the Exposition of Non-Division

322-4. Ārāmārāmavatthūnīti [V 0.0164] ettha (cūḷava. 321; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) ārāmo nāma pupphārāmo vā phalārāmo vā. Mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bibbohanādisayanāsanaṃ. Lohakumbhīādayo kāḷalohatambalohādimayā. Bhāṇako udakacāṭi. Pañcete avibhājiyāti bhājetvā na gahetabbā, gahitāpi saṅghasantakā evāti attho. Ettha pana ārāmo ārāmavatthūti paṭhamaṃ, vihāro vihāravatthūti dutiyaṃ, mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bibbohananti tatiyaṃ, lohakumbhī…pe… nikhādananti catutthaṃ, valli…pe… dārubhaṇḍaṃ mattikabhaṇḍanti pañcamanti evaṃ imāni rāsivasena pañca honti, sarupavasena anekāni honti. Honti cettha –

322-4. “Ārāma, ārāma grounds”—here (Cūḷavagga 321; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321), “ārāma” means a flower garden or a fruit garden. A bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, etc., are sleeping and sitting requisites. Iron pots, etc., are made of black iron, copper, etc. A bhāṇaka is a water pot. These five are not to be divided—they should not be taken after division; even if taken, they remain the property of the Saṅgha—this is the meaning. Here, first, the ārāma and ārāma grounds; second, the vihāra and vihāra grounds; third, the bed, chair, mattress, and pillow; fourth, the iron pot… up to… the spittoon; fifth, the vines… up to wooden and earthenware items—thus, these are five by way of aggregates, and numerous by way of their individual forms. Among these, there are—

“Dvisaṅgahāni dve honti, tatiyaṃ catusaṅgahaṃ;

Catutthaṃ navakoṭṭhāsaṃ, pañcamaṃ aṭṭhabhedana”nti. (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321);

“Two are collections of two, a third is a collection of four; a fourth has nine compartments, a fifth has eight subdivisions.” (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321);

325. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, avissajjiyāni na vissajjetabbāni saṅghena vā gaṇena vā puggalena vā, vissajjitānipi avissajjitāni honti. Yo vissajjeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (cūḷava. 321) vuttattā “bhājitāpi abhājitā”ti vuttaṃ. Eteti vuttappakārā pañcapi “garubhaṇḍānī”ti ca “avissajjiyānī”ti ca ca-saddena “avebhaṅgiyānī”ti ca vuccantīti attho.

325. “These five things, monks, are not to be given away—they should not be distributed by the Sangha, a group, or an individual. Even if given away, they remain not given away. Whoever gives them away incurs an offense of serious misconduct” (Cūḷavagga 321). Thus, it is said, “Even if divided, they are undivided.” These five, of the kind stated, are called “heavy goods,” and “not to be given away,” and also, by the word “ca,” “indivisible”—this is the meaning.

326-8. Idāni [M 0.0179] purimesu tīsu rāsīsu sabbassa garubhaṇḍattā te anāmasitvā pacchimesu dvīsu rāsīsu ekaccassa agarubhaṇḍassāpi atthitāya taṃ dassetuṃ ārabhantopi tesu dvīsu bahuvisayaṃ paṭhamaṃ dassetuṃ “valliḍḍhabāhumattāpī”tiādimāhāti ñātabbaṃ. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepo (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) – valli aḍḍhabāhumattāpi veḷu aṭṭhaṅgulāyatopi tiṇādi muṭṭhimattampīti ettha ādi-saddena muñjapabbajaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, paṇṇaṃ ekampi mattikā pākatā vā pañcavaṇṇā vā sudhākaṅguṭṭhaādikāti ādi-saddena sajjulasajātihiṅgulakādi vā tālapakkappamāṇāpi yehi kehici saṅghassa dinnā vā saṅghike tiṇakhettādimhi jātā vā rakkhitagopitabhūmibhāge uppannā tatthajātakā vā saṅghikā rakkhitā eva abhājiyāti attho.

326-8. Now, since all in the first three categories are heavy goods, without referring to them, and since in the latter two categories there are also some light goods, to show this, even when beginning to describe those two, first, to show the extensive scope, it is said, “vines half an arm’s length,” etc.—this should be understood. The summary here (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321) is: vines even half an arm’s length, bamboo even eight finger-breadths long, grass even a handful—here, the term “ādi” includes muñja and pabbaja grass. A single leaf, earthenware whether plain or five-colored, plaster from lime and chalk, etc.—the term “ādi” includes sajju-resin, lac, vermilion (hiṅgulaka), etc., even of the size of a ripe palm fruit. Whatever has been given to the Sangha or has grown in Sangha-owned grass fields, etc., or has arisen in protected and guarded areas—those born there are the Sangha’s, protected, and are not to be divided—this is the meaning.

Idāni [V 0.0165] ye cettha bhājitabbā, te dassetuṃ “niṭṭhite”tiādimāha, saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā kamme niṭṭhite bhājiyāti adhippāyo. Ettha pana yaṃ kiñci valliveḷutiṇapaṇṇamattikādi saṅghassa dinnaṃ vā saṅghike tiṇakhettādimhi jātakaṃ vā rakkhitagopitaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ, taṃ saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca niṭṭhite avasesaṃ puggalikakammepi dātuṃ vaṭṭati, agarubhaṇḍattā bhājitumpi labbhati. Senāsanatthāya rakkhitagopitameva garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, na itaraṃ. Sīhaḷadīpe tumūlasomavihāre saṅghassa pākavattampi tālapaṇṇaṃ vikkiṇitvā karīyati. Kasmā? Na hi tattha paṇṇena attho atthi, sabbepi iṭṭhakacchannā pāsādādayoti. Evaṃ aññatthāpi karīyati evāti vadanti.

Now, to explain what should be distributed here, the phrase “when completed” and so on is stated, meaning that distribution should occur when the Sangha’s or the shrine’s work is finished. Here, whatever has been given to the Sangha—such as vines, bamboo, grass, leaves, clay, etc.—or whatever has grown in the Sangha’s grass fields, etc., and has been protected and preserved, is heavy goods.
