The remainder of this, when the Sangha’s or shrine’s work is completed, may be given even for individual work; because it is then considered light goods, it may also be distributed. Only what has been protected and preserved for the sake of dwellings is considered heavy goods, not the rest. In Sri Lanka, at the Tumūlasoma Monastery, even the Sangha’s palm-leaves for cooking are sold and used. Why? Because there is no need for palm-leaves there, as all the mansions and other buildings are roofed with tiles. Thus, it is said that this is done elsewhere as well.

329. Idāni lohabhaṇḍādīsu ekantabhājetabbabhaṇḍaṃ dassetuṃ “pattādī”tiādimāha. Ettha (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 221) pana ādi-saddena lohathālakatamba [M 0.0180] kuṇḍikā kaṭacchu saraka añjani añjanisalākākaṇṇamalaharaṇīsūcisaṇḍāsakattarayaṭṭhiādīni gahitāneva. Tathāti bhājiyamevāti attho. Vippakatañca avippakatañca. Pādagaṇhakanti magadhanāḷiyā pañcanāḷiyā gaṇhanaṃ.

329. Now, to illustrate goods that must always be distributed, such as metal items, the phrase “bowls, etc.” is stated. Here (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 221), the term “etc.” includes metal plates, copper water pots, ladles, saucers, ointment boxes, ointment sticks, earwax removers, needles, tweezers, scissors, staffs, and so forth. The meaning is that these should indeed be distributed, both damaged and undamaged. “Pādagaṇhaka” means measuring with a Magadha nāḷi or a five-nāḷi measure.

331-2. Anuññātavāsi yaṃ sakkā sipāṭikāya pakkhipitvā pariharitunti vuttā. Tacchitāniṭṭhitanti vippakataṃ. Yadi tacchitaṃ, garubhaṇḍameva. Dantaṃ pana atacchitañca aniṭṭhitañca bhājiyameva. Aniṭṭhitaṃ mañcapādādikaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. Idāni mattikabhaṇḍaṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhūpakaraṇe”tiādimāha. Pattathālakakuṇḍikādibhikkhūpakaraṇe ca. Pādaghaṭakoti pādagaṇhanako ghaṭako ca mattikāmayo bhājiyo bhājetabboti attho. Saṅkhathālakampi bhājiyameva.

331-2. An authorized resident may carry whatever can be placed in a pouch, as was said. “Carved and unfinished” refers to something imperfectly made. If carved, it is indeed heavy goods. But ivory, if uncarved and unfinished, is divisible. Unfinished items like bed legs are heavy goods. Now, to show earthenware goods, he says, “for the monks’ use,” and so on. Bowls, dishes, water pots, and other items for the monks’ use, and a pādaghaṭaka, meaning a foot-washing pot or a clay pot, are divisible, meaning they should be distributed. Even a conch-shell dish is divisible.

333-4. Migacammādikaṃ kappiyacammaṃ bhājiyaṃ, sīhacammādikaṃ akappiyacammaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. Taṃ pana bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Eḷacammaṃ pana paccattharaṇagatikattā garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Idāni imāni pana pañca cīvarapiṇḍapātabhesajjānaṃ atthāya parivattetuṃ na vaṭṭati, garubhaṇḍena pana garubhaṇḍañca thāvarañca thāvarena thāvarameva parivattetvā paribhuñjitabbānīti dassetuṃ “garunā”tiādimāha. Tattha (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) garunāti garubhaṇḍena garubhaṇḍañca thāvarañca parivatteyyāti sambandho. Thāvarena ca thāvarameva parivatteyya, na garubhaṇḍanti adhippāyo. Pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu pacchimattayaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ, purimadvayaṃ thāvaranti veditabbaṃ[V 0.0166]. Tathā katvā ca bhuñjatūti evaṃ parivattetvā tato ābhataṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ paribhuñjatūti attho. Kathaṃ ñāyatīti ce? Vuttañhetaṃ parivāre-

333-4. The hide of a deer, etc., is permissible hide and is divisible, while the hide of a lion, etc., is impermissible hide and is heavy property. However, it is allowable to use it as a ground covering. The hide of a sheep or goat, due to its suitability as a sitting mat, is classified as heavy property. Now, these five things cannot be exchanged for the sake of robes, almsfood, or medicine. However, to show that heavy property may be exchanged for heavy property or permanent property, and permanent property only for permanent property, and that having been exchanged in this way, they may be used, the phrase “with heavy property,” etc., is stated. Here (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321), “with heavy property” means that heavy property may be exchanged for heavy property or permanent property—this is the connection. The intention is that permanent property should be exchanged only with permanent property, not with heavy property. Among the five categories, the last three are considered heavy property, while the first two are permanent property—this should be understood. “Having done so, one may use” means that having exchanged it in this way, the permissible items obtained therefrom may be used. If it is asked, “How is this known?” it is stated in the Parivāra—

“Avissajjiyaṃ [M 0.0181] avebhaṅgiyaṃ, pañca vuttā mahesinā;

Vissajjentassa paribhuñjantassa anāpatti,

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 479);

“Five things are declared by the Great Sage as not to be relinquished and indivisible. For one who relinquishes or uses them, there is no offense. This question was considered by the wise.” (Parivāra 479);

Ettha pana garubhaṇḍena garubhaṇḍañca thāvarañca thāvarena thāvarameva parivattanavidhiṃ sandhāya “vissajjantassa anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Puna tato nibbattañca catupaccayaṃ paribhuñjituṃ labbhatīti dīpetuṃ “paribhuñjantassa anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ imissā gāthāya adhippāyo. Sesanti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) ārāmādi abhājiyanti attho. Avebhaṅgiyavinicchayo.

Here, with reference to the method of exchanging heavy goods for heavy goods or permanent property, and permanent property only for permanent property, it is stated, “There is no offense for one who relinquishes.” Furthermore, to indicate that one can use the four requisites that arise from that, it is said, “There is no offense for one who uses.” This is the meaning of this verse. “The rest”—meaning gardens and the like—are not to be divided. This is the Determination on Indivisible Items.

Avebhaṅgiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Indivisible Items is completed.

41. Pakiṇṇakaniddesavaṇṇanā

41. Commentary on the Exposition of the Miscellaneous Section

335-6. Sadvārabandhane ṭhāne…pe… sayanto dukkaṭaṃ phuseti evarūpe ṭhāne divā sayantenāti sambandho. Sadvārabandhane (pārā. 77; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.77) pana ṭhāne yena kenaci parikkhitte abbhokāsepi rukkhamūlepi antamaso iminā lakkhaṇena yutte ākāsaṅgaṇepi sayantena dvāraṃ bandhitabbameva. Viññumhi puriseti bhikkhumhi vā sāmaṇere vā antamaso upāsakaārāmikesupi aññatarasmiṃ satīti attho. “Esa jaggissatī”ti ābhogo cāpi kappatīti kevalaṃ bhikkhuniṃ vā mātugāmaṃ vā āpucchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Savaseti attano vase, abahusādhāraṇaṭṭhāneti attho. Taṃ vinākāranti taṃ pubbe vuttappakāraṃ dvārathakanaābhogakaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ ākāraṃ vināti attho. Acittakāpattikiriyāyaṃ saṅkhepo.

335-6. In a place with a door to be fastened... if one lies down, one commits a dukkaṭa offense. The connection here is with one who lies down during the day in such a place. In a place with a door to be fastened (Pārā. 77; Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.77), that is, in any enclosed space, even in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or at least in an open courtyard endowed with this characteristic, the door must be fastened by one who is lying down. 'When there is an intelligent man' refers to a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or at least one among lay devotees or monastery attendants. The reflection, 'This one will stay awake,' is also allowable. It is not proper to ask only a bhikkhunī or a woman. 'In one's own dwelling' (`savāse`) means in a place that is not common to many. 'Without that mode' (`taṃ vinā ākāraṃ`) means without the aforesaid mode, that is, the act of fastening the door or making the reflection. This is a summary concerning an unintentional offense.

337. Ratanānīti [M 0.0182] muttādidasavidharatanāni. Dhaññanti sattavidhaṃ dhaññaṃ.

337. ‘Gems’ means the ten kinds of gems such as pearls and so on. ‘Grain’ means the seven kinds of grain.

338. Sitthatelodatelehīti [V 0.0167] ettha (cūḷava. 246; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 246) pana yo madhusitthakatelena vā udakamissakatelena vā aññena kenaci vikārena vā kese osaṇṭheti, dantamayādīsu yena kenaci phaṇena vā kocchena vā hatthena vā phaṇakiccaṃ karonto aṅgulīhi vā osaṇṭheti, tassa dukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho.

338. Herein (Cūḷavagga 246; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 246), for whoever anoints the hair with oil prepared with beeswax, or with oil mixed with water, or with any other preparation; or who, performing the function of a comb with any comb made of ivory and so on, or with a brush, or with the hand, anoints the hair with the fingers, there is a dukkaṭa offense—this is the meaning.

339. Nekapāvuraṇāti (cūḷava. 264) na ekapāvuraṇā. Tuvaṭṭayunti nipajjeyyuṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yadi ekapāvuraṇā vā ekattharaṇā vā ekamañce vā tuvaṭṭeyyuṃ, na vaṭṭati, dukkaṭaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekamhi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 264) vā bhājane na bhuñjeyyunti sambandho.

339. 'Not with a single covering' (Cūḷavagga 264) means not with one covering. `Tuvaṭṭeyyuṃ` means they should lie down. What is meant? If they should lie down together with one covering, or on one sheet, or on one bed, it is not proper; it is a dukkaṭa offense—this is what is meant. The connection is with 'they should not eat from a single bowl' (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 264).

340. Caturaṅgulato (cūḷava. 282; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 282) ūnaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ na khādeyyāti sambandho. Adhikaṭṭhaṅgulanti aṭṭhaṅgulato adhikaṃ. Tathāti na khādeyyāti attho. Akallako (cūḷava. 289) lasuṇaṃ na khādeyya.

340. The connection is: 'One should not chew a tooth-stick shorter than four finger-breadths' (Cūḷavagga 282; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 282). `Adhikaṭṭhaṅgulaṃ` means longer than eight finger-breadths. `Tathā` means one should not chew it. `Akallako`, one who is not sick, should not eat garlic (Cūḷavagga 289).

341. Hīnehi (pāci. 31 ādayo) vā ukkaṭṭhehi vā jātiādīhi eva ukkaṭṭhaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā “caṇḍālosī”tiādinā nayena ujuṃ vā “santi vā idhekacce caṇḍālā, venā, nesādā”tiādinā nayena aññāpadesena vā upasampannaṃ vā anupasampannaṃ vā akkosādhippāyaṃ vinā kevalaṃ davādhippāyena vade, dubbhāsitanti attho.

341. If, with reference to low or high birth and so on (Pācittiya 31 ff.), one should speak to one who is ordained or unordained either directly, in the manner of saying, 'You are an outcaste,' etc., or indirectly, in the manner of saying, 'There are some outcastes, bamboo-workers, and hunters here,' etc., speaking merely with an intention to jest and without an intention to revile, the meaning is that it is wrong speech.

342. Nakhe [M 0.0183] vā kese vā nāsalome (cūḷava. 275) vā dīghe na dhārayeti sambandho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, maṃsappamāṇena nakhe chinditu”nti (cūḷava. 274) ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dumāsikaṃ vā duvaṅgulaṃ vā”ti (cūḷava. 246) ca vuttaṃ. Na labbhaṃ vīsatimaṭṭhanti ettha ekanakhampi maṭṭhaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati eva. “Na bhikkhave vīsatimaṭṭhaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa (cūḷava. 274). Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, malamattaṃ apakaḍḍhitu”nti (cūḷava. 274) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā nakhato malamattaṃ apakaḍḍhituṃ vaṭṭati. Sambādhe lomahāraṇanti ettha sambādho nāma ubho upakacchakā muttakaraṇañca. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetu”nti (cūḷava. 275) hi vuttaṃ.

342. The connection is: one should not maintain long nails, hair, or nose-hair (Cūḷavagga 275). It has been said: 'I allow, monks, to cut nails to the level of the flesh' (Cūḷavagga 274), and 'I allow, monks, hair of two months' growth or two finger-breadths long' (Cūḷavagga 246). Regarding 'Polishing the twenty is not allowed': here it is not proper to polish even one nail. For it has been said: 'Monks, the polishing of the twenty (nails) should not be done. Whoever should have it done, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Cūḷavagga 274). And: 'I allow, monks, to remove just the dirt' (Cūḷavagga 274). Therefore, it is proper to remove just the dirt from the nails. Regarding 'Removing hair in a confined place': here 'a confined place' means both armpits and the genital area. For it has been said: 'I allow, monks, on account of an illness, to have hair removed in a confined place' (Cūḷavagga 275).

343. Yathāvuḍḍhanti [V 0.0168] vuḍḍhapaṭipāṭiyā laddhabbaṃ. Na bādheyyāti na vāreyya. Saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃvāti upāsakādīhi yathāvuḍḍhaṃ “ayyā paribhuñjantū”ti nissajjitvāva dinnaṃ senāsanādi. “Na bhikkhave uddissakatampi yathāvuḍḍhaṃ paṭibāhitabbaṃ. Yo paṭibāheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 313) hi vuttaṃ. Adhotapādehi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 324) vā allapādehi vā nakkameti sambandho. Sudhotapādakaṃ vāpīti dhotapādeheva akkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathevāti nakkameyya saupāhanoti attho. “Na bhikkhave adhotehi pādehi, allehi pādehi, saupāhanena senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ. Yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324), hi vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paccattharitvā nipajjitu”nti (cūḷava. 324) vuttattā paribhaṇḍakataṃ bhūmiṃ vā bhūmattharaṇasenāsanaṃ vā saṅghikaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ vā attano santakena paccattharaṇena paccattharitvāva nipajjitabbaṃ.

343. `Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ` (according to seniority) means it should be received in order of seniority. `Na bādheyya` (should not obstruct) means should not prevent. `Saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃ` (designated for the Sangha) refers to lodgings and so on given by lay devotees and others according to seniority after having relinquished them, saying, 'May the venerables make use of this.' For it has been said: 'Monks, what has been designated according to seniority should not be obstructed. Whoever should obstruct it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Cūḷavagga 313). The connection is: 'One should not step with unwashed feet or wet feet' (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 324). `Sudhotapādakaṃ` (a place for well-washed feet) means a place that should be stepped on only with washed feet. `Tatheva` (likewise) means one should not step on it while wearing footwear. For it has been said: 'Monks, a lodging should not be stepped on with unwashed feet, with wet feet, or with footwear. Whoever should step on it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Cūḷavagga 324). Since it has been said, 'I allow, monks, to lie down after spreading a covering' (Cūḷavagga 324), one should lie down only after spreading one's own covering over a prepared floor, or a lodging with a ground-covering, or a bed or chair belonging to the Sangha.

344. Saṅghāṭiyā [M 0.0184] na pallattheti adhiṭṭhitacīvarena vihāre vā antaraghare vā pallatthikā na kātabbāti attho. Parikammakataṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 324) bhittiādiṃ na apassaye. “Na bhikkhave parikammakatā bhitti apassetabbā. Yo apasseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā setabhitti vā cittakammakatā vā bhitti na apassayitabbā. Na kevalaṃ bhittiyeva, parikammakatā dvārakavāṭavātapānatthambhādayopi na apassayitabbā. Etthapi lomagaṇanāya eva āpattiyo veditabbā. Sante udake no na ācameti (cūḷava. 373; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 373) no na ācametuṃ, udakasuddhiṃ akātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho. Santeti vacanena asante anāpattīti dīpeti.

344. 'One should not sit cross-legged with the outer robe' means that one should not sit cross-legged with a determined robe, whether in a monastery or inside a house. One should not lean against a prepared wall and so on (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 324). For it has been said: 'Monks, a prepared wall should not be leaned against. Whoever should lean against it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Cūḷavagga 324). Therefore, one should not lean against a whitewashed wall or a wall with paintings. Not only walls, but also prepared doors, door-panels, windows, pillars, and the like should not be leaned against. Here too, the offenses should be understood as by the 'counting of hairs.' 'When water is available, one should not fail to rinse' (Cūḷavagga 373; Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 373) means it is not proper not to rinse, not to perform purification with water. By the word `sante` (when available), it shows that when it is not available, there is no offense.

345. Akappiyasamādāneti bhikkhuṃ vā sāmaṇerādike sesasahadhammike vā akappiye niyojentassa dukkaṭameva. “Na, bhikkhave, pabbajitena akappiye samādapetabbaṃ. Yo samādapeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 303) hi vuttaṃ. Sabhāgāya (mahāva. aṭṭha. 169) āpattiyā desanāyāti attho. Vatthusabhāgatā idha adhippetā, na āpattisabhāgatā. “Na bhikkhave sabhāgā āpatti desetabbā. Yo deseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 169) ca “na bhikkhave sabhāgā āpatti paṭiggahetabbā. Yo paṭiggaṇheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 169) ca vuttaṃ. Vatthusabhāgaṃ āpattiṃ āvi kātumpi na vaṭṭati, tena vuttaṃ “āvikamme ca dukkaṭa”nti. “Ahaṃ, āvuso, itthannāmaṃ [V 0.0169] āpattiṃ āpajjiṃ, taṃ ito vuṭṭhahitvā paṭikarissāmī”ti aññassa vacanaṃ āvikammaṃnāma.

345. 'In encouraging the improper': for one who engages a bhikkhu or other co-religionists such as novices in what is improper, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For it has been said: 'Monks, one who has gone forth should not encourage what is improper. Whoever should encourage it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Mahāvagga 303). Regarding 'confession of a similar offense' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 169): here similarity of the basis is intended, not similarity of the offense. For it has been said: 'Monks, a similar offense should not be confessed. Whoever should confess it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Mahāvagga 169); and 'Monks, a similar offense should not be accepted. Whoever should accept it, commits a dukkaṭa offense' (Mahāvagga 169). It is not proper even to make known an offense with a similar basis; therefore it was said, 'and in making it known, a dukkaṭa.' A statement to another such as, 'Friend, I have committed such-and-such an offense; having risen from this, I will make amends for it,' is called `āvikamma` (making known).

346. Itarassa [M 0.0185] tūti asuddhacittassa.

346. `Itarassa tu` (but for the other) means for one with an impure mind.

347. Porisanti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 284) purisappamāṇaṃ abhiruhituṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sati karaṇīye porisaṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhituṃ, āpadāsu yāvadattha”nti (cūḷava. 284) hi vuttaṃ.

347. `Porisaṃ` (to a man's height) (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 284) means it is proper to climb to the height of a man. For it has been said: 'I allow, monks, when there is a reason, to climb a tree to a man's height, and in times of calamity, as much as one wishes' (Cūḷavagga 284).

348. Parissāvanaṃ (cūḷava. 259; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 259) vinā aḍḍhayojanaṃ gacchantassa dukkaṭanti sambandho. “Addhānagamanasamayo nāma aḍḍhayojanaṃ gacchissāmīti bhuñjitabba”nti (pāci. 218) vuttaṃ, tasmā aḍḍhayojanameva antimaṃ addhānanti veditabbaṃ. Bhikkhuniyā ca mātugāmena ca saṃvidhānasikkhāpade “ekaddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya, antamaso gāmantarampī”ti (pāci. 182, 413) evaṃ visesetvā vuttattā “kukkuṭasampāte gāme gāmantare gāmantare āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 183, 414) vuttaṃ, na addhānalakkhaṇena. Yadi gāmantaraparicchedena addhānaṃ vuccati, gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadepi “addhānagamanasamayo nāma gāmantarampi gacchissāmīti bhuñjitabba”nti vadeyya, na ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā “na bhikkhave aparissāvanakena addhāno paṭipajjitabbo. Yo paṭipajjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sace na hoti parissāvanaṃ vā dhammakaraṇo vā, saṅghāṭikaṇṇopi adhiṭṭhātabbo iminā parissāvetvā pivissāmī”ti vuttaṭṭhānepi aḍḍhayojanavaseneva addhānaparicchedo veditabbo. Abhayagirivāsīnaṃ pana “dvigāvutavasena addhānaparicchedo”ti pāḷiyaṃ eva atthi. Yācamānassāti yācantassa. “Na ca bhikkhave addhānappaṭipannena bhikkhunā parissāvanaṃ yāciyamānena na dātabbaṃ. Yo na dadeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hi vuttaṃ.

348. The connection is that for one going half a yojana without a water-strainer, there is an offense of wrong-doing. It is said: 'The occasion for traveling is when one intends to go half a yojana; then one may eat.' Therefore, half a yojana should be understood as the limit of a journey. For a bhikkhunī and a woman, in the training rule on making an arrangement, it is specifically stated: 'one should set out on a journey along the same road, at least to another village.' Thus it is said: 'In a village within a cock's flight, between one village and another, there is a pācittiya offense,' but this is not by the definition of a journey. If a journey were defined by the interval between villages, then in the training rule on a group meal it would say: 'The occasion for traveling is when one intends to go even to another village; then one may eat,' but this was not said. Therefore, in the passage where it is said: 'Bhikkhus, one should not set out on a journey without a water-strainer. Whoever should set out would commit an offense of wrong-doing. If there is no water-strainer or water-pot, even the corner of the outer robe should be determined upon, thinking: “Having strained with this, I will drink,”' the definition of a journey should be understood as based on half a yojana. The Abhayagirivāsins, however, say: 'The definition of a journey is based on two gāvutas,' and this is in the Pāḷi itself. 'For one who asks' means for one who requests. For it is said: 'And, bhikkhus, a water-strainer should not be withheld by a monk on a journey when it is requested. Whoever would not give it would commit an offense of wrong-doing.'

349. Aññatra [M 0.0186] ābādhappaccayā kaṇṇanāsādike sesaṅge dukkaṭanti sambandho. Ābādhe sati aṅguliādīni chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Aṅgajātaṃ vā bījāni vā chindituṃ na vaṭṭati eva. Attaghātane [V 0.0170] ca dukkaṭanti sambandho. “Na ca bhikkhave attānaṃ ghātetabbaṃ. Yo ghāteyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hi vuttaṃ.

349. The connection is that except for reasons of illness, for cutting the ears, nose, or other limbs, there is an offense of wrong-doing. When there is an illness, it is permissible to cut off fingers and so on. But it is not permissible to cut off the male organ or the testicles. And in the case of taking one's own life, the connection is that there is an offense of wrong-doing. For it is said: 'And, bhikkhus, one should not take one's own life. Whoever should take it would commit an offense of wrong-doing.'

350. “Na ca bhikkhave paṭibhānacittaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ itthirūpakaṃ purisarūpakaṃ. Yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mālākammaṃ latākammaṃ makaradantakaṃ pañcapaṭika”nti (cūḷava. 299) vuttattā “cittapotthakarūpāni, na kare na ca kāraye”ti vuttaṃ. Bhuñjantanti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 316) vippakatabhojanaṃ. “Na bhikkhave vippakatabhojano bhikkhu vuṭṭhāpetabbo. Yo vuṭṭhāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 316) hi vuttaṃ.

350. Because it is said: 'And, bhikkhus, a figure painting of a woman's form or a man's form should not be commissioned. Whoever should commission one would commit an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, bhikkhus, floral work, creeper work, makara-tooth work, and five-strip work,' it is said: 'Figures in painting or on book covers, one should not make nor have them made.' 'Eating' means an interrupted meal. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu eating an interrupted meal should not be made to get up. Whoever should make him get up would commit an offense of wrong-doing.'

351. Yānānīti vayhaṃ ratho sakaṭaṃ sandamānikādīni gilānassa abhiruhituṃ kappanti, siviko ca kappati. Evaṃ sabbattha. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa yānaṃ, purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭakaṃ, sivikaṃ pāṭaṅki”nti (mahāva. 253) hi vuttaṃ.

351. 'Vehicles' means that a palanquin, a chariot, a cart, a sedan chair, and so on are allowable for a sick person to mount, and a litter is also allowable. So it is in all cases. For it is said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, a vehicle for the sick: one yoked with men, a hand-pushed cart, a litter, and a carrying-chair.'

352. Davanti keḷiṃ. “Na bhikkhave buddhaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā saṅghaṃ vā ārabbha davo kātabbo. Yo kareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pāci. 627) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā “kiṃ buddho silakabuddho, udāhu paṭibuddho”ti vā “kiṃ dhammo godhammo ajadhammo”ti vā “kiṃ saṅgho ajasaṅgho migasaṅgho”ti vā evamādinā nayena yo davaṃ karoti, tassa dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. “Tumhākaṃ [M 0.0187] cīvaraṃ dassāma, pattaṃ dassāmā”tiādinā nayena sāmaṇeraṃ vā upasampannaṃ vā aññassa antamaso dussīlassāpi parisabhūtaṃ attano upaṭṭhākakaraṇatthaṃ upalāḷane dukkaṭanti attho. “Na bhikkhave aññassa parisā apalāḷetabbā. Yo apalāḷeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hi vuttaṃ.

352. 'Sport' means play. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, sport should not be made concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Sangha. Whoever should do so would commit an offense of wrong-doing.' Therefore, it should be understood that for one who makes sport in such ways as, 'Is the Buddha a stone Buddha, or an awakened one?' or 'Is the Dhamma the cow-Dhamma or the goat-Dhamma?' or 'Is the Sangha the goat-Sangha or the deer-Sangha?', there is an offense of wrong-doing. The meaning is that there is an offense of wrong-doing in cajoling a novice or an ordained bhikkhu who belongs to another's assembly—even an immoral one—for the purpose of making him one's own attendant, by such means as saying, 'We will give you a robe, we will give you a bowl.' For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, another's assembly should not be cajoled away. Whoever should cajole it away would commit an offense of wrong-doing.'

353. Kāyaṃ (cūḷava. 411) vā ūruṃ vā nimittaṃ vā vivaritvā bhikkhunīnaṃ na dassayeti sambandho. Kaddamudakādinā tā bhikkhuniyo na siñceyyāti attho. Na kevalaṃ kaddamudakādikeneva, vippasannaudakarajanakaddamādīsupi yena kenaci osiñcantassa dukkaṭameva.

353. The connection is that one should not expose one's body, thigh, or private part to bhikkhunīs. The meaning is that one should not sprinkle those bhikkhunīs with muddy water and so on. Not only with muddy water and so on, but also with clear water, colored powder, mud, and so on—for one who sprinkles them with anything whatsoever, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

354. Bālanti ettha bālo nāma yo ovādaṃ gahetvā pātimokkhuddesakassa ārocetvā pāṭipade [V 0.0171] paccāharitabbanti na jānāti. Gilāno nāma yo ovādaṃ gahetvā uposathaggaṃ gantvā ārocetuñca paccāharituñca na sakkoti. Gamiyo nāma yo paṭidesaṃ gantukāmo.

354. Here, 'a fool' means one who, having received the exhortation, does not know that he should announce it to the Pātimokkha-reciter and report back in due course. A 'sick person' means one who, having received the exhortation, is unable to go to the Uposatha hall to announce it and report back. A 'traveler' means one who intends to go to another region.

“Na bhikkhave ovādo na gahetabbo. Yo na gaṇheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 414) ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā bālaṃ, ṭhapetvā gilānaṃ, ṭhapetvā gamikaṃ, avasesehi ovādaṃ gahetu”nti (cūḷava. 414) ca “na bhikkhave ovādo na paccāharitabbo. Yo na paccāhareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pāci. 415) ca vuttattā bhikkhunīhi terasiyaṃ vā cātuddasiyaṃ vā āgantvā “ayaṃ uposatho cātuddaso”ti vā “pannaraso”ti vā “kadā ayya uposatho”ti vā pucchite “cātuddaso”ti vā “pannaraso”ti vā “sve bhagini uposatho”ti [M 0.0188] vā ācikkhitabbaṃ. Tāhi bhikkhunīhi uposathadivase āgantvā “bhikkhunisaṅgho ayya bhikkhusaṅghassa pāde vandati, ovādūpasaṅkamanañca yācati, labhatu kira ayya bhikkhunisaṅgho ovādūpasaṅkamana”nti evaṃ yācitabbaṃ, taṃ vacanaṃ paṭiggahetvā uposathagge pātimokkhuddesakassa “bhikkhunisaṅgho, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghassa pāde vandati, ovādūpasaṅkamanañca yācati, labhatu kira, bhante, bhikkhunisaṅgho ovādūpasaṅkamana”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ. Pātimokkhuddesakenāpi sace tattha bhikkhunovādako atthi, “itthannāmo bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, taṃ bhikkhunisaṅgho upasaṅkamatū”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace natthi, “ko āyasmā ussahati bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”nti pucchitvā sace atthi aṭṭhahaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu, taṃ tattheva sammannitvā vuttanayeneva ovādappaṭiggāhakassa ārocetabbaṃ. Yadi natthi koci bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, “pāsādikena bhikkhunisaṅgho sampādetū”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena bhikkhunā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā pāṭipade bhikkhunīnaṃ “natthi koci bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, pāsādikena bhikkhunisaṅgho sampādetū”ti vattabbaṃ. Tāhipi “sādhu ayyā”ti sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Iminā nayena gaṇapuggalesupi vacanabhedo veditabbo.

Because it is said: 'Bhikkhus, the exhortation should not be refused. Whoever should refuse it would commit an offense of wrong-doing'; and 'I allow, bhikkhus, having excluded a fool, a sick person, and a traveler, for the rest to receive the exhortation'; and 'Bhikkhus, the exhortation should not be left unreported. Whoever should not report it back would commit an offense of wrong-doing,' when bhikkhunīs come on the thirteenth or fourteenth and ask, 'Is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?' or 'When, venerable sirs, is the Uposatha?' it should be declared, 'It is the fourteenth,' or 'It is the fifteenth,' or 'Tomorrow, sister, is the Uposatha.' On the Uposatha day, those bhikkhunīs should come and request thus: 'Venerable sirs, the Sangha of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the Sangha of bhikkhus and requests the approach for exhortation. May the Sangha of bhikkhunīs, venerable sirs, obtain the approach for exhortation.' Having accepted that statement, it should be announced in the Uposatha hall to the Pātimokkha-reciter: 'Bhante, the Sangha of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the Sangha of bhikkhus and requests the approach for exhortation. May the Sangha of bhikkhunīs, bhante, obtain the approach for exhortation.' The Pātimokkha-reciter, if there is an exhorter of bhikkhunīs agreed upon there, should say: 'The bhikkhu named so-and-so has been agreed upon as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Sangha of bhikkhunīs approach him.' If there is not, having asked, 'Which venerable one is able to exhort the bhikkhunīs?' if there is a bhikkhu endowed with the eight factors, having agreed upon him right there, it should be announced in the way stated to the receiver of the exhortation. If there is no bhikkhu agreed upon as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs, it should be said: 'Let the Sangha of bhikkhunīs act with conscientiousness.' That bhikkhu, having consented 'Good,' should say to the bhikkhunīs in due course: 'There is no bhikkhu agreed upon as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Sangha of bhikkhunīs act with conscientiousness.' They too should consent, 'Good, venerable sirs.' In this way, the difference in what is said should be understood also in the case of groups and persons.

355. Lokāyataṃ (cūḷava. 286; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 286) nāma vitaṇḍasatthaṃ. “Na bhikkhave āsittakūpadhāne bhuñjitabbaṃ. Yo bhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 264) vuttattā “peḷāyapi na bhuñjeyyā”ti vuttaṃ.

355. 'Lokāyata' is the name for the science of sophistry. Because it is said: 'Bhikkhus, one should not eat on a couch with stuffed cushions. Whoever should eat would commit an offense of wrong-doing,' it is said: 'One should not eat even from a large basket.'

356. Gihipārutaṃ [V 0.0172] na pārupeyya, gihinivāsanaṃ na nivāseyyāti attho. “Na bhikkhave gihinivatthaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ hatthisoṇḍakaṃ [M 0.0189] macchavāḷakaṃ catukaṇṇakaṃ tālavaṇṭakaṃ satavalikaṃ. Yo nivāseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 280) hi vuttaṃ. Parimaṇḍalato aññathā pārupanaṃ, sabbametaṃ gihipārutaṃ nāma. Taṃ pana na pārupetabbanti attho. Saṃvelliyanti ettha kacchaṃ bandhitvā na nivāseyyāti attho. Dāyanti (cūḷava. 283; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 283) araññaṃ. Nālimpayeyyāti sambandho.

356. The meaning is: one should not wear a householder's outer robe, one should not wear a householder's lower garment. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, a householder's garment should not be worn: the elephant's trunk style, the fish-tail style, the four-cornered style, the palmyra-fan style, the hundred-pleated style. Whoever should wear it would commit an offense of wrong-doing.' Wearing it otherwise than evenly all around—all this is called a householder's outer robe. The meaning is that this should not be worn. Here, 'by wrapping' means one should not wear it having tied a fold. 'In the wood' means the forest. The connection is with 'should not smear'.

357. Vaḍḍhiñca na payojaye, noñātake nappavārite na yāceti attho. Aññassāti ettha (cūḷava. 420; cūḷava. aṭṭha. 420) “tumhe paribhuñjathā”ti niyametvā dinnaṃ sahadhammikānampi dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Aggaṃ gahetvā vā katipāhaṃ bhutvā vā puna dadeyyāti attho.

357. The meaning is: 'And one should not practice usury'; one should not ask from non-relatives who have not issued an invitation. Here, regarding 'to another': what has been given with the stipulation 'You use this' is not allowable to be given even to those who share the Dhamma. The meaning is that having taken the first portion or having eaten for a few days, one should then give it.

358. Uddissa yācaneti ettha (pāci. aṭṭha. 679) “amhākaṃ vihāre itthannāmena idañcidañca kata”nti vā “karissantī”ti vā evaṃ uddissa rakkhaṃ yācaneti attho. Ñatvāñatvā vāti evaṃ “amhehi yāciyamānā imesaṃ daṇḍessantī”ti tesaṃ daṇḍinaṃ ñatvā vā añatvā vāti attho. Tehi pana daṇḍite so daṇḍo uddissa yācantānaṃ gīvāva bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ hoti evāti attho. “Iminā ca iminā ca idañca idañca kataṃ, ettakaṃ daṇḍaṃ gaṇhathā”ti sayaṃ daṇḍāpane pana assa daṇḍassa agghabhedena pārājikathullaccayadukkaṭā ñeyyāti attho.

358. Here, 'asking by specifying' means asking for protection by specifying, ‘In our monastery, so-and-so has done this and that,’ or ‘will do so.’ 'Knowing or not knowing' means knowing or not knowing that ‘when we ask, these people will punish them’—this is the meaning. But when they are punished by them, that punishment becomes a debt on the necks of those who asked by specifying. ‘By this person and this person, this and this has been done; take this much punishment’—in the case of causing punishment to be inflicted oneself, it should be understood that according to the value of the punishment, a pārājika, thullaccaya, or dukkaṭa offense is to be known—this is the meaning.

359. Anatthāya assa corassa bhāsiteti sambandho. Rājarājamahāmattādīhi tassa corassa daṇḍaṃ gaṇhante assa bhikkhussa tattakaṃ gīvāti attho.

359. The connection is with ‘spoken for the harm of that thief.’ When kings, royal ministers, and so on inflict punishment on that thief, the liability on that bhikkhu is that much—this is the meaning.

360. Vighāsaṃ [M 0.0190] (pāci. 825-826) vā uccāraṃ vā saṅkāraṃ vā muttaṃ vā pākārakuṭṭānaṃ bahi chaḍḍeyya, dukkaṭanti attho. Vaḷañje nāvalokiyāti imināva avaḷañjanakāle nāvaloketvā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Na kevalaṃ tattheva, atha kho harite vāpi vīhādināḷikerādiropime chaḍḍentassa dukkaṭamevāti attho.

360. If one should discard scraps, excrement, refuse, or urine outside the walls or fences, it is a dukkaṭa offense—this is the meaning. By the phrase ‘Vaḷañje nāvalokiyā,’ it is shown that it is allowable to discard without looking when the place is not in use. Not only there, but if one discards on green plants or on planted things like paddy or coconut palms, it is also a dukkaṭa offense—this is the meaning.

361. “Upahāraṃ karomā”ti vutteti pucchiteti adhippāyo.

361. The intention behind the utterance ‘Upahāraṃ karomā’ is that it was asked as a question.

362. Kīḷatthaṃ (pāci. 979; pāci. aṭṭha. 978) [V 0.0173] kataṃ rājāgāraṃ vā pokkharaṇiṃ vā uyyānaṃ vā cittāgāraṃ vā ārāmaṃ vā daṭṭhuṃ gacchato pade pade dukkaṭanti attho.

362. The meaning is that for one who goes to see a royal palace, a lotus pond, a park, a picture gallery, or a pleasure grove made for amusement, there is a dukkaṭa offense at every step.

363. Āsanena (cūḷava. 364) nave na paṭibāheyya, uṇhe (mahāva. 67, 78, 79; cūḷava. 376, 378, 380, 382) cīvaraṃ na nidaheyya. Gurunāti ācariyādinā paṇāmito khamāpeyyāti sambandho.

363. One should not obstruct a junior bhikkhu with a seat; one should not put away a robe in the heat. The connection is that when dismissed by a senior, such as a teacher, one should ask for forgiveness.

364. Āpattīhi ca sattahīti (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 26) sattahi āpattīhi bhikkhuṃ parammukhā akkosanena ca “assaddho appasanno bījabhojī”tiādinā aññeneva vā akkosanena ca dukkaṭanti adhippāyo.

364. The intention is that a dukkaṭa offense is committed by abusing a bhikkhu in his absence with reference to the seven classes of offenses, or with other abuse such as, ‘faithless, unconfident, a seed-eater,’ and so on.

365. Saddhādeyyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 361) cīvaraṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ vāti attho. “Na bhikkhave saddhādeyyaṃ vinipātetabbaṃ. Yo vinipāteyya, āpatti [M 0.0191] dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 361) hi vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mātāpitūnaṃ dātu”nti (mahāva. 361) vuttattā “labbhaṃ pitūna”nti vuttaṃ.

365. The meaning is: a faith-offering, that is, robes or almsfood. For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, a faith-offering should not be wasted. Whoever should waste it commits a dukkaṭa offense.’ Because it is said, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, giving to mother and father,’ the phrase ‘it is allowable for parents’ is stated.

366. Vassaṃvuttho aññatrāti sambandho, aññasmiṃ vihāreti attho. Aññatoti aññavihārato. “Na bhikkhave aññatra vassaṃvutthena aññatra cīvarabhāgo sāditabbo. Yo sādiyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 364) hi vuttaṃ. Tesanti tasmiṃ vihāre taṃ cīvaraṃ bhājetvā gaṇhituṃ yuttānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhuranikkhepato hoti bhaṇḍagghena kāriyoti attho.

366. The connection is with ‘one who has spent the rains elsewhere,’ meaning in another monastery. ‘Aññato’ means from another monastery. For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has spent the rains elsewhere should not consent to a share of robes elsewhere. Whoever should consent to it commits a dukkaṭa offense.’ The meaning is: for those bhikkhus in that monastery who are fit to receive a share after that robe has been distributed, it is a matter of laying down the burden; it should be done according to the value of the goods.

367. Saha antarena uttaroti santaruttaro, gāmaṃ na paviseyyāti attho. “Na bhikkhave santaruttarena gāmo pavisitabbo. Yo paviseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 362) hi vuttaṃ. Kallo vāti agilāno. Saupāhano gāmaṃ na paviseyyāti sambandho. “Na bhikkhave cāmaribījanī dhāretabbā. Yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 269), “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso bījaniyo vākamayaṃ usīramayaṃ morapiñchamaya”nti (cūḷava. 269) [V 0.0174] ca vuttattā “na dhāreyya cāmarīmakasabījani”nti vuttaṃ. Makasabījanī pana dantavisāṇadārudaṇḍakāpi vaṭṭati.

367. ‘Santaruttaro’ means with the inner robe and the upper robe; the meaning is that one should not enter a village thus. For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, a village should not be entered with the inner and upper robe. Whoever should enter commits a dukkaṭa offense.’ ‘Kallo vā’ means not being sick. The connection is that one should not enter a village wearing sandals. Since it is said, ‘Bhikkhus, a yak-tail fan should not be carried. Whoever should carry one commits a dukkaṭa offense,’ and, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, three kinds of fans: one made of bark, one of usīra grass, and one of peacock feathers,’ it is therefore stated, ‘one should not carry a yak-tail fan or a fly-whisk.’ However, a fly-whisk with a handle of ivory, horn, or wood is also allowable.

368. Ārāmato bahīti sambandho. “Na bhikkhave chattaṃ dhāretabbaṃ. Yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa chatta”nti ca vuttattā agilāno ārāmato bahi na labhati, cīvaraguttiyādiatthāya agilānopi labhatīti attho.

368. The connection is with ‘outside the monastery.’ Since it is said, ‘Bhikkhus, an umbrella should not be carried. Whoever should carry one commits a dukkaṭa offense,’ and, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, an umbrella for one who is sick,’ a bhikkhu who is not sick is not allowed one outside the monastery; but the meaning is that even one who is not sick is allowed one for such purposes as protecting one’s robes.

369. Gāheyya nubhatokājanti na gāheyya ubhatokājaṃ. Ekantarikakājakanti ekatokājañca antarakājañca[M 0.0192]. Sīsabhāro ca khandhabhāro ca kaṭibhāro ca sīsakkhandhakaṭibhārā. “Na bhikkhave ubhatokājaṃ haritabbaṃ. Yo hareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 281), “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ekatokājaṃ antarakājaṃ sīsabhāraṃ khandhabhāraṃ kaṭibhāraṃ olambaka”nti (cūḷava. 281) ca vuttattā ubhatokājameva na vaṭṭati, sesāni vaṭṭantīti veditabbā.

369. ‘Gāheyya nubhatokājaṃ’ means one should not take a double-ended carrying pole. ‘Ekantarikakājakanti’ means a single-ended pole and an intermediate pole. Head-load, shoulder-load, and hip-load are loads carried on the head, shoulder, and hip. Since it is said, ‘Bhikkhus, a double-ended carrying pole should not be used. Whoever should use one commits a dukkaṭa offense,’ and, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a single-ended pole, an intermediate pole, a head-load, a shoulder-load, a hip-load, and a hanging load,’ it should be understood that only the double-ended pole is not allowable; the rest are allowable.

370. Anokāsakatanti (mahāva. 153) yo paṭhamameva “karohi me āvuso okāsaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo”ti evaṃ akatokāsaṃ āpattiyā codeyya, tassa dukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho. Tathāti dukkaṭamevāti attho.

370. The meaning of ‘anokāsakataṃ’ is that if someone, from the very beginning, should charge another with an offense without having been given leave—that is, without first saying, ‘Friend, give me leave; I wish to speak to you’—it is a dukkaṭa offense for him. ‘Tathā’ means it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense.

371. Pakataṅgulena, na sugataṅgulenāti attho.

371. The meaning is: with a standard finger-breadth, not with the Sugata's finger-breadth.

372. Mūgabbatādiṃ (mahāva. 209; mahāva. aṭṭha. 209) titthiyabbataṃ yadi gaṇheyya, dukkaṭanti attho. Ādi-saddena govatakukkuravatādayo saṅgahitā. Tathāti (mahāva. 303; mahāva. aṭṭha. 303) nhāpitapubbako khurabhaṇḍaṃ yadi parihareyya, dukkaṭamevāti attho.

372. The meaning is that if one should undertake a heretical observance such as the vow of dumbness, it is a dukkaṭa offense. By the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), practices such as the cow-vow and the dog-vow are included. ‘Tathā’ means that if one who was formerly a barber should carry barber’s equipment, it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense.

373. Yaṃ kiñcīti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nhāpitatuṇṇakārakammādi yaṃ kiñci hatthakammanti attho. Tadanusāratoti hatthakammayācanānusāratoti attho. Sace evaṃ yācato hatthakammamūlameva deti, taṃ aññassa dāpetvā [V 0.0175] kāretuṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. Nikkammaṃ pana hatthakammavasena ayācitvāpi “ehi imaṃ karohī”ti kāretuṃ kappatīti attho. Yaṃ kiñciparasantakanti yaṃ kiñci dārutiṇādikaṃ aparasantakaṃ apariggahitaṃ āharāpetuṃ kappatīti adhippāyo.

373. ‘Whatever’ (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Kuṭikāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā) means any manual labor, such as the work of a barber or a tailor. ‘In accordance with that’ means in accordance with the request for manual labor. The meaning is that if, when one asks thus, a donor gives only the payment for the manual labor, it is allowable to have the work done by giving that payment to another. However, the meaning is that it is proper to have work done without wages, even without having asked for it as manual labor, by saying, ‘Come, do this.’ The intention of ‘whatever belonging to another’ is that it is proper to have anything un-owned and un-appropriated, such as wood or grass, brought.

374. Gihīnanti [M 0.0193] gihīnaṃ santakaṃ. Gopaketi rakkhake. Yattakaṃ deti, tattakaṃ gahetuṃ kappatīti attho. Yathāparicchedanti “divase divase ettakaṃ ucchunāḷikeraṃ ambapakkaṃ tumhe khādathā”ti paricchinditvā dinnameva tesu dentesu labbhatīti attho.

374. ‘Of householders’ means belonging to householders. ‘On the keepers’ means on the guards. The meaning is that whatever one gives, it is proper to take that much. ‘According to the delimitation’ means that only what is given after having been delimited—for instance, ‘Day by day you may eat this much sugarcane, coconut, or ripe mango’—is obtainable when they give from those things. This is the meaning.

375. Dvihāpajjeyyāti dvīhi āpajjeyya. Katamehi dvīhīti ce, te dassetuṃ “kāyavācāhī”ti vuttaṃ, “dvīhākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati, kāyena āpajjati, vācāya āpajjatī”ti (pari. 322) hi vuttaṃ. Kāyavācāhi āpattiṃ āpajjanto ca chahi ākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati, tāni dassetuṃ “alajjiñāṇakukkuccapakatattā”tiādimāha. Ettha (pari. 295) pana akappiyabhāvaṃ jānanto eva vītikkamaṃ karonto alajjitāya āpajjati nāma. Kappiyākappiyaṃ ajānitvā āpajjanto aññāṇatāya. Kappiyaṃ nu kho, no nu kho”ti saṃsaye uppanne tamabhivitaritvā vītikkamaṃ karonto kukkuccapakatattā āpajjati. Sahaseyyādiṃ āpajjanto satiplavā, satisammosāti attho. Acchamaṃsaṃ “sūkaramaṃsa”nti vā sūkaramaṃsaṃ “acchamaṃsa”nti vā khādanto akappiye kappiyasaññitāya ca kappiye akappiyasaññitāya ca āpajjatīti veditabbo.

375. ‘One would fall into an offense in two ways’ means one would fall into an offense by two means. If it is asked, ‘By which two?’ to show them, ‘by body and speech’ is said; for it is stated: ‘One falls into an offense in two ways: one falls by body, one falls by speech’ (Pari. 322). And one who falls into an offense by body and speech falls into an offense in six ways. To show these, he stated the passage beginning ‘through shamelessness, ignorance, being done with scruples.’ Here (Pari. 295), one who transgresses while knowing that something is improper is said to fall into an offense through shamelessness. One who falls into an offense without knowing what is proper and improper falls through ignorance. When doubt has arisen—‘Is this proper or not?’—one who transgresses after proceeding despite it falls into an offense because of acting with scruples. Falling into an offense such as lying down together is due to a lapse of mindfulness, that is, confusion of mindfulness. It should be understood that one falls into an offense through perceiving the improper as proper and the proper as improper when, for example, eating bear’s meat thinking it is pork, or eating pork thinking it is bear’s meat.

376. Alajjitāya vā aññāṇatāya vā āpattiṃ kāyavācāhi chādayeti attho. Eke vā ekasmiṃ vā. Liṅgeti liṅgaparivattanato. Evaṃ catudhā āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti attho. Tiṇavatthārakasamathaabbhānādīnaṃ vasena saṅghe āpatti vuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ nissajjanādīsu gaṇe. Ekassa santike vuṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭameva. “Yā āpattiyo [M 0.0194] bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi asādhāraṇā, tāhi āpattīhi anāpattī”ti (pārā. 69) vacanato liṅgaparivattane āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ ñātabbaṃ.

376. The meaning is that one conceals an offense by body or speech through shamelessness or ignorance. In the presence of a number of bhikkhus or of one. ‘By the characteristic’ means by the transformation of sex. The meaning is that emergence from an offense occurs in four ways. It should be understood that one emerges from an offense in the Sangha by means of procedures such as the covering-with-grass settlement and rehabilitation; and in a group for matters such as forfeiture. Emergence in the presence of one person is self-evident. Based on the statement, ‘As to those offenses of bhikkhus that are not shared with bhikkhunīs, one is in a state of non-offense in regard to them’ (Pārā. 69), emergence from an offense through transformation of sex is to be understood.

377. Paccayadvayeti cīvare ca piṇḍapāte ca. Na kevalañca ime eva, nimittakammampi na labbhateva, gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana na vuttaṃ. Tattha nimittakammaṃ nāma yaṃ kiñci [V 0.0176] paresaṃ paccayadānasaṃyojanakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ. Khādanīyaṃ gahetvā gacchante disvā “kiṃ khādanīyaṃ labhitthā”tiādinā nayena tassa pavatti veditabbā. Parikathā nāma yathā yathā taṃ labhati, tathā tathā parivattetvā kathanaṃ. “Etarahi bhikkhū piṇḍapātena kilamantī”tiādinā nayena tassa pavatti veditabbā. Obhāso nāma paccayappaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Viññatti pana pākaṭā eva. Tatiyeti senāsane. Senāsane pana nimittobhāsaparikathā vaṭṭanti, viññatti eva ekā na vaṭṭati. Tattha nimittakammaṃ nāma upāsake disvā senāsanatthaṃ bhūmiparikammakaraṇādi. Obhāso nāma “upāsakā, tumhe kuhiṃ vasathā”ti “pāsāde, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāsādo na vaṭṭatī”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ. Parikathā nāma “bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanaṃ sambādha”nti vacanaṃ. Seseti gilānapaccaye.

377. ‘In the two requisites’ refers to robes and almsfood. Not only in regard to these, but even making a sign is not allowable; however, for the ease of versification, it is not mentioned. Herein, making a sign means any bodily or verbal action connected with another's giving of requisites. Seeing someone carrying edible food and asking, “Did you get some edible food?” and so on—this is how its arising should be understood. Circumlocution means speaking in a roundabout way about how one might obtain something. For example, saying, “Nowadays, monks are exhausted by almsfood,” and so on—this is how its arising should be understood. Making an allusion means talk related to requisites. A request, however, is obvious. ‘The third’ refers to lodging. Regarding lodging, making a sign, making an allusion, and circumlocution are allowable; a request alone is not. Herein, making a sign means, upon seeing a lay follower, preparing the ground, and so on, for the sake of a lodging. Making an allusion means saying, “Lay followers, where do you live?” and when they reply, “In a mansion, venerable sir,” then asking, “Is a mansion not allowable for monks?” and so on. Circumlocution means saying, “The monks’ lodging is crowded.” ‘The rest’ refers to medicine for the sick.

378. Na ruhatīti na hoti. Accaye dānanti accayadānaṃ. Pañcasu sahadhammikesu yena kenaci kālaṃ karontena “mamaccayena mayhaṃ parikkhāro upajjhāyassa hotu, ācariyassa hotu, aññassa vā kassaci hotū”ti vutte tesaṃ na hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “na ruhatī”ti. Saṅghasseva ca taṃ hotīti yadi bhikkhusāmaṇerehi evaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ matepi bhikkhusaṅghasseva hoti, bhikkhunisikkhamānasāmaṇerīhi [M 0.0195] ce vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ mate bhikkhunisaṅghassa taṃ hotīti attho. Gihīnaṃ pana rūhatīti gihīnaṃ pana accayadānaṃ eva sabbesaṃ ruhatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

378. ‘Does not take effect’ means it does not happen. ‘A gift on passing away’ means a bequest. If, among the five kinds of co-religionists, anyone at the time of death says, “Upon my death, let my belongings go to my preceptor, teacher, or anyone else,” then it does not belong to them; therefore it is said, “Does not take effect.” And ‘it belongs only to the Sangha’ means that if monks or novices have said this, then upon their death it belongs only to the Sangha of monks; and if nuns, probationary nuns, or female novices have said this, then upon their death it belongs to the Sangha of nuns. ‘But for householders, it does take effect’ means that for all householders, a bequest does take effect.

379. Upassayeti bhikkhunivihāre. Dāyajjoti tassa parikkhārassa dāyajjo. Sesepīti sace bhikkhunisikkhamānasāmaṇeriyo bhikkhuvihāre kālaṃ karonti, tāsaṃ parikkhārānaṃ bhikkhusaṅghova dāyajjoti attho.

379. ‘In the residence’ means in a nunnery. ‘The heir’ means the heir to those requisites. ‘In the remaining cases’ means that if nuns, female probationers, or female novices die in a monastery of monks, the Sangha of monks is the heir to their requisites.

380. Purimassevāti ettha “imaṃ parikkhāraṃ netvā asukassa dehī”ti dinnaṃ purimasseva hotīti attho. “Asukassa dammī”ti dinnaṃ pana pacchimasseva hoti pariccajitvā dinnattā. Imaṃ vidhiṃ ñatvāva vissāsaggāhaṃ vā gaṇheyya, matakacīvaraṃ vā adhiṭṭheti sambandho. Matakacīvaraadhiṭṭhānaṃ nāma ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā kālaṃ ghosetvā thokaṃ āgametvā sace bhikkhū āgacchanti, tehi saddhiṃ bhājetabbāni, no ce āgacchanti, “mayhimāni cīvarāni pāpuṇantī”ti adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhite sabbāni tasseva honti, ṭhitikā pana na tiṭṭhati. Sace ekekaṃ uddharitvā “ayaṃ paṭhamabhāgo mayhaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ dutiyabhāgo”ti [V 0.0177] evaṃ gaṇhāti, gahitāni ca sugahitāni honti, ṭhitikā ca tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ pāpetvā gaṇhantenāpi adhiṭṭhitameva hoti.

380. Regarding ‘of the first,’ the meaning here is that if something is given with the instruction, ‘Take this requisite and give it to so-and-so,’ then it belongs to the first recipient. However, if it is given with the words, ‘I give this to so-and-so,’ then it belongs to the latter, because it is given after having been relinquished. Having understood this method, one may take something based on trust or determine a deceased person’s robes; this is the connection. The determination of a deceased person’s robes is as follows: after striking the bell and announcing the time, one should wait a short while. If monks arrive, the robes should be distributed among them. If they do not arrive, one should determine them, thinking, ‘May these robes come to me.’ When they have been thus determined, they all belong to that person, but the formal procedure is not established. If one takes them one by one, thinking, ‘This first share comes to me, this second share…,’ then they are well-taken, and the formal procedure is established. Even when one takes them after having obtained them in this way, it is still considered a determination.

381. Lohabhaṇḍe paharaṇiṃ ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ kappati, dārubhaṇḍe ca dārujaṃ pattañca pādukañca, pallaṅkañca āsandiñca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ kappati, mattikāmaye katakañca kumbhakārikañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ kappatīti attho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā paharaṇiṃ sabbaṃ lohabhaṇḍaṃ, ṭhapetvā āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ dārupattaṃ dārupādukaṃ sabbaṃ dārubhaṇḍaṃ, ṭhapetvā katakañca [M 0.0196] kumbhakārikañca sabbaṃ mattikābhaṇḍa”nti (cūḷava. 293) hi vuttaṃ. Ettha katakanti padumakaṇṇikākārena katamallakanti adhippetaṃ. Dhaniyasseva sabbamattikāmayā kuṭi kumbhakārikanti. Pakiṇṇakavinicchayo.

381. Among metal goods, everything is allowable except for a weapon. Among wooden goods, everything is allowable except for a wooden bowl, wooden sandals, a couch, and a chair. Among clay goods, everything is allowable except for a water-strainer and a potter’s-hut; this is the meaning. For it is said: ‘Monks, I allow all metal goods except for a weapon; all wooden goods except for a chair, a couch, a wooden bowl, and wooden sandals; and all clay goods except for a water-strainer and a potter’s-hut’ (Cūḷavagga 293). Here, ‘water-strainer’ is intended to mean a small pot made in the shape of a lotus pericarp. ‘Potter’s-hut’ refers to the potter Dhaniya’s hut, which was made entirely of clay. The Rulings on Miscellaneous Topics.

Pakiṇṇakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics is concluded.

42. Desanāniddesavaṇṇanā

42. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Teaching

382. Bhikkhubhāvassa (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.198) yo cāgo, sā pārājikadesanāti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ “visuddhāpekkhoti gihi vā hotukāmo upāsako vā hotukāmo ārāmiko vā hotukāmo sāmaṇero vā hotukāmo”ti (pārā. 198). Tasmā gihibhāvādikaṃyeva pārājikaṃ āpannassa visuddhi nāma, aññatarassa visuddhi eva natthi. “Chādeti jānamāpannaṃ, parivaseyya tāvatā”tiādinā nayena heṭṭhā vuttavidhiṃ sandhāya “yathāvuttena vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

382. The relinquishment of the state of a bhikkhu (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.198) is the meaning of the declaration of a pārājika offense. For it is said: ‘One who seeks purity, whether desiring to become a layperson, a male lay follower, a monastery attendant, or a novice’ (Pārā. 198). Therefore, for one who has committed a pārājika offense, purity is only the state of a layperson and so on; there is no other purity for such a one. The phrase ‘rehabilitation as described’ is stated with reference to the procedure mentioned below, according to the principle beginning with, ‘If one knowingly commits an offense and conceals it, one should live on probation for that long.’

383. Idāni vattabbataṃ sandhāya “eva”nti vuttaṃ.

383. Now, with reference to what should be spoken, ‘thus’ is stated.

384. Paṭidesemīti ārocemi. Etāni ahaṃ etānāhaṃ.

384. ‘I confess’ means ‘I announce.’ `Etānāhaṃ` is a contraction of `etāni ahaṃ`.

386. (Ka) yaṃ [V 0.0178] saṅgho gilānassa ticīvarena vippavāsasammutiṃ deti, taṃ aññatrāti attho.

386. (Ka) The meaning of ‘except’ is the permission granted by the Saṅgha for a sick bhikkhu to be away from the three robes.

(Kha) akālacīvaraṃ (pārā. 500) [M 0.0197] nāma “anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppannaṃ, atthate kathine sattamāse uppannaṃ, kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ, etaṃ akālacīvaraṃ nāmā”ti.

(Kha) The out-of-season robe (akālacīvara, Pārā. 500) is defined as: ‘That which arises during the eleven months when the kathina is not spread, that which arises during the seven months when the kathina is spread, or even that given during the season but designated—this is called an out-of-season robe.’

(Ga) purāṇacīvaraṃ (pārā. 505) nāma “sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññātikā nāma mātito vā pitito vā yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā asambandhā. Nisīdanapaccattharaṇadhovāpane dukkaṭaṃ.

(Ga) An old robe (purāṇacīvara, Pārā. 505) is defined as: ‘Even if worn once or used as a covering once.’ A non-relative (aññātikā) is one not related in kinship up to the seventh generation on the mother’s or father’s side. There is an offense of wrong doing in having a sitting cloth or a spread washed.

(Gha) aññatra pārivattakāti (pārā. 512) ettha harītakīkhaṇḍampi vaṭṭati. Cīvaraṃ nāma idha vikappanūpagapacchimato paṭṭhāya adhippetaṃ.

(Gha) In the phrase ‘Except by exchange’ (aññatra pārivattakā, Pārā. 512), even a piece of myrobalan is allowable. Here, ‘robe’ is intended to mean from the last one suitable for designation onwards.

(Ṅa) aññatra samayāti (pārā. 519) ettha “acchinnacīvaro vā hoti bhikkhu naṭṭhacīvaro vā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ samayanti attho.

(Ṅa) In the phrase ‘Except at the proper time’ (aññatra samayā, Pārā. 519), the meaning of ‘proper time’ is as stated: ‘The bhikkhu has had his robe stolen or has lost his robe.’

(Ca) “santaruttaraparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tato cīvaraṃ sāditabba”nti (pārā. 524) vuttattā “tatuttarī”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha pana “sace tīṇi naṭṭhāni honti, dve sāditabbāni. Dve naṭṭhāni, ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ, ekaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, na kiñci sāditabba”nti (pārā. 524) vuttaṃ.

(Ca) Because it is said, ‘At most, an inner and an outer robe may be obtained by that bhikkhu from that source’ (Pārā. 524), the phrase ‘beyond that’ (tatuttarī) is used. And here it is said: ‘If three are lost, two may be obtained. If two are lost, one may be obtained. If one is lost, nothing may be obtained’ (Pārā. 524).

(Cha-ja) “kīdisena te (pārā. 529), bhante, cīvarena attho, kīdisaṃ te cīvaraṃ cetāpemī”ti evaṃ appavāritoti attho. Vikappanti visiṭṭhakappaṃ adhikavidhānaṃ āpannaṃ. Idha purimaṃ ekassa, dutiyaṃ bahūnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, ettakaṃ nānattaṃ.

(Cha-ja) ‘What kind of robe do you need, venerable sir? What kind of robe shall I have made for you?’ (Pārā. 529)—this is the meaning of ‘uninvited’ (appavārito). `Vikappa` means a special rule, an additional regulation. Here, the former is stated with respect to one, the latter with respect to many—this is the only difference.

(Jha) atirekatikkhattunti ettha kenaci yaṃ kiñci akappiyavatthuṃ ānetvā “idaṃ kho me, bhante, āyasmantaṃ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṃ ābhataṃ, paṭiggaṇhatu āyasmā cīvaracetāpanna”nti vutte “na kho mayaṃ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma kālena kappiya”nti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ vutte sace so “atthi koci kappiyakārako”ti [M 0.0198][V 0.0179] vadati, cīvaratthikena ṭhapetvā pañca sahadhammike yo koci uddisitabbo “eso kho, āvuso, bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti, ettakameva vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ vutte sace dāyako tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “eso ayyassa cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā dassatī”ti vatvā gacchati, taṃ upasaṅkamitvā dvattikkhattuṃ codetabbo sāretabbo “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti, ettakameva vattabbaṃ, “dehi me cīvara”ntiādinā na vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ tikkhattuṃ codanāya taṃ cīvaraṃ labhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce labhati, chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ, na āsane nisīditabbaṃ, na āmisaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, na dhammo bhāsitabbo. “Kiṃ kāraṇā āgatosī”ti vutte “jānāhi, āvuso”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ. Sace nisajjādīni karoti, ṭhānaṃ bhañjati. Vattabhedadukkaṭañca āpajjatīti vadanti. Evaṃ pana appaṭipajjitvā atirekatikkhattuṃ codanāya atirekachakkhattuṃ ṭhānena sace nipphādeti, nissaggiyanti attho.

(Jha) In the phrase ‘more than three times’ (atirekatikkhattuṃ), if someone brings some unallowable item and says, ‘Venerable sir, this fund for a robe has been brought with the venerable one in mind; may the venerable one accept this fund for a robe,’ one should say, ‘Friend, we do not accept funds for a robe; we accept a robe when it is allowable and at the proper time.’ If, having been told this, he says, ‘Is there an attendant who makes things allowable?,’ the one who needs the robe should, excluding the five kinds of co-religionists, point someone out, saying only this: ‘Friend, this is the bhikkhus’ steward.’ If, having been told this, the donor places the unallowable item in his hand, says, ‘He will have a robe made for the master and give it,’ and departs, one should approach that person and prompt and remind him two or three times, saying only this: ‘Friend, I have need of a robe.’ One should not say things like, ‘Give me the robe.’ If by prompting him up to three times one receives that robe, this is proper. If one does not receive it, one should stand in silence for a maximum of six times. One should not sit on a seat, accept almsfood, or teach the Dhamma. If asked, ‘For what reason have you come?,’ one should say only this: ‘You know, friend.’ If one does sit down, etc., one breaks the standing. They say one also incurs an offense of wrong doing for breaking the observance. If, however, one does not act in this way, and obtains the robe by prompting more than three times or by standing for more than six times, it is to be forfeited; this is the meaning.

(Ña) santhataṃ (pārā. 544) nāma santharitvā kataṃ hoti avāyimaṃ. Ekakosiyaṃsunāpi ce missetvā karoti, nissaggiyaṃ.

(Ña) A felted rug (santhata, Pārā. 544) is something made by spreading out; it is not woven. If one makes it by mixing in even a single silk thread, it is to be forfeited.

(Ṭa) suddhakāḷakānanti (pārā. 547-549) aññehi amissitānanti attho. “Kāḷakaṃ nāma dve kāḷakāni jātikāḷakaṃ vā rajanakāḷakaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ.

(Ṭa) `Suddhakāḷakānaṃ` (Pārā. 547-549) means ‘of pure black,’ that is, unmixed with other colors. It is said: ‘“Black” means two kinds of black: natural black or dyed black.’

(Ṭha) anādiyitvā…pe… tulanti (pārā. 554) ettha pana yattakehi eḷakalomehi kattukāmo hoti, tesu dve koṭṭhāsā kāḷakānaṃ, eko odātānaṃ, eko gocariyānaṃ ādātabboti vinicchayo. Ekassāpi kāḷakalomassa atirekabhāge sati nissaggiyameva.

(Ṭha) Regarding ‘Without taking… they weigh’ (pārā. 554), here the ruling is this: of whatever amount of sheep’s wool one intends to use to make a rug, two parts of black, one part of white, and one part of tawny should be taken. If there is an excess portion of even a single black wool hair, it is to be forfeited.

(Ḍa) ūnakachabbassānīti [M 0.0199] (pārā. 562) chabbassato orabhāge.

(Ḍa) ‘Less than six years’ (pārā. 562) means on this side of six years, that is, before six years have been completed.

(Ḍha) nisīdanasanthataṃ (pārā. 567) pana kārāpentena purāṇasanthatassa ekapassato vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā chinditvā gahitaṭṭhānaṃ yathā vidatthimattaṃ hoti, evaṃ gahetvā ekadesaṃ vā santharitabbaṃ, vijaṭetvā vā santharitabbaṃ.

(Ḍha) When having a sitting-rug made (Pārā. 567), one should cut a round or square piece from one side of the old rug. It should be taken in such a way that the place from which it was taken is a span in size. It should then be incorporated by felting it in as a single piece, or by felting it in after having unraveled it.

(Ta) na [V 0.0180] kevalaṃ dhovāpane (pārā. 578) eva nissaggiyaṃ, rajanepi nissaggiyameva.

(Ta) It is to be forfeited not only when one has it washed (Pārā. 578), but also when one has it dyed.

(Da) rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇasseva (pārā. 589) paṭikkhittattā paṭiggahitaparivattane dosaṃ apassantā katākatādivasena anekavidhaṃ jātarūpaparivattanaṃ karonti, taṃ sandhāya “nānappakāraka”nti vuttaṃ.

(Da) Since only the acceptance of money is prohibited (Pārā. 589), some, not seeing any fault in exchanging what has been accepted, engage in various kinds of exchange of gold and silver, based on whether it is wrought or unwrought, and so on. It is with reference to this that the words ‘of various kinds’ were spoken.

387-9. Āpattiṃ desetvā pacchā kattabbaṃ dassetuṃ “athā”ti vuttaṃ. Gihiṃ vadeti sace tattha āgacchati ārāmiko vā upāsako vā, taṃ vadeyyāti attho. Evaṃ vutto so “iminā kiṃ āharāmī”ti ce vadeyyāti attho. Avatvāmanti “imaṃ vā imaṃ vā āharā”ti avatvāti attho. Vadeti “kappiyaṃ ācikkhitabba”nti (pārā. 584, 589) vacanato “pabbajitānaṃ sappi vā telaṃ vā madhu vā phāṇitaṃ vā vaṭṭatī”ti evaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ, “imaṃ nāma āharā”ti na vattabbameva. Dvepeteti dvepi ete rūpiyapaṭiggāhakañca rūpiyasabyohārikañcāti attho. Aññenāti antamaso ārāmikenāpi laddhabhāgo na kappati eva.

387-9. The word 'then' is stated to show what should be done after confessing the offense. 'He speaks to a layperson': this means if a monastery attendant or a male lay follower comes there, one should speak to him. 'If he says': this means if, having been spoken to thus, he should say, 'What shall I bring with this?' 'Without saying': this means without saying, 'Bring this or that.' 'He speaks': one should indicate what is allowable, in accordance with the text (Pārā. 584, 589): 'What is allowable should be indicated.' Thus one should state: 'Ghee, oil, honey, or molasses are allowable for renunciants.' One should certainly not say: 'Bring such and such a thing.' 'Both': this means both the one who accepts money and the one who engages in transactions with money. 'By another': this means that even a share obtained through a monastery attendant is not allowable.

390. Antamaso (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-4) tannibbattā rukkhacchāyāpi na kappatīti. Nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭiladdhampīti ettha yathā rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ katvā laddhavatthuto [M 0.0200] ābhataṃ na kappati, tathā kosiyamissakasanthatādittayampi na kappati. Na kevalaṃ tasseva, aññesampi na kappateva “aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 545, 550, 555) vuttattā.

390. At the very least, even the shade of a tree (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.583-4) produced from it is not allowable. Regarding ‘Even what is relinquished and reacquired’: here, just as an item brought from a thing obtained through a monetary transaction is not allowable, so too the triad of items beginning with the felted rug mixed with silk is not allowable. It is not allowable for others either, not just for that one, because it is said: ‘If one receives and uses what was made by another, there is an offense of wrong conduct’ (Pārā. 545, 550, 555).

391. Evaṃ no ce labhetha, so ārāmikādiko “imaṃ chaḍḍehī”ti saṃsiyo vattabboti attho. Evampi no ce labheyya, sammato bhikkhu chaḍḍeyyāti attho.

391. If he does not succeed in this way, the meaning is that the monastery attendant or the like should be told, 'Discard this.' If he does not succeed even in this way, the meaning is that an authorized bhikkhu should discard it.

392. Paṭiggahitarūpiyañca parivattitarūpiyañca sandhāya “etānī”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyapatto nāma “ūnapañcabandhanena pattena aññaṃ navaṃ pattaṃ cetāpeyya, nissaggiya”nti (pārā. 612) vuttapatto. So ca etāni ca saṅghe nissaṭṭhuṃ labbhareti sambandho. “Saṅghamajjhe nissajjitabbaṃ, bhikkhuparisāya nissajjitabba”nti (pārā. 584, 589) ca vuttattā na gaṇapuggalānaṃ [V 0.0181] nissajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sesāni pana tīṇi cīvarādivatthūni “nissajjitabbaṃ saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā”ti vuttattā (pārā. 463) saṅghādīnaṃ nissajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhāsantarenapīti pāḷiyā vattuṃ asakkontena damiḷabhāsādīsu aññatarāyapi nissajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti attho.

392. The word 'these' was spoken with reference to both accepted money and exchanged money. The 'second bowl' is the bowl mentioned in the rule (Pārā. 612): 'If a bhikkhu, having a bowl with fewer than five mends, should have another new bowl acquired, it is to be forfeited.' The connection is that that bowl and these items may be relinquished in the Sangha. And since it is said (Pārā. 584, 589), 'It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha; it should be relinquished in an assembly of bhikkhus,' it is not proper to relinquish them to a group or an individual. However, as it is said of the other three items—robes and so on—'It should be relinquished to the Sangha, or to a group, or to an individual' (Pārā. 463), it is proper to relinquish them to the Sangha and so on. 'Even in another language': this means that if one is unable to speak Pāli, it is proper to relinquish it in some other language, such as Tamil.

393. (Ka-ga) nānappakārakaṃ nāma “cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā, “antamaso cuṇṇapiṇḍopi dantakaṭṭhampi dasikasuttampī”ti (pārā. 595) pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Cetāpitoti (pārā. 613) yācitvā gahito.

393. (Ka-ga) 'Of various kinds' refers to what is stated in the Pāli text (Pārā. 595): 'robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, down to a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, and a needle-thread.' 'Having had it acquired' (Pārā. 613) means obtained by requesting.

394. Sammannitvāna pattagāhakaṃ saṅghassa pattantanti (pārā. 614; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. ūnapañcabaddhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) ya antimaṃ pattaṃ, taṃ tassa dāpayeti attho.

394. 'Having authorized a bowl-receiver... the Sangha's final bowl...' (Pārā. 614; Kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. Ūnapañcabaddhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā): the meaning is that the last bowl should be given to him.

395. (Kha) paridahitaṃ [M 0.0201] nissaggiyanti ettha (pārā. 626-628; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.628) pana ṭhatvā vassikasāṭikāya pariyesanakkhettaṃ karaṇakkhettaṃ nivāsanakkhettaṃ adhiṭṭhānakkhettanti catubbidhaṃ khettañca kucchisamayo piṭṭhisamayoti duvidho samayo ca veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Gimhānamāsesu pacchimamāsassa purimo aḍḍhamāso pariyesanakkhettaṃ, pacchimo karaṇakkhettañca nivāsanakkhettañca, pariyesitumpi vaṭṭati, adhiṭṭhātuṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Vassikā pana cattāro māsā pariyesanādīnaṃ catunnampi khettaṃ. Ete eva pañca māsā kucchisamayo nāma. Itare satta māsā piṭṭhisamayo, tattha satuppādakaraṇaṃ na vaṭṭati.

395. (Kha) Regarding '...is to be forfeited' (Pārā. 626-628; Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.628): here, in the case of the rains-bathing cloth, the fourfold field and the twofold period should be understood. The fourfold field is: the field of seeking, the field of making, the field of wearing, and the field of determination. The twofold period is: the belly period and the back period. How so? Of the summer months, the first half of the last month is the field of seeking; the second half is the field of making and the field of wearing. It is proper to seek it then, but not to determine it. The four months of the rains are the field for all four: seeking, etc. These five months are called the belly period. The other seven months are the back period; during that time it is not proper to have a cloth made from a new production.

(Ga) acchinnanti ettha “yo pana mama pattacīvarādīni vahanto mayā saddhiṃ carissatī”ti saññāya cīvaraṃ datvā puna sakasaññāya eva attano veyyāvaccaṃ akarontaṃ disvā acchindati, so imaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Kevalaṃ pariccajitvā dinnaṃ gahetumeva na labhati.

(Ga) 'Seizes back': here, a bhikkhu gives a robe with the thought, 'This person will carry my bowl, robes, etc., and travel with me.' Then, seeing that the person is not performing the service for him, he seizes it back with the same intention. He incurs this offense. One is not allowed to take back what has been given after having been completely relinquished.

(Gha) suttaṃ viññāpetvāti ettha cīvarakārasamayādīsu cīvarasibbanādīnamatthāya suttaṃ viññāpetvāti attho. Aññathā suttaṃ viññāpetumeva na vaṭṭati. Viññattiyā eva laddhatantavāyehīti [V 0.0182] attho. Suttatantavāyānaṃ akappiyabhāve sati dīghato vidatthimatte, tiriyantato hatthamatte vīte nissaggiyaṃ, ekato akappiyapakkhe dukkaṭaṃ.

(Gha) 'Having requested thread': here the meaning is having requested thread during the robe-making season for the purpose of sewing robes, etc. Otherwise, it is not proper to request thread. The meaning is 'from weavers from whom it was obtained by that very request.' If the thread and the weaving are unsuitable, and the cloth exceeds a span in length and a cubit in width, it is to be forfeited. If it is unsuitable on one count, there is an offense of wrong conduct.

(Ṅa) vikappaṃ āpannanti (pārā. 643) “idaṃ kho, āvuso, cīvaraṃ maṃ uddissa viyyati, āyatañca karotha vitthatañcā”tiādinā adhikaṃ vidhānaṃ āpannanti attho.

(Ṅa) 'Having made a stipulation' (Pārā. 643): the meaning is having made an excessive instruction, such as by saying, 'Friends, this robe is being woven for me; make it long and wide,' and so on.

(Ca) accekacīvaraṃ (pārā. 649-650) nāma senāya gantukāmādīhi dinnaṃ.

(Ca) An 'urgent robe' (Pārā. 649-650) is one given by those intending to go to war, and so on.

(Cha) atirekachārattanti (pārā. 654-655) [M 0.0202] chadivasato atirekaṃ. “Atthatakathinānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, pañca kappissanti, anāmantacāro asamādānacāro gaṇabhojanaṃ yāvadatthacīvaraṃ yo ca tattha cīvaruppādo, so nesaṃ bhavissatī”ti (mahāva. 306) vuttaānisaṃsesu cīvaramāse asamādānacāraṃ ṭhapetvā sesānisaṃsā labbhanti. Yadi asamādānacāro labbheyya, pāveyyakā bhikkhū vassaṃvutthā okapuṇṇehi cīvarehi na bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkameyyuṃ, yasmā taṃ na labhanti, tasmā cīvaramāsepi ticīvaraṃ ādāya eva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tasmā veditabbaṃ asamādānacāraparihāraṃ atthatakathinā eva labhanti, na itareti vadanti.

(Cha) 'For more than six nights' (Pārā. 654-655) means for more than six days. Among the benefits mentioned in the passage (Mahāva. 306), 'Bhikkhus, for you for whom the kathina has been spread, five things are allowable: wandering without taking leave, wandering without having determined the three robes, group meals, as much robe-cloth as you need, and whatever robe-cloth arises there will be for you'—of these, during the robe-month, the other benefits are obtained, except for wandering without having determined the three robes. If the benefit of wandering without having determined the three robes were obtainable, the bhikkhus from Pāvā, having completed the rains retreat, would not have approached the Blessed One with water-logged robes. Since they did not obtain that benefit, they approached the Blessed One even during the robe-month only after taking their three robes. Therefore, it should be understood that only those for whom the kathina has been spread obtain the exemption regarding wandering without having determined the three robes, not others—so they say.

397. (Kha) “ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ pāṭidesanīyāpattiṃ, dve, sambahulā pāṭidesanīyāpattiyo āpajji”nti imaṃ pana yesu potthakesu likhitaṃ, taṃ abhayagirivāsīnaṃ khuddasikkhāvasena dassitaṃ kira. Tattha “ahaṃ, āyasmā, sambahulā pāṭidesanīyā āpattiyo āpanno, tāyo paṭidesemi. Ahaṃ, āyasmā, ekaṃ pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ paṭidesemī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Amhākaṃ pana evaṃ desanāvidhānaṃ natthi. “Gārayhaṃ, āvuso, dhammaṃ āpajjiṃ asappāyaṃ pāṭidesanīyaṃ, taṃ paṭidesemī”ti (pāci. 553) vuttaṃ. Samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pāci. 553) “gārayhaṃ āvuso’tiādi paṭidesetabbākāradassana”nti vuttaṃ. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “tassā desetabbākāro gārayhaṃ āvuso’tiādinā nayena sikkhāpade dassitoyevā”ti vuttattā pāṭhe āgatanayeneva desanāvidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sace dve honti, “gārayhe, āvuso, dve dhamme āpajjiṃ asappāye pāṭidesanīye, te paṭidesemī”ti, “passatha, bhante, te dhamme”ti [M 0.0203] ca “gārayhe[V 0.0183], āvuso, sambahule dhamme āpajjiṃ asappāye pāṭidesanīye, te paṭidesemī”ti, “passatha, bhante, te dhamme”ti ca evaṃ yathānurūpaṃ desanāvidhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttappakāramevāti.

397. (Kha) "Venerable sir, I have committed one offense requiring acknowledgment, two, several offenses requiring acknowledgment." This is written in some books, and it is said to be shown in accordance with the Khuddasikkhā of the Abhayagiri residents. There, it is said: "Venerable sir, I have committed several offenses requiring acknowledgment; I acknowledge them. Venerable sir, I have committed one offense requiring acknowledgment; I acknowledge it." But for us, there is no such method of confession. It is said: "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable matter requiring acknowledgment; I acknowledge it" (Pāci. 553). In the Samantapāsādikā (Pāci. 553), it is said: "The showing of the way it should be acknowledged is by 'blameworthy, friend,' etc." In the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī (Kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) too, since it is said, "The way it should be confessed has been shown in the training rule itself by the method beginning with 'blameworthy, friend,'" the method of confession should be understood according to the method that has come down in the text. If there are two, the method of confession should be understood accordingly as: "Friend, I have committed two blameworthy, unsuitable matters requiring acknowledgment; I acknowledge them," and "Venerable sirs, see these matters." And if there are several: "Friend, I have committed several blameworthy, unsuitable matters requiring acknowledgment; I acknowledge them," and "Venerable sirs, see these matters." The rest is as has been stated.

398. Adesanāgāminiyanti (pari. 424 ādayo; pari. aṭṭha. 425) pārājikañca saṅghādisesañca na desayeti attho. Anāpattiñcāti anāpattiṃ eva “āpatti”nti na desaye. Lahukāpattimpi pubbe desitaṃ puna na desayeti sambandho, nānāsaṃvāsanissīmaṭṭhitānaṃ santike na desayeti attho. Catupañcahīti ettha samānavassikapavāraṇāyaṃ viya catūhi vā pañcahi vā ekato hutvā ekassa santike na desayeti attho. Dvinnaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ vā vaṭṭati. Kathaṃ desetabbanti ce? Ekassa santike tīhipi ekato nisīditvā “ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ pācittiyāpattiṃ āpajjiṃ, taṃ tumhamūle paṭidesemī”ti evaṃ attanā āpannaāpattivasena vutte tena “passasi, āvuso, taṃ āpatti”nti evaṃ tikkhattuṃ vutte “āma, bhante, passāmī”ti vā “āmāvuso passāmī”ti vā vutte puna tena “āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāthā”ti vā “saṃvareyyāsī”ti vā vutte “sādhu suṭṭhu saṃvarissāmī”ti vattabbaṃ, evaṃ desetabbaṃ. Manasāti vacībhedaṃ akatvā kevalaṃ citteneva na desayeti attho. Apakatattānanti antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassa vā ukkhittakassa vā uposatho pavāraṇā vā ṭhapitā honti, tassa santike na desayeti attho. Nānekāti nānāpattiyo “ekā”ti vatvā na desayeti attho. Ekā pana “sambahulā”ti desitā hotīti. Desanāvinicchayo.

398. The meaning of Adesanāgāminiyanti is that one does not confess a pārājika or saṅghādisesa offense. And anāpattiñcāti means one does not declare what is not an offense as 'an offense.' The connection is that even a minor offense previously confessed should not be confessed again; the meaning is that one should not confess in the presence of those of a different communion or those standing outside the boundary. Catupañcahīti here means that, as in the case of the Pavāraṇā for those of the same number of rains, one should not confess to one person when four or five are gathered together. It is permissible for two or three. If it is asked, 'How should one confess?' When three people have sat down together in the presence of one person, one should say, 'Venerable sir, I have committed a pācittiya offense, which I confess before you.' When this is stated by the one who has committed the offense, the other should say three times, 'Do you see this offense, friend?' When the response is, 'Yes, venerable sir, I see it,' or 'Yes, friend, I see it,' then the other should say, 'You should restrain yourselves in the future,' or 'Restrain yourself.' The reply should be, 'Good, I will restrain myself well.' This is how it should be confessed. Manasāti means one should not confess with the mind alone, without a verbal utterance. Apakatattānanti means that one should not confess in the presence of someone who has committed a final offense or has been suspended, for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been suspended. Nānekāti means not declaring multiple offenses as 'one.' However, one offense may be declared as 'several.' This is the determination of confession.

Desanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Confession is concluded.

43. Chandadānaniddesavaṇṇanā

43. The Commentary on the Exposition of Giving Consent

399. Kammappatte [M 0.0204] saṅghe samāgateti sambandho. Etena saṅghe asamāgate chandadānaṃ na ruhatīti dīpitaṃ hotīti vadanti. Etthāyaṃ vicāraṇā – pañcabhikkhuke vihāre ekassa chandapārisuddhiṃ [V 0.0184] āharitvā sesānaṃ uposathādikaraṇaṃ anuññātaṃ pāḷiyaṃ (pari. 496-497) aṭṭhakathāyañca (pari. aṭṭha. 487-488). Tesu eko chandadāyako, eko chandahārako, te muñcitvā na ettha sannipatito saṅgho tiṇṇaṃ samūhabhāvato, tasmā asamāgatepi dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Ārocentena pana samāgate eva ārocetabbaṃ. Idhāpi “hareyyā”ti vuttaṃ, na “deseyyā”ti. Tattha chandahārakena saddhiṃ kammappattānaṃ sannipāto veditabbo.
