399. The connection is with the Sangha, fit for a formal act, being assembled. This indicates, they say, that giving consent is not valid when the Sangha is not assembled. Here is a consideration: In a monastery with five bhikkhus, when one brings consent and purity, the others are permitted to perform the Uposatha and other acts, as stated in the Pāli and in the commentary. Among them, one is the giver of consent, and one is the bearer of consent; excluding these, the Sangha is not assembled here, since it is a group of three. Therefore, it is permissible to give consent even when the Sangha is not assembled. However, the one announcing it should do so only when the Sangha is assembled. Here too, 'he should bring' is said, not 'he should declare.' There, the assembly of those fit for the formal act, along with the bearer of consent, should be understood.

400. Idāni chandadānavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “ekaṃ bhikkhu”ntiādimāha (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā).

400. Now, to show the method of giving consent, he said, 'one bhikkhu,' and so on.

401. (Ka) “chandaṃ dammī”ti ettakameva alaṃ, “hara, ārocehī”ti imehi kiṃpayojananti ce? Vuccate – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe pārisuddhiṃ dentena chandampidātuṃ, santi saṅghassa karaṇīya”nti (mahāva. 165) vuttattā bhagavato āṇaṃ karontena “chandaṃ dammī”ti vuttaṃ. “Chandahārako ce, bhikkhave, dinne chande antarāmagge pakkamati, anāhaṭova hoti chando”ti (mahāva. 165) vuttattā chandahārakassa aññassa apakkamanatthāya pārisuddhiṃ dentena “idaṃ karohi evā”ti āṇāpentena “chandaṃ me harā”ti vuttaṃ. “Chandahārako ce, bhikkhave, dinne chande saṅghappatto sañcicca nāroceti, āhaṭo hoti chando, chandahārakassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 165) vuttattā “yaditvaṃ sañcicca nārocessasi, āpattiṃ āpajjissasi[M 0.0205], ārocehi evā”ti tassa ācikkhanto “ārocehī”ti āhāti evamettha imesaṃ padānaṃ sappayojanatā veditabbā. Evaṃ pārisuddhidānepīti.

401. (Ka) 'I give my consent'—is this alone sufficient? 'Carry it, announce it'—what is the purpose of these words?” It is said: Because it is stated, “I allow, bhikkhus, that on the Uposatha day, when giving purity, consent may also be given, since the Sangha has business to attend to,” one carrying out the Blessed One's command says, “I give my consent.” Because it is stated, “If, bhikkhus, the consent-bearer, having received consent, departs on the way, the consent is as good as not conveyed,” the one giving purity, so that the consent-bearer does not depart, commanding, “Do just this,” says, “Carry my consent.” Because it is stated, “If, bhikkhus, the consent-bearer, having received consent, arrives at the Sangha but deliberately does not announce it, the consent is considered conveyed, but the consent-bearer incurs an offense of wrong-doing,” one instructs him, “If you deliberately do not announce it, you will incur an offense—announce it,” and says, “Announce it.” Thus, the purposefulness of these words should be understood in this context. So too in giving purity.

402. Sesakammanti yadi saṅgho uposathagge aññaṃ apalokanādikammaṃ karoti, taṃ kammaṃ vibādhati, vikopetīti attho.

402. 'The remaining formal act': if the Sangha, in the Uposatha hall, performs another formal act such as an announcement, it obstructs that act, it spoils it—this is the meaning.

403. Dvayanti uposathañca sesakammañcāti attho. Nattanoti attano uposathaṃ na sampādeti.

403. 'Both' means both the Uposatha and the remaining formal act. 'Not for oneself' means one does not accomplish one's own Uposatha.

405. “Ekaṃsaṃ [V 0.0185] uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā”tiādikaṃ (mahāva. 213) sabbūpacāraṃ katvānāti attho.

405. 'Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down in the squatting position,' etc., means having performed all the proper formalities.

406. “Itthannāmena pavāraṇā dinnā”ti ārocetvā.

406. Having announced, 'The Pavāraṇā has been given by someone named so-and-so.'

408. Paṭijāneyya nāhaṭāti (mahāva. 164-165, 213) pāṭhe na āhaṭāti nāhaṭā, āhaṭā na hotīti attho. Tathā heyyāti vibbhamanādīni kareyyāti attho.

408. 'He might claim it was not brought': in the text, nāhaṭā is na āhaṭā (not brought); the meaning is it has not been brought. 'Similarly, he might behave improperly' means he might do things such as deceiving, etc.—this is the meaning.

409. Sutto vā nārocayeyya, āhaṭā hotīti sambandho. Anāpattivāti anāpatti eva. Chandadānavinicchayo.

409. If he is asleep or does not announce it, the connection is: it is considered brought. 'No offense' means there is indeed no offense. The Determination of Giving Consent.

Chandadānaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Giving Consent is concluded.

44. Uposathaniddesavaṇṇanā

44. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Uposatha

411. Suttuddeso saṅghasseva. Sesānanti dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā.

411. The recitation of the Sutta is for the Sangha alone. 'The remaining ones' means for two or three.

412. Pubbakaraṇe [M 0.0206] pubbakicce, pattakalle samāniteti sabbapaṭhamaṃ kattabbaṃ pubbakaraṇaṃ. Tadanantaraṃ kattabbaṃ pubbakiccaṃ nāma. Ettha –

412. Regarding preliminary preparations and preliminary duties, 'when it is brought to a state of fitness' means that the preliminary preparation is what should be done first. What should be done immediately after that is called the preliminary duty. Here:

“Sammajjanī padīpo ca, udakaṃ āsanena ca;

Uposathassa etāni, pubbakaraṇanti vuccati.

“Sweeping, a lamp, water, and a seat—these are called the preliminary preparations for the Uposatha.

“Chandapārisuddhiutukkhānaṃ, bhikkhugaṇanā ca ovādo;

Uposathassa etāni, pubbakiccanti vuccatī”ti –. (mahāva. aṭṭha. 168);

“Giving of consent and purity, announcement of the season, counting the bhikkhus, and the exhortation—these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.”

Evaṃ [V 0.0186] aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena pubbakaraṇañca pubbakiccañca veditabbaṃ.

Thus, according to the method stated in the commentary, both the preliminary preparations and the preliminary duties should be understood.

“Uposatho yāvatikā ca bhikkhū kammappattā,

Sabhāgāpattiyo ca na vijjanti;

Vajjanīyā ca puggalā tasmiṃ na honti,

Pattakallanti vuccatī”ti –. (mahāva. aṭṭha. 168);

“The Uposatha is said to be fit when as many bhikkhus as are qualified for the act are present, and there are no shared offenses, and no individuals who should be excluded are present.”

Vuttavasena pattakalle samānite, pajjiteti attho. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, pātimokkhuddesā. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ paṭhamo pātimokkhuddeso. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā cattāri pārājikāni uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ dutiyo pātimokkhuddeso. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā cattāri pārājikāni uddisitvā terasa saṅghādisese uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ tatiyo pātimokkhuddeso. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā cattāri pārājikāni uddisitvā terasa saṅghādisese uddisitvā dve aniyate uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ, ayaṃ catuttho pātimokkhuddeso. Vitthāreneva pañcamo. Ime kho bhikkhave pañca pātimokkhuddesā”ti (mahāva. 150) vuttattā so suttuddeso pañcadhā vibhāvitoti attho.

When it is brought to a state of fitness in accordance with what has been said, it is recited—this is the meaning. “Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha. First, having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by the Sutta—this is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. Second, having recited the Nidāna and recited the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by the Sutta—this is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha. Third, having recited the Nidāna, recited the four Pārājikas, and recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, the remainder should be announced by the Sutta—this is the third recitation of the Pātimokkha. Fourth, having recited the Nidāna, recited the four Pārājikas, recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, and recited the two Aniyatas, the remainder should be announced by the Sutta—this is the fourth recitation of the Pātimokkha. The fifth is the full one. These, bhikkhus, are the five recitations of the Pātimokkha,” thus it is stated; the meaning is that that recitation of the Sutta is distinguished in five ways.

413. Vināntarāyanti (mahāva. 150) [M 0.0207] rājantarāyādidasavidhaṃ antarāyaṃ vinā saṅkhepenuddeso vinivārito paṭikkhittoti attho. Therovāti saṅghattherova. Etthāti pañcasu uddesesu. “Dvīsu vā tīsu vā visadesu therova issaro”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā avattantepi antarāye saṃkhittena uddisituṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Kattha vuttanti ce? “Yo tattha bhikkhu byatto paṭibalo, tassādheyya”nti (mahāva. 155) vuttapāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yo tattha bhikkhu byatto paṭibaloti ettha kiñcāpi daharassāpi byattassa pātimokkho anuññāto, atha kho ettha ayamadhippāyo – sace saṅghattherassa pañca vā cattāro vā tayo vā pātimokkhuddesā nāgacchanti, dve pana akhaṇḍā suvisadā vācuggatā honti, therāyattova pātimokkho. Sace pana ettakampi visadaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, byattassa bhikkhuno āyattova hotī”ti attho vutto. Pāḷiyampi vuttameva “tehi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūhi eko bhikkhu sāmantā [V 0.0187] āvāsā sajjukaṃ pāhetabbo ‘gaccha, āvuso, saṃkhittena vā vitthārena vā pātimokkhaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā āgacchā’”ti (mahāva. 163).

413. 'Without obstacles' (vināntarāyaṃ) (Mahāva. 150) means without the ten kinds of obstacles such as royal interference, etc. The meaning is that the summary recitation is prevented, warded off, and rejected. 'The elder' (thero) means the Sangha's elder. 'Here' (ettha) means in these five recitations. 'In two or three clear sections, the elder alone is the authority,' so the commentary states. Therefore, even if no obstacle exists, it is fitting to recite in brief—this is the intention. If it is asked, 'Where is it stated?' In the commentary to the Pali passage that states: 'That bhikkhu who is skilled and capable, it depends on him' (Mahāva. 155). The commentary on 'That bhikkhu who is skilled and capable' says: 'Although here the Pātimokkha is permitted even to a young skilled bhikkhu, the meaning intended here is this: if the Sangha's elder cannot remember five, four, or three recitations of the Pātimokkha, but can recite two unbroken and very clear sections, then the Pātimokkha is dependent on the elder. But if he is unable to make even this much clear, then it is dependent on a skilled bhikkhu.' The Pali text itself also states, 'Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus should promptly send one bhikkhu from a neighboring monastery, saying, "Go, friend, and learn the Pātimokkha in brief or in detail and return"' (Mahāva. 163).

414. Uddisante vāti (mahāva. 172) pātimokkhe uddisiyamāne samā vā thokatarā vā yadi āgaccheyyuṃ, uddiṭṭhaṃ suuddiṭṭhaṃ, tehi saddhiṃ nisīditvā avasesakaṃ sotabbanti attho.

414. 'Uddisante vā' (Mahāva. 172): The meaning is that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, if an equal or fewer number arrive, what has been recited is well-recited; one should sit with them and listen to the remainder.

415. Uddiṭṭhamatte (mahāva. 172) vā sakalāya vā ekaccāya vā parisāya vuṭṭhitāya samā vā thokatarā vā yadi āgaccheyyunti sambandho. Pārisuddhinti pārisuddhiuposathaṃ. Kareyyesanti kareyya esaṃ, etesaṃ santiketi attho. Bahukātha ceti atha bahukā ce, puna āgatā bahukā ceti attho[M 0.0208],. “Uddissamāne, uddiṭṭhamatte ekaccāya vuṭṭhitāya sakalāya vuṭṭhitāyā”ti (mahāva. 172) āgatesu sabbavikappesu pubbakiccaṃ katvā puna ādito paṭṭhāya pātimokkhaṃ uddiseti attho.

415. 'Uddiṭṭhamatte' (Mahāva. 172): The connection is that if an equal or fewer number arrive just as it has been recited, or when the entire assembly or a part of it has risen. 'Pārisuddhiṃ' means the purification Uposatha. 'Kareyyesan' (kareyya esaṃ) means 'he should perform it for them,' that is, in their presence. 'Bahukātha ca' means 'but if they are many,' that is, if those who have come again are many. The meaning is that in all these possible cases of arrival—'while being recited, when it has been recited, when a part has risen, when the entire assembly has risen' (Mahāva. 172)—having completed the preliminary duties, he should recite the Pātimokkha again from the beginning.

416. Itarānanti āgantukānaṃ. Sacetaroti sace cātuddasikoti attho. Samānetarenuvattantūti samā vā ūnā vā itare āgantukā purimānaṃ āvāsikānaṃ anuvattantūti attho. Sacedhikāti āgantukā sace adhikā, purimā āvāsikā anuvattantūti attho. Sesepyayaṃ nayoti “āgantukānaṃ pannaraso hoti, āvāsikānaṃ cātuddaso”ti itarepi samathokā āgantukā āvāsikānaṃ anuvattantūtiādinā nayena vinicchayo veditabboti attho.

416. 'Itarānaṃ' means 'of the others,' that is, of the newcomers. 'Sacetaro' means 'if it is the other,' that is, 'if it is the fourteenth.' 'Samānetarenuvattantu' means that if the other newcomers are equal or fewer, they should follow the former resident bhikkhus—this is the meaning. 'Sacedhikā' means that if the newcomers are more numerous, the former resident bhikkhus should follow them—this is the meaning. 'This method applies to the rest as well' means that the decision should be understood by this method in the remaining cases as well, such as when 'the newcomers' day is the fifteenth and the residents' is the fourteenth,' where the other newcomers, being equal or fewer, should follow the residents, and so on.

417. Mūlaṭṭhāti āvāsikā. Samathokānaṃ āgantukānaṃ. Sāmaggiṃ dentu kāmatoti yadi icchanti, dentūti attho.

417. 'Mūlaṭṭhā' means 'the residents.' 'Samathokānaṃ āgantukānaṃ' means 'of the newcomers who are equal or fewer.' 'Sāmaggiṃ dentu kāmato' means 'let them give harmony willingly,' that is, 'if they wish, let them give it.'

418. No ce denti, āgantukehi bahi gantvāna uposatho kātabboti attho. Anicchāya sāmaggī deyyāti sambandho.

418. If they do not grant it, the meaning is that the newcomers should go outside and perform the Uposatha. The connection is with 'harmony should be given unwillingly' (anicchāya sāmaggiṃ deyya).

419. “Na bhikkhave pātimokkhuddesakena sañcicca na sāvetabbaṃ. Yo na sāveyya, āpatti [V 0.0188] dukkaṭassā”tivuttattā (mahāva. 154) “sāveyya sutta”nti vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pātimokkhuddesakena vāyamituṃ kathaṃ sāveyyanti, vāyamantassa anāpattī”ti (mahāva. 154) vuttattā “sañcicca assāventassa dukkaṭa”nti vuttaṃ.

419. Because it is stated (Mahāva. 154), "Bhikkhus, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should not intentionally fail to make it heard. Whoever does not make it heard commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," therefore 'should make the Sutta heard' (sāveyya suttaṃ) is stated. Because it is stated (Mahāva. 154), "Bhikkhus, I allow the reciter of the Pātimokkha to make an effort as to how to make it heard; for one who makes an effort, there is no offense," therefore 'for one who intentionally does not make it heard, there is a wrong-doing' (sañcicca assāventassa dukkaṭaṃ) is stated.

420. Tathāti [M 0.0209] dukkaṭanti attho. Kalloti agilāno. Pesitoti āṇatto. “Na bhikkhave therena āṇattena agilānena na sammajjitabbaṃ. Yo na sammajjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādi (mahāva. 159) vuttaṃ.

420. 'Tathā' means 'similarly,' that is, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 'Kallo' means 'not ill.' 'Pesito' means 'ordered.' As it is stated (Mahāva. 159), "Bhikkhus, one who is not ill, having been ordered by an elder, should not fail to sweep. Whoever does not sweep incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," etc.

421-3. Idāni pārisuddhiuposathaṃ dassetuṃ “sammajjitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Añjaliṃ (mahāva. 168) paggayhāti sambandho. Teti avasesā dve evaṃ samudīriyā vattabbāti attho. Ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgādikaraṇavasena samattapubbārambhena te dve bhikkhū navena evamīriyā vattabbāti attho.

Now, to explain the purification Uposatha (pārisuddhiuposatha), 'having swept' (sammajjitvā) and so forth is stated. The connection is with 'having raised the joined hands' (añjaliṃ paggayha) (Mahāva. 168). The meaning is that the remaining two should be addressed in this way. The meaning is that by arranging the upper robe over one shoulder and making a complete preliminary act, those two bhikkhus should be addressed anew in this way.

424-5. Idāni dvīhi kattabbaṃ dassetuṃ “dvīsu therenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, to show what should be done by two, 'when there are two, by the elder' (dvīsu therenā) is stated.

426. Ettāvatā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ pātimokkhaṃ uddisitu”nti (mahāva. 168) ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiṇṇaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 168) ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dvinnaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 168) ca vuttaṃ saṅghuposathañca pārisuddhiuposathañca dassetvā idāni yattha eko bhikkhu viharati, tassa anuññātaṃ adhiṭṭhānuposathaṃ dassetuṃ “pubbakicca”ntiādimāha. Ettha ca pubbakiccaṃ nāma sammajjanādikaṃyeva.

426. Up to this point, having shown the communal Uposatha (saṅghuposatha) and the purification Uposatha (pārisuddhiuposatha) by quoting, "Bhikkhus, I allow the recitation of the Pātimokkha for four" (Mahāva. 168), and "Bhikkhus, I allow the performance of the purification Uposatha for three" (Mahāva. 168), and "Bhikkhus, I allow the performance of the purification Uposatha for two" (Mahāva. 168), now, in order to show the determination Uposatha (adhiṭṭhānuposatha) allowed where a single bhikkhu dwells, he said, 'preliminary duties' (pubbakiccaṃ) and so on. And here, 'preliminary duties' means just sweeping and so forth.

427. Saṅghuposathapārisuddhiuposathaadhiṭṭhānauposathānaṃ vasena taṃ taṃ uposathaṃ yadi kayirunti sambandho.

427. The connection is with 'if one should perform the respective Uposatha'—that is, the communal Uposatha, the purification Uposatha, or the determination Uposatha—according to the case.

428. Vagge (mahāva. 173) ca samagge ca “vaggo”ti saññino ca “vaggo nu kho, samaggo nu kho”ti evaṃ vimatissa ca dukkaṭaṃ, “nassantete vinassantete, ko tehi attho”ti [V 0.0189] evaṃ [M 0.0210] anāgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ ñatvā bhedādhippāyena uposathaṃ karoto thullaccayaṃ hotīti attho. Tadubhayepi “samaggo”ti saññino anāpatti.

428. In the case of a faction (vagge) (Mahāva. 173) or a harmonious group (samagge), for one who perceives it as 'a faction' or is doubtful, thinking, 'Is it a faction or is it harmonious?'—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who, knowing of the existence of bhikkhus who have not yet arrived, performs the Uposatha with the intention of causing division, thinking, 'Let them be ruined, let them be destroyed, what is the use of them?'—there is a grave offense (thullaccaya)—this is the meaning. In both cases, if one perceives it as 'harmonious,' there is no offense.

429-430. Sesasahadhammikā nāma bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā cattāro. Abhabbassāti ettha paṇḍakatheyyasaṃvāsaka titthiyapakkantaka tiracchānagata mātughātaka pitughātaka arahantaghātaka bhikkhunidūsaka saṅghabhedaka lohituppādakaubhatobyañjanakā abhabbā gahitā. Ettha pana nāgamāṇavakādayo tiracchānagatapakkhikāti veditabbā. Etesaṃ nisinnaparisāyañca pātimokkhaṃ na uddiseti sambandho.

The 'remaining co-religionists' are the other four, excluding the bhikkhu. Here, 'those incapable' (abhabba) are taken to include: a eunuch, one who has entered the Sangha by stealth, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, and a hermaphrodite. Here, young nāgas and the like should be understood as included in the category of animals. The connection is that the Pātimokkha is not recited in an assembly where these are seated.

Tathāti yo pana saṅgho sabhāgāpattiko, sopi na uddise, parivutthena chandenapi na uddiseti attho. Ettha pana catubbidhaṃ pārivāsiyaṃ parisapārivāsiyaṃ rattipārivāsiyaṃ chandapārivāsiyaṃ ajjhāsayapārivāsiyanti.

Similarly, a Sangha that is collectively guilty of an offense should not recite; the meaning is that it should not be recited even with the consent of one living nearby. Here, there are four kinds of disqualification: disqualification of the assembly, disqualification by night, disqualification of consent, and disqualification by intention.

Ettha pana bhikkhū kenacideva karaṇīyena sannipatitā meghādīhi upaddutā “anokāsā mayaṃ, aññatra gacchāmā”ti chandaṃ avissajjetvāva uṭṭhahanti. Idaṃ parisapārivāsiyaṃ. Kiñcāpi parisapārivāsiyaṃ, chandassa pana avissaṭṭhattā kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Here, bhikkhus who have gathered for some business, being troubled by rain and so on, rise up, saying, 'We have no space; let us go elsewhere,' without having withdrawn their consent. This is a disqualification of the assembly. Although it is a disqualification of the assembly, since the consent has not been withdrawn, it is permissible to perform the formal act.

Punapi bhikkhūnaṃ “uposathādīni karissāmā”ti rattiṃ sannipatitvā dhammaṃ suṇantānaṃyeva aruṇo uggacchati. Sace “cātuddasikaṃ karissāmā”ti nisinnā, “pannaraso”ti kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pannarasikaṃ kātuṃ nisinnā, pāṭipade anuposathe uposathaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, aññaṃ pana saṅghakiccaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Idaṃ rattipārivāsiyaṃ nāma.

Again, for bhikkhus who have gathered at night thinking, 'We will perform the Uposatha and other duties,' dawn breaks while they are still listening to the Dhamma. If they sat down intending to perform the fourteenth-day observance, it is permissible to perform the fifteenth-day observance. If they sat down intending to perform the fifteenth-day observance, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha on the following day, which is a non-Uposatha day, but it is permissible to perform other formal acts of the Sangha. This is called being overtaken by night.

Puna [M 0.0211] bhikkhū “yaṃkiñcideva abbhānādikammaṃ karissāmā”ti sannipatitā honti, tatreko nakkhattapāṭhako evaṃ vadati “ajja nakkhattaṃ dāruṇa”nti, te tassa vacanena chandaṃ vissajjetvā tattheva nisinnā honti. Athañño āgantvā “kiṃ nakkhattena, karothā”ti vadati. Idaṃ chandapārivāsiyañceva ajjhāsayapārivāsiyañca. Tasmiṃ pārivāsiye puna chandapārisuddhiṃ anānetvā kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Idaṃ sandhāya “chandena parivutthenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Again, bhikkhus gather intending to perform some formal act such as rehabilitation, and one among them who reads the constellations says, 'Today the constellation is harsh.' At his words, they withdraw their consent and remain seated right there. Then another arrives and says, 'What does the constellation matter? Do it!' This is both being overtaken by consent and being overtaken by intention. In such a case, it is not permissible to perform the formal act without first restoring the purity of consent. It is with reference to this that it was said, 'when consent has been withdrawn.'

431. Āpannamāpattiṃ (mahāva. 169; mahāva. aṭṭha. 169) [V 0.0190] adesayitvāna vā “ahaṃ, āvuso, itthannāmāya āpattiyā vematiko, yadā nibbematiko bhavissāmi, taṃ āpattiṃ paṭikarissāmī”ti vatvā vimatiṃ anāvikatvāna vā “na ca bhikkhave anuposathe uposatho kātabbo aññatra saṅghasāmaggiyā”ti (mahāva. 183) vuttattā anuposathepi vā kātuṃ na ca kappatīti attho.

431. Either without having confessed a committed offense, or without having revealed one's doubt after saying, 'Venerable sirs, I am doubtful about such-and-such an offense; when I am free from doubt, I will deal with that offense,' or because it has been said: 'Bhikkhus, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day except for the sake of the Sangha's harmony,' it is not allowable to perform it even on a non-Uposatha day—this is the meaning.

432. “Na ca bhikkhave tadahuposathe sabhikkhukā āvāsā abhikkhuko āvāso vā anāvāso vā gantabbo aññatra saṅghena aññatra antarāyā”ti (mahāva. 181) vuttattā “aṭṭhitoposathāvāsā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 181) vuttaṃ. Na vaje na gacche. Adhiṭṭhātuṃ sīmameva vāti sace vihāre uposathaṃ karonti, uposathādhiṭṭhānatthaṃ sīmāpi nadīpi na gantabbā. Sace panettha koci bhikkhu hoti, tassa santikaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Vissaṭṭhauposathāpi āvāsā gantuṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ gato adhiṭṭhātumpi labhatīti. Uposathavinicchayo.

432. Because it has been said: 'Bhikkhus, on the Uposatha day, one should not go from a residence with bhikkhus to a residence without bhikkhus or to a non-residence, except with the Sangha or in case of an obstacle,' it is said: 'from a residence where the Uposatha is established.' One should not go; one should not leave. If they are performing the Uposatha in the monastery, one should not go even to the boundary or a river for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha. But if there is some bhikkhu there, it is permissible to go to him. It is also permissible to go from a residence where the Uposatha has been concluded, and having gone thus, one may undertake it. The Resolution on the Uposatha.

Uposathaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Uposatha is finished.

45. Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā

45. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Pavāraṇā

433. “Anujānāmi[M 0.0212], bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ saṅghe pavāretu”nti (mahāva. 215) vuttattā “sesā saṅghappavāraṇā”ti (mahāva. 215 ādayo) vuttā.

433. Because it has been said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, a Sangha of five to perform the Pavāraṇā,' it is said: 'the remaining are Sangha Pavāraṇās.'

434. Ajja pavāraṇāti ettha (mahāva. 215 ādayo) pana cātuddasikāya pavāraṇāya “ajja pavāraṇā cātuddasī”ti pubbakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ, pannarasiyaṃ “ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī”ti.

434. Here, regarding 'Today is the Pavāraṇā,' for the Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day, the preliminary duty should be performed by announcing: 'Today is the Pavāraṇā, the fourteenth'; and on the fifteenth: 'Today is the Pavāraṇā, the fifteenth.'

437. Theresu ukkuṭikaṃ nisajja pavārentesu sayaṃ pana navo yāva pavāreti, tāva ukkuṭikova acchatūti attho. “Na bhikkhave theresu ukkuṭikaṃ nisinnesu pavārayamānesu āsanesu [V 0.0191] acchitabbaṃ. Yo accheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tadamantarā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdituṃ, yāva pavāreti, pavāretvā āsane nisīditu”nti (mahāva. 211) hi vuttaṃ.

437. When the elder bhikkhus are sitting on their haunches performing the Pavāraṇā, a junior bhikkhu should himself remain on his haunches for as long as he performs the Pavāraṇā—this is the meaning. For it has been said: 'Bhikkhus, when the elder bhikkhus are sitting on their haunches performing the Pavāraṇā, one should not remain on a seat. Whoever should remain so, there is an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, bhikkhus, to sit on one's haunches in the meantime, for as long as one performs the Pavāraṇā; having performed the Pavāraṇā, one may sit on a seat.'

440-2. Evaṃ tevācikappavāraṇaṃ dassetvā idāni dvevācikaekavācikasamānavassikappavāraṇāsu kattabbaṃ dassetuṃ “dānenā”tiādimāha. Tattha dānenāti dānena vā. Dhammasākacchāti iminā dhammakathāsuttasaṅgāyanāvinayavinicchayādayo gahitā. Dānena vā dhammasākacchāya vā kalahena vā rattiyā khepitabhāvato tevācikāya okāse asati dasavidhe vā antarāye anurūpato uttiṃ ṭhapetvā pavāreyyāti sambandho.

440-2. Having thus shown the Pavāraṇā with three statements, now, in order to show what is to be done in the cases of the Pavāraṇā with two statements, with one statement, and for those of the same rains-residence, he says, 'by giving,' and so on. Here, 'by giving' means 'or by giving.' By 'Dhamma discussion' are included such things as Dhamma talks, Sutta recitations, Vinaya decisions, and so on. The connection is as follows: because the night has been spent in giving, or in Dhamma discussion, or in a quarrel, so that there is no opportunity for the Pavāraṇā with three statements, or because of one of the ten kinds of obstacles, one should perform the Pavāraṇā after having established an appropriate motion.

Idāni yathānurūpato ñatti ṭhapitā, taṃ dassetuṃ “suṇātu me”tiādimāha. Yathāṭhapitañattiyāti ettha sabbasaṅgāhikāceñattiṭhapitā, tevācikadvevācikaekavācikānaṃ vasena pavāretabbaṃ, samānavassikappavāraṇāva ekā na vaṭṭati. Sace “saṅgho tevācikaṃ pavāreyyā”ti ṭhapitā, tevācikā [M 0.0213] eva vaṭṭati, dvevācikādayo na vaṭṭanti. “Dvevācikaṃ pavāreyyā”ti vutte dvevācikañca tevācikañca vaṭṭati, ekavācikasamānavassikā na vaṭṭanti. “Ekavācikaṃ pavāreyyā”ti vutte pana samānavassikaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā vaṭṭanti. “Samānavassika”nti pana vutte sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti. Ādike cettha āhareti ettha pavāraṇāyapi pubbe uposathe vutte “yadi samā āgaccheyyu”ntiādike vāre āhareti attho.

Now, to show the motion established as appropriate, he says, 'Let the Sangha hear me,' and so on. Here, regarding 'according to the established motion': if an all-encompassing motion is established, the Pavāraṇā should be performed by way of three statements, two statements, or one statement; the Pavāraṇā for those of the same rains-residence alone is not permissible. If the motion is established as: 'Let the Sangha perform the Pavāraṇā with three statements,' only that with three statements is permissible; those with two statements, etc., are not permissible. When it is said: 'Let them perform the Pavāraṇā with two statements,' both that with two statements and that with three statements are permissible; that with one statement and that for those of the same rains-residence are not permissible. But when it is said: 'Let them perform the Pavāraṇā with one statement,' the others are permissible, setting aside that for those of the same rains-residence. But when it is said: 'for those of the same rains-residence,' all are permissible. Here, regarding 'one should adduce the initial cases,' the meaning is that one should adduce the initial cases stated previously in the Uposatha section that also apply to the Pavāraṇā, such as, 'if they should arrive in equal numbers,' and so on.

443. Idāni vattabbaṃ sandhāya “eva”nti vuttaṃ. Tivaggo ca catuvaggo ca ticatuvaggo.

443. Now, with reference to what is to be said, 'thus' is stated. A group of three and a group of four is a 'three-and-four-group'.

450. “Na bhikkhave sāpattikena pavāretabbaṃ. Yo pavāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 235) vuttattā sāpattikenapi vematikenapi pavāriyamāne āpattiṃ sarantenapi uposathe vuttanayena paṭipajjitabbaṃ. “Vagge samagge vaggoti-saññino vimatissa vā”tiādigāthāto paṭṭhāya yāva “antarāyaṃ va saṅghaṃ vā-dhiṭṭhātuṃ sīmameva vā”ti avasānagāthā, tāva sesā uposathe vuttā gāthāyoti adhippetā.

450. Because it has been said: 'Bhikkhus, one who has an offense should not perform the Pavāraṇā. Whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' one who has an offense, one who is doubtful, or one who remembers an offense while the Pavāraṇā is being performed should proceed in the manner stated for the Uposatha. Beginning from the verse, 'In a faction, perceiving it as a complete group, or being doubtful…' up to the concluding verse, '…or to determine an obstacle, or the Sangha, or even the boundary,' the remaining verses are intended as those stated in the Uposatha section.

451. Pavārite [V 0.0192] cāti (mahāva. 213 ādayo) paṭhamapavāraṇāya saṅghamhi pavāriteti adhippāyo. Ettha avutthoti pacchimikāya upagato apariniṭṭhitattā “avuttho”ti vuccati.

451. Regarding 'And when the Pavāraṇā has been performed,' the intention is that the Sangha has performed the Pavāraṇā of the first Pavāraṇā day. Here, 'one who has not resided' refers to one who has undertaken the later rains-residence; he is called 'one who has not resided' because he has not completed it.

452. Cātumāsinīti kattikapuṇṇamī. Ettha vutthavassā nāma pacchimikāya upagatā. Pavāraṇāvinicchayo.

452. 'The four-monthly' is the full moon of Kattika. Here, 'those who have completed the rains-residence' means those who undertook the later rains-residence. The Resolution on the Pavāraṇā.

Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Pavāraṇā is finished.

46. Saṃvaraniddesavaṇṇanā

46. Commentary on the Exposition of Restraint

453. Cakkhusotādibhedehīti (dī. ni. 1.213, 454; ma. ni. 1.411; a. ni. 4.198; dha. sa. 1352-1354; mahāni. 196) [M 0.0214] cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanasaṅkhātehi chahi indriyehīti attho. Rūpasaddādigocareti rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhammasaṅkhātesu chasu gocaresūti attho. Ettha pana hatthapādahasitakathitavilokitādibhedaṃ subhākāraṃ gahetvā ayoniso manasi karontassa abhijjhā uppajjati. “Anatthaṃ me acari, carati, carissatī”tiādinā (pari. aṭṭha. 329) nayena paṭighanimittaṃ gahetvā ayoniso manasi karontassa byāpādo uppajjati. Ettha pana itthipurisanimittaṃ vā subhanimittādikaṃ kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ aggaṇhitvā diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattādinā paṭipajjitvā asubhanimitte yoniso manasikāraṃ bahulīkarontassa abhijjhāya pahānaṃ hoti. “Anatthaṃ me acari, taṃ kutettha labbhā”tiādinā vā mettābhāvanādivasena vā yoniso manasi karontassa byāpādappahānaṃ hoti. Evamidaṃ saṅkhepato rūpādīsu kilesānubandhanimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlanti veditabbaṃ.

453. "By the diversity of eye, ear, etc.": This means by the six faculties designated as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "With forms, sounds, etc., as their objects": This means with the six objects designated as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangible objects, and mental phenomena. Here, when one attends improperly, having grasped a beautiful feature—the details of hands, feet, a smile, speech, or a glance—covetousness arises. When one attends improperly, having grasped a sign of aversion by way of thinking, "He has harmed me, is harming me, or will harm me," ill will arises. Here, however, for one who does not grasp the sign of a woman or a man, or any other beautiful sign that is a basis for the defilements, but practices in accordance with the principle "in the seen there will be only the seen," etc., and who frequently cultivates proper attention to the sign of the unattractive, covetousness is abandoned. For one who attends properly by way of thinking, "He has harmed me, but how can that be helped?" or by way of developing loving-kindness, etc., ill will is abandoned. Thus, in brief, the virtue of restraint of the faculties should be understood as having the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and features connected with the defilements in regard to forms, etc.

454.

454.

Niggaṇheyyāti nivāreyya;

“Yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ; (Ajitāti bhagavā,)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi;

Paññāyete pidhiyyare”ti –. (su. ni. 1041);

Niggaṇheyya (one should restrain) means nivāreyya (one should check). As it is said: "'Whatever streams there are in the world, Ajita,' said the Blessed One, 'mindfulness is their checking. I call it the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off.'" (Snp 1041)

Vuttattā [V 0.0193] “satimā sampajāno vā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha pana catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ sātthakasappāyagocaraasammohavasena. Saṃvaravinicchayo.

Because it has been said, it is stated: "mindful and clearly comprehending." Here, however, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose, of suitability, of the domain, and of non-delusion. The Determination of Restraint.

Saṃvaraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of Restraint is finished.

47. Suddhiniddesavaṇṇanā

47. Commentary on the Exposition of Purity

455. Desanā [M 0.0215] saṃvaro eṭṭhi, paccavekkhaṇa bhedatoti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.585; visuddhi. 1.19) desanāsuddhi saṃvarasuddhi pariyeṭṭhisuddhi paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti evaṃ catubbidhā suddhīti attho. Idāni tāhi suddhīhi visujjhanake dassetuṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarasammata”ntiādimāha.

455. Because of the verse fragment "confession, restraint, seeking, and reflection," the meaning is that purification is fourfold: purity by confession, purity by restraint, purity by seeking, and purity by reflection. Now, to show those who are purified by these purifications, the text states what begins with "consisting in the Pātimokkha restraint…"

456. “Puna evaṃ na karissa”nti cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvarā yasmā sujjhati indriyasaṃvaro, tasmā indriyasaṃvaro “saṃvarasuddhī”ti vuttoti sambandho.

456. The connection is this: because the restraint of the faculties is purified by the restraint that is the determination of mind, "I will not do so again," therefore the restraint of the faculties is called "purity of restraint."

457. Pahāyānesananti anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena uppādentassa paccayeti pāṭhaseso.

457. Pahāya anesanaṃ (having abandoned wrong livelihood): The rest of the passage is to be supplied as: "having abandoned wrong livelihood, for one who produces requisites in a righteous way."

458. “Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevāmi…pe… uppannānaṃ veyyābādhikānaṃ…pe… paramatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) ca evaṃ catūsupi paccayesu yathāvuttapaccavekkhaṇasujjhanāti attho. Ettha pana duvidhaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ paṭilābhakāle ca paribhogakāle ca. Paṭilābhakāle hi dhātuvasena vā paṭikkūlavasena vā paccavekkhitvā ṭhapitacīvarādīni tato uttari paribhuñjantassa anavajjova paribhogo, paribhogakālepi. Suddhivinicchayo.

458. "Wisely reflecting, I use the robe… for the relief of arisen painful feelings… for the utmost freedom from affliction." Thus, the meaning is that one is purified by reflection as stated in regard to all four requisites. Here, reflection is twofold: at the time of acquisition and at the time of use. For when one has reflected on the robes and other requisites at the time of their acquisition—either by way of the elements or by way of their repulsiveness—and has set them aside, for that person who later uses them, the use is blameless, even at the time of use. The Determination of Purity.

Suddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of Purity is finished.

48. Santosaniddesavaṇṇanā

48. Commentary on the Exposition of Contentment

459. “Cattārimāni[V 0.0194], bhikkhave, appāni ceva sulabhāni ca, tāni ca anavajjāni. Katamāni cattāri? Paṃsukūlaṃ, bhikkhave, cīvarānaṃ appañca sulabhañca, tañca anavajjaṃ. Piṇḍiyālopo, bhikkhave, bhojanānaṃ appañca sulabhañca, tañca anavajjaṃ. Rukkhamūlaṃ[M 0.0216], bhikkhave, senāsanānaṃ appañca sulabhañca, tañca anavajjaṃ. Pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ, bhikkhave, bhesajjānaṃ appañca sulabhañca, tañca anavajjaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri appāni ceva sulabhāni ca, tāni ca anavajjānī”ti (a. ni. 4.27; itivu. 101) vacanato “appenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

459. "Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless. What four? Among robes, bhikkhus, the rag-robe is of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless. Among foods, bhikkhus, alms-scraps are of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless. Among lodgings, bhikkhus, the root of a tree is of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless. Among medicines, bhikkhus, decomposing urine is of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless. These, bhikkhus, are the four things that are of little account, easy to obtain, and blameless." In accordance with this, it is said: "with little," etc.

Santuṭṭhoti ettha yathālābhayathābalayathāsāruppasantosānaṃ vasena ekekasmiṃ paccaye tayo tayo katvā catūsu paccayesu dvādasa santosā honti. Mattaññūti ettha (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.422; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.239; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.16; itivu. aṭṭha. 28; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 124-134) cattāro mattā pariyesanamattā paṭiggahaṇamattā paribhogamattā vissajjanamattāti. Itarītarena yāpento subharo nāma. Santosavinicchayo.

Santuṭṭho (content): Here, by way of the three kinds of contentment in regard to each single requisite—contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment according to what is suitable—there are twelve kinds of contentment in regard to the four requisites. Mattaññū (knowing moderation): Here, there are four kinds of moderation: moderation in seeking, moderation in accepting, moderation in using, and moderation in relinquishing. One who maintains oneself with anything whatsoever is called "easy to support." The Determination of Contentment.

Santosaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of Contentment is finished.

49. Caturārakkhaniddesavaṇṇanā

49. Commentary on the Exposition of the Four Protections

461-2. Asubhanti asubhabhāvanā. Ime cattāro caturārakkhā nāmāti adhippāyo. Idāni te dassetuṃ “ārakattādinā”tiādimāha. Ārakattādināti ettha ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi tāva catūhi kāraṇehi so bhagavā arahanti anussaritabboti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

"Unattractiveness" means the development of unattractiveness. These four are called the four protections—this is the meaning. Now, to show them, the text states what begins with 'because of being far,' etc. Here, 'because of being far, etc.' refers to: because of being far; because of destroying enemies and the spokes of the wheel; because of worthiness for requisites and the like; and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil. For these four reasons, that Blessed One should be recollected as an Arahant—this is the meaning. For it has been said—

“Ārakattā [V 0.0195] hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1; visuddhi. 1.130);

"Because of being far and because of having slain, that sage has slain the enemies which are the defilements; the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra are destroyed by him; he is worthy of requisites and so forth; he commits no evil in secret, therefore he is called an Arahant."

Bhagavā [M 0.0217] pana sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhito maggena savāsanakilesānaṃ hatattā, tasmā “ārakattā araha”nti vutto. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The Blessed One, however, stands exceedingly far from all defilements. Since by the path he has destroyed the defilements together with their latent tendencies, he is therefore called 'Arahant because of being far.' For it has been said:

“So tato ārakā nāma;

Yassa yenāsamaṅgitā;

Asamaṅgī ca dosehi,

Nātho tenārahaṃ mato”ti. (visuddhi. 1.125);

"He is therefore called 'far' (ārakā), from that with which he is unassociated; and being unassociated with faults, the Lord is therefore considered an Arahant."

Bhagavatā pana sabbakilesārayo hatā, tasmā “arīnaṃ hatattāpi araha”nti vutto. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The Blessed One has destroyed all the enemies which are the defilements; therefore, he is also called 'Arahant' because of destroying enemies. For it is said:

“Yasmā rāgādisaṅkhātā, sabbepi arayo hatā;

Paññāsatthena nāthena, tasmāpi arahaṃ mato”ti. (visuddhi. 1.126);

"Since all enemies, designated as lust and so forth, have been slain by the Lord with the sword of wisdom, therefore he is also considered an Arahant."

Yaṃ panetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhipuññābhisaṅkhāraapuññābhisaṅkhāraāneñjābhisaṅkhārāraṃ jarāmaraṇanemi “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vacanato āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe yojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ, tassa bhagavato bodhirukkhamūle sammappadhānavīriyapādehi catupārisuddhisīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakarañāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbe arā hatā. Tasmā “arānaṃ hatattā araha”nti vutto. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Moreover, this wheel of saṃsāra—which has rolled on since beginningless time, yoked to the chariot of the three realms, pierced by the axle that is the origin of the taints (in accordance with the phrase 'with the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance' (MN 1.103)), whose hub is made of ignorance and craving for existence, whose spokes are meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations, and whose rim is aging and death—all the spokes of this wheel were shattered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Standing firmly on the ground of the fourfold purity of virtue with the feet of right effort and energy, he took up the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma with the hand of faith. Therefore, he is called 'Arahant because of destroying the spokes.' For this has been said—

“Arā saṃsāracakkassa, hatā ñāṇāsinā yato;

Lokanāthena tenesa, arahanti pavuccatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.128);

"Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra are destroyed by the sword of wisdom by the Lord of the World, therefore he is called an Arahant."

Aggadakkhiṇeyyattā [V 0.0196] cīvarādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ uttamapūjāya ca yutto bhagavā, tasmā “paccayādīnaṃ arahattā ca araha”nti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Because the Blessed One is the foremost recipient of offerings and is worthy of requisites such as robes and so forth and of the highest veneration, he is therefore called 'Arahant' because of worthiness for requisites and the like. For it is said:

“Pūjāvisesaṃ [M 0.0218] saha paccayehi,

Yasmā ayaṃ arahati lokanātho;

Atthānurūpaṃ arahanti loke,

Tasmā jino arahati nāmameta”nti. (visuddhi. 1.129);

"Since this Lord of the World is worthy of special veneration together with requisites, and since in the world things are worthy in keeping with their meaning, therefore the Conqueror is worthy of this name."

Yathā loke keci paṇḍitamānino asilokabhayena raho pāpāni karonti, tathā bhagavā kadācipi na karoti, tasmā “pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā ca araha”nti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Just as in the world some who consider themselves wise commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill repute, the Blessed One never does so; therefore, he is called 'Arahant' because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil. For it is said:

“Yasmā natthi raho nāma, pāpakammesu tādino;

Rahābhāvena tenesa, arahaṃ iti vissuto”ti. (visuddhi. 1.130) –

"Since there is no secret place for such a one in evil deeds, therefore, because of the absence of secrecy, he is known as 'Arahant'."

Evaṃ ārakattādinā arahanti bhāvetabbaṃ.

Thus, one should cultivate the recollection of the Arahant by way of his quality of being far and so forth.

Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā pana sammāsambuddho. Sammāti ñāyeneva, abhiññeyye dhamme abhiññeyyato pariññeyye dhamme pariññeyyato pahātabbe dhamme pahātabbato sacchikātabbe dhamme sacchikātabbato bhāvetabbe dhamme bhāvetabbato evāti attho. Sāmañcāti attanāva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

And he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One because of having awakened to all things rightly and by himself. 'Rightly' means in the proper way: knowing things to be fully known as things to be fully known, fully understanding things to be fully understood as things to be fully understood, abandoning things to be abandoned as things to be abandoned, realizing things to be realized as things to be realized, and developing things to be developed as things to be developed—this is the meaning. 'By himself' means by himself alone. For it was said—

“Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇā”ti. (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 563);

"What was to be fully known has been fully known; what was to be developed has been developed; what was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O brahmin, I am Buddha."

“Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthādevamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā”ti evaṃ vutte navabhede bhagavato guṇe yā punappunaṃ uppajjanato satiyeva anussati, pavattitabbaṭṭhānamhiyeva vā pavattattā saddhāpabbajitassa [V 0.0197] kulaputtassa anurūpā satīti anussati, buddhaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati buddhānussati, yā evaṃ navavidhena pavattā sati[M 0.0219], sā buddhānussati nāmāti attho. Sabbākārena pana ācariyena buddhaghosena buddhānussati visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.123 ādayo) vuttā, atthikena pana tato paccāsīsitabbā.

"Indeed, the Blessed One is an Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One." When this is said, the mindfulness that arises again and again regarding the ninefold qualities of the Blessed One is indeed recollection; or, because it occurs only in the proper sphere, it is recollection appropriate for a faithful son of good family who has gone forth. Recollection that arises concerning the Buddha is called recollection of the Buddha. The mindfulness that operates in this ninefold manner is known as recollection of the Buddha—this is the meaning. Moreover, the recollection of the Buddha has been explained in all its aspects by the teacher Buddhaghosa in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.123 onwards); those who are interested should seek it there.

463-4. Caturārakkhāya sāyaṃpātaṃ bhāvetabbattā mettābhāvanaṃ dassentena therena sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena dassitāti veditabbā. Itarathā “attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye”ti (dha. pa. 129-130) vacanato sabbapaṭhamaṃ “ahaṃ sukhito homi, avero”tiādinā nayena bhāvetvāva attani cittaṃ niparibandhamānaṃ katvā pacchā ācariyupajjhāyādīsu kamena bhāvetabbā. Attani pana appanā na hoti. Gocaragāmamhi issare janeti sambandho. Tatthāti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165) gocaragāme. Sīmaṭṭhasaṅghato paṭṭhāya paricchijja paricchijjāti attho. Evaṃ mettaṃ bhāvento bhikkhusaṅghe mettāya sahavāsīnaṃ muducittaṃ janeti, athassa sukhasaṃvāsatā hoti. Sīmaṭṭhakadevatāsu mettāya mudukatacittāhi devatāhi dhammikāya rakkhāya susaṃvihitarakkho hoti. Gocaragāmamhi issarajane mettāya mudukatacittasantānehi issarehi dhammikāya rakkhāya surakkhitaparikkhāro hoti. Tattha manusse mettāya pasāditacittehi tehi aparibhūto hutvā vicarati. Sabbasattesu mettāya sabbattha appaṭihatacāro hoti.

463-4. Since the four protections should be developed morning and evening, it should be understood that the Elder showed the cultivation of loving-kindness by way of developing a meditation subject suitable for all situations. Otherwise, according to the statement, 'Having made oneself the example, one should neither kill nor cause to kill' (Dhp 129-130), one should first cultivate with the thought, 'May I be happy, free from enmity,' and so on, establishing the mind unhindered on oneself, and only afterwards should it be cultivated gradually towards teachers, preceptors, and so forth. However, absorption (appanā) does not occur with regard to oneself. In the alms-gathering village, there is a connection with the powerful people. 'There' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.165) refers to the alms-village. Starting from the Sangha within the boundary, it should be repeatedly demarcated—this is the meaning. A monk who cultivates loving-kindness in this way generates a gentle mind among the Sangha who dwell together in loving-kindness, and thus he lives in comfort. Among the deities within the boundary, with minds softened by loving-kindness, he is well-protected by the deities through righteous guardianship. In the alms-village, the powerful people, whose mind-streams are softened by loving-kindness, ensure his requisites are well-guarded through righteous protection. There, among people, he moves about unthreatened, their minds pleased by his loving-kindness. Toward all beings, his conduct is unobstructed everywhere due to loving-kindness.

465-6. Vaṇṇato ca saṇṭhānato ca okāsato ca disato ca paricchedato ca kesādikoṭṭhāse vavatthapetvāti sambandho. Ettha vaṇṇatoti (visuddhi. 1.110) kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇato. Saṇṭhānatoti tesaṃyeva saṇṭhānato. Okāsatoti “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imasmiṃ nāma okāse patiṭṭhito”ti evaṃ tassa tassa okāsato. Disatoti [M 0.0220] imasmiṃ sarīre nābhito uddhaṃ uparimā disā, adho heṭṭhimā disā, tasmā “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imissā nāma disāyā”ti disā vavatthapetabbā. Paricchedatoti sabhāgaparicchedato visabhāgaparicchedatoti dve paricchedā. Tattha “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso heṭṭhā ca upari ca tiriyañca iminā nāma paricchedo”ti evaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo veditabbo. “Kesā na lomā, lomā na kesā”ti evaṃ amissakavasena visabhāgaparicchedo.

465-6. The connection is established by defining the parts such as the hair, etc., in terms of color, shape, location, direction, and delimitation. Here, 'in terms of color' (as in Visuddhi. 1.110) refers to the color of the hair, etc. 'In terms of shape' refers to the shape of those same parts. 'In terms of location' means determining, 'This part is situated in such-and-such a location'; thus, the location of each part. 'In terms of direction' means that in this body, above the navel is the upper direction, below is the lower direction. Thus, one should define the direction by stating, 'This part belongs to such-and-such a direction.' 'In terms of delimitation' includes two types: delimitation of similar parts and delimitation of dissimilar parts. Among these, the delimitation of similar parts should be understood as, 'This part is delimited below, above, and around by such-and-such a boundary.' The delimitation of dissimilar parts is defined by distinction, such as, 'Hair is not body hair, and body hair is not hair.'

Evaṃ [V 0.0198] pañcahi ākārehi vavatthānākāraṃ dassetvā idāni manasi karontena evaṃ manasi kātabbanti taṃ dassetuṃ “anupubbato”tiādimāha. Tattha anupubbatoti sajjhāyakaraṇakālato paṭṭhāya “kesā nakhā”ti evaṃ ekantarikāya vā “lomā kesā”ti evaṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā vā na manasi kātabbaṃ, atha kho “kesā lomā”tiādinā nayena anupaṭipāṭiyā manasi kātabbaṃ, anupaṭipāṭiyā manasi karontenāpi nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇikaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cetaso vikkhepo paṭibāhitabbo. “Paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamma, muñcantassānupubbato”ti pāṭho gahetabbo. Evañhi sati bhāvanākkamena attho suviññeyyo hoti. “Kesā lomā”tiādipaññattiṃ amanasikatvā paṭikkūlabhāvena evaṃ cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Muñcantassānupubbatoti yo yo koṭṭhāso āpāthaṃ nāgacchati, taṃ taṃ anupubbato muñcantassāti attho.

Having shown the method of definition in these five ways, now, to show how one should attend to it, he states, 'beginning with "in due order," ' and so on. Here, 'in due order' means that from the time of recitation onwards, one should not attend to it by skipping parts, as in 'hair, nails,' etc., nor in reverse order like 'body hair, head hair,' etc., but rather in the proper sequence as 'head hair, body hair,' etc. Even when attending in due order, one should not do so too quickly or too slowly, and the scattering of the mind outwards to diverse objects should be prevented. The passage 'transcending the designation, releasing gradually' should be taken. For in this way, the meaning becomes easily understood through the progression of meditation. Without attending to the designation of 'head hair, body hair,' etc., the mind should be established in the repulsive aspect. 'Releasing gradually' means that as each part does not come into view, one releases it step by step—this is the meaning.

467. Idāni yathā paṭikkūlamanasikāro kātabbo, taṃ dassetuṃ “vaṇṇaāsayasaṇṭhānā”tiādimāha. Etehi vaṇṇādīhi koṭṭhāsehi paṭikkūlāti bhāvanāti sambandho. Ettha (vibha. aṭṭha. 356; visuddhi. 1.178) kesā tāva vaṇṇatopi paṭikkūlā. Tathā [M 0.0221] hi yāgubhattādīsu kesavaṇṇaṃ kiñci disvā jigucchanti. Saṇṭhānatopi paṭikkūlā. Tathā hi rattiṃ bhuñjantā kesasaṇṭhānaṃ makacivākādikaṃ chupitvā jigucchanti. Telamakkhanādivirahitānañca aggimhi pakkhittānañca gandho ativiya paṭikkūloti gandhatopi paṭikkūlā. Asuciṭṭhāne jātasūpeyyapaṇṇaṃ viya pubbalohitamuttakarīsapittasemhādinissandena jātattā āsayatopi paṭikkūlā. Gūtharāsimhi uṭṭhitakaṇṇikaṃ viya ekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsarāsimhi jātattā okāsatopi paṭikkūlā. Uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakaṃ vicchiddakaṃ vikkhāyitakaṃ vikkhittakaṃ hatavikkhittakaṃ lohitakaṃ puḷavakaṃ aṭṭhikanti imesu uddhumātakādīsu vatthūsu asubhākāraṃ gahetvā pavattā bhāvanā vā asubhaṃ nāmāti attho.

467. Now, to explain how the contemplation of the repulsive should be undertaken, it is said, "by color, origin, shape," etc. The connection is that the meditation is on these parts—color, etc.—as repulsive. Herein (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 356; Visuddhi. 1.178), first, head hair is repulsive by way of color. For example, seeing the color of hair in rice gruel, etc., disgusts one. It is also repulsive by shape, as when eating at night, touching the shape of hair resembling a bat’s wing, etc., disgusts one. The smell of hair devoid of oil or ointment, when thrown into a fire, is extremely repulsive—thus, it is repulsive also by smell. Since it is produced from a discharge of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, etc., like a succulent leaf in a cesspit, it is repulsive also by origin. Like a sprout rising from a dung heap, being born from a heap of thirty-one parts, it is repulsive also by location. The meaning is that the meditation that proceeds by grasping the aspect of foulness in these objects—the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut-up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm-infested, and a skeleton—is called 'the foul'.

468. Yaṃ panetaṃ arahantānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhasamucchedasaṅkhātaṃ samucchedamaraṇaṃ (visuddhi. 1.167), saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ khaṇikamaraṇaṃ, “rukkho mato, lohaṃ mata”ntiādi sammutimaraṇañca, na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Idha pana maraṇanti ekabhavapariyāpannassa jīvitindriyassa upacchedo adhippeto. Tampi kālamaraṇaṃ akālamaraṇanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha kālamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayena vā āyukkhayena vā ubhayakkhayena vā hoti, akālamaraṇaṃ upapīḷakaupacchedakakammavasena[V 0.0199]. “Maraṇaṃ me bhavissatī”ti vā “jīvitaṃ ucchijjissatī”ti vā “maraṇaṃ maraṇa”nti vā yoniso bhāvayitvānāti sambandho.

468. But the death intended here is not the final death of arahants, known as the cutting off of the round of suffering, nor the momentary death known as the breakup of formations, nor conventional death, as when one says, 'The tree is dead,' 'The metal is dead,' etc. Here, death means the cutting off of the life faculty included within a single existence. This is of two kinds: timely death and untimely death. Timely death occurs through the exhaustion of merit, or the exhaustion of the lifespan, or the exhaustion of both. Untimely death occurs through the force of oppressive or destructive kamma. The connection is made by wisely contemplating, 'Death will come to me,' or 'Life will be cut off,' or 'Death, death.'

469-70. Yassa pana ettāvatā upacārajjhānaṃ na uppajjati, tena vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānato sampattivipattito upasaṃharaṇato kāyabahusādhāraṇato āyudubbalato animittato addhānaparicchedato khaṇaparittatoti imehi aṭṭhahi ākārehi maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ, idāni [M 0.0222] te dassetuṃ “vadhakassevupaṭṭhāna”ntiādimāha. Asiṃ ukkhipitvā sīsaṃ chindituṃ ṭhitavadhako viya maraṇaṃ paccupaṭṭhitamevāti bhāvanā maraṇassati nāmāti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha. Sabbaṃ ārogyaṃ byādhipariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ yobbanaṃ jarāpariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ jīvitaṃ maraṇapariyosānaṃ, tasmā “ayaṃ yobbanādikāyasampatti tāvadeva sobhati, yāva maraṇasaṅkhātā vipatti na bhavissatī”ti evamādinā sampattivipattito ca, sattahākārehi upasaṃharaṇato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ yasamahattato puññamahattato thāmamahattato iddhimahattato paññāmahattato paccekabuddhato sammāsambuddhatoti. Tattha “idaṃ maraṇaṃ nāma mahāyasānaṃ mahāparivārānaṃ mahāsammatamandhātādīnampi upari patati, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayhaṃ upari na patissatī”ti evaṃ yasamahattato,

But for one for whom access concentration does not arise in this way, death should be recollected in these eight ways: as an executioner appearing, from success and failure, by comparison, from the body being common to many, from the frailty of life, as unindicated, from the limitedness of the lifespan, and from the shortness of the moment. Now, to show these, it is said, beginning with 'as an executioner appearing.' Just as an executioner stands ready to behead someone with a raised sword, so death is ever-present. This contemplation is called mindfulness of death—thus the connection. The same applies in all cases. All health ends in sickness, all youth ends in old age, all life ends in death. Therefore, one should reflect: 'This bodily success of youth and so on is beautiful only as long as the failure called death does not occur.' Death should also be recollected by comparison in seven ways: by greatness of fame, greatness of merit, greatness of strength, greatness of psychic power, greatness of wisdom, by reference to Paccekabuddhas, and by reference to Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. Herein, one should reflect: 'This death falls even upon those of great fame, great retinues, and highly esteemed rulers like Mandhātā; why then should it not fall upon me?' Thus, by greatness of fame,

“Jotiko jaṭilo uggo,

Meṇḍako atha puṇṇako;

Ete caññe ca ye loke,

Mahāpuññāti vissutā;

Sabbe maraṇamāpannā,

Mādisesu kathāva kā”ti. –

'Jotika, Jaṭila, Ugga, Meṇḍaka, and then Puṇṇaka; these and others who in the world were renowned for their great merit—all have met with death. What then to say of those like me?'

Evaṃ puññamahattato,

Thus, by greatness of merit,

“Vāsudevo baladevo, bhīmasenādayo mahā;

Balā maccuvasaṃ pattā, mādisesu kathāva kā”ti. –

'Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Bhīmasena, and other great heroes of mighty strength have fallen under the sway of death. What then to say of those like me?'

Evaṃ [V 0.0200] thāmamahattato,

Thus, by greatness of strength,

“Mahāmoggallānādīnaṃ mahiddhikānampi upari patati, mādisesu kathāva kā”ti evaṃ iddhimahattato, “sāriputtādīnaṃ mahāpaññānampi upari patati, mādisesu kathāva kā”ti [M 0.0223] evaṃ paññāmahattato. Evaṃ itaresampi paccekabuddhasammāsambuddhānampi mahantabhāvaṃ cintetvā “tesampi upari maraṇaṃ patati, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayhaṃ upari na patissatī”ti evaṃ upasaṃharaṇato ca, “ayaṃ kāyo bahusādhāraṇo ajjhattikānaṃyeva anekasatānaṃ rogānaṃ bāhirānaṃ ahivicchikādīnañcā”ti kāyabahusādhāraṇato ca, “assāsapassāsapaṭibaddhaṃ jīvita”ntiādinā nayena āyudubbalato ca,

'It falls even upon those of great psychic power like Mahāmoggallāna and others; what then of those like me?’—thus by greatness of psychic power. ‘It falls even upon those of great wisdom like Sāriputta and others; what then of those like me?’—thus by greatness of wisdom. And so, having considered the greatness of others too—Paccekabuddhas and Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones—‘Death falls even upon them; why then should it not fall upon me?’—thus by comparison. ‘This body is common to many—host to hundreds of internal ailments and external dangers like snakes and scorpions’—thus from the body being common to many. ‘Life is bound to the in-breath and out-breath,’ and so on—thus from the frailty of life.

“Jīvitaṃ byādhi kālo ca,

Dehanikkhepanaṃ gati;

Pañcete jīvalokasmiṃ;

Animittā na nāyare”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.20; jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.34) –

'Life, sickness, and time, the laying down of the body, and one's destination—these five in the living world are unindicated, not to be known.' (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.20; jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.34)

Evaṃ kālavavatthānassa abhāvato ca, “yo, bhikkhave, ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ jīvati appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.145) vuttattā evamādinā nayena addhānassa paricchedāca bhāvanā maraṇassati nāmāti attho. Khaṇaparittato ca maraṇassati bhāvetabbā.

Thus, from the absence of a fixed time, and because it is said, 'Bhikkhus, whoever lives long, lives a hundred years or a little more' (saṃ. ni. 1.145), and by the method beginning in this way, from the limitedness of the lifespan, the meaning is that this cultivation is called mindfulness of death. And mindfulness of death should be cultivated from the shortness of the moment.

“Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca,

Sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā,

Lahu so vattate khaṇo”ti. (visuddhi. 1.176) –

'Life and individuality, and mere pleasure and pain; bound to a single mind-moment, swiftly that moment passes.' (visuddhi. 1.176)

Hi vuttaṃ. Caturārakkhavinicchayo.

For it is said. The Analysis of the Four Protections.

Caturārakkhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Four Protections is completed.

50. Vipassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

50. Commentary on the Exposition of Insight

471-2. Nāmarūpaṃ [M 0.0224][V 0.0201] pariggayhāti ettha (visuddhi. 2.662 ādayo) nāmarūpapariggahaṃ kātukāmena tāva ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ avasesesu yaṃ kiñci jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni ca taṃsampayutte ca phassādayo dhamme lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasena paricchinditvā “sabbametaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato namanaṭṭhena nāma”nti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tato tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto “hadayavatthuṃ nissāya vattatī”ti passati, puna vatthussa paccayabhūtāni ca upādārūpāni ca passitvā “idaṃ sabbaṃ ruppanato vikārāpattito rūpa”nti pariggaṇhāti. Puna tadubhayaṃ “namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpa”nti evaṃ saṅkhepato nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti. Idaṃ sabbaṃ samathayānikavasena vuttaṃ. Vipassanāyāniko pana catudhātuvavatthānamukhena bhūtupādāyarūpāni paricchinditvā “sabbametaṃ ruppanato rūpa”nti passati. Tato evaṃ paricchinnarūpassa cakkhādīni nissāya pavattamānā arūpadhammāpi āpāthamāgacchanti. Tato sabbepi te arūpadhamme namanalakkhaṇena ekato katvā “etaṃ nāma”nti passati. So “idaṃ nāmaṃ, idaṃ rūpa”nti dvedhā vavatthapeti. Evaṃ vavatthapetvā “nāmarūpato uddhaṃ añño satto vā puggalo vā poso vā devo vā brahmā vā natthī”ti passati.

Herein, regarding 'one comprehends name-and-form' (visuddhi. 2.662 ādayo): one who wishes to undertake the comprehension of name-and-form should first, having set aside the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attain any of the remaining jhānas. Upon emerging, he should discern the jhāna factors such as initial application and their associated states such as contact by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. Then he should determine: 'All this, because it bends towards an object, is name in the sense of bending.' Next, seeking its condition, he sees that it occurs dependent on the heart-base. Then, seeing the derived materiality that is the condition for that base, he comprehends: 'All this, because it is afflicted, is form.' Again, he defines them both thus: 'Name has the characteristic of bending; form has the characteristic of being afflicted.' In this way he briefly defines name-and-form. All this is stated from the perspective of one on the vehicle of serenity. One on the vehicle of insight, however, first discerns the primary elements and derived materiality by way of the analysis of the four elements and sees: 'All this, because it is afflicted, is form.' Then, for him, the immaterial states that occur dependent on the eye, etc., based on this discerned form, also come into range. He then gathers all those immaterial states together under the characteristic of bending and recognizes: 'This is name.' Thus he defines them in two parts: 'This is name, this is form.' Having defined them thus, he sees: 'Apart from name-and-form, there is no other being, person, individual, god, or Brahmā.'

Yathāhi aṅgasambhārā, hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu, hoti sattoti sammuti. (saṃ. ni. 1.171);

Just as with an assemblage of parts, the word 'chariot' is used; so when the aggregates are present, there is the convention 'a being.' (saṃ. ni. 1.171)

Evameva pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu sati satto, puggaloti vā vohāramatto hotīti evamādinā nayena nāmarūpānaṃ yāthāvadassanasaṅkhātena diṭṭhivisuddhibhūtena ñāṇena nāmarūpaṃ pariggayhāti attho.

'In the same way, when the five aggregates subject to clinging are present, 'a being' or 'a person' is a mere designation.' By this method, with the knowledge that consists in seeing name-and-form as they really are, which constitutes the purification of view, one comprehends name-and-form. This is the meaning.

Tato [M 0.0225] tassa ca paccayanti puna tassa nāmarūpassa paccayaṃ pariggayhāti attho. Vuttanayena nāmarūpaṃ pariggaṇhitvā “ko nu kho imassa hetū”ti pariyesanto ahetuvādavisamahetuvādesu dosaṃ disvā rogaṃ disvā tassa nidānasamuṭṭhānaṃ pariyesanto vejjo viya tassa hetuñca paccayañca pariyesanto avijjā taṇhā upādānaṃ kammanti ime cattāro dhamme nāmarūpassa uppādapaccayattā “hetū”ti ca āhāraṃ upatthambhanassa paccayattā “paccayo”ti [V 0.0202] ca passati. “Imassa kāyassa avijjādayo tayo dhammā mātā viya dārakassa upanissayā honti, kammaṃ pitā viya puttassa janakaṃ, āhāro dhāti viya dārakassa sandhārako”ti evaṃ rūpakāyassa paccayapariggahaṃ katvā puna “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.43) nayena nāmakāyassapi hetupaccayaṃ pariggaṇhāti.

Then, the words 'and its condition' mean that he again comprehends the condition for that name-and-form. Having comprehended name-and-form in the way stated, he investigates, 'What, indeed, is the cause of this?' Like a physician who, having seen a disease, seeks its origin, he sees the fault in the theories of causelessness and of dissimilar causes. Investigating its cause and condition, he sees that ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma—these four states—are the 'generative cause' (hetu) for the arising of name-and-form, and that nutriment is the 'supportive condition' (paccaya). He understands: 'For this body, the three states beginning with ignorance are like a mother providing a foundation for a child; kamma is like a father who begets a son; and nutriment is like a wet-nurse who sustains the child.' Having thus comprehended the conditions for the material body, he again comprehends the cause and condition for the mental body by the method beginning: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises…' (SN 12.43).

Evaṃ pariggaṇhanto “atītānāgatāpi dhammā evameva pavattantī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ karoti. Tassa yā sā pubbantaṃ ārabbha “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ nu kho, kathaṃ nu kho, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”nti pañcavidhā vicikicchā vuttā, yāpi aparantaṃ ārabbha “bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho, kiṃ nu kho, kathaṃ nu kho, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhāna”nti pañcavidhā vuttā, yāpi etarahi vā pana paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha “ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hoti, ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī”ti chabbidhā vicikicchā vuttā, tā sabbāpi pahīyanti. Evaṃ paccayapariggahaṇena tīsu addhāsu [M 0.0226] kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ “kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhī”tipi “dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”ntipi “sammādassana”ntipi vuccati.

Comprehending in this way, one concludes: 'Past and future states also proceed in this same manner.' For him, the fivefold doubt concerning the past—'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist? What was I? How was I? Having been what, what did I become in the past?'—and the fivefold doubt concerning the future—'Will I exist in the future? Will I not? What will I be? How will I be? Having been what, what will I become in the future?'—and the sixfold doubt concerning the present—'Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will it go?'—all these doubts are abandoned. Thus, the knowledge established by having overcome doubt about the three periods of time through the comprehension of conditions is called 'purification by overcoming doubt,' 'knowledge of the stability of phenomena,' and 'right view.'

Ettha pana tisso lokiyapariññā ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā pahānapariññāti. Tattha “ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, vedayitalakkhaṇā vedanā”ti evaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paccattalakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena pavattā paññā ñātapariññānāma. “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā”tiādinā tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāpaññā tīraṇapariññā nāma. Tesu evaṃ pana dhammesu niccasaññādipajahanavasena pavattā lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanā pahānapariññā nāma. Tattha saṅkhārapariggahato paṭṭhāya yāva paccayapariggahā ñātapariññāya bhūmi. Kalāpasammasanato paṭṭhāya yāva udayabbayānupassanā tīraṇapariññāya bhūmi. Bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya pahānapariññāya bhūmi. Tato paṭṭhāya hi “aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ, nibbindanto nandiṃ, virajjanto rāgaṃ, nirodhento samudayaṃ, paṭinissajjanto [V 0.0203] ādānaṃ pajahatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.52) evaṃ pajahanto niccasaññādipahānasādhikānaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ ādhipaccaṃ hoti. Iti imāsu pariññāsu saṅkhāraparicchedassa ceva paccayapariggahassa ca sādhitattā iminā yoginā ñātapariññā adhigatā hoti.

Here, there are three mundane kinds of full understanding: full understanding as knowledge, full understanding as scrutiny, and full understanding as abandonment. Among these, the wisdom that proceeds by way of discerning the individual characteristics of those various states—such as, 'form has the characteristic of being afflicted, feeling has the characteristic of being experienced'—is called full understanding as knowledge. The insight-wisdom that takes characteristics as its object by applying the general characteristics—such as, 'form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent'—to those very states is called full understanding as scrutiny. The insight-wisdom that takes characteristics as its object and proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence, etc., in regard to those states is called full understanding as abandonment. Herein, the stage from the comprehension of formations up to the comprehension of conditions is the domain of full understanding as knowledge. The stage from the comprehension of groups up to the contemplation of rise and fall is the domain of full understanding as scrutiny. The stage from the contemplation of dissolution onwards is the domain of full understanding as abandonment. For from that point onwards, 'contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; being disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust; bringing about cessation, one abandons the origin; relinquishing, one abandons grasping' (Paṭis I 52). Thus, by abandoning in this way, the seven contemplations that accomplish the abandonment of the perception of permanence, etc., become predominant. Thus, among these kinds of full understanding, because the delimitation of formations and the comprehension of conditions have been accomplished, this yogi has attained full understanding as knowledge.

Puna “yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ hutvā abhāvato aniccaṃ, udayabbayappaṭipīḷitattā dukkhaṃ, avasavattittā anattā. Yā kāci vedanā, yā kāci saññā, ye keci saṅkhārā, yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ [M 0.0227] ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ hutvā abhāvato aniccaṃ, udayabbayappaṭipīḷitattā dukkhaṃ, avasavattittā anattā”ti evamādinā nayena kalāpasammasanaṃ karoti. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvāna saṅkhāre sammasanto”ti.

Again, 'Whatever form—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form, because it ceases to be after having been, is impermanent; because it is oppressed by rise and fall, is suffering; because it is not subject to one's will, is non-self. Whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, whatever consciousness—past, future, or present… far or near—all consciousness, because it ceases to be after having been, is impermanent; because it is oppressed by rise and fall, is suffering; because it is not subject to one's will, is non-self.' In this way, he performs the comprehension of groups. This is what is meant by 'contemplating the formations after applying the three characteristics.'

Evaṃ saṅkhāresu aniccadukkhaanattavasena kalāpasammasanaṃ katvā puna saṅkhārānaṃ udayabbayameva passati. Kathaṃ? “Avijjāsamudayā (paṭi. ma. 1.50) rūpasamudayo, taṇhākammaāhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo’ti evaṃ rūpakkhandhassa paccayasamudayadassanaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatī”ti evaṃ pañcahākārehi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. “Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho, taṇhākammaāhāranirodhā rūpanirodho’ti evaṃ rūpakkhandhassa paccayanirodhadassanaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passatī”ti evaṃ pañcahākārehi vayaṃ passati. Tathā “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo, taṇhākammaphassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo”ti vedanākkhandhassa, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. “Avijjānirodhā vedanānirodho, taṇhākammaphassanirodhā vedanānirodho”ti vedanākkhandhassa, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Evaṃ saññākkhandhādīsupi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – viññāṇakkhandhassa phassaṭṭhāne nāmarūpasamudayā, nāmarūpanirodhāti yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekekasmiṃ khandhe paccayasamudayavasena ca nibbattilakkhaṇavasena ca paccayanirodhavasena ca vipariṇāmalakkhaṇavasena ca udayabbayadassanena dasa [V 0.0204] dasa katvā paññāsa lakkhaṇāni [M 0.0228] vuttāni. Tesaṃ vasena evaṃ rūpassa udayo rūpassa vayoti paccayato ceva lakkhaṇato ca vitthārena manasikāraṃ karoti.

Having thus performed the comprehension of groups regarding formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, one again sees only the arising and passing away of formations. How? ‘With the arising of ignorance, form arises; with the arising of craving, kamma, and nutriment, form arises.’ Thus one sees the arising of the form aggregate in the sense of seeing the arising of its conditions, and also by seeing the characteristic of production. In this way one sees the arising of the form aggregate in five aspects. ‘With the cessation of ignorance, form ceases; with the cessation of craving, kamma, and nutriment, form ceases.’ Thus one sees the passing away of the form aggregate in the sense of seeing the cessation of its conditions, and also by seeing the characteristic of alteration. In this way one sees its passing away in five aspects. Similarly, for the feeling aggregate: ‘With the arising of ignorance, feeling arises; with the arising of craving, kamma, and contact, feeling arises,’ and one sees its arising by seeing the characteristic of production. ‘With the cessation of ignorance, feeling ceases; with the cessation of craving, kamma, and contact, feeling ceases,’ and one sees its passing away by seeing the characteristic of alteration. The same applies to the perception aggregate and the others. But there is this difference: for the consciousness aggregate, in place of contact, it should be connected as ‘with the arising of name-and-form’ and ‘with the cessation of name-and-form.’ Thus, for each aggregate, by seeing arising and passing away by way of the arising of conditions and the characteristic of production, and by way of the cessation of conditions and the characteristic of alteration, fifty characteristics are stated, ten for each. Based on these, one gives thorough attention to 'the arising of form, the passing away of form,' in detail, from the side of conditions and from the side of characteristics.

Tassevaṃ karoto “iti kira ime dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti ñāṇaṃ visadaṃ hoti. “Evaṃ kira ime dhammā anuppannā uppajjanti, uppannā nirujjhantī”ti niccaṃ navāva hutvā saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti. Na kevalañca niccaṃ navā, sūriyuggamane ussāvabindu viya, udakabubbuḷo viya, udake daṇḍarāji viya, āragge sāsapo viya, vijjuppādo viya ca parittaṭṭhāyino. Māyāmarīcisupinaalātacakkagandhabbanagarapheṇapiṇḍakadaliādayo viya nissārā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Ettāvatā cānena vayadhammameva uppajjati, uppannañca vayaṃ upetīti iminā ākārena samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitaṃ udayabbayānupassanaṃ nāma paṭhamaṃ taruṇavipassanāñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti, yassādhigamā āraddhavipassakoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

For one who does so, the knowledge becomes clear: ‘Indeed, these phenomena, not having been, come into being; having been, they vanish.’ ‘Thus, indeed, these phenomena, unarisen, arise; having arisen, they cease.’ Formations constantly appear as ever new. And not only are they constantly new, but like dewdrops at sunrise, like a water bubble, like a line drawn with a stick on water, like a mustard seed on an awl’s tip, and like a flash of lightning, they are short-lived. Like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a firebrand’s circle, a city of gandhabbas, a lump of foam, and a plantain trunk, they appear to be without substance. To this extent, having penetrated the fifty characteristics in this way—‘Only what is subject to vanishing arises, and what has arisen goes to vanishing’—one attains the first, tender insight-knowledge, called the contemplation of arising and passing away. With its attainment, one is reckoned as ‘one who has begun insight’.

Athassa āraddhavipassakassa kulaputtassa obhāso ñāṇaṃ pīti passaddhi sukhaṃ adhimokkho paggaho upaṭṭhānaṃ upekkhā nikantīti dasa vipassanupakkilesā uppajjanti.
