Ettha obhāso nāma vipassanākkhaṇe ñāṇassa balavattā lohitaṃ pasīdati, tena chavito obhāso nibbattati, taṃ disvā ayaṃ yogī “maggo mayā patto”ti tameva obhāsaṃ assādeti. Ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇamevetaṃ, saṅkhāre sammasantassa sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā pavattamānaṃ disvā pubbe viya “maggo”ti assādeti. Pītīti vipassanāpīti eva. Tassa hi tasmiṃ khaṇe pañcavidhā pīti uppajjati. Passaddhīti vipassanāpassaddhi. Tasmiṃ samaye neva kāyacittānaṃ daratho gāravatā kakkhaḷatā akammaññatā gelaññatā vaṅkatā hoti. Sukhaṃ vipassanāsukhameva. Tassa kira tasmiṃ [M 0.0229] samaye sakalasarīraṃ ṭhapitavaṭṭi viya abhisandayamānaṃ atipaṇītaṃ sukhaṃ uppajjati.

Then, for the clansman who has begun insight, ten imperfections of insight arise: illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and delight. Herein, illumination is this: at the moment of insight, because of the strength of knowledge, the blood becomes clear, and from that a radiance is produced in the complexion. Seeing this, the yogi savors that very illumination, thinking, ‘I have attained the path.’ Knowledge is just the insight-knowledge. When one is comprehending formations, seeing it proceed brilliantly and serenely, one savors it as the path, just as before. Rapture is just the insight-rapture. At that moment, the five kinds of rapture arise in him. Tranquility is the insight-tranquility. At that time there is no distress, heaviness, rigidity, unwieldiness, illness, or crookedness of body and mind. Bliss is just the insight-bliss. It is said that at that moment an exceedingly sublime bliss arises, suffusing his entire body like a wick soaking up oil.

Adhimokkho nāma vipassanākkhaṇe pavattā saddhā. Tasmiṃ khaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ ativiya pasādabhūtā balavatī saddhā uppajjati. Paggaho nāma vipassanāsampayuttaṃ vīriyaṃ. Tasmiñhi khaṇe asithilamanaccāraddhaṃ supaggahitaṃ vīriyaṃ uppajjati. Upaṭṭhānanti vipassanāsampayuttā sati. Tasmiñhi khaṇe supaṭṭhitā sati uppajjati. Upekkhāti duvidhā vipassanāvajjanavasena[V 0.0205]. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sabbasaṅkhāraggahaṇe majjhattabhūtavipassanupekkhāsaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇaṃ balavantaṃ hutvā uppajjati, manodvāre āvajjanupekkhā ca, sāva taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjentassa sūrā tikhiṇā hutvā vahati. Nikanti vipassanānikanti. Obhāsādīsu ālayaṃ kurumānā sukhumā santākārā nikanti uppajjati. Ettha obhāsādayo kilesavatthubhūtatāya “upakkilesā”ti vuttā, na akusalattā. Nikanti pana upakkileso ceva kilesavatthu ca. Paṇḍito pana bhikkhu obhāsādīsu uppannesu vikkhepaṃ agacchanto “obhāsādayo dhammā na maggo, upakkilesavinimuttaṃ pana vīthippaṭipannaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggo”ti maggañca amaggañca vavatthapeti. Tassevaṃ “ayaṃ maggo, ayaṃ na maggo”ti ñatvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ “maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhī”ti vuccati.

Resolution is the faith that occurs at the moment of insight. At that moment, a strong faith arises, which is an extreme lucidity for the mind and mental factors. Exertion is the energy associated with insight. At that moment, energy arises that is neither too lax nor too strained, but well-exerted. Establishment is the mindfulness associated with insight. At that moment, well-established mindfulness arises. Equanimity is twofold: that of insight and that of adverting. At that moment, the knowledge called equanimity of insight, which has become neutral in apprehending all formations, arises powerfully; and the equanimity of mind-door adverting also flows, keen and swift, as one adverts to this or that object. Delight is the delight in insight. A subtle, peaceful-seeming delight arises that forms an attachment to illumination and the other states. Herein, illumination and the others are called ‘imperfections’ because they are a basis for defilements, not because they are unwholesome in themselves. Delight, however, is both an imperfection and a basis for defilements. But a wise bhikkhu, when illumination and the others arise, does not fall into distraction but determines what is the path and what is not the path thus: ‘These phenomena such as illumination are not the path. The insight-knowledge that has entered the course, free from the imperfections, is the path.’ The knowledge of one who stands having known, ‘This is the path, this is not the path,’ is called the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and what is not path.

Ito paṭṭhāya aṭṭhavidhassa ñāṇassa vasena sikhāppattaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma hoti. Udayabbayānupassanāñāṇaṃ bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇanti imāni aṭṭha ñāṇāni nāma. Etāni nibbattetukāmena yasmā upakkilesehi abhibhūtaṃ hutvā lakkhaṇappaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ asamatthaṃ [M 0.0230] hoti cittaṃ, tasmā punapi udayabbayameva passitabbaṃ. Udayabbayaṃ passantassa aniccalakkhaṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ upaṭṭhāti, udayabbayappaṭipīḷitattā dukkhalakkhaṇañca “dukkhameva ca sambhoti, dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti cā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.171) passato anattalakkhaṇañca.

Henceforth, the insight-knowledge that has reached its peak by way of the eight kinds of knowledge is called the purification by knowledge and vision of the way. These are the eight knowledges: the knowledge of the contemplation of arising and passing away, the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution, the knowledge of the appearance of terror, the knowledge of the contemplation of danger, the knowledge of the contemplation of disenchantment, the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, the knowledge of the contemplation of reflection, and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations. For one who wishes to generate these, because the mind, being overwhelmed by the imperfections, is unable to penetrate the characteristics, one must again see arising and passing away. For one who sees arising and passing away, the characteristic of impermanence appears as it really is. And because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, the characteristic of suffering also appears; and for one who sees that ‘It is only suffering that comes to be, suffering that persists and passes away,’ the characteristic of non-self also appears.

Ettha ca aniccaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, dukkhaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, anattā anattalakkhaṇanti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Ettha aniccanti khandhapañcakaṃ. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā hutvā abhāvato vā. Aññathattaṃ nāma jarā, uppādavayaññathattaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, hutvā abhāvasaṅkhāto vā eko ākāravikāro. “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ. Kasmā? Abhiṇhaṃ paṭipīḷitattā. Abhiṇhappaṭipīḷanākāro dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ. “Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ anattā. Kasmā? Avasavattanato. Avasavattanākāro anattalakkhaṇaṃ. Imānipi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni udayabbayaṃ passantasseva ārammaṇāni honti.

Here, this distinction should be understood: between the impermanent and the characteristic of impermanence; between suffering and the characteristic of suffering; and between non-self and the characteristic of non-self. Here, ‘the impermanent’ refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because they have the nature of arising, vanishing, and altering, or because they cease to exist after having existed. ‘Alteration’ is aging. The characteristic of impermanence is this arising, vanishing, and alteration, or it is the change of state described as ceasing to exist after having existed. Based on the statement, ‘What is impermanent is suffering,’ those same five aggregates are suffering. Why? Because of being constantly oppressed. The mode of constant oppression is the characteristic of suffering. Based on the statement, ‘What is suffering is non-self,’ those same five aggregates are non-self. Why? Because they are not subject to control. The mode of not being subject to control is the characteristic of non-self. These three characteristics, too, are the objects for one who sees arising and passing away.

Punapi [V 0.0206] so rūpārūpadhammesu eva “aniccā”tiādinā vipassati, tassa saṅkhārā lahuṃ lahuṃ āpāthaṃ gacchanti. Tato uppādaṃ vā ṭhitiṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ akatvā tesaṃ khayavayanirodhe eva passato sati santiṭṭhatīti idaṃ bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma. Imassa uppādato paṭṭhāya assa yogino “yathā ime saṅkhārā pañcakkhandhā bhijjanti, evaṃ atītepi saṅkhārā bhijjiṃsu, anāgatepi bhijjissantī”ti nirodhameva passato sati santiṭṭhati, tassa bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ āsevantassa bahulīkarontassa sabbabhavayonigatiṭṭhitisattāvāsesu sabbe saṅkhārā jalitaaṅgārakāsuādayo viya mahābhayaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Etaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ nāma. Tassa taṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ āsevantassa [M 0.0231] sabbe bhavādayo ādittaaṅgārā viya, samussitakhaggā viya paccatthikā appaṭisaraṇā sādīnavā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Idaṃ ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma. Tassa evaṃ saṅkhāre ādīnavato passantassa bhavādīsu saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavattā sabbasaṅkhāresu ukkaṇṭhanā anabhirati uppajjati. Idaṃ nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma. Sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindantassa ukkaṇṭhantassa sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā muñcitukāmatā nissaritukāmatāva hoti. Idaṃ muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ nāma. Puna tasmā saṅkhāragatā muñcituṃ puna te eva saṅkhāre paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā tīraṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma, yo evaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre pariggaṇhanto tesu anattalakkhaṇassa sudiṭṭhattā “attā”ti vā “attaniya”nti vā aggaṇhanto saṅkhāresu bhayañca nandiñca pahāya saṅkhāresu udāsino hoti majjhatto, “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā na gaṇhāti, sabbasaṅkhāresu udāsino majjhatto tīsu bhavesu upekkhako, tassa taṃ ñāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ panetaṃ sabbasaṅkhārappavattaṃ vissajjetvā nibbānaninnaṃ nibbānapakkhandaṃ hoti, no ce nibbānaṃ santato passati, punappunaṃ “anicca”nti vā “dukkha”nti vā “anattā”ti vā tividhānupassanāvasena saṅkhārārammaṇameva hutvā pavattati.

Again, he contemplates material and immaterial phenomena by way of 'impermanent,' etc. For him, the formations swiftly become apparent. Then, without making their arising or persistence an object, his mindfulness becomes established on seeing only their destruction, passing away, and cessation—this is called the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution. From the arising of this, the yogin's mindfulness remains established on seeing only cessation, thinking: 'Just as these formations, the five aggregates, break up, so too did past formations break up, and so too will future formations break up.' As he cultivates and develops this knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, all formations in all kinds of existence, destinies, states, and abodes of beings appear to him as a great terror, like a pit of glowing embers. This is called the knowledge of the appearance of terror. As he cultivates this knowledge of the appearance of terror, all kinds of existence and so on appear to him as full of danger—like burning embers, like enemies with drawn swords, without refuge. This is called the knowledge of contemplation of danger. For one who sees formations in this way as full of danger, weariness and disenchantment with all formations arise. This is called the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment. For one who is weary and disenchanted with all formations, there arises the desire to be liberated from all that is formed, the desire to escape. This is called the knowledge of the desire for deliverance. Again, in order to be liberated from what is formed, he once more contemplates those very formations by applying the three characteristics. This determination is called the knowledge of contemplation by reflection. One who thus applies the three characteristics and comprehends the formations, having clearly seen the characteristic of not-self, no longer grasps them as 'self' or 'what belongs to self.' Abandoning both fear and delight in formations, he becomes equanimous and neutral towards them. He does not grasp at 'I' or 'mine' but remains indifferent and neutral towards all formations, equanimous towards the three kinds of existence. This knowledge is called the knowledge of equanimity towards formations. Now, this knowledge, having relinquished the process of all formations, inclines towards Nibbāna, slopes towards Nibbāna. If he does not yet see Nibbāna as peaceful, it continues to proceed with formations as its object, again and again, by way of the threefold contemplation of 'impermanent,' 'suffering,' or 'not-self.'

Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānañca etaṃ animitto appaṇihito suññatoti tiṇṇaṃ vimokkhānaṃ vasena vimokkhamukhabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā tiṭṭhati. Tisso hi anupassanā tīṇi vimokkhamukhānīti vuccanti. Ettha ca aniccato manasi karonto (paṭi. ma. 1.223-224) adhimokkhabahulo animittaṃ vimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Dukkhato manasi karonto passaddhibahulo appaṇihitaṃ vimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Anattato manasi karonto vedabahulo suññatavimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Ettha ca animitto [M 0.0232] vimokkhoti animittākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto [V 0.0207] ariyamaggo. So hi animittāya dhātuyā uppannattā animitto, kilesehi ca vimuttattā vimokkho. Eteneva nayena appaṇihitākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto appaṇihito, suññatākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto suññatoti veditabbo. Adhigatasaṅkhārupekkhassa kulaputtassa vipassanā sikhāppattā hoti. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāti etadeva. Etaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ āsevantassa bhāventassa tikkhatarā saṅkhārupekkhā uppajjati.

Thus established, this knowledge stands having reached the state of a gateway to liberation by way of the three liberations: the signless, the desireless, and the void. For the three contemplations are called the three gateways to liberation. Here, one who attends to impermanence, being abundant in resolution, attains the signless liberation. One who attends to suffering, being abundant in tranquility, attains the desireless liberation. One who attends to not-self, being abundant in wisdom, attains the void liberation. Here, the signless liberation is the noble path that proceeds having taken Nibbāna in its signless aspect as its object. Because it has arisen from the signless element, it is signless; and because it is liberated from the defilements, it is liberation. By this same method, the desireless liberation should be understood as the path that proceeds having taken Nibbāna in its desireless aspect as its object, and the void liberation as the path that proceeds having taken Nibbāna in its void aspect as its object. For a clansman who has attained equanimity towards formations, insight reaches its culmination. This itself is insight leading to emergence. For one who cultivates and develops this knowledge of equanimity towards formations, a sharper equanimity towards formations arises.

Tassa idāni maggo uppajjissatīti saṅkhārupekkhā saṅkhāre “aniccā”ti vā “dukkhā”ti vā “anattā”ti vā sammasitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Bhavaṅgā vuṭṭhāya saṅkhārupekkhāya āgatanayeneva aniccādiākārena manasi karitvā uppajjati manodvārāvajjanaṃ, tadeva manasi karoto paṭhamaṃ javanacittaṃ uppajjati, yaṃ “parikamma”nti vuccati. Tadanantaraṃ tatheva dutiyaṃ javanacittaṃ uppajjati, yaṃ “upacāra”nti vuccati. Tadanantarampi tatheva uppajjati javanacittaṃ, yaṃ “anuloma”nti vuccati. Idaṃ tesaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ. Avisesena pana tividhametaṃ āsevanantipi parikammantipi upacārantipi anulomantipi vuccati. Idaṃ pana anulomañāṇaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇāya vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya pariyosānaṃ hoti. Nippariyāyena pana gotrabhuñāṇameva vipassanāpariyosānanti vuccati. Tato paraṃ nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kurumānaṃ puthujjanagottaṃ atikkamamānaṃ nibbānārammaṇe paṭhamasamannāhārabhūtaṃ apunarāvaṭṭakaṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ pana ñāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiñca ñāṇadassanavisuddhiñca na bhajati, antarā abbohārikameva hoti, vipassanāsote patitattā pana vipassanāti vā [M 0.0233] saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā gotrabhuñāṇe niruddhe tena dinnasaññāya nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ vicikicchāsaṃyojananti tīṇi saṃyojanāni samucchedavasena viddhaṃsento sotāpattimaggo uppajjati. Tadanantaraṃ tasseva vipākabhūtāni dve tīṇi vā phalacittāni uppajjanti anantaravipākattā lokuttarānaṃ. Phalapariyosāne panassa cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otarati.

Now the path is about to arise for him. The equanimity towards formations, having comprehended formations as 'impermanent,' or 'suffering,' or 'not-self,' sinks into the life-continuum. Having emerged from the life-continuum, mind-door adverting arises, attending to formations in the same way as the preceding equanimity towards formations, by way of their impermanent nature, etc. As he continues to attend thus, the first impulsion consciousness arises, which is called 'preparation.' Immediately after, a second impulsion consciousness arises in the same way, which is called 'access.' Immediately after that, an impulsion consciousness arises in the same way, which is called 'conformity.' These are their specific names. But without distinction, these three are also called repetition, preparation, access, and conformity. This conformity knowledge is the culmination of the insight leading to emergence, which has formations as its object. Unqualifiedly, however, it is the change-of-lineage knowledge that is called the culmination of insight. Thereafter, taking cessation, Nibbāna, as its object, transcending the lineage of the worldling, the change-of-lineage knowledge arises, which is the first to take Nibbāna as object and is non-reverting. This knowledge does not belong to either the purification by knowledge and vision of the path or the purification by knowledge and vision, but is intermediate and unclassifiable. However, because it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is reckoned as insight. When the change-of-lineage knowledge has ceased after taking Nibbāna as its object, then, on the signal given by it, the path of stream-entry arises, taking Nibbāna as its object and demolishing by way of eradication the three fetters: the fetter of identity view, the fetter of clinging to rules and observances, and the fetter of doubt. Immediately after that, two or three fruition-cittas, which are its result, arise, owing to the immediacy of the result of the supramundane paths. At the end of the fruition, his consciousness sinks into the life-continuum.

Tato bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā paccavekkhaṇatthāya manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. So hi “iminā vatāhaṃ maggena āgato”ti maggaṃ paccavekkhati, tato “ayaṃ me ānisaṃso laddho”ti [V 0.0208] phalaṃ paccavekkhati, tato “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti pahīnakilese paccavekkhati, tato “ime nāma me kilesā avasiṭṭhā”ti uparimaggattayavajjhe kilese paccavekkhati, avasāne “ayaṃ me dhammo ārammaṇato paṭividdho”ti amataṃ nibbānaṃ paccavekkhati. Iti sotāpannassa ariyasāvakassa pañca paccavekkhaṇāni honti. Tathā sakadāgāmianāgāmīnaṃ. Arahato pana avasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Evaṃ sabbānipi ekūnavīsati honti. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedova ceso. Pahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇañhi sekkhānaṃ hoti vā, na vā. Evaṃ paccavekkhitvā so sotāpanno ariyasāvako tasmiṃyeva vā āsane nisinno aparena vā samayena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanubhāvaṃ karonto dutiyamaggaṃ pāpuṇāti, tadanantaraṃ vuttanayena phalañca. Tato vuttanayena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ anavasesappahānaṃ karonto tatiyamaggaṃ pāpuṇāti, vuttanayena phalañca. Tato tasmiṃyeva vā āsane nisinno aparena vā samayena rūparāgaarūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjānaṃ anavasesappahānaṃ karonto catutthamaggaṃ [M 0.0234] pāpuṇāti, vuttanayena phalañca. Ettāvatā cesa arahā nāma aṭṭhamo ariyapuggalo hoti mahākhīṇāsavo. Iti imesu catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma.

Then, having cut off the life-continuum, mind-door adverting arises for the purpose of reviewing. He reviews the path, thinking: 'Indeed, by this path have I come.' Then he reviews the fruit, thinking: 'This is the benefit I have obtained.' Next, he reviews the abandoned defilements, thinking: 'These defilements have been abandoned by me.' Then he reviews the remaining defilements—the defilements to be cut off by the three higher paths—thinking: 'These defilements remain in me.' Finally, he reviews the Deathless, Nibbāna, thinking: 'This is the Dhamma I have penetrated as my object.' Thus, for the noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, there are five kinds of reviewing. The same applies to the once-returner and the non-returner. For the arahant, however, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements. Thus, there are nineteen reviewings in all. This, however, is the maximum reckoning, for the reviewing of abandoned and remaining defilements may or may not occur for those in training. Having reviewed thus, that noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, while sitting in that very seat or at a later time, attenuates sensual lust and ill will and attains the second path, and subsequently the fruit in the way described. Then, in the way described, by abandoning sensual lust and ill will without remainder, he attains the third path, and the fruit in the way described. Then, while sitting in that very seat or at a later time, by abandoning lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance without remainder, he attains the fourth path, and the fruit in the way described. With that, he is the eighth noble person, called an arahant, a great one whose taints are destroyed. Thus, the knowledge in these four paths is called the purification by knowledge and vision.

Ettāvatā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlādīnaṃ vuttattā sīlavisuddhi ca mettāsubhādīnaṃ vuttattā cittavisuddhi ca nāmarūpapariggahādīnaṃ vasena diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhimaggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyo cāti satta visuddhiyo vuttā honti. Idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ paṭipadākkamaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “pāpuṇeyyānupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya”nti. Ettha sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmarāgo paṭigho rūparāgo aruparāgo māno uddhaccaṃ avijjāti ime dasa dhammā sabbasaṃyojanā nāma. Etesu sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsā sotāpattimaggavajjhā, kāmarāgapaṭighā dutiyamaggena tanubhūtā hutvā tatiyena samugghātaṃ gacchanti, sesāni pañca catutthenāti. Evaṃ anupubbena sabbasaṃyojanakkhayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇātīti veditabbaṃ.

Thus far, the purification of virtue through the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so on has been stated, and the purification of mind through loving-kindness, the contemplation of foulness, and so on has been stated. By means of the comprehension of name-and-form and so on, the purification of view, the purification by overcoming doubt, the purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, the purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and the purification by knowledge and vision—these seven purifications have been stated. This is said with reference to the gradual course of practice described thus: "He may reach, step by step, the destruction of all fetters." Here, these ten things are called 'all the fetters': identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, sensual desire, ill will, desire for form, desire for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. Among these, identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry. Sensual desire and ill will, having been attenuated by the second path, are completely eradicated by the third. The remaining five are eradicated by the fourth. Thus it should be understood that one gradually attains arahantship, which is designated as the destruction of all fetters.

Vipassanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Insight is finished.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Concluding Words

473-5. Adhisīlaadhicittānaṃ [V 0.0209] adhipaññāya ca sikkhanā uttari bhikkhukiccaṃ nāma natthi yasmā, ato ayaṃ khuddasikkhā samudāhaṭā.

Since there is no further task for a bhikkhu beyond the training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom, this 'Minor Training' has therefore been set forth.

Kenāti ce? Yassa therassa lokavicārino loke vicarantassa mahato kittisaddassa parissamo na sambhoti na hoti, kiṃ viya? Mālutasseva niccaso, yathā [M 0.0235] niccaṃ vicarantassa mālutassa parissamo natthi, evaṃ vicarantassa kittisaddassa parissamo natthi, tena dhammasirikena samudāhaṭāti sambandho.

If it is asked, 'By whom?' By that elder, the world-investigator, for whom, while wandering in the world, weariness from the great sound of his fame does not arise, does not occur. Like what? Just like the ever-moving wind. For just as there is no weariness for the wind that moves constantly, so there is no weariness for the sound of his fame that spreads. By that Dhammasirika it was set forth—this is the connection.

Ettāvatā ca –

And thus far—

Niṭṭhito khuddasikkhāya, samāsena vinicchayo;

Vitthāro pana etissā, sabbampi piṭakattayaṃ.

The concise analysis of the Minor Training is finished; its detailed explanation, however, is the entire Tipiṭaka.

Tasmā vitthārakāmena, sakale piṭakattaye;

Kattabbo sādaro ettha, itarena visesatoti.

Therefore, one who desires the detailed explanation should pay respect to the entire Tipiṭaka, and especially to this text, more so than to any other.

Khuddasikkhāvinicchayo.

The Analysis of the Minor Training.

Khuddasikkhā-purāṇaṭīkā niṭṭhitā.

The Old Sub-commentary on the Khuddasikkhā is finished.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddasikkhā-abhinavaṭīkā

The New Sub-commentary on the Khuddasikkhā

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Tilokatilakaṃ [V 0.0211][M 0.0237] vande, saddhammāmatanimmitaṃ;

Saṃsuṭṭhukatasambhattiṃ, jinaṃ janamanoramaṃ.

I venerate the Conqueror, the ornament of the three worlds, fashioned from the nectar of the true Dhamma, well-composed and revered, the delight of humankind.

Sāriputtaṃ mahāsāmiṃ, nekasatthavisāradaṃ;

Mahāguṇaṃ mahāpaññaṃ, namo me sirasā garuṃ.

With my head I bow to my teacher, Sāriputta, the great master, skilled in many sciences, of great virtue and great wisdom.

Khuddasikkhāya ṭīkā yā, purātanā samīritā;

Na tāya sakkā sakkaccaṃ, attho sabbattha ñātave.

The ancient sub-commentary on the Khuddasikkhā that was composed—by it, the meaning cannot be carefully understood everywhere.

Tatonekaguṇānaṃ [V 0.0212] yo, mañjūsā ratanānava;

Sumaṅgalasanāmena, tena paññavatā satā.

By that wise and good person named Sumaṅgala, who is a casket of many virtues, an ocean of gems;

Ajjhesito yatindena, sadāraññanivāsinā;

Savinicchayametissā, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Requested by the lord of ascetics who always dwells in the forest, I shall compose a commentary on its meaning, including an analysis.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

(Ka) etthāha – kimatthamāditovāyaṃ gāthā nikkhittā, nanu yathādhippetameva pakaraṇamārabhanīyanti? Vuccate – sappayojanattā[M 0.0238]. Sappayojanañhi taṃdassanaṃ tāya ratanattayappaṇāmābhidheyyakaraṇappakārappayojanābhidhānasandassanato. Tāni ca pana sappayojanāni anantarāyena ganthaparisamāpanādippayojanānamabhinipphādanato. Tathā hi sotūnamattano ca yathādhippetatthanipphādanaṃ ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇappayojanaṃ. Viditābhidheyyassa ganthassa viññūnamādaraṇīyatā abhidheyyakathanappayojanaṃ. Sotujanasamussāhajananaṃ karaṇappakārappayojanakathanappayojanaṃ. Vohārasukhatā pana abhidhānakathanappayojanaṃ.

Here one might say: For what purpose was this verse placed at the beginning? Should not the intended subject matter itself be started directly? It is said: Because it has a purpose. For that presentation is purposeful, as it shows the connection of the statements of the homage to the Triple Gem, the subject matter, the manner of composition, the purpose, and the title. And these purposeful statements accomplish such aims as the completion of the book without obstacles. Thus, for the listeners and for oneself, the fulfillment of the intended meaning is the purpose of making the homage to the Triple Gem. For the wise who know the subject matter, its being worthy of respect is the purpose of stating the subject matter. The generation of enthusiasm in the audience is the purpose of stating the manner of composition and its purpose. Ease of expression, however, is the purpose of stating the title.

Tattha vanditvā ratanattayanti iminā ratanattayappaṇāmo dassito, khuddasikkhanti iminā khuddabhūtānaṃ sikkhānaṃ idha paṭipādetabbatādīpanena abhidheyyaṃ, abhidheyyo ca nāmesa samuditena satthena vacanīyatthoti. Abhidhānañca pana imināva dassitaṃ tena atthānugatasamaññāparidīpanato. Samātikanti iminā karaṇappakāro, khuddasikkhanti iminā ca, tena khuddabhūtānaṃ sikkhānaṃ idha dassetabbabhāvappakāsanato. Ādito upasampanna sikkhitabbanti iminā payojanapayojanaṃ pana imināva sāmatthiyato dassitameva, tāsaṃ sikkhitabbappakāsanena hi sikkhane sati tammūlikāya diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthanipphattiyā saṃsijjhanato. Pakaraṇappayojanānaṃ sādhanasādhiyalakkhaṇo sambandho tannissayadassaneneva dassitoyevāti ayamettha samudāyattho.

Therein, by 'having venerated the Triple Gem,' the homage to the Triple Gem is shown. By 'the minor training,' the subject matter is indicated by pointing out that the minor trainings are to be expounded here; and the subject matter is the meaning to be conveyed by the collective text. Moreover, the title is shown by this very phrase, through its exposition of a name that accords with the meaning. By 'with its summary,' the manner of composition is shown, and also by 'the minor training,' as this clarifies the way the minor trainings are to be presented here. By 'from the beginning, one who is fully ordained should train,' the ultimate purpose is indeed shown by implication, for by indicating that these should be trained in, when the training is undertaken, the accomplishment of benefits in this life and the next, which are rooted in it, is achieved. The relationship between the purposes of the treatise, which has the characteristic of means and end, is shown precisely by seeing its dependence—this is the comprehensive meaning here.

Ayaṃ panetthāvayavattho – ratanattayaṃ vanditvā khuddasikkhaṃ pavakkhāmīti sambandho. Ratijananaṭṭhena [V 0.0213] ratanāni, buddhadhammasaṅghānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Atha vā cittīkatādinā kāraṇena ratanāni, buddhādayova ratanāni. Tathā ca vuttaṃ –

Now, this is the analysis of the parts. The connection is: 'Having venerated the Triple Gem, I will explain the Khuddasikkhā.' Because they generate delight (rati), they are 'gems' (ratanāni); this is a designation for the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Or alternatively, for reasons such as being esteemed (cittīkata), they are gems; the Buddha and the others are indeed the gems. And so it is said:

“Cittīkataṃ [M 0.0239] mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.223; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; udā. aṭṭha. 45; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50);

Cherished and of great price, incomparable, and rare to see; enjoyed by beings of surpassing worth, for that reason it is called a gem.

Tayo avayavā assāti tayaṃ, samudāyāpekkhaṃ ekavacanaṃ, avayavavinimuttassa pana samudāyassa abhāvato tīṇi eva ratanāni vuccanti. Ratanānaṃ tayaṃ ratanattayaṃ. Vanditvāti tīhi dvārehi namassitvā. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vandanā kāyena vandati, vacasā vandati, manasā vandatī”ti (a. ni. 3.155) hi vuttaṃ. Tattha viññattiṃ anuppādetvā kevalaṃ ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇavasena manodvāre bahulappavattā kusalacetanā manodvāravandanā. Taṃ taṃ viññattiṃ uppādetvā pana pavattā kāyavacīdvāravandanā. Sikkhitabbāti sikkhā, adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāvasena tisso sikkhā. Sikkhanañcettha yathākkamaṃ sīlādidhammānaṃ saṃvaraṇavasena, ekārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ samādhānavasena, ārammaṇajānanalakkhaṇappaṭivedhamaggapātubhāvapāpanavasena ca āsevanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññattha bahuvidhā sikkhā, idha tu saṅkhepanayattā appakādianekatthasambhavepi khudda-saddassa appakatthovettha yuttataroti khuddā appakā sikkhāti khuddasikkhā. Idha pana khuddasikkhāppakāsako gantho tabbohārūpacārato itthiliṅgavasena “khuddasikkhā”ti vuccati yathā “varuṇānagara”nti. Taṃ khuddasikkhaṃ. Pavakkhāmīti kathessāmi.

“It has three components,” thus it is a “triad” (tayaṃ); this is a singular noun used with reference to the collection. But since a collection does not exist apart from its components, they are spoken of as the “three gems.” A triad of gems is the “Triple Gem” (ratanattayaṃ). “Having venerated” means having paid homage with the three doors. For it is said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of veneration: one venerates with the body, one venerates with speech, one venerates with the mind” (AN 3.155). Here, the wholesome volition that arises frequently in the mind-door solely by way of recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, without producing a physical or verbal expression, is veneration by the mind-door. Veneration by the body-door and speech-door, however, occurs by producing their respective expressions. “What is to be trained in” is a “training” (sikkhā); there are three trainings: the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. Here, training should be seen as cultivation, respectively, by way of restraint in regard to the principles of virtue, etc.; by way of concentrating the mind and mental factors on a single object; and by way of bringing about the manifestation of the path of penetration, which has the characteristic of knowing the object. Elsewhere, trainings are of many kinds, but here, because of the concise method, although the word “khudda” can have several meanings such as “small,” the meaning “small” is most suitable. Thus, “small trainings” is “khuddasikkhā.” Here, however, the book that explains the minor training is called “Khuddasikkhā” in the feminine gender by transference of epithet, as in the case of “Varuṇānagara.” That is the “Khuddasikkhā.” “I will explain” means “I will tell.”

Kīdisanti āha “ādito upasampannasikkhitabba”ntiādi. Ādi-saddoyamatthi avayavavacano yathā “sabbādīni sabbanāmānī”ti. Atthi apādānavacano yathā “pabbatādīni khettānī”ti. Tatthāvayavavācī kammasādhano “ādiyatītyādī”ti. Itaro apādānasādhano “ādiyati etasmātyādī”ti[M 0.0240]. Tattha yo avayavavacano, tassedaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tasmā upasampannakkhaṇampi anto katvā ādibhūtā upasampannakkhaṇatoyeva paṭṭhāyāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Eva-saddo panettha sabbavākyānaṃ avadhāraṇaphalattā labbhati. To-paccayo avadhimhiyeva[V 0.0214], na ādhāre. Tattha hi topaccaye ādhāre vattamāne ādimhiyeva majjhaantānaṃ avayavabhūte upasampannakkhaṇeyevāti attho bhaveyya, tathā sati avadhāraṇanicchayo niyamoti atthantarattā ādikkhaṇaniyamena majjhādayo nivattiyeyyuṃ. Apādānavacanassāpi gahaṇe avadhibhūto upasampannakkhaṇo nivattiyeyya “pabbatādīni khettānī”ti ettha ādibhūtapabbatapariccāgena khettaggahaṇaṃ viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana ādhāratthopi vutto, so yathāvuttadosaṃ nātigacchati. Sabbattha “ṭīkāya”nti ca vutte ettheva purāṇaṭīkāyanti gahetabbaṃ. Āditoti iminā idaṃ dīpeti – atidullabhaṃ khaṇasamavāyaṃ labhitvā ālasiyadosena appaṭipajjantehi ca aññāṇadosena aññathā paṭipajjantehi ca ahutvā ādito paṭṭhāya nirantarameva tīsu sikkhāsu sammāpaṭipajjanavasena ādaro janetabboti.

What kind (of training) is it? It is said: “From the beginning, one should train after full ordination,” and so on. Here, the word “ādi” (beginning) has a partitive meaning, as in “all (sabbādīni) are pronouns (sabbanāmānī).” It also has an ablative meaning, as in “fields (khettānī) from the mountains (pabbatādīni).” There, the partitive sense is derived from the object, as in “one takes (ādiyati), hence ‘ādi.’” The other (ablative sense) is derived from the ablative, as in “one takes (ādiyati) from this (etasmā), hence ‘ādi.’” Here, the partitive meaning is what is intended. Therefore, including the moment of full ordination, the meaning here should be understood as: beginning precisely from that initial moment of full ordination itself. The word “eva” (only) here is used because it has the effect of emphasizing all the sentences. The suffix “-to” applies only to the limit (avadhi), not to the basis (ādhāra). For if the suffix “-to” were applied to the basis, the meaning would be that the middle and end, being parts, exist only in the initial moment of full ordination. If that were the case, the intention to specify would imply a restriction, and thus the middle and following moments would be excluded by the restriction to the initial moment, due to a different meaning. Even if the ablative meaning were taken, the moment of full ordination, being the limit, would be excluded—just as in “fields from the mountains,” where the taking of fields is understood by excluding the initial mountains. In the sub-commentary, however, the sense of basis (ādhāra) is also mentioned, but it does not escape the aforementioned fault. In all cases, when “in the sub-commentary” is mentioned, it should be taken to mean specifically the ancient sub-commentary here. By the word “ādito” (from the beginning), this is indicated: having obtained the exceedingly rare conjunction of opportune moments, one should not be like those who fail to practice due to the fault of laziness or who practice wrongly due to the fault of ignorance; rather, from the very beginning, diligence should be generated by practicing correctly and continuously in the three trainings.

Upasampannena upasampannāya ca sikkhitabbaṃ āsevitabbanti upasampannasikkhitabbaṃ, ekasesanayena upasampannatāsāmaññena vā upasampannāyapi etthevāvirodhoti upasampannena sikkhitabbanti samāso. Nanu adhisīlādayova sikkhitabbā, evaṃ sati kathaṃ pakaraṇaṃ sikkhitabbattena vuttanti? Nāyaṃ doso, sikkhāya sikkhitabbatte sati taddīpakaganthassāpi āsevitabbatā āpajjatīti. Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ vattabbavinicchayaṃ sakalampi saṅgahetvā mātikāya ṭhapanato saha mātikāyāti samātikaṃ. Tagguṇasaṃviññāṇoyaṃ bahubbīhi tassa khuddasikkhāsaṅkhātassa [M 0.0241] aññapadatthassa yo guṇo mātikāsaṅkhātaṃ visesanaṃ, tassa idha viññāyamānattā. Sukheneva hi gahaṇaṃ siyā mātikānusārena taṃ taṃ vinicchayaṃ olokentānaṃ saṃsayāpagamato.

What is to be trained and cultivated by a fully ordained man and woman is “upasampannasikkhitabbaṃ.” By the ekasesa method, or by the commonality of being fully ordained, there is no contradiction here even for a fully ordained woman; thus, “upasampannena sikkhitabbaṃ” is the compound. But shouldn’t only the higher virtues and so on be trained in? If so, how is the treatise said to be what is to be trained in? This is no fault, for when the training itself is to be cultivated, the text that illuminates it also becomes something to be cultivated. For the sake of easy comprehension, the entire matter to be stated and its analysis is gathered together and placed with the matrix, hence “together with the matrix” (samātikaṃ). This is a bahubbīhi compound denoting the quality of that; the quality of the other word’s meaning, which is called the “minor training,” is the distinguishing feature called the matrix, because it is recognized here. Indeed, comprehension becomes easy when, by following the matrix, one examines each analysis and dispels doubts.

Mātikāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Matrix

(Kha-ja) idāni [V 0.0215] “samātika”nti vuttattā mātikāpadāni tāva uddisituṃ “pārājikā ca cattāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Etthāha – tīsu sikkhāsu adhisīlasikkhāva kasmā paṭhamaṃ vuttāti? Sabbasikkhānaṃ mūlabhūtattā. “Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) hi vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi mahāsāvajjattā mūlacchejjavasena pavattanato sabbapaṭhamaṃ jānitabbāti pārājikāva paṭhamaṃ vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Mātikāpadānaṃ pana attho tassa tassa mātikāpadassa niddesavaseneva viññāyatīti na idha visuṃ dassayissāma. Aviññāyamānaṃ pana tattha tattheva pakāsayissāma.

(Kha-ja) Now, since “together with the matrix” (samātikaṃ) has been stated, the matrix terms are first recited, beginning with “And there are four pārājikas,” and so on. Here it is asked: Why is the training in higher virtue stated first among the three trainings? Because it is the root of all trainings. For it is said: “A wise person, established in virtue, develops mind and wisdom” (SN 1.23; Peṭakopadesa 22; Milindapañha 2.1.9). Furthermore, because of their great gravity and because they lead to cutting off the root, it should be understood that the pārājikas are stated first among all, as they are to be known first. As for the meaning of the matrix terms, it will be understood through the explanation of each matrix term itself, so we will not elaborate on it separately here. However, what is not understood we will clarify in the appropriate places.

Idāni uddiṭṭhapadānukkamena niddesaṃ ārabhanto “pārājikā ca cattāro”ti paṭhamaṃ mātikāpadaṃ uddhari. Evamuparipi. Idāni pārājikāyo uddisitvā uddiṭṭhapadānukkamena niddesaṃ ārabhanto “garukā navā”ti dutiyaṃ padaṃ uddharītiādinā yathāyogaṃ vattabbaṃ. Tattha sikkhāpadaṃ atikkamitvā āpattiṃ āpannā puggalā tāya parājayantīti parājiyā. Teyeva pārājikā upasaggassa vuddhiṃ katvā ya-kārassa ka-kārakaraṇena. Te pana gaṇanaparicchedavasena cattāroti attho.

Now, beginning the explanation in the order of the terms laid down, the first matrix term, “And there are four pārājikas,” is cited. And so on for what follows. Now, having cited the pārājikas, beginning the explanation in the order of the terms laid down, the second term, “Nine are grave,” is cited, and so on, as appropriate. There, individuals who, having transgressed a training rule, incur an offense, are defeated by that—hence, they are parājiya. Those very ones are pārājika through the augmentation of the prefix and the changing of the “ya” sound to “ka.” But they are four by way of numerical delimitation—this is the meaning.

1. Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Explanation of the Pārājikas

1-2. Idāni te dassetuṃ “maggattaye”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha maggattayeti ettha [M 0.0242] maggā ca nāma tiṃsa maggā. Manussāmanussatiracchānagatavasena hi tisso itthiyo. Tattha tiracchānagatāya ayaṃ paricchedo –

1-2. Now, to explain them, the section beginning “in the three paths” has been commenced. Similarly, what follows should be connected appropriately. Here, regarding “in the three paths,” there are indeed thirty paths. For there are three types of females, according to whether they are human, non-human, or animal. Here, this is the delineation for the animal:

“Apadānaṃ ahī macchā, dvipadānañca kukkuṭī;

Catuppadānaṃ majjārī, vatthu pārājikassimā”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.55);

For the footless, snakes and fish; for the two-footed, the hen; for the four-footed, the cat—these are the grounds for a pārājika offense.

Tāsaṃ vaccapassāvamukhamaggavasena tayo tayo katvā nava maggā, tathā ubhatobyañjanakānaṃ, purisānaṃ pana vaccamukhamaggavasena dve dve katvā cha, tathā paṇḍakānanti tiṃsa. Tesaṃ taye. Kīdiseti āha “santhatasanthate”ti. Santhate asanthateti padacchedo. Na santhataṃ asanthataṃ. Tasmiṃ asanthate. Na-kāro ettha “abrāhmaṇo”tiādīsu viya payirudāse, taṃ kiriyāyuttassa tādisassa aññassa vatthuno vidhānena santhatassa vatthuno payirudāsanaṃ pariccajanaṃ payirudāsoti. Na pasajjappaṭisedhe, santhataṃ pasajja patvā tassa “brāhmaṇo na bhavissatī”tiādīsu viya na nisedhoti. Vā-saddo panettha vacanayuttibaleneva labbhati, tassa paliveṭhetvā, anto vā pavesetvā vatthādinā kenaci paṭicchanne vā appaṭicchanne vāti attho. Tathābhūte allokāse pakativātena asamphuṭṭhe tintappadese. Nimittanti aṅgajātaṃ. Santiādi tabbisesanaṃ. Santi attaniyaṃ. Saṃ-saddo hi attani attaniye ca vattati. Santhataṃ asanthatanti yathāvuttanayena paṭicchannaṃ vā appaṭicchannaṃ vā. Upādiṇṇanti anaṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ. Kittakanti āha “tilamattampī”ti. Tilassa mattaṃ sākallaṃ yassa taṃ tilamattaṃ[V 0.0216]. “Mattaṃ sākallaṃ nicchaye”ti hi nighaṇḍu. Etthāpi avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho, tilabījappamāṇampīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ taṃ? Nimittaṃ, pavesanaṃ vā. Api-saddo sambhāvane, “tilabījamattampī”ti sambhāvīyati, adhike kā [M 0.0243] nāma kathāti idamettha sambhāvanaṃ, evaṃbhūtaṃ saṃ aṅgajātaṃ yathāvutte maggattaye tilamattampi pavesanto bhikkhu cuto paribhaṭṭho, pārājiko nāma hoti sāsanatoti viññāyati gammamānatthassa saddassa payogaṃ pati kāmācārattā. Kīdisoti āha “anikkhittasikkho”ti. Nikkhittasikkho pana abhikkhukattā pariccatto. Tattha nikkhittā ohitā pariccattā paccakkhātā sikkhā etenāti viggaho. Yathālakkhaṇaṃ na nikkhittasikkho anikkhittasikkho. Tattha cittakhettakālappayogapuggalavijānanavasena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ ñatvā tadabhāvena apaccakkhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For women, by way of the passages for excrement, urine, and mouth, three each make nine passages. Similarly for hermaphrodites. For men, by way of the passages for excrement and mouth, two each make six. Likewise for eunuchs—thus thirty. Of these, three. What kind? He says, 'in the covered or uncovered.' The word division is 'covered, uncovered.' 'Not covered' is 'uncovered.' In that which is uncovered. The negative particle here, as in 'not a brahmin,' etc., serves as exclusion by association (payirudāsa). That is, exclusion by association is the abandonment of a covered object by the stating of another object of that kind, which is connected with the action. It is not a direct negation (pasajjappaṭisedha). It is not a negation, as in 'he will not be a brahmin,' etc., by directly applying to the covered object. Here, the word 'or' (vā) is understood solely by the force of the context of the statement. Its meaning is: having wrapped it around, or having inserted it inside, whether covered by cloth or anything else, or uncovered. Similarly, in such a dark place, untouched by natural wind, in a moist region. The sign (nimitta) is the genital organ. 'Owned,' etc., is its qualifier. 'Owned' means belonging to oneself. For the prefix 'saṃ-' indeed applies to oneself and what belongs to oneself. 'Covered or uncovered' means, as explained, either concealed or unconcealed. 'Seized' (upādiṇṇa) means not devoid of bodily sensitivity. How much? He says, 'even the size of a sesame seed.' 'Tilamattaṃ' means that of which the measure (mattaṃ) is the entirety of a sesame seed. For the lexicon states, 'measure means entirety in determination.' Here too, the analysis by parts implies the aggregate meaning; it is said to be even the size of a sesame seed. What is that? The sign, or the insertion. The word 'even' (api) is for possibility: 'even the size of a sesame seed' is considered possible—what more need be said for more? This is the possibility here. It is understood that a monk who inserts such a genital organ, even the size of a sesame seed, into the aforementioned three passages, is fallen, ruined, and is called a pārājika in the Dispensation, due to the freedom of usage of the word with respect to the meaning that is to be understood. What kind? He says, 'one who has not discarded the training.' One who has discarded the training, however, is one who has renounced it by not being a monk. There, the analysis is: 'discarded' (nikkhittā) means laid aside, given up, rejected, renounced, by him, the training. 'Anikkhittasikkho' means one who has not discarded the training according to the characteristic. There, the renunciation of the training should be understood by way of the mind, field, time, application, and knowledge of the person, and non-renunciation by the absence thereof.

Tattha upasampannabhāvato cavitukāmatācittaṃ cittaṃ nāma. “Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādīni “gihīti maṃ dhārehi, upāsako, ārāmiko, sāmaṇeroti maṃ dhārehī”ti “alaṃ me buddhenā”tiādīni cha khettapadāni khettaṃ nāma. “Paccakkhāmī”tiādinā vutto vattamānakāloyeva kālo nāma. Yāya kāyaci bhāsāya vasena vācasikappayogova payogo nāma. Anummattādiko paccakkhāto ca manussajātiko sova puggalo nāma. Paccakkhātakassa vacanasamanantarameva “ayaṃ ukkaṇṭhito”ti vā “gihibhāvaṃ patthayatī”ti vā sotuno jānanaṃ vijānanaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Here, the thought of wishing to fall away from the state of being ordained is called 'mind' (citta). The six phrases—'I renounce the Buddha,' and so on; 'Consider me a layperson,' 'Consider me a lay follower,' 'Consider me a monastery attendant,' 'Consider me a novice,' and 'Enough of the Buddha for me,' and so on—are called 'field' (khetta). The present moment when one utters phrases like 'I renounce,' and so on, is called 'time' (kāla). The verbal application by way of whatever language is called 'application' (payoga). The person who renounces, such as one who is not insane, and is of human birth, is called 'person' (puggala). Immediately after the statement of renunciation, the listener's knowing—whether 'This one is disgusted' or 'He desires the lay state'—is called 'knowledge' (vijānana). This should be understood.

Tattha naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ pana piḷakaṃ vā cammakhilaṃ vā lomaṃ vā pavesantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Akkhināsakaṇṇacchiddavatthikosesu, satthakādīhi katavaṇe vā methunarāgena nimittaṃ pavesantassa thullaccayaṃ. Avasesasarīresu upakacchakādīsu dukkaṭaṃ. Tiracchānagatānaṃ hatthiassagogadrabhaoṭṭhamahiṃsādīnaṃ nāsāya thullaccayaṃ, vatthikose thullaccayameva. Sabbesampi tiracchānagatānaṃ akkhikaṇṇavaṇesu dukkaṭaṃ. Tathā avasesasarīre [M 0.0244] kāyasaṃsaggarāgena, methunarāgena vā jīvamānakapurisassa vatthikosaṃ appavesanto nimittena nimittaṃ chupati, dukkaṭaṃ. Bahi nikkhantadantesu vāyamantassa pana thullaccayanti ayamettha savinicchayo atthavaṇṇanakkamo.

Here, however, for one who inserts a boil, or a skin tag, or a hair into a place where bodily sensitivity is destroyed, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who inserts the sign (nimitta) with sexual desire into the eye, nose, ear aperture, or genital area, or into a wound made by a knife or similar tools, there is a thullaccaya offense. For the remaining parts of the body, such as the armpits, etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense. For animals—such as elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, buffalo, etc.—inserting into the nose incurs a thullaccaya offense, and into the genital area, it is indeed a thullaccaya offense. For all animals, inserting into the eye, ear, or a wound is a dukkaṭa offense. Similarly, for the remaining parts of the body, if one touches a sign with a sign out of desire for bodily contact or sexual desire—without inserting into the genital area of a living male—there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, for one who makes an effort with teeth protruding outward, there is a thullaccaya offense. This is the detailed determination and the order of the meaning here.

Idāni pavesanaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ attupakkameneva, parūpakkamenāpi hoti, tatrāpi sādiyantova [V 0.0217] cuto hotīti dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha atha vāti ayaṃ nipāto, nipātasamudāyo vā pakkhantarārambhe. Pavesanañca ṭhitañca uddhāro ca paviṭṭhañca pavesana…pe… paviṭṭhāni, itarītarayogadvando. Itarītarayogo nāma aññamaññatthopādānatāti pavesanādīni ṭhitādiatthānipi hontīti paviṭṭha-saddopi pavesanādiattho hoti, tatoyevettha tasmā bahuvacanasambhavo. Aññathā dvande avayavatthapadhānattā ekatthavācakāpi paviṭṭha-saddā kathaṃ bahuvacanappasaṅgo. Samāhāre vā dvando. Khaṇoti kālaviseso. So ca yogavantānaṃ khaṇantaravinimutto natthīti pavesana…pe…paviṭṭhāniyeva khaṇoti kammadhārayo, abhede bhedaparikappanāya vā pavesana…pe… paviṭṭhānaṃ khaṇoti chaṭṭhītappuriso. Tassa sādako, tasmiṃ vā sādako pavesana…pe… sādako. Khaṇa-saddo panettha paccekaṃ yojetabbo dvandasamāsattā, pavesanakālaṃ ṭhitakālaṃ uddhārakālaṃ paviṭṭhakālaṃ, tasmiṃ vā sādiyantoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ sevanacittapaccupaṭṭhānena sādako bhikkhu cutoti yojetabbaṃ. Tattha yathāvuttappadesassa antokaraṇaṃ pavesanaṃ nāma. Yāva uddharaṇārambhā nivattaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.58) pana mātugāmassa sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ patvā sabbathā vāyamato oramitvā ṭhitakālaṃ sandhāya “sukkavissaṭṭhisamaye”ti [M 0.0245] vuttaṃ. Yāva aggā nīharaṇaṃ uddhāro nāma. Yāva pavesanārahaṭṭhānā antokataṃ paviṭṭhaṃ nāma.

Now, to show that 'entry' (pavesanaṃ) occurs not only by one's own effort but also by the effort of others, and that even then one falls only if one consents, the phrase 'or alternatively' (atha vā) and so on is stated. Here, 'or alternatively' (atha vā) is a particle, or a group of particles, for introducing an alternative side. Entry (pavesana), remaining (ṭhita), withdrawal (uddhāra), and entered (paviṭṭha)—these, i.e., entry... up to entered, form a reciprocal compound (itarītarayogadvanda). A reciprocal compound means the mutual inclusion of meanings. Thus, the terms 'entry' and so on also have the meanings of 'remaining' and so on, and likewise, the word 'entered' (paviṭṭha) also has the meaning of 'entry' and so on. For this very reason, the plural form is possible here. Otherwise, in a compound, since the individual components are primary, how could the plural apply to the word 'entered,' even if it denotes a single meaning? Alternatively, it could be an aggregative compound (samāhāre dvando). 'Khaṇa' means a specific moment. And for those engaged (in the act), there is no moment free from that. Thus, 'entry... up to entered' itself is the moment, forming a descriptive compound (kammadhāraya). Alternatively, by conceiving a distinction in what is undifferentiated, 'the moment of entry... up to entered' is a genitive tatpurisa (chaṭṭhītappuriso). Its consenter, or the consenter in that (moment)—entry... up to the consenter. Here, the word 'moment' (khaṇa) should be connected individually due to the reciprocal compound, meaning the moment of entry, the moment of remaining, the moment of withdrawal, the moment of being entered—or while consenting in that (moment). Thus, the meaning here should be understood in this way. In this way, it should be connected that the monk who consents, due to the arising of the mind of indulgence, falls. Here, making it internal to the aforementioned region is called 'entry' (pavesanaṃ). Remaining (ṭhitaṃ) is its cessation until the beginning of withdrawal. In the commentary (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.58), however, 'at the time of emission' (sukkavissaṭṭhisamaye) is stated with reference to the period of remaining, having reached the emission of semen of a woman and having completely exerted oneself and then ceased. Withdrawal (uddhāro) is pulling out up to the tip. Entered (paviṭṭhaṃ) is what has been made internal up to the place suitable for entry.

Paṭhamaṃ.

First.

3-4. Idāni dutiyaṃ dassetuṃ “ādiyeyyā”tiādimāha. Tattha adinnaṃ theyyacittena ādiyeyya…pe… saṅketaṃ vītināmaye, pārājiko bhaveti sambandho. Adinnanti manussasāmikehi kāyavācāhi na dinnaṃ. Theyyacittenāti thenoti coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ na-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā dvittena. Bhavanti etasmā abhidhānabuddhīti bhāvo, saddappavattinimittaṃ jātiguṇādi. Idha pana avaharaṇacittasaṅkhātaṃ dabbaṃ theyyaṃ. Theyyañca taṃ cittañcāti theyyacittaṃ, tena. Ādiyeyyāti ārāmādiṃ abhiyuñjitvā gaṇheyya. Hareyyāti haranto gaṇheyya. Avahareyyāti upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “dehi me bhaṇḍa”nti vuccamāno “na mayā gahita”ntiādīni vadanto gaṇheyya. Iriyāpathaṃ kopeyyāti bhaṇḍahārakassa gamanādiiriyāpathaṃ vicchinditvā gaṇheyya. Kopaṃ katvā gaṇhātīti hi etasmiṃ atthe “kopī”ti [V 0.0218] nāmadhātu. Ṭhānā cāveyyāti ṭhapitaṭṭhānato cāveyya. Saṅketaṃ vītināmayeti parikappitaṭṭhānaṃ vā suṅkaghātaṃ vā atikkāmeyya.

Now, to explain the second pārājika, he says, beginning with 'he would take.' Here, the connection is: 'he would take what is not given with the intention to steal... up to... he would pass the agreed signal, he becomes a pārājika.' 'What is not given' (adinnaṃ) means what is not given by human owners through body or speech. 'With the intention to steal' (theyyacittena): 'theno' is a thief; the state of being a thief is 'theyya,' formed by changing the 'na' to 'ya' and doubling it. 'Bhāva' is that from which the understanding of a term arises, the cause of the application of a word, such as genus or quality. Here, however, theft (theyya) is the thing designated as the mind of taking away. And that theft is the mind, thus 'the intention to steal' (theyyacitta), by means of that. 'He would take' (ādiyeyya) means he would seize it, having laid claim to a park or the like. 'He would carry away' (hareyya) means he would seize it while carrying. 'He would steal' (avahareyya) means he would seize a deposited object, saying 'I did not take it,' etc., when told 'Give me the object.' 'He would disrupt the movement' (iriyāpathaṃ kopeyya) means he would seize it by interrupting the movement, such as walking, of the object's carrier. For in this sense, 'he takes having caused disruption,' the denominative verb is 'kopī.' 'He would remove from its place' (ṭhānā cāveyya) means he would remove it from the place where it was put. 'He would pass the agreed signal' (saṅketaṃ vītināmaye) means he would go beyond the prearranged place or the customs barrier.

Ettha ca ārāmādiabhiyuñjane, sāmikassa vimatuppādanadhuranikkhepe, bhaṇḍahārakassa sīsabhārāmasanaphandāpanakhandhoropane, upanikkhitte “dehi me bhaṇḍa”nti codiyamānassa “nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti bhaṇanavimatuppādanadhuranikkhepe, thalaṭṭhassa theyyacittenāmasanaphandāpanaṭhānācāvane cāti catūsu paccekaṃ yathākkamaṃ dukkaṭathullaccayapārājikāyo veditabbā. “Sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ nessāmī”ti [M 0.0246] paṭhamadutiyapādasaṅkāmane, parikappitasuṅkaghātaṭṭhānato paṭhamadutiyapādātikkāme cāti dvīsu paccekaṃ kamena thullaccayapārājikāyo veditabbā. Ayamettha saviññāṇakāviññāṇakamissakattā nānābhaṇḍavasena yojanā. Ekabhaṇḍavasena pana sassāmikassa dāsassa vā tiracchānagatassa vā yathāvuttena abhiyogādinā nayena ādiyanaharaṇādivasena yojanā daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, in laying claim to a park, etc., culminating in the owner laying down the burden of ownership through the arising of doubt; in the touching, shaking, or lowering from the head to the shoulder of a porter's load; in the laying down of the burden through the arising of doubt by saying, 'I did not take it,' when reproached with, 'Give me the goods,' regarding a deposited item; and in touching, shaking, or moving from its place something on the ground with the intention of theft—in these four cases, offenses of dukkaṭa, thullaccaya, and pārājika should be understood respectively for each stage. In moving the first or second foot with the thought, 'I will take the goods along with the porter'; and in crossing beyond the prearranged customs barrier with the first or second foot—in these two cases, offenses of thullaccaya and pārājika should be understood in sequence for each. Here, this application is in terms of various goods, because it is a mixture of animate and inanimate things. However, in the case of a single item, the application should be understood in terms of taking, carrying away, etc., a slave or an animal belonging to an owner, by the method of laying claim, etc., as stated.

Apica imāni cha padāni vaṇṇayantena nānābhaṇḍaekabhaṇḍasāhatthikapubbappayogatheyyāvahārasaṅkhāte pañcapañcake samodhānetvā pañcavīsati avahārā dassetabbā chappadantogadhattā sabbesampi avahārānaṃ. Te pana avahārā yena kenaci abhiyogādiākāranānattamattena bhinnāti taṃvasena pañcapañcakaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Evaṃ saṃvaṇṇitañhi idaṃ adinnādānapārājikaṃ suvaṇṇitaṃ nāma hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha purimāni dve pañcakāni “ādiyeyyā”tiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ padānaṃ vasena labbhanti. Yaṃ panetaṃ “saṅketaṃ vītināmaye”ti chaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ, taṃ tatiyapañcamesu pañcakesu nissaggiyaparikappāvahāravasena yojetabbaṃ.

Moreover, in explaining these six terms, one should demonstrate twenty-five instances of appropriation by combining the five groups of five—designated as various goods, single goods, by one's own hand, prior application, and thieving appropriation—since all appropriations are included within these six terms. These appropriations, however, are distinguished by the mere diversity of modes such as laying claim, etc.; it is on account of that difference that the name 'five groups of five' has arisen. Thus, it should be understood that this pārājika offense of taking what is not given, when so explained, is well-expounded. Of these, the first two groups of five are obtained based on the five terms beginning with 'he would take.' But this sixth term, 'he would pass the agreed signal,' should be connected to the third and fifth groups of five by way of appropriation by relinquishment and by pre-arrangement.

Tattha sāhatthika-saddena upacārato taṃsahacaritapañcakaṃ gahetvā “sāhatthikañca taṃ pañcakañcā”ti vā “sāhatthikādi pañcaka”nti majjhepadalopavasena vā sāhatthikapañcakaṃ. Evamuparipi. Taṃ pana sāhatthiko āṇattiko nissaggiyo atthasādhako dhuranikkhepo cāti. Tattha sako hattho sahattho, sahatthena nibbatto sāhatthiko. Evaṃ āṇattiko. Suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsānaṃ anto ṭhatvā bahi nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, so eva nissaggiyo. Kālaṃ aniyametvā āṇattassa bhaṇḍaggahaṇato [M 0.0247] ca parassa telakumbhiyā pādagghanakaṃ telaṃ avassaṃ pivanakānaṃ upāhanādīnaṃ nikkhittānaṃ telapātanato ca puretarameva pārājikasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ [V 0.0219] sādhetīti atthasādhako. So pana āṇāpanappayogo, upāhanādīnaṃ nikkhepappayogo ca. Ārāmābhiyoge ca upanikkhittabhaṇḍe ca tāvakālikabhaṇḍadeyyānamadāne ca dhurassa nikkhepo dhuranikkhepo.

Herein, by the term 'sāhatthika,' the group of five associated with it is taken figuratively, thus forming 'sāhatthikapañcaka' either as 'sāhatthika and that fivefold group' or by eliding the middle term as 'sāhatthika, etc., fivefold group.' The same applies to the others. Now, these are: sāhatthika (by one's own hand), āṇattika (by command), nissaggiya (by relinquishment), atthasādhaka (accomplishing the purpose), and dhuranikkhepa (laying down the burden). Herein, one's own hand is 'sahattha,' and what is done by one's own hand is 'sāhatthika.' Similarly, 'āṇattika.' Relinquishment (nissaggo) is standing inside the prearranged customs area and placing the goods outside; that itself is 'nissaggiya.' 'Atthasādhaka' is so called because it accomplishes the purpose—classified as pārājika—even before the act is complete, as in the taking of goods by one commanded without a fixed time, and in spilling oil from another's oil pot onto a foot-wiper, or spilling oil onto deposited drinking vessels, sandals, and so forth. This refers to the application of a command and the application of leaving behind sandals and such. 'Dhuranikkhepa' is the laying down of the burden in laying claim to a park, in the case of deposited goods, and in not giving goods that should be given for a time.

Pubbappayogapañcakaṃ nāma pubbappayogo sahappayogo saṃvidhāvahāro saṅketakammaṃ nimittakammanti. Tattha āṇāpanaṃ bhaṇḍaggahaṇato pubbattā pubbappayogo nāma. Ṭhānācāvanakhilasaṅkāmanappayogena saha vattamāno sahappayogo. Saṃvidhāya sammantayitvā gatesu ekenāpi bhaṇḍe ṭhānā cāvite sabbesaṃ avahāro saṃvidhāvahāro. Saṅketakammanti pubbaṇhādikālaparicchedavasena sañjānanakaraṇaṃ. Nimittakammaṃ nāma saññuppādanatthaṃ akkhinikhaṇanādikaraṇaṃ.

The fivefold group of prior application is called: prior application, concurrent application, appropriation by arrangement, action by signal, and action by sign. Among these, commanding (āṇāpanaṃ) is called prior application because it is prior to the taking of goods. Concurrent application is that which occurs simultaneously with an action such as moving from a place or moving a post. Appropriation by arrangement is when, after arranging and agreeing, even if the goods are moved from their place by one person, it is an appropriation for all. Action by signal is the act of establishing recognition by defining a time, such as forenoon. Action by sign is an act such as winking the eye for the purpose of producing a signal.

Theyyāvahārapañcakaṃ pana sayameva dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Nanu ca chappadantogadhattā “sabbesampi avahārāna”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati “atha vā”ti pakkhantaravasena visuṃ viya idaṃ pañcakaṃ kasmā vuttanti? Nanu avocumhā “yena kenaci abhiyogādiākāranānattamattena bhinnā”ti, etādisassa bhedassa sambhavato pakkhantaravasenāpi yujjatīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Imassa pañcakassa visuṃ uddharitvā vacanaṃ pana pasiddhivasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, kusa-saddena kusasaṅkāmanamadhippetaṃ abhedopacārena. Theyyañca balañca kuso ca channañca parikappo ca theyyā…pe… parikappaṃ, dīgho sandhivasena. Tena avahārako pārājiko bhaveti sambandho. Yo pana paṭicchannena avahārako, so atthato [M 0.0248] paṭicchannassa avahārako hotīti dvandasamāsantogadhattepicassa virodhābhāvobhāvasādhano cāyaṃ channa-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Tattha sandhicchedanādīni katvā vā tulākūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇakūṭādīhi vañcetvā vā gaṇhanto theyyāvahārako. Balakkārena parasantakaṃ gaṇhanto balāvahārako. Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā gaṇhanto kusāvahārako. Tiṇapaṇṇādīhi yaṃ kiñci paṭicchādetvā pacchā kassa paṭicchannassa avahārako paṭicchannāvahārako. Sāṭakādibhaṇḍavasena, gabbhadvārādiokāsavasena vā parikappetvā gaṇhanto parikappāvahārako. Ettha pana parikappitabhaṇḍaggahaṇe parikappitaparicchedātikkame ca pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, to present the fivefold group of appropriation by theft, he says, beginning with 'or else.' But was it not said, 'of all appropriations,' because they are included within the six terms? If so, why is this fivefold group mentioned separately with 'or else,' as if it were a different alternative? Did we not say, 'they are distinguished by the mere diversity of modes such as laying claim, etc.'? Since such a distinction is possible, it is fitting to state it as an alternative. It should be understood that the separate enumeration of this fivefold group is due to common usage. By the word 'kusa,' the moving of a lot (kusa) is intended, by a metaphor of non-difference. Theft, force, lot, concealment, and pre-arrangement—these are the five... the long vowel is due to sandhi. The connection is: by this, the appropriator becomes a pārājika. And this word 'channa' (concealed) should be understood as denoting an action, without contradiction, even though it is included in a dvandva compound, for one who appropriates by means of concealment is, in effect, an appropriator of what is concealed. Herein, one who takes by making a breach in a wall, etc., or by deceiving with false scales, false measures, or counterfeit coins, is an appropriator by theft. One who takes another’s property by force is an appropriator by force. One who takes by moving a lot is an appropriator by lot. One who covers something with grass, leaves, etc., and later appropriates what has been concealed, is an appropriator by concealment. One who takes by pre-arranging goods like cloth or by means of a secret door, etc., is an appropriator by pre-arrangement. Herein, a pārājika offense should be understood in the taking of the pre-arranged goods and in transgressing the pre-arranged boundary.

Idāni panettha vinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ “bhaṇḍakālagghadesehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha adinnādāne bhaṇḍañca kālo ca aggho ca deso ca tehi ca paribhogena ca vinicchayo kātabboti attho[V 0.0220]. Tattha avahaṭabhaṇḍassa sassāmikassāmikabhāvaṃ sassāmikepi sāmikānaṃ sālayanirālayabhāvañca upaparikkhitvā sālayakāle ce avahaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kātabbo vinicchayo bhaṇḍena vinicchayo. Nirālayakāle ce avahaṭaṃ, pārājikaṃ natthi, sāmikesu puna āharāpentesu dātabbaṃ. Tadeva hi bhaṇḍaṃ kadāci mahagghaṃ, kadāci appagghaṃ, tasmā yasmiṃ kāle bhaṇḍaṃ avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva kāle yo tassa aggho, tena kātabbo vinicchayo kālena vinicchayo. Navabhaṇḍassa yo aggho, so pacchā parihāyati, tasmā sabbadā pakatiagghavasena akatvā kātabbo vinicchayo agghena vinicchayo. Bhaṇḍuṭṭhānadese bhaṇḍaṃ appagghaṃ hoti, aññattha mahagghaṃ, tasmā yasmiṃ dese bhaṇḍaṃ avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva dese agghena kātabbo vinicchayo desena vinicchayo. Paribhogena [M 0.0249] sāṭakādino bhaṇḍassa aggho parihāyati, tasmā tassa paribhogavasena parihīnāparihīnabhāvaṃ upaparikkhitvā kātabbo vinicchayo paribhogena vinicchayo.

Now, to present the judgment here, it is said: 'By the object, time, value, and place,' and so on. Here, in the case of taking what is not given, the meaning is that judgment should be made by the object, the time, the value, the place, and by its use. Herein, concerning the stolen object, one must examine whether it has an owner or is without an owner, and if it has an owner, whether the owners are attentive or inattentive. If the object is stolen when the owner is attentive, the judgment should be made by appraising the object; this is judgment by the object. If the object is stolen when the owner is inattentive, there is no pārājika offense, but if the owners ask for it back, it must be returned. The very same object is sometimes of high value and sometimes of low value; therefore, judgment should be made based on the value at the time the object was stolen; this is judgment by time. The value of a new object declines later; therefore, judgment should not always be made based on its original value; this is judgment by value. An object is of low value in the place where it originates, but of high value elsewhere; therefore, judgment should be made based on the value in the place where the object was stolen; this is judgment by place. Through use, the value of an object such as a garment decreases; therefore, one must examine whether its value has diminished through use or not and then make the judgment; this is judgment by use.

Dutiyaṃ.

The Second.

5-7. Idāni tatiyaṃ dassetuṃ “manussaviggaha”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha manussaviggahaṃ kalalato paṭṭhāya jīvamānakamanussajātikānaṃ sarīraṃ. Cicca pāṇoti saññāya saddhiṃyeva “vadhāmi na”nti vadhakacetanāya cetetvā pakappetvā. Jīvitā vā viyojayeti yo bhikkhu jātiuṇṇaṃsunā samuddhaṭatelabindumattaṃ kalalarūpakāle tāpanādīhi vā tato vā uddhamapi tadanurūpena upakkamena rūpajīvitindriyopakkame sati tadāyattavuttino arūpajīvitassāpi voropanasambhavato ubhayajīvitā voropeyya. Vā-saddo vikappe. Maraṇacetanoti maraṇe cetanā yassa so maraṇādhippāyo. Satthahārakanti jīvitaṃ haratīti hārakaṃ, satthañca taṃ hārakañcāti satthahārakaṃ, taṃ. Assa manussaviggahassa. Upanikkhipeti samīpe nikkhipeyya vā. Etena thāvarappayogaṃ dasseti. Gāheyya maraṇūpāyanti “satthaṃ vā āhara, visaṃ vā khādā”tiādinā nayena maraṇatthāya upāyaṃ gāhāpeyya vā. Etena āṇattippayogo dassito. Vadeyya maraṇe guṇanti kāyavācādūtalekhāhi “yo evaṃ marati, so dhanaṃ vā labhatī”tiādinā nayena maraṇe guṇaṃ pakāseyya vā. Ubhayattha adhikāravasena vā-saddo āharitabbo. So bhikkhu cutoti sambandho, sāsanatoti viññāyati.

Now, to present the third [rule], the passage beginning with 'human form' is introduced. Here, 'human form' refers to the body of living human beings, starting from the embryonic stage (kalala). 'Intending to kill' means having intended and planned with the intention to kill, together with the perception, 'I will kill him.' 'Or deprives of life' means that if a monk—even at the kalala embryonic stage, which is like a drop of oil lifted up by the tip of a fine wool thread, or later, by means of heating and so on, or by a corresponding effort—when there is an attack on the material life-faculty, since it is possible also to destroy the immaterial life which is dependent on that, he would deprive the being of both lives. The word 'or' indicates an alternative. 'With the intention of death' means one whose intention is death. As for 'a life-taking weapon' (satthahārakaṃ): that which takes life is a 'taker' (hāraka), and a weapon that is a taker is a 'life-taking weapon'. That is for this human form. 'Or places it nearby' means he might place it close by. This illustrates the method of a fixed device. 'Or might cause another to take up a means of death' means he might cause another to take up a means for death with instructions such as, 'Bring a weapon,' or 'Eat poison.' This illustrates the method of command. 'Or might speak of the benefit in death' means he might proclaim the merits of death through body, speech, a messenger, or writing, such as, 'Whoever dies in this way obtains wealth,' and so on. In both places, the word 'or' should be supplied according to the context. The connection is: 'that monk is fallen'; it is understood as 'from the Dispensation'.

Idāni panassa chabbidhe payogedassetuṃ “payogā”tiādimāha. Tattha sāhatthi…pe… iddhivijjāmayā [V 0.0221] payogāti ime [M 0.0250] cha payogāti sambandho. Ka-kāralopena panettha “sāhatthī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā anekatthe anekataddhitasambhavena sahatthassāyaṃ payogo sāhatthīti padasiddhi veditabbā. Sāhatthi ca nissaggo ca āṇatti ca thāvaro cāti dvando. Iddhi ca vijjā ca, tāsamimeti iddhivijjāmayā, iddhimayo vijjāmayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Payogāti ime chappayogā nāma hontīti attho. Tattha sayaṃ mārentassa kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā paharaṇaṃ sāhatthiko payogo. Dūre ṭhitaṃ māretukāmassa kāyādīhi ususattiādīnaṃ nissajjanaṃ nissaggo. “Asukaṃ nāma mārehī”tiādinā āṇāpentassa āṇāpanaṃ āṇatti, opātakhaṇanaṃ apassenasaṃvidhānaṃ asiādīnaṃ upanikkhipanādi thāvaro. Māraṇatthaṃ kammavipākajāya iddhiyā payojanaṃ iddhimayo. Kammavipākajiddhi ca nāmesā rājādīnaṃ rājiddhiādayo. Tattha piturañño sīhaḷindassa dāṭhākoṭanena cūḷasumanakuṭumbiyamāraṇe rājiddhi daṭṭhabbā, tadatthameva athabbaṇādivijjāya parijappanaṃ vijjāmayo payogo.

Now, to explain its six kinds of employment, he begins with 'employments,' and so on. Herein, the connection is that these six employments are: personal action… and those consisting of psychic power and magical knowledge. Here, it is said as 'sāhatthī' through the elision of the letter 'ka'. Alternatively, the word-formation 'sāhatthī' should be understood as 'this is the employment of one's own hand,' due to the possibility of various taddhita suffixes in various meanings. 'Sāhatthi ca nissaggo ca āṇatti ca thāvaro ca' is a dvandva compound. Psychic power and magical knowledge—'consisting of them' is 'iddhivijjāmayā', which means 'consisting of psychic power' and 'consisting of magical knowledge'. The meaning is that these are called the six employments. Herein, for one who kills by oneself, striking with one's own body or with something connected to the body is the employment of personal action. For one wishing to kill from a distance, the discharge of arrows, spears, and so on from one's body is the employment of discharge. For one who commands, the act of commanding, saying, 'Kill so-and-so,' and so on, is the employment of command. Digging a pitfall, arranging a trap, placing swords, and so on nearby is the employment of a fixed device. The use of psychic power arisen from kamma-result for the purpose of killing is the employment consisting of psychic power. This psychic power arisen from kamma-result is, for instance, the royal power of kings and others. Herein, the royal power should be seen in the killing of the householder Cūḷasumana by the tooth-cleaner of the king who was Sīhaḷinda's father. For that very purpose, the muttering of magical knowledge like that of the Atharva Veda is the employment consisting of magical knowledge.

Evaṃ chappayoge dassetvā tesu āṇattippayogassa niyāmake dassetuṃ “kālā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathāvuttaṃ āṇattiṃ niyamenti saṅketavisaṅketatāvasena paricchindantīti āṇattiniyāmakā. Te pana kālo ca vatthu ca āvudhañca iriyāpatho cāti cattāro, tathā kiriyāviseso okāsoti gaṇanaparicchedavasena cha hontīti attho. Tattha kālo pubbaṇhādi yobbanādi ca. Vatthu māretabbo satto. Āvudhaṃ asiādi. Iriyāpatho māretabbassa gamanādi. Kiriyāviseso vijjhanādi. Okāso gāmādi. Yo hi “ajja, sve”ti aniyametvā “pubbaṇhe mārehī”ti vutto yadā kadāci pubbaṇhe māreti, natthi visaṅketo. Yo pana “pubbaṇhe”ti [M 0.0251] vutto majjhanhādīsu māreti, visaṅketo hoti, āṇāpakassa anāpatti. Evaṃ kālassa saṅketavisaṅketatāvasena niyāmakatā veditabbā. Imināva nayena vatthuādīsupi vinicchayo veditabboti.

Having thus shown the six modes of employment, to indicate the determining factors for the command mode of employment, 'time,' and so on, is stated. Herein, the determiners of command are those that define the command as previously described, by way of agreement with and disagreement from the specification. These are four: time, object, weapon, and posture; and, by way of numerical division, they are six, including specific action and location. Herein, time refers to the forenoon, etc., and youth, etc. The object is the being to be killed. The weapon is a sword, etc. Posture is the movement, etc., of the one to be killed. Specific action is piercing, etc. Location is a village, etc. For if one is told, 'Kill in the forenoon,' without the time being specified as 'today' or 'tomorrow,' and one kills at some time in the forenoon, there is no disagreement. But if one, having been told 'in the forenoon,' kills at noon or later, there is a disagreement, and the one who gave the command incurs no offense. Thus, the determining role of time should be understood by way of agreement with and disagreement from the specification. In the same way, the judgment should be understood for the object and the other factors.

Tatiyaṃ.

The Third.

8-9. Idāni catutthaṃ dassetuṃ “jhānādibheda”ntiādimāha. Tattha attani nosantaṃ attupanāyikañca paccuppannabhavassitañca aññāpadesarahitañca jhānādibhedaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vā ekekaṃ katvā vā kāyena vā vācāya vā viññattipathe dīpento nādhimāniko ñāte cuto bhaveti [V 0.0222] sambandho. Tattha attani sakasantāne nosantaṃ anuppannattāyeva avijjamānaṃ, ettha nosantoti atthe tappuriso. Jhānādibhedanti jhānaṃ ādi yassa “vimokkhasamādhi samāpatti ñāṇadassana maggabhāvanā phalasacchi kiriyākilesappahānavinīvaraṇatācittassa suññāgāre abhiratī”ti (pārā. 198) vuttassa so jhānādi, sova bhedo visesoti samāso. Taṃ jhānādibhedaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ. Attupanāyikanti “ayaṃ mayi atthī”ti ārocanavasena attani upanīyati, “ahaṃ vā ettha sandissāmī”ti attā upanīyati ettha dhammeti vā attupanāyiko, jhānādibhedo, taṃ. Paccuppannabhavassitanti paccuppannabhavo nāma idāni vattamāno attabhāvo, tannissitoti samāso, so ca jhānādibhedoyeva, taṃ.

Now, to present the fourth [rule], he begins with 'the distinction of jhāna, etc.,' and so on. Herein, the connection is: a monk who is not conceited, who displays by body or by speech in the path of communication a distinction of jhāna, etc.—which is not present in himself, is self-referential, is based on the present existence, and is without indirect reference—either by dividing it into sections or by taking each one individually, is fallen when it is known. Here, 'not present in oneself' means non-existent, precisely because it has not arisen in one's own continuum. Here, 'nosanta' is a tappurisa compound in the sense of 'not present'. The term 'jhānādibheda' is a compound where jhāna is the beginning of that which is described as 'liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandonment of defilements, freedom from obstructions, and delight in an empty dwelling' (Pārā. 198); that is the 'jhāna, etc.,' and that itself is the 'distinction' or special quality. That 'distinction of jhāna, etc.' is a superior human state. The term 'attupanāyika' (self-referential) means that it is brought near to oneself by way of declaration, as in 'this exists in me,' or alternatively, it is the dhamma where the self is brought near, as in 'I am to be found in this'; that is the self-referential 'distinction of jhāna, etc.' The term 'paccuppannabhavassita' (based on the present existence) is a compound meaning 'based on that,' where 'present existence' refers to the individual existence presently occurring; and that too is the very 'distinction of jhāna, etc.'

Aññāpadesarahitanti “yo te vihāre vasi, so bhikkhu paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjī”tiādinā (pārā. 220) nayena aññassa apadeso, tena rahito cattoti tappurisasamāso, so rahito tenāti vā bahubbīhi, jhānādibhedova[M 0.0252], taṃ. Koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vāti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjiṃ, paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji”ntiādinā nayena koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vā. Ekekaṃ katvā vāti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjiṃ, dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji”ntiādinā nayena ekekaṃ katvā vā. Ettha ca ekanti ṭhite vicchāyaṃ dvittaṃ. Ettha pana katvāti karaṇakiriyāya ekekavasena bhinnassa jhānādino atthassa sambandhanicchā vicchāti veditabbā. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “koṭṭhāsaṃ vāti ettha ‘jhānalābhī, vimokkhalābhī, samādhilābhī, samāpattilābhīmhī’ti evamādinā nayena koṭṭhāsato vāti attho”ti ca “ekekaṃ vāti ‘paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, dutiyassa jhānassa lābhīmhī’ti evamādinā nayena ekekaṃ vāti attho”ti ca vuttaṃ.
