So pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca avuttakkamoti veditabbo. Kāyena vāti hatthamuddādivasena kāyena vā. Vācāti ettha ya-kāro luttaniddiṭṭho “alajjitā”tiādīsu viya. Viññattipatheti kāyavacīviññattīnaṃ gahaṇayogye padese ṭhatvāti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Dīpentoti “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇena ayaṃ dhammo mayi atthī”ti pakāsento. Nādhimānikoti appatte pattasaññitāsaṅkhāto adhiko māno, so natthi etassāti nādhimāniko, bhikkhu. Ñāteti viññunā manussajātikena sikkhāpaccakkhāne vuttanayena viññāte sati cuto bhave sāsanatoti viññāyati. Aññāpadesena dīpayato pana thullaccayaṃ. Ettha ca –

Regarding aññāpadesarahita (without reference to another): a reference to another is in the manner of, 'The monk who lived in your monastery attained the first jhāna,' etc. (Pārā. 220). 'Devoid of that' (tena rahito) is a tappurisa compound; or, 'one who is devoid of that' (so rahito tena) is a bahubbīhi. This refers to a distinction of jhāna, etc. The phrase 'by dividing into sections' (koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vā) means by dividing into sections in the manner of, 'I attained the first jhāna, then the second jhāna; I attained the first jhāna, then the third jhāna,' etc. The phrase 'or one by one' (ekekaṃ katvā vā) means one by one in the manner of, 'I attained the first jhāna; I attained the second jhāna,' etc. Here, when eka stands, there is a doubling in the sense of repetition. Here, however, katvā (having done) should be understood as repetition (vicchā) due to the desire to connect the meaning of jhāna, etc.—which is distinct by being one by one—through the act of doing. In the Subcommentary, however, it is said: 'Here, "by sections" means in the manner of, "I am a gainer of jhāna, I am a gainer of liberation, I am a gainer of concentration, I am a gainer of meditative attainment," etc., by sections.' And: 'Here, "one by one" means in the manner of, "I am a gainer of the first jhāna, I am a gainer of the second jhāna," etc., one by one.' This should be understood as a sequence not stated in the Pāli or the Commentary. The phrase 'by body' (kāyena vā) means by the body, such as through hand gestures, etc. In the word vācā, the ya syllable is understood to be elided, as in alajjitā, etc. The phrase 'in the path of communication' (viññattipathe) should be supplied as 'standing in a place suitable for grasping bodily and verbal communications.' The word 'declares' (dīpento) means revealing, 'This quality exists in me due to this and that reason.' The term nādhimānika (not conceited) means a monk for whom there is no excessive conceit, which is reckoned as the assumption of having attained what has not been attained. The word 'known' (ñāte) means that when known by a wise human being, according to the method stated for renouncing the training, it is understood that he has fallen from the Dispensation. However, for one who declares by reference to another, there is a grave offense. Here, moreover—

Dukkaṭaṃ [V 0.0223] paṭhamasseva, sāmantamiti vaṇṇitaṃ;

Sesānaṃ pana tiṇṇampi, thullaccayamudīritanti.

A wrongdoing for the first one, described as bordering; but for the remaining three, a grave offense is stated.

Catutthaṃ.

Fourth.

10. Idāni [M 0.0253] catunnampi cetesamasaṃvāsataṃ abhabbatañca dīpetuṃ “pārājikete”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ete cattāro pārājikā puggalā yathā pure pubbe gihikāle, anupasampannakāle ca viya asaṃvāsāti sambandho. Saha vasanti yasmā sabbepi lajjino etesu kammādīsu na ekopi tato bahiddhā sandissatīti ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatāti ime tayo saṃvāsā nāma. Tattha apalokanādikaṃ catubbidhampi saṅghakammaṃ sīmāparicchinnehi pakatattehi bhikkhūhi ekato kattabbatā ekakammaṃ nāma. Tathā pañcavidhopi pātimokkhuddeso ekato uddisitabbattā ekuddeso nāma. Paññattaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato samasikkhatā nāma. Natthi te saṃvāsā etesanti asaṃvāsā. “Abhabbā”tiādīsu bhikkhubhāvāyāti tumatthe sampadānavacanaṃ, tasmā yathā sīsacchinno jīvituṃ abhabbo, evaṃ cattārome puggalā bhikkhubhāvāya bhikkhū bhavituṃ abhabbāti attho.

10. Now, to explain the inability to associate with these four and their disqualification, he begins with 'these are pārājika offenders' (pārājikete), etc. The connection is that these four pārājika individuals are 'disqualified from association' (asaṃvāsa), just as they were previously during their lay life and before their higher ordination. Since all conscientious persons live together, and not a single one among them is seen outside of these actions, etc., these three are called 'association': one action, one recitation, and equal training. Herein, 'one action' is the performance together of all four kinds of Saṅgha actions, beginning with formal declaration, by properly ordained monks within a defined boundary. Similarly, 'one recitation' is the recitation together of the fivefold Pātimokkha. Moreover, 'equal training' is the fact that the established training rules must be equally observed by all conscientious individuals. They have no association with these, hence they are 'disqualified from association.' In the phrase 'unable' (abhabbā), etc., 'for the state of a monk' (bhikkhubhāvāya) is a dative case in the sense of purpose. Therefore, just as a beheaded person is unable to live, so too these four individuals are unable to become monks—this is the meaning.

11. Idāni pariyāyāṇattīhi sambhavante dassetuṃ “pariyāyo cā”tiādimāha. Pariyāyo ca āṇatti ca tatiye manussaviggahe labbhatīti sambandho. Tattha kāyādīhi yathāvuttehi “yo evaṃ marati, so dhanaṃ vā labhatī”ti evamādiviññāpako byañjanabhūto kāyavacīpayogo pariyāyo. Iminā idaṃ dīpeti – yathā adinnādāne “ādiyeyyā”ti (pārā. 92) vuttattā pāriyāyakathāya muccati, na idha evaṃ. “Saṃvaṇṇeyyā”ti (pārā. 172) pariyāyakayāyapi na muccatīti. “Dutiye panā”tiādīsu attho pākaṭoyeva. Evamuparipi pākaṭamupekkhissāma.

11. Now, to show how these arise through indirect means and formal instructions, he begins with 'there is also an indirect means' (pariyāyo ca), etc. The connection is that 'indirect means' and 'command' are obtained in the third [Pārājika], the case of a human being. Herein, an indirect means is a bodily or verbal mode of employment that is a signifying expression, as previously described by bodily actions, etc., such as 'one who dies in this way obtains wealth,' etc. By this, he indicates that just as in the case of taking what is not given, one is freed by indirect speech because 'he may take' (Pārā. 92) is stated, it is not so here. Even by indirect speech like 'he may praise' (Pārā. 172), one is not freed. In the phrase 'but in the second case,' etc., the meaning is quite clear. Similarly, we will pass over what is clear in the following sections.

12. Idāni methunadhammādīnaṃ aṅgāni dassetuṃ “sevetū”tiādimāha. Sevetukāmatācittanti methunaṃ sevetuṃ [M 0.0254] kāmetīti sevetukāmo, tassa bhāvo nāma taṇhā, tāya sevetukāmatāya sampayuttaṃ cittanti tappuriso. Methunadhammassāti mithunānaṃ itthipurisānaṃ idanti methunaṃ, tameva dhammoti methunadhammo. Idha pana upacāravasena pārājikāpatti methunadhammo nāma. Atha [V 0.0224] vā methunena jāto dhammo pārājikāpatti methunadhammo, tassa methunadhammassa methunadhammapārājikāpattiyā. Aṅgadvayanti aṅgānaṃ kāraṇānaṃ dvayaṃ. Budhāti vinayadharā viññuno.

12. Now, to show the factors of sexual misconduct, etc., he says, beginning with “he should engage.” “Mind with the desire to engage” (sevetukāmatācitta) means one who desires to engage in sexual intercourse—this is called sevetukāma; its state is craving. The compound sevetukāmatācitta means the mind associated with that desire to engage. “Of sexual misconduct” (methunadhammassa) means that which is common to pairs, to male and female, is sexual intercourse (methuna); that very thing is called sexual misconduct (methunadhamma). Here, however, by way of extension, the pārājika offense is called sexual misconduct. Alternatively, the dhamma that arises from sexual intercourse is the pārājika offense of sexual misconduct; thus, “of sexual misconduct” refers to the pārājika offense of sexual misconduct. “Two factors” (aṅgadvaya) means a pair of causes. “The wise” (budhā) means those versed in the Vinaya, the intelligent.

13. Manussasanti manussānaṃ saṃ manussasaṃ, tadāyattavatthukā ca. Etena petatiracchānagatāyattaṃ nivatteti. Tathāsaññīti tathā tādisā saññā tathāsaññā, sā assa atthīti tathāsaññī. Parāyattasaññitā cāti attho. Bhāvappadhānā ime niddesā, bhāvapaccayalopo vā “buddhe ratana”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 6.3) viya. Evamuparipi īdisesu. Theyyacittanti thenabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ cittañca. Vatthuno garutāti bhaṇḍassa pādaatirekapādārahabhāvena garutā ca. Ūnapañcamāsake vā atirekamāsake vā thullaccayaṃ. Māsake vā ūnamāsake vā dukkaṭaṃ. Avahāroti pañcavīsatiyā avahārānaṃ aññatarena avaharaṇañcāti ime pañca adinnādānahetuyo adinnādānapārājikāpattiyā aṅgāni.

13. ‘Property of a human’ (manussasaṃ) means the property of humans, and an object dependent on them. This excludes dependence on departed spirits and animals. ‘Having such perception’ (tathāsaññī) means having a perception that is such, of such a kind; it means that one has such a perception. It also means the perception of dependence on another. These explanations emphasize the state; or it is the elision of the affix of state, as in ‘the Buddha is a jewel’ (Khu. Pā. 6.3), and similarly in such instances above. ‘Thieving mind’ (theyyacitta) means a mind that is of the nature of thievery. ‘Heaviness of the object’ (vatthuno garutā) means the object’s heaviness by being worthy of a quarter or more than a quarter. For less than five māsakas, or for more than a māsaka, it is a grave offense. For a māsaka, or for less than a māsaka, it is a wrongdoing. ‘Appropriation’ (avahāra) means appropriating by any of the twenty-five ways of appropriating. These five factors are the causes of taking what is not given, the constituents for the pārājika offense of taking what is not given.

14. Pāṇo mānussakoti manussajātisambandho pāṇo ca, pāṇoti hi vohārato satto, paramatthato pana jīvitindriyaṃ vuccati. Pāṇasaññitāti pāṇoti saññitā ca, ghātanaṃ ghāto, so eva cetanā ghātacetanā, “vadhāmi na”nti evaṃ pavattā sā ca, taṃsamuṭṭhito sāhatthikādīnaṃ channamaññataro payogo ca, tena payogena maraṇañcāti ete yathāvuttā pañca vadhahetuyo pāṇaghātāpajjitabbaāpattiyā aṅgānīti attho.

14. “A human being” (pāṇo mānussako) means a life connected to human birth; and “life” (pāṇa), in conventional terms, signifies a being, but ultimately it is called the life-faculty. “Perception of a living being” (pāṇasaññitā) means the perception of a living being. “Killing” (ghātana) is the act of slaughter; that very intention is the intention to kill (ghātacetanā), which proceeds as “I will slay him.” And any one of the six applications arising from that intention, such as by one’s own hand; and death caused by that application—these five factors, as stated, are the causes of killing and the constituents for incurring the offense of killing.

15. Attani [M 0.0255] asantatāti uttarimanussadhammassa santāne avijjamānatā ca. Pāpamicchatāyārocanāti yā sā “idhekacco dussīlo samāno ‘sīlavāti maṃ jano jānātū”tiādinā (vibha. 851) nayena vuttā pāpaicchatāya samannāgatā, tāya uttarimanussadhammassa ārocanā ca. Tassāti yassa āroceti, tassa. Manussajātitāti manussānaṃ jāti yassa, tassa bhāvo manussajātitā, sā ca, naññāpadesoti na aññāpadeso aññāpadesābhāvo ca, tadeva jānananti taṅkhaṇaṃyeva vijānanañcāti imāni pañca ettha asantadīpane asmiṃ santāne avijjamānauttarimanussadhammappakāsananimitte pārājike aṅgāni hetuyoti attho.

15. “Absence in oneself” (attani asantatā) means the non-existence of a higher human quality in one’s continuum. “Declaration out of evil desire” (pāpamicchatāyārocanā) means the declaration of a higher human quality by one who is possessed of evil desire, as described in the manner: “Here, someone of bad character, being immoral, wishes, ‘May people know me as virtuous’” (Vibh. 851). “To him” (tassa) means to whom one declares it. “Human birth” (manussajātitā) means the state of one who has a human birth, that is, the state of being human. “Not another pretext” (naññāpadeso) means not another pretext, that is, the absence of another pretext. “Knowing it then” (tadeva jānanaṃ) means knowing it at that very moment. The meaning is that these five are the constituents, the causes, here in this pārājika offense, which is characterized by the declaration of a non-existent higher human quality in this continuum.

16. Evaṃ tesamasaṃvāsatābhabbatādīni dassetvā idāni na te cattārova, atha kho santaññepīti [V 0.0225] te sabbepi samodhānetvā dassento “asādhāraṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha asādhāraṇāti pārājikā dhammā adhippetā. Teneva cettha pulliṅganiddeso. Tasmā bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūhi asādhāraṇā pārājikā dhammā cattāro cāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Upacāravasena tu ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikādikā pārājikāpannā pariggayhanti. Tāsu yā avassutā avassutassa manussapurisassa akkhakānaṃ adho jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ kapparānañca upari kāyasaṃsaggaṃ sādiyati, ayaṃ ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā. Yā pana aññissā bhikkhuniyā pārājikaṃ paṭicchādeti, sā vajjappaṭicchādikā. Yā ukkhittakaṃ bhikkhuṃ tassā diṭṭhiyā gahaṇavasena anuvattati, sā ukkhittānuvattikā. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena tintassa hatthaggahaṇaṃ saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ kāyasaṃsaggatthāya purisassa hatthapāse ṭhānaṃ ṭhatvā sallapanaṃ saṅketagamanaṃ purisassāgamanasādiyanaṃ [M 0.0256] paṭicchannokāsavavisanaṃ hatthapāse ṭhatvā kāyopasaṃharaṇanti imāni aṭṭha vatthūni yassā avassutāya, sā aṭṭhavatthukā nāma.

16. Having thus shown their unfitness for communion, incapability, and so on, now, to show that it is not just those four, but that there are indeed others as well—thus, bringing them all together, he says, beginning with “not shared.” Herein, “not shared” (asādhāraṇā) refers to the intended pārājika offenses. For this reason, the masculine gender is used here. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: the four pārājika offenses are not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus. By way of extension, however, those who have committed offenses such as ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā are included as having committed a pārājika. Among these: One who, being lustful, consents to bodily contact with a lustful man, below the collarbones and above the kneecaps and elbows, is called ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā. One who conceals another bhikkhunī’s pārājika offense is called vajjappaṭicchādikā. One who follows a suspended bhikkhu by adopting his views is called ukkhittānuvattikā. The eight grounds for a lustful bhikkhunī are: taking a man’s hand, taking the edge of his robe, standing within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of bodily contact, standing and conversing with him, going to an appointment, consenting to his coming, entering a concealed place, and standing within arm’s reach and drawing the body near. A bhikkhunī for whom these eight grounds exist, being lustful, is called aṭṭhavatthukā.

Abhabbakā ekādasa cāti ettha paṇḍako theyyasaṃvāsako titthiyapakkantako tiracchānagato mātughātako pitughātako arahantaghātako bhikkhunidūsako saṅghabhedako lohituppādako ubhatobyañjanakoti ime abhabbā ekādasa ca. Tesu paṇḍakoti opakkamikanapuṃsakapaṇḍakā ca paṇḍakabhāvapakkhe pakkhapaṇḍako ca idha adhippetā. Āsittausūyapaṇḍakānaṃ pana pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca na vāritā. Theyyasaṃvāsako pana liṅgatthenakādivasena tividho. Tattha sayaṃ pabbajitattā liṅgamattaṃ thenetīti liṅgatthenako. Bhikkhuvassagaṇanādikaṃ saṃvāsaṃ thenetīti saṃvāsatthenako. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya evaṃ paṭipajjantepi eseva nayo. Yathāvuttamubhayaṃ thenetīti ubhayatthenako. Ṭhapetvā pana imaṃ tividhaṃ –

And there are eleven who are incapable: a eunuch, one who lives in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, one who causes schism in the Saṅgha, one who maliciously sheds a Buddha's blood, and a hermaphrodite—these are the eleven who are incapable. Among them, “eunuch” (paṇḍaka) here refers to an opakkamika-paṇḍaka, a napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka, and a pakkha-paṇḍaka. However, ordination and higher ordination are not prohibited for āsitta-paṇḍakas or usūya-paṇḍakas. The one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is of three kinds, beginning with a thief of the outward signs. Here, one who has gone forth by himself and steals only the outward signs (of a monk) is called a thief of the outward signs (liṅgatthenaka). One who steals communion (with monks), such as the counting of the years of seniority, is called a thief of communion (saṃvāsatthenaka). The same principle applies to one who, having renounced the training, continues to act in this way. One who steals both as described is called a thief of both (ubhayatthenaka). But excluding these three kinds—

Rājadubbhikkhakantāra-rogaveribhayena vā;

Cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ vā, liṅgaṃ ādiyatīdha yo.

Either due to fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies; or for the sake of obtaining robes, whoever here adopts the outward sign;

Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānaso;

Theyyasaṃvāsako nāma, tāva esa na vuccatīti. (mahāva. aṭṭha. 110; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā);

He does not consent to communion, and as long as his intention is honest, for that long he is not called 'one who lives by theft.' (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 110; Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. First Pārājika Commentary);

Titthiyapakkantakādayo [V 0.0226] tu taṃtaṃvacanatthānusārena veditabbā. Tiracchānagato pana ṭhapetvā manussajātikaṃ avaseso sabbo veditabbo. Ime ekādasa puggalā bhikkhubhāvāya abhabbattā pārājikāpannasadisatāya “pārājikā”ti vuccanti. Vibbhantā bhikkhunīti gihinivāsananivatthā bhikkhunī ca. Sā hi ettāvatā pārājikā. Mudukā piṭṭhi yassa, so ca. So hi anabhiratiyā pīḷito yadā attano [M 0.0257] aṅgajātaṃ attano vaccamukhamaggesu paveseti, tadā pārājiko hoti.

Those who have gone over to other sects and so on should be understood according to the meaning of their respective terms. As for an animal, it should be understood as any being except for a human. These eleven individuals are called ‘pārājika’ because they are incapable of becoming bhikkhus and are similar to one who has committed a pārājika offense. A deranged bhikkhunī (vibbhantā bhikkhunī) refers to a bhikkhunī who wears the clothes of a householder; for by that much she is defeated. Also, one with a soft back (mudupiṭṭhika). He, afflicted by discontent, becomes defeated when he inserts his own sexual organ into his own anus or mouth.

17-18. Lambamānamaṅgajātametassāti lambī. So yathāvuttesu pavesito pārājiko. Mukhena gaṇhanto aṅgajātaṃ parassa cāti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito parassa suttassa vā matassa vā aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gaṇhāti, so parassa aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gaṇhanto ca. Tatthevābhinisīdantoti yo anabhiratiyā pīḷito tattheva parassa aṅgajāte vaccamaggena abhinisīdati, so cāti ete dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiyā abhāvepi magge maggappavesanahetu methunassa anulomikā cattāro ca. Idhāgatā cattāroti idha khuddasikkhāyaṃ yathāvuttā methunadhammā pārājikādayo cattāro cāti samodhānā piṇḍīkaraṇavasena catuvīsati pārājikā bhavantīti seso. Ettha ca gāthābandhavasena rassaṃ katvā “parājikā”ti vuttaṃ. Etthāha – mātughātakādayo tatiyaṃ pārājikaṃ āpannā, bhikkhunidūsako, mudupiṭṭhikādayo cattāro ca paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannā evāti kuto catuvīsatīti? Vuccate – mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idha anupasampannā eva adhippetā. Mudupiṭṭhikādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā pana ekena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ appaṭisevino honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttāti.

17-18. One whose sexual organ hangs down is a lambī. When it is inserted into the aforementioned passages, he is defeated. And 'one who takes another's sexual organ with the mouth': one who, afflicted by discontent, takes into his mouth the sexual organ of another who is asleep or dead, he is 'one who takes another's sexual organ with the mouth.' And 'one who sits down upon it': one who, afflicted by discontent, sits down upon another's sexual organ with his anus. These four are conducive to sexual intercourse, being a cause for the insertion of an orifice into an orifice, even in the absence of a two-by-two union. The four that have come here, that is, the four pārājikas beginning with sexual intercourse, as stated here in the Khuddasikkhā—by combining and aggregating them, there are twenty-four pārājikas; this is the rest. And here, for the sake of the verse meter, it is shortened and said as ‘parājikā’. On this, someone might say: “Those who kill their mother and so on have committed the third pārājika; the violator of a bhikkhunī, the one with a soft back, and the other four have committed the first pārājika—so how are there twenty-four?” It is said: The four, beginning with the matricide, are here intended as being unordained. The four, beginning with the one with a soft back, although included under the first pārājika, are mentioned separately because, in one way, they are not partakers of sexual intercourse.

Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Pārājika is finished.

2. Saṅghādisesaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Saṅghādisesa Offenses

19. Vuṭṭhānassa garukattā garukāti saṅghādisesā vuccanti. Navāti tesaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo. Nanu “navā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, “terasā”ti vattabbanti? Nāyaṃ doso, cirenāpajjitabbe [V 0.0227][M 0.0258] cattāro yāvatatiyake ṭhapetvā vītikkamakkhaṇeyeva āpajjitabbā paṭhamāpattikā vuccantīti. Idāni te dassetuṃ “mocetukāmatā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sukkassāti āsayadhātunānattato nīlādivasena dasavidhe sukke yassa kassaci sukkassa. Mocetukāmatāti mocetukāmatāya, ya-kāro luttaniddiṭṭho. Iminā pana vacanena mocanassāda muccanassāda muttassādamethunassāda phassassāda kaṇḍuvanassāda dassanassāda nisajjanassāda vācassāda gehasitapema vanabhaṅgiya saṅkhātesu ekādasassādesu ekaṃyeva mocanassādaṃ dasseti.

19. Because rehabilitation is a grave matter, they are called ‘grave offenses’ (garuka); this refers to the saṅghādisesas. ‘Nine’ is their numerical count. But why is ‘nine’ said, when ‘thirteen’ should be said? This is no fault. Setting aside the four yāvatatiyaka offenses, which are incurred over time, only the initial offenses, which are incurred at the very moment of transgression, are spoken of. Now, to show these, the text begins with ‘desiring to release.’ Here, ‘of semen’ refers to any semen whatsoever among the ten kinds, such as blue, etc., which are due to the diversity of the element of intention. ‘Desiring to release’ stands for ‘by the desire to release’; the letter ‘ya’ is indicated as elided. By this statement, however, among the eleven pleasures—namely, the pleasure of releasing, the pleasure of being released, the pleasure of what has been released, the pleasure of sexual intercourse, the pleasure of touch, the pleasure of scratching, the pleasure of seeing, the pleasure of sitting, the pleasure of speaking, domestic affection, and forest flirtation—only the pleasure of releasing is indicated.

Tattha mocanāya assādo sukhavedanā mocanassādo. Muccane attano dhammatāya muccane assādo muccanassādo. Evaṃ sabbattha sattamītappurisena attho daṭṭhabbo. Imehi pana navahi padehi sampayuttaassādasīsena rāgo vutto. Gehanissitesu mātādīsu pemaṃ gehe sitaṃ pemanti gehasitapemaṃ, iminā sarūpeneva rāgo vutto. Santhavakaraṇatthāya itthiyā pesitapupphādi vanabhaṅgiyaṃ, iminā ca vatthuvasena rāgo vutto. Methunassādopi itthiyā gahaṇappayogena veditabbo. Sabbattheva ca pana cetanānimittupakkamamocane sati visaṅketābhāvo veditabbo. Upakkamma hatthādinā nimitte upakkamitvā. Aññatra supinantenāti supinoyeva supinanto “kammameva kammanto”tiādīsu viya anta-saddassa tabbhāvavuttittā. Taṃ supinantaṃ vinā vimocayaṃ sukkaṃ vimocento samaṇo yo koci bhikkhu garukaṃ garukāpattisaṅkhātaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ phuse phuseyya, āpajjeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca ajjhattarūpabahiddhārūpaubhayarūpaākāsekaṭikampanasaṅkhātesu catūsu upāyesu sati rāgūpatthambhādīsu [M 0.0259] ca kālesu yena kenaci aṅgajāte kammaññataṃ patte “ārogyatthāyā”tiādīsu yena kenaci adhippāyena adhippāyavatthubhūtaṃ yaṃ kiñci sukkaṃ mocanassādacetanāya eva nimitte upakkamma mocento saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjatīti sabbathā adhippāyo daṭṭhabbo.

Here, the pleasure in releasing is the pleasant feeling of releasing. The pleasure in being released, by its own nature of being released, is the pleasure of being released. Thus, in all cases, the meaning should be understood by the locative compound. Moreover, by these nine terms, lust is spoken of under the heading of associated pleasure. Affection for mother and others dependent on the home is called “home-dependent affection”; by this very form, lust is indicated. And “flirting in the forest” refers to flowers and so on sent by a woman for the purpose of making acquaintance; by this, lust is indicated by way of the object. The pleasure of sexual intercourse should also be understood by the act of taking hold of a woman. And in all cases, when there is intention, effort towards the object, and release, the absence of ambiguity should be understood. “Effort” means having made an effort towards the object with the hand and so on. “Except in dreaming” means only in dreaming, just as in expressions like “the deed is the doing,” the suffix “-anta” expresses the state of being that. It is said that any monk who, apart from that dreaming, releases semen, would touch, that is, would commit, a grave offense, which is classified as a saṅghādisesa. And here, in the four methods—internal form, external form, both forms, and shaking the hips in the air—and at times when lust is supported and so on, when the sexual organ has become workable in any way, and with any intention, such as “for the sake of health,” if he, with the intention of pleasure in releasing, makes an effort towards the object and releases any semen that is the object of his intention, he commits a saṅghādisesa. This is the full meaning to be understood in every way.

Paṭhamo.

The first.

20. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgavāti kāye saṃsaggo, tasmiṃ rāgo, so assa atthīti vantu, kāyasaṃsaggarāgasamaṅgīti attho. Samaṇo itthisaññīti sambandho. Upakkammāti kāyena vāyamitvā. Manussitthiṃ samphusantoti antamaso lomenapi parāmasanto garukaṃ phuseti yojanā. Manussabhūtā amatā itthī manussitthī. Tattha “kāyasaṃsaggarāgavā”ti iminā mātupemādiṃ[V 0.0228], itthiyā gahitamokkhādhippāyañca paṭikkhipati. Itthiyā vematikassa, paṇḍakapurisatiracchānagatasaññissa ca thullaccayaṃ. Itthiyā pana kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhāmasane, kāyappaṭibaddhena kāyāmasane ca yakkhīpetīpaṇḍakānaṃ kāyena kāyāmasane ca purisatiracchānagatitthīnaṃ kāyena kāyāmasanepi dukkaṭaṃ, tathāyakkhīādīnaṃ kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhādīsu ca. Matitthiyā pana thullaccayaṃ. Itthiyā pana phusiyamāno sevanādhippāyopi sace kāyena na vāyamati, anāpatti.

20. “One with lust for bodily contact” means: there is contact with the body, and lust for it; he has that, thus he is “one endowed with lust for bodily contact”—this is the meaning. The connection is with “a monk perceiving a woman.” “Making an effort” means having exerted effort with the body. “Touching a human woman” means that even by stroking with a hair, he touches a grave offense—this is the connection. A human woman is a woman who is a human being and not dead. Here, by “one with lust for bodily contact,” it excludes affection for one’s mother and so on, and also the intention of seizing a woman or being released by her. For one who is doubtful about a woman, or perceives her as a eunuch, a male, or an animal, there is a grave offense. However, for touching something attached to a woman's body with one's own body, or for touching her body with something attached to one's own body, there is a minor offense. And for touching the body of a yakkha, peta, or paṇḍaka with one's own body, and also for touching the body of a man or an animal with one's own body, there is a minor offense. Likewise for a yakkha and so on, in cases of touching with the body something attached to the body, and so on. For a dead woman, however, there is a grave offense. However, if a monk is touched by a woman, even if he has the intention of intimacy, if he does not exert bodily effort, there is no offense.

Dutiyo.

The second.

21. Tathāti itthisaññī. Suṇantinti viññattipathe ṭhatvā attano vacanaṃ suṇantiñca. Viññuñcāti duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullasallakkhaṇasamatthañca manussitthiṃ. Maggaṃ vāti vaccamaggapassāvamaggānaṃ vasena maggaṃ vā methunaṃ vā ārabbhāti sambandho. Duṭṭhullavācārāgenāti [M 0.0260] duṭṭhā ca sā asaddhammappaṭisaṃyuttatāya thūlā ca lāmakajanasādhāraṇatāyāti duṭṭhullā. Sāva puna vācā duṭṭhullavācā. Tassaṃ assādasampayutto rāgoti samāso, tena. Obhāsitvāti vaṇṇāvaṇṇayācanādivasena asaddhammavacanaṃ vatvā. Asuṇantiyā pana dūtena vā paṇṇena vā ārocite anāpatti. Tattha dvinnaṃ maggānaṃ vasena vaṇṇāvaṇṇehi, methunayācanādīhi vā “sikharaṇīsi, sambhinnāsi, ubhatobyañjanakāsī”ti imesu tīsu aññatarena akkosavacanena vā obhāsantassa saṅghādiseso, adhakkhakaubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ ādissa vaṇṇādibhaṇane thullaccayaṃ, tathā yakkhīpetīpaṇḍakānaṃ vaccamaggapassāvamagge ādissa vaṇṇādibhaṇane methunayācanādīsupi. Tesaṃ pana adhakkhakādike dukkaṭaṃ, tathā manussitthīnaṃ ubbhakkhake adhojāṇumaṇḍale kāyappaṭibaddhe ca.

21. “Thus” means perceiving a woman. “Listening” means one who stands within range of communication and listens to his words. And “discerning” means a human woman capable of discerning what is lewd and what is not. “Or the path” is the connection, meaning concerning the path—either the excretory or urinary passage—or concerning sexual intercourse. “With lust for lewd speech”: it is corrupt because it is associated with improper conduct, and it is vulgar because it is common among lowly people; thus, it is lewd. That very speech is lewd speech. The lust associated with the pleasure in it is a compound; by that lust. “Having spoken” means having spoken improper words by way of praise, dispraise, solicitation, and so on. If the woman does not hear it, however, whether it is conveyed by a messenger or a letter, there is no offense. Here, for one who speaks with praise or dispraise concerning the two passages, or solicits for sex, or speaks any of these three insulting words—“You are a sikharinī,” “you are promiscuous,” “you are a hermaphrodite”—it is a saṅghādisesa offense. For speaking praise and so on referring to the area below the navel and above the knees, it is a grave offense. Similarly, for speaking praise and so on referring to the excretory or urinary passages of female yakkhas, petas, or eunuchs, or for soliciting them for sex, it is also a grave offense. However, for those beings, regarding the area below the navel and so on, it is a minor offense. Likewise, for human women, regarding the area above the navel, below the knees, or things attached to the body, it is a minor offense.

Tatiyo.

The third.

22. Attakāmupaṭṭhānanti methunadhammasaṅkhātena kāmena upaṭṭhānaṃ kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ. Attano atthāya kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā kāmīyatīti kāmaṃ, attano kāmaṃ attakāmaṃ, sayaṃ methunarāgavasena patthitanti attho. Attakāmañca taṃ upaṭṭhānañcāti attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ. Tassa vaṇṇo guṇo, taṃ. Vatvāti “yadidaṃ kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, etadaggaṃ upaṭṭhānāna”nti kāmupaṭṭhāne vaṇṇaṃ [V 0.0229] antamaso hatthamuddāyapi itthīti saññī pakāsetvāti attho. Vācāti vācāya yakāralopavasena. Methunayuttenāti methunayuttāya, liṅgavipallāsavasena tāya “arahasi tvaṃ mayhaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ dātu”ntiādikāya methunadhammappaṭisaṃyuttāya vācāya methunayācane methunarāginoti sambandho. Methunerāgo, so assa atthīti methunarāgī, tassa. Garu hotīti garukāpatti hotīti attho. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Ettha [M 0.0261] pana paṇḍake paṇḍakasaññino thullaccayaṃ, tasmiṃyeva itthisaññino dukkaṭaṃ.

22. “Praising the provision of sensual pleasure for oneself” means: the provision of sensual pleasure, which is designated as the sexual act, is “provision of sensual pleasure.” The provision of sensual pleasure for one’s own sake is “provision of sensual pleasure for oneself.” Alternatively, “sensual pleasure” is what is desired; “one’s own sensual pleasure” means what is desired by oneself due to lust for sexual intercourse. And that which is one’s own sensual pleasure and also a provision is “provision of sensual pleasure for oneself.” Its praise is its virtue; that. “Having spoken” means having praised the provision of sensual pleasure by saying, “This which is called the provision of sensual pleasure is the foremost of provisions,” even to the point of indicating it to one perceived as a woman with a hand gesture—this is the meaning. “By speech” is by way of the elision of the letter ‘y’ from the instrumental form. “Connected with sexual intercourse”: the connection is with one who is lustful for sex in a sexual request made with speech connected with the sexual act—by way of gender disagreement—such as, “You ought to give me the sexual act.” He has lust for sex, so he is “one lustful for sex”; for him. “It is grave” means it becomes a grave offense—this is the meaning. The letter ‘m’ is for euphonic conjunction. Here, however, in the case of a eunuch, for one who perceives him as a eunuch, it is a grave offense; for one who perceives that same one as a woman, it is a minor offense.

Catuttho.

The fourth.

23. Itthiyā vā purisassa vā sandesaṃ paṭiggahetvāti sambandho. Itthiyā vāti “dasa itthiyo māturakkhitā piturakkhitā”tiādinā (pārā. 303) ca “dasa bhariyāyo dhanakkītā chandavāsinī”tiādinā (pārā. 303) ca vuttāya vīsatividhāya itthiyā vā purisassa vā taṃsambandhavasena tesaṃ mātādīnaṃ vā. Sandesanti itthiyā vā purisena vā ubhinnaṃ mātādīhi vā “ehi, bhante, itthannāmaṃ itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti vuttaṃ jāyampatibhāvasannissitaṃ sandesavacanaṃ. Paṭiggahetvāti “sādhū”ti kāyena vā vācāya vā sampaṭicchitvā. Vīmaṃsitvāti yattha pesito, tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ upaparikkhitvā vā upaparikkhāpetvā vā. Haraṃ paccāti itthī vā puriso vā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchatu vā, mā vā, yehi pesito, tesaṃ paccāharanto vā harāpento vā, jāyampatibhāvo hotu vā, mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Imāya tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso ca, dvīhi aṅgehi paṇḍake ca aṅgattayenāpi thullaccayaṃ, ekena dukkaṭaṃ. Keci pana “haraṃ pacchā”ti vipāṭhaṃ parikappetvā “pacchā hara”nti yojenti, taṃ na sundaraṃ paccāti upasaggattā. Padassa upari atthe sajjento pakāsento gacchatīti hi upasaggo nāma, tasmā “pati ā”ti upasaggānaṃ “hara”ntimassa padassa upari bhavitabbanti.

23. The connection is with “having received a message from a woman or a man.” “From a woman” refers to the twenty kinds of women mentioned, such as the “ten women protected by their mother, protected by their father,” and so on, and the “ten wives, such as those bought with wealth, living by consent,” and so on; or from a man; or from their mothers and so on by way of their connection to them. “Message” means a message-word dependent on the state of being husband and wife, spoken by a woman, or by a man, or by the mothers and so on of both, such as, “Come, venerable sir, and say this to such-and-such a woman or man.” “Having received” means having accepted it with body or speech by saying, “Very well.” “Having investigated” means having examined or having caused to be examined the intention of those to whom one is sent. “Bringing back” means that whether the woman or man accepts by saying, “Very well,” or not, and whether he brings back or causes to be brought back the reply to those who sent him, and whether the state of being husband and wife comes to be or not—this is not the cause. With the fulfillment of these three factors, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. For a eunuch, with two factors, and also with three factors, it is a grave offense; with one factor, it is a minor offense. Some, however, imagine the variant reading “haraṃ pacchā” and construe it as “pacchā hara” (bring it later), but that is not good, because `paccā` is a prefix. A prefix is so called because it goes before a word, attaching to and clarifying its meaning. Therefore, the prefixes `pati` and `ā` should be before the final word `hara`.

Pañcamo.

The fifth.

24. Saṃyācitaparikkhāranti saṃ attanā yācito vāsiādiko parikkhāro yassā, taṃ. Adesitavatthukanti uttidutiyakammena adesitaṃ vatthu kuṭikaraṇappadeso yassāti [M 0.0262] viggaho, taṃ. Pamāṇātikkantanti [V 0.0230] idāni majjhimassa purisassa tisso vidatthiyo sugatavidatthi nāma, tāya “dīghaso dvādasa vidatthiyo sugatassa vidatthiyā tiriyaṃ sattantarā”ti (pārā. 348) evaṃ vuttappamāṇaṃ ekatobhāgenāpi atikkantā pamāṇātikkantāti taṃ tiriyaṃ catuhatthasaṅkhātaheṭṭhimappamāṇe sati dīghato vuttappamāṇato kesaggamattampi vaḍḍhetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tato ūnake, dīghato ca vaḍḍhite ayaṃ kuṭisaṅkhaṃ na gacchatīti. “Mayhaṃ vāsāgāraṃ eta”nti evaṃ attā uddeso etissāti attuddesā. Kuṭinti ullittādikaṃ kuṭiṃ katvāti sambandho. Tattha ullittā nāma anto uddhaṃmukhaṃ littā. Avalittā nāma bahi adhomukhaṃ littā. Ubhayathā ullittāvalittā. Katvāti antobhūtakāritatthavasena kārāpetvā vā.

24. ‘Saṃyācitaparikkhāra’ means one for whom requisites, such as an axe, have been requested by oneself. ‘Adesitavatthuka’ means one for whom the site, the place for building a hut, has not been indicated by a formal act of the Saṅgha involving a motion and one announcement. ‘Pamāṇātikkanta’ refers to exceeding the standard measure. Now, for a middle-sized man, three of his spans are called a Sugata span. By that span, the prescribed measure is ‘twelve Sugata spans in length and seven inside in width’ (Pārā. 348). Exceeding this prescribed measure even by a single part is called ‘exceeding the measure.’ When the width is at the lower limit of four cubits, it is not permissible to increase the length beyond the prescribed measure even by a hair’s breadth. If it is less than that in width, and the length is increased, this does not count as a hut. ‘This is my dwelling’ means that it is self-designated. ‘A hut’ is connected with having made a hut with plastering and so on. Herein, ‘plastered inside’ means plastered upward on the inside. ‘Plastered outside’ means plastered downward on the outside. ‘Plastered both inside and outside’ means plastered in both ways. ‘Having built’ means having it built, in the sense of being the internal agent.

Tatthāyaṃ vatthudesanakkamo – tena kuṭikārakena bhikkhunā kuṭivatthuṃ sodhetvā saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā padabhājane (pārā. 349) vuttanayena saṅghaṃ tikkhattuṃ yācitvā sabbe vā saṅghapariyāpannā, saṅghena vā sammatā dve tayo bhikkhū tattha netabbā. Tehi ca kipillikādīhi soḷasahi upaddavehi virahitattā anārambhaṃ anupaddavaṃ dvīhi catūhi vā balibaddehi yuttena sakaṭena ekacakkaṃ nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāne ekaṃ bahi katvā āviñchituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāya “saparikkamana”nti sallakkhetvā sacepi saṅghappahonakā honti, tattheva, no ce, saṅghamajjhaṃ gantvā tena bhikkhunā yācitehi padabhājane (pārā. 50, 51) vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya vatthu desetabbanti. Adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ kuṭiṃ karissāmīti sabbappayoge dukkaṭaṃ, idāni dvīhi piṇḍehi niṭṭhānaṃ gamissatīti paṭhamapiṇḍadāne [M 0.0263] thullaccayaṃ, dutiyadānena lepe saṅghaṭite sace adesitavatthukā eva vā hoti, pamāṇātikkantā eva vā, eko saṅghādiseso, sārambhaaparikkamanatāya dve ca dukkaṭānīti sace ubhayavipannā, dve ca saṅghādisesā dve ca dukkaṭānīti sabbaṃ ñeyyaṃ.

Herein, this is the procedure for designating the site: The monk who is to build the hut should first clean the site, then approach the Saṅgha. Arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, he should pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, sit squatting, raise his joined palms, and request the Saṅgha three times in the manner described in the Padabhājana (Pārā. 349). All those belonging to the Saṅgha, or two or three monks appointed by the Saṅgha, should be taken there. They should observe that the site is free from the sixteen dangers, such as ants, that it is undisturbed and safe, and that it has space for circumambulation, being suitable for a cart with two or four oxen to be pulled, with one wheel placed outside in a spot where water does not collect. If the monks present are sufficient to constitute a Saṅgha, the site should be designated right there. If not, having gone into the midst of the Saṅgha, the site should be designated by those monks who were requested, using the formal act with a motion and one announcement as described in the Padabhājana (Pārā. 50, 51). If one intends to build a hut that is on an undesignated site or exceeds the measure, every effort entails a dukkaṭa offense. When it is about to be completed with two lumps of plaster, at the application of the first lump, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. With the application of the second, when the plaster is set, if the hut is on an undesignated site or exceeds the measure, there is one Saṅghādisesa offense. If it is also troublesome and without space for circumambulation, there are two dukkaṭa offenses. If it is deficient in both ways, that is, on an undesignated site and exceeding the measure, then two Saṅghādisesa offenses and two dukkaṭa offenses are incurred. All this should be understood.

Chaṭṭho.

Sixth.

25. Mahallakanti sassāmikabhāvena saṃyācitakuṭito mahantabhāvena, vatthuṃ desāpetvā pamāṇātikkamenāpi kātabbabhāvena ca mahantatāya mahattaṃ lāti ādadātīti mahallako. Mahattalaka iti ṭhite ttassa lopo lassa ca dvittaṃ, taṃ. Vasanaṃ attho payojanaṃ vasanattho, tāya[V 0.0231]. Ettha pana adesitavatthubhāve eko saṅghādiseso. Sesaṃ anantarasadisameva. Idha ca tattha ca leṇaguhātiṇakuṭipaṇṇacchadanagehesu aññataraṃ kārentassa ca kuṭimpi aññassa vāsatthāya vāsāgāraṃ vā ṭhapetvā uposathāgārādīsu aññataratthāya karontassa ca anāpatti.

25. ‘Mahallaka’ (a large dwelling) is so called because it takes (`lāti`) or obtains greatness (`mahattaṃ`) from its greatness (`mahantatāya`) in being large (`mahantabhāvena`) compared to a hut built from requested materials, in having an owner, and in being able to be built even exceeding the measure after having the site designated. When the form is ‘mahattalaka,’ there is elision of ‘tt’ and doubling of ‘l’, hence ‘mahallaka.’ ‘For the purpose of dwelling’ (`vasanattho`) means for the use or purpose (`attho payojanaṃ`) of dwelling (`vasanaṃ`). Here, however, if the site has not been designated, there is one Saṅghādisesa offense. The rest is just like the preceding case. And in both this rule and the previous one, there is no offense for one who causes any of these to be made: a cave, a rock shelter, a grass hut, or a leaf-roofed house; nor for one who makes a hut or a dwelling for another’s use, or for some other purpose such as an Uposatha hall.

Sattamo.

Seventh.

26. Amūlakena antimena vatthunāti sambandho. Amūlakenāti dassanasaṅkhātassa, savanasaṅkhātassa, diṭṭhasutamutavasena pavattaparisaṅkāsaṅkhātassa ca mūlassa abhāvena natthi mūlametassāti amūlakaṃ, tena. Taṃ pana so āpanno vā hotu, no vā, etaṃ idha appamāṇaṃ. Tattha bhikkhuñca mātugāmañca tathārūpe ṭhāne disvā parisaṅkati, ayaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkā. Andhakāre vā paṭicchanne vā bhikkhussa ca mātugāmassa ca vacanaṃ sutvā aññassa atthibhāvaṃ ajānanto parisaṅkati, ayaṃ sutaparisaṅkā. Dhuttānaṃ itthīhi saddhiṃ [M 0.0264] paccantavihāresu pupphagandhasurādīhi anubhavitvā gataṭṭhānaṃ disvā “kena nu kho idaṃ kata”nti vīmaṃsanto tattha kenaci bhikkhunā gandhādīhi pūjā katā hoti, bhesajjatthāya ariṭṭhaṃ vā pītaṃ, so tassa gandhaṃ ghāyitvā “ayaṃ so bhavissatī”ti parisaṅkati. Ayaṃ mutaparisaṅkā nāma. Antimena cāti tato paraṃ vajjābhāvena ante bhavattā antimeneva. Vatthunāti bhikkhuno anurūpesu ekūnavīsatiyā pārājikesu dhammesu aññatarena pārājikena dhammena. Ca-kāro panettha avadhāraṇe, tena saṅghādisesādiṃ nivatteti. Atha vā ca-kāro aṭṭhānappayutto.

26. The connection is with a groundless, ultimate matter. ‘Groundless’ means that it has no root, because there is no root in terms of what is called seeing, what is called hearing, or what is called suspicion arising from what was seen, heard, or sensed. Whether or not the monk has actually committed the offense is immaterial here. In this case, seeing a monk and a woman in such a situation, one suspects—this is suspicion based on sight. Or, hearing the voices of a monk and a woman in darkness or a concealed place without knowing of the presence of anyone else, one suspects—this is suspicion based on hearing. Or, seeing a place where libertines have enjoyed flowers, perfumes, liquor, and so on, with women in border monasteries, and wondering, ‘Who did this?’—if a monk has made offerings of perfumes there, or if he drank ariṭṭha, a medicinal drink, for medicinal purposes, and one smells that scent and thinks, ‘This must be him,’ one suspects—this is called suspicion based on sensing. ‘Ultimate’ means that because there is no further offense beyond it, it is ultimate. ‘Matter’ refers to a pārājika offense, any one of the nineteen pārājika offenses appropriate for a monk. The particle ‘ca’ here serves as an emphasis, thereby excluding Saṅghādisesa and other offenses. Alternatively, the particle ‘ca’ is used without a specific purpose.

Codento vā codāpentovācāti yojetabbo. Cāvetunti brahmacariyā cāvanatthāya. Etena ekaṃ cāvanādhippāyaṃ gahetvā avasese akkosādhippāyavuṭṭhāpanādhippāyādike sattādhippāye paṭikkhipati. Suṇamānanti idaṃ “codento”tiādīnaṃ kammapadaṃ, iminā parammukhā codanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Parammukhā pana sattahi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Codentoti “vatthusandassanā āpattisandassanā saṃvāsappaṭikkhepo sāmīcippaṭikkhepo”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.385-386) saṅkhepato vuttānaṃ catunnaṃ codanānaṃ vasena sayaṃ codento vā. Codāpento vāti parena yena kenaci codāpento vā. Tasmā yo bhikkhussa samīpe ṭhatvā “tvaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ sevi, assamaṇosī”tiādinā vatthusandassanavasena vā “tvaṃ methunadhammāpattiṃ āpannosī”tiādinā āpattisandassanavasena vā “assamaṇosi, natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā [V 0.0232] pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā, assamaṇosī”tiādinā saṃvāsappaṭikkhepavasena vā abhivādanādisaṃvāse paṭikkhitte assamaṇoti kasmāti puṭṭhassa “assamaṇosī”tiādivacanehi sāmīcippaṭikkhepavasena vā antamaso [M 0.0265] hatthamuddāya eva vāpi etamatthaṃ dīpayato “karotu me āyasmā okāsaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo”ti evaṃ okāse akārite vācāya saṅghādiseso ceva dukkaṭañca, okāsaṃ kāretvā codentassa pana saṅghādisesova daṭṭhabbo.

‘To make one fall away’ means for the purpose of making one fall away from the holy life. By this, the single intention of making one fall away is taken, while the remaining seven intentions, such as the intention to insult or the intention to remove, are rejected. ‘While listening’ is the object of ‘accusing’ and so on; by this, accusing someone in their absence is rejected. However, for one who speaks in the absence of another regarding the seven classes of offenses, there is a dukkaṭa offense. ‘Accusing’ refers to personally accusing someone based on the four types of accusations briefly stated as: ‘pointing out the basis, pointing out the offense, rejecting communal life, and rejecting proper conduct’ (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.385-386). ‘Causing someone to be accused’ means having someone else accuse, by any means. Therefore, for one who stands near a monk and, indicating this matter by saying, ‘You have engaged in sexual intercourse, you are not an ascetic,’ and so on—by way of pointing out the basis; or by saying, ‘You have committed an offense of sexual intercourse,’ and so on—by way of pointing out the offense; or by saying, ‘You are not an ascetic; there is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or formal act of the Saṅgha with you; you are not an ascetic,’ and so on—by way of rejecting communal life; or, when communal life such as paying respects is rejected and one is asked why, one replies with words such as, ‘You are not an ascetic’—by way of rejecting proper conduct; or even by merely gesturing with the hand—if one does so without having been given leave after saying, ‘Venerable, grant me leave, I wish to speak to you,’ it is both a Saṅghādisesa and a dukkaṭa offense. But for one who accuses after having been given leave, only a Saṅghādisesa offense should be understood.

Aṭṭhamo.

Eighth.

27. Aññassāti khattiyādijātikassa parassa. Kiriyanti methunavītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ kiriyaṃ. Tenāti aññassa vītikkamasaṅkhātassa methunavītikkamasandassanena karaṇabhūtena. Lesenāti yassa jātiādayo tato aññampi vatthuṃ lissati uddiṭṭhe vitthāraṃ silissati vohāramattenevāti jātiādayova “lesā”ti vuccanti, tena jātilesanāmalesādinā lesena. Aññanti yo vītikkamanto diṭṭho, tato aparampi bhikkhuṃ cāvetuṃ antimena vatthunā codayanti sambandho. Kathaṃ? Koci khattiyajātiyo vītikkamanto diṭṭho, tato aññaṃ attano veriṃ khattiyajātikaṃ bhikkhuṃ passitvā taṃ khattiyaṃ jātilesaṃ gahetvā “khattiyo mayā diṭṭho vītikkamanto, tvaṃ khattiyo pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosī”ti codeti codāpeti vā. Evaṃ nāmalesādayopi veditabbā. Sesā vinicchayakathā aṭṭhame vuttasadisāyeva.

27. ‘Of another’ means of another person of a caste such as a Khattiya. ‘Action’ means the action designated as the transgression of sexual intercourse. ‘By that’ means by the instrumental cause which is the observation of the transgression of sexual intercourse, designated as the transgression of another. ‘By a pretext’ (lesa) means that by which caste, etc., or even another matter, adheres, or in the detailed explanation, is connected by mere expression; thus caste, etc., are called ‘pretexts.’ By that pretext, such as the pretext of caste, the pretext of name, etc. ‘Another’ means that they charge another monk, different from the one who was seen transgressing, with the final matter in order to disrobe him; this is the connection. How? Someone of the Khattiya caste is seen transgressing. Then, seeing another monk of the Khattiya caste—an enemy of his—he takes that pretext of caste and charges him, saying, ‘A Khattiya was seen by me transgressing; you are a Khattiya—you have committed a pārājika offense!’ or he causes another to charge him. In the same way, the pretexts of name and other things should be understood. The remaining discussion on the legal decision is just as was stated in the eighth.

Navamo.

Ninth.

28. Ettāvatā “garukā navā”ti uddiṭṭhe vitthārato dassetvā idāni tesu āpannesu paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassetuṃ “chādeti jānamāpanna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo bhikkhu attanā āpannaṃ saṅghādisesāpattiṃ āpattivasena vā vatthuvasena vā jānaṃ jānanto yāvatā [M 0.0266] yattakāni ahāni chādeti paṭicchādeti, tāvatā tattakāni ahāni tassa parivāso hotīti evaṃ padasandhivasena attho veditabbo. Tattha paṭicchannaparivāso suddhantaparivāso samodhānaparivāsoti tividho parivāso. Tesaṃ pana atisaṅkhepanayena mukhamattepi dassite vitthāravinicchayapavesopāyasambhavo siyāti mukhamattaṃ dassayissāma.

28. Having thus explained in detail what was pointed out as “the nine serious offenses,” now, to show the way to proceed with regard to those who have incurred them, what was said beginning with “he conceals, knowing he has incurred” was stated. Herein, a monk who, knowing he has incurred a Saṅghādisesa offense, whether knowing it as an offense or knowing its basis, conceals or covers it up for as many days as he does so—for that many days his probation lasts—in this way, the meaning should be understood by connecting the words. Herein, probation is of three kinds: probation for a concealed offense (paṭicchannaparivāsa), probation based on a period of purity (suddhantaparivāsa), and probation by consolidation (samodhānaparivāsa). However, even if only the bare outlines of these are shown, there might be a way to enter into a detailed determination, so we will show just a bare outline.

Tattha [V 0.0233] paṭicchannaparivāso nāma yathāpaṭicchannāya āpattiyā dātabbo, tasmā paṭicchannadivase ca āpattiyo ca sallakkhetvā sace ekāhappaṭicchannā hoti, “ahaṃ, bhante, sambahulā āpattiyo āpajjiṃ ekāhappaṭicchannāyo”tiādinā khandhake (cūḷava. 98-99) āgatanayena yācāpetvā “suṇātu me bhante saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu sambahulā āpattiyo āpajji ekāhappaṭicchannāyo”tiādinā khandhake āgatanayeneva kammavācaṃ vatvā parivāso dātabbo. Ekaṃ āpajjitvā “sambahulā”ti vinayakammaṃ karontassāpi vuṭṭhātīti “sambahulā”ti vuttaṃ. Nānāvatthukāsupi eseva nayo. Atha dvīhādippaṭicchannā honti, pakkhaatirekapakkhamāsaatirekamāsasaṃvaccharaatirekasaṃvaccharappaṭicchannā vā, “dvīhappaṭicchannāyo vā”tiādinā vatvā yo yo āpanno hoti, tassa tassa nāmañca gahetvā yojanā kātabbā.

Herein, probation for a concealed offense (paṭicchannaparivāsa) is to be given in accordance with the offense as it was concealed. Therefore, after taking note of both the days of concealment and the offenses, if it was concealed for one day, one should have him request it by saying, “Venerable sirs, I have incurred several offenses concealed for one day,” and so forth, in the manner stated in the Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga 98-99). Then, the probation should be given by reciting the formal act in the manner stated in the Khandhaka: “Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has incurred several offenses concealed for one day,” and so forth. Even if one has incurred a single offense, if one performs the disciplinary act as if for “several,” it is still valid—hence, “several” is stated. The same method applies to offenses with different grounds. If they are concealed for two days or more—such as for more than a fortnight, more than a month, or more than a year—one should state “concealed for two days,” and so forth, and taking the name of each one who has incurred an offense, the phrasing should be applied.

Kammavācāpariyosāne ca sace appabhikkhuko āvāso hoti, sakkā ratticchedaṃ anāpajjantena vasituṃ, tattheva “parivāsaṃ samādiyāmi, vattaṃ samādiyāmī’ti vattaṃ samādāya tattheva saṅghassa “ahaṃ, bhante, sambahulā saṅghādisesā āpattiyo āpajjiṃ ekāhappaṭicchannāyo”tiādinā ārocetvā puna āgatāgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [M 0.0267] ārocentena pakatattena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekacchanne sahavāso, tena ca vināvāso, āgantukādīnaṃ upacāragatānaṃ anārocanāti etesu ekenāpi ratticchedañca vattabhedañca akatvā parivatthabbaṃ.

At the conclusion of the recitation of the formal act, if the monastery has few monks and it is possible to stay without incurring an interruption of the night, one should undertake the observance right there by saying, “I undertake the probation, I undertake the observance.” Having undertaken the observance, one should inform the Saṅgha right there, saying, “Venerable sirs, I have incurred several Saṅghādisesa offenses, concealed for one day,” and so on, and then one must inform the monks as they arrive. One should undergo probation without causing an interruption of the night or a breach of the observance by even one of these: living under the same roof with a regular monk, living apart from him, or not informing visiting monks who have entered the precincts.

Sace na sakkā hoti parivāsaṃ sodhetuṃ, nikkhittavattena vasitukāmo hoti, tattheva saṅghamajjhe vā ekassa puggalassa vā santike “parivāsaṃ nikkhipāmi, vattaṃ nikkhipāmī”ti parivāso nikkhipitabbo. Nikkhittakālato paṭṭhāya pakatattaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Athānena paccūsasamaye ekena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ parikkhittassa vihārassa parikkhepato, aparikkhittassa parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvā mahāmaggato okkamma paṭicchannaṭṭhāne nisīditvā antoaruṇeyeva vattaṃ samādiyitvā ārocetabbaṃ. Sace bahi ṭhitānampi saddaṃ suṇāti, passati vā, dūraṃ gantvāpi ārocetabbaṃ, anārocente ratticchedo ceva vattabhedadukkaṭañca. Sace ajānantasseva upacārasīmaṃ pavisitvā gacchanti, ratticchedova hoti, na vattabhedo. Aruṇe uṭṭhite tassa santike vattaṃ nikkhipitvā vihāraṃ gantabbaṃ. Evaṃ yāva rattiyo pūrenti, tāva parivatthabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva paṭicchannaparivāso.

If he is unable to complete the probation, and wishes to live with the observance set aside, the probation should be set aside right there—whether in the midst of the Saṅgha or in the presence of an individual—by saying, “I set aside the probation, I set aside the observance.” From the moment it is set aside, he stands in the position of a regular monk. Then, at dawn, he should, together with one monk, having gone beyond two stone-throws from the boundary of a circumscribed monastery, or from a place suitable for circumscription if it is uncircumscribed—having stepped aside from the main road—and having sat down in a concealed spot, he should undertake the observance before the first light of dawn and announce it. If he hears or sees even those standing outside, he must go farther away to announce it. If he fails to announce it, there is an interruption of the night and a dukkata offense for breaking the observance. If they enter the proximity boundary while he is unaware of their passing, there is only an interruption of the night, not a breaking of the observance. When dawn has risen, he should, after setting aside the observance in the presence of that monk, return to the monastery. He must live this way until the nights are completed. This, then, is probation for a concealed offense (paṭicchannaparivāsa).

Suddhanto [V 0.0234] duvidho cūḷasuddhanto mahāsuddhantoti. Tattha yo “upasampadato paṭṭhāya yattakaṃ nāma kālaṃ ahaṃ suddho”ti jānāti, tattakaṃ apanetvā tato avasese rattiparicchede ekato katvā dātabbaparivāso cūḷasuddhanto. Yo pana sabbaso rattipariyantaṃ na jānāti nassarati, tattha ca vematiko, tassa dātabbo mahāsuddhanto. Āpattipariyantaṃ jānātu vā, mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ.

Probation based on a period of purity (suddhanta) is of two kinds: minor suddhanta (cūḷasuddhanta) and major suddhanta (mahāsuddhanta). Herein, for one who knows, “From the time of my higher ordination, for such a period I was pure,” that period should be excluded and the remaining portions of nights combined into one; the probation to be given then is minor suddhanta. But for one who does not know or remember the full extent of the nights, and is uncertain about it, major suddhanta should be given. Whether he knows the extent of the offense or not, this is irrelevant.

Samodhānaparivāso [M 0.0268] nāma tividho odhānasamodhāno agghasamodhāno missakasamodhānoti. Tattha yo niṭṭhitaparivāsopi vā niṭṭhitamānattopi vā anikkhittavatto aññaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā purimāpattiyā samā vā ūnatarā vā rattiyo paṭicchādeti, tassa mūlāya paṭikassanena te parivutthadivase ca mānattaciṇṇadivase ca odhunitvā makkhetvā purimāya āpattiyā mūladivasaparicchede pacchā āpannaṃ āpattiṃ samodahitvā puna ādito paṭṭhāya dātabbaparivāso odhānasamodhāno nāma. Sace kassaci ekāpatti ekāhappaṭicchannā, dvīhappaṭicchannā, evaṃ yāva dasāhappaṭicchannā, tāsaṃ agghena samodhāya tāsaṃ dasāhappaṭicchannavasena avasesānaṃ ekāhappaṭicchannādīnampi dātabbaparivāso agghasamodhāno nāma. Yo pana nānāvatthukā āpattiyo ekato katvā dātabbaparivāso missakasamodhāno nāma. Dānavidhi pana sabbattha khandhake (cūḷava. 134 ādayo) āgatanayeneva veditabbo.

Probation by consolidation (samodhānaparivāsa) is of three kinds: consolidation by covering (odhānasamodhāna), consolidation by value (agghasamodhāna), and consolidation by mixing (missakasamodhāna). Herein, when someone who has completed probation or completed mānatta, but whose observance has not been set aside, incurs another offense and conceals it for the same number of nights as, or fewer than, the previous offense—for him, by being sent back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassanena), those days spent in probation and the days spent in mānatta are to be shaken off and discarded. Then, having consolidated the later-incurred offense with the previous offense under its original day-count, the probation to be given again from the beginning is called consolidation by covering. If someone has offenses concealed for one day, two days, and so on up to ten days, the probation to be given for all of them, by consolidating them according to their highest value, based on the ten-day concealment, is called consolidation by value. But the probation that is given when offenses based on different grounds are combined is called consolidation by mixing. The method of giving it, however, should be understood everywhere according to the way stated in the Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga 134 onwards).

Evaṃ parivutthaparivāso bhikkhu mānattaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mānanabhāvaṃ cha rattiyo akhaṇḍaṃ katvā careyya kareyya, sampādeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha saṅghena gaṇena puggalena kataṃ tena bhikkhunā saṅghamajjhe vattaṃ samādāpetvā “ahaṃ, bhante, sambahulā āpattiyo āpajji”ntiādinā khandhake vuttanayena yācāpetvā tattheva vuttanayena mānattadānādayopi veditabbā. Imināpi vattaṃ nikkhipitukāmena ce vattaṃ nikkhipitvā catūhi pañcahi saddhiṃ parivāse vuttappakāraṃ padesaṃ gantvā purimanayeneva heṭṭhā vuttaṃ sahavāsādiṃ antamaso catūhi ūnattā ūne gaṇe caraṇadosañca vajjetvā paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Appaṭicchannāpattikassa pana parivāsaṃ adatvā mānattameva dātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ciṇṇaṃ kataṃ pariniṭṭhāpitaṃ mānattaṃ yena[M 0.0269], taṃ bhikkhuṃ. Vīsati saṅgho gaṇo assāti vīsatīgaṇo dīghaṃ katvā, so saṅgho abbheyya sampaṭiccheyya, abbhānakammavasena osāreyyāti vuttaṃ hoti, avheyyāti vā attho. Etthāpi samādānaārocanayācanāni, kammavācā ca khandhake vuttanayena veditabbā.

Thus, a monk who has completed parivāsa should practice mānatta—the state of being honored by the monks—for six consecutive nights without interruption, as has been said. Herein, the observance given by the Saṅgha, by a group, or by an individual, should be undertaken by that monk in the midst of the Saṅgha, and he should cause it to be requested by saying, “Venerable sirs, I have incurred numerous offenses,” and so forth, in the manner stated in the Khandhaka. The giving of mānatta and so forth should also be understood in the same manner as stated there. If he wishes to set aside the observance, having set aside the observance, he should go to a place of the kind stated regarding parivāsa, together with four or five monks, and he should proceed in the former manner, avoiding the fault of cohabitation and so forth mentioned below, at least avoiding the fault of practicing in a group that is deficient, being less than four. However, for one whose offense is not concealed, mānatta itself should be given without giving parivāsa. When mānatta has been observed, done, and completed in this way by him, that monk—a Saṅgha of twenty, or a group of twenty (the long vowel indicates this)—that Saṅgha should rehabilitate him, accept him, release him by means of the act of rehabilitation, as has been said, or the meaning is “should call back.” Herein too, the undertaking, announcement, requests, and formal motion should be understood in the manner stated in the Khandhaka.

29. Evaṃ [V 0.0235] tesu paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassetvā idāni chādanassa aṅgāni dassetuṃ “āpattī”tiādimāha. Tattha na ukkhitto anukkhitto, natthi antarāyo assāti anantarāyo. Sakatthe ttapaccayavasena vā, pahuno bhāvo pahuttaṃ, taṃ assatthīti saddhādivasena vā pahutto. Anukkhitto ca anantarāyo ca pahutto cāti dvando, tesaṃ bhāvo anukkhittādiguṇo anukkhitta…pe… pahuttatā. Āpatti ca anukkhitta…pe… pahuttatā ca āpatti…pe… pahuttatāyo. Ma-kāro padasandhijo. Tathā tena pakārena āpattiādīsu catūsu āpattādipakārena saññī tathasaññī rassavasena. Tassa bhāvo tathasaññitā, yathāvuttaāpattādisaññitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ca-kāro vuttasamuccayattho. Kamanaṃ patthanaṃ kāmo, chādetuṃ kāmo chādetukāmo. Iti yathāvuttā nava, atha chādanā cāti evaṃ dasa ca tāni aṅgāni cāti, tehi. Aruṇuggamamhi aruṇasaṅkhātassa paṭhamabālasūriyaraṃsino uggamane sati channā hoti, āpattīti seso.

29. Having thus shown the manner in which one should proceed in these cases, now, to explain the factors of concealment, he states what begins with “offense.” Herein, “not suspended” (anukkhitto) means not suspended. “Without obstacle” (anantarāyo) means there is no obstacle for him. Or, [the word `pahuttaṃ` is formed] by means of the suffix `-tta` in its own sense. The state of being able is competence (`pahuttaṃ`). Or, 'competent' (`pahutto`) means one who possesses that, as in the case of faith and so forth. Not suspended, without obstacle, and competent—this is a dvandva compound. Their state is the quality of not being suspended, etc.—not suspended... competence. An offense and not suspended... competence—these are offenses... competences. The letter “m” is for euphonic conjunction. Similarly, in the four cases beginning with “offense,” being aware in the manner of offenses, etc., he is “thus-aware” (tathasaññī), by shortening the vowel. The state of that is “thus-awareness” (tathasaññitā), meaning the awareness of offenses, etc., as stated. The particle “ca” has the meaning of combining what has been stated. The act of desiring, the wish, is “desire” (kāmo). “Desire to conceal” (chādetukāmo) means desiring to conceal. Thus, there are nine as stated, and then concealment itself, making ten—these are the ten factors. When dawn rises, when the rising of the first rays of the sun, called dawn, occurs, it is concealed. “An offense” is the remainder.

Tatthāyamadhippāyo – yo bhikkhu rājacoraaggiudakamanussaamanussavāḷasarīsapajīvitabrahmacariyantarāyānaṃ dasannamekassāpi natthitāya anantarāyiko samāno anantarāyikasaññī hutvā bhikkhuno santikaṃ gantuñceva ārocetuñca sakkuṇeyyatāya [M 0.0270] pahu samāno pahusaññī hutvā tividhaukkhepanīyakammākaraṇena anukkhitto samāno anukkhittasaññī hutvā garukāpattīti saññī garukaṃyeva āpattiṃ chādetukāmo hutvā chādeti, tassāyaṃ āpatti ca channā hotīti. Sace panettha anāpattisaññī vā hoti aññāpattikkhandhasaññī vā vematiko vā, acchannā honti. Ārocentena pana “mama ekāpattiṃ āpannabhāvaṃ jānāhī”tiādinā nayena ārocetabbaṃ. Sace pana vatthusabhāgāpattikassa āroceti, tāva tappaccayā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati.

Herein, this is the meaning: A bhikkhu who, being free from danger due to the non-existence of any one of the ten dangers—from kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild animals, creeping things, danger to life, or obstacles to the holy life—and perceiving himself as free from danger; being capable of approaching and informing a bhikkhu, and perceiving himself as capable; not being under suspension due to the non-performance of the three kinds of acts of suspension, and perceiving himself as not under suspension; perceiving it as a grave offense, and desiring to conceal a grave offense, conceals it—for him, that offense is concealed. But if in this case he perceives it as no offense, or perceives it as belonging to another category of offenses, or is in doubt, it is not concealed. However, one who informs should inform in such a way as to say, “Know that I have committed an offense,” and so on. But if he informs one who has an offense of the same kind, he incurs a dukkaṭa on that account.

Saṅghādisesaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅghādisesa Exposition is concluded.

3. Cīvaraniddesavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Robe Exposition

30. “Khomañca [V 0.0236] koseyyañcā”tiādinā napuṃsakaviggahena dvande kate khoma…pe… bhaṅgāni. Tattha khomanti gacchajāti. Upacārato pana khomena khomasuttena vāyitanti taddhitena upacārena vā khomaṃ khomapaṭacīvaraṃ, tathā avasesāni. Sāṇaṃ sāṇavākasuttehi vāyitaṃ cīvaraṃ. Bhaṅgaṃ khomasuttādīni sabbāni ekaccāni vā vomissetvā vāyitacīvaraṃ. Vākamayameva vāti keci. Kambalanti manussalomaṃ vāḷalomañca ṭhapetvā sesalomehi vāyitaṃ. Etānīti khomādīni yathāvuttāni. Saha anulomehīti sānulomāni. Jātito kappiyāni cha cīvarāni bhavanti.

30. When a dvanda compound is formed with a neuter gender analysis, such as 'khoma and koseyya,' etc., then khoma… [and so on, up to] bhaṅga. Here, 'khoma' means a kind of plant. By figurative usage, however, 'khoma' means a khoma cloth or khoma robe, woven from khoma or khoma threads; or it is a figurative taddhita formation. Similarly for the rest. Sāṇa is a robe woven from hemp or bark threads. Bhaṅga is a robe woven by mixing all or some of khoma threads and so on. Some say it is made entirely of bark fiber. Kambala is woven from the remaining hairs, excluding human hair and wild animal hair. These, namely khoma and so on, are as stated. 'Saha anulomehi' means 'with their conformable kinds' (sānulomāni). By nature, there are six kinds of allowable robes.

31. Idāni “dukūla”ntiādinā tesaṃ anulomāni dasseti. Tattha dukūlanti dukūlasaṅkhātena kenaci vākavisesena vāyitaṃ cīvaraṃ. Cevāti samuccaye, so upari ākaḍḍhitabbo. Paṭṭuṇṇanti paṭṭuṇṇesu jātaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ. Desavācino [M 0.0271] bahuvacanantāti bahuvacanena viggaho. Tathā somārā ca cīnā ca, tesu jātaṃ somāracīnajaṃ. Imāni tīṇi pāṇakehi katasuttamayāni. Ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā jātaṃ iddhijaṃ, taṃ pana khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ. Devadinnanti devehi dinnaṃ kapparukkhe nibbattaṃ cīvaraṃ. Tadetaṃ dukūlādi tassa tassa yathāvuttassa khomādino anulomikaṃ hoti. Tattha lomāni anugataṃ anulomaṃ, yathā sesalomāni anugataṃ lomaṃ tadanukūlattā “anuloma”nti vuccati, tathā taṃjātiyakaṃ yesaṃ kesañci anukūlaṃ sabbampi ruḷhīvasena “anuloma”nti vuccati. Tameva anulomikaṃ, anukūlanti attho. Kathaṃ? Dukūlaṃ sāṇassa anulomaṃ, paṭṭuṇṇādīni tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni, iddhijaṃ devadinnañca khomādīnamanulomanti.

31. Now, with 'dukūla,' etc., he shows their conformable kinds. Here, 'dukūla' means a robe woven from a certain kind of bark fiber called dukūla. The word 'ca' is for aggregation; it should be drawn from what follows. Paṭṭuṇṇa means that which is produced in Paṭṭuṇṇa. The analysis is with the plural, as it is a term for a country. Similarly, 'somāra' and 'cīna' refer to that which is produced in Somāra and Cīna. These three are made of threads produced by insects. Iddhija is that which arises by the power of merit of the 'Come-Bhikkhus'; however, it is one of the khoma types and so on. Devadinna is a robe given by devas, produced from the wish-fulfilling tree. Thus, this dukūla and so on is conformable to each of the previously mentioned khoma and so on. Here, 'anuloma' means 'following the hair,' just as hair that follows the other hairs is called 'anuloma' because of being agreeable to it; similarly, anything of that kind that is agreeable to anyone is, by common usage, called 'anuloma.' That itself is 'anulomika,' meaning 'agreeable.' How so? Dukūla is conformable to sāṇa; paṭṭuṇṇa and so on, these three, are conformable to koseyya; and iddhija and devadinna are conformable to khoma and so on.

32-3. Evaṃ sānulomāni cīvarāni dassetvā idāni adhiṭṭhānādikaṃ dassetuṃ “ticīvara”ntiādimāha. Tattha avuttepi avassaṃ vattabbatāya sabbattha ca-saddo ajjhāharitabbo, ticīvarañca…pe… kaṇḍucchādiñca adhiṭṭheyya na vikappeyyāti sambandho. Tattha tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ samāhāro ticīvaraṃ. Parikkhārañca taṃ coḷañcāti parikkhāracoḷaṃ. Vassassa yoggā vassikā, sāva sāṭikā vassikasāṭikā. Puñchati anenāti puñchanaṃ, mukhassa puñchanaṃ mukhapuñchanaṃ. Nisīdanti etthāti nisīdanaṃ, mukhapuñchanañca nisīdanañca mukhapuñchananisīdanaṃ[V 0.0237]. Sayanasukhādiṃ paṭicca attharīyatīti paccattharaṇaṃ, tadeva paccattharaṇakaṃ. Kaṇḍuṃ chādetīti kaṇḍucchādi. Adhiṭṭhaheti “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādinā navannaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā adhiṭṭheyya. Na vikappeyyāti tassa tassa nāmaṃ gahetvā na vikappeyya, tassa tassa pana nāmaṃ aggahetvā “imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vikappeyyāti adhippāyo. Etthāti imesu navasu [M 0.0272] cīvaresu. Ticīvaranti ticīvaranāmena adhiṭṭhitaṃ. Tathā hi adhiṭṭhānato pubbe visuṃ ticīvaraṃ nāma natthi saṅghāṭiādippahonakassa paccattharaṇādivasenāpi adhiṭṭhātuṃ anuññātattā. Taṃ vinā ekāhaṃ ekadivasampi. Na vaseyyāti aladdhasammutiko bhikkhu avippavāsasīmato aññattha vāsaṃ na kareyyāti attho. Evaṃ sati ticīvarañca nissajjitabbaṃ hoti, pācittiyañca āpattiṃ āpajjatīti dīpeti. Nisīdanaṃ vinā cātumāsaṃ na vaseyyāti sambandho. Catunnaṃ māsānaṃ samāhāro catumāsaṃ, tameva cātumāsaṃ. Taṃ accantasaṃyogavasena.

Having thus shown the robes along with their related kinds, he now begins with 'the three robes' and so on, in order to show determination and so forth. Here, even if not stated, the particle 'ca' should be supplied everywhere due to necessity, and the connection is: 'The three robes... and so on... and the itch-covering cloth should be determined, not shared.' Here, 'ticīvara' is the collective term for the three robes. That which is an accessory and a cloth is an 'accessory cloth'. Suitable for the rains is a 'rainy-season cloth'; that very garment is a 'rainy-season garment'. That with which one wipes is a 'wiping-cloth'; a wiping-cloth for the face is a 'face-wiping-cloth'. That on which one sits is a 'sitting-cloth'; a face-wiping-cloth and a sitting-cloth are referred to by the compound 'face-wiping-and-sitting-cloth'. That which is spread down for the sake of comfort in lying down and so on is a 'spread'; that very thing is a 'small spread'. That which covers an itch is an 'itch-covering cloth'. One should determine by taking up each of the nine names, saying, 'I determine this outer robe,' and so on. 'One should not share it' means one should not share it by taking up its specific name; however, without taking up its specific name, one may share it by saying, 'I share this robe with you'—this is the intended meaning. 'Here' means among these nine robes. 'The three robes' means that which is determined by the name 'the three robes.' For before the determination, there is no separate thing called 'the three robes,' because it is permitted for a cloth sufficient for an outer robe and so on to be determined even as a spread and so on. Without it, even for a single day... 'one should not dwell' means a bhikkhu who has not obtained permission should not dwell elsewhere, outside the boundary of non-separation. When this is so, it is shown that the three robes must be relinquished, and one incurs a pācittiya offense. 'Without the sitting-cloth, one should not dwell for four months'—this is the connection. 'Catumāsa' is the collective term for four months; that very thing is 'cātumāsa.' This is in the sense of absolute connection.

34. Idāni “ima”ntiādinā “adhiṭṭheyyā”ti vuttamadhiṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Saṅghāṭiṃ “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭhaheti sambandho. Tattha adhiṭṭhaheti hatthapāse ṭhitaṃ evaṃ adhiṭṭheyya. Ahatthapāsanti hatthassa pāso samīpo hatthapāso, aḍḍhateyyahatthabbhantaro. Dvādasahatthabbhantarotipi vadanti. Natthi hatthapāso etissāti ahatthapāsā, taṃ etanti adhiṭṭhaheti sambandho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Antogabbhe vā uparipāsāde vā tadaheva gantvā nivattanayogge padese vā ṭhitaṃ cīvaraṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato dūre ṭhitampi adhiṭṭhātabbantipi vadanti. Sesesupīti uttarāsaṅgādikaṇḍuppaṭicchādipariyantesupi avasesacīvaresu. Ayaṃ nayoti ayameva nayo. Yathā saṅghāṭiyā, evaṃ “imaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādi vuttanayovāti vuttaṃ hoti. Adhiṭṭhahantena pana hatthena gahetvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyena vā adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, vacībhedamattaṃ katvā vācāya vā. Parikkhāracoḷaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhanti ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷampi adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

34. Now, with 'this' and so on, he shows the determination that was mentioned with 'should determine.' The connection is: one should determine the outer robe by saying, 'I determine this outer robe.' Here, 'should determine' means one should determine it thus while it is within arm's reach. 'Not within arm's reach' (ahatthapāsa): the vicinity of the hand is 'arm's reach' (hatthapāso), which is within two and a half cubits. Some say within twelve cubits. That which is not within arm's reach is ahatthapāsā; the connection is that one should determine it thus. What is meant? It is meant that having gone to an inner chamber, or an upper storey, or a place from which it is possible to return on the same day, and having marked the robe that is there, one should determine it by saying, 'I determine that outer robe.' They also say that it can be determined even if it is located far away. 'In the remaining ones too' means in the remaining robes, up to and including the upper robe and the itch-covering cloth. 'This is the method' means this is the very same method. It is said that just as with the outer robe, so too with 'I determine this upper robe,' and so on, it is in the manner stated. However, when determining, one should take it with the hand, make a bodily gesture, and having made a mental application with the thought, 'I determine this outer robe,' it should be determined by body, or by voice after making a mere vocal utterance. An 'accessory cloth' is a principal item for storing away; it is also allowable to determine an accessory cloth as one of the three robes.

35. Idāni [M 0.0273] evaṃ adhiṭṭhahato aññaṃ laddhā adhiṭṭhātukāmena paccuddharitvā adhiṭṭhātabbanti dassetuṃ “adhiṭṭhahanto”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅghāṭi pabhuti ādi yassa taṃ saṅghāṭippabhuti. Etaṃ “adhiṭṭhahanto”ti etthāpi “adhiṭṭheyyā”ti etthāpi kammapadaṃ, “pubbacīvara”nti [V 0.0238] ettha pana visesanaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Paccuddharitvāti pariccajitvā. Parikkhāracoḷanāmena adhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapitavatthehi saṅghāṭiādīni karoti, niṭṭhite rajane ca kappe ca imaṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ paccuddharitvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Pattādhiṭṭhahaneti pattassa adhiṭṭhāne. Tathāti ca yathā cīvare, tathā pattepi adhiṭṭhānādikaṃ sabbanti attho. Ettha pana “imaṃ pattaṃ, etaṃ patta”nti vā viseso.

35. Now, to show that for one who has thus determined, upon acquiring another robe and wishing to determine it, he must determine it after having relinquished the previous one, he begins with 'while determining' and so on. Here, saṅghāṭippabhuti means that which has the outer robe and so forth as its beginning. This word is the object in both 'while determining' and 'should determine,' but in 'previous robe' it stands as a qualifier. 'Having relinquished' (paccuddharitvā) means having given up. One makes outer robes and so on from cloths that have been determined and set aside under the name 'accessory cloth'; when the dyeing and cutting are finished, this 'accessory cloth' should be relinquished and they (the new robes) should be determined again. 'In the determination of the bowl' (pattādhiṭṭhahane): 'similarly' means that just as with the robes, so too with the bowl, everything, including determination and so on, is the same. Here, however, the difference lies in saying 'this bowl' or 'that bowl'.

36. Idāni paccuddhāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “eta”ntiādimāha. Tattha imaṃ va iti vā-saddo rassaṃ katvā niddiṭṭho, so iti-saddato paraṃ yojetabbo, tasmā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā saṃseti sambandho veditabbo. Saṃseti vadeyya. Evanti yathā nāmena saṅghāṭi paccuddharitabbā, tathā uttarāsaṅgādīnīti attho. Vidūti paccuddharetimassa kattupadaṃ, paññavāti attho. Sabbatthāpi dūrāsannatādī vuttanayena veditabbā.

36. Now, to show the method of relinquishing, he begins with 'that' (etaṃ) and so on. Here, the particle vā is indicated with a shortened vowel (va) after imaṃ and iti; it should be connected after the word iti. Therefore, the connection should be understood as: one should say either, 'I relinquish that outer robe,' or 'I relinquish this outer robe.' 'Should say' (saṃseti) means vadeyya. 'Thus' (evaṃ) means that just as the outer robe is to be relinquished by name, so too are the upper robe and so on. 'The wise one' (vidū) is the agent of paccuddhareyya, meaning 'the intelligent person.' In all cases, distance, proximity, and so on should be understood in the manner previously stated.

37-8. Idāni saṅghāṭiādīnaṃ channaṃ pamāṇaparicchedaṃ dasseti “saṅghāṭī”tiādinā. Pacchimo anto pacchimanto, tena, pacchimakoṭiyāti attho. Dīghasoti dīghato. Muṭṭhiyā sahitaṃ pañcakaṃ yassā sā muṭṭhipañcakā, liṅgavipallāsavasena pana muṭṭhipañcako. Muṭṭhi-saddenettha upacāravasena katamuṭṭhiko hatthova vutto. Sugatassa cīvarato ūnāti samāso. Apīti vuttasamuccaye, tena [M 0.0274] yathāvuttapacchimappamāṇā ca ayañca uttamappamāṇāti attho. “Pacchimantenā”ti idaṃ muṭṭhittikañca tiriyanti etthāpi anuvattetvā attho veditabbo. Ca-saddo “uttamantena sugatacīvarūnāpi vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ samuccinoti. Tattha idāni majjhimassa purisassa tisso vidatthiyo ekā sugatavidatthi, tāya vidatthiyā nava vidatthiyo dīghato sugatacīvarappamāṇaṃ, tiriyaṃ cha vidatthiyo, taṃ pana vaḍḍhakihatthena dīghato terasa hatthā ekā ca vidatthi, tiriyato nava hatthā honti. Taṃvasena ubhayattha ūnatā viññātabbā.

Now, he shows the specific measurements of the six items, beginning with the outer robe, with the phrase 'the outer robe' and so on.
