'The lowest limit' (pacchimo anto) is pacchimanto; by this is meant 'by the minimum limit.' 'Lengthwise' (dīghaso) means dīghato. That which is five with a fist is muṭṭhipañcakā; however, due to a change of gender, it is muṭṭhipañcako. Here, by the word 'fist' (muṭṭhi), the hand made into a fist is figuratively meant. 'Less than the Sugata’s robe' is a compound. 'Also' (api) is an inclusive conjunction; by this is meant that both the aforementioned minimum measure and this maximum measure are included. The phrase 'by the lowest limit' (pacchimantenā) should be understood by carrying it forward to apply here also to the three fist-spans and to 'breadthwise.' The particle 'ca' includes this: 'It is permissible even if it is less than the Sugata's robe by the maximum limit.' In this regard, for a man of medium size, three of his spans make one Sugata-span. By that span, the measure of the Sugata's robe is nine spans in length and six spans in breadth. By a carpenter’s cubit, however, this is thirteen cubits and one span in length, and nine cubits in breadth. The deficiency in both cases should be understood in this way.

Uttarāsaṅgopi tattakovāti dassetuṃ “tathā ekaṃsikassapī”ti āha. Eko aṃso ekaṃso, tattha kātabbanti taddhite ekaṃsikaṃ. “Antaravāsako”ccādinā nivāsanaṃ dasseti. Tattha antaraṃ majjhapadeso, antare majjhe kaṭippadese vāso vatthaṃ antaravāso, soyeva antaravāsako. Cāpīti samudāyo, eko vā samuccayo. Aḍḍhena tatiyo bhāgo aḍḍhateyyo. Ettha dvinnaṃ hatthakoṭṭhāsānaṃ sampuṇṇānaṃ tatiyakoṭṭhāsasaṃsijjhane karaṇabhūtā aḍḍha-saddaniddiṭṭhā yā vidatthi[V 0.0239], sāva tatiyoti niddiṭṭhoti upaḍḍhahatthasaṅkhāto tatiyo bhāgo aḍḍhateyyo. So ca nānantarena dvihatthatatiyatā labbhatīti dve hatthā, ekā ca vidatthi aḍḍhateyyo. Taṃsanniyogena panettha antaravāsakova aḍḍhateyyoti veditabbo. Dve hatthā yassāti bāhiratthasamāso. Pārupanenāpi sakkā nābhiṃ paṭicchādetunti “dvihattho”ti vuttaṃ. Vā-saddo aḍḍhateyyaṃ vikappeti. Tiriyassa antoti chaṭṭhītappuriso, tiriyameva antoti vā kammadhārayo “gāmanto”tiādīsu viya.

To show that the upper robe is also of that size, it is said: 'Likewise, for the one-shouldered robe.' One shoulder is 'ekaṃso'; that which is to be worn thereon is 'ekaṃsikaṃ', formed with a taddhita suffix. With 'antaravāsako,' and so on, the lower garment is indicated. Therein, 'antara' means the middle region; a cloth worn in the middle or on the waist region is an 'antaravāso,' which is the same as 'antaravāsako.' The particle 'ca' is for aggregation, or it is a single conjunction. 'Aḍḍhateyya' is the third part with a half. Herein, the span ('vidatthi') indicated by the word 'aḍḍha' (half), which is the means for completing the third portion after two full cubit-portions, is itself designated as the third. Thus, 'aḍḍhateyya' is the third part, reckoned as half a cubit. And this is not obtained without an intermediary after the two cubits; thus, two cubits and one span is 'aḍḍhateyya.' In this connection, it should be understood that the 'antaravāsako' is 'aḍḍhateyya'. The word 'dvihattho' is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning 'that which has two cubits'. Since it is possible to cover the navel even by wearing it, it is called 'two-cubits long.' The particle 'vā' offers an alternative to 'aḍḍhateyya.' 'Tiriyassa anto' is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound; or 'tiriyameva anto' is a karmadhāraya compound, as in examples such as 'gāmanto'.

39. “Nisīdanassā”tiādinā [M 0.0275] nisīdanacīvaraṃ dasseti. Ettha nisīdanaṃ nāma same bhūmibhāge eḷakalomāni uparūpari santharitvā kañjikādīhi siñcitvā kato dvīsu ṭhānesu phālitattā tīhi dasāhi yutto parikkhāraviseso. Vidatthī dveti dve vidatthī. Visālato puthulato.

39. By 'For a sitting cloth,' etc., the sitting-cloth is indicated. Herein, a sitting cloth is a specific requisite made by spreading goat's hair in layers over a flat surface, sprinkling it with sour rice-gruel, etc., and which, being split in two places, is endowed with three borders. 'Vidatthī dve' means two spans. 'Visālato' means in breadth or width.

40. “Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī”tiādinā kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ dasseti. Tattha kaṇḍūti hi na atthato nānaṃ, taggahaṇena panettha piḷakassāvathullakacchābādhaṃ gayhati. Kaṇḍuṃ yathāvuttaṃ piḷakādiṃ paṭicchādetīti kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi. Paṭicchadanaṃ vā paṭicchādo, yathāvuttakaṇḍuyā paṭicchādo kaṇḍuppaṭicchādo, so assa atthīti kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī, tassa. Tiriyanti tiriyato.

40. By 'Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī' (a covering for itching), etc., a covering for itching is indicated. Herein, 'itching' (kaṇḍū) does not differ in meaning, but by this term, boils, oozing sores, or thick scabies are included. That which covers the aforementioned itching, such as boils and the like, is called a 'kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi.' Or, the act of covering is 'paṭicchādo'; the covering for the aforementioned itching is 'kaṇḍuppaṭicchādo'; one who possesses this is 'kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī'; 'tassa' refers to him. 'Tiriyaṃ' means breadthwise.

41. “Vassikā”tiādinā vassikasāṭikaṃ dasseti, taṃ suviññeyyaṃ.

41. By 'Vassikā' (rainy-season robe), etc., the rainy-season robe is indicated; this is easily understood.

42. Evaṃ pamāṇavantānaṃ pamāṇaṃ dassetvā vuttappamāṇātikkame dosaṃ, kesañci pamāṇābhāvagaṇanābhāvañca dassetuṃ “etthā”tiādimāha. Tattha etthāti vuttappamāṇavantesu cīvaresu. Taduttari tato vuttappamāṇato uttari nipātena uttari-saddena tappuriso. Karontassa sampādentassa. Chedanapācittīti chedanena sahitā pācitti, atirekaṃ chinditvā pācittiyaṃ desetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttappamāṇato pana atirekañca ūnakañca “parikkhāracoḷa”nti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Yena mukhaṃ puñchanti, taṃ mukhasambandhīti mukhassa coḷanti samāse dvando. Ākaṅkhitaṃ icchitaṃ pamāṇanti kammadhārayo. Tametesamatthīti ākaṅkhitappamāṇikā. Ettha ca ticīvarādīsu avuttepi gaṇanavibhāge paccattharaṇamukhapuñchanaparikkhāracoḷe ṭhapetvā ādito paṭṭhāya [M 0.0276][V 0.0240] chakkamekekameva vaṭṭati. Mukhapuñchanacoḷāni paccattharaṇāni ca bahūnipīti viññātabbaṃ.

42. Having thus shown the measure for those that have a measure, to point out the fault of exceeding the stated measure, and to show that for some there is no measure or counting, it begins with 'etthā,' etc. Herein, 'etthā' refers to robes that have a stated measure. 'Taduttari' (beyond that) is a tatpuruṣa compound with the particle 'uttari' (beyond) from 'tato vuttappamāṇato' (from that stated measure). 'Karontassa' means 'for one who makes' or 'completes it'. 'Chedanapācitti' means a pācittiya offense accompanied by cutting; it is said that having cut the excess, a pācittiya offense is to be confessed. However, both what exceeds and what falls short of the stated measure should be determined as 'accessory cloth.' That with which one wipes the mouth is related to the mouth; 'cloth of the mouth' ('mukhassa coḷaṃ') in a compound is a dvandva. 'Desired measure' ('ākaṅkhitappamāṇa') is a karmadhāraya compound. 'They possess that' means they are of the desired measure. Herein, although a division by number is not stated for the three robes and so on, with the exception of the ground-sheet, the face-wiping cloth, and the accessory cloth, only one of each of the six types of robes is allowable from the beginning. It should be understood that many face-wiping cloths and ground-sheets are allowable.

43. Gaṇanāti ettha napuṃsakassa itthivacanena yogābhāvā “na dīpitā”ti liṅgaṃ vipariṇāmetvā sambandhitabbaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na pakāsitāti attho. Tiṇṇaṃ panetesaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavaseneva vuttaṃ, vikappanūpagapacchimena pacchimappamāṇaṃ atthiyeva. Idāni yasmā tattha taṃ sabbaṃ na dīpitaṃ, tasmā vikappanūpagathavikādi sabbaṃ ekaṃ “parikkhāracoḷa”nti, bahūni ekato katvā “parikkhāracoḷānī”tipi vatvā adhiṭṭhātabbanti dassento “tathā”tiādimāha. Iminā parikkhāracoḷaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhanti dasseti. Thavikādiṃ thavikā ādi yassa parissāvanādinoti samāso. Vikappassa upagaṃ vikappiyaṃ, tañca upari vakkhati.

43. Regarding 'counting' (gaṇanā) here—since there is no grammatical connection of the neuter word with the feminine word, the gender should be altered to 'na dīpitā' (not shown, feminine) and connected; the meaning is that it is not explained in the commentary. However, for these three, it is stated only by way of the highest limit; the minimum measure indeed exists with the final part subject to determination. Now, since all that is not indicated there, it begins with 'tathā' (thus), etc., to show that all the items subject to determination, such as the bag, etc., should be determined as one 'accessory cloth,' or by grouping many together, as 'accessory cloths.' By this, it shows that the 'accessory cloth' is a particular category for requisites. 'Thavikādiṃ' (bag, etc.) is a compound meaning 'that which has a bag as its beginning,' such as a water strainer. 'Vikappiyaṃ' is what is subject to determination, and that will be explained further on.

44. Idāni tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ paṭibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “ahatā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ahatena navena adhotena kappaṃ sadisaṃ ahatakappaṃ, ekavāradhotaṃ. Ahatañca ahatakappañca ahatāhatakappāni, vatthāni, tesaṃ. Dve guṇā paṭalāni yassa sāti duguṇā. “Guṇo paṭalarāsīsū”ti hi abhidhānappadīpikā. Duguṇā dupaṭṭā, uttarasmiṃ dehabhāge āsañjīyatīti ukkarāsaṅgo. Ekaccaṃ ekapaṭṭaṃ assa atthīti ekaccī, ekapaṭṭoti attho. Nipāto vā ekaccīti. Tathāti samuccaye, antaravāsako cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upamāyaṃ vā, yathā uttarāsaṅgo ekacciyo, evaṃ antaravāsakoti attho.

44. Now, to show the distinction pertaining to the three robes, the passage beginning with 'ahatā' (unbeaten) is introduced. Herein, 'ahata' means new, unwashed; 'ahatakappa' (like unbeaten) is similar, meaning washed once. 'Ahata' and 'ahatakappa' together are 'ahatāhatakappāni' (unbeaten and like-unbeaten cloths); 'tesaṃ' refers to these fabrics. 'Duguṇā' (double) means that which has two layers ('guṇā' or 'paṭalāni'). For the Abhidhānappadīpikā says, 'Guṇa is used in the sense of a layer or a heap.' 'Duguṇā' means two-layered. 'Uttarāsaṅgo' (upper robe) is so called because it is fastened ('āsañjīyati') on the upper ('uttarasmiṃ') part of the body. 'Ekaccī' means having one layer ('ekapaṭṭaṃ'); the meaning is single-layered. Or, 'ekaccī' is a particle. 'Tathā' (thus) is for conjunction, meaning 'and the lower robe' is also spoken of. Or it is a simile: just as the upper robe is single-layered, so is the lower robe—this is the meaning.

45. “Utū”ti anekautu gahitāti ututo dīghakālato uddhaṭā utuddhaṭā, tesaṃ pilotikānanti attho. Sesāti uttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakā. Paṃsu viya kucchitaṃ [M 0.0277] ulati pavattatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, rathikāsusānasaṅkārakūṭādīnaṃ yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ coḷakhaṇḍaṃ, tasmiṃ. Yā yā rucīti abyayībhāve yathāruci, yāvadatthaṃ satapaṭṭampi vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

45. By 'utū' is meant gathered over many seasons ('anekautu gahitā'); thus 'utuddhaṭā' means taken up after a long time. The meaning is 'their rags' ('tesaṃ pilotikānaṃ'). 'Sesā' (the rest) refers to the upper robe and the lower robe. 'Paṃsukūlaṃ' (rag-heap cloth) is so called because, being despised ('kucchitaṃ'), it is found ('ulati pavattatī') like dust ('paṃsu viya'); it refers to a piece of cloth lying anywhere, such as in streets, cemeteries, or on rubbish heaps. 'Yā yā rucī' (whatever one pleases) forms the avyayībhāva compound 'yathāruci' (according to preference); the intention is that as many as are needed, even a hundred patches, are allowable.

46. Idāni tīsu chinditvā kātuṃ appahontesu kātabbavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “tīsū”tiādimāha. Tattha ticīvarasamudāyato ekadesabhūtānaṃ dvinnamekassa ca saṅkhāguṇena niddhāriyamānattā tīsūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Ekavacanassa bahvatthena yogābhāvato dvicīvarasaṅkhātabahvatthavasena [V 0.0241] vacanaṃ vipariṇāmetvā yāni pahonti, tāni dve vāpi chinditabbāni, yaṃ pahoti, taṃ ekaṃ vā chinditabbanti yojetabbaṃ. Pahontīti pacchimacīvarappamāṇachinnakāni pahonti. Apīti sambhāvane, tīsu kā kathāti attho. Anvādhinti āgantukapattaṃ. Anu pacchā ādhīyatīti anvādhi, yaṃ cīvarassopari saṅghāṭiākārena āropetabbaṃ. Anādiṇṇanti anāropitaṃ anvādhikaṃ. Na dhāreyyāti iminā yadi dhāreyya, dukkaṭanti dīpeti.

46. Now, to explain the procedure for those unable to cut and make robes from three pieces of cloth, it begins with 'tīsū' (in three), etc. Herein, since two or one, being a part of the aggregate of the three robes, are being determined by their numerical quality, 'tīsu' is in the locative case of determination. Because there is no grammatical connection of the singular word with the plural meaning, the word should be altered to express the plural meaning of 'two robes', and it should be construed thus: 'those that are sufficient, even those two should be cut, or that which is sufficient, even that one should be cut.' 'Pahonti' (are sufficient) means pieces cut to the size of the minimum robe are sufficient. 'Api' (even) is used in the sense of possibility; the meaning is 'what need to speak of three?' 'Anvādhi' refers to a newcomer's bowl. The term 'anvādhi' is so called because it is placed ('ādhīyati') after ('anu'); it also applies to that which is to be placed over the robe in the manner of an outer cloak. 'Anādiṇṇaṃ' means an unplaced extra robe. By 'na dhāreyya' (should not wear), it indicates that if one were to wear it, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

47-8. Idāni “ticīvaraṃ na vaseyya vinekāha”nti vuttānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ avippavāsalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “gāme”tiādinā udositasikkhāpade (pārā. 471 ādayo) vuttaparihāramāha. Tattha gāme vā…pe… vihāre vā ticīvaraṃ nikkhipitvāti sambandho. Tattha “paṭo daḍḍho”tiādīsu viya avayavepi samudāyavohāravasena tīsu ekampi “ticīvara”nti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhusammutiyaññatrāti saṅghena gilānassa bhikkhuno dīyamānaṃ cīvarena vippavāsasammutiṃ vinā. Vippavatthunti ekūpacāranānūpacāragāmādito bahi, atha vā nivesanādīnaṃ, tattha ca gabbhovarakānaṃ cīvarassa vā hatthapāsaṃ atikkamma cīvarena vippayutto [M 0.0278] hutvā vasituṃ. Ettha ca gāmādīnaṃ ekūpacāranānūpacāratā ekakulanānākulasantakassa gāmādino parikkhepassa, parikkhepokāsassa ca vasena satthaabbhokāsānaṃ sattabbhantaravasena ca veditabbā. Tattha eko abbhantaro aṭṭhavīsatihattho hoti. Ettha ca nivesanādīni gāmato bahi sanniviṭṭhānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ visuṃ gāmassa gahitattā, tathā udositādīhi aññaṃ nivesanaṃ.

Now, to explain the characteristic of non-separation regarding the three robes mentioned in the phrase, 'one should not live without the three robes for a single day,' he states the allowance mentioned in the training rule concerning what has been set aside (Pārā. 471ff.), beginning with 'in a village,' and so on. Therein, the connection is 'having deposited the three robes in a village or... or in a monastery.' In this context, just as in cases like 'the cloth is burnt,' even a single item among the three is called 'the three robes' by way of collective usage. 'Except by the agreement of the bhikkhus' means without the permission for separation from his robe, granted by the Sangha to a sick bhikkhu. 'To live separated' means to dwell outside a village, etc., whether it has a single precinct or not, or outside residences, etc., and therein inner chambers and cells, having gone beyond the hand's reach of the robe and become disjoined from it. Here, whether villages, etc., have a single precinct or not is to be understood by means of the enclosure of a village belonging to a single or multiple families, the space of the enclosure, and by means of the seven `abbhantaras` for roofed and open spaces. Therein, one `abbhantara` is twenty-eight cubits. Here, residences, etc., are to be understood as situated outside the village, because the village is mentioned separately; likewise, a residence is distinct from an `udosita` and so on.

Tattha udosito nāma yānādīnaṃ bhaṇḍānaṃ sālā. Pāsādo dīghapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Nāvā ca aṭṭo ca māḷo ca ārāmo ca nāvā…pe… ārāmaṃ, tasmiṃ. Aṭṭo nāma paṭirājādīnaṃ paṭibāhanatthaṃ iṭṭhakāhi kato bahalabhittiko catupañcabhūmiko patissayaviseso. Māḷo ekakūṭasaṅgahito caturassapāsādo. Ārāmo pupphārāmo vā phalārāmo vā. Sattho ca khettañca khalañcāti dvando. Sattho nāma jaṅghasattho vā sakaṭasattho vā. Khalaṃ vuccati dhaññakaraṇaṃ. Dumo nāma dumamūlaṃ chāyāya phuṭṭhokāso upacāravasena. Abbhokāso pana agāmake araññeva adhippeto.

There, an udosita is a hall for vehicles and goods. A pāsāda is a long mansion. A hammiya is a mansion with a flat roof. A ship, a fort, a pavilion, and a park—in that [location, meaning in a ship... or in a park]. A fort (aṭṭo) is a special kind of shelter built with bricks, with thick walls and four or five stories, intended to repel enemy kings and others. A pavilion (māḷo) is a square mansion with a single peak. A park (ārāmo) is either a flower garden or a fruit orchard. A caravan, a field, and a threshing floor—this is a dvanda compound. A caravan (sattho) refers to either a foot caravan or a cart caravan. A threshing floor (khala) is called a place for processing grain. A tree (dumo) means the base of the tree, a shaded open space touched by its shade, by way of convention. However, an open space (abbhokāso) specifically refers to a place without houses, that is, the wilderness itself.

49. Idāni “etaṃ…pe… saṅghāṭi”ntiādinā navannameva paccuddhāro vutto, na pana tesaṃ [V 0.0242] kālaparicchedoti taṃ dassetuṃ “rogā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha devadatto dattoti nāmekadesenāpi nāmavohārato vassikasāṭikāva “sāṭikā”ti pakaraṇavasena gammamānatthattā vuttā. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādikā ca rogavassānapariyantā. Rogā ca vassānā ca māsā rogavassānā, te tadatikkamena paccuddharitabbatāya pariyantā yāsanti viggaho.

49. Now, by the phrase beginning 'this... up to the `saṅghāṭi`,' the relinquishment of only the nine items is stated, but not their time limit. To indicate that, the phrase beginning 'due to illness' is introduced. Therein, the rains-cloth is called simply 'cloth' because its meaning is understood from the context, by the convention of naming by a part of the name, just as Devadatta is called Datta. Likewise, the itch-covering is limited by illness and the rains. The analysis is: illness and the rains are the limits for those cloths, because they must be relinquished when that period is exceeded.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Vassikasāṭikā vassānamāsātikkame kattikapuṇṇamāya eva paccuddharitabbā. Tathā kaṇḍuppaṭicchādikā [M 0.0279] ābādhesu vūpasantesūti vuttaṃ hoti. “Paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā”ti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) vuttaṃ. Ettha pana keci ācariyā “paccuddharitvāti vassikasāṭikabhāvato apanetvā”ti vadiṃsu, taṃ na yujjati. Paccuddhāravinayakammavisayeyeva paccuddhāra-saddassa diṭṭhattā, “cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) pāḷivacanato ca. “Cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātu”nti ca catunnaṃ māsānaṃ adhiṭṭhānena saha accantasaṃyogo dassitoti na tena adhiṭṭhānabhedo viññāyati. Teneva kurundaṭṭhakathāyampi “vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ, tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vacanato kattikapuṇṇamāya eva paccuddharitvā hemante vikappetabbāti vuttaṃ. Tasmā “vassikasāṭikā vassānamāsātikkamenāpi kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi ābādhavūpasamenāpi adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatī”ti (kaṅkā. aṭṭha. kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi paccuddhāravasenāpi adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti evamattho gahetabbo. Evañhi sati sabbaṭṭhakathāyo samenti, yutti ca aviruddhā hontīti. Tato paranti paccuddhārato upari. Vikappeyyāti kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ paccuddharitvā vikappeyya. Vassikasāṭikaṃ kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ paccuddharitvā hemantassa paṭhamadivase vikappeyya, evaṃ asati dukkaṭanti adhippāyo. Sesāti apare satta cīvarāni sesā. Natthi pariyantaṃ vuttasadiso kālaparicchedo etesanti apariyantikā.

What is meant? The rains-cloth must be relinquished upon the passing of the months of the rains, specifically on the full moon day of Kattika. Similarly, it is meant that the itch-covering is to be relinquished when the ailments have subsided. For it is stated in the commentary (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.469): 'Having relinquished it, it should be placed under joint ownership.' Here, however, some teachers have said, '“Relinquishing” means removing it from its state as a rains-cloth.' That is not correct, because the word 'relinquishment' is seen only in the domain of the Vinaya act of revocation, and because of the Pāli statement (Mahāva. 358): 'One should determine it for four months, and after that, place it under joint ownership.' And by 'determine it for four months,' a complete connection with the determination for four months is shown, so a break in the determination is not to be understood from this. For that very reason, in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā too, it is said: 'According to the Pāli (Mahāva. 358), “One should determine it for the four months of the rains, and after that, place it under joint ownership,” it should be relinquished on the full moon day of Kattika and placed under joint ownership in the winter.' Therefore, it is said (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Kathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā): 'The rains-cloth loses its determination upon the passing of the months of the rains, and the itch-covering upon the subsiding of ailments.' In the Mātikāṭṭhakathā as well, the meaning should be taken thus: 'The determination is also lost by means of relinquishment.' For when this is so, all the commentaries are in agreement, and the reasoning is not contradicted. 'After that' means after the relinquishment. 'One should place it under joint ownership' means that after relinquishing the itch-covering, one should place it under joint ownership. One should relinquish the rains-cloth on the full moon day of Kattika and place it under joint ownership on the first day of winter. The intention is that if this is not done, it is an offense of wrong-doing. 'The rest' means the other seven robes are the remainder. They are 'without limit' because for them there is no time limit similar to the one mentioned.

50. Idāni paccattharaṇādikaṃ cīvaracatukkaṃ sadasādikaṃ vaṭṭati, nāparanti dassetuṃ “paccattharaṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha parikkhāro ca mukhapuñchanañcāti dvando. Parikkhāramukhapuñchanameva coḷakanti kammadhārayo. Dvandasamāsante suyyamānattā pana coḷaka-saddo parikkhāra-saddato ca paraṃ daṭṭhabbo [M 0.0280] “parikkhāracoḷaka”nti. Taṃ pana sāmaññajotanāya visesepi avaṭṭhānato ṭhapetvā pañca cīvarāni parikkhāracoḷanāmenādhiṭṭhitāni avasesaṃ [V 0.0243] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paccattharaṇañca parikkhāramukhapuñchanacoḷakañca paccattharaṇa…pe… coḷakañca nisīdanañcāti etaṃ cīvaracatukkaṃ sadasampi arattampi anādiṇṇakappampi labbhanti sambandho. Sadasanti saha yāhi kāhici dasāhīti sadasaṃ. Sadasake labbhamāne adasampi labbhatevāti sadasampi adasampi pupphadasampīti ettha attho. Pi-saddo vuttāvuttasampiṇḍanattho. Arattanti nīlapītādirajanena arañjitampi. Pi-saddena rañjitanīlapītādikampi anādiṇṇakappampīti. Ādiṇṇo kappo yassa natthīti taṃ anādiṇṇakappampi. Pi-saddena ādiṇṇakappampi.

50. Now, to show that the fourfold set of robes, beginning with the ground-sheet, is allowable with a fringe and so on, but not others, he said 'the ground-sheet,' etc. Therein, 'requisite-cloth' and 'face-wiping cloth' form a dvanda compound. 'Requisite-and-face-wiping cloth' is simply a 'cloth' (`coḷaka`)—a karmadhāraya compound. However, because the word `coḷaka` is commonly heard at the end of a dvanda compound, it should be understood as coming after the word `parikkhāra`, as in `parikkhāracoḷaka`. But that (`parikkhāracoḷa`) should be understood as the remainder—setting aside the five robes determined by the name `parikkhāracoḷa`—because it serves as a general indicator while also applying in specific cases. The connection is that this fourfold set of robes—the ground-sheet, the requisite-cloth, the face-wiping cloth, and the sitting-cloth—is obtainable even with a fringe, even undyed, and even without the proper marking. 'With a fringe' (`sadasaṃ`) means together with any sort of fringe. The meaning here is that when something with a fringe is obtainable, something without a fringe is obtainable as well—hence, 'even with a fringe, even without a fringe, even with a flower-patterned fringe.' The particle `pi` serves to include what is said and unsaid. 'Undyed' (`arattaṃ`) means not colored with dye such as blue or yellow. By the particle `pi` [in `arattampi`], one that is colored is also included. 'Without the proper marking' (`anādiṇṇakappaṃ`) means that for which the proper marking has not been applied. By the particle `pi` [in `anādiṇṇakappampi`], one with the proper marking is also included.

Nanu ca “na bhikkhave sabbanīlakāni cīvarāni dhāretabbānī”tiādinā (mahāva. 372) sabbanīlakasabbapītakasabbalohitakacīvarāni sāmaññena paṭikkhittānīti kathamidaṃ cīvaracatukkaṃ sadasādikaṃ vaṭṭati, kathañca anādiṇṇakappampi vaṭṭatīti? Vuccate – “tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu kusacīraṃ nivāsetvā”tiādinā uppannavatthūsu (mahāva. 371) “na bhikkhave kusacīraṃ…pe… titthiyaddhajo dhāretabbo. Yo dhāreyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”tiādinā (mahāva. 371) uppannavatthuvaseneva nivāsanapārupanasaṅkhātadhāraṇassa paṭikkhittattā ca tattheva aṭṭhakathāyañca (mahāva. aṭṭha. 372) “sabbanīlakādīni rajanaṃ dhovitvā puna rajitvā dhāretabbāni, na sakkā ce honti dhovituṃ, paccattharaṇāni vā kātabbāni, dupaṭṭacīvarassa vā majjhe dātabbāni, acchinnadasadīghadasāni dasā chinditvā dhāretabbāni, kañcukaṃ labhitvā phāletvā rajitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, veṭhanepi eseva nayo”ti nivāsanapārupanavaseneva dhāraṇaparibhogānaṃ [M 0.0281] vuttattā ca dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpade (pāci. aṭṭha. 368) “yaṃ nivāsetuṃ vā pārupituṃ vā sakkā hoti, tadeva cīvaranti veditabba”nti pañcannaṃyeva kappabinduno anuññātattā ca ticīvarakaṇḍuppaṭicchādivassikasāṭikasaṅkhātāni pañca cīvarāni kāyaparihāriyāneva adasāni asabbanīlakādīni kappiyarajanarajitāni ādiṇṇakappāniyeva honti, na niyamena nivattitāni parāni cattārīti cīvaracatukkameva sadasādikaṃ anādiṇṇakappampi vaṭṭatīti.

But is it not so that by the text beginning, 'Monks, robes that are entirely blue are not to be worn' (Mahāvagga 372), robes that are entirely blue, entirely yellow, and entirely red are generally rejected? How then are these four robes, with fringes and so on, allowable? And how are they allowable even without being marked with a kappa-mark? It is said: In the origin stories beginning, 'At that time, a certain bhikkhu, having put on a robe of kusa grass...' (Mahāvagga 371), and by the text beginning, 'Monks, a robe of kusa grass... a heretics' banner is not to be worn. Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of grave transgression' (Mahāvagga 371), the wearing, described as putting on a lower or upper robe, is rejected only in accordance with the origin story. And in the commentary on that very passage (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 372), it is said: 'Robes that are entirely blue and so on are to be worn after washing out the dye and re-dyeing them. If they cannot be washed, they should be made into ground-cloths, or they should be placed in the middle of a double-layered robe. Those with uncut fringes or long fringes are to be worn after cutting the fringes. Having obtained a jacket, it is allowable to tear it up, dye it, and use it. This is the same method for head-cloths.' And because the wearing and use are spoken of only in terms of lower and upper robes, and because in the training rule on making a discoloration mark (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 368) it is said, 'Only that which can be worn as a lower robe or put on as an upper robe is to be known as a robe,' and because the kappa-mark is permitted for only five robes—namely, the three robes, the cloth for covering sores, and the rains-cloth—these five robes, being for personal use, must be without fringes, not entirely blue and so on, dyed with a proper dye, and marked with a kappa-mark. The other four are not necessarily so restricted. Therefore, the four robes, with fringes and so on, are allowable even without being marked with a kappa-mark.

51. Sesacīvarapañcakaṃ adasaṃyeva rajitaṃyeva ādiṇṇakappaṃva kappatīti yojanā. Rajitanti kappiyarajanena rajitaṃ. Nisīdanassa yathāvuttenatthena sabbattha adasatthaṃ nisedhetuṃ “sadasaṃva nisīdana”nti vuttaṃ. Sati hi sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ hoti.

51. The connection is that the five remaining robes are allowable only if they are without a fringe, only if dyed, and only if marked with a kappa-mark. 'Dyed' means dyed with a proper dye. To prohibit the meaning of 'without a fringe' everywhere for the sitting-cloth, in accordance with the stated meaning, it is said, 'the sitting-cloth is with a fringe.' For a qualifier is meaningful when there is a possibility and a deviation.

52. Idāni [V 0.0244] anadhiṭṭhite anissaṭṭhe ca kā pavattīti taṃ dassetuṃ “anadhiṭṭhita”ntiādimāha. Tattha anadhiṭṭhitanti ticīvarādivasena anadhiṭṭhitaṃ. Anissaṭṭhanti yassa kassaci dānalakkhaṇena adinnaṃ. Vikappetvā paribhuñjayeti vakkhamānanayena ekabahubhāvaṃ, sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca sallakkhetvā vikappetvā paccuddharitvā paribhuñjeyya. Vakkhamānanayena pana viññāyatīti “paccuddharitvā”ti na vuttaṃ.

52. Now, to show what the procedure is when it is not determined and not relinquished, he says, 'not determined,' and so on. Therein, 'not determined' means not determined as the three robes and so on. 'Not relinquished' means not given to anyone, which has the characteristic of a gift. 'One should use it after having shared it' means that, according to the method to be explained, having taken note of whether it is one or many, and whether it is present or not present, one should share it, rescind the sharing, and then use it. However, since it is understood by the method to be explained, 'having rescinded' is not stated.

Idāni “vikappetvā”ti vuttaṃ kīdisaṃ taṃ heṭṭhimantena vikappiyanti āha “hatthā”tiādi. Tattha hattho dīghena yassa taṃ hatthadīghaṃ. Tatoti tasmā hatthato. Upaḍḍho hatthassa dutiyo bhāgo vidatthisaṅkhāto vitthārena yassa taṃ upaḍḍhavitthāraṃ.

Now, regarding what was said, 'having shared it,' he says, 'from the hand,' and so on, to show by what kind of following text it is to be shared. Therein, that which has a hand-breadth in length is 'a hand-breadth long.' 'From that' means from that hand-breadth. Half, the second part of a hand-breadth, is called a span; that which has this in width is 'a half-span in width.'

53. Idāni yathāvuttavidhānaṃ tecīvarikasseva vasena, aparo pana aññathā paṭipajjatīti taṃ dassetuṃ “ticīvarassā”tiādimāha[M 0.0282]. Tattha nāmenādhiṭṭhitāni tīṇi cīvarāni etassāti ticīvaro. Tassa vinayatecīvarikassāti attho, na parikkhāracoḷanāmena adhiṭṭhitacīvarassa. Vinayatecīvarikassa pana udositasikkhāpade vuttaparihāro natthi. Parikkhāracoḷiyoti parikkhāracoḷamassa atthīti ṇikena ya-kāro. Sabbanti sakalaṃ navavidhampi cīvaraṃ. Tathā vatvāti ekabahubhāvaṃ, sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādinā vatvā. Adhiṭṭhatīti adhiṭṭhāti.

53. Now, to show that the procedure as stated is by way of one who possesses the three robes, but another practices otherwise, he says, 'of the three-robed one,' and so on. Therein, 'one who possesses the three robes' (ticīvaro) is one for whom the three robes are determined by name. The meaning is 'of one who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya,' not of one who has determined a robe by the name 'requisite-cloth.' For one who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya, however, there is no allowance as stated in the training rule on what has been stored. 'One who has a requisite-cloth' (parikkhāracoḷiyo) means 'he has a requisite-cloth'; the 'ya' is due to the suffix '-ṇika.' 'All' means the entire nine kinds of robes. 'Having spoken thus' means having known whether it is one or many, and whether it is present or not present, and having spoken the words beginning, 'I determine this requisite-cloth.' 'He determines' (adhiṭṭhati) is adhiṭṭhāti.

54. Adhiṭṭhitacīvaraṃ pana paribhuñjato kathaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti taṃ dassento “acchedā”tiādimāha. Tattha acchedo ca vissajjanañca gāho ca vibbhamo cāti dvando. Acchedo nāma corādīhi acchinditvā gahaṇaṃ. Vissajjanaṃ paresaṃ dānaṃ. Gāho vissāsena gahaṇaṃ. Vibbhamo sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya gihibhāvūpagamanaṃ. Tadāpi tassa aññassa dāne viya cīvarassa nirālayabhāvena pana pariccāgoti. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana bhādiso bhikkhuyevāti adhiṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatīti atthaṃ vikappetvā bhikkhuniyā gihibhāvūpagamanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ, kāraṇaṃ panettha amhākaṃ garūhiyeva sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.469) “bhikkhuniyā ‘hīnāyāvattanenā’ti visesetvā avuttattā bhikkhuniyā hi gihibhāvūpagamane adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ visuṃ vattabbaṃ natthi tassā vibbhamaneneva assamaṇībhāvato”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu ca bhikkhuno appaccakkhātasikkhassa gihibhāvūpagamanena adhiṭṭhānavijahanena nirālayabhāvo kāraṇabhāvena [V 0.0245] vutto, evaṃ sati parivattaliṅgassa natthi nirālayabhāvoti kathamassa adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti? Saccametaṃ, tathāpi buddhamataññūhi aṭṭhakathācariyehi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.69) “yaṃ panassa bhikkhubhāve [M 0.0283] adhiṭṭhitaṃ ticīvarañca patto ca, taṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati, puna adhiṭṭhātabba”nti vuttattā natthettha dosoti.

54. Now, showing how the determination lapses for one using a determined robe, he says, 'by theft,' and so on. Therein, 'by theft, by relinquishment, by taking, and by falling away' is a dvanda compound. 'Theft' (acchedo) is the taking by robbers and others after having snatched it. 'Relinquishment' (vissajjanaṃ) is giving to others. 'Taking' (gāho) is taking with familiarity. 'Falling away' (vibbhamo) is attaining the state of a householder without having renounced the training. Even then, just as in the case of giving it to another, it is a relinquishment through the robe's state of having no attachment. In the subcommentary, however, it is said that a bhikkhunī's attaining the state of a householder is not to be taken here, having construed the meaning that the determination does not lapse, as in 'such as a bhikkhu only.' This should not be accepted. The reason for this is that our own teachers have stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.469): 'Since it is not stated specifically for a bhikkhunī with the phrase "by reverting to a lower state," there is no need to state separately that a bhikkhunī's determination lapses upon attaining the state of a householder, because she becomes a non-ascetic simply by that falling away from the state of a recluse.' But is it not so that for a bhikkhu who attains the state of a householder without having renounced the training, the state of having no attachment is stated as the reason for the lapse of determination? If so, for one whose gender has changed, there is no state of having no attachment, so how does his determination lapse? This is true. Nevertheless, because the commentary teachers, who knew the Buddha's intention, have stated in the commentary (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.69), 'As for the three robes and the bowl that were determined by him in the state of a bhikkhu, that determination lapses; they must be determined anew,' there is no fault here.

Māraṇaliṅgasikkhāti uttarapadalopena upacārena vā liṅgaparivattanaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānañca “liṅgasikkhā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Iti ete aṭṭha sabbesu navasu cīvaresu adhiṭṭhānassa viyogo vippavāso, tassa kāraṇā hontīti pāṭhaseso. Ticīvarassa pana na kevalaṃ imeyeva aṭṭha, vinividdhachiddañca adhiṭṭhānaviyogakāraṇanti liṅgavacanañca parivattetvā yojetabbaṃ. Tattha abbhantare ekassapi tantuno abhāvena vinividdhaṃ vinivijjhitvā gatachiddaṃkaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ vinividdhachiddaṃ. Tattha saṅghāṭiyā ca uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghantato vidatthippamāṇassa, tiriyantato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇassa, antaravāsakassa pana dīghantato vidatthippamāṇasseva tiriyantato caturaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, sūcikammaṃ katvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sūcikammaṃ karontena ca chinditvā dubbalaṭṭhānāpanayanena chiddaṃ adassetvā kātabbaṃ.

The change of gender and the renunciation of the training are also called 'liṅgasikkhā', either by elision of the latter word or by metaphor. Thus, these eight are the separation, the dissociation, from the determination with regard to all nine robes; 'they are the causes of it' is the remainder of the text. For the three robes, however, not only these eight, but also a hole pierced right through is a cause for the separation from the determination; the gender and number should be changed and connected. Therein, a 'hole pierced right through' (vinividdhachiddaṃ) is a hole the size of the back of the little fingernail, which has gone through by being pierced, due to the absence of even a single thread inside. Therein, for the outer robe and the upper robe, a hole within an area measuring a span in length and eight finger-breadths in width, and for the lower robe, within an area measuring a span in length and four finger-breadths in width, breaks the determination. Having done needlework, it must be determined anew. And when doing the needlework, it should be done by cutting away and removing the weak spot, after making the hole disappear.

55. Idāni akappiyāni dassetuṃ “kusā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kusā ca vākā ca phalakāni ca, tesaṃ cīrāni kusa…pe… cīrāni. Tattha kusena ganthetvā kataṃ kusacīraṃ. Tathā vākena ganthetvā kataṃ vākacīraṃ, tāpasānaṃ vakkalaṃ. Phalakasaṇṭhānāni phalakāni sibbitvā kataṃ phalakacīraṃ. Kesavālajanti kesehi ca vālehi ca jātaṃ vāyitaṃ kambalanti sambandho. Ulūkapakkhājinakkhipeti ulūkānaṃ kosiyasakuṇānaṃ pakkhaṃ pakkhena kataṃ nivāsanañca ajinakkhipaṃ salomaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinamigānaṃ cammañca dhārayato thullaccayanti sambandho.

55. Now, to show what is unsuitable, 'kusa' and so forth is stated. Herein, kusa grass, bark, and wooden planks—their robes are 'kusa... robes.' Therein, a robe made by plaiting kusa grass is a kusa-robe. Similarly, a robe made by weaving with bark is a vāka-robe, the bark-cloth of ascetics. A robe made by sewing together pieces shaped like planks is a phalaka-robe. 'Kesavālaja' is connected with a blanket woven from human hair and animal hair. 'Ulūkapakkhājinakkhipeti' is connected with a grave offense for one who wears a garment made from the feathers of owls, that is, kosiya birds, and a hide garment, that is, the skin of a deer with its fur and hooves.

56. Kadalerakakkadussesūti kadaliyo ca erako ca akko ca, tesaṃ dussāni vatthāni, tesu ceva makacivākehi [M 0.0284] kate potthake cāpi dukkaṭaṃ. Nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Kadalidussādisaddena taṃdhāraṇamadhippetaṃ, tasmā taṃdhāraṇanimittaṃ dukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho. Evaṃ sabbattha. “Nīlako cā”tiādinā dvando. Sabbā nīlaka…pe… kaṇhakāti kammadhārayo. Nīlādivaṇṇayogena [V 0.0246] vatthaṃ nīlādi. Nīlakaṃ umāpupphavaṇṇaṃ. Mañjeṭṭhaṃ mañjeṭṭhikavaṇṇaṃ. Pītaṃ kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Lohitaṃ jayasumanapupphavaṇṇaṃ. Kaṇhakaṃ addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇaṃ. Sabba-saddo panettha paccekaṃ yojetabbo.

56. 'Kadalerakakkadussesūti' means kadali (banana plant), eraka (a type of grass), and akka (Calotropis gigantea)—the cloths made from them; and in the case of coverings made from them with makaci wool, there is also an offense of wrong-doing. This locative case is in the sense of a reason. By the term 'kadali cloth, etc.,' the wearing of them is intended; therefore, the meaning is that there is an offense of wrong-doing for the reason of wearing them. Thus it is in all cases. By 'nīlaka and so forth' a dvanda compound is formed. 'All are nīlaka... up to kaṇhaka' is a descriptive compound (kammadhārayo). A cloth is called 'nīla,' etc., due to its connection with the color blue, etc. 'Nīlaka' is the color of the umā flower. 'Mañjeṭṭha' is the color of the mañjeṭṭhika flower. 'Pīta' is the color of the kaṇikāra flower. 'Lohita' is the color of the jayasumana flower. 'Kaṇhaka' is the color of the addāriṭṭhaka. Here, the word 'sabba' (all) should be applied to each one individually.

57. Mahā…pe… ratteti mahāraṅgo ca mahānāmaraṅgo ca, tehi ratte. Etthāpi puna suyyamānaṃ sabbasaddamanuvattiyaṃ, “sabbamahāraṅgaratte”tiādinā attho veditabbo. Iminā ca asabbanīlakādi kappiyarajanarajitaṃ paribhuñjantassa natthi dosoti dīpeti. Tattha mahāraṅgo satapadipiṭṭhivaṇṇo. Mahānāmaraṅgo sambhinnavaṇṇo, so pana paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇo hoti, padumavaṇṇotipi vadanti. Tirīṭaketi taṃ nāmaka rukkhatace. Acchinnadīghadasaketi sabbaso acchinnattā acchinnā ca majjhe chinnattā dīghā ca sā dasā ca vatthakoṭi yassāti aññapadatthasamāso. Phalapupphadaseti aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā katā phalasadisā dasā “phalā”ti vuccanti, ketakādi pupphasadisāni “pupphānī”ti ca, phalā ca pupphā ca dasā yassa, phalasadise dase, pupphasadise dase cāti attho. Veṭhaneti sīsaveṭhane. Tathāti iminā sabbanīlakādīsu dukkaṭaṃ atidisati. Sabbanti kusacīrādikaṃ sakalaṃ. Acchinnaṃ cīvaraṃ yassa so labhatīti sambandho.

57. 'Mahā...pe...ratte' means dyed with mahāraṅga and mahānāmaraṅga. Here too, by carrying forward the word 'sabba' which is heard again, the meaning should be understood as 'all dyed with mahāraṅga,' and so forth. And by this, it is shown that there is no fault for one who uses a cloth that is not entirely blue, etc., dyed with a permissible dye. Therein, mahāraṅga is the color of a centipede's back. Mahānāmaraṅga is of a mixed color; it is the color of a yellow leaf, though some say it is the color of a lotus. 'Tirīṭake' refers to the bark of the tree of that name. 'Acchinnadīghadasake' is a possessive compound (aññapadatthasamāso) meaning 'that which has a long, uncut fringe,' because it is uncut as a whole, and the fringe, which is the edge of the cloth, is long because it is cut into in the middle. 'Phalapupphadase' means 'that which has fruit-like and flower-like fringes.' Fringes made by sewing them together, resembling fruits, are called 'fruits,' and those resembling flowers like the ketaka are called 'flowers.' Thus, the meaning is 'having fringes resembling fruits and fringes resembling flowers.' 'Veṭhane' refers to a head-wrap. By 'Thus,' the offense of wrong-doing is extended to all cases of blue, etc. 'All' refers to the entirety of the kusa-grass robe, etc. The connection is: 'one whose robe is uncut obtains it'.

Cīvaraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Robes is concluded.

4. Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of Dyes

58. Mūlañca [M 0.0285] khandho ca taco ca pattañca phalañca pupphañca, tesaṃ pabhedoti chaṭṭhītappuriso. Atha vā pabheda-saddassa kammasādhanatte tāniyeva pabhedoti kammadhārayo, tato. Rajanti etehīti rajanāni, mūlādīni. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cha rajanāni mūlarajana”ntiādinā (mahāva. 344) bhagavatā anuññātattā vuttaṃ “rajanā chappakārāni, anuññātāni satthunā”ti.

58. The root, the trunk, the bark, the leaf, the fruit, and the flower—'their distinctions' (tesaṃ pabhedo) is a genitive determinative compound (chaṭṭhītappuriso). Alternatively, if the word 'pabheda' is taken in an instrumental sense, then those very things are the distinctions, forming a descriptive compound (kammadhārayo). From that, 'dyes' (rajanāni) are so called because one dyes (rajanti) with them, that is, with roots and so forth. Because it was permitted by the Blessed One in the passage beginning, 'I allow, bhikkhus, six dyes: root-dye' (Mahāvagga 344), it is said: 'There are six kinds of dyes, permitted by the Teacher.'

59. Mūleti [V 0.0247] mūlarajane haliddiṃ vivajjiya sabbaṃ labbhanti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha. Mañjeṭṭhi ca tuṅgahārako cāti dvando. Alli-saddena nīli-saddena ca tesaṃ gacchajātīnaṃ pattāni gahitāni upacārena, tathā lodda-saddena kaṇḍula-saddena ca taco, kusumbha-saddena kiṃ suka-saddena ca pupphāni. Teneva ca tāni napuṃsakāni. Tuṅgahārako nāma eko kaṇṭakarukkho, tassa haritālavaṇṇaṃ khandharajanaṃ hoti. Allipattena ekavāraṃ gihiparibhuttaṃ rajituṃ vaṭṭati. Phalarajane sabbampi vaṭṭati.

59. Regarding 'root' (mūle): in the case of root-dye, the connection is that all are permissible, having excluded turmeric. Thus it is in all cases. 'Mañjeṭṭhi and tuṅgahāraka' is a dvanda compound. By the words 'alli' and 'nīli,' the leaves of those plant species are taken metaphorically; similarly, by the words 'lodda' and 'kaṇḍula,' the bark is taken; and by the words 'kusumbha' and 'kiṃsuka,' the flowers. For that reason, they are in the neuter gender. Tuṅgahāraka is the name of a certain thorny tree; its trunk-dye is the color of orpiment. With an alli leaf, it is permissible to dye once that which has been used by a householder. In the case of fruit-dye, all are permissible.

Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Dyes is concluded.

5. Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Bowl

60. Ayopatto nāma ayasā kāḷalohena nibbatto patto. Jātiyā ukkaṭṭhādīnaṃ sāmaññavasena. Pamāṇatoti paricchedato. Tayo pattāti pāṭhaseso.

60. An 'iron bowl' (ayopatto) is a bowl made from iron, that is, black metal. 'By type' refers generally to the superior kind and so forth. 'By measure' (pamāṇato) means by limitation. 'Three bowls' is the remainder of the text.

61. “Magadhesū”ti vattabbe magadheti vacanavipallāsena vā “paccāsā satī”tiādīsu viya su-saddalopena vā [M 0.0286] vuttaṃ. Nāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhitanti ettha magadhāpekkhopi nāḷi-saddo dvaya-saddena samāso hoti gammakattāti nāḷiyā dvayaṃ nāḷidvayaṃ. Tattha magadhanāḷi nāma aḍḍhaterasapalā hoti. Ettha ca aḍḍhaterasapalāni māsānanti vadanti. Nāḷidvayena pamitā taṇḍulā sukoṭṭitaparisuddhā anupahatapurāṇasālitaṇḍulā nāḷidvayataṇḍulā, tehi sādhitaṃ pacitanti attho. Odananti sammā sampāditaṃ avassāvitodanaṃ. Sūpanti odanassa catutthabhāgappamāṇaṃ nātighanaṃ nātitanukaṃ hatthahāriyaṃ sabbasambhārasaṅkhataṃ muggasupaṃ. Byañjanañca tadūpiyanti tassa odanassa upiyaṃ anurūpaṃ yāva carimālopappahonakaṃ macchamaṃsādibyañjanañca ukkaṭṭho gaṇhātīti sambandho.

61. Although 'Magadhesu' should be said, 'Magadhe' is stated either through a change of expression or through the elision of the suffix 'su,' as in 'paccāsā satī,' etc. In 'nāḷidvayataṇḍulasādhitaṃ' (cooked with two nāḷis of rice), the word 'nāḷi,' though referring to the Magadhan measure, is compounded with the word 'dvaya' because it is intelligible; thus, 'nāḷidvayaṃ' means a pair of nāḷis. Therein, a Magadhan nāḷi is thirteen and a half palas. And here, they say that thirteen and a half palas are māsas. 'Nāḷidvayataṇḍulā' are well-pounded, pure, undamaged, old sāli rice grains measured by two nāḷis; 'cooked with them' is the meaning. 'Odana' means properly prepared, undrained rice. 'Sūpa' means mung bean soup, in a quantity of one-quarter of the rice, neither too thick nor too thin, able to be taken by hand, and prepared with all ingredients. 'Byañjanañca tadūpiyaṃ' means curries of fish, meat, etc., suitable and appropriate for that rice, sufficient up to the last morsel. The connection is that the superior bowl holds this.

62. Tassāti yathāvuttaodanādino. Upaḍḍhoti upaḍḍhaṃ nāḷikodanādi assa atthīti upaḍḍho. Eva-kārena atirekaṃ nivatteti. Tatoti yathāvuttanāḷikodanādito. Ukkaṭṭhato ukkaṭṭho [V 0.0248] ca omakomako ca apattoti yojanā. Omakato omako omakomako. Iminā puna pattadvayadassanena pamāṇato tayopi pattā vibhāgato nava hontīti dīpeti. Tattha yasmiṃ magadhanāḷidvayataṇḍulodanādikaṃ sabbampi vaḍḍhanapakkhe ṭhitaṃ pakkhittaṃ sace pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, suttena vā hīrena vā chindantassa suttassa vā hīrassa vā heṭṭhimantaṃ phusati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti antogatameva, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho nāma patto. “Ekaṃ nāḷikodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ vuttanayeneva heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimo nāma patto”tiādinā majjhimamajjhimomakamajjhimukkaṭṭhā ca “yattha upaḍḍhanāḷikodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati[M 0.0287], ayaṃ omako nāma patto”tiādinā omakaomakomakaomakukkaṭṭhā ca pattā ukkaṭṭhe vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Tesu dve apattā bhājanaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbā, nādhiṭṭhānūpagā, na vikappanūpagā.

62. 'Tassa' refers to the aforementioned rice and so forth. 'Upaḍḍho' is so called because it has half a nāḷi of rice, etc. 'Tato' refers to the aforementioned nāḷi of rice and so forth. The connection is that from the superior grade, the superior-superior and the inferior-inferior are not proper bowls. From the inferior, the inferior is the inferior-inferior. By this showing of two further bowls, it is indicated that the three bowls by measure become nine by division. Therein, if all the food, beginning with rice from two Magadhan nāḷis, when placed in it while being served, stands level with the lower line of the bowl's rim, or if, when leveling it with a thread or a strip of palm-leaf, it touches the lower edge of the thread or strip, this is called the superior bowl. If it stands heaped up, having surpassed that line, this is called the superior-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line but remains inside, this is called the superior-superior bowl. By the passage beginning, 'If one nāḷi of rice and so forth, when all placed inside, stands level with the lower line in the manner described, this is called the middle bowl,' the middle-middle, middle-inferior, and middle-superior bowls should be understood. And by the passage beginning, 'Where half a nāḷi of rice and so forth, when all placed inside, stands level with the lower line, this is called the inferior bowl,' the inferior-inferior, inferior-middle, and inferior-superior bowls should be understood in the same way as explained for the superior. Among these, two are not proper bowls; they are to be used as mere vessels, and are not fit for determination or for sharing.

63. Kappo sako atirekapatto dasāhaparamaṃ dhāreyyāti yojanā. Tattha kappoti kappiyo. Sakoti attano santako. Kappiyattā pana attasantakattā ca sattannampi adhiṭṭhānavikappanūpagatā veditabbā. Tattha ayopatto pañcahi pākehi, mattikāpatto dvīhi pākehi pakko adhiṭṭhānūpago ca vikappanūpago ca, tathā ubhopi kākaṇikamattassāpi mūlassa anavasesetvā dinne, sabbaso attasantakatte viññāte ca adhiṭṭhānavikappanūpagāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atirekapattoti anadhiṭṭhitāvikappitatāya atirekapatto. Adhiṭṭhānapaccuddhārā panettha cīvare vuttāva. Vikappentena pana pattānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ, sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sammukhādibhedo panettha cīvare vakkhamānanayena veditabbo. Dasāhaparamanti dasa ahāni paramo paricchedo assāti dahāhaparamo, kālo, taṃ. Accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Dhāreyyoti paribhogavasena dhāretabbo. Tasmiṃkāle atināmite patto nissaggiyo hotīti yojanā. Atināmiteti atikkāmite nissaggiyo hoti, ekādase aruṇuggamane saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā padabhājanīye (pārā. 602) vuttanayena patto nissajjitabbo hoti, tathā sati pācittiyāpatti cassa hotīti adhippāyo.

63. The connection is: 'An allowable extra bowl of one's own may be kept for a maximum of ten days.' Herein, 'kappo' means allowable. 'Sako' means one's own possession. However, because of their allowability and being one's own possession, all seven types of bowls should be understood as subject to determination and assignment. Here, an iron bowl processed by five firings and a clay bowl processed by two firings are both subject to determination and assignment. Similarly, both should be regarded as subject to determination and assignment when given without retaining even the value of a small coin, and when fully recognized as one's own possession. 'Extra bowl' means a bowl that is extra due to not being determined or assigned. The determination and withdrawal of determination regarding robes have already been stated here. However, when assigning bowls, one should know whether the bowls are singular or plural, present or not present, and then say, 'This bowl' or 'These bowls,' or 'That bowl' or 'Those bowls,' followed by, 'I assign it to you.' The distinctions of face-to-face and so on should be understood here in the same way as will be explained for robes. 'For a maximum of ten days' means that ten days is its maximum limit, which is the time. This is the accusative case used to denote continuous duration. 'May be kept' means it should be kept for use. The connection is that if that time is exceeded, the bowl becomes subject to forfeiture. 'Exceeded' means if it is gone beyond, it becomes subject to forfeiture. At dawn on the eleventh day, the bowl must be forfeited to the Sangha, a group, or an individual, according to the method explained in the Pārājika commentary (p. 602). If that is so, one also incurs a pācittiya offense—this is the meaning.

64. “Acchedā”tiādi [M 0.0288] cīvare vuttanayattā uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – maraṇuddhaṭāti [V 0.0249] uddharaṇaṃ uddhaḷaṃ, paccuddhāro. Maraṇañca uddhaṭañca maraṇuddhaṭā, tasmā. Chiddenāti yena kaṅgusitthaṃ nikkhamati ceva pavisati ca, tena mukhavaṭṭito heṭṭhā dvaṅgulachiddena. Pattādhiṭṭhānamujjhatīti patto adhiṭṭhānaṃ ujjhati vissajjati.

64. 'By being taken away' and so on is self-evident, as it follows the method stated in the section on robes. This, however, is the specific point: 'removed by death' means removal, taking away, or withdrawal. It is 'death' and 'removal', hence 'removed by death'. 'By a hole' means by a two-finger-wide hole below the rim, through which a millet grain can exit and enter. 'The determination of the bowl is abandoned' means the bowl gives up, it relinquishes its determination.

65. Idāni “patta”ntiādinā aññathā pariharaṇe dukkaṭaṃ dasseti. Tattha sodakaṃ pattaṃ na paṭisāmeyyāti yojanā. Na paṭisāmeyyāti guttaṭṭhāne na nikkhipeyya, “sodakaṃ pattaṃ uṇhe na ca otape”tiādinā ca yojanīyaṃ. Na ca otapeti neva īsakaṃ tāpeyya. Na nidaheti nirudakaṃ katvāpi bhusaṃ na nidaheyya, vodakaṃ katvā īsakaṃ tāpeyyātipi byatirekattho. Bhūmyā na ṭhapeti kharāya bhūmiyā na ṭhapeyya. Yattha pana vaṇṇo na dussati, evarūpāya mattikāya paribhaṇḍakatāya bhūmiyā vā tathārūpāya eva vālikāya vā nikkujjitvā ukkujjitvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. No ca laggayeti bhittikhilādīsu na olambeyya.

65. Now, with the phrase 'a bowl,' and so on, it shows that there is an offense of wrong-doing in handling it improperly. Here, the connection is: 'One should not put away a bowl with water.' 'Should not put away' means one should not place it in a safe place. And it should be construed with the phrase, 'a bowl with water should not be placed in the heat or exposed to the sun,' and so on. 'Nor expose to the sun' means one should not heat it even slightly. 'Should not place down' means that even after making it waterless, one should not heat it intensely; the contrary meaning is that after making it wet, one may heat it slightly. 'Should not be placed on the ground' means one should not place it on rough ground. However, where the color is not damaged, it is permissible to place it upside down or right-side up on such earthen ground prepared as a stand, or on similar sandy ground. 'And should not be hung' means one should not suspend it on wall-pegs and so on.

66. “Miḍḍhante vā”tiādinā vatvā pattaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na ca kappatīti yojetabbaṃ. Miḍḍhanteti āḷindakamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ miḍḍhīnaṃ ante. Sace pana parivattetvā tattheva patiṭṭhāti, evarūpāya vitthiṇṇāya miḍḍhiyā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Paribhaṇḍante vāti bāhirapasse katāya tanukāya miḍḍhikāya ante vā. Ettha vā-saddo samuccaye, so ca paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Aṅke pana aṃsabaddhakena aṃsakūṭe laggetvā ṭhapetuñca vaṭṭati. Chattepi bhaṇḍakena saddhiṃ bandhitvā vā aṭṭaṃ katvā vā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mañcepi aññena saddhiṃ bandhitvā ṭhapetuṃ, aṭaniyaṃ bandhitvā olambetuṃ vaṭṭati.

66. Having stated 'Or at the edge of a ledge,' and so on, it should be construed that it is not permissible to place a bowl. 'At the edge of a ledge' means at the edge of ledges such as those on a veranda. But if, upon rolling over, it remains there, it is permissible to place it on such a wide ledge. 'Or at the edge of a utensil-rack' means at the edge of a narrow ledge made on the outer side. Here, the word 'or' has the sense of a conjunction, and it should be applied to each case. On the lap, however, it is permissible to place it, and also to attach it to the point of the shoulder with a shoulder strap. On an umbrella, too, it is permissible to place it by tying it with a carrying-strap or by making a support for it. On a bed, too, it is permissible to place it by tying it together with something else, or to hang it by tying it to a bed-post.

67. Pattena ucchiṭṭhodakañca calakaṭṭhikañca na nīhareyyāti sambandho. Ucchiṭṭhodakanti mukhavikkhālanodakaṃ. Calakāni ca [M 0.0289] cabbetvā apaviddhāmisāni aṭṭhikāni macchamaṃsaaṭṭhikāni ca calakaṭṭhikaṃ. Pattaṃ paṭiggahaṃ katvā hatthaṃ dhovitumpi hatthadhotādi udakampi patte ākiritvā nīharitumpi anucchiṭṭhaṃ suddhapattaṃ ucchiṭṭhahatthena gaṇhitumpi na vaṭṭati. Macchamaṃsaphalāphalādīni khādanto yaṃ tattha aṭṭhiṃ vā calakaṃ vā chaḍḍetukāmo hoti, taṃ patte ṭhapetuṃ na labhati. Mukhato nīhaṭaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci puna akhāditukāmo patte ṭhapetuṃ na labhati. Siṅgiverādīni ḍaṃsitvā puna ṭhapetuṃ labhati. Pattahatthoti patto hatthe yassāti viggaho. “Pattahattho, kavāṭa”nti ca upalakkhaṇametaṃ. Yattha katthaci sarīrāvayave pana pattasmiṃ [V 0.0250] sati yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetuṃ, ghaṭikaṃ vā ukkhipituṃ, sūciṃ vā kuñcikāya avāpurituṃ na labhati. Aṃsakūṭe pana pattaṃ laggetvā yathāsukhaṃ avāpurituṃ labhati.

67. The connection is that one should not remove leftover water, scraps, and bones with the bowl. 'Leftover water' means water for rinsing the mouth. 'Scraps and bones' means scraps, bones from which the flesh has been chewed and discarded, and fish and meat bones. It is not permissible to wash one's hands using the bowl as a receptacle, to pour water from washing hands and so on into the bowl to carry it away, or to take an unused, clean bowl with a hand that has touched leftovers. While eating fish, meat, fruits, and non-fruits, if one wishes to discard a bone or a scrap, one is not allowed to place it in the bowl. Furthermore, one is not allowed to place in the bowl anything taken from the mouth that one does not intend to eat again. One is allowed to bite ginger and similar things and place them back. 'Bowl-in-hand' is analyzed as 'one who has a bowl in their hand.' 'Bowl-in-hand, door-panel' is an illustrative example. When one has a bowl on any part of the body, one is not allowed to use any part of the body to open a door-panel, lift a latch, or open a bolt with a key. However, having attached the bowl to the point of the shoulder, one is allowed to open them as one wishes.

68. Bhūmiyā bhūmisambandhī ādhārako, tasmiṃ dantavallivettādīhi kate valayādhārake ca ekadārunā kate dāruādhārake ca bahūhi daṇḍehi kate daṇḍādhārake ca yattha ṭhapito patto yathā parivattitvā na paripatati, tathā suṭṭhu sajjite tasmiṃ pattassupari pattoti evarūpe duve patte ṭhapeyyāti padatthayojanā. Bhamakoṭisadiso pana dāruādhārako tīhi daṇḍakehi baddho daṇḍādhārako ca ekassapi pattassa anokāso, tattha ṭhapetvāpi hatthena gahetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Bhūmiyanti kaṭasārakādinā atthatāya bhūmiyā pana nikkujjitvā vā paṭikujjitvā vā ekaṃ pattaṃ ṭhapeyyāti yojanā.

68. On the ground means on a stand connected to the ground. On such a stand—be it a ring-stand made of ivory, creepers, rattan, or the like; a wooden stand made from a single piece of wood; or a stand made from many sticks—that is so well-prepared that a bowl placed on it will not fall over when it rolls, one may place two bowls, one on top of the other. This is the connection of the meaning of the words. However, a wooden stand resembling the point of a spinning top, or a stand made of three sticks bound together, is not a suitable place for even one bowl; even if placed there, one must sit holding it by hand. 'On the ground' means on ground that is spread with a mat of rushes or the like; the connection is that one may place a single bowl on it, either upside down or right side up.

69. Idāni akappiyapatte dasseti “dārū”tiādinā. Tattha suvaṇṇameva sovaṇṇaṃ. Dāru ca rūpiyañca sovaṇṇañca maṇi ca veḷuriyañca dāru…pe… veḷuriyāni, tehi nibbattā dāru…pe… mayā[M 0.0290]. Dīgho pana “veḷuriyāmayā”ti gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ kato. Evamuparipi tādisaṃ viññeyyaṃ. Tattha indanīlādi maṇi nāma. Kaṃso ca kāco ca tipu ca sīsañca phalikā ca tambaloho cāti dvando, tehi jātā kaṃsa…pe… jā. Tattha kaṃsa-saddena vaṭṭalohopi saṅgahito. Setaṃ tipu, kaṇhaṃ sīsaṃ.

69. Now, with 'wooden,' and so on, it shows the unallowable bowls. Here, 'golden' means made of gold. Wood, silver, gold, gems, and beryl are listed as 'wood... beryl'; bowls made from them are 'wooden... made of beryl'. The long vowel in 'made of beryl' is for the sake of metrical ease. This should be understood in the following cases as well. Here, 'gem' means sapphire and so on. 'Bronze, glass, tin, lead, crystal, and copper' is a coordinative compound; 'bronze-born... born' are those produced from them. Here, the word 'bronze' also includes bell-metal. Tin is white, lead is black.

70. Chavasīsamayoti chavassa matamanussassa sīsaṃ sīsakapālaṃ, tena nibbatto chavasīsamayo. Ghaṭi ca tumbañca, tesaṃ kaṭāho, tehi jātāti ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā. Tattha ghaṭīti ghaṭoyeva. Tumbaṃ alābu. Iti ime sabbe pattā akappiyā vuttā, dukkaṭavatthukā ca vuttāti yojanā. Tattha rūpiyādīsu catūsu sace gihī bhattaggesu suvaṇṇataṭṭakādīsu byañjanaṃ katvā upanāmenti, āmasituṃ na vaṭṭati. Kaṃsakācaphalikajāni pana taṭṭakādīni bhājanāni puggalikaparibhogeneva na vaṭṭanti, saṅghikaparibhogena vā gihivikaṭāni vā vaṭṭanti. Ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā pana labhitvā pariharituṃ na vaṭṭanti, tāvakālikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭanti.

70. 'Made of a skull' (chavasīsamayo) means the head of a dead human being, the cranium; that which is made from it is chavasīsamayo. A pot (ghaṭi), a gourd (tumba), and a potsherd (kaṭāha) from them; those born from these are called ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā. Herein, ghaṭī means simply a pot, and tumba means a gourd. Thus, all these bowls are declared unsuitable and are the basis for a dukkaṭa offense; this is the connection. Among the four types—silver, etc.—if householders prepare curry in golden or silver saucers and the like in dining halls and offer it, it is not permissible to touch it. However, vessels such as saucers made of bronze, glass, or crystal are not permissible for personal use, but are permissible for the Sangha's use or if altered by householders. As for those born from a pot, gourd, or potsherd, it is not permissible to obtain and keep them, but it is permissible to use them for the time being.

Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Bowl is concluded.

6. Thālakaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dish

71-2. Dāru [V 0.0251] …pe… veḷuriyāmayā akappiyā, phalikākācakaṃsajā thālakā gihisantakā saṅghikā ca kappiyā, tumbaghaṭijā tāvakālikā kappiyāti sambandho. Kappanti parikappanti avirodhibhāvenevāti kappā, tathā kappiyā. Na kappā akappā. Saṅghassa ime saṅghikā. Tāva-saddo avadhimhi. Tāva bhojanāvadhibhūto kālo etāsanti tāvakālikā[M 0.0291], bhuñjitvā chaḍḍetabbā, na pariharitabbāti adhippāyo.

71-2. Wooden …pe… those made of beryl are unallowable. Dishes made of crystal, glass, or bronze—whether belonging to householders or the Sangha—are allowable. Those made of gourds or pots are allowable for temporary use; this is the connection. They are suitable (kappanti), they are considered (parikappanti) as being unopposed, thus they are suitable (kappā), and likewise allowable (kappiyā). What is not suitable is unallowable. These belonging to the Sangha are saṅghika. The word tāva is in the sense of a limit. 'For temporary use' (tāvakālikā) means the time is limited to the meal; after eating, they should be discarded and not kept—this is the intention.

Thālakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Dish is concluded.

7. Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of Refusal

73. Yena iriyāpathena upalakkhito pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ yaṃ kiñci bhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno ayaṃ bhikkhu kappiyānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ hatthapāsopanītānaṃ pavārito, tato iriyāpathato aññena iriyāpathena anatirittakaṃ yāvakālikaṃ bhuñjeyya ce, imassa pācitti hotīti padatthayojanā. Bhuñjanatthāya paṭiggahaṇe pana dukkaṭaṃ. Tattha iriyāya kāyikakiriyāya patho pavattanūpāyo iriyāpatho, ṭhānagamananisajjanasayanāni. Pavāreti paṭikkhipatīti pavārito, atha vā pavāraṇaṃ paṭikkhipanaṃ pavāritaṃ, tamassa atthīti pavārito, katappavāraṇo katappaṭikkhepoti attho, atha vā parivesakena vārīyatīti pavārito paṭikkhepito. Anatirittakanti yaṃ pavāretvā āsanā vuṭṭhahantassa “alametaṃ sabba”nti evaṃ atirittakaraṇādīhi sattahi vinayakammākārehi kappiyaṃ kataṃ, tañca “ajja vā yadā vā icchati, tadā khādissatī”ti āhaṭaṃ, gilānātirittañca atirittaṃ adhikanti vuccati, tato aññaṃ anatirittakaṃ anadhikanti attho. Kusalaṃ cittaṃ pātetīti pācitti, tasmā itthiyaṃ timhi ta-kārassa ca-kāre, dvitte ca pācitti. Yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhato āpatti dukkaṭassa, ajjhohāre ajjhohāre āpatti dukkaṭassa.

73. This is the explanation of the meaning of the words: If this bhikkhu, while eating any of the five kinds of food, is characterized by a certain posture and has refused the five kinds of allowable food brought within arm’s reach, and then eats non-leftover yāvakālika food in a different posture from that, a pācittiya offense occurs for him. However, for receiving it for the purpose of eating, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Herein, 'posture' (iriyāpatho) is the path, the means of proceeding, for a bodily action: standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. 'Refused' (pavārito) means one who rejects. Or, refusal (pavāraṇaṃ) is rejection; he who has this is 'one who has refused' (pavārito), meaning one who has made a refusal, one who has made a rejection. Or, he is refused by the server, thus he is 'refused' (pavārito), rejected. The following is called 'leftover' (atiritta), meaning 'extra' (adhika): that which, for one who has refused and is rising from his seat, has been made allowable by the seven Vinaya procedures for making something leftover, such as saying, 'This is enough for all'; and that which has been brought with the thought, 'He may eat it today or whenever he wishes'; and what is leftover for the sick. What is other than that is 'non-leftover' (anatirittakaṃ), meaning 'not extra'. 'Pācitti' is so called because it causes a wholesome mind to fall. Therefore, in the feminine, with the suffix -ti, the letter 't' becomes 'c', and with doubling, it becomes pācitti. For receiving yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika items for the purpose of eating, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for each act of swallowing, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

74. Idāni [M 0.0292][V 0.0252] yāya pavāritā, sā pañcaṅgasampannāyeva pavāraṇā nāma hotīti dassetuṃ “asana”ntiādimāha. Tattha asananti bhuñjamānassa bhuñjanaṃ. Iminā yaṃ vippakataṃ bhojanaṃ, taṃ dasseti. Bhojanañcevāti pavāraṇappahonakaṃ bhojanañceva hotīti. Abhihāroti dāyakassa kāyena pavāraṇappahonakassa abhiharaṇaṃ, na vācāya. Samīpatāti aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇasaṅkhātā samīpatā ca. Ettha pana sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, āsanassa pacchimantato paṭṭhāya, sace ṭhito, paṇhiantato paṭṭhāya, sace nipanno, yena passena nipanno, tassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya dāyakassa ṭhitassa vā nisinnassa vā nipannassa vā ṭhapetvā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa orimantena paricchinditvā aḍḍhateyyahatthapāso veditabbo. Kāyavācāpaṭikkhepoti tassa abhihaṭabhojanassa aṅgulicalanādikāyavikārena vā “ala”ntiādinā vacīvikārena vā paṭikkhipanaṃ. Iti imehi pañcahaṅgehi pavāraṇā pakārayuttavāraṇā pañcaaṅgāti sambandho. Pañca aṅgāni yassā sā pañcaaṅgā.

74. Now, to show that the refusal (pavāraṇā) is called a proper refusal only when endowed with five factors, the text begins with 'asana,' etc. Herein, 'asana' means the act of eating while one is eating. This indicates the food that has been started. 'Bhojanañceva' means that the food is specifically sufficient for the refusal. 'Abhihāro' refers to the donor physically bringing the food sufficient for the refusal, not verbally. 'Samīpatā' means proximity, defined as being within a distance of two and a half cubits. Here, if a monk is sitting, the measurement starts from the back edge of the seat; if standing, from the heels; if lying down, from the edge of the side on which he is lying. From the donor’s position—whether standing, sitting, or lying down—after setting aside an outstretched hand, the nearest part is measured, and the distance should be understood as two and a half cubits. 'Kāyavācāpaṭikkhepo' refers to rejecting the offered food either by a bodily gesture like moving a finger or by a verbal expression like saying 'enough.' Thus, by these five factors, the refusal (pavāraṇā), a prevention endowed with qualities, has five factors; this is the connection. That which has five factors is called 'pañcaṅgā' (five-factored).

75. Idāni etesu odanādipañcavidhaṃ bhojanaṃ dassetvā tāni ca puna vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “odano”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sālīti rattasāliādikā sabbāpi sālijāti. Vīhīti sabbāpi vīhināmikā vīhijāti. Kaṅgūti setarattakāḷabhedā sabbāpi kaṅgujāti. Kudrūso nāma kāḷakodravo. Varako nāma setavaṇṇo kodravo. Yavagodhumesu pana bhedo natthi. Evaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ sānulomānaṃ sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ bhojjayāgu cāti sambandho. Bhojjayāgu cāti uṇhaṃ vā sītalaṃ vā bhuñjantānaṃ bhojanakāle gahitaṭṭhāne odhi paññāyati, sā bhojjayāgu. Ca-saddena odano cāti sambandho[M 0.0293], odano nāmāti attho. Sace pana bhatte udakakañjikakhīrādīni ākiritvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti denti, kiñcāpi tanukā hoti, pavāraṇaṃ janeti. Sace pana udakādīsu pakkhipitvā pacitvā denti, yāgusaṅgahameva gacchati. Sace pana tanukāyapi yāguyā sāsapamattampi macchamaṃsakhaṇḍaṃ vā nhāru vā pakkhittaṃ hoti, pavāraṇaṃ janeti.

75. Now, having shown the five kinds of food such as cooked rice, the text begins with 'odano' (cooked rice) to further elaborate by classifying them. Herein, 'sālī' refers to all varieties of rice, including red rice. 'Vīhī' refers to all types of rice called vīhi. 'Kaṅgū' includes all varieties of foxtail millet, whether white, red, or black. 'Kudrūso' is black kodrava. 'Varako' is white kodrava. As for barley and wheat, there are no further subdivisions. Thus, the seven kinds of grains mentioned above, along with their varieties, and edible gruel, are related. 'Bhojjayāgu' refers to gruel, whether hot or cold, which is taken at mealtime, where a boundary is discerned at the place it is taken; this is edible gruel. The particle 'ca' connects it to 'odano', meaning it is also considered a staple food. However, if water, rice-water, milk, etc., are poured over cooked rice and one is told, 'Take the gruel,' even if it is thin, it constitutes a refusal. But if they are mixed in with water, etc., and cooked before being given, it is included simply as gruel. Even if a tiny amount—like a mustard seed—of fish, meat, or tendon is added to thin gruel, it constitutes a refusal.

76. Sāmākāditiṇaṃ kudrūsake saṅgahaṃ gataṃ, varakacorako varake saṅgahaṃ gato, nīvāro ceva sāliyaṃ saṅgahaṃ gatoti yojanā. Sāmākāditiṇanti sāmāko ādi yassa, tameva tiṇaṃ tiṇadhaññanti samāso.

76. Grasses such as sāmāka are included under kudrūsaka. Varakacoraka is included under varaka. Nīvāra is included under sāli (rice). This is the connection. The compound 'sāmākāditiṇa' means 'grasses of which sāmāka is the first,' and that very grass is a 'grass-grain' (tiṇadhañña).

77. Bhaṭṭhadhaññamayoti [V 0.0253] kharapākabhajjitehi sattavidhehi dhaññehi koṭṭetvā kato, antamaso cuṇṇampi kuṇḍakampi sattu nāmāti attho. Samapākabhajjitānaṃ pana ātapasukkhānaṃ vā taṇḍulānaṃ sattu vā kuṇḍakāni eva vā na pavārenti. Yavena sambhavo uppatti assāti yavasambhavo, kummāso kummāso nāma. Muggādīhi kato pana pavāraṇaṃ na janeti. Kappiyo cāti kappiyoyeva maṃso “maṃso”ti vuttoti yojanā. Cāti avadhāraṇe. Akappiyo pana paṭikkhipitabbova. Paṭikkhittopi na pavāreti. Udake sambhavo yassa so maccho nāma. Dvīsu panetesu sace yāguṃ pivantassa yāgusitthamattesupi macchakhaṇḍesu vā maṃsakhaṇḍesu vā ekaṃ khāditaṃ ekaṃ hatthe vā patte vā hoti, so ce aññaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Dvepi khāditāni honti, mukhe sāsapamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ natthi, sacepi aññaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti.

77. 'Made of roasted grain' (Bhaṭṭhadhaññamaya) refers to what is made by pounding the seven kinds of grains that are roasted hard. Even flour or bran is called 'sattu.' However, sattu or bran made from rice grains that are roasted soft or are sun-dried do not generate a refusal. Yavasambhava means 'that which has barley as its origin or source,' and this is called 'kummāsa.' However, what is made from mung beans and the like does not generate a refusal. 'Kappiyo ca' means 'only permissible meat is called meat'—this is the connection. The word 'ca' is for emphasis. However, impermissible meat must be rejected. Even if rejected, it does not generate a refusal. 'Maccha' means 'that which arises in water.' Regarding these two, if someone drinking gruel has eaten one piece of fish or meat, even if only the size of a grain of gruel, and another piece remains in his hand or bowl, and he rejects another, he generates a refusal. But if both pieces have been eaten, and not even a mustard-seed-sized remnant remains in the mouth, even if he rejects another, he does not generate a refusal.

78. Idāni “kīdisaṃ bhuñjanto kinti vatvā upanītaṃ kiṃ nāma nisedhento pavāreti nāmā”ti codanaṃ manasi nidhāyāha “bhuñjanto”tiādi[M 0.0294]. Tattha kappaṃ vā akappaṃ vā pañcasu bhojanesu yaṃ kiñci bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto bhikkhu tannāmena tesaṃ pavāraṇājanakabhojanānaṃ nāmena vā “ima”nti sāmaññena vā vatvā abhihaṭaṃ hatthapāsopanītaṃ kappaṃ kappiyaṃ yathāvuttabhojanaṃ nisedhayaṃ nisedhayanto pavāreyyāti padatthasambandho. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yena ce akappiyamaṃsañca kuladūsanavejjakammauttarimanussadhammārocanasāditarūpiyādīhi nibbattaṃ akappiyabhojanañca tathā aññañca kappiyaṃ vā akappiyaṃ vā ekasitthamattampi ajjhohaṭaṃ hoti, so sace pattamukhahatthesu yattha katthaci bhojane sati sāpekkhova aññaṃ hatthapāse ṭhitena “odanaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādinā pavāraṇappahonakasseva nāmena vā “ima”nti sāmaññavaseneva vā kāyeneva abhihaṭaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ kappiyameva bhojanaṃ kevalaṃ vā missaṃ vā kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhipati pavāretīti. “Ākira ākira, koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā pūrehī”ti pana vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

78. Now, bearing in mind the question, 'While eating what kind of food, and what having been presented with what words, and rejecting what, is it called performing pavāraṇā?' he says, 'while eating,' and so on. Here, a monk eating any of the five kinds of food, whether permissible or impermissible, rejects a permissible food, as described, that has been brought within arm's reach, offered by its name, or the name of those foods that occasion a pavāraṇā, or generally as 'this'—by rejecting it, he performs pavāraṇā. This is the connection of the terms. The meaning here is this: If a monk has consumed even a single morsel of impermissible meat, or impermissible food obtained through corrupting families, medical practice, proclaiming superior human states, accepted silver, etc., or any other permissible or impermissible food, and if, while food remains anywhere in his bowl, mouth, or hand, and with expectation, he rejects another item that is within arm's reach—which has the characteristics mentioned and is sufficient for a pavāraṇā, and whether it is purely permissible or mixed—then by rejecting it with gesture or speech, he performs pavāraṇā. However, it is permissible to say, 'Heap it on, heap it on! Pound it down and fill it up!'

79-80. Idāni ye pavāraṇaṃ na janenti, te dassetuṃ “lājā”tiādimāha. Tattha lājā…pe… phalādīni pavāraṇaṃ na janentīti sambandho. Lājāti sāliādīhi katā lājā. Taṃsattubhattānīti tehi lājehi katā sattu ceva bhattāni ca. Gorasoti gunnaṃ raso khīrādi. Suddhakhajjakoti macchamaṃsehi asammissatāya suddhakhajjako. Sattuyo piṇḍetvā kato apakko sattuguḷo pana sattumodakasaṅkhāto pavāreti. Taṇḍulāti samapākabhajjitānaṃ sāliādīnaṃ [V 0.0254] taṇḍulā, bhajjitataṇḍulā eva vā. Bhaṭṭhapiṭṭhanti suddhaṃ yaṃ kiñci bhajjitaṃ piṭṭhaṃ. Puthukāti sāliādīnaṃ puthukā. Puthukā hi tantiāgamayuttiyā visumpi gayhati, ekatopi, tasmā vuttāvasesānaṃ puthukāveḷuādīnaṃ bhattanti ca sambandho. Veḷūti tesaṃ [M 0.0295] taṇḍulā vuccanti. Puthukā ca veḷu ca, te ādayo yesanti samāso. Ca-saddo panettha sabbatthāpi yojetabbo. Ādi-saddena kandamūlaphalānipi gayhanti. Vuttāvasesānanti vuttehi sattavidhehi dhaññehi avasesānaṃ. Rasayāgūti rasehi pakkamaṃsādīhi sammissā yāgu. Rasopi tādisova. Suddhayāgūti maṃsādīhi amissā suddhayāgu. Phalādīnīti ādi-saddena kandādīnampi gahaṇaṃ. Api cāti nipāto, nipātasamudāyo vā samuccaye, so paccekaṃ yojetabbo.

Now, to show those things which do not occasion a pavāraṇā, he says 'lājā,' etc. Here, lājā... etc., and fruits, etc., do not occasion a pavāraṇā—this is the connection. 'Lājā' is puffed rice made from sāli rice and the like. 'Taṃsattubhattāni' means sattu and meals made from those puffed grains. 'Gorasa' is the product of cattle, such as milk and so on. 'Suddhakhajjaka' is pure snack food, unmixed with fish or meat. However, an uncooked ball of sattu, made by kneading sattu, which is called a sattumodaka, does occasion a pavāraṇā. 'Taṇḍulā' means grains of sāli rice and the like that are roasted until evenly cooked, or simply roasted grains. 'Bhaṭṭhapiṭṭha' is any pure roasted flour. 'Puthukā' are flattened grains of sāli rice and the like. Indeed, puthukā are taken both separately and together according to the reasoning of the textual tradition; therefore, there is also a connection with 'meals' for the remaining mentioned items, puthukā, veḷu, etc. 'Veḷu' refers to their grains. The compound means 'those of which puthukā and veḷu are the beginning.' The word 'ca' should be applied everywhere here. The word 'ādi' also includes roots and tubers. 'Vuttāvasesānaṃ' refers to the remaining items beyond the seven kinds of grain mentioned. 'Rasayāgu' is gruel mixed with savory juices like cooked meat and so on. 'Rasa' also refers to such things. 'Suddhayāgu' is pure gruel, unmixed with meat and so on. 'Phalādīni' includes roots and so on with the word 'ādi.' 'Api ca' is a particle, or a collection of particles, for inclusion; it should be applied to each item.

81. Idāni yasmā sattahi vinayakammākārehi yaṃ atirittaṃ akataṃ, tattha pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ, byatirekato atirittakate natthi, tasmā atirittaṃ karontena evaṃ kātabbanti dassento “pavāritenā”tiādimāha. Tattha pavāritena vuṭṭhāya atirittaṃ na kātabbaṃ, bhojanaṃ abhuttena ca atirittaṃ na kātabbanti sambandho. Bhojananti pavāraṇappahonakabhojanaṃ. Abhuttenāti ekasitthamattampi abhuttāvinā. Yena yaṃvā pure katanti ettha ca eva-saddo dīghaṃ katvā niddiṭṭho, so ca ajjhāhaṭena taṃ-saddena sambandhīyati, tasmā yena bhikkhunā yaṃ bhojanaṃ pure pubbe atirittaṃ kataṃ, teneva tameva atirittaṃ na kātabbanti yojetvā attho veditabbo. Tasmā kappiyaṃ kāretvā bhuñjantassa aññaṃ āmisaṃ ākiranti, taṃ so puna kātuṃ na labhati, tasmiṃ bhojane kariyamāne paṭhamakatena saddhiṃ kataṃ hotīti. Aññasmiṃ pana tena vā aññena vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

81. Now, since a pācittiya offense is stated for when the 'excessive' act is not performed according to the seven modes of a disciplinary act, and conversely, there is no offense when it is performed, therefore, showing how one who makes it excessive should act, he says 'pavāritena,' etc. Here, the connection is that one who has performed pavāraṇā should not make food excessive after rising, and one who has not eaten should not make the food excessive. 'Bhojana' means food sufficient to occasion a pavāraṇā. 'Abhuttena' means without having eaten even a single morsel. In 'yena yaṃvā pure kataṃ,' the word 'eva' is indicated with a long vowel, and it is connected with the supplied word 'taṃ'; therefore, the meaning should be understood by connecting it thus: 'the monk who previously made a particular food excessive should not make that same food excessive again.' Therefore, if one has had food made permissible and is eating, and others offer additional savory food, he is not able to make that excessive again, because if that food were to be made excessive, it would be considered as done together with what was first made excessive. However, it is permissible for him or another to do so for a different meal.

82. “Kappiya”ntiādīni “karonto”ti etassa kammapadāni. Kappiyañceva gahitañceva uccāritañceva hatthapāsagañceva yāvakālikaṃ atirittaṃ karonto “alametaṃ sabba”nti evaṃ bhāsatūti [M 0.0296] yojanā.
