Tatthayaṃ phalaṃ vā kandamūlādi vā pañcahi samaṇakappehi kappiyaṃ kataṃ, yañca kappiyamaṃsaṃ vā kappiyabhojanaṃ vā, etaṃ kappiyaṃ nāma. Gahitanti bhikkhunā paṭiggahitaṃ. Uccāritanti kappiyaṃ kāretuṃ āgatena bhikkhunā īsakampi ukkhittaṃ vā apanāmitaṃ vā, taṃ pana atirittakārakena “alametaṃ sabba”nti vuttena kātabbaṃ. Hatthapāsaganti kappiyaṃ kāretuṃ āgatena hatthapāsaṃ gataṃ. Atirittaṃ karontoti īdisaṃ catubbidhākārasampannaṃ bhojanaṃ atirittaṃ karonto pavāretvā āsanā avuṭṭhito vā appavāretvāpi [V 0.0255] sabbathā bhutto vāti evaṃ duvidhavinayakammākārasampanno bhikkhu. Alametaṃ sabbanti evaṃ bhāsatūti alametaṃ sabbaṃ iti evaṃ bhāsatu. Evaṃ sattavidhaṃ vinayakammākāraṃ sampādento vacībhedaṃ katvā sakimpi evaṃ vadeyyāti attho.

82. 'Kappiya,' etc., are the objects of 'making.' The explanation is that one who makes excessive what is permissible, what has been received, what has been handled, what is within arm's reach, and what is for a limited time, should say, 'This is enough, all of this!' Here, fruit or root vegetables, etc., made permissible by the five means suitable for recluses, or permissible meat or permissible food—this is called 'permissible.' 'What has been received' means what has been accepted by a monk. 'What has been handled' means what has been slightly lifted up or moved away by a monk who has come to have it made permissible; this, however, is to be done by the one making it excessive after he has said, 'This is enough, all of this!' 'What is within arm's reach' means what has come within arm's reach of one who has come to have it made permissible. 'One who makes excessive' refers to a monk endowed with two kinds of disciplinary acts: one who, making excessive such a food endowed with four characteristics, has either performed pavāraṇā and has not risen from his seat, or, without having performed pavāraṇā, has eaten in every way. 'Should say, "This is enough, all of this!"' means he should speak thus: 'This is enough, all of this!' The meaning is that one accomplishing the sevenfold manner of a disciplinary act, having made a verbal declaration, should say it even just once.

83. Kappiyaṃ karontena pana anupasampannassa hatthe ṭhitaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Tenāha “na kare…pe… hatthaga”nti. Upasampannato añño anupasampanno, tassa hatthe gataṃ anupasampannahatthagaṃ. Pesayitvāpīti sace tattha añño byatto bhikkhu natthi, yattha atthi, tattha pesayitvāpi. Taṃ atirittakataṃ akārako atirittakārakato añño sabbo pavāritopi appavāritopi bhuñjituṃ labbhateti sambandhanīyaṃ. Pavāritena pana mukhañca hatthañca sodhetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ.

83. However, one making something permissible should not do so for an item that is in the hand of an unordained person. Therefore, it is said: 'One should not do... up to... hand-held.' An unordained person is other than an ordained one; that which has gone into his hand is called 'hand-held by an unordained person.' 'Even by sending' means: if there is no competent monk there, one may do so by sending it to where there is one. That which has been made excessive—anyone other than the one who made it excessive, whether he has performed pavāraṇā or not, may eat it. This is how it should be connected. However, one who has performed pavāraṇā should clean his mouth and hands before eating.

Pavāraṇāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of pavāraṇā is finished.

8. Kālikaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Exposition of Time-Periods

84. Kālikāti majjhanhikapacchimayāmasattāhayāvajīvappavattisaṅkhāto kālo etesamatthīti kālikā, sabbepi [M 0.0297] khajjabhojjaleyyapeyyasaṅkhātā atthā. Te pana gaṇanaparicchedato cattāro honti. Kiṃ te appaṭiggahitāpi sabhāveneva kālikavohāraṃ labhanti, udāhu aññathāpīti āha “paṭiggahitā”ti, paṭiggahitāyeva te yāvakālikādi kālikavohāralābhino, no aññathāti adhippāyo. Idāni te dasseti “yāvakālika”ntiādinā. Tattha aruṇuggamanato yāva ṭhitamajjhanhiko, tāva paribhuñjitabbattā yāva majjhanhikasaṅkhāto kālo assāti yāvakālikaṃ, piṭṭhakhādanīyādikaṃ vatthu, ṭhitamajjhanhikato paṭṭhāya taṃ paribhuñjituṃ na sakkā, kālaparicchedajānanatthaṃ kālatthambho vā yojetabbo, kālantare vā bhattakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yāva rattiyā pacchimasaṅkhāto yāmo, tāva paribhuñjitabbato yāmo kālo assāti yāmakālikaṃ. Paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ nidhetabbato sattāho kālo assāti sattāhakālikaṃ. Ṭhapetvā udakaṃ avasesaṃ sabbampi paṭiggahitaṃ yāvajīvaṃ [V 0.0256] pariharitvā sati paccaye paribhuñjitabbato jīvassa yattako paricchedo yāvajīvaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti yāvajīvikaṃ.

84. Things are called `kālika` because they have a time reckoned as up to midday, up to the last watch of the night, for seven days, or for life. All these are substances reckoned as chewable food, edible food, lickable food, and drinkable liquids. These are four in terms of their reckoning and limits. Do these, even if not accepted, naturally acquire the designation of `kālika`, or is it otherwise? It is said, 'accepted'—the meaning is that only when accepted do they acquire the designation of `kālika`, such as `yāvakālika` and so on, not otherwise. Now, these are shown by the terms 'yāvakālika' and so on. Here, that which is to be consumed from sunrise until standing midday is `yāvakālika`, because it has a time reckoned as up to midday; this refers to substances like flour-based food. After standing midday, it is not possible to consume it. To know the time limit, either a time marker should be set or the meal should be completed within the designated time. That which is to be consumed up to the last watch of the night is `yāmakālika`, because it has a time reckoned as a watch. That which is to be accepted and stored for seven days is `sattāhakālika`, because it has a time reckoned as seven days. Except for water, all other accepted items that are kept for life and consumed when the occasion arises are `yāvajīvika`, because it has a limit as long as life, which is for life.

Nanu ca aññattha viya “yāvajīvika”nti ettha kālasutiyā abhāve kathaṃ “cattāro kālikā”ti yujjatīti? Yujjati, sogatānaṃ khandhavinimuttasseva kālassābhāvato jīvasaṅkhātassa jīvitindriyassa khandhasaṅgahitattā sopi kāloyevāti. Nanu cettha “yāvakālika”ntiādinā niddiṭṭhāneva “kālikā”ti vuttāni, “kālikānī”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti? Nedamevaṃ viññeyyaṃ, “kālika”ntiādīni vatthusambandhena vuttāni, “kālikā”ti pana sāmaññantaravasena atthasaddasambandhena vuttanti natthi virodhoti.

But indeed, how can 'four `kālika`s' be justified here, as in the case of 'yāvajīvika', when there is no mention of the word 'time'? It is justified, because for Buddhists, since there is no time apart from the aggregates, and because the life faculty, which is reckoned as life, is included within the aggregates, even that is time. But here, when `yāvakālika` and so on are specified, shouldn't `kālikāni` (neuter plural) be said instead of `kālikā` (masculine plural)? This should not be understood thus. `Kālika` and so on are stated in relation to the substance, whereas `kālikā` is stated in a general sense, in connection with the word 'attha' (thing/substance). Therefore, there is no contradiction.

85. Idāni tesu “piṭṭha”ntiādinā yāvakālikaṃ dasseti. Tattha piṭṭhaṃ mūlaṃ phalanti piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ mūlakhādanīyaṃ phalakhādanīyañca[M 0.0298]. Tattha sattannaṃ tāva dhaññānaṃ dhaññānulomānaṃ aparaṇṇānañca piṭṭhaṃ panasalabujaambāṭakadhotatālapiṭṭhādikañceti tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena 03 manussānaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyakiccasādhakaṃ piṭṭhaṃ piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ. “Adhotaṃ tālapiṭṭhaṃ khīravallipiṭṭha”ntiādinā gaṇiyamānānaṃ gaṇanāya anto natthi, khādanīyabhojanīyakiccasādhakabhāvoyeva panetesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, subahuṃ vatvāpi imasmiṃyeva lakkhaṇe ṭhātabbanti na vitthārayāma. Evaṃ sabbattha. Tambakataṇḍuleyyādimūlaṃ mūlakhādanīyaṃ. Panasalabujanāḷikerādiphalaṃ phalakhādanīyaṃ. Khajjanti sakkhalimodakādipubbaṇṇāparaṇṇamayaṃ khādanīyañca. Gorasoti khīradadhitakkasaṅkhāto gunnaṃ raso ca. Dhaññabhojananti sānulomānaṃ dhaññānaṃ odanasattukummāsasaṅkhātabhojanañca. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “sānulomāni sattadhaññāni ca pañcavidhabhojanañcā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na yuttaṃ, dhaññānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇe payojanābhāvā, payojanasambhave ca phalaggahaṇeneva tesaṃ gahaṇasambhavato.

85. Now, among these, `yāvakālika` is shown by 'flour' and so on. There, `piṭṭha` (flour), `mūla` (roots), and `phala` (fruits) refer to flour-based food, root-based food, and fruit-based food. Among these, first, the flour of seven kinds of grains, grains similar to them, and other pulses, as well as flour from jackfruit, breadfruit, hog plum, washed palmyra flour, and so on—in various regions, these are the customary food of people, serving the purpose of chewable and edible provisions. This is called flour-based food. 'Unwashed palmyra flour, milk-vine flour,' and so on—there is no limit to the enumeration of such items. Their defining characteristic is simply their ability to serve as chewable and edible provisions. Even if much is said, it must be understood within this defining characteristic—we will not elaborate further. This applies in all cases. Root-based food includes roots such as turmeric, taro, and the like. Fruit-based food includes fruits such as jackfruit, breadfruit, coconut, and the like. Chewable food refers to things made from earlier and later crops, such as sugar lumps, sweetmeats, and so on. Milk products refers to the essence of cows, such as milk, curd, and buttermilk. Grain-based meals refers to meals prepared from grains and similar grains, such as cooked rice, flour-meal, and gruel. In the sub-commentary, it is said, 'seven kinds of grains and their similars, and five types of meals,' but this is not correct. There is no purpose in separately listing grains, and where a purpose exists, their inclusion is already accomplished by the inclusion of fruits.

Yāgusūpappabhutayoti yāgu ca sūpañca, taṃ pabhuti yesaṃ teti ete yāvakālikā hontīti sambandho. Ettha ca pabhuti-saddena macchamaṃsasaṅkhātaṃ dhaññabhojanato avasiṭṭhaṃ bhojanañca piṭṭhamūlaphalakhādanīyato avasiṭṭhaṃ kandakhādanīyaṃ, muḷālakhādanīyādiñca saṅgaṇhāti. Tesu dīgho ca bhisakandādi vaṭṭo ca uppalakaṇḍādi kandakhādanīyaṃ, padumamūlādi ca taṃsadisaṃ erakamūlādi ca muḷālakhādanīyaṃ, tālādīnaṃ kaḷīrasaṅkhātā matthakā matthakakhādanīyaṃ, ucchukkhandhādayo [V 0.0257] nīluppalādīnaṃ daṇḍakkhandhakādi khandhakhādanīyaṃ, tambakataṇḍuleyyādīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ pattakhādanīyaṃ, ucchutacova eko saraso tacakhādanīyaṃ, tambakasiggupupphādi pupphakhādanīyaṃ, labujaṭṭhipanasaṭṭhiādikaṃ aṭṭhikhādanīyaṃ.

Porridge, soup, and so forth—this refers to porridge and soup, and those of which these are the chief; these are `yāvakālika`. Here, the term 'and so forth' includes food reckoned as fish and meat, which remains from grain-based food; and it includes food of bulbs, food of edible stalks, and so on, which remain from flour, root, and fruit foods. Among those, long bulbous roots such as lotus root, and round bulbous roots such as water lily stems, are bulbous-root food. Lotus roots and things similar to them, and fibrous roots like erakamūla, are edible-stalk food. The soft tops, reckoned as shoots, of palmyra palms and the like are top-food. The stalks of sugarcane and the stem-stalks of blue lotuses and the like are stem-food. The leaves of things like turmeric and taro are leaf-food. The succulent bark of sugarcane alone is bark-food. The flowers of turmeric and moringa are flower-food. The seeds of breadfruit, jackfruit, and the like are seed-food.

86. “Madhū”tiādinā [M 0.0299] yāmakālikaṃ dasseti. Madhu ca muddikā ca sālūkañca cocañca mocañca ambañca jambu cāti dvando. Muddikā phalepi itthiyaṃ, phale sesā napuṃsake, “jambu” iti phalavācī napuṃsakasaddantaraṃ, tato jātaṃ madhupānādi madhu…pe… jambujaṃ, tañca phārusañca pānakanti yojanā. Tattha madhujaṃ pānaṃ nāma muddikānaṃ jātirasaṃ udakasambhinnaṃ katvā katapānaṃ. Taṃ attanā kataṃ purebhattameva sāmisaṃ nirāmisampi vaṭṭati. Anupasampannehi kataṃ labhitvā pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattaṃ pana nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Esa nayo sabbapānesu. Muddikajaṃ pānaṃ nāma muddikānaṃ udake madditvā katapānaṃ. Tathā sesapānāni yathānurūpaṃ veditabbāni, sālūkaṃ rattuppalādīnaṃ sālūkaṃ. Cocaṃ aṭṭhikakadaliphalaṃ. Mocaṃ anaṭṭhikaṃ. Imāni aṭṭha pānāni sītānipi ādiccapākānipi vaṭṭanti, aggipākāni pana na vaṭṭanti. Tenāha “nāggisantatta”nti.

86. By 'honey' and so on, `yāmakālika` is shown. Honey, grape, lotus root, seeded banana, seedless banana, mango, and rose apple—these form a compound. `Muddikā` is feminine even when referring to the fruit; the rest are neuter when referring to the fruit. `Jambu` is another neuter word referring to the fruit. The construction is: the drink produced from these, from honey-drink and so on up to rose-apple drink, and `phārusa` drink, are drinks. Here, 'honey-drink' means a drink made by mixing the natural juice of grapes with water. If made by oneself, it is allowable before the meal, whether with or without solid food. But if made by those not fully ordained, having been received before the meal, it is allowable before the meal even with solid food; after the meal, however, it is allowable only without solid food. This rule applies to all drinks. 'Grape-drink' means a drink made by squeezing grapes in water. Likewise, the remaining drinks should be understood accordingly. `Sālūka` is the edible root of red lotuses and so on. `Coca` is a banana fruit with seeds. `Moca` is without seeds. These eight drinks are allowable whether cooled or sun-baked, but they are not allowable if fire-heated. Therefore, it is said, 'not heated by fire.'

87-8. Avasesāni pana vettatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapitthakaramandādikhuddakaphalapānāni aṭṭhapānagatikāneva. Tenāha “sānulomāni dhaññāni, ṭhapetvā phalajo raso”ti. Ekassa pana vakkhamānānañca “puppharaso”tiādīnaṃ “sītodamadditādiccapāko vā yāmakāliko”ti iminā sambandho veditabbo. Tālanāḷikerapanasalabujaalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalatipusaeḷālukaphalānīti nava mahāphalāni, sabbañca aparaṇṇaṃ sattadhaññāni anulomentīti saha anulomehīti sānulomāni. Sānulomadhaññānaṃ pana raso yāvakāliko. “Sānulomāni dhaññānī”ti phalāni viññāyanti. Phalasutiyā “sesaphalajo”ti vattabbe gamyamānattā na vuttaṃ. Madhukapupphamaññatrāti madhukapupphaṃ ṭhapetvā. Pakkaḍākajanti pakkehi yāvakālikehi ḍākehi jātaṃ rasaṃ. Sītamudakaṃ sītodaṃ, khīrode viya sītode [M 0.0300] madditoti tappuriso. Ādicca-saddo ātape vattati upacāratoti ādicce pāko yassāti samāso.

87-8. The remaining small fruit-drinks, such as those from cane, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, and karamanda, are indeed of the eight drinks category. Hence it is said: 'Grains with their similars, except for the juice born of fruit.' However, for one and for those to be mentioned later, such as 'flower juice' and so on, the connection should be understood through this phrase: 'whether crushed in cold water or sun-ripened, it is `yāmakālika`.' The nine great fruits are: palmyra fruit, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, gourd, pumpkin, a type of gourd, cucumber, and a type of cucumber. And all pulses are similar to the seven grains, thus they are `sānuloma` (with similars). However, the juice of grains with their similars is `yāvakālika`. 'Grains with their similars' are understood as fruits. In the context of fruits, although 'juice born of remaining fruits' should be said, it is not said because it is understood. 'Except for madhuka flowers' means excluding madhuka flowers. 'Born of ripe `ḍāka`s' refers to juice produced from ripe `ḍāka`s that are `yāvakālika`. `Sītodaṃ` is cold water; 'crushed in cold water' is a tatpurisa compound, like in `khīroda`. The word `ādicca` is used figuratively for sunshine; hence, 'that which is ripened by the sun' is a compound.

89. Sattāhakālikaṃ dasseti “sappī”tiādinā. Tattha sattāhakālikāti yathāvuttāni sappiādīni sattāhakālikāni. Idāni sappiādīni vibhajati “sappī”tiādinā. Tattha yesaṃ [V 0.0258] gomahiṃ sādīnaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappi sappi nāmāti “sappī”tiādinā sappilakkhaṇamāha. Akappiyamaṃsasappinopi kappiyasambhave tattha sattāhātikkame dukkaṭassa vakkhamānattā nissaggiyavatthumeva cettha dassetuṃ “yesaṃ maṃsamavārita”nti vuttaṃ. Khīrādīsu hi tesamakappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Navanītassa sappisadisatāya navanītalakkhaṇaṃ visuṃ na vuttaṃ. Upari sappipiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā sītalapāyāsaṃ denti, yaṃ pāyāsena asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ sattāhakālikaṃ, missitaṃ pana ādiccapākaṃ katvā parissāvitaṃ, tathā khīraṃ pakkhipitvā pakkatelampi, tesu navanītaṃ nāma navuddhaṭaṃ. Tena kataṃ pana sappi.

89. The seven-day allowable is shown by 'ghee' and so on. Here, 'seven-day allowable' refers to ghee and so on, as previously mentioned. Now, ghee and so on are distinguished by 'ghee' and so on. Here, the characteristic of ghee is stated by 'ghee' and so on, meaning that the ghee of those whose meat, such as that of cows and buffaloes, is permissible, is called ghee. Even if there is ghee from impermissible meat, since an offense of wrong-doing will be stated for exceeding seven days when a permissible source is available, the phrase 'whose meat is not forbidden' is stated here to show only the item requiring relinquishment. Indeed, among milk and so on, there is nothing impermissible. Due to the similarity of fresh butter to ghee, the characteristic of fresh butter is not stated separately. They give cool rice porridge, placing a lump of ghee on top; that which is not mixed with the porridge is a seven-day allowable. But if it is mixed, it must be sun-cooked and strained; likewise for oil cooked by adding milk. Among these, fresh butter is that which is newly extracted. But what is made from that is ghee.

90. Tilā ca vasā ca eraṇḍāni ca madhukāni ca sāsapā cāti dvando. Tehi sambhavo yassāti bāhirattho, taṃ telaṃ nāmāti attho. Khuddā khuddamadhumakkhikā ca bhamarā ca khuddabhamaraṃ, khuddajantukattā napuṃsakekavacanaṃ. Madhuṃ karontīti madhukariyo, tā eva makkhikā madhukarimakkhikā, khuddabhamarameva madhukarimakkhikāti kammadhārayo. Tāhi kataṃ madhu madhu nāmāti attho. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana visuṃ madhukarī-saddaṃ vikappetvā “daṇḍakesu madhukarā madhukarimakkhikā nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Madhupaṭalaṃ vā madhusitthakaṃ vā sace madhunā makkhitaṃ, madhugatikameva. Tumbalakānaṃ cīrikānañca niyyāsasadisaṃ madhu pana [M 0.0301] yāvajīvikaṃ. Raso nikkasaṭo ādi yassā sā rasādi. Ādi-saddena phāṇitādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, sā ucchuvikati. Pakkāti avatthukapakkā vā, phāṇitaṃ phāṇitaṃ nāmāti attho. Sītūdakena katamadhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ pana phāṇitagatikameva. Ambaphāṇitādīni yāvakālikāni. Etāni yathāvuttāni sappiādīni purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogenāpi, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya pana tāni ca pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitāni ca sattāhaṃ nidahitvā nirāmisaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbāni.

90. Sesame, fat, castor beans, madhuka seeds, and mustard seeds—this is a dvanda compound. The meaning is that what is produced from these external sources is called oil. Small honeybees and bumblebees are 'small bumblebees'; being tiny creatures, the term is in the neuter singular. Those that make honey are 'honey-makers'; those very bees are 'honey-making bees'; 'small bumblebee' itself is 'honey-making bee'—this is a karmadhāraya compound. The meaning is that what is made by them is called honey. In the sub-commentary, however, analyzing the word 'madhukarī' separately, it is stated: 'In the Daṇḍaka forest, some honey-makers are called madhukarimakkhikā.' A honeycomb or beeswax, if smeared with honey, follows the same rule as honey. However, the honey resembling the sap of Tumbalaka and Cīrika trees is allowable for life. That which has extracted essence and so on as its basis is 'rasādi'. By the term 'ādi', molasses and the like are included; that is a sugarcane product. The meaning is that molasses is called molasses, which is cooked, or cooked without its raw material. Molasses made from madhuka flowers with cold water, however, follows the same rule as molasses. Mango molasses and the like are allowable for the day. These items, as previously mentioned—ghee and so on—may be consumed even with meat before the meal. From after the meal onwards, however, these, and those received after the meal, must be stored for seven days and then consumed without meat.

91. Idāni odissa anuññātavasāya pākato vibhāgaṃ dassetvā tato sappiādīnaṃ dassetuṃ “savatthū”tiādimāha. Tattha purebhattaṃ sāmaṃ vā attanā eva. Vā-saddena parehi vā. Amānusā manussavasārahitā. Vasā acchādīnaṃ akappiyānaṃ, sūkarādīnaṃ kappiyānañca sattānaṃ vasā. Savatthupakkā sattāhakālikā hotīti seso. Savatthupakkāti savatthukaṃ katvā pakkā. Ayamettha adhippāyo – sace pana vasaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā pacitvā telaṃ parissāvitaṃ sattāhāni nirāmisaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Atha parehi kataṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ, purebhattaṃ sāmisampi [V 0.0259] vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva, no ce, dukkaṭaṃ hotīti. Kāriye kāraṇopacārena panettha “vasā”ti telameva vuttaṃ, vasā pana yāvakālikāva.

91. Now, having shown the division concerning the preparation of specifically permitted fat, he then states, beginning with 'with its substance', to show the rules for ghee and so on. Here, this means it is prepared either by oneself, or, indicated by the word 'or', by others. 'Non-human' means devoid of human fat. Fat is the fat of unallowable animals like bears and of allowable animals like pigs. The remainder of the phrase explains that 'fat cooked with its substance is allowable for seven days'. 'Cooked with its substance' means cooked together with its raw material. The meaning here is this: if fat is received before the meal, cooked, and the oil strained, it is to be consumed without meat for seven days. But if it is prepared by others and received before the meal, it is allowable even with meat before the meal; from after the meal onwards, it must be without meat, otherwise, it is an offense of wrong-doing. For the effect, by metaphorical application of the cause, the term 'fat' here refers to oil, but fat itself is only allowable for the day.

Ṭīkāyaṃ pana vasāya “sattāhakālike āgataṭṭhānaṃ natthīti vadantī”ti vatvā “taṃ upaparikkhitabba”nti vasāya sattāhakālikattamāsaṃkiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kimettha upaparikkhitabbaṃ? Bhesajjaṃ anujānatā bhagavatā “yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisāyanīyāni bhesajjāni, seyyathidaṃ – sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitaṃ, tāni paṭiggahetvā [M 0.0302] sattāhaparamaṃ sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbānī”ti (pārā. 622) sappiādīnameva sattāhakālikattaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhesajjakkhandhakepi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni pañca bhesajjāni paṭiggahetvā kālepi vikālepi paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 260) tāni pañceva “bhesajjānī”ti vatvā telaṃ niyamato “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasaṃ kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttaṃ. Bhesajjasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyañca (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci vasa”ntiādinā vasātelassa vidhānaṃ dassetvā “aññesaṃ yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ vatthuṃ pacituṃ na vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vadatā aṭṭhakathācariyena yāvakālikesu vasaṃ ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ vatthuṃ pacituṃ na vaṭṭatīti ayamettha attho dīpitoti vasā “yāvakālikāyevā”ti viññāyatīti ko ettha sukhumo nayoti.

In the sub-commentary, however, regarding fat, it is stated, 'They say there is no instance where the seven-day allowance applies,' and then it is said, 'This should be investigated,' thus stating that the seven-day allowability of fat is doubtful. What is to be investigated here? When the Blessed One permitted medicines, he said: 'Those medicines that are suitable for sick monks, namely, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—these may be received and stored for a maximum of seven days before being consumed.' Here, the seven-day allowance is mentioned only for ghee and the like. In the Chapter on Medicines, too, it is said: 'I allow, monks, these five medicines to be received and consumed at the proper time or at the improper time.' Having called these five 'medicines', oil is specifically regulated: 'I allow, monks, fats as medicines—bear fat, fish fat, crocodile fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—to be received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, mixed at the proper time, and consumed with the allowance for oil.' And in the commentary on the Training Rule on Medicines, after showing the regulation for fat-oil with 'except for human fat, any other fat,' and so on, the commentary master, by stating 'for other items allowable for the day, it is not at all allowable to cook the substance,' clarifies that the meaning here is that it is not permissible to cook the substance of other items allowable for the day, setting aside fat from among them. Thus, it is understood that fat is 'only allowable for the day'. What subtle point is there here?

Aññesaṃ vasātelato paresaṃ yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ yesaṃ tesaṃ yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ sappiādīnaṃ vatthuṃ yāvakālikasaṅkhātaṃ khīrādikaṃ na paceti sambandho. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yathā sattāhaparibhogatthāya vasaṃ kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle pacituṃ vaṭṭati, na evaṃ sappiādīnaṃ vatthubhūtaṃ khīrādiyāvakālikaṃ, taṃ pana sattāhaparibhogatthāya kālepi na vaṭṭati. Tāni hi yadi taṃ paṭiggahetvā sayaṃ katāni, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭanti savatthukappaṭiggahitattā, sāmisaṃ na vaṭṭanti sāmaṃpakkattā, purebhattampi na vaṭṭanti yāvakālikavatthuto vivecitattā. Parehi katāni pana purebhattaṃ sāmisampi [M 0.0303] vaṭṭanti attanā apakkattā. Yāvajīvikāni tu sāsapamadhukaeraṇḍaaṭṭhīni telakaraṇatthaṃ paṭiggahetvā tadaheva kataṃ telaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ, dutiyadivase kataṃ chāhaṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ yāva sattamadivase kataṃ tadaheva vaṭṭati, uggate aruṇe nissaggiyaṃ[V 0.0260], aṭṭhame divase anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, uggahitena yena kenaci vatthunā katasadisaṃ hoti. Telatthāya paṭiggahitasāsapādīnaṃ sattāhātikkamena dukkaṭaṃ. Nibbattitaṃ sappi vā navanītaṃ vā kālepi vikālepi paṭiggahetvā pacituṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ pana tadahu purebhattampi sāmisaṃ na vaṭṭati, saṃsaggato yāvakālikampi sāmaṃpakkaṃ siyāti nirāmisaṃ pana sattāhampi vaṭṭati.

The connection is this: unlike fat-oil, one may not cook the yāvakālika substance, such as milk, of other yāvakālika items, namely ghee and so on. The meaning here is this: just as it is permissible to receive fat at the proper time for seven-day use and to cook it at the proper time, the same does not apply to a yāvakālika item like milk which is the substance of ghee and so on; that is not allowable for seven-day use even if received at the proper time. For if one receives such items and prepares them oneself, they are not allowable after the meal because they were received with their substance; they are not allowable with meat because they are cooked by oneself; and they are not allowable even before the meal because the product has been separated from its yāvakālika substance. However, if prepared by others, they are allowable even with meat before the meal, since one did not cook them oneself. But as for lifelong items, such as mustard seeds, madhuka seeds, and castor beans received for the purpose of making oil, oil made on that same day is allowable for seven days. Oil made on the second day is allowable for six days, and so on, until oil made on the seventh day is allowable only on that day. At the break of dawn, it becomes an item for relinquishment; on the eighth day, it is not to be consumed, and becomes like something made with any forfeited item. For mustard seeds and the like received for making oil, if kept beyond seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing. As for ghee or fresh butter that has been produced, it is permissible to receive and cook it at the proper or improper time. However, on that very day, it is not allowable even before the meal if it contains meat, because through this association, it would become like a self-cooked yāvakālika item. But if it is without meat, it is allowable for seven days.

92. Idāni “haliddi”ntiādinā yāvajīvikaṃ dasseti. Tattha “haliddi nāma nisā”tiādinā vuccamānepi pariyāyavacane sammoho siyāti na taṃvacanena bhusaṃ sammohayissāma, tasmā tāni upadesatova veditabbāni. Tattha “haliddi”nti binduāgamena vuttaṃ. Upacārena tu mūlādīni haliddādisaddena vuttāni. Tā haliddādayo keci itthiliṅgāyeva. Mūlaphale vacattañca…pe… bhaddamuttañca ativisāti padacchedo. Pañcamūla-saddena cūḷapañcamūlamahāpañcamūlāni gahitāni. Ādi-saddena vajakalimūle jaraṭṭhanti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

92. Now, beginning with 'turmeric' (haliddi), he indicates items allowable for life (yāvajīvika). Here, even though synonymous terms are stated, such as 'turmeric is called nisā,' confusion might arise. Therefore, we will not excessively confuse the reader with such terms; they should be understood through instruction alone. Here, 'haliddi' is stated with the insertion of a dot. However, by convention, roots and so on are referred to by the term 'turmeric' and similar words. Some of these—turmeric and the like—are only feminine in gender. 'Roots and fruits' (mūlaphale) and also... 'bhaddamutta' and 'ativisā' — this is the word division. By the term 'five roots' (pañcamūla), the lesser five roots (cūḷapañcamūla) and the greater five roots (mahāpañcamūla) are included. By the term 'and so on' (ādi-saddena), the inclusion of terms such as 'vajakalimūla,' 'jaraṭṭha,' and so on is intended.

93-5. Goṭṭhaphalanti madanaphalanti vadantīti. Tīṇi phalāni yassaṃ saṅgahitaṃ sā tiphalā. Eraṇḍakādīnanti ādi-saddena jātirukkhādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sulasādīnaṃ paṇṇanti sambandho. Ādi-saddena asokādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sūpeyyapaṇṇanti tambakataṇḍuleyyādisūpayoggapaṇṇaṃ. Ucchuniyyāsaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbo [M 0.0304] niyyāso ca sarasaṃ ucchujaṃ tacañca ṭhapetvā sabbo taco cāti sambandho. Tattha hiṅgukaṇikāraniyyāsādi sabbo niyyāso nāma. Nirasaucchutacādi sabbo taco nāma. Loṇaṃ sāmuddādi. Lohaṃ ayatambādi. Silā kāḷasilādi.

93-5. They say 'goṭṭhaphala' means 'madanaphala'. That in which three fruits are collected is called 'tiphalā'. By the term 'etc.' (ādi-saddena) in 'eraṇḍakādīni', the inclusion of jātirukkha, etc., is meant. The connection is 'leaves of sulasa and so on' (sulasādīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ). By the term 'etc.', the inclusion of asoka, etc., is meant. 'Sūpeyyapaṇṇa' means leaves suitable for soup, like tambakataṇḍuleyya, etc. The connection is: having excluded sugarcane sap (ucchuniyyāsa), all sap; and having excluded succulent sugarcane bark (sarasaṃ ucchujaṃ taca), all bark. Here, 'all sap' means hiṅgu and kaṇikāra sap, etc. 'All bark' means non-succulent sugarcane bark, etc. 'Salt' (loṇa) means sea salt, etc. 'Metal' (loha) means iron, copper, etc. 'Stone' (silā) means black stone, etc.

96. Suddhasitthanti madhunā amakkhitaṃ. Madhumakkhitaṃ pana sattāhakālikaṃ. Yañca kiñci sujhāpitanti dujjhāpitaṃ akatvā sujjhāpitaṃ yaṃ kiñci ca. Vikaṭādippabhedanti vikaṭaṃ gūthamattikāmuttachārikāsaṅkhātaṃ ādi yassa, so pabhedo yassāti bāhirattho, taṃ. Yaṃ kiñci cāti sambandho. Ettha pana ādi-saddena kandakhādanīye khīrakākolādayo, muḷālakhādanīye haliddisiṅgiveramūlādayo, matthakakhādanīye haliddisiṅgiverakaḷīrādayo, khandhakhādanīye uppalapaṇṇadaṇḍādayo, pupphakhādanīye campakapupphādayo, aṭṭhikhādanīye madhukaṭṭhieraṇḍasāsapādayo, piṭṭhakhādanīye adhotatālapiṭṭhādayo ca saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā.

96. 'Pure beeswax' (suddhasittha) means that which is not smeared with honey. What is smeared with honey, however, is allowable for seven days. 'And whatever is well-cooked' (yañca kiñci sujhāpitaṃ) means whatever is well-cooked, not ill-cooked. 'That which is a variety of vikaṭa and so on' (vikaṭādippabheda) means that of which 'vikaṭa' (designated as feces, clay, urine, and ashes) is the beginning, and that which has that as its variety; this is the external meaning. The connection is 'and whatever else'. Here, by the term 'and so on' (ādi-saddena), the following are to be understood as included: for 'edible tubers' (kandakhādanīya), milk, kākola, etc.; for 'edible rhizomes' (muḷālakhādanīya), turmeric, ginger roots, etc.; for 'edible tops' (matthakakhādanīya), turmeric, ginger shoots, etc.; for 'edible stems' (khandhakhādanīya), lotus leaf stalks, etc.; for 'edible flowers' (pupphakhādanīya), campaka flowers, etc.; for 'edible seeds' (aṭṭhikhādanīya), madhuka seeds, castor, mustard, etc.; and for 'edible flours' (piṭṭhakhādanīya), unwashed palm flour, etc.

97. Idāni [V 0.0261] sabbaso yāvajīvikaṃ dassetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā vuttāni ca avuttāni ca ekato sampiṇḍetvā tattha lakkhaṇaṃ ṭhapento “mūla”ntiādimāha. Tattha “sāro”ti vattabbe “sāra”nti liṅgavipallāsenāha. “Sāro bale thiraṃse cā”ti hi nighaṇḍu. Āhāraṭṭhanti āhārena jāto attho payojanaṃ āhārattho, sova āhāraṭṭho, taṃ āhārakiccanti vuttaṃ hoti.

97. Now, because it is impossible to show in full what is permissible for a lifetime, he combines what has been stated and what has not been stated, and, establishing the characteristic therein, says 'root' (mūla), etc. Here, where 'sāro' should be said, 'sāra' is stated due to a change of gender. For the lexicon states: 'Sāro means strength and firmness.' 'For the purpose of food' (āhāraṭṭhaṃ): the purpose or benefit that arises from food is the 'food-purpose' (āhārattho); that itself is the purpose of food. This is to say, it is called the 'function of food'.

98. Idāni catūsu kappiyākappiyādivibhāgaṃ dasseti “sabbā”tiādinā. Tattha sabbe kālikā, tesaṃ sambhogo anubhavoti samāso. Kāleti pubbaṇhakāle. Sabbassāti gilānāgilānassa. Sati paccayeti tīsu [M 0.0305] yāmakālikaṃ pipāsādikāraṇe sati, sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikañca gelaññakāraṇe satīti attho, kālato vigato vikālo, tasmiṃ, yāmakālikaṃ vikāle āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇe, sattāhakālikaṃ pana yāvajīvikañca tadatthāya paṭiggahaṇamattepi dukkaṭaṃ.

98. Now, he shows the division concerning the four types of requisites into allowable, unallowable, etc., with 'all' (sabbā), and so on. Here, the compound is 'all the time-limited items, their partaking' (sabbe kālikā, tesaṃ sambhogo), meaning their use or enjoyment. 'In the proper time' (kāle) means in the forenoon. 'For all' (sabbassa) means for both the sick and the healthy. 'When there is a condition' (sati paccaye) means that when there is a reason such as thirst, the period-allowable is permissible; and when there is a reason of illness, the seven-day and the lifelong allowables are permissible. 'Wrong time' (vikāla) is that which is devoid of the proper time. In that wrong time, for consuming the period-allowable for the purpose of nourishment, and for merely receiving the seven-day and lifelong requisites for that purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

99. Ubhoti yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikañca. Tattha yāvakālikaṃ attano kālātikkantaṃ vikālabhojanabhikkhāpadena pācittiyaṃ janayati, yāmakālikaṃ yāmātikkantaṃ sannidhisikkhāpadena. Ete ubhopi antovutthañca sannidhiñca janayantīti sambandho. “Antovutthaṃ sannidhi”nti bhāvappadhānoyaṃ niddeso, antovutthattaṃ sannidhittañcāti attho.

99. 'Both' refers to the time-allowable (yāvakālika) and the period-allowable (yāmakālika). Herein, the time-allowable, when its own time has passed, gives rise to a pācittiya offense under the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time. The period-allowable, when its period has passed, gives rise to an offense under the training rule concerning stored food. Both of these give rise to being kept overnight and to accumulation—this is the connection. 'Kept overnight, accumulation' (antovutthaṃ sannidhi) is an explanation emphasizing the state, meaning the state of being kept overnight and the state of being accumulated.

100. Atināmiteti atikkāmite. Pācittīti sattāhātikkantaṃ bhesajjasikkhāpadena nissaggiyapācittiyāpatti ca hotīti attho. Sace dvinnaṃ santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ avibhattaṃ hoti, sattāhātikkame dvinnampi anāpatti, paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Pāḷināruḷheti pāḷiyaṃ anāruḷhe sappiādimhi satta ahāni atināmiteti sambandho. Sappīti manussādīnaṃ sappi. Ādi-saddena tesaṃyeva navanītaṃ, nāḷikerāditelaṃ, sītodakena kataṃ madhukapupphaphāṇitañca saṅgahitaṃ.

100. 'Exceeded' (atināmite) means surpassed. 'Pācitti' means that if seven days are exceeded, there is also an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya) under the training rule concerning medicine. If something belonging to two people is received by one and remains undivided, there is no offense for either even after seven days have passed, but it is not allowable to use it. 'Not mentioned in the Pāḷi' (pāḷināruḷhe) refers to exceeding seven days in the case of ghee, etc., which are not stipulated in the Pāḷi; this is the connection. 'Ghee' means ghee from humans, etc. The word 'etc.' includes butter from the same, coconut oil, and molasses made from madhuka flowers with cold water.

101. Nissaṭṭhaladdhanti nissaṭṭhaṃ vinayakammavasena nissajjitañca taṃ laddhañca puna tathevāti nissaṭṭhaladdhaṃ. Taṃ gahetvāti seso. Nissajjanavidhānaṃ pana vakkhamānanayena veditabbaṃ. “Naṅga”ntiādi upalakkhaṇamattaṃ. Tena makkhitāni kāsāvādīni ca pana aparibhogāniyeva[V 0.0262]. Aññassa pana kāyikaparibhogo vaṭṭati. Vikappentassa sattāhe sāmaṇerassāti ettha [M 0.0306] ṭīkāyaṃ “idaṃ sappiṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”tiādinā tesaṃ tesaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā sammukhāparammukhāvikappanavasena atthaṃ dassetvā taṃ sādhayantehi avikappite vikappitasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti āpattivāre pāḷi āhaṭā. “Sace upasampannassa vikappeti, attano eva santakaṃ hoti, paṭiggahaṇampi na vijahatī”ti dosaṃ vatvā anupasampannassa vikappane attasantakattābhāvo, paṭiggahaṇavijahanañca payojanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha vadāma – āpattivāre “avikappite”tiādipāḷiyeva natthi, “anadhiṭṭhite adhiṭṭhitasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, avissajjite vissajjitasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”ntiādinā (pārā. 624) pāḷiyā āgatattā tadanurūpameva anāpattivāre “adhiṭṭheti, vissajjetī”tiādināva pāḷi āgatā. Yadi bhaveyya, vaṇṇanīyaṭṭhānatāya aṭṭhakathāya bhavitabbaṃ, na cettha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vijjati. Anupasampannassa vikappane ca kathaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati sikkhāpaccakkhānādīsu chasu paṭiggahaṇavijahanakāraṇesu vikappanassa anantogadhattā, tasmā nāyamettha atthoti.

101. 'Relinquished and reacquired' (nissaṭṭhaladdhaṃ) means that which has been relinquished through a disciplinary act and then reacquired in the same manner. 'Taking that' is the remainder. The procedure for relinquishment, however, should be understood according to the method to be explained. 'Ploughshare' (naṅga), etc., are merely illustrative. Therefore, robes, etc., smeared with it are indeed unusable. However, physical use by another is allowable. Regarding 'for one who assigns to a novice within seven days' (vikappentassa sattāhe sāmaṇerassāti), in the subcommentary, the Pāḷi concerning offense cases is cited: 'If those attempting to accomplish that, by taking their respective names and demonstrating the meaning through face-to-face or indirect assignment, saying "I assign this ghee to you," etc., perceive something unassigned as assigned, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).' Further, stating the fault: 'If one assigns it to an ordained monk, it becomes his own property, and the receipt is not relinquished,' it is said that the purpose in assigning to an unordained person is the non-existence of it being one's own property and the relinquishing of the receipt. Here, we say: In the offense cases, there is no Pāḷi such as 'avikappite,' etc.; instead, because the Pāḷi comes as 'Perceiving something undetermined as determined is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession, perceiving something unrelinquished as relinquished is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession,' etc. (Pārā. 624), correspondingly, in the non-offense cases, the Pāḷi comes only as 'determines, relinquishes,' etc. If it existed, it would have to be in the commentary, as it is a point to be explained, but it is not found in the commentary. Moreover, how does receipt cease in assigning to one unordained, since assignment is not included among the six causes for the ceasing of receipt, such as renunciation of the training? Therefore, this is not the meaning here.

Mayamettha evamatthaṃ bhaṇāma – vikappentassāti ettha vikappanaṃ saṃvidahanaṃ “cittasaṅkappo”tiādīsu viya, ubhayattha pana upasaggehi nānattamattaṃ, tasmā antosattāhe sāmaṇerassa yassa kassaci vikappentassa saṃvidahantassa pariccāgasaññaṃ pariccāgacetanaṃ pariccāgādhippāyaṃ uppādentassa anāpattīti attho. Idañca mahāsumattheravādamolubbha vuttaṃ. Vuttañhi “tena cittenā”tiādīsu pāḷivacanesu adhippāyaṃ dassentena, “idaṃ kasmā vuttaṃ. Evañhi antosattāhe datvā pacchā paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjantassa anāpattidassanattha”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.625). Mahāpadumatthero panāha “sattāhātikkantassa pana [M 0.0307] paribhoge anāpattidassanatthamidaṃ vutta”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.625). Ayameva vādo tesu sundarataro. Sattāhe makkhanādiṃ adhiṭṭhato ca aññassa dadatopi ca anāpattīti sambandho. Ādi-saddena abbhañjanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ayametthādhippāyo – sappiādiṃ abbhañjanādiṃ madhuṃ arumakkhanaṃ, phāṇitaṃ gharadhūpanaṃ adhiṭṭhato anāpattīti. Aññassāti upasampannassa vā anupasampannassa vā.

Here we explain the meaning thus: In 'vikappentassa' (for one who assigns), 'vikappana' is 'arranging' (saṃvidahanaṃ), as in 'cittasaṅkappa' (thought-conception), etc.; in both cases, the prefixes merely indicate a difference. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no offense for one who, within seven days, assigns, arranges, or generates for a novice or for anyone whatsoever the perception of relinquishment, the intention to relinquish, or the resolve to relinquish. This is stated based on the view of the Elder Mahāsuma. For it is stated, showing the intention in the Pāḷi passages such as 'with that thought' (tena cittenā): 'Why is this said? It is to show that there is no offense for one who gives something within seven days and later regains and uses it.' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.625). However, the Elder Mahāpaduma says: 'This is stated to show that there is no offense in using it after seven days have passed.' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.625). This very view is the better one among them. The connection is that there is no offense for one who determines on butter and the like within seven days, or for one who gives them to another. The word 'etc.' includes anointing and so forth. The meaning here is this: There is no offense for one who determines on ghee and the like for anointing, honey for applying to wounds, or molasses for fumigating a house. 'To another' means to one who is ordained or to one who is not ordained.

102. Yāvakālikaādīni attanā saha saṃsaṭṭhāni sabbhāvaṃ gāhāpayantīti sambandho. Sabbhāvanti sassa attano bhāvo dvitte sabbhāvo, taṃ. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ, tasmā. Evamudīritanti [V 0.0263] evaṃ “vikappentassa sattāhe”tiādinā vuttaṃ. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yasmā attanā saṃsaṭṭhāni attano bhāvaṃ gāhāpayanti yāvakālikādīni, tasmā sattāhātikkāmitāni sattāhakālikāni pācittiyajanakāni saṃsaṭṭhāni attasaṃsaṭṭhānipi pācittiyajanakāni karontīti avikappanādimhi sati byatirekato pācittiyāpattiparidīpakaṃ “vikappentassā”tiādikaṃ vākyattayaṃ vuttanti. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “idāni vakkhamānaṃ sandhāya evanti vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vakkhamānassa atītaudīritattāyogato kathaṃ yujjatīti. Evamudīritanti vā pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca evameva vuttanti attho. Eva-saddo avadhāraṇe.

102. The connection is that the time-allowable items, etc., when associated with oneself, cause one to take on their own nature. 'Sabbhāva' is from 'sa-bhāva' (one's own nature); when the 'sa' is doubled, it becomes 'sabbhāva'. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means 'because it is so, therefore.' 'Evamudīrita' (thus stated) refers to what was said beginning with 'for one who assigns within seven days.' The meaning here is this: because the time-allowable items, etc., when associated with oneself, cause one to take on their own nature, therefore, the seven-day items, having exceeded the seven days, make the items with which they are associated productive of a pācittiya offense, and also make the items associated with oneself productive of a pācittiya offense. Thus, when there is no assignment, etc., the three statements beginning with 'for one who assigns' are stated to illuminate, by way of contrast, the falling into a pācittiya offense. In the subcommentary, however, it is said: 'It is said "thus" with reference to what is about to be stated.' How is that fitting, since it is inappropriate for something that is about to be said to have been stated in the past? Alternatively, 'Evamudīrita' means that it is stated in this very way in the Pāḷi and in the commentary. The word 'eva' is for emphasis.

103-5. Idāni attasaṃsaṭṭhānaṃ yāvakālikādīnaṃ sabbhāvagāhāpanaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “pure”tiādimāha. Tattha sattāhanti satta ahāni yassa taṃ sattāhaṃ, sattāhakālikaṃ. Ca-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, so sattāhañca yāvajīvikañcāti yojetabbo. Sesakālikasammissanti sesehi tadahu paṭiggahitehi kālikehi yāvakālikayāmakālikasaṅkhātehi sammissaṃ. Pācittīti [M 0.0308] sannidhisikkhāpadena pācitti. Tadahu paṭiggahitanti tasmiṃyeva dine purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ. Tadahevāti tasmiṃyeva dine purebhattameva. Sesanti sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikañca. Evanti yāme eva paribhuñjayeti vijānīyanti sambandho. Itaranti sattāhakālikato aññaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Now, to show specifically the causing to take on their own nature of the time-allowable items, etc., that are associated with oneself, he says 'pure,' etc. Herein, 'sattāhaṃ' means that which has seven days, that is, 'sattāhakālika' (a seven-day allowable). The word 'ca' (and) is used in the wrong place; it should be connected as 'sattāhañca' (and a seven-day allowable) and 'yāvajīvikañca' (and a lifelong allowable). 'Sesakālikasammissaṃ' means mixed with the remaining kālikas received on that same day, namely those designated as morning-allowable and watch-allowable. 'Pācitti' is a pācittiya offense under the training rule concerning storing. 'Tadahu paṭiggahitaṃ' means received before the meal on that very day. 'Tadaheva' means only before the meal on that very day. 'Sesaṃ' refers to the seven-day allowable and the lifelong allowable. The connection for 'Evaṃ' (thus) is that it should be understood as 'one should use only within the watch (yāma).' 'Itaraṃ' means the other, the lifelong allowable, which is different from the seven-day allowable.

Kālikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Time-Allowables is concluded.

9. Paṭiggāhaniddesavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Exposition of Acceptance

106. Dātuṃ kāmetīti dātukāmo, tassa abhihāro īsakampi oṇamanādinābhiharaṇanti tappuriso, hatthassa pāso hatthapāso. Ruḷhīvasena tu aḍḍhateyyahattho hatthapāso nāma. So ca sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, āsanassa pacchimantato paṭṭhāya, sace ṭhito, paṇhiantato paṭṭhāya, sace nipanno, yena passena nipanno, tassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya dāyakassa nisinnassa ṭhitassa vā ṭhapetvā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa orimantena paricchinditvā veditabbo. Eraṇakkhamanti thāmamajjhimena purisena eraṇassa ukkhipanassa [V 0.0264] khamaṃ yoggaṃ. Vatthusaddāpekkhaṃ napuṃsakattaṃ. Tidhā denteti kāyakāyappaṭibaddhanissaggiyānaṃ vasena tīhi pakārehi dāyake dadamāne. Tattha yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena antamaso pādaṅguliyāpi dīyamānaṃ kāyena dinnaṃ nāma hoti, kaṭacchuādīsu yena kenaci dīyamānaṃ kāyappaṭibaddhena, kāyato pana kāyappaṭibaddhato vā mocetvā hatthapāse ṭhitassa kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā pātiyamānaṃ nissaggiyena payogena dinnaṃ nāma. Dvidhā gāhoti kāyakāyappaṭibaddhānaṃ vasena dvīhi pakārehi yehi kehici [M 0.0309] dīyamānassa gahaṇaṃ. Evaṃ paṭiggaho pañcaṅgoti yojanā. Pañcaṅgoti pañca aṅgāni yassāti bahubbīhi.

106. 'Dātukāma' is one who desires to give. 'His offering' (tassa abhihāro) is the act of presenting (abhiharaṇaṃ), even by a slight bending down and so forth; this is a tappurisa compound. The hand's reach is 'hatthapāsa'. By convention, however, 'hatthapāsa' is a distance of two and a half cubits. And that should be understood by measuring from the back edge of the seat, if the bhikkhu is seated; from the heel, if he is standing; or if he is lying down, from the furthest edge of the side on which he is lying, and delimiting it by the inner edge of whatever limb of the donor (whether seated or standing) is nearest, excluding the outstretched hand. 'Eraṇakkhama' means suitable and fit for a man of average strength to lift an 'eraṇa' (a type of weight). The neuter gender is with reference to the word 'vatthu' (object). 'Tidhā dente' (when giving in three ways) refers to when a donor is giving in three manners: by means of the body, by means of what is connected to the body, and by means of forfeiture. Therein, what is given with any part of the body, even with a toe, is called 'given by the body'. What is given with something connected to the body, such as a ladle, is called 'given by what is connected to the body'. But what is made to fall by the body or by what is connected to the body, having been released from the body or from what is connected to the body for one who is standing within the hand's reach, is called 'given by the application of forfeiture'. 'Dvidhā gāho' (receiving in two ways) is the receiving of what is given by someone in two ways: by means of the body and by means of what is connected to the body. The construction is: "Thus, acceptance is five-factored." 'Pañcaṅgo' (five-factored) is a bahubbīhi compound meaning "that which has five parts."

107. Idāni aneraṇakkhame ca kismiñci kāyappaṭibaddhe ca paṭiggahaṇārohanaṃ dassetuṃ “asaṃhāriye”tiādimāha. Tattha asaṃhāriyeti ānetumasakkuṇeyye phalakapāsāṇādimhi. Tatthajāteti tesuyeva rukkhādīsu jāte kiṃsukapaduminipaṇṇādike. Ciñcaādīnaṃ sukhume paṇṇeti sambandho. Tāni hi sandhāretuṃ na sakkonti. Tesaṃ pana sākhāsu vaṭṭati. Ādi-saddena “aṅga”ntiādikaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vā-saddo samuccaye. Asayhabhāreti thāmamajjhimapurisena sahituṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkuṇeyye bhāre. Sabbesaṃ paṭiggaho “na rūhatī”ti iminā sambandho.

107. Now, to show when acceptance is valid with regard to something that is not 'eraṇakkhama' and something connected to the body, he says 'asaṃhāriye' and so on. Here, 'asaṃhāriye' refers to what is immovable, such as planks, stones, and so forth. 'Tatthajāte' refers to what grows on those very things, such as trees, for example, kiṃsuka blossoms, lotus leaves, and so forth. The connection of 'ciñca' (tamarind) and so forth is with a delicate leaf. For these are not able to support anything. On their branches, however, it is permissible. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), he includes 'aṅga' (limb), and so forth. The word 'vā' is in the sense of conjunction. 'Asayhabhāre' refers to a load that cannot be borne or supported by a man of average strength. The acceptance of all these is connected with the phrase 'is not valid' (na rūhati).

108. Idāni paṭiggahaṇavijahanaṃ dasseti “sikkhā”tiādinā. Tattha sikkhāmaraṇaliṅgehīti sikkhāpaccakkhānena ca maraṇena ca liṅgaparivattanena ca. Anapekkhavisaggatoti natthi apekkho etassāti anapekkho, sova visaggo, tato ca. Acchedāti corādīhi acchinditvā gahaṇena. Anupasampannadānāti anupasampannassa dānena. Ca-saddo sabbattha ānetabbo. Gāhoti paṭiggahaṇaṃ. Upasammatīti vijahati.

108. Now he shows the abandonment of acceptance with 'sikkhā' and so on. Therein, 'sikkhāmaraṇaliṅgehi' means: by renouncing the training, by death, and by a change of gender. 'Anapekkhavisaggato' means: from the relinquishment by one who is without expectation—'anapekkho' is one for whom there is no expectation, and that itself is the relinquishment ('visaggo'). 'Acchedā' means: by seizure, that is, by the seizing and taking by thieves and so on. 'Anupasampannadānā' means: by giving to one who is not fully ordained. The word 'ca' should be supplied in each case. 'Gāho' means acceptance. 'Upasammati' means it is abandoned ('vijahati').

109-10. Idāni appaṭiggahitaṃ paribhoge dosaṃ dassetuṃ “appaṭiggahita”ntiādimāha. Tattha sabbanti catukālikapariyāpannaṃ sakalampi. Idāni appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ dassetuṃ “suddha”ntiādimāha. Tattha suddhaṃ nātibahalaṃ udakañca tathā aṅgalaggaṃ avicchinnaṃ danta…pe… gūthakañca loṇa…pe… karīsakañca kappateti sambandho. Tattha suddhanti rajareṇūhi aññarasena [M 0.0310] ca asammissatāya parisuddhaṃ. Nātibahalanti yaṃ kasitaṭṭhāne bahalamudakaṃ viya mukhe vā hatthe vā na laggaṃ, taṃ. Avicchinnanti aṅgato vicchinditvā [V 0.0265] na gataṃ. Dantāni ca akkhīni ca kaṇṇañca dantakkhikaṇṇaṃ pāṇyaṅgattā, tassa gūthakanti tappuriso. Loṇaṃ sarīruṭṭhitaṃ. Siṅghāṇīti siṅghāṇikā. Vicchinnaṃ na paṭiggahetabbaṃ.

109-10. Now, to show the fault in using what is unaccepted, it is said, ‘unaccepted,’ and so on. Herein, ‘all’ includes everything encompassed by the four time-limited categories of requisites. Now, to show what may be used without being accepted, it is said, ‘pure,’ and so on. Herein, the connection is that pure, not-too-thick water, and similarly, what is attached to the body and unbroken—such as the discharge from teeth, etc., and salt, etc., from dung—are permissible. Herein, ‘pure’ means unmixed with dust, dirt, or other flavors. ‘Not-too-thick’ means that which, like thick water in a plowed field, does not stick to the mouth or hands. ‘Unbroken’ means what has not become separated from the body by being cut off. ‘Discharge from teeth, eyes, and ears’ is a determinative compound, as they are parts of the body. ‘Salt’ refers to that which has arisen from the body. ‘Mucus’ means nasal mucus. What is severed should not be accepted.

111. Idāni “gūthā”tiādinā kālodissaṃ dasseti. Tathāvidheti sappadaṭṭhakkhaṇādike tathāvidhe kāle. Tathā tādiso vidho kālo etassāti bahubbīhi. Seveyyāti sevanaṃ kareyya, paribhuñjeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Asante kappakāraketi ettha dubbacopi asamatthopi kappiyakārako asantapakkheyeva tiṭṭhatīti veditabbo. Kālodissattā pana chārikāya asati alladāruṃ rukkhato chinditvā kātuṃ, mattikāya asati bhūmiṃ khaṇitvāpi mattikaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

111. Now, with ‘feces,’ and so on, a specific time is shown. ‘In such a case’ refers to such a time, like the moment of being bitten by a snake, and so forth. ‘A time of such a kind belongs to this’ is a relative compound. ‘One should use’ means ‘one should make use of’ or ‘one should consume’—this is what is meant. Regarding ‘when there is no steward,’ it should be understood that even a steward who is difficult to instruct or incapable is considered to be in the category of ‘unavailable.’ However, because of the specific nature of the time, if there is no charcoal, it is permissible to cut green wood from a tree to make it; and if there is no clay, it is permissible to dig into the ground to obtain clay.

112. Durūpaciṇṇeti duṭṭhuṃ upaciṇṇaṃ āmaṭṭhaṃ durūpaciṇṇaṃ. Sace bhikkhu appaṭiggahitaṃ sāmisaṃ bhājanaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānato apanetvā āmasati, pidhānaṃ āmasati, upari ṭhitakacavarādiṃ chaḍḍeti, tatthajātakaphaliniyā sākhāya vā valliyā vā gahetvā vā cāleti, durūpaciṇṇaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmiṃ dukkaṭanti sambandho. Phalarukkhaṃ pana apassayituṃ vā tattha kaṇṭakaṃ vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Araññe patitaambaphalādiṃ “sāmaṇerassa dassāmī”ti āharitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Rajokiṇṇeti rajasā okiṇṇe, tasmiṃ pattādike yaṃ kiñci paṭiggaṇhato vinayadukkaṭaṃ hotīti attho. Sace piṇḍāya carantassa patte rajaṃ patati, paṭiggahetvā bhikkhā gaṇhitabbā[M 0.0311]. “Paṭiggahetvā dethā”ti vuttepi ākiranti, hatthato amocenteneva paṭiggāhāpakassa santikaṃ netvā paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Sace mahāvāto tato tato rajaṃ pāteti, na sakkā hoti bhikkhaṃ gahetuṃ, “anupasampannassa dassāmī”ti suddhacittena ābhogaṃ katvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ pana tena dinnaṃ vā vissāsena vā paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

112. ‘Improperly handled’ means wrongly handled or touched. If a monk moves a food-bowl that has not been accepted from its place and handles it, touches the lid, discards refuse placed on top, or grasps and shakes a fruit-bearing branch or vine growing there, it is called ‘improperly handled.’ The connection is that in such a case, it is a ‘dukkaṭa’ offense. However, it is permissible to lean against a fruit tree or to tie a thorn there. In the wilderness, if a fruit like a mango has fallen, one may bring it with the thought, ‘I will give it to a novice,’ and offer it. ‘Dust-covered’ means covered with dust. The meaning is that if one receives anything like a bowl in such a state, it incurs a Vinaya ‘dukkaṭa’ offense. If dust falls into a bowl while one is going for alms, the almsfood should be accepted. Even if, when told, ‘Accept this and give it,’ they scatter the alms, one should, without letting go of the bowl from one's hand, bring it near the offerer and accept it. If a strong wind scatters dust from all sides, making it impossible to accept alms, one may, with a pure mind, make an intention thinking, ‘I will give it to an unordained person,’ and take it. Then, if it is given by that person or received with trust, it is permissible to consume it.

Athāti vakkhamānārambhe. Uggahappaṭiggaheti uggahitthāti uggaho, uggahitaṃ, tassa paṭiggaho, tasmiṃ. Appaṭiggahitabhāvaṃ jānato attanā eva uggahetvā gahaṇeti adhippāyo. Mātāpitūnaṃ atthāya pana appaṭiggahetvā telādīni, chāyatthāya sākhādīni vā gahetvā pacchato bhuñjitukāmatāya paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Ucchuādīsu phālitesu malaṃ na paññāyati, mūlabhesajjādīni pisantānaṃ vā koṭṭentānaṃ vā nisadanisadapotakaudukkhalamusalāni khīyanti, dantantare laggaṃ sukhumaāmisaṃ hoti, raso na paññāyati, abbohārikaṃ. Antovuttheti [V 0.0266] akappiyakuṭiyā chadanabbhantare vuttheti attho. Sayaṃpakketi attanā yattha katthaci pakke. Sace vāsiādiṃ tāpetvā takkādīsu pakkhipati, ettāvatāpi sāmapākato na muccati. Purimakālikadvaye punapākañhi ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ bhikkhuno pacituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sacepissa uṇhayāguyā sulasipaṇṇādīni vā siṅgiveraṃ vā pakkhipanti, cāletuṃ na vaṭṭati. Uttaṇḍulaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā pidahituṃ na vaṭṭati. Antopakketi akappiyakuṭiyā anto pakke. Sabbattha dukkaṭanti sambandho.

‘Now’ is at the beginning of what is to be said. ‘Grasping and accepting’ means the acceptance of what has been grasped. The intention is the taking of it by grasping it oneself, while knowing its unaccepted state. For the sake of one's parents, however, it is permissible to take things like oil and so forth without formal acceptance, or branches and so forth for shade, and then, desiring to partake of them later, to accept and consume them. In sugarcane and the like, when split, no impurity is apparent. When grinding or pounding root medicines, etc., the grinding stone, the upper grinding stone, mortar, and pestle wear out. Fine food particles stuck between the teeth are subtle food, the taste of which is not discernible; this is insignificant. ‘Dwelling inside’ means dwelling inside an unsuitable hut, within the roof covering. ‘Self-cooked’ refers to something cooked by oneself, wherever it may be. If one heats a tool like an adze and places it in whey and so forth, even then, it is not freed from being considered self-cooked. Indeed, apart from re-cooking items from the first two time-categories, it is not permissible for a monk to cook any food. If they add basil leaves or ginger or the like to his hot gruel, it is not permissible for him to stir it. Having received rice with uncooked grains, it is not permissible to cover it. ‘Cooked inside’ means cooked inside an unsuitable hut. The connection is that in all cases, there is a ‘dukkaṭa’ offense.

Paṭiggāhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Acceptance is concluded.

10. Akappiyamaṃsaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Exposition of Unallowable Meat

113-4. Manussahatthiassānañca [M 0.0312] …pe… uragassa ca yaṃ maṃsañca, yaṃ uddissakatamaṃsañca, appaṭivekkhitaṃ yañca maṃsaṃ, tesu maṃsesūti evaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo. Tattha sīsagīvātaraṅgena carantā acchavisesāva taracchā. Uragassāti iminā sabbāpi dīghajāti saṅgahitā. Uddissakatamaṃsanti bhikkhuṃ uddisitvā kataṃ uddissakataṃ, tañca taṃ maṃsañca. Ettha ca maṃsa-ggahaṇena macchānampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ upalakkhaṇavasena, ca-saddena vā. Pañcasupi sahadhammikesu yaṃ kiñci uddissakataṃ sabbesampi na kappati, tampi adiṭṭhaasutaaparisaṅkitatāya tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ vaṭṭati. Appaṭivekkhitanti anupaparikkhitaṃ, anāpucchitanti attho. Āpattibhīrukena hi rūpaṃ sallakkhentenāpi pucchitvā paṭiggahetabbaṃ paribhuñjitabbañca. Manussānaṃ maṃsesu thullaccayanti yojanā. Thūlo accayo etthāti rasse, dvitte ca thullaccayaṃ. Pārājikasaṅghādisesehi ṭhapetvā ito adhikaṃ vajjaṃ natthi. Sesesūti avasesesu ekādasasu.

113-4. The meaning should be understood by applying this to the following kinds of meat: the flesh of humans, elephants, horses… and so on… and the flesh of a snake, and whatever flesh is specially prepared, and any flesh not properly examined. Herein, hyenas are a kind of bear that move with a wave-like motion of their head and neck. By the term ‘snake,’ all long-bodied creatures are included. ‘Specially prepared flesh’ is flesh prepared having designated a monk; it is that specially prepared meat. And here, by the mention of ‘flesh,’ the inclusion of fish should be understood by way of indication, or by the word ‘and.’ Among the five kinds of co-religionists, anything specially prepared for any of them is not permissible for any of them. However, even that is allowable if it is pure in three aspects: not seen, not heard, and not suspected to have been prepared for one. ‘Not properly examined’ means not scrutinized or not inquired about. For one who fears an offense, even while observing its appearance, one should inquire before accepting and consuming it. The connection is that regarding human flesh, a grave offense is incurred. ‘Grave offense’ (`thullaccaya`) is so called because the transgression is gross; whether in its short or doubled form, it is a grave offense. Apart from offenses of defeat and of formal meeting of the Sangha, there is no fault greater than this. ‘In the remaining cases’ refers to the other eleven.

115. Idāni manussādīnaṃ aṭṭhiādīnipi akappiyānīti dassetuṃ “aṭṭhipī”tiādimāha. Pi-saddo “lohita”ntiādīsupi anuvattetabbo. Esanti manussādīnaṃ dasannaṃ. Vasāsu pana ekā manussavasā na vaṭṭati. Khīrādīsu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Uddissakataṃyeva [V 0.0267] sacittakanti yojanā. Sacittakanti uddissakatabhāvajānanacittena saha vattatīti sacittakaṃ. Vatthuvītikkamavijānanacittena hi sacittakattaṃ. Ettha ca sacittakattaṃ āpattiyā eva, na ca maṃsassa, tathāpi maṃsasīsena āpatti eva vuttāti viññātabbanti.

115. Now, to show that even the bones and other parts of humans and so on are unallowable, it is said, ‘even bones,’ and so on. The word ‘even’ should also be applied to terms like ‘blood’ and so on. ‘These’ refers to the ten kinds, of humans and so on. However, among the fats, only human fat is not allowed. Among milk and similar substances, there is nothing declared unallowable. The connection is that only what is specially prepared is a conscious offense. ‘Conscious offense’ (`sacittaka`) means what occurs together with the mind that knows the state of being specially prepared. The state of being a conscious offense arises from the mind that knows the transgression regarding the object. And here, the state of being a conscious offense applies only to the offense, not to the meat itself; nevertheless, it should be understood that the offense is stated under the heading of meat.

Akappiyamaṃsaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Unallowable Meat is concluded.

11. Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Rules on Forfeiture

116-7. Rūpiyena [M 0.0313] arūpiyaṃ rūpiyañca itarena rūpiyañca parivatteyyāti sambandho. Tattha rūpiyenāti rūpiyasaṅkhātena nissaggiyavatthunā. Arūpiyanti arūpiyasaṅkhātaṃ dukkaṭavatthuṃ kappiyavatthuñca. Itarenāti arūpiyena. Nissaggīti nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, pubbabhāge kattabbassa vinayakammassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nissaggo assa atthīti nissaggi, kiṃ taṃ? Pācittiyaṃ. Rūpiyassa mūlaggahaṇe pana rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

116-7. The connection is: ‘One might exchange a monetary item for a non-monetary one, and a monetary one for the other.’ Herein, ‘with a monetary item’ refers to an object designated as monetary, which is an item requiring forfeiture. ‘A non-monetary one’ refers to a non-monetary item, which may be an item entailing a `dukkaṭa` offense or a permissible item. ‘With the other’ means with a non-monetary item. ‘Requiring forfeiture’ (`nissaggi`): forfeiture (`nissagga`) is relinquishment (`nissajjana`); this is the name for a disciplinary act to be performed in the preliminary stage. It is called `nissaggi` because it has (`ī`) forfeiture (`nissagga`). What is it? A `pācittiya` offense. However, in the case of accepting the value of a monetary item, it is a `nissaggiya pācittiya` offense under the training rule on accepting monetary items.

Idāni rūpiyādiṃ dassetuṃ “idhā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kahā…pe… māsakaṃ idha rūpiyanti sambandho. Tattha kahāpaṇo nāma suvaṇṇamayo vā rajatamayo vā etarahi pakatikahāpaṇo vā. Sajjhūti rajataṃ. Siṅgīti suvaṇṇabhedo, tathāpi cettha sāmaññena suvaṇṇamadhippetaṃ. Vohārūpagamāsakanti vohāraṃ kayavikkayaṃ upagacchatīti vohārūpagaṃ, tañca taṃ māsakañca. Taṃ pana samuṭṭhāpitarūpañca asamuṭṭhāpitarūpañca lohadāruādimayaṃ vuccati. Idha rūpiyanti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade rūpiyaṃ nāmāti attho. Vatthamuttādi kappaṃ dukkaṭavatthuñca itaranti yojanā. Tattha vatthañca muttā ca ādi yassāti samāso. Ādi-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo “vatthādi muttādī”ti. Tattha paṭhamena ādi-saddena kappāsasuttāparaṇṇādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci kappiyavatthuṃ, dutiyena maṇi saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ lohitaṅko masāragallaṃ sattadhaññāni dāsidāsakhettavatthupupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti idaṃ dukkaṭavatthuṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vatthādikappiyavatthuṃ, muttādidukkaṭavatthuñca itaraṃ aññaṃ arūpiyaṃ nāmāti attho.

Now, to show what constitutes money and the like, the text begins with 'here,' and so on. Herein, 'a kahāpaṇa...pe... a māsaka' is connected with 'money here.' Herein, a kahāpaṇa is one made of gold or silver, or nowadays a common kahāpaṇa. 'Sajjhū' is silver. 'Siṅgī' is a type of gold, yet here gold is generally intended. 'Vohārūpagamāsaka' means that which enters into trade, i.e., buying and selling, and that is a māsaka. It is said to be of manufactured or unmanufactured form, made of metal, wood, and so on. 'Money here' means 'what is called money in this training rule.' The construction is: 'cloth, pearls, and so on are allowable, and the other things are objects of a dukkaṭa offense.' Here, 'vatthamuttādi' is a compound meaning 'cloth, pearls, and the like.' The word 'ādi' (and so on) should be applied to each: 'cloth and so on,' 'pearls and so on.' Here, by the first 'and so on,' any allowable item is included, such as cotton thread, other grains, and so on. By the second, it includes objects of a dukkaṭa offense: gems, conch shells, stone, coral, rubies, cat's-eye gems, the seven kinds of grain, male and female slaves, fields, land, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so on. The meaning is that allowable items beginning with cloth, and other items beginning with pearls which are objects of a dukkaṭa offense, are called 'non-monetary'.

118. Ettāvatā [V 0.0268] rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ dassetvā idāni kappiyabhaṇḍe kayavikkayaṃ dassetumāha “ima”ntiādi. Tattha [M 0.0314] “imaṃ gahetvā imaṃ dehi, imaṃ kara, imaṃ ānayā”ti vā “imaṃ bhutvā imaṃ dehi, imaṃ kara, imaṃ ānayā”ti vā “imaṃ demi, imaṃ dehi, imaṃ kara, imaṃ ānayā”ti vā kayavikkaye samāpanne nissaggīti yojanā. Tattha imanti taṇḍulādiṃ. Bhutvāti odanādiṃ bhuñjitvā. Imaṃ dehīti etaṃ vatthādikaṃ dehi. Imaṃ karāti etaṃ rajanapacanādiṃ karohi. Imaṃ ānayāti etaṃ rajanakaṭṭhādiṃ ānehi. Imaṃ demīti etaṃ vatthādikaṃ tava demi. Samāpanneti kate. Tasmā kappiyaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ parivattentena aññātakehi saddhiṃ “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti, “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ, “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti vadato kayavikkayanti vuttā tisso āpattiyo. Mātāpitūhi pana saddhiṃ kayavikkayamattaṃ mocentena parivattetabbaṃ. Ayañhi kayavikkayo ṭhapetvā pañcasahadhammike avasesehi gihipabbajitehi na vaṭṭati. Sace pana navakammāni kāreti, aṭṭhakathāpamāṇena pācittiyamattaṃ desetabbaṃ.

118. Having thus explained transactions with money, now, to explain the buying and selling of allowable goods, he says, 'this,' and so on. Here, the construction is that when buying and selling is concluded with phrases such as 'Take this and give this, do this, or bring this,' or 'Having consumed this, give this, do this, or bring this,' or 'I give this; give this, do this, or bring this,' it requires forfeiture. Herein, 'this' refers to rice and the like. 'Having consumed' means having eaten cooked rice and the like. 'Give this' means give this cloth or similar item. 'Do this' means do this dyeing or cooking. 'Bring this' means bring this dye-wood or the like. 'I give this' means I give this cloth or similar item to you. 'Concluded' means done. Therefore, for one exchanging allowable goods with those who are not relatives, saying 'give this' is an improper request (viññatti); saying 'take this' is a destruction of what is given in faith; and saying 'with this, give this' is buying and selling—thus, three offenses are stated. With one's parents, however, one should exchange while avoiding mere buying and selling. For this buying and selling is not permissible with the remaining householders and renunciants, except for the five kinds of co-residents. But if one has new construction work done, only a pācittiya offense should be confessed, according to the commentary.

119-120. Idāni pariṇāmanavasena āpattibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “attano”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – saṅghassa nataṃ lābhaṃ attano pariṇāmeyya, nissaggi. Aññato puggalassa pariṇāmeyya, pācitti. Aññassa saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā pariṇāmeyya, dukkaṭaṃ. Aññassa puggalassa vā cetiyassa vā nataṃ lābhaṃ attano vā saṅghassa vā aññapuggalassa vā aññacetiyassa vā pariṇāmeyya, dukkaṭanti yojanā. Tattha natanti kāyena vā vacasā vā ninnaṃ kataṃ. Lābhanti labhitabbaṃ cīvarādi. Aññato aññasmiṃ puggale vā cetiye vā, cetiye pana dukkaṭaṃ. Aññassāti cetiyādino antamaso sunakhassa. Aññato vāti cetiyādimhi vā. Saṅghassāti pana idaṃ kākakkhigoḷakañāyena “nataṃ pariṇāmeyyā”ti ubhayattha parivattati. Nissaṭṭhaṃ sakasaññāya na [M 0.0315] dadeyya vā, dukkaṭanti sambandho. Aññathā aññena pakārena, theyyasaññāya na dadeyya ceti vuttaṃ hoti. Itaranti vatthuvasena aññaṃ pārājikaṃ thullaccayaṃ dukkaṭañca hotīti attho.

119-120. Now, to explain the different offenses by way of transference, the text begins with 'one's own,' and so on. Here is the meaning in brief: if one transfers a gain intended for the Sangha to oneself, it requires forfeiture. If one transfers it to another individual, it is a pācittiya offense. If one transfers it to another Sangha or to a shrine, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If one transfers a gain intended for another individual or a shrine to oneself, to the Sangha, to another individual, or to another shrine, it is a dukkaṭa offense—this is the construction. Herein, 'intended' means made inclined by body or speech. 'Gain' means what is to be received, such as robes. If one transfers it to another individual, it is a pācittiya offense. To another Sangha or shrine, but in the case of a shrine, it is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Another' means from a shrine and so on, down to even a dog. 'From another' means from a shrine or the like. As for 'for the Sangha,' this, by the maxim of the crow's eye, revolves to connect with both instances of 'should transfer what is intended.' The connection is: if one does not give what has been relinquished, perceiving it as one's own, it is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Otherwise' means in another way; that is to say, if one does not give it with the perception of theft. The meaning of 'other' is that, depending on the object, it becomes another offense: pārājika, thullaccaya, or dukkaṭa.

Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Nissaggiya Rules is concluded.

12. Pācittiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pācittiya Rules

121. Musā [V 0.0269] …pe… haraṇeti nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tassa “pācitti vuttā”ti iminā sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha. Musāvādeti nipātena saddhiṃ tappuriso. Pubbepi jānitvā vacanakkhaṇepi jānantassa musābhaṇananimittanti attho. Bhaṇanañca nāma idha abhūtassa vā bhūtataṃ, bhūtassa vā abhūtataṃ katvā kāyena vā vācāya vā viññāpanappayogo. Pārājikasaṅghādisesācāravipattiyo amūlikāya codentassa yathākkamaṃ saṅghādisesapācittiyadukkaṭāni. Anupadhāretvā sahasā bhaṇantassa, “aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññaṃ bhaṇantassa yassa bhaṇati, so na suṇāti, tassa ca anāpatti.

121. In 'false speech...pe... stealing,' the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; its connection is with the phrase 'a pācittiya is declared.' This applies everywhere. 'Musāvāde' (in false speech) is a tatpurisa compound with the particle 'musā.' The meaning is: it is a cause for uttering a falsehood for one who knows it beforehand and also knows it at the moment of speaking. And 'uttering,' in this context, is the act of communication, by body or by speech, making what is not true appear true, or what is true appear not true. For one who groundlessly accuses another of failures in conduct such as pārājika, saṅghādisesa, or other misconduct, the offenses are, respectively, saṅghādisesa, pācittiya, and dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one who speaks hastily without consideration, for one who intends to say one thing but says another, or if the person to whom one speaks does not hear.

Omasati amanāpatāya kaṇṇesu vijjhati viya etena, omasati vāti omaso, so cāyaṃ vādoca, tasmiṃ. Dīgho pana gāthābandhavasena. Evaṃ sabbattha. Hīnukkaṭṭhesu ca jātināmagottavayakammasippaābādhaliṅgakilesaāpattiakkosasaṅkhātesu dasasu bhūtena vā abhūtena vā “khattiyosi, caṇḍālosī”tiādinā kāyena vā vācāya vā anaññāpadesena bhikkhuno khuṃsetukāmatāya akkosavacaneti attho. “Santi idhekacce caṇḍālā”tiādinā aññāpadesena vā “corosi, vikārīsi, mātughātakosī”tiādīhi pāḷimuttapadehi vā bhikkhussa, yathā vā [M 0.0316] tathā vā anupasampannaṃ, parammukhā pana sabbampi akkosantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Kevalaṃ davakamyatāya vadato pana sabbattha dubbhāsitaṃ.

One disparages (omasati) with this, or it disparages, as if piercing the ears with unpleasantness; thus it is called disparagement (omaso). And this refers to speech. The long vowel, however, is due to the meter of the verse. This applies everywhere. The meaning is: abusive speech, with the intention to humiliate a monk, concerning the ten categories of inferior and superior—namely birth, name, clan, age, occupation, craft, illness, physical characteristics, defilements, and offenses—whether true or untrue, using words like, 'You are a khattiya,' 'You are an outcaste,' and so on, by body or by speech, without indirect reference. Or, by indirect reference, as in, 'There are some outcastes here,' or with words not found in the Pāli canon, such as, 'You are a thief,' 'You are deformed,' 'You are a matricide,' and so on, whether to a monk or, in any case, to one not fully ordained. However, for one who insults any of these behind their back, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But for one who speaks merely with a desire for jest, it is in all cases wrong speech (dubbhāsita).

Pesuññaharaṇeti pisuṇassa bhāvo pesuññaṃ. Attano piyakamyatāya vā parassa paresu bhedādhippāyena vā jātiādīhi omasantassa bhikkhuno vacanaṃ sutvā bhikkhussa tassa pesuññassa haraṇe. Anupasampannassa haraṇe dukkaṭaṃ. Padaṃ padaṃ padaso, vicchāyaṃ so, koṭṭhāsena koṭṭhāsenāti attho. Saṅgītittayāruḷho tipiṭakadhammo, anāruḷho ca rājovādādiko dhammo nāma, tena saha padasoti nipātassa tatiyātappuriso. Padasodhammeti ekakkharādinā koṭṭhāsena koṭṭhāsena anupasampannena saddhiṃ yathāvuttadhammabhaṇaneti attho. Padasodhammabhaṇanañhi padasodhamma-saddena upacārena vuttaṃ. Anupasampannena saddhiṃ ekato uddesaggahaṇe sajjhāyakaraṇe, taṃsantike uddesaggahaṇādike ca tena saddhiṃ ekato yebhuyyena paguṇaṃ ganthaṃ bhaṇantassa osārentassa khalitaṭṭhāne “evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti ekato bhaṇantassapi anāpatti.

In 'carrying of slander': slander (pesuñña) is the state of a slanderer (pisuṇa). It is the carrying of that slander to a monk, after having heard the words of another monk who was disparaging someone regarding birth and so on, either from a desire to endear oneself or with the intention of causing division between that person and others. Carrying it to one who is not fully ordained is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Padaso' means word by word, syllable by syllable, portion by portion. The Dhamma that was established in the three recitations is the Tipiṭaka Dhamma, and that which was not established, such as advice to kings and so on, is also called Dhamma. 'Padaso' with that (Dhamma) is a tatiyā-tappurisa compound with the particle. 'Padasodhamma' means reciting the aforementioned Dhamma portion by portion, beginning with single syllables, together with one who is not fully ordained. The 'reciting of padasodhamma' is spoken of metaphorically by the term 'padasodhamma.' There is no offense in taking up a recitation or making a rehearsal together with one who is not fully ordained, nor in taking up a recitation and so on in their presence, nor when reciting a text that is mostly familiar together with them, bringing it to a conclusion, and, when there is a mistake, reciting it together, saying, 'Recite it like this.'

Antamaso [V 0.0270] vatthādinā yena kenaci sabbacchannaṃ chadanaṃ anāhacca diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhenāpi sabbaparicchinnaṃ yebhuyyenachannaṃ yebhuyyenaparicchinnañca senāsanaṃ agāranti adhippetaṃ. Tatraṭṭho pana bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā antamaso pārājikavatthubhūto tiracchānagatopi antamaso tadahujātā itthīpi upacārato agāra-saddena vuccati. Saha agārenāti sāgāro, bhikkhu. Upacāreneva ca pana anupasampannena, mātugāmena ca saha seyyakappanaṃ sāgārabhāvo nāmāti gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghasammataṃ senāsanapaññāpakādibhedaṃ upasampannaṃ ayasakāmā hutvā bhikkhūhi yena ca ujjhāpenti avajānāpenti avaññāya olokāpenti, lāmakato [M 0.0317] vā cintāpenti, taṃ vacanaṃ ujjhāpanakaṃ. Yena khīyanti sabbattha tassa avaṇṇaṃ pakāsenti, taṃ khīyanaṃ.

Even if covered by anything such as a cloth, without disturbing any covering, a dwelling enclosed all around by a wall one and a half cubits high, mostly covered or mostly enclosed, is intended by the term 'dwelling.' Therein, except for a bhikkhu, even an animal that is the basis for a pārājika offense, or even a female born that very day, is conventionally called a 'dwelling.' 'With a dwelling' (`saha agārena`) means `sāgāra`; this refers to a bhikkhu. Furthermore, it should be understood that arranging a sleeping place together with an unordained person or a woman constitutes 'being with a dwelling.' That speech by which bhikkhus, desiring ill-repute, cause an ordained person—one approved by the Saṅgha, such as a lodging designator—to be complained about, despised, looked upon with contempt, or thought of as base, is 'complaining.' That by which they vex him, spreading his dispraise everywhere, is 'vexation.'

122. Talanti hatthatalamadhippetaṃ. Taggahaṇena pana kāyova talaṃ. Sattīti kāyappaṭibaddhā satti āvudhaviseso, upalakkhaṇattā pana sabbampi kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ satti. Talañca satti ca talasatti. Idha pana kopena bhikkhussa talasattiuggiraṇaṃ talasatti. Sace pana viraddho pahāraṃ deti, na paharitukāmatāya dinnattā dukkaṭaṃ, paharitukāmatāya pācittiyaṃ, anupasampanne dukkaṭaṃ, mokkhādhippāyassa anāpatti.

122. 'Tala' is intended to mean the palm of the hand. However, by this term, the body itself is also taken as 'tala.' 'Satti' is a type of weapon attached to the body; however, by extension, anything attached to the body is a 'satti.' 'Tala' and 'satti' together are 'talasatti.' Here, however, a bhikkhu's raising of the 'talasatti' out of anger is 'talasatti.' If, having missed, he gives a blow, it is a dukkaṭa offense because it was not given with the intention to strike. If given with the intention to strike, it is a pācittiya offense. Against an unordained person, it is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense if the intention is for release.

Paññattena vadato upasampannassa vā tena vuccamānadhammassa vā anādarakaraṇaṃ anādaro. Anupasampannassa tena vuccamānassa vā upasampannena, parena vā apaññattena vā vuccamānassa anādare dukkaṭaṃ.
