Showing disregard for an ordained person who speaks according to what is prescribed, or for the Dhamma being spoken by him, is 'disregard.' In showing disregard for an unordained person, or for what is said by him, or for what is said by an ordained person, or by another, or for what is said not according to what is prescribed, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

“Ūnavasso tvaṃ maññe”tiādinā bhikkhuno kukkuccassa uppādanaṃ anupasampannassa dukkaṭaṃ.

Causing scruples to arise in a bhikkhu by saying, 'You are, I suppose, deficient in rains,' and so on, is a pācittiya offense. In the case of an unordained person, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Anāpucchā gāmappavesaneti pakativacanena pucchitumanurūpaṃ antoupacārasīmāya dassanūpacāre bhikkhuṃ disvā “vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchāmī”ti anāpucchitvā vikāle gāmappavesane. Dīgho pana sandhivasena. Āpadāsu anāpatti.

'Entering the village without asking' means: when it is appropriate to ask a bhikkhu in the normal way, having seen one within sight-range inside the inner boundary, one enters the village at an improper time without asking him, 'I ask permission to enter the village at an improper time.' The long vowel, however, is due to euphonic combination. There is no offense in times of calamity.

Paramparabhojaneti paro ca paro ca paramparā ma-kāro sandhivasena, tasmā paramparā uppattavisayaapādānavacanaṃ, parato parato laddhā bhuñjaneti attho. Ayamettha adhippāyo – pañcahi [V 0.0271] bhojanehi nāmaṃ gahetvā nimantitassa yena yena paṭhamaṃ nimantito, tassa tassa bhojanato uppaṭipāṭiyā, “mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī”ti vā “vikappemī”ti [M 0.0318] vā ādinā sammukhā vā parammukhā vā avikappetvā vā aññato aññato pañcabhojanādīni laddhā bhuñjamāneti. Gilānacīvaradānacīvarakārasamaye anāpatti.

'Paramparabhojana': 'one after another' is `paramparā`; the letter 'm' is due to euphonic combination. Therefore, `paramparā` is a word in the ablative case indicating the sphere of origin. The meaning is: eating after having received from one after another. Here, this is the intended meaning: for one who has been invited by name for the five kinds of food, to eat the five kinds of food and so on, having received them from another place, out of the proper order of the meal from the person by whom one was first invited, without having transferred it either face-to-face or in one's absence by saying, 'I give you my expectation of a meal,' or 'I transfer it,' etc. There is no offense during a time of illness, a time of giving robes, or a time of making robes.

123. Seyyaṃ senāsanāni vā anuddharitvā gamaneti sambandho. Vā-saddo samuccaye. Tattha “bhisi cimilikā uttarattharaṇaṃ bhūmattharaṇaṃ taṭṭikā cammakkhaṇḍo nisīdanaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāro”ti (pāci. 116) vuttāsu dasasu seyyāsu ekampi attano vassaggane gahetvā saṅghike sabbappaṭicchanne gutte senāsane santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā yathā ṭhapitaṃ upacikādīhi na khajjati, tathā ṭhapanavasena anuddharitvā parikkhittassa ārāmassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa upacāraṃ atikkamitvā gamane ca, tathā mañcapīṭhatisikocchasaṅkhātāni senāsanāni vassakāle ajjhokāse santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā anupasampannena anuddharitvā thāmamajjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātaṃ atikkamitvā gamane cāti attho. Yathāvuttato pana aññattha dukkaṭaṃ.

123. The connection is with 'leaving without putting away bedding or lodgings.' The word 'vā' is used inclusively. Among the ten kinds of bedding mentioned—'a mattress, felt rug, upper covering, ground covering, mat, piece of leather, sitting cloth, under-covering, a spread of grass, a spread of leaves'—if one takes any of these for one’s own rainy-season share, spreads it or has it spread in a Saṅgha lodging that is completely covered and protected, and then leaves without putting it away in such a manner that it is not eaten by termites and other creatures, as it was placed, having gone beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery or the precincts of an unenclosed one; and similarly, in the case of lodgings designated as beds, chairs, bolsters, and wicker chairs, having spread them or had them spread in the open during the rainy season, one leaves without putting them away, having gone beyond the range of a clod-throw by a man of average strength—this is the meaning. However, in other cases than as stated, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Itthiyā addhānagamaneti “gacchāma bhagini, gacchāma ayyā”ti aññamaññaṃ saṃvidahitvā “ajja vā sve vā”tiādinā niyamitakālavisaṅketaṃ akatvāpi dvāravisaṅketaṃ maggavisaṅketaṃ katvāpi itthiyā saddhiṃ addhānamaggagamaneti attho.

'Traveling on a journey with a woman' means: having made an arrangement with each other, saying, 'Let us go, sister,' or 'Let us go, noble lady,' and then traveling on a long road with a woman, even without having made an appointment for a specific time such as 'today or tomorrow,' but having made an appointment regarding the gate or the path. This is the meaning.

Ekekāya nisīdaneti ekena ekāti ekekā, tassā nisajjāyāti attho. Ekena saha ekissā nisajjaṃ vinā ekāya saha ekassa nisajjaṃ nāma natthīti ekāya saha ekassa nisajjāyaṃ sati nisinnassa bhikkhuno pācittiyanti adhippāyo. “Ekāyekanisīdane”ti vā pāṭho.

'Sitting one-on-one' means one with one, that is, the act of sitting with her. There is no sitting of one male with one female without the sitting of one female with one male. The intended meaning is that when a bhikkhu sits with a woman one-on-one, it is a pācittiya offense. Alternatively, the reading is 'ekāyekanisīdane.'

124. Rūpādīnaṃ [M 0.0319] upasaṃhārena, bhayānakakathākathanena vā upasampannassa bhiṃsāpane. Anupasampannassa dukkaṭaṃ.

124. It is an offense for frightening an ordained person by presenting sights and so on, or by telling a frightening story. In the case of an unordained person, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Ākoṭane [V 0.0272] upasampannassa antamaso uppalapattenāpi pahāradāne. Anupasampannassa antamaso tiracchānagatassapi dukkaṭaṃ. Mokkhādhippāyassa anāpatti.

It is an offense for striking, which is giving a blow to an ordained person, even with a lotus petal. In the case of an unordained person, or even an animal, it is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense if the intention is for release.

Saṅghamajjhe vinayadharena anuyuñjiyamānassa pucchitato aññassa vādo aññena aññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ aññavādo. Tatheva pucchiyamānassa akathetukāmatāya vihesanaṃ tuṇhībhāvo vihesā. Aññavādakassa vihesakassa ca ñattidutiyakammena aññavādakavihesakakamme kate puna aññavāde vihesāya pācittiyaṃ. Anāropite pana kamme dukkaṭaṃ. Kiñci vītikkamaṃ disvā “āvuso, idaṃ nāma tayā kata”nti vutte taṃ na kathetukāmo tuṇhībhūto saṅghaṃ vihesetīti vihesako. Anācāraṃ ācaritvā saṅghamajjhe āpattiyā, vatthunā vā anuyuñjiyamāne taṃ akathetukāmo “ko āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno”tiādinā nayena aññehi vacanehi taṃ vacanaṃ paṭicchādento yo aññaṃ vadati, ayaṃ aññavādako nāma.

In the midst of the Saṅgha, when one is being questioned by a Vinaya-holder, a speech other than what was asked, or responding to one thing with another, is 'evasive speech.' Similarly, when one is being questioned, vexing by being silent out of an unwillingness to speak is 'vexation.' For one who engages in evasive speech or vexation, after the formal act with motion and one announcement has been carried out regarding evasive speech and vexation, if they again engage in evasive speech or vexation, it is a pācittiya offense. If the formal act has not yet been imposed, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If someone sees a transgression and says, 'Friend, this was done by you,' but the other, unwilling to speak, remains silent and thus vexes the Saṅgha, this is a 'vexatious one.' If one behaves improperly and, when questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha about an offense or its basis, does not wish to speak and conceals the matter with other statements like, 'Who is at fault? At fault in what?'—one who speaks otherwise in this way is called an 'evasive speaker.'

Duṭṭhullaṃ nāma pārājikasaṅghādisesā, idha pana saṅghādisesova. Pakāso ca chādo ca pakāsachādo, duṭṭhullassa pakāsachādoti tappuriso. Abhiṇhāpattikassa bhikkhuno āyatiṃ saṃvaratthāya āpattipariyantaṃ kulapariyantañca katvā vā akatvā vā tikkhattuṃ apaloketvā kātabbaṃ. Bhikkhusammutiṃ ṭhapetvā anupasampannassa “ayaṃ asuciṃ mocetvā saṅghādisesaṃ āpanno”tiādinā nayena vatthunā saddhiṃ āpattiṃ ghaṭetvā tassa duṭṭhullassa pakāsane ārocane ca, tasseva yena kenaci upāyena ñatvā chādane ca, aduṭṭhullārocane chādane [M 0.0320] ca, anupasampannassa pana purimapañcamasikkhāpade itarā duṭṭhullepi dukkaṭaṃ.

A 'gross offense' means a pārājika or a saṅghādisesa. Here, however, it is only a saṅghādisesa. 'Disclosure' and 'concealment' is `pakāsachādo`; 'the disclosure and concealment of a gross offense' is a `tappurisa` compound. For a bhikkhu who is a frequent offender, for the sake of future restraint, whether or not a limit on offenses and a limit on families has been set, a formal act should be carried out after announcing it three times. Without the consent of the bhikkhus, it is an offense to disclose or announce that gross offense to an unordained person—for instance, 'This one, having emitted impurity, has committed a saṅghādisesa,' thus connecting the offense with its basis; and to conceal it, having learned of it by some means. It is also an offense to announce or conceal what is not a gross offense. However, to inform an unordained person about other gross offenses related to the first five training rules is also a dukkaṭa offense.

Hāsodaketi ettha hāse udaketi padavibhāgo veditabbo. Yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena hasādhippāyassa upakacchakādīsu hāse phusane. Hāsanimittañhi phusanaṃ hāso. Anupasampanne dukkaṭaṃ. Udake hāseti uparigopphake udake hasādhippāyassa ummujjananimujjanena kīḷāya. Kīḷā hi idha hāsoti vutto. Nāvāya kīḷato, hatthādinā kaṭṭhādinā vā udakaṃ hanato antamaso bhājanagatakañjikādīnipi khipanakīḷāya kīḷato dukkaṭaṃ. Ahasādhippāyassa anāpatti.

Herein, in 'hāsodake', the division of words should be understood as 'hāse' and 'udake'. 'Hāse' means in touching, in places such as the armpits, with any bodily limb, with the intention of amusement. For touching for the sake of amusement is 'hāso'. For one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing. 'Hāse in udake' means playing by diving and surfacing with the intention of amusement in water above the ankles. For here, play is called 'hāso'. For one who plays in a boat, or strikes the water with a hand or a stick, or even plays by throwing sour gruel and so forth contained in a vessel, it is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense if there is no intention of amusement.

Nicchubhane vihārāti saṅghikavihārato bhikkhuno nikkaḍḍhananikkaḍḍhāpane. Ettha ca ekappayoge [V 0.0273] ekā, nānāpayoge dvāragaṇanāya āpattiyo. Puggalikanikkaḍḍhane, tassa parikkhāranikkaḍḍhane, anupasampannassa pana tassa parikkhārassa vā nikkaḍḍhane dukkaṭaṃ. Na sammāvattantānaṃ antevāsikasaddhivihārikānaṃ vā nikkaḍḍhane, attano vissāsikassa vihārā nikkaḍḍhane, bhaṇḍanakārakassa pana sakalasaṅghārāmato nikkaḍḍhane anāpatti.

Regarding 'expelling from a dwelling,' this means expelling or causing to be expelled a bhikkhu from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha. Herein, in a single attempt, there is one offense; in various attempts, the offenses are according to the count of doors. In expelling from a personal dwelling, in expelling his requisites, or in expelling one who is not fully ordained or his requisites, it is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense in expelling pupils or co-residents who do not behave properly, in expelling a trusted person from one's own dwelling, or in expelling a quarrelsome person from the entire monastery.

Anupakhajja sayaneti “vuḍḍho, gilāno, saṅghena dinno”ti jānitvā mañcapīṭhānaṃ vā tassa bhikkhuno pavisantassa vā nikkhamantassa vā upacāraṃ anupakhajja anupavisitvā saṅghike vihāre “yassa sambādho bhavissati, so pakkamissatī”ti adhippāyena nisīdananisajjanavasena sayane. Puggalike dukkaṭaṃ.

Regarding 'lying down encroaching,' this means that in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing, 'He is senior, sick, or it was given by the Saṅgha,' one lies down by way of sitting or reclining, having entered and encroached upon the vicinity of the bed or chair of that bhikkhu who is entering or leaving, with the intention, 'Whoever is inconvenienced will leave.' In a personal dwelling, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

Ettha ca pācittīti uddisitvā kānici pasiddhāni dassitāni. Avuttāni pana tādisāni imināva sāmaññavacanena saṅgahetvā [M 0.0321] veditabbāni. Kathaṃ? Acelakādiaññatitthiyānaṃ yassa kassaci āmisassa sahatthā dāne ca, sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitamacchamaṃsakhīradadhisaṅkhātānaṃ paṇītabhojanānaṃ attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjane, rāgapariyuṭṭhitaitthipurisassa yogge kule anupavisitvā nisajjanakappane, pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantito tasmiṃ bhutte vā abhutte vā santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchitvā purebhattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ vā yasmiṃ kule nimantito, tato gilānacīvaradānakārasamayaṃ ṭhapetvā aññasmiṃ aññakulappavesane, ṭhapetvā ekadivasaṃ aññasmiṃ dine āvasathapiṇḍassa agilānena hutvā bhuñjane, rattiparicchedaṃ vā bhesajjaparicchedaṃ vā katvā pavāritato uttari aññatra puna pavāraṇāya aññatra niccappavāraṇāya viññāpane, aññatra tathārūpapaccayā gāmato nikkhantasenādassanāya gamane, paccayenapi gantvā tirattato uttari senāya vāse, tassa ca vasantassa yuddhaṭṭhānabalagaṇaṭṭhānasenānivesaanīkadassanatthaṃ gamane, piṭṭhādīhi katamajjasaṅkhātasurāya, pupphādīhi kataāsavasaṅkhātamerayassa ca pāne, padīpujjalapattapacanādikāraṇaṃ vinā visibbitukāmatāya agilānassa aggino jālanajālāpane, kappabinduṃ anādāya navacīvaraparibhoge, sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetvā apaccuddhāya paribhoge, bhikkhusantakapattādino antamaso hasādhippāyenapi apanidhāne apanidhāpane, sañcicca tiracchānagatassa jīvitavoropane, sañcicca yathādhammaṃ nihatādhikaraṇassa punakammāya ukkoṭane, sañcicca theyyasatthena saddhiṃ saṃvidhāya ekaddhānagamane, bhikkhūhi sikkhāpadehi vuccamānassa aññaṃ avicāretvā [V 0.0274] “na tattha sikkhissāmī”ti bhaṇane, sikkhāpadavivaṇṇane, imesaṃ “sutvā oramissāmī”ti adhippāyaṃ vinā vivādāpannānaṃ upassutiṭṭhāne, dhammikānaṃ kammānaṃ chandaṃ datvā pacchā khīyanadhammāpajjane, saṅghe vinicchaye vattamāne chandaṃ adatvā [M 0.0322] pakkamane, samaggena saṅghena cīvaraṃ datvā pacchā khīyanadhammāpajjane, aññatra ajjhārāmā ajjhāvasathā vā ratanassa vā ratanasammatassa vā uggaṇhanauggahāpane pācittiyanti.

Here, after reciting 'a training entailing confession,' some well-known offenses have been shown. However, those not mentioned should be understood as included under this general statement. How? For example: giving any edible item directly by hand to a naked ascetic or follower of another sect; eating fine foods such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, or curds after requesting them for oneself; entering a household suited for a man or woman infatuated with lust and arranging to sit down; being invited to any of the five foods, and whether having eaten or not, entering another household before or after the meal without informing an available bhikkhu, except at the time of giving a robe or for a sick person's reason; apart from one day, on another day, eating an alms-portion from a lodging when not sick; requesting further from a person who has offered an invitation, after a limit on the night or on medicine has been established, except for a renewed invitation or a perpetual invitation; going to see an army that has gone forth from the village, except for a suitable reason; even having gone with a reason, staying with the army for more than three nights; and while staying there, going to see the battlefield, the place of the array of forces, the army encampment, or the battle line; drinking liquor called surā, made from flour and so forth, and intoxicants called meraya, made from flowers and so forth; lighting a fire or causing it to be lit when not ill, for the sake of warming oneself, without a reason like lighting a lamp or cooking leaves; using a new robe without applying a determination mark; using a robe that one has oneself assigned to another, without first revoking that assignment; hiding or causing to be hidden a bowl or other item belonging to a bhikkhu, even as a joke; intentionally depriving an animal of life; intentionally stirring up again for a new procedure a legal issue that has been settled according to the Dhamma; intentionally going on a journey together with a caravan of thieves, having made an arrangement; when being admonished by bhikkhus regarding the training rules, replying without reflection, 'I will not train in that'; disparaging the training rule; standing to eavesdrop on those who are in dispute, without the intention of desisting after hearing them; having given consent for a legitimate act, later finding fault with it; leaving without giving consent while the Saṅgha is conducting a legal procedure; a robe having been given by a united Saṅgha, later finding fault with it; picking up or causing another to pick up treasure or what is considered treasure, except within a monastery or a lodging—these entail a confession.

Pācittiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Pācittiya is concluded.

13. Samaṇakappaniddesavaṇṇanā

13. The Commentary on the Exposition of What is Allowable for a Recluse

125. Samaṇakappāti samaṇavohārā. Bhavanti, ahesunti vā bhūtā, vattamāne, bhūte vā tappaccayo. Viruḷhamūlādibhāvaṃ āpajjitvā vaḍḍhamānakānaṃ, vaḍḍhitvā mahantabhāvaṃ pattānañca rukkhalatādisaṅkhātānaṃ bhūtānaṃ gāmo, bhūtā eva vā gāmo samūho bhūtagāmo. Tassa samārambho chedanaphālanādi, tasmiṃ. Nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummaṃ, taṃhetu pācittiyaṃ hotīti attho. Katakappiyaṃ samaṇakappiyaṃ bhaveti sambandho. Tattha kataṃ kappiyaṃ yassāti bahubbīhi. Kenāti āha “nakhenā”tiādi.

125. The term 'samaṇakappa' refers to the conventions of a recluse. 'Bhūtā' (beings) can be understood as 'they are,' 'they were,' or the 'ta' suffix is used in the present or past tense. 'Bhūtagāma' (plant kingdom) refers to a collection of beings such as trees and creepers that have attained the state of having well-grown roots, are growing, and have grown to a large size; or the beings themselves are the collection, hence 'bhūtagāma'. The 'samārambha' (undertaking) of this involves cutting, splitting, and so forth, and it is in that context. This locative case is in the sense of a cause, meaning that because of it, an offense entailing confession occurs. The connection is that what has been made allowable becomes allowable for a recluse. Therein, 'that for which something is made allowable' is a bahubbīhi compound. By what? He says, 'by the nail,' and so forth.

126. Idāni yassa samārambho, taṃ bhūtagāmaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “sa mūlā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Soti bhūtagāmo. Bhavituṃ uppajjituṃ payojetīti kāritantā tappaccayo, pabhāvito uppāditoti attho. Atha vā pabhavanaṃ pabhavo, uppatti, sova pabhavo, pabhāvaṃ karotīti nāmadhātuto kattari tappaccayo, pabhāvito uppannoti attho. Mūlañca khandho ca bījañca aggañca phaḷu ca mūla…pe… phaḷūni. Phaḷu nāma pabbaṃ. Tāniyeva bījāni, tehi pabhāvito uppādito, atha vā tehi avadhibhūtehi, kāraṇabhūtehi vā pabhāvito uppannoti kamena vikappadvaye samāsadvayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha mūlabījaṃ nāma haliddisiṅgiverādi.

126. Now, to show that plant kingdom which is the object of this undertaking, the passage beginning 'sa mūlā' and so forth is commenced by dividing it. 'So' refers to the plant kingdom. 'Pabhāvito' means 'caused to exist' or 'produced,' with the suffix 'ta' from the causative stem. Alternatively, 'pabhava' means 'origin' or 'arising'; that very origin is 'pabhava,' and 'pabhāvito' means 'arisen' or 'produced,' with the suffix 'ta' in the agentive sense from a nominal root. The list is 'roots, trunks, seeds, shoots, and nodes' (mūla…pe… phaḷūni). 'Phaḷu' means a joint. These are indeed seeds; by them it is produced or generated; or, by them as the basis or as the cause, it is produced or arisen. In order, two alternatives and two compounds should be understood. Herein, 'root-seed' refers to turmeric, ginger, and so forth.

Khandhabījaṃ [M 0.0323] nāma assatthanigrodhādi. Bījabījaṃ nāma pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇādi. Aggabījaṃ nāma [V 0.0275] hiriverādi. Phaḷubījaṃ nāma ucchunaḷādi. Tattha mūlabījādīni pañca bījagāmo. Tannibbatto rukkhalatādi bhūtagāmo.

Trunk-seed refers to trees such as the assattha and nigrodha, and so forth. Seed-seed refers to grains such as early grains and late grains, and so forth. Shoot-seed refers to plants such as hirivera, and so forth. Node-seed refers to plants such as sugarcane and reed, and so forth. Herein, these five, beginning with root-seed, constitute the seed kingdom. Trees, creepers, and the like that arise from them constitute the plant kingdom.

Idāni tesu bījagāmasamārambhe dukkaṭaṃ dasseti aparaddhena. Bhūtagāmaviyojitaṃ bījaṃ ārambhe dukkaṭanti sambandho. Bhūtagāmato viyojitanti tappuriso. Bījanti bhūmiyaṃ ropitamaropitampi niggatavidatthimattapattavaṭṭipi mūlabījāni. “Ārambhe”ti kitakapaccayassa yoge avutte kammani chaṭṭhuppattiyaṃ vikappena ubhayattha dutiyā. Ārambheti samārambhe. Tasmā “imaṃ pupphaṃ phalaṃ vā jāna, imaṃ kappiyaṃ karohī”tiādinā kappiyavacanena bhūtagāmato viyojitaṃ bījajātaṃ bījagāmaparimocanatthaṃ puna kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paribhuñjibhabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ aggiparijitaṃ satthaparijitaṃ nakhaparijitaṃ abījaṃ nibbattabījaññeva pañcama”nti (cūḷava. 250) vuttesu pañcasu nakhaparijitādīni tīṇi dassitāni.

Now, regarding the undertaking of these of the seed kingdom, a dukkaṭa offense is shown by the transgression. The connection is: a dukkaṭa offense occurs in undertaking a seed separated from the plant kingdom. 'Separated from the plant kingdom' is a tatpurisa compound. 'Seeds' are root-seeds, whether planted in the ground or not, even those that have emerged with a circle of leaves the size of a span. Regarding 'ārambhe' (in undertaking), in the usage of the kṛta suffix, when the object is unexpressed, the sixth case arises optionally, or the second case in both instances. 'Ārambhe' means 'in undertaking'. Therefore, a type of seed separated from the plant kingdom should be made allowable again by a declaration of allowability, such as, 'Know this flower or fruit; make this allowable,' for the purpose of releasing it from the seed kingdom, and then it may be consumed. Among the five mentioned in the Cūḷavagga (250)—'Monks, I allow the consumption of fruit by five ascetic conventions: fire-purified, knife-purified, nail-purified, seedless, and the fifth, that from which the seed has been removed'—the three, beginning with nail-purified, are shown.

127. Idāni avasiṭṭhāni dve dassetuṃ “nibbattabīja”ntiādikaṃ paṭhamaddhaṃ āha. Tattha nibbattabījanti nibbattaniyanti nibbattaṃ, nipubba vatu vattanetimasmā tappaccayo, nibbattaṃ bījaṃ yassa taṃ nibbattabījaṃ, bījaṃ nibbattetvā visuṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ ambapanasādi. Nobījaṃ nāma taruṇambaphalādi. Idāni bījagāmabhūtagāmesu kappiyakaraṇappakārādivisesaṃ dassento “kaṭāhā”tiādimāha. Tattha kaṭāhena baddhaṃ bījaṃ yesanti bāhirattho.

127. Now, to explain the remaining two, he stated the first half beginning with 'nibbattabīja'. Therein, 'nibbattabīja' means that from which the seed has been removed. 'Nibbatta' is derived from the root 'vat' (to be) preceded by 'ni', with the suffix 'ta'; it means 'produced' or 'removed'. 'Nibbattabīja' is that from which the seed has been removed—such as mangoes, jackfruits, and so on, which are to be consumed after removing the seed and setting it apart. 'Nobīja' refers to young mango fruits and the like. Now, to show the particular methods for making things of the seed kingdom and plant kingdom allowable, he begins with 'kaṭāhā' and so on. Therein, the external meaning is 'those whose seeds are bound by a pot'.

128. Bhājane bhūmiyampi vā ekābaddhesu bījesu ekasmiñca kappiye kateti yojanā. Bījesūti bījagāmabhūtagāmesu[M 0.0324]. Bhūtagāmopi hi idha “bīja”nti ruḷhīvasena vuccati.

128. The application is: when, among seeds bound together in a vessel or on the ground, one is made allowable. 'In seeds' means in the seed kingdom and the plant kingdom. For here, the plant kingdom is also called 'seed' by customary usage.

129. Nikkhitteti ṭhapite. Kappiyaṃ puna kareyyāti jātamūlapaṇṇabhāvato bhūtagāmattā bhūtagāmato parimocitaṃ bījagāmaparimocanatthaṃ puna kappiyaṃ kāreyyāti attho. Tenāha “bhūtagāmo hi so tadā”ti. Hi-saddo hetumhi. Tadāti mūle ca paṇṇe ca jātakāle sace mūlamattaṃ sañjāyati, uparibhāge sace aṅkuro jāyati, heṭṭhābhāge chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Mūlamattesu vā [V 0.0276] pana paṇṇamattesu vā niggatesu sacepi ratanappamāṇāpi sākhā nikkhamanti, bījagāmasaṅgahitā honti.

129. 'Nikkhitteti' means 'placed'. 'Kappiyaṃ puna kareyyāti' means that because it has become rooted and leafed, and is thus of the plant kingdom, it should be made allowable again for the purpose of releasing it from the plant kingdom and for releasing it from the seed kingdom. For this reason, it is said, 'For it is of the plant kingdom at that time.' The particle 'hi' is in the sense of a reason. 'Tadā' refers to the time when roots and leaves have sprouted. If only the root portion has developed, or if a sprout has appeared in the upper portion, it is allowable to cut the lower part. However, once the root portions or the leaf portions have emerged, even if branches the size of a gem sprout, they are included in the seed kingdom.

130. Udakasambhavo sevālo ca cetiyādīsu sevālo ca bhūtagāmovāti sambandho. Ādi-saddena pākārādiggahaṇaṃ. Yadi dve tīṇi paṇṇāni na jāyanti, aggabījasaṅgahaṃ gacchati. Sukkho pana sammajjitabbo. Mūlapaṇṇe viniggate bījopi bhūtagāmovāti sambandho. Paṇṇeti iminā aṅkuramattaṃ paṭikkhipati.

130. The connection is: algae born of water and algae on shrines and so forth are also of the plant kingdom. By the word 'and so forth,' walls and the like are included. If two or three leaves do not grow, it is included in the category of shoot-seed. When dry, however, it should be swept away. The connection is: when roots and leaves have emerged, the seed is also of the plant kingdom. By 'leaf,' it excludes a mere sprout.

131. Ghaṭādipiṭṭhe sevālo ca ahichattakamakuḷañca dukkaṭasseva vatthūnīti sambandho. Piṭṭheti iminā anto abbohārikoti dasseti. Phullanti phullitaṃ ahichattakaṃ. Abyavahārikanti āpattivohārayoggaṃ na hotīti attho.

131. The connection is: algae on the surface of a pot and so forth, and a mushroom bud, are indeed grounds for a dukkaṭa offense. By 'surface,' it shows that the inside is not a matter for transaction. 'Phulla' means a bloomed mushroom. 'Abyavahārika' means that it is not suitable for the legal transaction of an offense.

132. Allarukkhe lākhāniyyāsachattāni vikopiya gaṇhato tattha akkharaṃ chindato vāpi pācittīti sambandho. Tatthāti allarukkhe. “Vikopaya”nti potthakesu pāṭho dissati, so apāṭho paṭhamantatāya kāraṇābhāvato. “Vikopiyā”ti pana pāṭho gahetabbo. Vikopiyāti [M 0.0325] iminā avikopetvā gahaṇe anāpattīti dīpeti.

132. The connection is: for one who takes lac, resin, or bark from a living tree by scraping it off, or for one who cuts a letter there, there is a pācittiya offense. 'There' means on a living tree. The reading 'vikopaya' is found in manuscripts, but that is an incorrect reading because there is no reason for it to be a nominative ending. The reading 'vikopiyā' should be taken instead. By 'vikopiyā,' it is shown that there is no offense in taking it without scraping.

133. Dārumakkaṭakādināti āṇiṃ koṭṭetvā dāruyantaṃ katvā tattha kaṇṭakaṃ olambenti, etaṃ dārumakkaṭakaṃ nāma. Ādi-saddena kaṇṭakabandhanādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tiṇādiṃ chindituṃ, gaṇṭhikaṃ kātuñca na kappatīti yojanā. Chinditunti chindanaṃ.

133. 'By a wooden monkey and so forth' means: having hammered in a peg and made a wooden device, they hang a thorn on it—this is called a wooden monkey. By the word 'and so forth,' thorn-bindings and the like are included. The application is: it is not allowable to cut grass and so forth, or to make a knot. 'Chindituṃ' means cutting.

134. Bhūtagāmaṃ vāti bhūtagāmaṃ vā. Bījaṃ vāti bījagāmaṃ vā. “Chinda vā”tiādinā sabbattha vā-saddo yojetabbo. Paca vāti pacanaṃ karohīti vā. “Paṭa” iti vā pāṭho, tassa uppādehīti attho. “Imaṃ rukkhaṃ chindāhī”tiādinā pana avatvā “rukkhaṃ chindā”tiādinā aniyametvā vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

134. 'Bhūtagāmaṃ vā' means 'or the plant kingdom'. 'Bījaṃ vā' means 'or the seed kingdom'. The particle 'vā' should be connected everywhere, as in 'cut or,' and so forth. 'Paca vā' means 'do the cooking'. Or there is the reading 'paṭa,' which means 'produce it'. However, instead of saying 'cut this tree,' and so on, it is allowable to speak without specifying, by saying 'cut a tree,' and so on.

135. Imanti [V 0.0277] etaṃ rukkhādiṃ. Imaṃ sodhehīti ettha iti-saddaṃ katvā attho vattabboti.

135. 'Imam' means this tree and so forth. Here, in the phrase 'Imaṃ sodhehi' (Clean this), the meaning should be stated by using the particle 'iti'.

Samaṇakappaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on ascetic conventions is concluded.

14. Bhūminiddesavaṇṇanā

14. The Explanation of the Exposition on Grounds.

136. Yāsu vutthaṃ pakkañca kappati, tā kappiyā bhūmiyo sammuti ca sammutikuṭi ca…pe… gahapati ca gahapatikuṭi cāti imā catasso hontīti yojetvā attho veditabbo. Tattha bhesajjakkhandhake (mahāva. 295) vuttāya uttidutiyakammavācāya, apalokanakammavasena vā sāvetvā sammā uttisampannaṃ karīyatīti sammuti, thambhānaṃ bhittipādānaṃ vā uggamanaṃ uddhaṃ katvā ṭhapanaṃ, “kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vācāya sāvanañca [M 0.0326] antaṃ yassā sā ussāvanantā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “thambhappatiṭṭhānañca vacanapariyosānañca samakālaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 295). Nisādanaṃ pavisanaṃ sannivesanaṃ nisādo, gunnaṃ viya nisādo etissāti gonisādi. Bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā sesasahadhammikā sabbe ca devamanussā idha gahapatīti sāmaññena adhippetā. Ettha pana gahapatisambandhinī kuṭi dīghena gahapatī.

136. The meaning should be understood by connecting thus: these four are the permissible grounds where dwelling and cooking are allowed: the 'agreement' (sammuti) and the 'agreement-hut' (sammutikuṭi)... and the 'householder' (gahapati) and the 'householder-hut' (gahapatikuṭi). Therein, 'sammuti' is so called because it is properly established by the formal act with a motion and two announcements, as stated in the chapter on medicines (Mahāvagga 295), or by the act of seeking consent. That which has as its limit the raising and setting up of pillars or wall-footings and the announcement with the words, 'We are making a permissible hut,' is 'ussāvanantā'. And so it is said: 'The setting up of the pillars and the conclusion of the statement are allowable simultaneously' (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 295). 'Nisāda' is sitting down, entering, settling. 'Gonisādi' is so called because its 'nisāda' is like that of cattle. Here, excluding a monk, all other co-religionists and all devas and humans are generally intended by 'gahapati'. Here, however, the hut related to a householder is 'gahapatī' with a long vowel.

“Yaṃ pana akappiyabhūmiyaṃ sahaseyyappahonake gehe vuttha”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 295) aṭṭhakathāvacanato yaṃ saṅgho ākaṅkhati vihāraṃ vā aḍḍhayogaṃ vā pāsādaṃ vā hammiyaṃ vā guhaṃ vā leṇādiṃ vā, tesampi sāmaññavacanaṃ viññāyatīti taṃtaṃlakkhaṇappattā sahaseyyappahonakā leṇādayo catūsveva kuṭīsu antogadhāti veditabbaṃ. Imāsu catūsu sahaseyyappahonake padese yaṃ saṅghikaṃ puggalikaṃ vā bhikkhusantakaṃ ekarattampi antovutthaṃ anupasampannena pakkañca yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikañca antovutthaantopakkasaṅkhaṃ na gacchati, ko pana vādo itaradvaye. Taṃ pana akappiyabhūmiyampi vutthaṃ pakkañca vaṭṭati. Tena vuttaṃ “yāsu vutthaṃ pakkañca kappatī”ti.

From the commentary’s statement (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 295), 'Whatever has been stored overnight in a dwelling suitable for co-residence on unallowable ground,' it should be understood that whatever the Saṅgha might wish for—a monastery, a gabled building, a mansion, a storied building, a cave, or a lodging, and so on—since a general term is understood for them too, those lodgings and so on that have their respective characteristics and are suitable for co-residence are included within these four huts. In these four places suitable for co-residence, whatever belongs to the Saṅgha, to an individual, or is in the possession of a monk, if it is stored overnight inside or cooked by an unordained person, it is not counted as 'stored inside' or 'cooked inside'. What then to say of the other two cases? That, however, is allowable even if stored overnight and cooked on unallowable ground. Therefore it is said: 'on which storing overnight and cooking are allowable'.

137. Vāsatthāya kate saṅghike vā ekasantake vā sahaseyyappahonake gehe kappiyākuṭi [V 0.0278] laddhabbāti sambandho. Tattha vāsatthāyāti iminā avāsatthāya kataṃ nivatteti. Ekasantaketi ekassa bhikkhuno santake. Kappiyākuṭīti bhāvappadhānoyaṃ niddeso, na hi gehe gehaṃ laddhuṃ yujjatīti kappiyakuṭitāti attho. Dīgho pana gāthāvasena, kappiyā kuṭitāti vā visesanavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahaseyyappahonaketi ettha sahaseyyappahonakaṃ [M 0.0327] vāsāgāralakkhaṇe vuttalakkhaṇaṃ senāsanaṃ.

137. The connection is that a permissible hut is to be obtained in a dwelling made for habitation, whether belonging to the Sangha or to an individual, which is suitable for shared sleeping. Herein, ‘for habitation’ excludes that which is not made for habitation. ‘Belonging to an individual’ means belonging to a single monk. ‘Permissible hut’ (kappiyākuṭi) is a designation where the abstract sense is primary, for it is not fitting to obtain a house within a house; thus, the meaning is ‘the state of being a permissible hut.’ The long vowel, however, is used for metrical reasons, or it should be understood as a qualification, as in ‘a permissible hut.’ Herein, ‘suitable for shared sleeping’ refers to a lodging that has the characteristics stated in the definition of a dwelling place.

138. Idāni tā kuṭiyo kamena dassetvā tattha paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ, tāsaṃ sabbathāpagamañca dassetuṃ “gehe”tiādimāha. Tattha “kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti evamīrayanti sambandho. Iṭṭhakā ca thambhā ca “iṭṭhakāthambhā”ti vattabbe rasso. Iṭṭhakathambhā ādi yassa bhittipāsādassāti bahubbīhi. Pacchā paṭhamasaddena kammadhārayo. “Ṭhapeyya ce, sā ussāvanantikā”ti evaṃ ce-sā-sadde yojetvā attho veditabbo.

138. Now, having shown those huts in sequence, to explain the procedure to be followed there and to show their complete removal, he says, “in a house,” etc. Here, the connection is to be understood as, “We make a permissible hut, we make a permissible hut,” thus they speak. Bricks and pillars—when it should be said “iṭṭhakāthambhā,” it is shortened. “Brick-pillars,” etc., is a bahubbīhi compound meaning “that which has brick-pillars as its beginning,” referring to a wall or mansion. Afterward, with the first word, it becomes a kammadhāraya compound. The meaning of “If one were to place it, that would be until the announcement” should be understood by connecting the words “ce” and “sā” in this way.

139. Sakalo aparikkhitto ārāmopi vāti sambandho. Senāsanaṃ parikkhittaṃ vā hotu, aparikkhittaṃ vā, na taṃ pamāṇaṃ.

139. The connection is that even the entire unenclosed monastery is included. Whether the lodging is enclosed or unenclosed, that is not the standard.

140. Aññehi kappiyakuṭiyā atthāya dinno vā tesaṃ santako vāti yojanā.

140. The construction is: whether given by others for the purpose of a permissible hut, or belonging to them.

141. Avirodhabhāvena kappanīyā kappā, kappa sāmatthiyamiccetasmā itthiyaṃ āpaccaye rūpaṃ, na kappā akappā, akappā ca sā kuṭi ceti akappakuṭi, tāya. Sappiādīti iminā sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikañca gahitaṃ.

141. By virtue of being fit to be made permissible, it is kappā; from the meaning of ‘permissibility’ (kappa) or ‘capability’ (sāmatthiya), the form kappā is derived with the feminine ā suffix. Not kappā is akappā; and that hut which is akappā is an akappakuṭi; by that. By “ghee, etc.,” both seven-day and lifetime allowances are included.

142. Tehevāti akappakuṭiyaṃ vutthasappiādīhi eva saddhiṃ sattāhakālikasaṃsaṭṭhatāya “sattāhaṃ kappate”ti vuttaṃ. Sāmiseti āmisasaṅkhātena purimadvayena sahite. Sāmapākatāti sāmaṃ attanā pāko etassāti sāmapākaṃ, sattāhakālikena saha pakkaṃ sāmisaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ, tassa bhāvo sāmapākatā. Sayaṃ pakkaṃ taṃ attanā saṃsaṭṭhatāya tampi āmisaṃ sāmapākagatikaṃ karotīti tassa sāmapākatā hotīti adhippāyo.

142. ‘By those very ones’ (teheva) means that it is said, “It is permissible for seven days,” because of being mixed with a seven-day allowance, along with that very ghee, etc., that has been kept in an impermissible hut. ‘With substance’ (sāmise) means together with the former two, which are reckoned as substance. ‘The state of being self-cooked’ (sāmapākatā) means: that which is cooked by oneself is ‘self-cooked’ (sāmapāka). Sāmapākatā is the state of a lifetime allowance that is substantial and has been cooked together with a seven-day allowance. The intention is that because it is cooked by oneself, through being mixed with it, it renders even that substance into one belonging to the self-cooked category; therefore, it has the state of being self-cooked.

143. Adhiṭṭhitāti [M 0.0328] patiṭṭhitā. Eva-saddo tiṭṭhatisaddassa ante daṭṭhabbo.

143. ‘Adhiṭṭhitā’ means ‘patiṭṭhitā’ (established). The word ‘eva’ should be understood at the end of the word ‘tiṭṭhati’.

144. Sabbesūti [V 0.0279] thambhādīsu sakalesu. Jahitaṃ vatthu kuṭibhūmi yassā jahitavatthukā. Parikkhitte jahitavatthukāti sambandho. Sesāti itarā dve kuṭiyo. Chadanavibbhamāti chadanassa vināsā. Etthāpi “jahitavatthukā”ti ānetabbanti.

144. ‘In all’ (sabbesu) means in all, such as pillars, etc., in their entirety. ‘Having an abandoned site’ (jahitavatthukā) means that whose site, the hut-ground, is abandoned. The connection is “in an enclosed place having an abandoned site.” ‘The rest’ (sesā) means the other two huts. ‘From the destruction of the roof’ (chadanavibbhamā) means from the collapse of the roof. Here too, “having an abandoned site” should be supplied.

Bhūminiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Description of Grounds is concluded.

15. Upajjhācariyavattaniddesavaṇṇanā

15. The Commentary on the Description of the Duties toward the Preceptor and Teacher

145. “Idaṃ tayā dukkataṃ, dubbhāsita”ntiādīni vatvā codanato, attano vajjaṃ assarantassa satuppādavasena sāraṇato, sammā paṭipattiyaṃ sāraṇato pavattāpanato vā vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyati bhusaṃ cintetīti upajjhā. Upajjhā eva upajjhāyo. “Evaṃ tayā buddhavacanaṃ sajjhāyitabbaṃ, evaṃ atikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ paṭikkamitabba”ntiādinā ācārasikkhāpane ācarati pavattatīti ācariyo. So ca nissayapabbajjāupasampadādhammācariyavasena catubbidho. Upajjhā ca ācariyo ca upajjhācariyā, te. Nissāya vasamānoti iminā nissayapabbajjāupasampadādhammantevāsikesu yo nissāya vasati, taṃ dasseti. Catūsu hi tesu nissayantevāsikena yāva ācariyaṃ nissāya vasati, tāvasabbaṃ ācariyavattaṃ kātabbaṃ, netarehi. Itarehi, nissayamuttakehipi yāva cīvararajanaṃ, tāva ca arativinodanādikañca vattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Anāpucchitvā pattacīvaradānādimhi pana etesaṃ anāpatti. Saddhivihārikassa pana upajjhāyānaṃ yāva cīvararajanaṃ, tāva ca arativinodanādikañca akarontassa nissayamuttakassāpi amuttakassāpi āpattiyeva. Ekaccassa pattadānādito [M 0.0329] paṭṭhāya amuttanissayasseva āpatti. Tesu majjhe dve ācariyassa yāvajīvaṃ bhārā. Itare pana yāva samīpe vasanti, tāvadeva, tasmā ācariyenāpi tesu sammā vattitabbaṃ, upajjhāyena saddhivihārikesu vattabbameva natthi. Supesaloti piyaṃ sīlamassāti pesalo, vuddhi, ya-lopena ī-kārassa attakaraṇena, suṭṭhu pesalo supesalo, sikkhākāmoti attho. “Dantakaṭṭha”ntiādi “dade”timassa kammaṃ. Dadeti sammā ādarena yathādhippāyaṃ dadeyyāti attho. Kāleti tadanurūpe kāle.

145. Because he reproaches, saying, ‘This is a wrongdoing by you, ill-spoken,’ etc.; because he reminds one who does not remember his own fault by causing mindfulness to arise; or because he causes one to proceed by reminding him of right practice—he intensely reflects upon and considers faults and blamelessness. Thus he is a preceptor (upajjhā). The upajjhā is indeed the upajjhāya. Because he acts and proceeds in instructing in the training of conduct, saying, ‘Thus should the Buddha’s word be recited by you, thus should you go forward, thus should you return,’ etc., he is a teacher (ācariyo). He is fourfold: a teacher of dependence, of the going forth, of ordination, and of the Dhamma. The preceptor and the teacher are the upajjhācariyā. By ‘dwelling in dependence,’ he indicates one who dwells in dependence among the pupils of dependence, of the going forth, of ordination, and of the Dhamma. For among these four, as long as a pupil of dependence dwells in dependence on the teacher, all the duties to the teacher must be fulfilled, but not so by the others. The others, even those free from dependence, must perform duties such as dyeing robes and dispelling discontent up to a certain point. However, for them, there is no offense in giving a bowl, robe, etc., without asking permission. But for a co-resident, if he does not perform duties for the preceptor, such as dyeing robes and dispelling discontent, an offense is committed, whether he is free from dependence or not. For some, the offense of giving a bowl, etc., applies only to one who is not free from dependence. Among these pupils, two kinds are a lifelong responsibility for the teacher. The others, however, are so only as long as they dwell nearby. Therefore, the teacher must also behave properly toward them; as for the preceptor toward his co-residents, there is nothing more to be said. ‘Very amiable’ (supesalo) means one whose character is dear (piyaṃ sīlam assa) is amiable (pesalo); through lengthening, elision of ‘ya,’ and vowel modification, it becomes ‘pesalo.’ ‘Very amiable’ (supesalo) means desirous of training. ‘Tooth-stick,’ etc., is the object of ‘should give.’ ‘Should give’ means one should give properly and with care, as intended. ‘At the proper time’ means at a time suitable for that.

146. Patte [V 0.0280] ca…pe… cīvare ca vattaṃ careti sambandho. Careti kareyya. Tattha nīcaṃ katvā sādhukaṃ aparighaṃsantena dhovanaṃ, muhuttaṃ uṇhe otāpanaṃ, ṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ upaparikkhitvā cammādinā kenaci antarahitāya nikkhipanaṃ patte vattaṃ. Gāmaṃ pavisantānaṃ nivāsanakāyabandhanasaṅghāṭidānaṃ, dhovitvā sodakapattassa dānaṃ gāmappavese vattaṃ. Yadi ākaṅkhanti, parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca nātidūranaccāsanne gamanaṃ, pattapariyāpannaggahaṇañca gamane vattaṃ. Nivattente pana paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā āsanapaññāpanaṃ, pādodakādiupanikkhipanaṃ, pattacīvarappaṭiggahaṇaṃ āgame āgamane vattaṃ. Bhaṇantānaṃ antarā kathāanopātanaṃ sabbattha vattaṃ. Āsanapaññāpanaṃ, uṭṭhitesu āsanauddharaṇaṃ, pādapīṭhakathalānaṃ upanikkhipanaṃ, paṭisāmanañca āsane pādapīṭhe pādakathale ca vattaṃ. Dhotapādaṭṭhapanakaṃ pādapīṭhaṃ. Aññaṃ kathalaṃ. Upāhanā ca cīvarañcāti dvando, tasmiṃ. Sukkhaallacoḷehi puñchanaṃ upāhanāya vattaṃ. Sinnacīvarassa muhuttaṃ otāpanaṃ, caturaṅgulaṃ kaṇṇaṃ ussāretvā cīvarasaṃharaṇañca cīvare vattaṃ.

146. The connection is that one should perform the duties regarding the almsbowl... and the robe. ‘Perform’ (care) means ‘should do’ (kareyya). Therein, washing it thoroughly, having lowered it, without rubbing it roughly; drying it briefly in the sun; inspecting the place for storage and then placing it down with something like leather intervening—this is the duty regarding the almsbowl. Giving the lower robe, waistband, and outer robe to those entering the village; giving a washed almsbowl with water—this is the duty upon entering the village. If they wish, walking neither too far nor too close, having worn the lower robe and wrapped the outer robe evenly, and taking what is contained in the almsbowl—this is the duty while walking. When returning, however, arriving first, preparing a seat, setting out foot-water and so forth, and receiving the almsbowl and robe—this is the duty upon returning. Not interrupting the speech of those speaking is the duty in all cases. Preparing a seat, clearing the seat after they have risen, setting out footstools and mats, and tidying up the seat, footstool, and mat—these are the duties regarding them. A footstool is for placing washed feet. The other is a mat. ‘Footwear and robe’ is a dvanda compound; regarding these: wiping the footwear with dry or wet cloths is the duty regarding footwear. For a damp robe, drying it briefly, raising the corner by four finger-widths, and then folding the robe—this is the duty regarding the robe.

147. Paribhojanīya…pe… passāvaṭṭhānisu ca vihārasodhane ca puna paññāpane ca vattaṃ tathāti sambandho. Vaccañca [M 0.0330] passāvo ca vaccapassāvā. Tiṭṭhati etthāti ṭhānī, kuṭi. Vaccapassāvānaṃ ṭhānīti tappuriso. Atha vā tiṭṭhati etthāti ṭhānaṃ, soyeva samāso, vaccapassāvassa ca patanaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti iṭṭhagehādi. Paribhojanīyañca pānīyañca vaccapassāvaṭṭhānī ca pari…pe… ṭṭhānī. Tāsu tesu vā. Pādodakauṇhasītanahānodakappaṭiyādāpanaṃ paribhojanīye vattaṃ. Pātabbapānīyena pucchanaṃ upaṭṭhāpanañca pānīye vattaṃ. Sammajjanapānīyaupaṭṭhāpanaṃ vaccapassāvaṭṭhānīsu vattaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ pattacīvarādīni harāpetvā ekamante nikkhipanādi, ullokato paṭṭhāya makkaṭasantānaṃ ohāretvā sammajjanañca vihārasodhane vattaṃ. Otāpetvā sodhetvā papphoṭetvā atiharitvā yathāṭhāne bhūmattharaṇādipaññāpanaṃ puna paññāpane vattaṃ. Tathāti iminā “care”ti idaṃ atidisati.

147. The connection is that one should likewise perform the duties regarding things for use... and latrines, and in cleaning the monastery, and in setting things in order again. 'Vaccapassāvā' means feces and urine. 'Ṭhānī' is a place where something stands, a hut. 'Vaccapassāvānaṃ ṭhānī' is a determinative compound. Alternatively, 'ṭhāna' is a place where something stands, and it is the same compound; it refers to the place where feces and urine fall, such as a privy or the like, which one possesses. Things for use, drinking water, and latrines... or in those places. Preparing foot-water, warm water, cold water, and bathing water is the duty regarding things for use. Asking for potable water and providing it is the duty regarding drinking water. Sweeping and providing water is the duty at the latrines. First, having the bowl, robe, and so forth carried away and set aside in one place, then sweeping from the skylight downwards to remove cobwebs—this is the duty in cleaning the monastery. After airing, cleaning, shaking out, and carrying them back, arranging the floor coverings and so forth in their proper places—this is the duty in setting things in order again. By 'thus,' the word 'should perform' is extended.

148. Vihāraṃ sodhento bhikkhu paṭivāte vā saṅgaṇe vā pānīyasāmantā vā sayanāsanaṃ na papphoṭeyyāti sambandho. Pānīya-saddena paribhojanīyañca saṅgahitaṃ. Paṭivāteti uparivāte. Saṅgaṇeti bahūnaṃ samosaraṇe vivaṭappadese. Sayanāsanaṃ nāma bhūmattharaṇamañcādi.

148. The connection is that a monk cleaning the dwelling should not shake out bedding and seating against the wind, or in a crowded place, or near drinking water. By the word 'drinking water,' water for general use is also included. 'Against the wind' means upwind. 'In a crowded place' means in an open area where many gather. 'Bedding and seating' refers to floor coverings, beds, and so forth.

149. Nhāne vattaṃ care, nhātassa kātabbe careti sambandhassa purisādhīnatāya sambandho veditabbo[V 0.0281]. Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇagattaparikammakaraṇaṃ nahāne vattaṃ. Kātabbe careti gattato udakasammajjananivāsanadānādikicce pavatteyyāti attho. “Vanappagumbe”tiādīsu viya sissa e-kārādesaṃ rūpaṃ, tasmā kātabbaṃ vattaṃ careyyāti yojetvā veditabbaṃ. Budhā pana “nhāne nhātassa kātabbe vattaṃ care”ti yojetvā atthaṃ vadanti. Evaṃ sati kātabba-saddassa kammasādhanattā vattameva kātabbaṃ nāmāti “vatte vattaṃ care”ti vuttaṃ [M 0.0331] viya hotīti virujjhati. “Nahātena nahātassā”ti vā pāṭho, udake gattaparikammena theraṃ paṭhamaṃ nahāpetvā sayampi nahātenāti attho. Pāḷiyampi “nahātena paṭhamataraṃ uttaritvā”ti (mahāva. 67) atthi. Atha raṅgapāke dhovane sibbane ca vattaṃ careti sambandho, rajanapāke cīvaradhovane cīvarasibbane cāti attho. Rajanto cīvare theve ṭhite na vajeti sambandho. Rajantoti cīvaraṃ rajanto. Theveti rajanabindumhi.

149. One should perform the duty regarding bathing, and one should perform the duty to be done for one who has bathed—this connection should be understood as dependent on the person. Receiving the robe and attending to the body is the duty regarding bathing. 'Should perform the duty to be done' means one should engage in actions such as wiping water from the body and offering the lower robe. As in 'vanappagumbe' and so on, it is a form with the substitution of 'e' for 'i'; therefore, it should be understood by connecting it as 'one should perform the duty that is to be done.' The wise, however, explain the meaning by connecting it as 'one should perform the duty for the one who has bathed, in the matter of bathing.' If so, since the word 'kātabba' is formed in the sense of the object, the duty itself becomes what is to be done, as if it were said 'one should perform a duty in relation to a duty,' which is contradictory. Alternatively, the reading is 'by one who has bathed, for one who has bathed,' meaning, having first bathed the elder by attending to his body with water, and then having bathed oneself. In the Pāli Canon, it also exists as 'having bathed first and emerged' (Mahāva. 67). Furthermore, the connection is that one should perform duties related to preparing dyes, washing, and sewing; this means preparing dyes for robes, washing robes, and sewing robes. The connection is that while dyeing, when a drop of dye is on the robe, one should not move it. 'While dyeing' means while dyeing the robe. 'Theve' means on the drop of dye.

150. Ekaccassāti ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ verino puggalassa pattaṃ vā cīvarāni vā kiñcanaṃ parikkhāraṃ vā na dadeyya na gaṇheyya vāti sambandho. Tattha na dadeyya na gaṇheyyāti paṭisāmanatthāyapi na dadeyya, na gaṇheyya vāti attho. “Ākiñcana”ntiādīsu viya kiñcana-saddo daṭṭhabbo, tassa kiñcīti attho. Kiñcinanti vā pāṭho, kiñci naṃ parikkhāranti yojanā. Padasiddhivasenettha nanti ta-saddappayogo kato.

150. 'For a certain person'—this is the connection: one should not give to, nor take from, a person hostile to one’s teachers or preceptors a bowl, robes, or any requisite. Here, 'should not give, should not take' means one should not give even for safekeeping, nor should one take—this is the meaning. The word 'kiñcana' should be understood as in 'ākiñcana' and so on; its meaning is 'anything.' Alternatively, the reading is 'kiñcinaṃ'; the construction is 'kiñci naṃ parikkhāraṃ' (any requisite of his). Here, 'naṃ' is a usage of the pronoun 'ta', employed for the sake of word formation.

151-2. Pacchato kātunti pacchāsamaṇaṃ kātuṃ. Tassāti ekaccassa. Pacchatoti pacchāsamaṇo hutvā. Ninnetunti ekaccassa nīharituṃ. Sabbattha anāpucchā na vaṭṭatīti yojetabbaṃ. Kiccayaṃ vāti veyyāvaccādi yaṃ kiñci kiccaṃ vā. Kiccameva kiccayaṃ, kassa yo “seniyo”tiādīsu viya. Parikammaṃ vāti piṭṭhiparikammādiparikammaṃ. Attano kārāpetuṃ vāti ekaccena attano kārāpetuṃ vā. Kātuṃ vāti tassa attanā kātuṃ vā.

151-2. 'To make a follower' means to make one a junior monk. 'For him' means for a certain person. 'As a follower' means having become a junior monk. 'To lead away' means to remove a certain person. It should be connected that in all cases, it is not proper without asking permission. 'Or any duty' means any service or whatever duty. 'Kiccayaṃ' is simply 'kicca'; the suffix '-ya' is added, as in 'seniyo' and so on. 'Or attendance' means attendance such as massaging the back, etc. 'Or to have one’s own done' means to have one's own done by a certain person. 'Or to do' means to do it oneself for that person.

153. Sīmato niggatā bahibhūtā nissīmā, taṃ. Ācariyupajjhāyesu avatvā dūraṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gatesupi apassantena [M 0.0332] gāmo pavisitabbo. Diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya pana āpucchituṃyeva vaṭṭati. Attano kiccayaṃ vāpīti attano sīmāyapi pattapacanacīvararajanādikaṃ sakaṃ karaṇīyaṃ vāpi kātuṃ.

153. Having gone out from the boundary, being outside, is 'nissīmā'; this refers to that. Even when one's teachers and preceptors have gone far on their alms-round without being told, one should enter the village without being seen by them. But from the point where one is seen, it is proper to ask permission. 'Or one’s own duty' means to perform one’s own tasks, such as cooking in the bowl, dyeing robes, and so on, which are one's own duties, even within one's own boundary.

154. Aratinti [V 0.0282] sāsane anabhiratiṃ. Saṅghāyattesu kammesūti parivāsāditajjanīyādīsu saṅghappaṭibaddhesu kammesu. Ussukkaṃ vāpīti ācariyupajjhāyesu garudhammaṃ ajjhāpannesu, kammārahesu ca “kinti nu kho saṅgho parivāsaṃ dadeyyā”tiādinā ussāhaṃ vāpi.

154. 'Discontent' means dissatisfaction with the Dispensation. 'In matters dependent on the Sangha' means in actions connected with the Sangha, such as probation, censure, and so forth. 'Or eagerness' means eagerness concerning teachers and preceptors who have committed a serious offense or are eligible for a formal act, thinking, 'How might the Sangha grant probation?' and so forth.

155. Gilānesu upaṭṭheyyāti “pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato gilānupaṭṭhāko alaṃ gilānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ, paṭibalo hoti bhesajjaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ, sappāyāsappāyaṃ jānāti, asappāyaṃ apanāmeti, sappāyaṃ upanāmeti, mettacitto gilānaṃ upaṭṭhāti no āmisantaro, ajegucchī hoti uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā kheḷaṃ vā vantaṃ vā nīhātuṃ, paṭibalo hoti gilānaṃ kālena kālaṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetuṃ samādapetuṃ samuttejetuṃ sampahaṃsetu”nti (mahāva. 366) evaṃ vuttapañcaṅgasamannāgatena hutvā gilānesu upaṭṭhaheyyāti attho. Iminā sabbehipi ācaritabbaṃ gilānavattaṃ upadisati. Vuṭṭhānanti gelaññā vuṭṭhitaṃ. Āgameti āgameyya, olokeyyāti attho. Upajjhācariyehi ca saddhivihārikaantevāsikesu yadi te gilānā honti, ādito paṭṭhāya cīvare rajanapariyosānañca arativinodanādikañca vattaṃ, agilānesu pana uddesaparipucchā ovādānusāsaniyā anuggahopattacīvarādidānañcāti sabbaṃ kātabbaṃ. Teneva heṭṭhā vuttaṃ “tasmā ācariyenāpi [M 0.0333] tesu sammā vattitabbaṃ, upajjhāyena saddhivihārikesu vattabbameva natthī”ti.

155. One should attend to the sick—this means: 'Bhikkhus, an attendant of the sick who is endowed with five qualities is competent to attend to the sick: he is capable of preparing medicine; he knows what is suitable and unsuitable, removes what is unsuitable, and provides what is suitable; he attends to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness, not for material gain; he is not disgusted at removing feces, urine, saliva, or vomit; and he is capable of instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the sick from time to time with a talk on the Dhamma.' Thus, having become endowed with these five qualities, one should attend to the sick. By this, the duty towards the sick that should be practiced by all is taught. 'Recovery' means having recovered from illness. 'One should await' means one should wait for, one should look after—this is the meaning. And by preceptors and teachers, if their co-residents and pupils are sick, from the beginning the duties up to the completion of dyeing the robes, the dispelling of discontent, and so on, should be performed. For those who are not sick, however, everything should be done, such as giving instruction and questioning, advice and admonition, help, and the giving of bowl, robes, and so on. For that reason, it was said below: 'Therefore, a teacher should also act rightly towards them; for a preceptor, there is nothing to be said regarding his co-residents.'

Upajjhācariyavattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the duties towards preceptors and teachers is concluded.

16. Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikaniddesavaṇṇanā

16. The Explanation of the Section on the Place for Feces and Urine.

156. Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikanti ṭhānamhi ṭhāne vā bhavaṃ vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikaṃ. Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vaccaṃ na kareyyāti sambandho. Ye ye vuḍḍhā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, āgatappaṭipāṭiṃ hitvā vuḍḍhappaṭipāṭiyāti attho. Vaccanti upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, passāvañca nahānañca na kareyyāti adhippāyo. Tadeva samattheti “yātānupubbiyā”tiādinā. Yātānupubbiyāti yātānaṃ gatānaṃ anupubbi [V 0.0283] anukkamo yātānupubbi, tāya. Vacca…pe… titthañcāti etaṃ tayaṃ labbhatīti attho, bhikkhunāti viññāyati.

156. 'Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānika' means that which pertains to the place for feces and urine. The connection is: 'One should not defecate according to seniority.' 'According to seniority' means according to the seniority of those who are senior, abandoning the order of arrival—this is the meaning. 'Defecation' is merely an indication; the intention is that one should not urinate or bathe there either. This is supported by 'according to the sequence of those who have gone,' and so on. 'According to the sequence of those who have gone' means by the sequence, the order, of those who have gone. The meaning is that these three—feces... and bathing place—are obtained; it is understood 'by a bhikkhu'.

157. Ubbhajitvā ca sahasā ca no paviseyyāti sambandho. Ubbhajitvāti cīvaraṃ dūratova ukkhipitvā. Sahasāti sīghaṃ. Ukkāsitvā paviseyyāti yojanā.

157. The connection is: 'One should not enter having hitched up one's robe nor hastily.' 'Having hitched up' means lifting the robe from afar. 'Hastily' means swiftly. The construction is: 'One should enter after clearing one's throat.'

158. Vaccapassāvadoṇīnaṃ bahīti sambandho. Ubhayanti vaccampi passāvampi.

158. The connection is with 'outside' regarding the receptacle for feces and urine. 'Both' refers to both feces and urine.

159. Kūpeti vaccāvāṭe. Kaṭṭhanti avalekhanakaṭṭhaṃ. Pharusenāti kharena avalekhanakaṭṭhena. Uhatañcāpīti attanā vā parena vā uhatañcāpi vaccamakkhitañcāpīti attho. Dhovayeti sati udake, udake asati kaṭṭhenapi sodheyya.

159. 'In a pit' means in a latrine pit. 'Stick' means a scraping stick. 'Harshly' means with a rough scraping stick. 'Uhatañcāpi' means even if it has been removed by oneself or another, and even if it is smeared with feces. 'Wash' means to wash if water is available; if not, one should clean it even with a stick.

160. Na nikkhameti na nikkhameyya. Capu capūti anukaraṇaṃ, vicchāyaṃ dvitte capu capu katvāti kiriyāvisesanaṃ. Nācameyyāti na dhoveyya. Sati pana udake ācamitabbaṃ, asati yena [M 0.0334] kenaci puñchitvā gantabbaṃ, sabbasādhāraṇaṭṭhāne ca ācamanakumbhiyā udakaṃ na sesetabbaṃ. Uklāpanti kacavaraṃ. Visodhayeti vihārasodhane viya vaccapassāvakuṭiyo, pariveṇakoṭṭhake ca sammajjeyya. Sabbattheva ca pana vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ.

160. 'Na nikkhameti' means one should not depart. 'Capu capu' is an onomatopoeia; in its reduplicated form, 'having made a capu capu sound' is an adverbial modifier. 'Nācameyyāti' means one should not wash. But if water is available, one should rinse; if not, one should wipe with whatever is available and proceed. And in a common place, water in the rinsing pot should not be left over. 'Uklāpa' means refuse. 'Visodhayeti' means, as in cleansing the monastery, so one should sweep the latrines and the surrounding cells. And in every breach of duty, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition concerning the place for feces and urine is concluded.

17. Āpucchakaraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

17. Commentary on the Exposition on Asking Permission

161. Āpucchakaraṇanti āpucchāya karaṇaṃ. Anajjhiṭṭhovāti anāṇattova, ayācito eva vā. Na ca vissajeti pucchitapañhaṃ na vissajjeyya ca, āpucchitvā vā yācito vā yathāvuttametaṃ kātuṃ labhatīti adhippāyo.

161. 'Āpucchakaraṇa' means the act of asking permission. 'Anajjhiṭṭho' means without being commanded, or even without being requested. 'Na ca vissajeti' means one should not answer a question that has been asked. The intention is that one is permitted to do this as stated only after having asked or having been requested.

162. Āpucchitvā [V 0.0284] kathentassāti attano vuḍḍhaṃ āpucchitvā dhammādikaṃ bhāsantassa. Puna vuḍḍhatarāgameti puna aññassa vuḍḍhatarassa āgamane satīti attho. Punaāpucchanaṃ natthīti bhāsitabbaṃ ṭhapetvā puna āpucchanakiccaṃ natthīti attho. Saṅghatthere asati āraddhampi aṭṭhapetvā kathentassāpi eseva nayo. Bhattagge anumodato ca āpucchanaṃ natthīti sambandho. Anumodatoti dāyakehi yācitassa taṃtaṃpuññānumodanavasena dhammakathaṃ karoto ca. Anumodanañca therādheyyaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave therena bhikkhunā bhattagge anumoditu”nti (cūḷava. 362) hi vuttaṃ. “Sace manussā attano abhirucikena ekena anumodanaṃ kārenti, neva tassa anumodato āpatti, na mahātherassa bhāro hoti. Upanisinnakathāyameva hi manussesu [M 0.0335] kathāpentesu mahāthero āpucchitabbo”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cuḷava. aṭṭha. 362) vuttaṃ.

162. 'Of one speaking having asked permission' means of one speaking about the Dhamma and so forth after asking permission from one's elder. 'When a more senior elder arrives again' means when another, more senior elder arrives. 'There is no need to ask permission again' means that, apart from what is to be spoken, there is no further duty of asking permission. This same principle applies even for one who speaks without setting aside what has been started, when the elder of the Saṅgha is not present. 'While giving thanks in the meal hall, there is no need to ask permission' is the connection. 'Giving thanks' refers to giving a Dhamma talk at the request of donors, by way of dedicating their merit. The giving of thanks is the elder's responsibility. 'I allow, monks, for a monk who is an elder to give thanks in the meal hall' (Cūḷavagga 362) is stated. 'If people have the giving of thanks done by one according to their own liking, there is no offense for the one giving thanks, nor is it a burden for the senior elder. Only when people are prompted to speak in conversation while seated nearby should the senior elder be asked for permission,' as stated in the commentary (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 362).

163. Vuḍḍhena ekavihārake vasanto cāti sambandho. Vuḍḍhenāti vuḍḍhena saddhiṃ. Ekavihāraketi savanūpacāre khuddakavihāre, na mahāvihāre. Kucchitatthe hi kappaccayo. Na sajjhāyeyyāti sajjhāyanaṃ na kareyya.

163. 'And dwelling in a single small dwelling with an elder' is the connection. 'With an elder' means together with an elder. 'In a single small dwelling' refers to a small dwelling within earshot, not a large monastery. For the suffix -ka is in the sense of 'contemptible.' 'Should not recite' means one should not perform recitation.

164. “Dhammaṃ na bhāsaye”tiādīsu anāpucchāti sambandhitabbaṃ. Na ca vijjhapeti na ca nibbāyeyya. Vātapānañca ālokasandhiphalakaṃ kavāṭañca dvāraphalakaṃ vātapānakavāṭaṃ vā na vivareyya na thakeyya cāti na-kāro sabbattha yojetabbo.

164. In 'should not teach the Dhamma,' etc., 'without asking permission' should be connected. 'And one should not extinguish' means one should not put it out. The negative particle 'na' should be applied everywhere to 'should not open' and 'should not close' the window, the light-opening panel, the door panel, or the window-door.

165. Ekacaṅkame vuḍḍhena caṅkamantopi yena vuḍḍho, tena parivattayeti yojanā. Yena tenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, yattha vuḍḍho, tatthāti attho, vuḍḍhaṃ ohāya aññato na gantabbanti adhippāyo. Soti navako. Enanti vuḍḍhaṃ. Sabbattha dukkaṭaṃ. Ayañhi khandhakadhammatā yattha na-kārena paṭisedho, tattha dukkaṭanti.

165. 'Even while walking on the same walking path with an elder, one should turn in the direction the elder turns' is the construction. 'Yena tena' is an instrumental expression used in the locative sense, meaning 'wherever the elder is.' The intention is that one should not go elsewhere, leaving the elder behind. 'He' refers to the junior monk. 'Him' refers to the elder. In all these cases, it is a dukkaṭa offense. For this is the nature of the Khandhaka rules: wherever there is a prohibition with the negative particle 'na,' it entails a dukkaṭa offense.

Āpucchakaraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition on asking permission is concluded.

18. Nagganiddesavaṇṇanā

18. Commentary on the Exposition on Nakedness

166. “Vaje”tiādīsu [V 0.0285] na-saddo sambandhitabbo. Tattha pana yathānurūpabhojanādikaṃ kammavacanaṃ ajjhāharitvā “bhojanaṃ na bhuñje”tiādinā attho veditabbo.

166. In ‘vaje’ and so forth, the word ‘na’ should be connected. There, however, by supplying an object of the action appropriate to the context, such as ‘food,’ the meaning should be understood as ‘one should not eat food’ and so forth.

167. Na [M 0.0336] kareti hatthakammādikaṃ parikammaṃ sayampi na kareyyāti attho. Paṭicchādīsūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ, jantāgharudakavatthappaṭicchādīnaṃ majjheti attho. Parikamme duve kappiyāti sambandho. Parikammeti jantāghare udakepi upajjhāyādīnaṃ kattabbaparikammavisaye, na abhivādanādīsu. Duveti jantāgharaudakappaṭicchādayo. Chādenti etāyāti chādi, vatthassa chādi vatthacchādi. Sabbatthāti sabbakammesūti.

167. 'One should not do' means one should not oneself perform services such as hand-work. ‘Paṭicchādīsu’ is a locative of specification; the meaning is ‘among coverings for the steam-bath, water, and cloth’. ‘In service, two are allowable’ is the connection. ‘In service’ refers to the sphere of service to be rendered to preceptors and others in the steam-bath or with water, not in matters like paying respects and so forth. ‘Two’ refers to the coverings for the steam-bath and for water. ‘A covering’ is that by which they cover; the covering for a cloth is ‘vatthacchādi’. ‘In all cases’ means ‘in all actions’.

Nagganiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Nakedness is concluded.

19. Nhānakappaniddesavaṇṇanā

19. Commentary on the Exposition on Allowable Things in Bathing

168. Kappanaṃ kappiyatā kappo, nhāne kappo nhānakappo. Navako therānaṃ purato upari vā na ca nhāyeyyāti sambandho. Na cāti nayeva. Puratoti abhimukhe. Uparīti nadiyā upari.

168. ‘Kappanaṃ’ is making allowable; ‘kappiyatā’ is allowableness; ‘kappo’ is what is allowable; what is allowable in bathing is ‘nhānakappo’. ‘A junior monk should not bathe in front of or upstream from the elders’ is the connection. ‘Na ca’ means ‘certainly not’. ‘Purato’ means ‘in front of’. ‘Upari’ means upstream on a river.

169-171. Kuṭṭatthambhataruṭṭāne kāyaṃ na ghaṃsayeti sambandho. Tattha kuṭṭaṃ nāma iṭṭhakadārusilābhitti. Thambho nāma nahānatitthe nikhanitvā ṭhapito. Tarūti rukkho. Aṭṭānaṃ nāma tacchetvā aṭṭhapadākārena rājiyo chinditvā nahānatitthe nikhātaphalakaṃ. Gandhabbahatthena vā…pe… mallakena vā kāyaṃ sarīrena vā aññamaññaṃ na ghaṃsayeti sambandho. Gandhabbahatthenāti dārumayahatthena. Kuruvindakasuttiyāti kuruvindakapāsāṇacuṇṇāni lākhāya bandhitvā kataguḷikāvaliyā suttena āvuṇitasuttiyā. Mallakenāti makaradantake chinditvā padumakaṇṇikasaṇṭhānena katamallakena. Sarīrenāti attano kāyena. Aññamaññassa aññamaññaṃ kiriyākaraṇasaṅkhāte [V 0.0286] kiriyābyabhihāre dvittaṃ. Kapāla…pe… puthupāṇi ca sabbesaṃ vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Kapālañca iṭṭhakā ca, tāsaṃ khaṇḍāni. Puthupāṇīti puthu nānā [M 0.0337] pāṇi puthupāṇi, hatthaparikammaṃ ruḷhīvasena. Sabbesanti gilānāgilānānaṃ. Gilānassa akatamallakaṃ vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Akatamallakaṃ nāma katamallakaviparītaṃ. Pheṇaṃ nāma samuddapheṇanti.

169-171. ‘One should not rub the body on a wall, pillar, tree, or platform’ is the connection. Here, ‘kuṭṭaṃ’ means a wall made of bricks, wood, or stone. ‘Thambho’ means a pillar fixed in the bathing place. ‘Tarū’ means a tree. ‘Aṭṭānaṃ’ means a plank, dug into the bathing place, which has been planed and has lines cut in the shape of an eight-squared board. ‘One should not rub the body against another with a hand-shaped tool… or with a scraper, or with one’s own body’ is the connection. ‘Gandhabbahatthena’ means with a wooden hand. ‘Kuruvindakasuttiyā’ refers to a string made by binding ruby powder with lac into a row of small balls, which is wound with thread. ‘Mallakena’ means with a scraper shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, made by cutting a 'makara-tooth'. ‘Sarīrena’ means with one’s own body. The reduplication of ‘aññamaññassa aññamaññaṃ’ is in the sense of repetition of action, denoted as action and counter-action. ‘A potsherd… and a ‘puthupāṇi’ are allowable for all’ is the connection. ‘Kapālañca’ refers to potsherds and bricks, and their fragments. ‘Puthupāṇī’ means ‘various hands’; by convention, it means hand-service. ‘Sabbesaṃ’ means for both the sick and the not-sick. ‘For the sick, an unadorned scraper is allowable’ is the connection. ‘Akatamallakaṃ’ means the opposite of an adorned scraper. ‘Pheṇaṃ’ refers to sea-foam.

Nhānakappaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Allowable Things in Bathing is concluded.

20. Avandiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

20. Commentary on the Exposition on Those Unworthy of Veneration

172. Ukkhittoti āpattiyā adassane appaṭikamme ca ukkhittako pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge ukkhittakoti tividho ukkhittako. Nānāsaṃvāsako nāma laddhinānāsaṃvāsakopi kammanānāsaṃvāsakopi. Garukaṭṭho cāti pārivāsiko mūlāyapaṭikassanāraho mānattāraho mānattacārī abbhānāraho ca idha garukaṭṭhoti adhippeto. Imehi pana aññamaññaṃ vandituṃ vaṭṭatīti.

172. ‘Ukkhitto’ means one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one suspended for not renouncing a wrong view; thus, there are three kinds of suspended persons. ‘Nānāsaṃvāsako’ means one of different communion by doctrine and one of different communion by act. ‘Garukaṭṭho’ here is intended to mean one who is on probation, one who is deserving to be sent back to the beginning, one who is deserving penance, one who is undergoing penance, and one who is deserving rehabilitation. However, it is allowable for these to venerate each other.

Avandiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Those Unworthy of Veneration is concluded.

21. Cammaniddesavaṇṇanā

21. Commentary on the Exposition on Hides

173. Migā ca ajā ca eḷakā ca, tesaṃ cammānīti samāso. Ajo chagalako. Eḷako meṇḍako. Mige dasseti “rohite”tiādinā. Rohitā-diggahaṇaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, vātamigamigamātukādīpi ettheva saṅgayhanti.

173. The compound is ‘the hides of them: deer, goats, and sheep’. ‘Ajo’ is a goat. ‘Eḷako’ is a ram. It indicates deer by ‘rohita’ and so forth. The inclusion of ‘rohita’ and so forth is merely an illustration; antelope, does, and the like are also included here.

174. Anuññātattayāti [V 0.0287] anuññātā yathāvuttacammattayato. Amānusaṃva sabbaṃ cammaṃ thavikopāhane kappatīti sambandho. Thavikā satthakakosakādīti.

174. ‘Anuññātattayā’ means permitted in respect of the three kinds of hides mentioned above. The connection is: ‘All non-human hides are allowable for bags and footwear.’ ‘Thavikā’ means knife sheaths and so forth.

Cammaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Hides is concluded.

22. Upāhananiddesavaṇṇanā

22. Commentary on the Exposition on Footwear

175. Navā [M 0.0338] guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā majjhadese na kappantīti sambandho. Navāti ekavārampi appaṭimukkā. Tattha guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā catupaṭalato paṭṭhāya vuccanti. Sambhave byabhicāre ca visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ bhavatīti “majjhadese”ti visesanaṃ amajjhadesaṃ byabhicaratīti amajjhadese guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā kappantīti veditabbaṃ. Tathā navāti iminā anavā majjhadesepi. Iminā pana vākyena majjhadesepi ekavārampi paṭimukkā, aññattha tu sabbāpi guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā vaṭṭanti, na sesāti āpannaṃ, tathāpi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ekapalāsikaṃ upāhana”nti (mahāva. 245) vuttattā ekapaṭalikāpi vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Sabbassāti majjhadese paccantimepi gilānāgilānassa sabbassa. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ajjhārāme upāhanaṃ dhāretu”nti (mahāva. 249) hi sāmaññena anuññātaṃ. Sabbatthāti gāme vā araññe vā ārāmato aññatra. Akallakassa cāti gilānasseva.

175. The connection is: ‘New footwear with multiple layers are not allowable in the Middle Country.’ ‘Navā’ means not worn even once. Here, ‘guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā’ are said to be those from four layers upwards. Since a qualification is meaningful when there is possibility and exception, the qualification ‘in the Middle Country’ implies an exception for non-Middle Country regions; thus, it should be understood that in non-Middle Country regions, footwear with multiple layers are allowable. Similarly, by ‘navā’ (new), it is implied that non-new ones are allowable even in the Middle Country. However, by this statement, it is implied that those worn even once are allowable even in the Middle Country, and elsewhere all footwear with multiple layers are allowable, and not the others; nevertheless, since it is stated, ‘Monks, I allow footwear with a single layer’ (Mahāvagga 245), it should be understood that even single-layered ones are allowable. ‘Sabbassa’ means for all, both sick and healthy, in the Middle Country and the border regions. For it is generally permitted, as stated, ‘Monks, I allow the wearing of footwear within the monastery’ (Mahāvagga 249). ‘Sabbattha’ means in villages or forests, or outside the monastery. ‘Akallakassa ca’ means for the sick only.

176-9. Sabba…pe… rattā ca upāhanā sabba…pe… vicchikāḷikā ca…pe… dīpīnaṃ cammehi ca majjāra…pe… cammehi ca parikkhaṭā ca upāhanā saṅkamanīyā pādukā ca koci dhāreyya, dukkaṭanti yojanā. Odātāya pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca abhāvepi anulomavasenettha vuttaṃ viya dissati. Nīlako ca odāto cātiādinā dvando. Sabbeva nīlaka…pe… kaṇhakā yāsanti samāso. “Mahāraṅgā”tiādīsu appayuttepi sabba-sadde pakaraṇavasena yojetvā attho veditabbo.

176-9. The connection is: ‘If anyone were to wear footwear that is entirely… red… or with scorpion-like designs… or made from the hides of leopards… or adorned with the hides of cats… or walking sandals, it is a wrong-doing.’ Even in the absence of the pure Pāḷi and the commentary, it appears to be stated here in accordance with what is conformable. ‘Blue and white’ and so forth is a dvanda compound. ‘All which are blue… black’ is the compound. In ‘Mahāraṅgā’ and so forth, even if the word ‘sabba’ (all) is not explicitly used, the meaning should be understood by connecting it according to the context.

“Atthā [V 0.0288] pakaraṇā liṅgā, ocityā kāladesato;

Saddatthā vibhajīyanti, na saddāyeva kevalā”ti. –

‘Meanings are distinguished by import, context, gender, propriety, time, and place; the meanings of words are distinguished, not merely the words themselves.’

Hi [M 0.0339] vuttaṃ. Citrāti vicitrā. Nīlapītādī vaddhāyeva yāsanti samāso. Ādi-saddena odātādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tittirapattasadiso vicitto vaṇṇo tittirapatta-saddena gahito. Tametesamatthīti tittirapattikā. Meṇḍassa ca ajassa ca visāṇasadisā vaddhā yāsanti bāhirattho. Tā pana kaṇṇikaṭṭhāne meṇḍakaajavisāṇasaṇṭhāne vaddhe yojetvā katā. Esa nayo vicchikāḷikādīsu. Paṇhipidhānatthaṃ tale khallaṃ baddhaṃ yāsanti viggaho. Jaṅghato sabbapādappaṭicchādanakaṃ puṭaṃ baddhaṃ yāsanti bahubbīhi. Tūlaṃ picu puṇṇaṃ yāsanti aññapadattho. Paliguṇṭhetīti paliguṇṭho, uparipādatalamattappaṭicchādakabandho, tena yojetvā katā pāliguṇṭhimā, vicitrā hi taddhitavutti. Vicchikānaṃ aḷasadisaṃ naṅguṭṭhasadisaṃ baddhametāsanti vicchikāḷikā. Sīhabyagghuddājinadīpīnaṃ cammehi cāti pakaraṇato ajinā nāma migā. Ulūkā pakkhibiḷārā. Saṅkamanti gacchanti etāhīti saṅkamanīyā. Tā pana tālapaṇṇādīhi katā saṃhāriyā.

For it is said. ‘Citrā’ means variegated. ‘Those which are bound with blue, yellow, and so forth’ is the compound. By the word ‘ādi’, white and so forth are included. A variegated color resembling a partridge’s feather is referred to by the word ‘tittirapatta’. That which possesses this quality is called ‘tittirapattikā’. The external meaning is ‘which have bindings resembling the horns of a ram and a goat’. These, however, are made by fitting bindings shaped like ram and goat horns in the place of the ear-piece. This principle applies to ‘vicchikāḷikā’ and so on. The analysis is: ‘which have a piece of leather bound to the sole for covering the heel’. ‘Which have a covering bound from the shin, covering the entire foot’ is a bahubbīhi compound. ‘Which are filled with cotton or kapok’ is its other meaning. ‘Paliguṇṭho’ is that which wraps around, a band covering only the upper part of the sole; ‘pāliguṇṭhimā’ is made by fitting it with this, for the formation of derived nouns is varied. ‘Vicchikāḷikā’ are those to which something resembling a scorpion’s sting or a tail is bound. ‘With the hides of lions, tigers, otters, and leopards’—from the context, ‘ajina’ means deer. ‘Ulūkā’ are owls and cats. ‘Saṅkamanīyā’ are those by which one walks or goes. These, however, are foldable, made of palm leaves and so on.

180. Sakalaṃ ekadesaṃ vā puñchitvāvāti yojanā. Khallakādikanti ādi-saddena meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikādikaṃ sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhātīti.

180. The connection is: ‘having wiped the whole or a part’. ‘Khallakādikaṃ’—by the word ‘ādi’, it includes all such things as ram’s horn bindings and the like.

Upāhananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Footwear is concluded.

23. Anolokiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

23. Commentary on the Exposition on Not Looking

181. Sārattoti saṃratto, sañjātarāgacittoti attho. Itthiyāti tadahujātāyapi paṭasatanivatthāya anokāsupanijjhāyane antamaso tiracchānagatānampi dukkaṭameva. Bhikkhādāyiyāti upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, itthī vā hotu puriso vā, bhikkhādānasamaye asārattenāpi mukhaṃ [M 0.0340] na ulloketabbaṃ. Ujjhānaṃ lāmakato saṃcintanaṃ, kopo, tattha saññā assāti [V 0.0289] ujjhānasaññī. Idha pana gilānopi na muccati. Ādāse udakapatteti iminā sesesu kaṃsapattādīsu kañjiyādīsu ca mukhanimittaṃ paññāyati, tesaṃ saṅgaho. “Sañchavi nu kho me vaṇṇo, no, jiṇṇo nu khomhi, no”ti pana oloketuṃ vaṭṭati. Assāti bhikkhuno.

181. ‘Sāratto’ means ‘saṃratto,’ that is, ‘having a mind in which lust has arisen.’ ‘Itthiyā’: in the case of a woman, even one born that very day and clad in a hundred pieces of cloth, in improper gazing, it is a wrong-doing even towards animals at the very least. ‘Bhikkhādāyiyā’ is merely an indication; whether it is a woman or a man, at the time of giving alms, one should not look up at their face even without lust. ‘Ujjhānaṃ’ is thinking of something as base, anger; one who has that perception is ‘ujjhānasaññī.’ Here, however, even the sick are not exempt. ‘In a mirror or a water bowl’: by this, it is understood that the reflection of the face is visible in other things such as bronze bowls, rice-gruel, etc.; these are included. However, it is permissible to look to see, “Is my skin-color good? No, am I old? No.” ‘Assa’ refers to the monk.

Anolokiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Not Looking is concluded.

24. Añjanīniddesavaṇṇanā

24. Commentary on the Exposition on Eye-Salve

182. Vaṭṭā vā aṭṭhasoḷasaṃsā vā maṭṭhā añjanī vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Aṭṭha ca soḷasa ca aṃsā koṇā yassā sāti viggaho. Soḷasaṃsapadesavibhattāya aṭṭhaṃsāsutiyā aṭṭhaṃsapadesavibhattā caturaṃsāpi sāmatthiyā gayhatīti ñātabbaṃ. “Ujukameva pana caturaṃsāvā”ti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) vuttaṃ. Añjanīti añjananāḷi. Mūle tissopi lekhā vaṭṭantīti yojanā. Mūleti bunde, heṭṭhatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Lekhāti vaṭṭalekhā. Bandhituṃ gīvāyaṃ ekā eva lekhā vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Bandhitunti pidhānabandhanatthaṃ.

182. The construction is: ‘A smooth eye-salve container, whether round or with eight or sixteen sides, is permissible.’ The analysis of this is: ‘That which has eight and sixteen sides or corners.’ It should be understood that by implication, a four-sided container divided into eight sections is also included, just as an eight-sided one is divided into sixteen sections. Indeed, it is said in the commentary (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.85), “But it could be a straight, four-sided one.” ‘Añjanī’ means an eye-salve tube. The construction is: ‘At the base, even three lines are permissible.’ ‘Mūle’ means at the base, that is, at the bottom. ‘Lekhā’ means a circular line. The connection is that only one line around the neck is permissible for binding. ‘Bandhituṃ’ means for the purpose of fastening the lid.
