183. Yaṃ kiñci rūpanti itthirūpādi yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ. Mālādikammanti mālākammaṃ latākammaṃ. Aḍḍhacandādīti ettha ādi-saddena agghiyādikaṃ gahitaṃ. Etthāti añjaniyaṃ.

183. ‘Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ’ means any form whatsoever, such as a woman's form, etc. ‘Mālādikammaṃ’ means garland-work and creeper-work. ‘Aḍḍhacandādi’: here, the word ‘ādi’ (etc.) includes things such as a vessel for offerings, etc. ‘Ettha’ means on the eye-salve container.

184. Thavikāti añjanithavikā. Sipāṭīti khurasipāṭikā. Salākāpi acittakā labbhāti sambandho. Salākāti añjanisalākā. Natthi cittametissāti acittakā. Tādisaṃ [M 0.0341] pana labhitvā upāhanāyo viya nāsetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

184. ‘Thavikā’ means an eye-salve pouch. ‘Sipāṭī’ means a razor case. The connection is that even an undecorated applicator is permissible. ‘Salākā’ means an eye-salve applicator. ‘Acittakā’ means ‘it has no decoration.’ However, having obtained such a thing, one should use it until it is destroyed, like footwear.

185. Aṭṭhi-saddena manussaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci aṭṭhi gahitaṃ.

185. By the word ‘aṭṭhi,’ any bone is taken, excluding human bone.

186. Dhūmanettāti dhūmanāḷikā, nissa ā-kārādesavasena vuttaṃ. Satthakadaṇḍānīti satthadaṇḍā[V 0.0290]. Natthuṃ denti etāyāti natthudānā. Aniyamena hi nadādito vā ī. Tehi saṅkhanābhiādīhi nibbattā tammayā.

186. ‘Dhūmanetta’ means a smoking tube; it is said by way of substituting ‘ā’ for the root vowel. ‘Satthakadaṇḍāni’ means knife handles. ‘Natthudānā’ means ‘that by which snuff is administered.’ For the suffix ‘ī’ is added without restriction from words like ‘nada’ etc. Those made from conch-shell centers, etc., are made of that material.

Añjanīniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition on Eye-Salve is concluded.

25. Akappiyasayananiddesavaṇṇanā

25. Commentary on the Exposition on Unsuitable Beds

187-9. Akappiyāni sayanānīti uccāsayanamahāsayanāni. Padhānavasena pana “sayanānī”ti vuttaṃ, pīṭhādayopi ettheva saṅgayhanti añjanī-saddena avasesāni viya. Āsandi ca…pe… ubhatorattūpadhānakañceti etāni akappiyānīti sambandho. Tattha āsandīti sugataṅgulena atirekaṭṭhaṅgulapādakāni mañcapīṭhāni. Tattha pīṭhaṃ nāma mañco viya nātidīghaṃ vuccati. Tividhaṃ tūlametissā atthīti tūlī, pakatitūlikā. “Pallaṅkoti pādesu vāḷarūpāni ṭhapetvā kato”ti ṭhapanassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 254) vuttattā ṭhapanañca yathākathañci hoti, yutti ca hotīti, “tattheva sīharūpādiṃ dassetvā kato pana vaṭṭatīti vadantī”ti yaṃ ṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ “kimiti evaṃ vadantī”ti vatvā paṭikkhipitabbaṃ. “Akappiyarūpakato akappiyamañco pallaṅko nāmā”ti hi [M 0.0342] sārasamāsepi. Āsandī pallaṅko uccāsayanaṃ, sesā mahāsayanaṃ. Paṭikā uṇṇāmayo setattharaṇo. Gono caturaṅgulādhikalomo mahākojavo. Cittakaṃ vānavicitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Uṇṇā eḷakalomaṃ. Paṭalikā ghanapupphikā. Vikatīti sīhabyagghādirūpavicitto. Uddalomīti ekato uggatalomo. Ekantalomikāti ubhato uggatalomo.

187-9. "Unsuitable beds" means high beds and luxurious beds. However, the term "beds" is used here in a primary sense, and seats and the like are also included, just as the remaining items are included under the term "añjanī." The connection is that the āsandī and so on, up to the ubhatorattūpadhānaka, are unsuitable. Herein, "āsandī" refers to beds or seats with legs exceeding eight Sugata-fingerbreadths. Among these, a "pīṭha" is called a seat that is not excessively long, like a bed. Because it has three kinds of stuffing, it is called "tūlī," a natural mattress. Regarding "pallaṅka," since it is said in the commentary (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 254) that "it is made by placing animal figures at the feet," and since such placement can be of any kind and is reasonable, what is said in the ṭīkā (subcommentary) that "it is permissible if made by depicting lion figures, etc., there" should be rejected by saying, "Why do they say so?" For in the Sārasamāsa too, it is said, "An unsuitable bed, made in an unsuitable form, is called a pallaṅka." The āsandī and pallaṅka are high beds, while the rest are luxurious beds. "Paṭikā" is a white woolen coverlet. "Gono" is a large fleecy rug with hair exceeding four fingerbreadths. "Cittakaṃ" is a variegated woolen spread with figures. "Uṇṇā" is sheep’s wool. "Paṭalikā" is a thickly flowered rug. "Vikatī" is ornamented with figures of lions, tigers, etc. "Uddalomī" has hair raised on one side. "Ekantalomikā" has hair raised on both sides.

Kuttaṃ soḷasannaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ ṭhatvā naccanayoggo. Koseyyaṃ ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyasuttamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ, kaṭṭissaṃ ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ. Hatthino ca assā ca rathā cāti senaṅgānaṃ bahutte samāhāradvando, hatthiassarathe tesaṃ piṭṭhīsu attharāti tappuriso. Ajinappaveṇīti ajinānaṃ ajinamigacammānaṃ mañcappamāṇena dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbitā paveṇī. Kadalimigānaṃ idaṃ kadalimigaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Cammaṃ, pavaro ca so paccattharo cāti [V 0.0291] pavarapaccattharo, so ca taṃ setavatthassa upari atthatañca, kadalimigañca taṃ pavarapaccattharañcāti samāso, pavarapaccattharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ setavatthassa upari pattharitaṃ kadalimigappavarapaccattharaṇanti attho. Taṃ kira evaṃ karonti. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana yathāvuttadvayena atthataṃ aññameva kiñci vuttaṃ, taṃ na yuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī dhāretabbā”tiādinā (mahāva. 254) visuṃ attharaṇānameva vuttattā. Tesu hi vuttesu tadatthataṃ vuttameva siyā, tathā ca vuttaṃ heṭṭhā visuṃ paṭikādikanti.

"Kuttaṃ" is a rug suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand and dance upon. "Koseyyaṃ" is a coverlet made of silk thread, interwoven with jewels; "kaṭṭissaṃ" is one made of silk floss, interwoven with jewels. "Hatthino ca assā ca rathā ca" (elephants, horses, and chariots) is a collective compound due to the multitude of army components; "hatthiassarathe" is a dependent determinant compound meaning "coverings on the backs of elephants, horses, and chariots." "Ajinappaveṇī" refers to a series of hides, that is, skins of deer, stitched together after being made into two or three layers the size of a bed. "Kadalimigaṃ" (a kadalimiga hide): what is that? A hide. And a superior coverlet (pavarapaccatthara) as well—thus "pavarapaccatthara." And that is spread over a white cloth, and that kadalimiga hide and that superior coverlet—thus the compound. The meaning is: a superior coverlet of kadali-deer hide, designated as a superior coverlet, spread over a white cloth. They say it is made in this way. However, what is said in the ṭīkā about something else being spread by means of the two previously mentioned items is not correct, because in the phrase "an ajinappaveṇī should be used," etc. (Mahāva. 254), separate coverings are mentioned. For if those had been mentioned, their being spread would have already been stated; and so it is stated separately below, as in the case of the paṭikā and so on.

Salohitavitānanti etaṃ “ubhatorattūpadhānaka”ntimassa visesanaṃ. Lohitavitānena saha vattamānanti samāso. Setavitānampi heṭṭhā akappiyapaccattharaṇe sati na vaṭṭati. Rattaṃ upadhānaṃ sīsūpadhānaṃ pādūpadhānañca rattūpadhānakaṃ, ubhato mañcassa sīsapādanikkhepanaṭṭhāne rattūpadhānakanti [M 0.0343] alopasamāso. Yaṃ pana ekameva upadhānaṃ ubhayapassesu rattādivaṇṇaṃ vicitraṃ, taṃ pamāṇayuttameva vaṭṭati. Tatridaṃ pamāṇaṃ – vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ, majjhe muṭṭhiratanaṃ, dīghato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ vā dviratanaṃ vā. Paribhuñjatoti iminā karontassa kārāpentassa katthaci chedanakaṃ pācittiyanti dīpeti.

"Salohitavitānaṃ" (with a red canopy) is a qualification of the last item, "ubhatorattūpadhānakaṃ" (with red pillows at both ends). It is a compound meaning "existing together with a red canopy." A white canopy is also not allowable if there is an unsuitable coverlet beneath it. "Rattūpadhānakaṃ" means a red head-pillow and a red foot-pillow; and "ubhatorattūpadhānakaṃ" means red pillows at both ends of the bed where the head and feet are placed—this is an unelided compound. However, if there is a single pillow that is variegated with red and other colors on both sides, it is allowable only if it meets the proper measurements. Here are the measurements: in width, at three corners, the distance between two corners should be a span and four fingerbreadths, with one fist-cubit in the middle; in length, it should be one and a half cubits or two cubits. "Paribhuñjati" (uses it) indicates that for one who makes it, has it made, or cuts it anywhere, there is a pācittiya offense for cutting; this is indicated.

190. Dhammāsane ca bhattagge ca ghare cāpi āsandādittayā sese gihisantake gihivikaṭe sati nisīdituṃ labbhatīti ajjhāhāro padasambandho veditabbo. Gihisantaketi iminā saṅghikampi upalakkheti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā tīṇi āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ tūlikaṃ gihivikaṭa”nti (cūḷava. 314) sāmaññena vuttaṃ. Sāmaññajotanāya pana visesepi avaṭṭhānato āsandādittayāti ettha dhammāsane āsandādittayā seseti yojetvā attho gahetabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyañhi “āsandī pallaṅko gonako”tiādipāḷikkame āsandādidvayamādito hitvā “gonakādīni saṅghikavihāre vā puggalikavihāre vā mañcapīṭhakesu attharitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti, dhammāsane pana gihivikaṭanīhārena labbhanti, tatrāpi nipajjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) vuttaṃ. Bhattaggaṃ nāma vihāre dānaṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammāsanaṃ pana yattha katthaci. Ghareti antaraghare. Nisīdituṃ labbhateti iminā nipajjituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Saṃkhipanaṃ antokaraṇaṃ saṅkhepo, bhūmattharaṇe saṅkhepo assa sayanassāti samāso. Tasmiṃ bhūmattharaṇe antokaraṇabhūmattharato bhūmattharaṇamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sayituñcāti attano kappiyapaccattharaṇaṃ attharitvā sayituñca nisīdituñca. “Paribhaṇḍakataṃ bhūmiṃ vā bhūmattharaṇasenāsanaṃ [V 0.0292] vā saṅghikamañcapīṭhaṃ vā attano santakena paccattharaṇena paccattharitvāva [M 0.0344] nipajjitabba”nti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 324) vuttaṃ. Idañca āsandādīnampi aññathattakaraṇe paribhoge lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “anujānāmi bhikkhave, āsandiyā pāde chinditvā paribhuñjituṃ, pallaṅkassa vāḷe bhinditvā paribhuñjituṃ, tūlikaṃ vijaṭetvā bibbohanaṃ kātuṃ, avasesaṃ bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātu”nti (cūḷava. 320).

190. "On the Dhamma seat, in the dining hall, and inside a house—except for the three beginning with āsandī—when there are remaining items that are a householder’s property or furniture, it is permissible to sit." This connection of words should be understood as being supplied. By "householder’s property," what belongs to the Sangha is also indicated. For it is said generally (in Cūḷava. 314): "Monks, I allow a householder's furniture, except for three: an āsandī, a pallaṅka, and a tūlikā." However, for the sake of clarifying the general rule, since it applies even to specific cases, the meaning here should be taken by construing "on the Dhamma seat" with "on the remaining items apart from the three beginning with āsandī." For in the commentary (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 320), following the Pali sequence "āsandī, pallaṅka, gonaka," etc., it is said, excluding the first two (āsandī and pallaṅka): "Gonaka and the like, whether in a Sangha dwelling or a personal dwelling, when spread on beds or benches, are not to be used. However, on a Dhamma seat, they are permissible according to a householder’s usage, but lying down on them is not allowed." The dining hall refers to the place for giving food in the monastery. The Dhamma seat, however, is wherever it may be. "Ghare" means within a house. "It is permissible to sit" indicates that lying down is not allowed. "Saṃkhipanaṃ" is making compact, "antokaraṇaṃ" is putting inside, "saṅkhepo" is contraction. The compound "bhūmattharaṇe saṅkhepo assa sayanassāti" means "its bed is a contraction on the ground covering." In that ground covering, it should be seen as the ground covering itself, rather than a ground covering that is made compact. "To sleep" means spreading one’s own allowable coverlet and then sleeping and sitting. For in the commentary (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 324), it is said: "A prepared piece of ground or a ground-covering seat, or a Sangha bed or bench, should only be lain upon after spreading one’s own allowable coverlet over it." This also serves as a defining statement for the use of āsandī and the like when altered. For the Blessed One has said: "Monks, I allow you to cut the legs of an āsandī and then use it, to break off the animal figures of a pallaṅka and then use it, to unravel a tūlikā and make a headrest, and to make the rest into a ground covering."

191. Caturaṃsapīṭhā ca…pe… pañcaṅgā ca uccapādakā kappantīti atthato vacanaṃ vipallāsetvā sambandhitabbaṃ, “kappiyā”ti iminā vā sambandho veditabbo. Tattha cattāro aṃsā koṇā yesaṃ, te ca te pīṭhā cāti samāso. Tiṇṇaṃ apassayānaṃ, catunnañca pādānaṃ vasena satta aṅgāni yesanti samāso. Ekāpassayassa vasena pañcaṅgā. Caturaṃsapīṭhānaṃ visuṃ kappiyabhāvassa vuttattā sattaṅgādayo pana dīghāti viññāyanti. Pāḷiyaṃ bhattaggassa ekayoganiddiṭṭhattā ekayoganiddiṭṭhānaṃ saha vā pavatti, saha vā nivattīti ghareti iminā bhattaggassapi gahaṇaṃ. Eva-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, tasmā tūlonaddhā mañcapīṭhā ghare vā bhattagge vā nisīditumeva kappantīti sambandho. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi “tena kho pana samayena manussā bhattagge antaraghare tūlonaddhaṃ mañcampi pīṭhampi paññapenti. Bhikkhū kukkuccāyantā nābhinisīdanti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gihivikaṭaṃ abhinisīdituṃ, na tveva abhinipajjitu”nti (cūḷava. 314). Te pana karontassa vā kārāpentassa vā uddālanakaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

191. The words 'four-cornered seats... and five-membered high-footed ones are permissible' should be connected by transposing their meaning. Alternatively, the connection should be understood with the word 'permissible'. Here, 'four-cornered seats' (caturaṃsapīṭhā) is a compound meaning 'seats (pīṭhā) which have four corners (aṃsā koṇā)'. The compound 'seven-membered' (sattaṅgāni) means 'having seven members by way of three supports and four feet'. The 'five-membered' (pañcaṅgā) means 'by way of one support'. Since the permissibility of four-cornered seats is stated separately, the seven-membered ones and so on are understood to be long. In the Pāli, since the dining hall (bhattagga) is designated as a single application, it is included by the term 'house' (ghara), for things designated by a single application either occur together or cease together. The word 'eva' is used inappropriately here; therefore, the connection is that cotton-stuffed beds and seats are permissible only for sitting in the house or dining hall. Here is the Pāli passage: 'At that time, people prepared cotton-stuffed beds and seats in the dining hall inside the house. The monks, being scrupulous, did not sit on them. They reported the matter to the Blessed One. He said: “I allow, monks, to sit on household furniture, but not to lie down on it”' (Cūḷavagga 314). For one who makes them or has them made, there is an offense of expiation involving destruction (uddālanaka pācittiya).

192. Sānulomānaṃ channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ chavi etāsanti viggaho. Pañca bhisīti coḷāditūlagaṇanāya pañcakā vuttā. Sabbatthāti vihāramañcapīṭhādīsu sabbattha.

192. The analysis (viggaha) is: 'skin is for them one of the six conforming robes'. 'Five mattresses' (pañca bhisī) refers to the pentad mentioned in the enumeration of stuffing such as cloth-rags. 'Everywhere' (sabbattha) means everywhere, such as in monasteries, on couches, and on seats.

193. Tūlattayanti [M 0.0345] simbalirukkhādīnaṃ khīravalliādīnaṃ erakādīnaṃ tiṇānaṃ tūlattayaṃ. Bhisigabbho coḷādiko pañcavidho bhisigabbho. Migapakkhinaṃ lomānīti etaṃ sabbanti seso. Miga-saddeneva sabbepi sīhādayo catuppadā, pakkhi-saddena sabbepi haṃsamorādayo gahitā. Nanu ca bhisigabbhasaddantogadhāya uṇṇāya migapakkhilomānampi gahaṇasabbhāvepi tesaṃ visuṃ gahaṇe sati punaruttidoso āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati manussalomapariccāgavibhāvanappayojanasabbhāvato. Nanu ca evampi dosoyeva, “manussalomamuṇṇāya”ntiādinā [V 0.0293] bhisigabbhānaṃ upari nīyamānattā gamyate bibbohanepi ayameva bhisigabbhoti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi na doso, gamyamānatthassa saddassa payogaṃ pati kāmacāroti. Masūrake tūlavajjā anuññātāti vipariṇāmetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Masūrakaṃ nāma cammachavikā bhisīti vadanti.

193. 'Three kinds of stuffing' (tūlattaya) refers to the three kinds of stuffing from silk-cotton trees, etc., milk-vines, etc., and grasses like eraka, etc. A 'mattress stuffing' (bhisigabbho) is of five kinds, such as cloth-rags, etc. 'The hairs of animals and birds'—this completes the list. By the term 'animals' (miga), all four-footed creatures such as lions are included; by the term 'birds' (pakkhi), all creatures such as geese and peacocks are included. Now, is there not a fault of repetition if the hairs of animals and birds are mentioned separately, even though they are already included in the term 'mattress stuffing' (bhisigabbha) by way of wool (uṇṇā)? There is no fault, because the purpose is to demonstrate the exclusion of human hair. But is there not still a fault, since by saying 'human hair, wool,' etc., it is understood that these mattress stuffings are dealt with above, and thus this too is a mattress stuffing even in the case of a pillow (bibbohana)? True, but still there is no fault, because with regard to the intended meaning, the usage of the word is optional. 'In the case of a masūraka, [stuffings] are allowed, with the exception of cotton'—this should be connected by transposing the words. 'Masūraka' is what they call a leather-hide mattress.

194. Uṇṇāyaṃ manussalomañca paṇṇe suddhaṃ tamālakañca pupphañca appaṭivekkhitaṃ āsanañceva na labbhanti sambandho. Manussalomanti iminā na kevalaṃ idha eḷakalomameva uṇṇā, atha kho kappiyākappiyamaṃsajātīnaṃ pakkhicatuppadānaṃ lomampīti dasseti. Pupphanti piyaṅgubakulapupphādi. Tamālakasaddeneva upacārato pattaṃ gahetvā “tamālaka”nti vuttaṃ. Appaṭivekkhitanti anupaparikkhitaṃ. Kīdisaṃ pana paṭivekkhitabbaṃ, kīdisaṃ na paṭivekkhitabbanti? Yaṃ vinicchayato viññātaṃ, taṃ na paṭivekkhitabbaṃ, itaraṃ hatthena parāmasantena paṭivekkhitabbaṃ.

194. The connection is that human hair in wool, a clean tamālaka leaf, and an uninspected flower and seat are not permissible. By 'human hair' (manussaloma) it is shown that here 'wool' (uṇṇā) is not only sheep's hair, but also the hair of birds and four-footed animals, whether their flesh is permissible or impermissible. 'Flower' (puppha) refers to flowers like the piyaṅgu and bakula. The term 'tamālaka' is used figuratively, taking the leaf by way of convention. 'Uninspected' (appaṭivekkhita) means 'unexamined'. But what should be inspected, and what should not? What is known through discernment need not be inspected; the rest should be inspected by touching with the hand.

Akappiyasayananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of unsuitable sleeping arrangements is finished.

26. Samānāsanikaniddesavaṇṇanā

26. Commentary on the Exposition of Sharing the Same Seat

195. Tivassantaramekamāsanaṃ [M 0.0346] bhikkhūnaṃ anuññātanti sambandho. Tattha ekasmiṃ āsane mañcādike dvinnaṃ āsanaṃ nisīdanaṃ ekamāsanaṃ. Ma-kāro sandhijo. Kīdisanti āha “tivassantara”nti. Tiṇṇaṃ vassānamantarametassāti tivassantaro, dvīhi vassehi mahantataro vā daharataro vā bhikkhu, so assa atthīti tivassantaraṃ, tivassantaravantanti attho. Yo pana ekena vassena mahantataro vā daharataro vā ekavassoyeva vā, tabbantatāya vattabbameva natthi. Atha vā tivassantaranti karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tivassantarena saddhinti attho. Tameva samattheti “sattavasse”ccādinā.

195. The connection is that monks are allowed to share a single seat (ekamāsana) with a three-year interval (tivassantara). Here, 'a single seat' (ekamāsana) means two people sitting on one seat, such as a couch. The letter 'm' is a euphonic addition (sandhija). What kind? He says, 'three-year interval'. It means 'having an interval of three years'. That is, a monk who is older or younger by two years has this 'three-year interval'. But if one is older or younger by just one year, or of the same seniority, there is no need to discuss that interval at all. Alternatively, 'three-year interval' (tivassantara) is a usage in the instrumental sense, meaning 'together with a three-year difference'. The same is supported by the phrase 'seven years,' etc.

196. Muni [V 0.0294] anuññāsīti sambandho. Sabbehevāti samānāsanikaasamānāsanikehi sabbeheva saddhiṃ.

196. The connection is: the Sage allowed it. 'With all' (sabbeheva) means together with all, whether they are ones who may share a seat (samānāsanika) or ones who may not share a seat (asamānāsanika).

197. Dīghāsanaṃ dasseti “anta”ntiādinā. Yaṃ tiṇṇaṃ nisīdituṃ pahoti, taṃ antaṃ dīghāsananti sambandho. Antanti pacchimaṃ. Adīghāsane pana samānāsanikā nisīdituṃ labbhantīti dassento “mañcake”tiādimāha. Sabbattha ayathākaraṇato dukkaṭanti.

197. It indicates a long seat (dīghāsana) with the word 'end' (anta), etc. The connection is that a seat sufficient for three to sit is a long seat, indicated by 'end'. 'End' (anta) means 'last' or 'farthest'. But to show that those who may share a seat (samānāsanikā) are allowed to sit on a non-long seat, he says 'on a couch' (mañcake), etc. In all cases, for acting improperly, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Samānāsanikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of sharing the same seat is finished.

27. Asaṃvāsaniddesavaṇṇanā

27. Commentary on the Exposition of Non-communion

198. Ukkhittoti kammanānāsaṃvāsakasaṅkhāto āpattiyā adassane, appaṭikamme, pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge ukkhittako. Anupasampannoti sikkhamānasāmaṇerasāmaṇerisikkhāpaccakkhātasaṅkhāto anupasampanno. Chinnamūlakoti [M 0.0347] antimavatthuajjhāpanno. Ukkhittakesu “dhammavādino ete”ti uppannāya laddhiyā nānābhūto saṃvāso etassāti nānāsaṃvāso, ukkhittānuvattakasaṅkhāto laddhinānāsaṃvāsako. Sīmato niggatā nissīmā, sīmantarikā bahisīmā ca, tattha hatthapāse cepi ṭhito, sīmānānāsaṃvāsako nissīmaṭṭhito. Vehāyase ākāse ṭhito vehāyasaṇṭhito bindāgamena. Tattha “nānāsaṃvāso cā”tiādinā samāhāradvandepi kvaci napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ byabhicaratīti napuṃsakattābhāvo yathā “maggāmaggo”ti. Ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatāti ayaṃ tividhopi saṃvāso nāma. So yesaṃ natthi, te asaṃvāsā. Ete hatthapāsato bahikaraṇavasena vajjetabbā. Etesu hi tividhe ukkhittake sati uposathādikaṃ kammaṃ karontassa pācittiyaṃ, itaresu dukkaṭanti.

198. One who is suspended (`ukkhitto`) is one known as `kammanānāsaṃvāsaka` (one of different communion due to a formal act); an `ukkhittaka` is one suspended for not acknowledging an offense, not making amends, or not relinquishing a wrong view. One who is unordained (`anupasampanno`) refers to a probationer (sikkhamāna), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), or one who has renounced the training. One who is root-cut (`chinnamūlako`) is one who has committed a final offense. Among the suspended, one whose communion is different on account of the view that has arisen, 'These are speakers of the Dhamma,' is called `nānāsaṃvāso` (one of different communion), being one known as `laddhinānāsaṃvāsako` (one whose communion differs due to doctrine), a follower of the suspended. Those who have gone beyond the boundary are `nissīmā` (outside the boundary), `sīmantarikā` (between boundaries), and `bahisīmā` (outside the boundary); one who stands outside the boundary, even if within arm's reach there, is a `sīmānānāsaṃvāsako` (one whose communion differs due to the boundary). One standing in the sky (`vehāyase ākāse ṭhito`) is `vehāyasaṇṭhito` (one situated in the sky), by way of a nasal insertion. Here, in phrases like 'nānāsaṃvāso ca,' etc., even in a collective compound (samāhāradvanda), the neuter gender is sometimes deviated from, hence the absence of neuter gender, as in 'maggāmaggo' (path and non-path). A single formal act, a single recitation, and equal training—these three are called `saṃvāsa` (communion). Those for whom these are absent are `asaṃvāsā` (not in communion). These should be avoided by keeping them beyond arm's reach. Among these, for the three types of suspended individuals, if one performs a formal act like the Uposatha, it is a pācittiya offense; for the others, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Asaṃvāsaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Non-communion is finished.

28. Kammaniddesavaṇṇanā

28. Commentary on the Exposition of Formal Acts

199. Vaggena [V 0.0295] adhammakammañca samaggena adhammakammañca vaggena dhammakammañca samaggena dhammakammañcāti cattāri kammāni hontīti seso. Tattha vaggena adhammakammanti vaggena saṅghena karaṇīyaṃ adhammakammaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Vaggoti ca samūho vuccati, so ca catuvaggādikaraṇīyādīsu yāvatikānaṃ kammappattānaṃ asammukhībhāvena, chandārahānaṃ chandānāharaṇena, sammukhībhūtānañca paṭikkosanena, tesu ekenāpi vā idha adhippeto. Adhammakammanti ettha pana dhammo nāma “uttidutiye ce, bhikkhave, kamme ekāya uttiyā kammaṃ karoti, na ca kammavācaṃ anussāveti, adhammakamma”ntiādinā (mahāva. 387) ekāyeva ñattiyā[M 0.0348], tathā dvīhi ñattīhi ekāyeva vā kammavācāya, tathā dvīhi kammavācāhīti āgatāya ca tathā hāpanaaññathākaraṇabhāvena ñattikammaṃ ṭhapetvā ñatticatutthe ca kamme āgatāya ca akammārahassa tajjanīyapabbājanīyapaṭisāraṇīyaniyassatividhaukkhepanīyānaṃ sattannaṃ kammānaṃ karaṇavasena, kammārahassa ca virādhetvā karaṇavasena āgatāya ca pāḷiyā viparītā ca pāḷi, upasampadādikammavasena āgatā ca pāḷi, sammukhāvinayasativinayaamūḷhavinayapaṭiññākaraṇayebhuyyasikātassapāpi- yasikātiṇavatthārakasaṅkhātānaṃ sattannaṃ kammānaṃ yathālābhakaraṇavasena āgatā ca pāḷi, tena karaṇīyaṃ apalokanañattiñattidutiyañatticatutthasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ dhammakammaṃ, tappaṭipakkhaṃ adhammakammaṃ. Tabbipariyāyena samaggo dhammakammañca veditabbaṃ. Dhammo yathāvuttā pāḷi assa atthi, dhammena kataṃ vāti dhammikaṃ. Tabbiparītaṃ adhammikaṃ. Catutthaṃyevāti tesu catūsu kammesu catunnaṃ pūraṇaṃ samaggena dhammikaṃ. Sesakammānaṃ bhāvena bhikkhunā dukkaṭassa bhavanaṃ lakkhīyatīti sesakammesūti bhāvalakkhaṇe sattamī. Dukkaṭanti kuppānaṃ adhammakammavaggakammānaṃ katattā dukkaṭaṃ.

199. There are four kinds of formal acts: an unlawful formal act by a faction, an unlawful formal act by a complete assembly, a lawful formal act by a faction, and a lawful formal act by a complete assembly—this is the remainder. Herein, 'an unlawful formal act by a faction' refers to an unlawful formal act to be performed by a factional Sangha. The same principle applies throughout. 'Faction' means a group, and it is intended here to refer to a situation where those eligible to participate in the formal act are not present, where consent is not obtained from those from whom it should be, or where those who are present object—even one of these. As for 'unlawful formal act,' the Dhamma is defined as: 'If, monks, in a formal act with a second announcement, one performs the act with one announcement and does not recite the formal proclamation, it is an unlawful formal act,' and so on (Mahāvagga 387). An unlawful formal act is one that has come about by way of a single motion, or two motions, or a single formal proclamation, or two formal proclamations, or by way of omission or alteration in a formal act with a motion, as opposed to a formal act with a motion and three proclamations. It also refers to the performance of the seven formal acts—censure, banishment, reconciliation, subordination, and the three kinds of suspension—on one who is not liable for them, or by performing them incorrectly on one who is liable. Similarly, it refers to formal acts like higher ordination performed contrary to the Pāli text, as well as the performance of the seven kinds of settling legal questions—resolution in the presence of, resolution by mindfulness, resolution for past insanity, resolution on admission, resolution by majority, verdict for specific depravity, and covering with grass—when performed as available. The fourfold formal act—apalokana, ñatti, ñattidutiya, ñatticatuttha—is considered a 'lawful formal act,' while its opposite is an 'unlawful formal act.' Conversely, a 'lawful formal act by a complete assembly' should be understood. 'Lawful' (dhammika) means that which has the Dhamma, that is, the Pāli text as stated, or that which is done in accordance with the Dhamma. Its opposite is 'unlawful' (adhammika). 'The fourth only' means that among these four formal acts, the fourth one is the lawful act by a complete assembly. By the nature of the remaining formal acts, a bhikkhu is understood to incur a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing); thus, 'in the remaining formal acts' is a locative of characteristic. 'Wrongdoing' refers to the fault incurred by performing invalid, unlawful, or factional formal acts.

200. Idāni yadidaṃ samaggena dhammikaṃ nāma, taṃ yehi saṅghehi kātabbaṃ, tesaṃ pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “catuvaggo”tiādimāha. Catvādīnaṃ saṅkhyeyavuttittā catunnaṃ vaggotiādinā viggaho. Dasavīsativaggikoti dasannaṃ vīsatiyā ca vaggabhedavasena dasavīsatīnaṃ vaggoti viggaho, ṇiko sakatthe. Vīsatiyā vaggo, atirekena sahito vīsativaggoti viggaho.

200. Now, to show the distinctions of those Sanghas by whom this which is called a lawful act by a complete assembly should be done, he begins with 'the group of four,' etc. Because of the enumerable nature of four and so on, the analysis is, 'a group of four,' and so on. 'The group of ten or twenty' is analyzed as, 'by way of the division into groups of ten and twenty, it is a group of ten or twenty,' the suffix 'ika' being used in its own sense. 'A group of twenty, combined with a surplus, is a group of more than twenty'—this is the analysis.

201-2. Pañcannaṃ kammānaṃ niyameti “catū”tiādinā. Abbhānaṃ upasampadaṃ pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā [V 0.0296] catuvaggo cātiādinā yojetvā [M 0.0349] sabbakammesu kammappattoti dīpitoti yojetabbaṃ. Tattha tattha ca-saddo catuvaggādayo kammapattikiriyāyaṃ samuccinoti. Idha pana sabba-saddo abbhānādīnaṃ kesañci ṭhapitattā padesasabbe gayhati. Kammapattoti kammassa patto yutto anurūpo. Itaroti vīsativaggo atirekavīsativaggo. Sabbakammesūti ettha pana sabba-saddo sabbasabbe. Nanu ca vīsativaggassa kammappattabhāvesati atirekavīsativaggassa pagevāti viññāyati. Tathā sati so kasmā vuttoti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi so catuvaggādinā saṅghena kattabbakammaṃ ūnakatarena na vaṭṭati, atirekena pana vaṭṭatīti ñāpanatthaṃ vutto.

201-2. It regulates five types of formal acts with 'four,' etc. Except for rehabilitation, higher ordination, and invitation, it should be construed that by connecting with 'the group of four,' etc., suitability for all formal acts is indicated. There, the word 'ca' (and) includes the group of four, etc., in the action of being suitable for the formal act. But here, the word 'sabba' (all) is taken as a partial 'all' because some, such as rehabilitation etc., are excluded. 'Kammappatto' means one who has attained to, is connected with, or is suitable for the formal act. 'Itara' (the other) refers to the group of twenty and the group of more than twenty. 'In all formal acts'—here, however, the word 'sabba' (all) means 'all-inclusive all.' Now, if the group of twenty is suitable for the formal act, it is obvious that the group of more than twenty is even more so. If so, why was it stated? True, even so, a formal act to be performed by the Sangha comprised of the group of four, etc., is not proper with fewer than required, but is proper with more—this was stated to make this known.

203. Idāni catuvaggādikena chandāharaṇena pūretabboti dasseti “catū”tiādinā. Pārājikādibhāvamanāpannattā pakatiyā sabhāveneva ṭhito attā yesaṃ, pakato vā tatoyeva kammesu avigato attā yesaṃ teti pakatattakā, pārājikaukkhittakaladdhinānāsaṃvāsakehi aññe. Pareti ekasīmaṭṭhā tādisāyeva aññe. Sesepīti avasese pañcavaggādikaraṇīyepi.

203. Now, it is shown how to complete the groups of four and so on by taking consent: 'four' and so on. Those whose inherent nature remains unchanged because they have not incurred states such as defeat (pārājika), or whose inherent nature is such that they have not deviated from those formal acts, are called pakatattaka (those of inherent nature), that is, those other than the defeated (pārājika), the suspended (ukkhittaka), and those whose communion differs due to doctrine (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka). Others are those who stand in one boundary, being just like those others (i.e., sīmānānāsaṃvāsaka). Even in the remaining cases, such as those involving formal acts requiring a group of five and so on, this method should be used.

204. Idāni vatthuñattianussāvanasīmādivipattito, kammavipattīsu parisato ca paṭikkosato ca kammassa kuppākuppabhāvaṃ tattha ca āpattiādiṃ dassetuṃ “catū”tiādi māha. Catuvaggādikattabbaṃ asaṃvāsagaṇapūraṃ vā kammārahagaṇapūraṃ vā kammañca garukaṭṭhagaṇapūraṃ vā parivāsādikammañcāti yojanā. Ettha ca kammāraho garukaṭṭhato añño, nikkhittavatto pana garukaṭṭho gaṇapūrako hotiyeva. Katanti catuvaggādinā kataṃ.

204. Now, to explain the validity or invalidity of the formal act, and the offenses involved therein, due to flaws in the basis, motion, announcement, boundary, etc., and due to faults in the assembly or objections to the formal act, the text states 'four' and so on. The meaning is to be connected thus: the formal act to be performed by a group of four or more, or by a complete group for declaring non-communion, or by a complete group of those eligible for formal acts, or by a complete group including a gravely-offended monk, or it is a formal act such as probation and so on. Here, one who is eligible for the formal act is different from one who has reached the grave stage, but one whose practice has been suspended is indeed at the grave stage and completes the group. 'Done' refers to what has been carried out by the group of four or more.

205. Vāreyyāti antarāye asati antamaso ekopi vāreyyāti attho. Antarāyeti pāpehi kariyamāne [M 0.0350] jīvitabrahmacariyantarāye sati. Anantarāyikā ce na vārenti, dukkaṭaṃ. Diṭṭhāvinti attano attano diṭṭhiṃ laddhiṃ “adhammakammaṃ idaṃ, na metaṃ khamatī”ti aññamaññaṃ āvi kareyyunti seso. Ekodhiṭṭhānanti eko bhikkhu “na metaṃ khamatī”ti adhiṭṭhānaṃ kareyyāti seso. Tatodhikāti tīhi adhikā. Te pana saṅghattā pahonti attano kammaṃ nittharituṃ.

205. 'They should prevent' means that even if there is no obstacle, at least one should prevent; that is the meaning. 'Obstacle' refers to an obstacle to life or the holy life when evil actions are being performed. If they do not prevent when there is no obstacle, it is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Having made known their view' means each one, having their own view or doctrine, should openly declare to one another, 'This is an unlawful formal act; this is not pleasing to me'; the rest follows. 'One resolves' means a single monk may make a resolution, 'This is not pleasing to me'; the rest follows. 'More than that' means more than three. They, however, being a Sangha, are able to bring their own formal act to completion.

206. Khittacitto nāma ummattako. Dukhaṭṭitoti vedanaṭṭo. Na rūhatīti gayhattaṃ na rohatīti attho.

206. 'Distraught mind' means one who is insane. 'Afflicted by suffering' means afflicted by pain. 'Does not take root' means it does not take hold; that is the meaning.

207. Antamaso [V 0.0297] anantarassāpi ārocentassa pakata…pe… bhikkhunoti sambandho. Ekasīmāyaṃ tiṭṭhatīti ekasīmaṭṭho. Samo saṃvāso assāti samasaṃvāso. Ekasīmaṭṭho ca so samasaṃvāso ca, pakatatto ca so ekasīmaṭṭhasamasaṃvāso ca, so cāyaṃ bhikkhu cāti sabbattha kammadhārayo, tassa. Ettha pana avipannasīlo pakatattoti adhippeto. Ārocentassāti attano laddhiṃ pakāsentassa. Rūhatīti paṭikkhepo ruhati.

207. The connection is with 'of a `pakatatta` monk... who is informing, and who is, at the very least, not causing an obstacle.' 'Stays within one boundary' means one who is located in a single boundary. 'Equal in communion' means he has equal communion. 'Located in one boundary and with equal communion,' and 'he is of inherent nature and located in one boundary with equal communion,' and 'this is a monk'—in all cases, it is a determinative compound, referring to him. Here, however, 'one of unbroken virtue' is intended by 'pakatatta'. 'Informing' means declaring one's own doctrine. 'Takes root' means the rejection takes root.

208. Dhammikaṃ kammanti dhammena kattabbaṃ apalokanādikammaṃ. Paṭikkoseyyāti nivāreyya. Tirokkhā kāyasāmaggiṃ vā chandaṃ vāti vā-saddaṃ netvā attho netabbo. Tirokkhāti parammukhā. So sammukhā-saddo viya nipāto, atha vā akkhā indriyavisayato tiro bahīti atthoti.

208. 'Lawful formal act' means a formal act that should be done lawfully, such as acts requiring formal announcement, etc. 'Should reject' means should prevent. Regarding 'out of sight of bodily presence or consent,' the meaning should be understood by construing the word 'or' with each term. 'Out of sight' means turned away. It is a particle, like the word 'face-to-face,' or alternatively, it means outside the range of the senses, external.

Kammaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Formal Acts is concluded.

29. Micchājīvavivajjanāniddesavaṇṇanā

29. Commentary on the Exposition of Avoiding Wrong Livelihood

209. Āgamma jīvanti etenāti ājīvo, ko so? Paccayapariyesanavāyāmo. Micchāya ājīvo, tassa [M 0.0351] vivajjanā micchājīvavivajjanā. Sā panāyaṃ atthato “idha bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno”ti (vibha. 508) evaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasampattiyā paṭipattidassanavasena āgato ācāro ceva yathākkamena pārājikasaṅghādisesathullaccayapācittiyapāṭidesanīyadubbhāsitadukkaṭānaṃ kāraṇabhūtassa ājīvahetupaññattānaṃ abhūtārocanasañcarittaaññāpadesabhūtārocanapaṇītabhojanaviññatti bhikkhunibhojanaviññattisūpodanaviññattisikkhāpadānaṃ vītikkamassa ca kuhanalapananemittikatā nippesikatā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāti evamādīnañca pāpadhammānaṃ vasena pavattaṃ micchājīvaviratisaṅkhātaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlañca. Tassā pana kassaci idha dassanaṃ yathā dassetumāraddhaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṅkhātāya adhisīlasikkhāya, caturārakkhavipassanāvasena āgatānaṃ adhicittaadhipaññāsaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ sikkhānañca upakārakadhammaparidīpanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, evamīdisaṃ [V 0.0298] viññeyyaṃ, taṃ dasseti “dāru”ntiādinā. Tattha “dāru”ntiādīni “dade”ti etassa pattikammaṃ. Cuṇṇaṃ sirīsacuṇṇādinahāniyacuṇṇaṃ. Nhānamukhodakanti nhānañca mukhañca, tassa udakanti samāso. Ādi-saddena paṇṇādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Kulasaṅgahāti kulasaṅgahakaraṇena.

209. That by which they live is livelihood. What is that? The effort to seek requisites. Livelihood by wrong means is wrong livelihood; its avoidance is the avoidance of wrong livelihood. In meaning, this is the conduct that comes by way of showing the practice of the perfection of Pātimokkha restraint, as in: “Here, a monk dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort” (Vibh. 508). And it is also the virtue of livelihood purity, called abstinence from wrong livelihood, which proceeds by way of such evil qualities as deceit, flattery, hinting, belittling, and seeking gain with gain, and by way of the transgression of the training rules declared for the sake of livelihood—which are the cause of Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dubbhāsita, and Dukkaṭa offenses—namely, the training rules concerning false boasting, acting as a go-between, hinting by another pretext, boasting of what is true, requesting fine food, requesting food from a bhikkhunī, and requesting soup and rice. The showing of this here for someone is undertaken to demonstrate the higher virtue training, called Pātimokkha restraint, and for the purpose of clarifying the supportive qualities for the two trainings, called higher mind and higher wisdom, which come by way of the fourfold guarding of insight; thus, this is to be understood. It is shown by “wood,” etc. Here, “wood,” etc., are the objects of “should give.” Powder: powder for bathing, such as sirīsa powder. Water for bathing and face: a compound of “bathing” and “face,” meaning “water for that.” The word “etc.” includes leaves and so forth. Service to families: by rendering service to families.

210. Paribhaṭati paresaṃ dārake pariharatīti paribhaṭo, paribhaṭassa kammaṃ pāribhaṭako, sakatthe tameva pāribhaṭakatā. Alaṅkaraṇādinā kuladārakapariharaṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Muggassa sūpo muggasūpo, soyeva muggasuppo. Yathā muggasūpe paccamāne kocideva muggo na paccati, avasesā paccanti, evaṃ yassa puggalassa vacane kiñcideva saccaṃ hoti, sesaṃ alikaṃ, ayaṃ puggalo muggasūpasadisatāya upacārena “muggasuppo”ti vuccati, tassa bhāvo muggasuppatā[M 0.0352]. Saccālikena jīvitakappanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Gharavatthuādisambandhinī vijjā vatthuvijjā. Pāribhaṭakatā cātiādinā dvando napuṃsakattābhāve pāri…pe… vijjā, tāya. Rasso pana gāthābandhavasena, tathā dīgho. Pahiṇānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kamme tesaṃ tesaṃ niyuñjanaṃ paheṇaṃ. Ādarena dūtena kāretabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ dūtakammaṃ. Pisanaṃ pesanaṃ, jaṅghāya pādena pesanaṃ jaṅghapesanaṃ, tamassa atthīti jaṅghapesaniyaṃ. Tesaṃ tesaṃ gihīnaṃ gāmantaradesantarādīsu sāsanapaṭisāsanaharaṇassetamadhivacanaṃ.

210. One who tends to others’ children is called a `paribhaṭa`; the work of a `paribhaṭa` is `pāribhaṭaka`, and in its own sense, that very state is `pāribhaṭakatā`. This is a name for tending to the children of a family by means of adornment and the like. Soup made from mung beans is `muggasūpa`, and that same is `muggasuppo`. Just as when mung bean soup is cooking, some mung beans do not cook while the rest do, so too, if in a person’s speech some part is true while the rest is false, that person, by analogy with mung bean soup, is figuratively called a `muggasuppa`; the state of being such is `muggasuppatā`. This is a designation for making a living by means of truth and falsehood. Knowledge relating to house sites and so forth is `vatthuvijjā`. The dvanda compound beginning with `pāribhaṭakatā ca`, in the absence of the neuter gender, becomes `pāri…pe… vijjā`, by that. The short vowel, however, is due to the constraints of meter, and likewise the long vowel. Appointing messengers to various tasks is `paheṇaṃ`. Any task to be done with care by a messenger is `dūtakamma`. Grinding is `pisanaṃ`, sending is `pesanaṃ`; sending by leg, that is, by foot, is `jaṅghapesanaṃ`; the practice of this is `jaṅghapesaniyaṃ`. This is a designation for the carrying of messages and replies for various householders to other villages, countries, and so forth.

211. Lābhāsāya lañjadānaṃ anuppadānaṃ. Sambuddhappaṭikuṭṭhena buddhagarahitena aṅgavijjānakkhattavijjāsupinavijjābhūtavijjādinā aññena vā.

211. Giving a bribe with the desire for gain is `anuppadāna`. [This is done] by means of arts despised by the Perfectly Enlightened One, reviled by the Buddha, such as divination, astrology, dream interpretation, spirit lore, or any other.

212. Aññātakānaṃ appavāritānaṃ viññāpanaṃ viññatti, yācanavasena pavatto kāyavacīpayogo. Buddhappaṭikuṭṭhena micchājīvena paccayapariyesanā anesanā. Abhūtassa attani avijjamānassa uttarimanussadhammassa ullapanaṃ kathanaṃ abhūtullapanā. Kuhanādīhīti kuhanālapanādīhi. Tattha lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa paccayappaṭisevanasāmantajappanairiyāpathasaṇṭhāpanavasena janavimhāpanā kuhanā. Vihāraṃ āgate manusse disvā “kimatthāya bhonto āgatā, kiṃ bhikkhū nimantetu”nti vā “mayi rājā pasanno, asuko ca asuko ca rājamahāmatto pasanno”ti vā ādinā nayena ālapanā lapanā. Khādanīyaṃ gahetvā gacchante disvā “kiṃ khādanīyaṃ labhitthā”tiādinā nayena nimittakaraṇādi nemittakatā. “Assaddho appasanno”tiādinā nayena garahaṇāni ca “etaṃ ettha kathethā”tiādinā nayena vācāya [V 0.0299][M 0.0353] ukkhipanādi ca nippesikatā. Appena lābhena bahukaṃ vañcetvā gahetuṃ icchanaṃ lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā. Kuladūsādīti ettha ādi-saddena rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇarūpiyasaṃvohārā saṅgayhantīti.

212. Requesting from those who are not relatives and have not given an invitation is `viññatti` (requesting), which is bodily and verbal effort proceeding in the manner of asking. Seeking requisites by means of wrong livelihood despised by the Buddha is `anesanā` (unseemly search). Uttering and declaring higher human qualities not present in oneself is `abhūtullapanā` (false boasting). “By means of deceit, etc.” means by deceit, flattery, and so forth. Therein, `kuhanā` (deceit) is deceiving people by relying on gain, honor, and fame, by means of the use of requisites, whispering, and composing one's posture. Seeing people arrive at the monastery and saying, “Why have you come, sirs? To invite the monks?” or “The king is pleased with me, and such-and-such royal ministers are also pleased,” and so on—this kind of address is `lapanā` (flattery). Seeing someone carrying food and saying, “What food did you get?” and so on—this kind of hinting is `nemittakatā`. Disparaging by saying, “He is faithless and unconfident,” and so on, and extolling with speech by saying, “You should speak about this here,” and so on—this is `nippesikatā` (belittling). Desiring to obtain much by deceiving with a little gain is `lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā` (seeking gain with gain). In “corrupting families, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes accepting gold and silver and engaging in transactions with them.

Micchājīvavivajjanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Avoiding Wrong Livelihood is concluded.

30. Vattaniddesavaṇṇanā

30. Commentary on the Exposition of the Observances

213. Saupāhano…pe… cīvaraṃ sīse karitvā vā āgantuko ārāmaṃ na paviseti sambandho. Sachattoti sīse katachattena sachatto. Oguṇṭhitoti sasīsaṃ pārupito. “Parikkhittassa vihārassa parikkhepo, aparikkhittassa parikkhepārahaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ upacārasīmāsamīpaṃ patvā upāhanāomuñcanādisabbaṃ katvā ārāmo pavisitabboti ayamettha byatirekaladdho attho.

213. The connection is that a visitor should not enter the monastery wearing sandals... or carrying a robe on his head. ‘With an umbrella’ means with an umbrella held over the head. ‘Covered up’ means having the head completely covered. ‘The boundary of an enclosed monastery is its enclosure; for an unenclosed monastery, the boundary is the area suitable for enclosure’—this means that upon reaching the vicinity of the boundary, one should remove sandals and perform all such actions before entering the monastery. This is the inferred meaning here.

214. Pānīyena pāde na dhoveyyāti sambandho. Paṭikkamanaṃ patvā ekamante pattacīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā patirūpe nisajja pucchitvā pānīyaṃ pātabbaṃ, paribhojanīyena yathāvuttaṃ pādā dhovitabbāti adhippāyo. Vuḍḍhatare āvāsikepi ca abhivādeyyāti iminā vassaṃ pucchitvā navakena āvāsikena abhivādāpetabbanti dīpeti. Puccheyya sayanāsananti “katamaṃ senāsanaṃ pāpuṇāti, ajjhāvutthaṃ anajjhāvutthaṃ vā”ti senāsanaṃ puccheyya. Idañca pucchāya lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Tasmā āvāsikavatte vuttamajjhāvutthādikañca pucchitabbaṃ. Sace “anajjhāvuttha”nti vadanti, kavāṭaṃ ākoṭetvā muhuttaṃ āgametvā ghaṭikaṃ ugghāṭetvā kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetvā bahi ṭhitena ulloketvā pavisitvā sabbaṃ senāsanavattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Āgantukavattaṃ.

214. The connection is that one should not wash the feet with drinking water. Upon arriving at the place of retreat, having put down the bowl and robe in a suitable spot, one should sit down properly, ask, and then drink the water. The intention is that the feet should be washed with water for washing as previously described. ‘One should also pay respects to the senior resident’—this indicates that after asking about the rains-residence seniority, the resident should have the newcomer pay respects. ‘One should ask about the lodging’—meaning, ‘Which lodging is available, whether it has been occupied or unoccupied,’ one should inquire about the lodging. And this is a characteristic statement regarding the inquiry. Therefore, one should also ask about what has been said in the resident’s observances regarding occupied lodgings, etc. If they say, ‘Unoccupied,’ one should knock on the door, wait a moment, lift the bolt, open the door, stand outside and look in, then enter and perform all the observances related to the lodging. These are the observances of a guest.

215-6. Gamiko [M 0.0354] pakkameyyāti sambandho. “Paṭisāmetvā”tiādīnimassa pubbakiriyāpadāni. Dārumattikabhaṇḍakanti ettha mañcapīṭhādidārubhaṇḍaṃ rajanabhājanādimattikābhaṇḍaṃ. Paṭisāmetvāti atthi ce anovassake saṇṭhapetvā. Thaketvānāti dvāravātapānehi pidhāya[V 0.0300]. Sādhukaṃ saṅgopetvānāti catūsu pāsāṇesu mañcaṃ paññapetvā mañce mañcassa, pīṭhe pīṭhassa āropanena senāsanassa uparūpari puñjakaraṇena sādhukaṃ saṅgopanaṃ katvā. Na cāti neva. Gamikavattaṃ.

215-216. The connection is that ‘the departing monk should depart’. ‘Having put away,’ etc., are the preceding verbal actions for this. ‘Wooden and earthenware items’—here, wooden items include beds, benches, etc., and earthenware items include dye vessels, etc. ‘Having put away’ means, if there are any, storing them in a place protected from rain. ‘Having closed up’ means closing the doors and windows. ‘Having carefully gathered them’ means erecting the bed on four stones, arranging the lodging neatly by stacking beds on top of beds and benches on top of benches, thus carefully gathering things together. ‘And not’ means not at all. This is the departing monk’s observance.

217-8. Āvāsikoti idaṃ “paññapeyyā”tiādīnaṃ kattupadaṃ. Navakammakaraṇādibhāranittharaṇatāya āvāso vihāro assa atthīti āvāsiko. Yassa pana kevalaṃ vihāre nivāsanamattaṃ atthi, so nevāsiko. Ubhopi te idha āvāsika-saddena saṅgahitā. Pādodappabhutinti ettha pabhuti-saddena pādapīṭhapādakathalikānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Paccuggantvāna pattacīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāti yojanā. Paññape sayanāsananti “etaṃ tumhākaṃ senāsanaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti evaṃ sayanāsanaṃ paññapeyya, pakāseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

217-218. ‘Resident’ is the subject of terms like ‘should assign,’ and so forth. A resident (āvāsika) is one who has a dwelling, a monastery, because of bearing the burden of tasks such as new construction. However, one who merely dwells in the monastery is an inhabitant (nevāsiko). Both are included here under the term ‘resident.’ In ‘beginning with foot-washing water,’ the word ‘beginning with’ includes footstools and foot-basins. The connection is: ‘Having gone forth to greet, one should take the bowl and robe.’ ‘One should assign lodging’ means one should assign or point out the lodging by saying, ‘This lodging is allotted to you.’ This is what is meant.

219. Ajjhāvutthanti pubbe bhikkhūhi nivutthaṃ. Gocarāgocaraṃ vadeti “bhikkhācāragāmo dūro, āsanno”ti vā, “kālasseva piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ, divā vā”ti evaṃ gocarañca, “micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ vā gāmo, paricchinnabhikkho vā”tiādinā agocarañca vadeyyāti attho. Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānānītiādīnipi “vade”ti imasseva kammavacanāni. Sekhasammutinti yassa saddhassa kulassa saṅgho sekhasammutiṃ deti, taṃ kulañca.

219. ‘Previously occupied’ means previously occupied by monks. He speaks about what is a suitable and unsuitable alms-resort, saying, ‘The alms-gathering village is far,’ or ‘near,’ or ‘One should go for alms at the proper time, or in the daytime,’ thus explaining what is a suitable resort. And he should explain what is an unsuitable resort by saying, ‘It is a village of those with wrong view,’ or ‘alms are limited there,’ and so on. This is the meaning. Similarly, places for defecation and urination, and so forth, are also objects of the verb ‘should explain.’ ‘Designation for trainees’ refers to the faithful family to which the Sangha gives the designation for trainees, and that family.

220. Pavesanikkhame kālanti “kesuci ṭhānesu vāḷamigā vā amanussā vā honti, imaṃ kālaṃ pavisitabbaṃ nikkhamitabbañcā”ti [M 0.0355] evaṃ pavesanikkhame ca kālaṃ. Etaṃ pana āsanapaññapanādikaṃ sabbaṃ vattaṃ vuḍḍhatare āgate cīvarakammādiṃ vā nātigilānassa bhesajjaṃ vā ṭhapetvāpi kātabbaṃ. Mahāgilānassa pana bhesajjameva kātabbaṃ. Cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ karontenāpi tassa vattaṃ kātuṃ ārabhitabbaṃ. Paṇḍito hi āgantuko “karohi tāva bhesajjaṃ, cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjāhī”ti ca vadeyya. Apica bījanena bījitabbo, pādāpissa dhovitabbā, telena makkhitabbā. Piṭṭhi ce āgilāyati, sambādhetabbā. Navakassa pana āgantukassa “idamāsanaṃ, ettha nisīdā”tiādinā ācikkhitabbanti dassento “nisinnoyevā”tiādimāha. Nisinnoyevāti iminā “ṭhitoyevā”tiādiṃ upalakkheti. Samuddiseti ādarena vadeyya. Āvāsikavattaṃ.

220. ‘The time for entering and leaving’ means: ‘In some places there are wild animals or non-human beings; one should enter and leave at this time.’ Thus, he should also explain the time for entering and leaving. However, all these observances, such as preparing seats, should be performed for a more senior monk who has arrived, even setting aside tasks like robe-making or preparing medicine for one who is not seriously ill. For one who is seriously ill, however, medicine itself should be prepared. Even while performing the observance for the shrine courtyard, one should begin to perform the observance for the visitor. For a wise visitor might say, ‘First prepare the medicine, then sweep the shrine courtyard.’ Furthermore, he should be fanned with a fan, his feet should be washed, and oil should be applied to them. If his back aches, it should be massaged. To show that for a newly arrived visitor one should point out, ‘This is a seat, sit here,’ and so on, he said ‘while he is seated,’ etc. By ‘while he is seated,’ it also indicates ‘while he is standing,’ and so forth. ‘He should address’ means he should speak with respect. The Observance for a Resident Monk.

“Vatta”nti [V 0.0301] pana sāmaññena niddiṭṭhattā na there bhikkhū atiallīyitvā nisīditabbaṃ, mahātherassa nisinnāsanato ekaṃ dve āsanāni ṭhapetvā “nisīdā”ti vutte nisīditabbaṃ, na navāpi bhikkhū āsanena paṭibāhitabbā, na saṅghāṭiṃ ottharitvā nisīditabbaṃ, saddaṃ akatvā udakakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ, yathā sūpassa okāso hoti, evamattāya odano gaṇhitabbo, therena bhikkhunā “ṭhapetvā appakaṃ odanādikaṃ sabbaṃ sabbesaṃ samakaṃ sampādehī”ti vattabbaṃ, na tāva therena bhuñjitabbaṃ, bhuttāvinā na tāva udakaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, bhattaggato nivattantehi yathānurūpaṃ nikkhamitvā viraḷāya pāḷiyā gantabbanti evamādikañca tadanurūpaṃ sekhiyavattañca sampādetabbanti idaṃ bhattaggavattañca sādhukaṃ ataramānena gāmo pavisitabbo, “iminā pavisissāmi, iminā nikkhamissāmī”ti nivesanaṃ pavisantena sallakkhetabbaṃ, nātisahasā pavisitabbaṃ, nātisahasā nikkhamitabbaṃ, nātidūre naccāsanne [M 0.0356] ṭhātabbaṃ, nāticiraṃ ṭhātabbaṃ, nātilahukaṃ nivattitabbaṃ, dātukāmatākāraṃ ñatvā ṭhātabbaṃ, yo paṭhamaṃ gāmato paṭikkamati, tena āsanapaññapanādi sabbaṃ kātabbaṃ, yo pacchā, tena āsanuddharaṇādi sabbaṃ kātabbanti evamādikañca tadanurūpaṃ sekhiyavattañca sampādetabbanti idaṃ piṇḍacārikavattañca kātabbaṃ.

Since ‘observance’ is stated generally, elder monks should not sit crowding each other. When a great elder is seated, one should sit down when told, ‘Sit,’ after leaving one or two seats vacant from his. New monks should not be pushed away from a seat. One should not sit having spread out the outer robe. The water-duty should be done without making a sound. Cooked rice should be taken in such a quantity that there is room for curry. The elder monk should say, ‘Setting aside a little of the cooked rice and so forth, provide all of it equally to everyone.’ The elder should not eat yet. Water should not yet be accepted by one who has eaten. When returning from the meal hall, one should depart appropriately and go in a spaced-out line. Such conduct and other appropriate training rules should be fulfilled. This is the observance for the meal hall. And the village should be entered carefully and without haste. When entering a house, one should note, ‘I will enter by this way, I will leave by this way.’ One should not enter too hastily; one should not leave too hastily. One should not stand too far away, nor too close. One should not stand for too long; one should not turn back too quickly. Having understood the sign of their desire to give, one should stand. The one who returns first from the village should do everything, such as preparing the seats. The one who returns last should do everything, such as clearing away the seats. Such conduct and other appropriate training rules should be fulfilled. This is the observance for the alms-round.

Senāsanaṭṭhāne sabbaṃ vattañca sampādetvā tato nikkhamitvā sādhukaṃ nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca ataramānena gāmo pavisitabbotiādi sabbaṃ piṇḍacārikavattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Pānīyaparibhojanīyaaggiaraṇisahitakattaradaṇḍā upaṭṭhapetabbā, nakkhattapadāni sakalāni vā ekadesāni vā uggahetabbāni, disākusalena bhavitabbanti idaṃ āraññikavattañca uddiṭṭhaṃyeva hotīti avagantabbanti.

Having fulfilled all the observances at the lodging place, one should then depart. Having carefully dressed in the lower and upper robes, one should enter the village without haste—all the observances for the alms-round should be performed. Water for drinking and for use, a fire-drill, and a staff should be kept ready. All or some of the positions of the constellations should be learned, and one should be skilled in the directions—it should be understood that this, the forest-dweller’s observance, has also been indicated.

Vattaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Observances is concluded.

31. Vikappanāniddesavaṇṇanā

31. The Commentary on the Exposition of Designation.

221. Sammukhā parammukhāti sassa mukhaṃ, parassa mukhanti viggaho, sammukhena parammukhenāti attho. Sammukhāvikappanā parammukhāvikappanāti bhedā duve vikappanā vuttāti yojanā[V 0.0302]. Bhedāti visesato. Atha vā sassa mukhaṃ mukhasambandhivacanaṃ assā vikappanāyāti samāso. Tathā parammukhā. Sammukhā ca parammukhā ca, tassā bhedo, tato. Sammukhāya sammukhavikappanāya. Byattassāti vikappanavidhānaṃ paccuddhāravidhānañca jānantassa.

221. ‘In the presence of’ (sammukhā), ‘in the absence of’ (parammukhā): the analysis is ‘one’s own presence’ (sassa mukhaṃ), ‘another’s presence’ (parassa mukhaṃ); the meaning is ‘by one’s own presence,’ ‘by another’s presence.’ The connection is: the two kinds of designation, designation in the presence of (sammukhāvikappanā) and designation in the absence of (parammukhāvikappanā), are stated as divisions. ‘Divisions’ means specifically. Or alternatively, the compound is: ‘one’s own presence’ (sassa mukhaṃ) is a word relating to one’s presence in this designation. Similarly for ‘in the absence of’ (parammukhā). ‘In the presence of’ and ‘in the absence of,’ its division, from that comes ‘by that in the presence of’ (sammukhāya), meaning ‘by designation in the presence of.’ ‘Of a competent person’ (byattassa) means of one who knows the procedure for designation and the procedure for revocation.

222. Tenāti yassa santike vikappeti, tena bhikkhunā. Paribhogādikanti paribhogaṃ vissajjanaṃ adhiṭṭhānañca.

222. ‘By him’ (tena) means by that monk in whose presence one designates. ‘Use, and so forth’ (paribhogādikaṃ) means use, giving away, and determination.

224-5. Aparā [M 0.0357] sammukhāvekāti ettha vā-saddo pakkhantare, atha vāti attho, api-saddattho vā vā-saddo, so aparā-saddato paraṃ daṭṭhabbo, aparāpi ekā sammukhāvikappanā atthīti attho. Kathanti āha “bhikkhussā”tiādi. “Pañcannaṃ sahadhammīna”nti vuttattā “tissassa bhikkhuno”tiādīsu tissāya bhikkhuniyā tissāya sikkhamānāya tissāya sāmaṇeriyā tissassa sāmaṇerassātipi viññātabbaṃ.

224-225. Here, in ‘aparā sammukhāvikappanā ekā,’ the word ‘vā’ indicates an alternative, meaning ‘or’; or the word ‘vā’ has the meaning of ‘api’ (also). It should be understood as coming after the word ‘aparā,’ so the meaning is: ‘there is also another designation in the presence of.’ How so? He says, ‘of the monk,’ and so forth. Since it is said ‘of the five co-religionists,’ in phrases like ‘of the monk Tissa,’ it should also be understood as ‘of the nun Tissa,’ ‘of the female probationer Tissa,’ ‘of the female novice Tissa,’ and ‘of the male novice Tissa.’

226. Parammukhāvikappanāti parammukhena vikappanena, parammukhāvikappanāti vā gahetabbaṃ, parammukhāvikappanā kathanti attho.

226. ‘Designation in the absence of’ (parammukhāvikappanā) means by designation in the absence of (parammukhena vikappanena), or it should be taken as ‘designation in the absence of’; the meaning is ‘how is designation in the absence of done?’

227. Mittoti daḷhamitto. Sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamattamitto. Ettha pana dvinnaṃ vikappanānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Sammukhāvikappanāya tāva sayaṃ vikappetvā parena paccuddharāpeti, teneva sā sammukhāvikappanā nāma jātā. Parammukhāvikappanāya pareneva vikappāpetvā pareneva paccuddharāpeti, teneva sā parammukhāvikappanā nāma jātāti idamettha nānākaraṇanti.

227. ‘A friend’ (mitto) means a firm friend. ‘An acquaintance’ (sandiṭṭho) means a friend who is merely seen. Here, what is the difference between the two designations? In designation in the presence of, one first designates it oneself and then has it revoked by another; for that reason it comes to be called ‘designation in the presence of.’ In designation in the absence of, one has it designated by another and has it revoked by another; for that reason it comes to be called ‘designation in the absence of.’ This is the difference here.

228. Dūrasantikattekattanti ettha āsannadūrabhāvo adhiṭṭhāne vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

228. Here, in the phrase ‘oneness in being far and near,’ the state of being near or far should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on determination.

229. Dasāhaṃ…pe… paccāsāya sati māsakaṃ nādhiṭṭhitavikappitaṃ nissaggiṃ nuppādayatīti sambandho. Dasa ahāni samāhaṭāni dasāhaṃ. Sabbattha accantasaṃyoge dutiyā. Tattha yaṃ divasaṃ cīvaraṃ uppannaṃ, tassa yo aruṇo, so uppannadivasanissito, tasmā cīvaruppādadivasena saddhiṃ ekādase aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ hotīti āha “dasāha”nti. Māsamekaṃ vāti “anatthate kathine ekaṃ [M 0.0358] pacchimakattikamāsa”nti (pārā. 649 atthato samānaṃ) vuttattā [V 0.0303] kathinatthate pañca māseti labbhati. Kathinaṃ atthataṃ yasmiṃ vihāreti samāso. Pāripūratthanti pāripūri attho yassāti viggaho. Kiriyāvisesanaṃ, pāripūrippayojanaṃ katvāti attho. Ūnassāti yattakena kayiramānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ cīvaraṃ pahoti, tattakatābhāvato ūnassa ekādasamāsasattamāsasaṅkhāte piṭṭhisamaye uppannassa mūlacīvarassa. Paccāsā satīti “saṅghādito yato kutoci lacchāmī”ti evaṃ satiyā paccāsāyāti attho. Ubhayampi ya-kāralopena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Satīti vā nipāto, liṅgavipallāsena vāha. Ettha pana byatirekavasena dasāhātikkamanādīsu nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ veditabbanti.

229. Ten days... (etc.)... when there is expectation, for a month, a robe not determined or designated does not give rise to a forfeiture—this is the connection. Ten days collected make “dasāhaṃ.” Everywhere, the accusative case is used for continuous association. Therein, the dawn of the day on which the robe arose is dependent on the day of its arising. Therefore, he says “dasāhaṃ” because it becomes subject to forfeiture at the eleventh sunrise, including the day the robe arose. And “for one month”... since it is stated (Pārā. 649, similar in meaning) “when the Kathina is not laid out, one is the last Katthika month,” therefore, when the Kathina is laid out, five months are obtained. “Kathinaṃ atthataṃ yasmiṃ vihāre” is a compound meaning “in which monastery the Kathina is laid out.” “Pāripūratthaṃ”—the analysis is “whose purpose is completion.” It is an adverb, meaning “having made completion the purpose.” “Ūnassa” (of the incomplete) means of the original robe that arose in the subsequent period, reckoned as the eleventh or seventh month, which is incomplete due to the lack of sufficient determination to make the robe last. “Paccāsā sati” means “with expectation present,” that is, “with the expectation, ‘I will obtain it from somewhere, from the Saṅgha or from another source.’” Both are indicated by the elision of the letter ‘ya.’ Or ‘sati’ is a particle, or it is stated with a change of gender. Here, however, by way of contrast, it should be understood that by exceeding the ten days, etc., a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred.

Vikappanāniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Designation is concluded.

32. Nissayaniddesavaṇṇanā

32. The Commentary on the Exposition of Dependence.

230. Byattassāti “kāriya”nti kitakayoge kattari chaṭṭhī. Byatto ca nāma “pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā anissitena vatthabbaṃ, āpattiṃ jānāti, anāpattiṃ jānāti, lahukaṃ āpattiṃ jānāti, garukaṃ āpattiṃ jānāti, ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni honti suvibhattāni suppavattīni suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā anissitena vatthabba”nti (mahāva. 103) evaṃ vuttabyatto ca bahussutabyatto ca veditabbo.

230. “Byattassa” means that “kāriya” is in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) in the sense of the agent (kattari) when connected with a kṛtya affix. And a skilled one (byatto) is spoken of thus: “Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities should live independently: he knows an offense, he knows a non-offense, he knows a light offense, he knows a heavy offense, and both his Pātimokkhas are well-recited, well-divided, well-established, well-defined, according to the suttas and according to the minor details. Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities should live independently” (Mahāvagga 103). Thus, “byatto” should be understood as both the skilled one spoken of thus and the skilled one who is very learned (bahussuta).

Tattha suvibhattānīti suṭṭhu vibhattāni padapaccābhaṭṭhasaṅkaradosavirahitāni. Suppavattīnīti paguṇāni vācuggatāni. Suvinicchitāni [M 0.0359] suttasoti khandhakaparivārato āharitabbasuttavasena suṭṭhu vinicchitāni. Anubyañjanasoti akkharapadapāripūriyā suvinicchitāni akkhaṇḍāni aviparītakkharāni. Etena aṭṭhakathā dīpitā. Aṭṭhakathāto hi esa vinicchayo hotīti. Bahussutabyatto pana yena sabbantimena paricchedena dve mātikā paguṇā vācuggatā, pakkhadivasesu dhammasavanatthāya suttantato cattāro bhāṇavārā, sampattānaṃ parisānaṃ parikathanatthāya andhakavindamahārāhulovādaambaṭṭhasadiso eko kathāmaggo, saṅghabhattamaṅgalāmaṅgalesu anumodanatthāya tisso [V 0.0304] anumodanā, uposathappavāraṇādijānanatthaṃ kammākammavinicchayo, samaṇadhammakaraṇatthaṃ samādhivasena vipassanāvasena vā arahattamaggapariyosānamekaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ettakaṃ uggahitaṃ, svāyaṃ vuccati. Natthi nissāya kāriyanti ācariyādiṃ nissāya vāsena kattabbaṃ natthi. “Nissayakāriya”nti vā pāṭho, nissayena kāriyanti samāso. Jīvassa yattako paricchedo yāvajīvaṃ.

There, “suvibhattāni” (well-divided) means well divided, free from the faults of mixing words and their re-arrangement. “Suppavattīnī” (well-established) means familiar and memorized. “Suvinicchitāni suttaso” (well-defined according to the suttas) means well-defined by way of the suttas to be drawn forth from the Khandhaka and Parivāra. “Anubyañjanaso” (according to the minor details) means well-defined in the completeness of letters and words, unbroken, with no incorrect letters. By this, the commentary is indicated, for this discrimination comes from the commentary. Moreover, a learned and skilled person is one who, at the very least, has two mātikās familiar and memorized, four recitations from the Suttanta for hearing the Dhamma on the fortnight days, one discourse path like the Andhakavinda, Mahārahulovāda, or Ambaṭṭha Sutta for speaking to assembled gatherings, three expressions of appreciation for Saṅgha meals and auspicious or inauspicious ceremonies, a discrimination of action and non-action for knowing Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, etc., and one meditation subject culminating in the path of arahantship through concentration or insight for performing the ascetic’s duty—this much is learned, this one is called [bahussutabyatto]. “Natthi nissāya kāriyaṃ” (nothing needs to be done relying [on another]) means there is nothing to be done by dwelling dependent on a teacher, etc. Alternatively, the reading is “nissayakāriyaṃ,” a compound meaning “to be done with dependence.” “Jīvassa yattako paricchedo” (the extent of life) means “yāvajīvaṃ” (as long as life lasts).

231. Tena nissāya vasantena evaṃ nissayo gahetabboti dassetuṃ “ekaṃsa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ekaṃsanti eko aṃso assa cīvarassāti viggaho. Kiriyāvisesanaṃ vā bhummatthe vā upayogavacanaṃ, ekasmiṃ aṃseti attho. Añjali karapuṭo. Yāvatatiyakaṃ vadeti upasampadāya saṭṭhivassena sattativassena vāpi byattassa navakassa santike yāvatatiyakaṃ vacanaṃ kareyya. Yāvatatiyo vāro assāti kiriyāvisesanasamāso. Āyasmatoti āyasmantaṃ. Vacchāmīti vasāmi. Upajjhaṃ gaṇhantenāpi “upajjhāyo me, bhante, hohī”ti gahetabbaṃ. Taṃ pana “ācariyo”ti ettha “upajjhāyo”ti vacanaṃ visesoti ettha vācābhedato [M 0.0360] na visuṃ vuttaṃ. Na kevalamettha nissayupajjhāyagahaṇe, gāmappavesanādīsupi evameva katvā “ahaṃ āvuso”ti vā “bhante”ti vā vatvā “gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchāmī”tiādinā vattabbaṃ.

231. To show how one living in dependence should take dependence, “ekaṃsaṃ” and so on are stated. “Ekaṃsaṃ”—the analysis is “one shoulder is for this robe.” Or, it is an adverbial modifier, or a word used in the locative sense, meaning “on one shoulder.” Añjali is the cupped hands. “Yāvatatiyakaṃ vadeti” means that even one who has been ordained for sixty or seventy years should make a statement up to three times in the presence of a skilled junior monk. “Yāvatatiyo vāro assa” is an adverbial compound meaning “it is the third time for him.” “Āyasmatoti” means “to the venerable one.” “Vacchāmi” means “I will dwell.” Even one taking a preceptor should take him saying, “Venerable sir, be my preceptor.” However, the term “upajjhāyo” here instead of “ācariyo” indicates a distinction, but it is not stated separately due to the difference in the words. Not only in taking dependence and a preceptor, but also in matters like entering a village, one should similarly, having said, “Friend” or “Venerable sir,” state “I request permission to enter the village,” and so forth.

232. Nissayapaṭippassaddhiṃ dasseti “pakkante”tiādinā. Pakkanteti upajjhāye ācariye saddhivihārike antevāsike ca gāmādīsu yattha katthaci āpucchitvā vā anāpucchitvā vā gate. Tesu yena kenaci “asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ gacchāmī”ti vutte tesuyeva yena kenaci “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitepi taṃ taṃ niyamaṃ atikkamitvā pakkantepi anāpucchā pana upacārasīmātikkamena pakkantepi nissayo sammati paṭippassambhati. Pakkhasaṅkanteti titthiyapakkhasaṅkante cāpi vibbhante cāpi maraṇena ca taṅkhaṇaññeva paṭippassambhati. Āṇatti nāma “paṇāmemi ta”nti vā “mā idha pavisā”tiādikā nissayappaṇāmanā. Tāya paṇāmitena ācariyupajjhāyā khamāpetabbā. Akhamantesu daṇḍakammaṃ katvā tasmiṃ vihāre mahāthere gahetvāpi sāmantavihāre bhikkhū gahetvāpi khamāpetabbā. Na khamanti ce, ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ sabhāgānaṃ santike vasitabbaṃ. Yena kenaci kāraṇena na sakkā hoti tatra ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ sabhāgānaṃ santike vasituṃ, taṃyeva vihāraṃ āgantvā aññassa santike nissayaṃ gahetvā vasitabbaṃ. Tattha “pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ saddhivihārikaṃ [V 0.0305] appaṇāmento upajjhāyo sātisāro hoti, paṇāmento anatisāro hoti. Upajjhāyamhi nādhimattaṃ pemaṃ hoti, nādhimatto pasādo hoti, nādhimattā hirī hoti, nādhimatto gāravo hoti, nādhimattā bhāvanā hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi…pe… hoti (mahāva. 68). Pañcahi, bhikkhave[M 0.0361], aṅgehi samannāgataṃ antevāsikaṃ appaṇāmento ācariyo…pe… hotī”ti (mahāva. 81) vuttattā pana asammāvattante antevāsikasaddhivihārike appaṇāmentā ācariyupajjhāyā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjantīti veditabbaṃ. Bhāvanāti mettābhāvanā. Upajjhāyasamodhānaṃ pana tassa dassanasavanavasena veditabbaṃ.

232. The text explains the relinquishment of dependence with the phrase “pakkante” and so on. “Pakkante” means when the preceptor, teacher, co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika), or resident pupil (antevāsika) has departed for a village or any other place, whether having taken leave or not. Even if one of them says, “I am going to such and such a village,” and it is accepted with “Very well” by another, if they depart transgressing that particular agreement, or if they depart without asking permission by transgressing the boundary of proximity, the dependence ceases and is relinquished. Relinquishment also occurs at the moment of going over to a sectarian faction, disrobing, or dying. “Āṇatti” refers to the formal dismissal of dependence, such as saying, “I dismiss you,” or “Do not enter here,” and so on. One who has been dismissed in this way must seek forgiveness from the teacher or preceptor. If they do not forgive, disciplinary action should be taken; forgiveness must be sought even by bringing in the senior elders of that monastery or the monks of neighboring monasteries. If they do not forgive, one must reside in the presence of the teacher, preceptor, or their associates. If it is impossible to stay near the teacher, preceptor, or their associates for any reason, one must return to that same monastery and take dependence under another. There, it is said: “A preceptor who does not dismiss a co-resident pupil endowed with five qualities incurs an offense, but one who dismisses does not incur an offense. The co-resident pupil does not have excessive affection, excessive faith, excessive shame, excessive respect, or excessive cultivation toward the preceptor. These five qualities… (Mahāvagga 68). Similarly, a teacher who does not dismiss a resident pupil endowed with five qualities… (Mahāvagga 81).” Therefore, it should be understood that if teachers or preceptors fail to dismiss misbehaving resident pupils or co-resident pupils, they incur a dukkaṭa offense. “Bhāvanā” refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness. The establishment of a connection with the preceptor should be understood by way of seeing and hearing.

233. Alajjinti –

233. Those who are shameless are—

“Sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjati;

Āpattiṃ parigūhati;

Agatigamanañca gacchati;

Ediso vuccati alajjipuggalo”ti. (pari. 359) –

“He deliberately commits an offense; he conceals the offense; and he follows a wrong course; such a one is called a shameless person.”

Evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ alajjiṃ. Nissayaṃ dentenāpi lajjinoyeva dātabbaṃ. “Na bhikkhave alajjīnaṃ nissayo dātabbo. Yo dadeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 120) hi vuttaṃ. Adiṭṭhapubbassa katipāhaṃ ācāraṃ upaparikkhitvā dātabbaṃ. Apubbanti ettha sambandhisaddattā pubba-saddena pubbavāso gahito, natthi pubbo assāti apubbaṃ, navanti vuttaṃ hoti. Cattāri pañca vā parimāṇametesanti viggaho. Ettha pana parimāṇa-saddasannidhānena saṅkhyeyyavācinopite saṅkhyāmattavācino hontīti catupañcasaṅkhyāparimāṇameva saṅkhyeyyamāha, tasmā viggahapadatthehi bhinno aññapadattho sambhavatīti samāso. Vā-saddassa yo vikappattho, tattha cāyaṃ samāso, cattāri vā pañca vā, catupañca ahāni, tesaṃ ahānaṃ samāhāro catupañcāhaṃ. Bhikkhusabhāgatanti samāno bhāgo lajjitāsaṅkhāto koṭṭhāso yesaṃ, bhikkhūhi sabhāgā, tesaṃ bhāvo bhikkhusabhāgatā, taṃ, pesalabhāvanti attho. “Thero lajjī”ti jānantena pana pakatiyā nissayadānaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0362] gatena ca tadaheva gahetabbo, ekadivasampi parihāro natthi. Sace [V 0.0306] “okāse alabhante paccūsasamaye gahessāmī”ti sayati, aruṇaṃ uggatampi na jānāti, anāpatti. Laddhaparihārenāpi vasituṃ vaṭṭatīti.

The shameless one is of the characteristic thus stated. Even when giving dependence, it should be given only to one who is conscientious. For it is said: “Monks, dependence should not be given to the shameless. Whoever gives it incurs a dukkaṭa offense” (Mahāvagga 120). For one not seen before, dependence should be given after observing their conduct for a few days. Here, in the word ‘apubba’ (not former), because it is a relative term, ‘prior residence’ is understood by the word ‘pubba’ (former). ‘Not having a former’ means there is no prior; thus, it is said to mean ‘new.’ The analysis is ‘four or five as their measure.’ Here, due to the proximity of the word ‘measure,’ even terms that denote countable things become merely indicative of quantity. Thus, it refers to a countable thing with a measure of four or five. Therefore, the compound has a meaning different from the literal meaning of its constituent words, a meaning that arises from another word; this is a compound. The word ‘vā’ (or) has the sense of alternation, and in that sense this compound is formed: ‘four or five,’ ‘four or five days’; the collection of these days is ‘catupañcāhaṃ’ (a period of four or five days). ‘Bhikkhusabhāgatā’ means the state of those who have a common share, that is, the portion known as conscientiousness; this means a virtuous nature. However, if one knows, “The elder is conscientious,” and has gone to the usual place for giving dependence, it should be taken on that very day; there is no allowance even for a single day. If one lies down thinking, “If I do not get an opportunity, I will take it at dawn,” and does not know even when the dawn has arisen, there is no offense. It is permissible to stay even with an allowance obtained.

234. “Labbhatī”ti kammani nipphannattā avuttakattāti “addhikassā”tiādīsu kattari sāmivacanaṃ, “addhikenā” tiādi vuttaṃ hoti. “Sallakkhentenā”ti pana sarūpeneva niddiṭṭhaṃ. Vasitunti vuttakammaṃ. Bhāve hi tuṃ-paccayo, vāsoti attho. Yācitassāti “gilānupaṭṭhākassa cā”ti ettha visesanaṃ. Sace pana “yācāhi ma”nti vuccamānopi gilāno mānena na yācati, gantabbaṃ. Araññe vā sallakkhentena phāsukanti yattha vasantassa paṭiladdhataruṇasamathavipassanāvisesabhāgitāvasena phāsu hoti, tasmiṃ araññe tādisaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ sallakkhentena āraññakena. Dāyake asanteti padacchedo. Tāvāti avadhimhi, addhikādīhi yāva nissayadāyako labbhati, tāva, āraññakena pana “paṭirūpe nissayadāyake sati nissāya vasissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā yāva āsāḷhipuṇṇamā, tāvāti attho. “Sace pana āsāḷhimāse ācariyo nāgacchati, yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabbaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 121). Antovasse pana nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitabbaṃ, nissayo ca gahetabbo”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 121) hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

234. Regarding ‘labbhati’ (it is obtained): because it is formed in the passive voice and the agent is unexpressed, in cases like ‘addhikassa’ (for the traveler), the genitive case is used for the agent; it means ‘by the traveler.’ However, ‘sallakkhentena’ (by one who considers) is expressed in its own form. ‘Vasituṃ’ (to dwell) is the expressed action; indeed, the suffix ‘-tuṃ’ is in the sense of an abstract noun, meaning ‘dwelling.’ ‘Yācitassa’ (of one who is asked) is a qualifier here in the phrase ‘and for the attendant of the sick.’ But if the sick person, even when told, “Ask me,” does not ask out of pride, one should go. Or in the wilderness, by one considering what is comfortable: ‘comfortable’ refers to a place where, for one dwelling there, it is comfortable by way of partaking in the special qualities of newly-acquired serenity and insight; a forest-dweller should consider such a comfortable dwelling in such a wilderness. The word division is ‘dāyake asante ti’ (when there are no donors). ‘Tāva’ (so long) is in the sense of a limit: for the traveler and others, it means until a giver of dependence is obtained. But for the forest-dweller, having made the resolution, “If a suitable giver of dependence is present, I will dwell in dependence,” it means until the full moon of Āsāḷha. For it is stated in the commentary: “But if in the month of Āsāḷha the teacher does not come, one should go where dependence is obtained” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 121). “However, within the rainy season, one must dwell in a fixed residence and take dependence” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 121).

Amhākaṃ pana keci antevāsikattherā “na bhikkhave vassaṃ na upagantabbaṃ. Yo na upagaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā’ti (mahāva. 186) ca ‘na bhikkhave tadahu vassūpanāyikāya vassaṃ anupagantukāmena sañcicca āvāso atikkamitabbo. Yo atikkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā’ti (mahāva. 186) pāḷivacanato kenaci kāraṇena [M 0.0363] nissayaṃ alabhamānenapi na sakkā antovasse vassaṃ anupagantuṃ. ‘Antovasse panā’tiādīsu pana ca-saddo anvācayattho, tasmā tenāpi vassaṃ upagantabbamevā”ti vadiṃsu.

Some of our resident elder disciples said: “Monks, one should not fail to enter the rains residence. Whoever fails to enter incurs a dukkaṭa offense” (Mahāvagga 186). And also, “Monks, on the day for entering the rains, one who does not wish to enter the rains residence should not intentionally pass beyond a dwelling. Whoever passes beyond incurs a dukkaṭa offense” (Mahāvagga 186). Due to these Pāli statements, even if one cannot obtain dependence for any reason, it is not possible not to enter the rains residence during the rains.
