Furthermore, in the phrase ‘but during the rains, etc.,’ the word ‘ca’ has an accumulative meaning; therefore, even by such a one, the rains residence must be entered.” Thus they spoke.

Mayaṃ panettha evamavocumha “bhagavatā anupagamane dukkaṭaṃ anantarāyikasseva vuttaṃ, teneva ‘kenaci antarāyena purimikaṃ anupagatena pacchimikā upagantabbā’ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 185) vuttaṃ. Antarāyo ca nāma antarā vemajjhe etīti antarāyo, yo koci bādhakappaccayatāya adhippeto vuccati ‘na labhanti patirūpaṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ, eseva antarāyoti pakkamitabba’ntiādīsu (mahāva. 201) viya, tasmā bādhakappaccayatā adhippetā[V 0.0307]. Nissayālābhopi antarāyotveva viññāyati. Sakkā hi vattuṃ ‘antarāyo vassūpagamo sannissayattā taruṇasamathavipassanālābhīnaṃ katokāso viyā’ti. Taruṇasamathavipassanālābhīnampi hi katokāsepi ‘sace pana āsāḷhimāse ācariyo nāgacchati, yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabba’nti daḷhaṃ katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 121) vuttaṃ. Amhākaṃ garūhi ca sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.121) ‘ācariyaṃ āgamentasseva ce vassūpanāyikadivaso hoti, hotu, gantabbaṃ tattha, yattha nissayadāyakaṃ labhatī’ti vassūpanāyikadivasepi nissayatthāya gamanameva vuttaṃ. Atha ca pana mahākāruṇikopi bhagavā ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānupaṭṭhākena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena yāciyamānena anissitakena vatthu’nti (mahāva. 121) gilānavisayepi nissayaṃ garukaṃ katvā paṭṭhapesi. Yaṃ pana anissayaṃ, taṃ anantarāyaṃ nissayamuttakassa vassūpagamanaṃ viya. Apica nāvāya gacchantassa pana vassāne āgatepi nissayaṃ alabhantassa anāpattīti nāvāya [M 0.0364] gacchatoyeva āveṇikā anāpattikatā vuttā. Tasmā nissayālābho bādhakappaccayo vassūpagamanassa, na vassūpagamanaṃ nissayassāti antarāyoyeva nissayālābho. Tatoyeva ṭīkāyaṃ ‘antovasse pana anissitena vatthuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti vuttaṃ. Tasmāyeva ca ‘antovasse panā’tiādīsu nissayadāyake sati nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitabbañca nissayo gahetabbo ca hotīti gamanakiriyāya khīyamānatāvasena ca-saddo samuccayo gahetabbo”ti.

Herein we said this: “The Blessed One spoke of a dukkaṭa for not entering only in the case of one who has no obstacle. For that reason, it is stated in the commentary: ‘By one who has not entered the earlier rains-residence due to some obstacle, the later one should be entered’ (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 185). An ‘obstacle’ (antarāya) is so called because it ‘comes in between’ (antarā eti). It is said to refer to any obstructive condition, as is meant in such passages as: ‘They do not find a suitable attendant; this itself is an obstacle, so one should depart’ (Mahāva. 201). Therefore, an obstructive condition is what is meant. The non-obtaining of dependence is also to be understood as an obstacle. For it can be said: ‘For those who are attaining new serenity and insight, entering the rains-residence is an obstacle because it requires dependence, just as it might be to an opportunity that has arisen.’ Indeed, even for those attaining new serenity and insight, even when an opportunity has arisen, the commentary firmly states: ‘But if the teacher does not arrive in the month of Āsāḷha, one must go where dependence can be obtained’ (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 121). Moreover, our teachers in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.121) say: ‘If the day for entering the rains arrives while one is awaiting the teacher, so be it; one must go where one can find a giver of dependence.’ Thus, even on the day of entering the rains, going for the sake of dependence is what is stated. And yet the greatly compassionate Blessed One established dependence as important even in the case of illness, saying: ‘Monks, I allow a monk who is nursing the sick, if he cannot obtain dependence though he seeks it, to dwell without dependence’ (Mahāva. 121). But that which is without dependence is without obstacle, like the entering of the rains for one who is exempt from dependence. Furthermore, for one traveling by boat, even if the rains have arrived and he cannot obtain dependence, there is no offense—this special exemption from offense is stated specifically for one traveling by boat. Therefore, the non-obtaining of dependence is an obstructive condition for entering the rains, not that entering the rains is for obtaining dependence; thus, the non-obtaining of dependence is itself the obstacle. For this very reason, the sub-commentary says: ‘But during the rains, dwelling without dependence is not permissible.’ And for this reason, in passages like ‘but during the rains,’ etc., when a giver of dependence is present, one must dwell in a fixed residence and dependence must be taken; the particle ‘ca’ should be taken as conjunctive, by way of the cessation of the act of traveling.”

Nissayaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition on dependence is concluded.

33. Kāyabandhananiddesavaṇṇanā

33. Explanation of the Exposition on the Girdle

235. Bandhīyati anenāti bandhanaṃ, kāyassa bandhanaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ, natthi kāyabandhanametassāti akāyabandhano. Dukkaṭanti sañcicca vā asañcicca vā paviseyya ce, dukkaṭaṃ. Asatiyā gato yattha sarati, tattheva bandheyyāti sambandho. Gatoti antogāmaṃ gato. Saritvā yāva na bandhati, na tāva piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ.

235. ‘That by which one is bound’ is a binding (bandhana). The body’s binding is a girdle (kāyabandhana). ‘He has no girdle’ means he is without a girdle (akāyabandhano). ‘Dukkaṭa’ means that if one should enter, whether intentionally or unintentionally, it is a dukkaṭa offense. The connection is: having gone unmindfully, wherever one remembers, one should tie it right there. ‘Gone’ means gone into a village. Having remembered, for as long as one does not tie it, one should not walk for alms.

236. “Paṭṭikā”tiādinā [V 0.0308] sabbasaṅgāhakaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ niddisati. Paṭṭikāti pakativītā vā macchakaṇṭakakhajjūripattavāyimā vā. Sūkarānaṃ antaṃ sūkarantaṃ. Idha pana taṃsadisaṃ vuccati. Caturassaṃ akatvā sajjitaṃ muddikakāyabandhanampi saṅgahetvā “ekā rajjū”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana rajjukaṃ bandhantena ekaguṇameva katvā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, majjhe bhinditvā diguṇaṃ katvā bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Diguṇaṃ pana akatvā satavārampi punappunaṃ āvijjhitvā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ pana ekampi na vaṭṭati[M 0.0365]. Bahurajjuke ekato katvā ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ “bahurajjuka”nti na vattabbaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Tadanulomikāti tesaṃ paṭṭikāsūkarantānaṃ dvinnaṃ dve ime yathākkamamanulomikā.

236. By ‘Paṭṭikā’ and so on, a body-strap that includes all types is indicated. ‘Paṭṭikā’ means either plainly woven, or woven in the pattern of fish bones or date palm leaves. ‘Sūkaranta’ means pig’s intestines, but here, something similar is meant. Even a ring-shaped body-strap prepared without being made four-cornered is included; thus, it is said, ‘one rope.’ However, when tying such a rope, it is allowable to tie it only as a single strand; it is not allowable to fold it in the middle and tie it as a double strand. But without making it double, it is allowable to wind it again and again even a hundred times and tie it; however, even one in the shape of a bracelet is not allowable. If many ropes are made into one by being continuously wrapped with a single rope, it should not be called ‘many-roped’; that is allowable. ‘Corresponding to these’ means that these two correspond respectively to those two, the paṭṭikā and the sūkaranta, in due order.

237-8. Paṭṭikā kīdisī vaṭṭatīti āha “macchā”tiādi. Paṭṭikā macchakaṇṭakakhajjūripattā vā maṭṭhā vā labbhāti sambandho. Kaṇṭaka-saddena patta-saddena ca tadākāro vuccati, upacārato hi macchānaṃ kaṇṭakākāro ca khajjūrīnaṃ pattākāro ca etissāti samāso. Maṭṭhāti pakativītā. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “ete macchakaṇṭakādayo maṭṭhā vikārarahitā paṭṭikā ca tadantogadhāti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ tesamantogadhatā? Yato tāniyeva paṭṭikā nāmāti. Tathā ca vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pakativītā vā macchakaṇṭakavāyimā vā paṭṭikā vaṭṭatī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 278). Ettha pana macchakaṇṭakeyeva khajjūripattaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ. Catassopi dasā labbhāti sambandho. Catassoti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vuttaṃ, tasmā tato ūnāpi vaṭṭanti. Anteti kāyabandhanassa ubhayante diguṇasuttakaṃ labbhanti sambandho. Guṇo bandhanabhūtaṃ suttakaṃ guṇasuttakaṃ. “Guṇo paṭalarāsīsu, ānisaṃse ca bandhane”ti hi abhidhānappadīpikā. Dvinnaṃ guṇasuttakānaṃ samāhāro diguṇasuttakaṃ. Taṃ dasāmukhassa thirabhāvāya koṭṭetuṃ vaṭṭati, na sobhanatthaṃ. Tenāha “mālādi”ntiādi.

237-8. What kind of paṭṭikā is allowable? He says, ‘Of fish,’ etc. The connection is: a paṭṭikā of fish-bone pattern, date-palm-leaf pattern, or plain is allowable. By the word ‘thorn’ (kaṇṭaka) and the word ‘leaf’ (patta), their shape is meant; for, metaphorically, the shape of fish bones and the shape of date palm leaves are attributed to it—this is the compound. ‘Plain’ (maṭṭhā) means plainly woven. However, in the sub-commentary it is said: ‘The intention is that these fish-bone patterns and the like, being plain and free from any artificial alteration, and also the paṭṭikā, are included within them.’ How are they included within them? Because they themselves are called paṭṭikā. And so it is said in the commentary: ‘A paṭṭikā that is plainly woven or woven in a fish-bone pattern is allowable’ (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 278). Here, however, the date-palm-leaf pattern is included in the fish-bone pattern. All four fringes are also allowable—this is the connection. ‘Four’ is stated as the maximum limit; therefore, fewer are also allowable. ‘At the ends’ means a double-threaded cord is allowable at both ends of the body-strap—this is the connection. A cord that is a binding is a ‘binding-cord’ (guṇasuttaka). For the Abhidhānappadīpikā states: ‘Guṇa is used for layers, heaps, benefit, and for binding.’ The combination of two binding-cords is a ‘double-threaded cord’ (diguṇasuttaka). It is allowable to attach it to the opening of the fringe for stability, not for adornment. Therefore, he says, ‘A garland, etc.’

Mālādiṃ kakkaṭacchādiṃ kuñjaracchādiñca dassetvā guṇasuttakakoṭṭitā paṭṭikā na kappatīti sambandho. “Mālādi”ntiādīsu ādi-saddena tādisaṃ yaṃ kiñci vikārarūpaṃ gayhati. Kakkaṭānaṃ viya acchīni, tāni ādīni yassāti samāso. Tathā kuñjaracchādinti.

Having shown a garland, etc., a crab-eye pattern, etc., and an elephant-eye pattern, etc., the connection is that a paṭṭikā decorated with a binding-cord is not allowable. In ‘a garland, etc.’ and so on, by the word ‘etc.’ any such altered form is included. ‘That which has eyes like crabs, and so on’—this is the compound. Similarly for ‘elephant-eye pattern, etc.’

239. Ghaṭakanti [M 0.0366] ghaṭakākāravaṭṭalekhārūpaṃ. Makaramukhādinti ettha makaramukhaṃ nāma makaramukhasaṇṭhānaṃ[V 0.0309]. Bindu pana āgamavasena vutto. Ādi-saddena deḍḍubhasīsādivikārarūpaṃ yaṃ kiñci saṅgayhati. Dasāmukheti dasānaṃ mukhabhūte ante etāni na kappantīti sambandho. Vidhe ubhante ghaṭakā lekhā aññaṃ cittakañca na kappantīti sambandho. Ghaṭakāti ghaṭakato. Lekhāti lekhāya. Pañcamiyā lopo. Vidheti kāyabandhanassa pāsante dasāmūle tassa thirabhāvatthaṃ kattabbe dantavisāṇādimaye vidhe.

239. ‘Ghaṭaka’ means a form of circular line in the shape of a small pot. Here, ‘makaramukha’ means a shape like a makara’s face. The bindu, however, is stated by way of scriptural tradition. By the word ‘etc.’ any altered form whatsoever, such as the head of a water-snake, is included. ‘At the opening of the fringes’ (dasāmukhe) means these are not allowable at the ends, which are the openings of the fringes—this is the connection. At the fastenings at both ends, pot-designs, lines, and other decorations are not allowable—this is the connection. ‘Ghaṭakā’ is from ‘ghaṭakato.’ ‘Lekhā’ is from ‘lekhāya.’ The fifth case ending is elided. ‘Vidhe’ refers to the fastening made of ivory, horn, etc., to be made at the side of the body-strap at the root of the fringe for the sake of its stability.

240. Deḍḍubhakanti udakasappasīsasadisaṃ. Murajanti nānāvaṇṇehi suttehi murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “murajanti bahurajjuke ekato saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekāya rajjuyā paliveṭhetvā katarajjū”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ “bahurajjuke ekato katvā”tiādinā heṭṭhā vuttaaṭṭhakathāvacanena virujjhati. Maddavīṇanti pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kalābukanti bahurajjukaṃ. Tesaṃ “na kappatī”ti iminā sambandho. Dve majjhimāti majjhe bhavā murajamaddavīṇasaṅkhātā dve.

240. ‘Deḍḍubhaka’ means resembling the head of a water snake. ‘Muraja’ means made by wrapping with threads of various colors in the shape of the rim of a muraja drum. However, in the sub-commentary it is said: ‘Muraja means a rope made by gathering many ropes together, pulling them tight, and wrapping them with a single rope.’ This contradicts the statement of the commentary mentioned above, which begins, ‘If many ropes are made into one.’ ‘Maddavīṇā’ means having the shape of a bracelet. ‘Kalābuka’ means many-roped. The connection for these is with ‘is not allowable.’ ‘The two middle ones’ means the two that are in the middle, designated as muraja and maddavīṇā.

241. Gaṇṭhiyo cāpīti cīvarassa gaṇṭhiyo cāpi. Tammayāti tehi veḷuādīhi nibbattā. Pasaṅgena panetaṃ vuttanti.

241. ‘Knots and also’ (gaṇṭhiyo cāpi) refers to the knots of the robe as well. ‘Made of that’ (tammayā) means produced from those, such as bamboo, etc. This, however, is said incidentally.

Kāyabandhananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the body-strap is concluded.

Sumaṅgalappasādaniyā nāma ṭīkāya

In the Sub-commentary named Sumaṅgalappasādanī.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first recitation portion is concluded.

34. Pathavīniddesavaṇṇanā

34. Commentary on the Exposition of Earth

242. Jātājātāti [M 0.0367] duvidhāti jātā pathavī ajātā pathavīti pathavī duvidhāti attho. Iminā jātapathaviñca ajātapathaviñca dasseti. Tāsaṃ vibhāgaṃ dasseti “suddhā”tiādinā. Suddhamattikapaṃsukā ca adaḍḍhā ca bahumattikapaṃsukā ca cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhapaṃsumattikarāsi ca jātā pathavīti sambandho. Mattikā ca paṃsu cāti dvando. Suddhā appasakkharāditāya mattikā paṃsavo yassāti bāhirattho. Adaḍḍhāti uddhanapacanādivasena tathā tathā [V 0.0310] adaḍḍhā. Sā pana visuṃ natthi, suddhamattikādīsu aññatarāva veditabbā. Cattāro māsā, tehi sahito atireko kālo, tasmiṃ ovaṭṭhoti samāso. Ovaṭṭhoti yena kenaci udakena ovaṭṭho. Budhā pana “ākāsato vuṭṭhaudakeneva, na aññattha paharitvā patitabindunā”ti vadanti, “ovaṭṭho”ti sāmaññena vuttattā ca “pokkharaṇiyā ṭhitatanukaddamo vaṭṭati, bahalo tu na vaṭṭatī”ti (pāci. aṭṭha. 86) vuttattā ca “vinayavinicchaye sampatte garuke ṭhātabba”nti vinayalakkhaṇato ca na taṃ yujjatīti amhākaṃ khanti. Paṃsumattikānaṃ rāsi paṃsumattikarāsi. Catu…pe… vaṭṭho paṃsumattikarāsi yassāti aññapadattho, kammadhārayo vā.

242. ‘Born and unborn means twofold’ means that earth is twofold: born earth and unborn earth. By this, he indicates both born earth and unborn earth. He shows their distinction by ‘pure,’ and so on. The connection is that pure clay and dust, unbaked, clay and dust in abundance, and a heap of dust and clay rained upon for more than four months, is born earth. ‘Clay and dust’ is a dvanda compound. The external meaning is: pure clay and dust, on account of having little gravel and so on. ‘Unbaked’ means not baked in an oven or by other such means. This, however, does not exist separately; it should be understood as one of the pure clay, etc. ‘Four months, and an additional period with them, in which it was rained upon’—this is the compound. ‘Rained upon’ means rained upon by any water whatsoever. The wise, however, say, ‘Only by water rained from the sky, not by drops that have fallen after striking something else.’ But since ‘rained upon’ is stated generally, and since it is said, ‘Thin mud standing in a pond is allowable, but thick is not’ (Pāci. Aṭṭha. 86), and from the characteristic of the Vinaya that ‘when a serious Vinaya decision is reached, one must stand by it,’ that is not our view. A heap of dust and clay is a ‘heap of dust and clay.’ ‘Four… rained upon… a heap of dust and clay’ is an aññapadattha compound, or a kammadhāraya.

243. Vālukā ca daḍḍhā ca yebhuyyasakkharādimahīpi ca cātumāsomavaṭṭhako vuttarāsi ca dutiyā bhūmīti sambandho sakkharā ca pāsāṇā ca marumbā ca kathalā ca vālukā cāti dvando. Suddhā sakkhara…pe… vālukā yassāti viggaho. Hatthamuṭṭhinā gahetabbappamāṇā sakkharā, tato upari pāsāṇā, kaṭasakkharā marumbā, kapālakhaṇḍāni kathalāti veditabbā. Dutiyāti ajātā. Vuttarāsīti vutto mattikapaṃsusirā.

243. The connection is that sand, baked earth, ground mostly consisting of gravel and so on, and the aforesaid heap rained upon for less than four months, is the second type of ground. ‘Gravel, stones, coarse sand, potsherds, and sand’ is a dvanda compound. The analysis is: ‘pure gravel… up to sand.’ It should be understood that gravel (sakkharā) is of a size that can be grasped by the fist; larger than that are stones (pāsāṇā); coarse gravel (kaṭasakkharā) is coarse sand (marumbā); and fragments of pottery are potsherds (kathalā). ‘Second’ means unborn. ‘Aforesaid heap’ refers to the aforesaid heap of clay and dust.

244. Kīdisī [M 0.0368] yebhuyumattikādīti āha “dve bhāgā”tiādi. Yassa bhūmiyāti yassā bhūmiyā. Sesesupīti yebhuyyapaṃsuyebhuyyasakkharayebhuyyapāsāṇādīsu.

244. Regarding what kind of ground is mostly clay and so on, he says, ‘Two parts,’ and so on. ‘Yassa bhūmiyā’ means ‘yassā bhūmiyā.’ ‘In the remaining cases also’ means in cases of ground that is mostly dust, mostly gravel, mostly stone, and so on.

245. “Pācittī”tiādinā tattha vinicchayaṃ dasseti. Jāte jātasaññissa khaṇane pācittīti sambandho. Jāteti jāte bhūmibhāge, liṅgavipallāso vā, jātāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jāte dveḷhassa vimatissa dukkaṭanti sambandho. Jāte ajātasaññissa anāpatti. Tathā āṇāpane anāpattīti yojanā. Ajātasaññissāti ajātāti saññā ajātasaññā, sā assa atthīti ajātasaññī, tassa.

245. By ‘pācittiya,’ and so on, he shows the legal decision in that case. The connection is: for one who perceives it as born, there is a pācittiya offense for digging in born earth. ‘In born’ (jāte) means in a portion of ground that is born; or it is a change of gender, meaning it is said as ‘in the born’ (jātāya). The connection is: for one who is doubtful or uncertain about born earth, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who perceives born earth as unborn, there is no offense. Likewise, the construction is that there is no offense in ordering. ‘For one who perceives it as unborn’ (ajātasaññissa) is explained as: the perception ‘it is unborn’ is ‘perception of the unborn’ (ajātasaññā); one who has this is ‘one who perceives it as unborn’ (ajātasaññī); for him.

246. Ekāyāṇattiyā ekāti sace sakiṃ āṇatto divasampi khaṇati, āṇāpakassa ekā eva āpattīti attho. Vācaso āpattīti sambandho. Vācasoti vicchāyaṃ so, vācāya vācāyāti attho.

246. ‘One per instruction’ (ekāyāṇattiyā ekā) means that if, having been instructed once, one digs even for a day, for the one who gave the instruction there is only one offense. The connection is ‘an offense by speech’ (vācaso āpatti). ‘By speech’ (vācaso) is an indeclinable in the distributive sense, meaning ‘for each word’.

247. “Imaṃ ṭhānaṃ khaṇa vā”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. “Ettha aggiṃ jālehi vā”ti yojanā[V 0.0311]. “Vattu”nti idaṃ “na vaṭṭatī”ti imassa kattupadavacananti attho. Atha vā “imaṃ ṭhānaṃ khaṇā”tiādippakāro vacanāya na vaṭṭatīti attho. Niyametvāti iminā “āvāṭaṃ khaṇa, kandaṃ khaṇā”tiādinā aniyametvā vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti.

247. It should be connected with ‘Or dig this spot,’ and so on. The construction is ‘Or light a fire here.’ ‘To say’ (vattuṃ) means that this is the agent-word for ‘it is not allowable’ (na vaṭṭati). Alternatively, the meaning is that a manner of speech such as ‘Dig this spot’ is not allowable. By this word ‘having specified’ (niyametvā), it is shown that it is allowable to speak without specifying, such as ‘Dig a pit, dig a root,’ and so on.

248. “Imassa thambhassa āvāṭaṃ jāna vā, kappiyaṃ karohi vā”ti ca “mattikaṃ jāna vā, mattikaṃ āhara vā, mattikaṃ kappiyaṃ karohi vā”ti ca edisaṃ vacanaṃ vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Etaṃ viya dissatīti edisaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? “Mattikaṃ dehī”tiādikaṃ upameyyaṃ. “Mattikaṃ jānā”tiādikaṃ pana [M 0.0369] upamānaṃ, tesaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ yā kappiyasaṅkhātā samānadhammatā, sā upamā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ amhehi subodhālaṅkāre “upamānopameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ siyopamā”ti. Aññathā upamānabhūtaakkharāvaḷisadisīyeva, akkharāvaḷi upameyyaṃ siyā. Vākye viya-saddoyeva pana upamānaṃ jotetīti veditabbaṃ.

248. The connection is that such speech is allowable as: ‘Know the hole for this post, or make it allowable,’ and ‘Know the clay, or bring the clay, or make the clay allowable.’ ‘Such’ (edisaṃ) means ‘it appears like this.’ What is that? ‘Give clay,’ and so on, is the object of comparison (upameyya). But ‘Know the clay,’ and so on, is the standard of comparison (upamāna). The common property between this standard and object of comparison, known as suitability (kappiya), is the simile (upamā). Thus it was said by us in the Subodhālaṅkāra: ‘The commonality of property between the standard and object of comparison is a simile.’ Otherwise, the object of comparison would be a string of letters just like the string of letters that is the standard of comparison. It should be understood that in a sentence, it is only the word ‘like’ (viya) that illuminates the standard of comparison.

249. Pathaviyā asambaddhaṃ sukkhakaddamaādikañca tanukaṃ ussiñcanīyakaddamañca kopetuṃ labbhanti sambandho. Kaddamaādikanti ettha ādi-saddena udakena gataṭṭhāne udakapappaṭako nāma hoti, yaṃ vātappahārena calati, taṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ussiñcanīyakaddamanti ghaṭehi ussiñcituṃ sakkuṇeyyakaddamaṃ.

249. The connection is that it is allowable to disturb dry mud and the like that is not connected to the earth, as well as thin mud that can be bailed out. Here, in ‘mud and the like’ (kaddamaādikaṃ), by the word ‘like’ (ādi-saddena), it includes what is called water-scum in places where water has receded, which moves when blown by the wind. ‘Mud that can be bailed out’ (ussiñcanīyakaddamaṃ) refers to mud that can be bailed out with pots.

250. “Cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhaṃ gaṇḍuppāda”ntiādinā sambandhitabbaṃ. Gaṇḍaṃ pathaviyā gaṇḍasadisaṃ mattikarāsiṃ uppādentīti gaṇḍuppādā. Idha pana tehi uṭṭhāpito gūtho “gaṇḍuppāda”nti niddiṭṭho. Potthakesu pana “gaṇḍuppādo”ti pāṭho dissati. Taṃ “na kopaye”ti ettha kammena bhavitabbanti na yujjati. Mūsikukkiranti mūsikānaṃ ukkiro khaṇitvā bahi kataṃ paṃsurāsi mūsikukkiroti. Leḍḍādinti ettha leḍḍunti kasitaṭṭhāne naṅgalacchinnamattikāpiṇḍaṃ. Ādi-saddena gāvīnaṃ khuracchinnaṃ kaddamaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

250. It should be connected with ‘a molehill that has stood for more than four months,’ and so on. ‘Molehills’ (gaṇḍuppādā) are those that produce a heap of soil resembling a lump, a lump on the earth. Here, however, the dung raised by them is designated as ‘molehill’ (gaṇḍuppāda). However, in some books the reading ‘gaṇḍuppādo’ is found. That is not suitable, because it must be the object in ‘one should not disturb’ (na kopaye). ‘A mouse-heap’ (mūsikukkira) means the excavated earth of mice; a heap of dust dug and put outside is a mouse-heap. Here, in ‘clods and the like’ (leḍḍādi), ‘clod’ (leḍḍu) means a lump of earth cut by a plow in a plowed field. By the word ‘like’ (ādi-saddena), it includes mud cut by the hooves of cattle.

251-2. Udakasantike patite vāpiādīnaṃ kūle ca pāsāṇe lagge raje ca navasoṇḍiyā patite raje ca abbhokāsuṭṭhite vammike ca mattikākuṭṭe ca tathāti sambandho. Tathāti iminā kūlādike cātumāsādhikovaṭṭhaṃ vā sabbaṃ na kopayeti idaṃ atidisati. Iṭṭhakakuṭṭako vaṭṭatīti āha “yebhuyyā”tiādi. Yebhuyyena kathalā etthāti yebhuyyakathalā, bhūmi[V 0.0312], tiṭṭhati etthāti ṭhānaṃ[M 0.0370], yebhuyyakathalāya ṭhānaṃ, tasmiṃ. Iṭṭhakakuṭṭako yebhuyyakathalā viya hotīti adhippāyo. Kuṭṭakaṃ kopentassa anāpattīti adhippāyo. Iṭṭhakāya kato kuṭṭakoti samāso.

The connection is that it is the same for dust fallen near water, and on the bank of a pond and so on, for dust sticking to stones, for dust fallen on fresh cow dung, for an anthill that has arisen in the open air, and for an earthen wall. By ‘thus’ (tathā), this is extended: one should not disturb any of these, whether on a bank and so on having stood for more than four months, or all of them. He says that a brick wall (iṭṭhakakuṭṭako) is allowable, with ‘mostly,’ and so on. ‘A place of mostly gravel’ (yebhuyyakathalā) means ‘mostly gravel is here,’ i.e., ground. ‘A place’ (ṭhānaṃ) means ‘it stands here.’ ‘In the place of mostly gravel’ (yebhuyyakathalāya ṭhānaṃ). The intention is that a brick wall is like a place of mostly gravel. The intention is that there is no offense for one who disturbs a wall. ‘A wall made of brick’ (iṭṭhakāya kato kuṭṭako) is a compound.

253-5. Sañcāletvā bhūmiṃ vikopayaṃ thambhādiṃ gaṇhituṃ vāti sambandho. Tattha vikopayanti karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ, vikopayatāti attho. Aññathā kathamettha paṭhamāpasaṅgo. Paṭhamā hi “bhava”nti vutte siyā, na ca “gaṇhitu”ntiādīsu tuṃ-paccayehi vutto koci atthi, yadā bhāve tuṃ-paccayo, tadā na kiñci vuttaṃ hotīti, “na kappatī”ti padhānakiriyāyapi heṭṭhā vuttanayena kattā aññoyevāti evaṃ sabbattha. Tatiyatthe tu sati ito cito sañcāletvā bhūmiṃ vikopayatā thambhādiṃ gaṇhituṃ na kappatīti atīva yujjati. Dhārāyāti passāvadhārāya. Visamaṃ samaṃ kātuṃ sammuñjanīhi ghaṃsituṃ vāti yojanā. Visamanti visamaṭṭhānaṃ. “Padaṃ dassessāmī”ti bhūmiṃ bhindanto caṅkamituṃ vāti sambandho. Bhindantoti bhindatā. Kaṇḍurogī vā taṭādīsu aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ ghaṃsitunti yojanā. Kaṇḍurogīti kaṇḍuroginā. Ca-saddo avadhāraṇe.

The connection is: ‘or to take a post and so on, shaking and disturbing the ground.’ Here, ‘disturbing’ (vikopayaṃ) is a personal ending in the instrumental sense; the meaning is ‘by one who disturbs’ (vikopayatā). Otherwise, how could the nominative case be appropriate here? For the nominative would be used if ‘bhava’ were stated, but in ‘to take’ (gaṇhituṃ) and so on, no agent is expressed by the ‘tuṃ’ suffix. When the ‘tuṃ’ suffix denotes the action itself, nothing is expressed. Therefore, the agent of the main verb ‘it is not allowable’ (na kappati) is also another, by the method stated below—thus in all cases. But when it is in the instrumental sense, then ‘it is not allowable for one who disturbs the ground, shaking it from here and there, to take a post and so on’ fits very well. ‘By a stream’ (dhārāya) means by a stream of urine. The construction is: ‘or to rub with brooms to make the uneven even.’ ‘Uneven’ (visamaṃ) means an uneven place. The connection is: ‘or to walk while breaking the ground, thinking, “I will show the path.”’ ‘Breaking’ (bhindanto) means ‘by one who breaks’ (bhindatā). The construction is: ‘or a person with an itch-disease rubbing their limbs on a bank and so on.’ ‘A person with an itch-disease’ (kaṇḍurogī) means ‘by a person with an itch-disease’ (kaṇḍuroginā). The particle ‘ca’ is for emphasis.

256-7. Suddhacittassāti pathavibhedādhippāyavirahena parisuddhacittassa.

‘For one with a pure mind’ (suddhacittassa) means for one whose mind is purified through the absence of the intention to break the earth and so on.

258. Aggissa anupādāne kapāle vā anupādānāya iṭṭhakāya vā aggiṃ pātetuṃ vā avase sati bhūmiyaṃ pātetuṃ vā labbhateti sambandho. Upādānaṃ indhanaṃ, na upādānaṃ anupādānaṃ, tasmiṃ. Vaso pabhuttaṃ. “Vaso pabhutte āyatte”ti hi nighaṇḍu. Na vaso avaso, tasmiṃ apabhutteti [M 0.0371] attho. Patitaṭṭhāneyeva upādānaṃ datvā aggiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sukkhakhāṇukasukkharukkhādīsu ca aggiṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana “pathaviṃ appattameva nibbāpetvā gamissāmī”ti deti, vaṭṭati, pacchā nibbāpetuṃ na sakkoti, avisayattā anāpatti. “Bhūmiyaṃ pātehī”ti evampi vattuṃ na vaṭṭatīti.

258. The connection is that it is allowable to drop a fire onto a potsherd without fuel or onto a brick without fuel, or, if there is no alternative, to drop it onto the ground. ‘Upādāna’ means fuel. ‘Not upādāna’ is ‘anupādāna,’ without fuel; on that. ‘Vasa’ means control. For the lexicon states: ‘Vasa means control, power.’ ‘Not vasa’ is ‘avasa’; on that, meaning ‘without control.’ It is allowable to make a fire by providing fuel only in the place where it has fallen. And it is not allowable to set fire to dry stumps, dry trees, and the like. But if one gives it thinking, ‘I will extinguish it before it even reaches the ground and then go,’ it is allowable. If afterwards one is not able to extinguish it, there is no offense because it is beyond one’s scope. It is also not allowable to say, ‘Drop it onto the ground.’

Pathavīniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Earth is concluded.

35. Parikkhāraniddesavaṇṇanā

35. Commentary on the Exposition of Requisites

259-60. Chatte [V 0.0313] anto bahi ca pañcavaṇṇehi suttehi sibbituñca paṇṇe girikūṭaaḍḍhacandādiṃ chindituñca na vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Chatteti tālapaṇṇe chatte. Girikūṭaṃ nāma makaradantakaṃ, ādi-saddena tādisaṃ aññaṃ vikārarūpaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Ghaṭakanti gehatthambhesu viya kayiramānaṃ ghaṭakaṃ. Daṇḍeti chattadaṇḍe. Lekhāti tahiṃ tahiṃ dinnā lekhā. Sādisanti dīghena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Bundamhi mūle.

The connection is that it is not allowable to sew an umbrella inside and out with five-colored threads, nor to cut the leaves into shapes like mountain peaks, half-moons, and so on. ‘On an umbrella’ (chatte) means on a palm-leaf umbrella. ‘Mountain-peak’ (girikūṭa) is a ‘makara-tooth’ design; by the word ‘like’ (ādi), other such decorative shapes are included. ‘Pot-shape’ (ghaṭaka) means a pot-shape made like those on house pillars. ‘On the staff’ (daṇḍe) means on the umbrella-staff. ‘Line’ (lekhā) means a line made here and there. ‘Similar’ (sādisaṃ) is what is specified as long. ‘At the base’ (bundamhi) means at the root.

261. Thiratthaṃ chatte ekavaṇṇena sibbituṃ vā pañjaraṃ vinandhituṃ vā vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Sibbitunti anto bahi ca sibbituṃ. Ekavaṇṇenāti nīlādinā ekavaṇṇena. Pañjaranti chattadaṇḍagāhakasalākapañjaraṃ. Thiratthanti iminā na vaṇṇamaṭṭhatthāyāti dasseti. Bandhituṃ daṇḍe lekhā vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Bandhitunti vātappahārena acalanatthaṃ chattamaṇḍalikaṃ rajjukehi gahetvā bandhanatthāya. Lekhāvāti valayamiva ukkiritvā katā lekhā eva. Vaṭṭatīti yadipi na bandhati, rajjukehi bandhituṃ yuttaṭṭhānattā vaṭṭati.

261. The connection is that it is allowable to sew the umbrella with a single color for durability, or to bind the frame. ‘To sew’ (sibbituṃ) means to sew both inside and outside. ‘With a single color’ (ekavaṇṇena) refers to a single color, such as blue, etc. ‘Frame’ (pañjara) means the frame of ribs that holds the umbrella handle. ‘For durability’ (thiratthaṃ) indicates that this is not for the sake of ornamentation. The connection is that grooves on the handle for binding are allowable. ‘For binding’ (bandhituṃ) means for the purpose of holding and binding the umbrella canopy with cords so that it does not move when struck by the wind. ‘Grooves’ (lekhā) refers to lines made by carving them out like rings. ‘It is allowable’ (vaṭṭati) means that even if one does not bind them, it is permissible because they are a suitable place for tying cords.

262. Cīvare ante vāpi paṭṭamukhe vāpi veṇipi vā saṅkhalikāpi vā aññaṃ sūcivikāraṃ vā pāḷikaṇṇikaādikaṃ kappabinduvikārampi [M 0.0372] vā na ca kappatīti sambandho. Anteti cīvarapariyante, anuvāteti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭṭamukheti paṭṭakoṭiyaṃ, dvinnaṃ paṭṭānaṃ saṅghaṭitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Veṇīti varakasīsākārena sibbanaṃ. Saṅkhalikāti biḷālabandhanākārena sibbanaṃ. Aññaṃ sūcivikāraṃ vāti cīvaramaṇḍanatthāya kayiramānaṃ aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci sūcikammavikāraṃ vā. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana “satapadisadisaṃ aññaṃ vā sūcivikāraṃ na kappatī”ti sāmaññena vuttaṃ. “Cīvaramaṇḍanatthāya nānāsuttakehi satapadisadisaṃ sibbantā āgantukapaṭṭaṃ ṭhapenti, aññampi yaṃ kiñci sūcikammavikāraṃ karonti, sabbaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā pana nānāvaṇṇehi vā hotu, ekavaṇṇena vā hotu, cīvaramaṇḍanatthāya saṃsibbantānaṃ sūcikammavikāraṃ sandhāya vuttanti cīvaresu phālitaṭṭhānassa thirabhāvatthaṃ satapadisadisampi sibbituṃ vaṭṭatīti amhākaṃ khanti. Pāḷi-saddena, kaṇṇika-saddena ca kappa-saddalopena vā upacārena vā pāḷikappādayova gahitā. Pāḷi ca kaṇṇikā ca pāḷikaṇṇikāyo, tā ādi yassa aññassa tādisassāti viggaho. Tattha nīlāvaḷiādisaṇṭhānāya [V 0.0314] bindupantiyā yathā sobhati, tathā kayiramāno pāḷikappo. Tatheva bindusamūhe katthaci dassetvā kayiramāno kaṇṇikakappo.

262. It is not permissible to have on a robe, at its edge or at the end of a strip, a braid, a chain-pattern, other needlework, or a decoration of dots such as a `pāḷi` or a `kaṇṇikā`—this is the connection. ‘Ante’ refers to the border of the robe, meaning along the hem. ‘Paṭṭamukhe’ refers to the end of a strip, meaning the place where two strips are joined. ‘Veṇī’ means sewing in a pattern resembling the head of a varaka grain. ‘Saṅkhalikā’ means sewing in a pattern resembling a cat’s collar. ‘Aññaṃ sūcivikāraṃ’ refers to any other kind of needlework done for the ornamentation of the robe. However, in the Sub-commentary, it is generally stated, ‘A centipede-like pattern or other needlework is not permissible.’ Since the Commentary states, ‘For the sake of ornamentation, they sew with various threads, placing an extra piece of cloth with a centipede-like pattern, or they do any other kind of needlework—none of this is permissible,’ it refers to needlework done for ornamentation, whether with multiple colors or a single color. However, in our understanding, sewing something similar to a centipede-like pattern is permissible if it is for reinforcing a torn part of the robe. The terms ‘pāḷi’ and ‘kaṇṇikā’ are understood as referring to ‘pāḷikappa’ and so forth, either by elision of the word ‘kappa’ or by metaphor. The analysis is ‘pāḷi and kaṇṇikā are pāḷikaṇṇikāyo, and these are the beginning of other similar things.’ Therein, a ‘pāḷikappa’ is made in the shape of a blue line or similar, with a row of dots, so that it appears beautiful. Similarly, a ‘kaṇṇikakappa’ is made by displaying clusters of dots in certain places.

263. Gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭāti gaṇṭhino ca pāsakassa ca patiṭṭhānaṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbā paṭṭā. Vaṭṭatīti ettha “gaṇṭhipāsakā”ti katvā “catukoṇāva vaṭṭantī”ti atthato vacanaṃ vipallāsetvā yojetabbaṃ. Agghiyanti cetiyasaṇṭhānena sibbanaṃ. Mūle ca agge ca ekasadisaṃ katvā muggarākārena sibbanaṃ muggaro. Vikāranti vikāro, liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Etthāti gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭesu.

263. ‘Gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭā’ refers to the straps to be placed at the point where the knot and the loop are secured. Here, in relation to ‘vaṭṭati,’ by taking it as ‘gaṇṭhipāsakā,’ the statement ‘they are permissible only at the four corners’ should be construed by transposing the words according to the sense. ‘Agghiya’ means stitching in the form of a stupa. ‘Muggaro’ means stitching in the shape of a hammer, making the base and the top equal. ‘Vikāraṃ’ stands for ‘vikāro’; it is stated with a change of gender. ‘Ettha’ applies to the ‘gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭā.’

264. Koṇasuttāti [M 0.0373] napuṃsakaniddeso, gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭānaṃ koṇehi nīhaṭasuttakoṭiyo. Pīḷakāti tāniyeva nivattetvā pīḷakākārena katāni. Duviññeyyāvāti tesaṃ antesu ekavāraṃ gaṇṭhikaraṇena vā puna nivattetvā sibbanena vā duviññeyyā eva. Gandhaṃ telaṃ vāti gandhaṃ vā telaṃ vā. Kañcikapiṭṭhakhalikaādīnipi vaṭṭanti.

264. ‘Koṇasutta’ is a neuter designation, referring to the ends of threads drawn out from the corners of the ‘gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭā.’ ‘Pīḷakā’ means those same threads turned back and fashioned in the shape of a ‘pīḷakā’ (a small knot or button). ‘Duviññeyyā’ means they are indeed difficult to discern, either by knotting them once at their ends or by turning them back and stitching. ‘Gandhaṃ telaṃ vā’ means either perfume or oil. Items such as bodices, back-boards, and pegs are also permissible.

265. Maṇināti masāragallādipāsāṇena. Na ca ghaṭṭeyyāti neva ghaṭṭeyya. Aññena vāti muggaramusalādinā. Aṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanāni pana tathā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Doṇiyaṃ katvā na ca ghaṃseyyāti pakkarajanākiraṇadoṇiyaṃ ṭhapetvā bhūmiyaṃ jaṇṇukāni nihantvā ito cito ca āvijjhitvā neva ghaṃseyyāti attho.

265. ‘Maṇinā’ refers to a precious stone such as masāragalla. ‘Na ca ghaṭṭeyya’ means one should not strike it at all. ‘Aññena vā’ means with a hammer, pestle, or similar tool. However, it is permissible to make shoulder straps and body bindings in that way. ‘Doṇiyaṃ katvā na ca ghaṃseyya’ means that, having placed it in a trough for scattering dye, one should not rub it by kneeling on the ground and swirling it to and fro.

266-7. Kaṇṇakoṇakasuttānīti cīvararajanakāle lagganatthāya anuvāte catūsu koṇesu ca pāsakaṃ katvā bandhitāni suttāni, yāni “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇṇasuttaka”nti (mahāva. 344) evaṃ anuññātāni. Kaṇṇasaṅkhātā koṇā kaṇṇakoṇakā, tesu suttāni. Gaṇṭhikapāsakapaṭṭesu pana kaṇṇakoṇakasuttānaṃ duviññeyyānameva kappiyatā heṭṭhā vuttāti cīvare ratteyeva tesaṃ chinditabbatā natthi, kaṇṇakoṇakasuttānaṃ chinditabbatāya vuttattā anuvātehi nikkhamitasuttānipi chinditabbānīti veditabbaṃ. Dhammakaraṇe chattavaṭṭiyaṃ lekhaṃ ṭhapetvā lekhā na vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Chattavaṭṭiyanti chattassa mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ. Lekhāti upari vā heṭṭhā vā kucchiyaṃ vā aññā lekhā. Kuñcikāya ca pipphale ca maṇikā ca pīḷakā ca na vaṭṭantīti [V 0.0315] sambandho. Maṇikāti ekā vaṭṭamaṇi. Pīḷakāti sāsapamattikā muttarājisadisā bahuvaṭṭalekhā. Daṇḍamhīti pipphaladaṇḍake.

266-7. ‘Kaṇṇakoṇakasuttāni’ refers to threads tied at the four corners with loops for attachment in a draught during the dyeing process, which are permitted by the phrase ‘Bhikkhus, I allow ear-threads’ (Mahāva. 344). The corners, designated as 'ears', are `kaṇṇakoṇakā`, and the threads are in them. However, regarding the knot-and-loop straps, since it was stated below that only corner-threads that are difficult to discern are permissible, they are not to be cut when the robe is dyed; but since corner-threads in general are stated as needing to be cut, it should be understood that even threads that have come out from the hanging-cords are to be cut. The construction is that on the water-strainer, apart from a line on the rim, another line is not permissible. ‘Chattavaṭṭiyaṃ’ means on the rim of the water-strainer. ‘Lekhā’ refers to another line, whether above, below, or on the body. On a key and on a `pipphala`, a gem and a `pīḷakā` are not permissible—this is the connection. ‘Maṇikā’ is a single round gem. ‘Pīḷakā’ refers to a mustard-seed-sized, many-circled line resembling a string of pearls. ‘Daṇḍamhi’ refers to the handle of the `pipphala`.

268-9. Araṇiyaṃ [M 0.0374] mālādi ca pattamaṇḍale bhittikammañca na vaṭṭatīti sambandhitabbaṃ. Araṇiyanti uttarāraṇi adharāraṇi araṇidhanukañca sāmaññena gahitaṃ. Pattamaṇḍaleti tipusīsādimaye pattamaṇḍale. Ettha pana makaradaṇḍakaṃ vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhāti kattarayaṭṭhiyā heṭṭhā. Uddhanti tassāyeva upari.

268-9. It should be connected that on a fire-stick, garlands and the like, and on a bowl-stand, and wall-paintings are not permissible. ‘Araṇiyaṃ’ generally refers to the upper fire-stick, the lower fire-stick, and the fire-stick bow. ‘Pattamaṇḍale’ refers to bowl-stands made of tin, lead, and the like. Here, however, the makara-handle is permissible. ‘Heṭṭhā’ means below the knife-handle. ‘Uddhaṃ’ means above the same.

270-3. Sammuñjanimhīti sammuñjaniyā liṅgavipallāso. Avāritanti itthirūpaṃ pana vāritaṃ. Sovaṇṇamayampīti suvaṇṇamayampi. Visāṇanāḷi nāma visāṇamayā nāḷi. Ettha pana avuttānipi yāni kānici ārakaṇḍakadantakaṭṭhachedanapānīyaghaṭapānīyauḷuṅkacuṇṇabhājanādīni vuttānaṃ anulomānīti veditabbāni. Yo panettha vinayaññū tādisaṃ parikkhāraṃ disvā chindeyya vā chindāpeyya vā, anupavajjo soti veditabbanti.

270-3. ‘Sammuñjanimhi’ is a gender inversion of ‘sammuñjanī’ (broom). ‘Avārita’ means that a female form, however, is prohibited. ‘Sovaṇṇamayampi’ means even if made of gold. ‘Visāṇanāḷi’ means a tube made of horn. Here, it should be understood that even unmentioned items such as awl-cases, tooth-stick cutters, water pots, drinking ladles, powder boxes, and so on, are permissible if they are in conformity with what has been stated. It should be understood that if a Vinaya expert, seeing such an accessory, cuts it or has it cut, he is blameless.

Parikkhāraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of Requisites is concluded.

36. Bhesajjaniddesavaṇṇanā

36. The Explanation of the Exposition of Medicines

274-5. Janassa bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ dātuṃ vattuñca na labbhatīti sambandhiyaṃ. Labbhatīti ettha “bhikkhunā”ti kattā “bhesajja”nti vuttakammaṃ. Nanu ca kātunti bhāvasādhanattā tassa avuttakammenāpi bhavitabbaṃ bhāve vihitakitakappaccayānaṃ payoge kammakārakassāpi icchitabbattāti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi padhānabhūtakammasattiyā abhidhāne sati appadhānakitakakiriyābhisambandhena guṇībhūtā kammasatti abhihitā viya viññāyati. Tathā ca vuttaṃ amhehi yogavinicchaye “padhānānuyāyitāya janavohārāya padhānasatyābhidhāne guṇasatti abhihitā viya pakāsatī”ti. Janassāti āgatāgatajanassa. Sahadhammīnañca pitūnañca tadupaṭṭhākabhikkhunissitabhaṇḍūnañca veyyāvaccakarassa ca bhikkhācariyaviññattisakehi [M 0.0375] bhesajjakaraṇaṃ labbhanti sambandho[V 0.0316]. Tattha sahadhamminanti saha caritabbo dhammo sīlasaddhāpaññāsaṅkhāto sahadhammo, so etesamatthīti sahadhammino, bhikkhu bhikkhunī sikkhamānā sāmaṇero sāmaṇerīti pañca, tesaṃ. Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro ekasesanayena, ubhinnaṃ sāmaññaniddeso vā, tesaṃ. Bhikkhunissito nāma yo vihāre sabbakammāni karonto bhikkhuṃ nissāya vasati. Bhaṇḍu nāma yo pabbajjāpekkho yāva pattacīvaraṃ paṭiyādiyati, tāva vihāre vasati, so paṇḍupalāso. Veyyāvaccakarassāti attano upaṭṭhākassa. Etesu pana mātāpitaro sace rajjepi ṭhitā paccāsīsanti, akātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Mātaraṃ anāmasantena sabbaṃ parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Pitā pana sahatthena nahāpanasambāhanādīni katvā upaṭṭhātabbo.

274-5. In this connection, it is not permissible for a person to prepare medicine, to give it, or to speak about it. Here, in 'it is permissible,' the agent is 'by a monk' and the object is 'medicine' (which is stated). But since 'to prepare' (kātuṃ) has an abstract verbal sense (bhāvasādhana), should it not also be possible with an unstated object, given that in the use of participles (kitaka-paccaya) prescribed for the abstract sense (bhāva), the objective case (kammakāraka) is also intended? True, but even so, when the primary objective power is expressed, the subordinate objective power, being secondary due to its connection with the non-primary verbal action, is understood as if expressed. And thus it has been said by us in the Yogavinicchaya: 'In common usage, due to following the primary, when the primary power is expressed, the subordinate power appears as if expressed.' By 'for a person' is meant for any person who comes. The connection is that the preparation of medicine is permissible for co-religionists, parents, their attendants, those dependent on a monk, bhaṇḍus, and those who perform services, by means of one's own resources, by going for alms, or by making a request. Here, 'co-religionists' (sahadhammīnaṃ) means those who have the 'co-Dhamma,' which is the Dhamma to be practiced together, consisting of virtue, faith, and wisdom; thus they are 'co-religionists.' These are five: monks, nuns, female probationers, novice monks, and novice nuns; for them. By 'parents' (pitūnaṃ) is meant father and mother by the ekasesa method, or a general designation for both; for them. A 'monk's dependent' (bhikkhunissita) is one who resides in the monastery performing all duties while relying on a monk. A 'bhaṇḍu' is one who, aspiring for ordination, resides in the monastery until robes and bowls are prepared; he is like a pale leaf. By 'one who performs services' (veyyāvaccakara) is meant one's own attendant. Among these, however, if parents—even if they are rulers—express a wish, it is not proper to refuse. For a mother, all services should be performed without touching her. A father, however, should be attended to by performing bathing, massaging, and other services with one's own hand.

276. Pitā ca mātā ca bhātā ca bhaginī cāti dvando pitā…pe… bhaginiyo. Mahanto ca cūḷo ca, mahācūḷā ca te pitā…pe… bhaginiyo cāti kammadhārayo. Tā ādi yesanteti aññapadattho. Mahācūḷa-saddā pitādi-saddehi paccekaṃ yojetabbā “mahāpituno cūḷapituno”tiādinā. Ādi-saddena panettha pitucchā mātulo, tesaṃ dasannampi yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā puttaparamparañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tesaṃ sake bhesajjakaraṇaṃ labbhanti yojanā. Tesaṃ mahāpitādīnaṃ santake sati tena bhesajjakaraṇaṃ labbhatīti attho. Nāti natthi ce. Attaniyeti bhikkhuno attano santake satīti attho. Dātabbaṃ tāvakālikanti tāvakālikaṃ katvā dātabbanti attho. Te pana sace paṭidenti, gahetabbaṃ, no ce denti, na codetabbā. Yāva tassa dānaṃ, tāva kālo assāti tāvakālikaṃ. Ṇiko samāsante.

276. Father, mother, brother, and sister—this is a dvanda compound, 'father... up to... sisters.' The great and the small, and the great-small—these are father... up to... sisters, forming a kammadhāraya compound. That which has them as its beginning is an aññapadattha compound. The words 'mahā' (great) and 'cūḷa' (small) should be individually connected to the words for father, etc., as in 'for the great father, for the small father,' and so on. Here, by the term 'etc.' are included the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle, encompassing up to the seventh generation of these ten relatives and the line of descendants. The construction is that the preparation of medicine is permissible for them when it belongs to them. The meaning is that when it is in the possession of these great fathers and others, the preparation of medicine by means of it is permissible. 'If there are no relatives' (nāti natthi ce) means if there are no relatives. By 'belonging to oneself' (attaniye) is meant when it is in the monk's own possession. By 'to be given temporarily' (dātabbaṃ tāvakālikaṃ) is meant that it should be given by making it temporary. If they, however, return it, it may be accepted; if they do not give it, they should not be urged. It is 'temporary' (tāvakālikaṃ) meaning 'as long as that gift lasts, that is the time.' The suffix 'ṇika' is at the end of the compound.

277. Bhesajjakaraṇādīti [M 0.0376] ādi-saddena anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍadānādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, hi-saddo hetumhi, hi yasmā etesu kuladūsanādayo na ruhanti, tasmā tesaṃ bhesajjakaraṇaṃ labbhaṃ, attaniye ca sati dātabbanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Na rūhatīti na rohati nappavattati na hoti, āpattiṃ na janetīti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ atthāya ñātisāmaṇerehi vā bhesajjaṃ āharāpetabbaṃ, attano atthāya vā āharāpetvā dātabbaṃ. Tehipi “upajjhāyādīnaṃ āharissāmā”ti vattasīsena āharitabbaṃ. Sace aññepi ye gilānā hutvā vihāraṃ pavisanti, tesaṃ sabbesampi apaccāsīsantena bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ. Saddhaṃ kulaṃ hoti bhikkhusaṅghassa mātāpituṭṭhānīyaṃ, tatra ce koci gilāno hoti, tassatthāya “bhante, itthannāmassa [V 0.0317] rogassa kiṃ bhesajjaṃ karontī”ti kappiyaṃ katvā pucchanti, idañcidañca gahetvā karontīti vaṭṭati, bhikkhūhi aññamaññaṃ vā kathā kātabbā.

277. By 'the preparation of medicine, etc.' (bhesajjakaraṇādi) is meant the inclusion of the giving of alms-food untouched by hand, etc., by the term 'etc.' (ādi-saddena). The word 'hi' is in the sense of a reason: for since in these cases, offenses such as corrupting families do not arise, therefore, the preparation of medicine is permissible for them, and when it is in one's own possession, it should be given. This is how the meaning should be understood here. By 'does not arise' (na rūhati) is meant it does not grow, does not occur, does not happen; the intention is that it does not produce an offense. For their sake, medicine should be caused to be brought by novice relatives, or caused to be brought for one's own sake and then given. They too should bring it with the thought, 'We will bring it for our preceptors, etc.,' as a matter of duty. If others, being sick, enter the monastery, medicine should be prepared for all of them without expecting anything in return. A faithful family is like a mother and father to the community of monks. If someone there is sick, for their sake they may ask an allowable person, 'Venerable sir, what medicine do they prepare for such-and-such an illness?' It is proper to say, 'They prepare it by taking this and that.' Monks may also discuss it among themselves.

278. Channaṃ mātādīnañca dāmarikacorassa issariyassa anāmaṭṭho piṇḍapāto dātuṃ avāritoti yojetabbaṃ. Channanti mātādīnaṃ channaṃ majjhe. Mātādīnanti bhikkhunissitaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesānaṃ pañcannaṃ mātādīnaṃ. “Channa”nti pana yojanāya aṭṭhakathāya virujjhati. Tattha hi “mātāpitūna”ntiādinā bhikkhunissitaṃ ohāya satteva vuttā. Ācariyabuddhadattattherena ca tatheva vuttaṃ –

278. It should be construed that the alms-food untouched by hand is not prohibited to be given to the six, beginning with the mother, and to the robber chief and the ruler. By 'the six' is meant among the six, beginning with the mother. By 'beginning with the mother' is meant the remaining five, beginning with the mother, excluding the monk's dependent. However, the interpretation of 'six' contradicts the commentary. For there, beginning with 'mother and father,' seven are mentioned, excluding the monk's dependent. And the Elder Ācariya Buddhādatta also stated it in the same way—

“Anāmaṭṭhopi dātabbo, piṇḍapāto vijānatā;

Dvinnaṃ mātāpitūnampi, tadupaṭṭhāyakassa ca.

Even alms-food untouched by hand should be given by one who knows; To both mother and father, and also to their attendant.

“Issarassāpi dātabbo, coradāmarikassa ca;

Bhaṇḍukassattano ceva, veyyāvaccakarassapī”ti. (vinaya vi. 493-495);

Even to the ruler it should be given, and to the robber chief; And to one's own bhaṇḍu, and also to one who performs services.

Dāmarikacorassāti [M 0.0377] rajjaṃ patthayamānassa pākaṭacorassa. Anāmaṭṭhoti apabbajitassa hatthato laddhā attanā aññena vā pabbajitena aggahitaaggo, ayaṃ anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāto. Paṭisanthāro “vihārappattaṃ āgantukaṃ vā daliddādiṃ vā disvā ‘pānīyaṃ pivā’ti dātabbaṃ, pādamakkhanatelaṃ dātabbaṃ, kāle āgatassa yāgubhattaṃ, vikāle āgatassa sace taṇḍulā atthi, taṇḍulā dātabbā, sayanaṭṭhānaṃ dātabbaṃ, corānaṃ pana saṅghikampidātabba”nti vutto. Avasesapaṭisanthāro pana apaccāsīsantena kātabbo. Tathā dhammapaṭisanthāropi yassa kassaci dātabbova.

By 'robber chief' (dāmarikacorassa) is meant a notorious thief desiring sovereignty. By 'untouched by hand' (anāmaṭṭho) is meant alms-food received from the hand of a non-renunciant, the top portion of which has not been taken by oneself or another renunciant; this is anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāta. Hospitality (paṭisanthāro) is described thus: 'Upon seeing a guest who has arrived at the monastery, or a poor person, etc., one should give them water to drink, provide foot-ointment oil, give rice-gruel or cooked rice at the proper time; if there are rice grains when they arrive at an improper time, rice grains should be given, a sleeping place should be given; but even property of the Sangha should be given to thieves,' it is said. But the remaining hospitality should be done without expecting anything in return. Similarly, the hospitality of the Dhamma should also be given to anyone whatsoever.

279. Tesanti aññātakādīnaṃ gihīnaṃ. Kayirāti “bhaṇathā”ti vutte kareyya. “Na karomā”ti vutte sace vippaṭisārino bhavissanti, kātabbaṃ. Nattanoti attano suttodakehi na kayirāti yojanīyaṃ. Evaṃ sāmaññena paritte paṭipajjanavidhiṃ dassetvā idāni āṭānāṭiyaparitte paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “bhaṇitabba”ntiādimāha. Bhaṇāpenteti “bhaṇathā”ti [V 0.0318] ajjhesanapubbakaṃ payojente. Parittaṃ sāsanogadhanti paṭhamameva āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃ abhaṇitvā sāsanapariyāpannaṃ mettasuttaṃ dhajaggasuttaṃ ratanasuttanti imāni suttāni sattāhaṃ bhaṇitvā yathāparikammaṃ parittaṃ āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ bhaṇitabbanti yojanā.

279. By 'them' (tesaṃ) is meant laypeople such as strangers, etc. By 'should do' (kayirā) is meant one should do it if told, 'Recite.' If they say, 'We will not do it,' and then become regretful, it should be done. By 'not by oneself' (nattano) is meant that it should be construed as 'one should not do it with one's own thread and water.' Having thus shown the method of practicing the protective verses in general, the text now begins with 'should be recited' (bhaṇitabbaṃ) to explain the method of practicing the Āṭānāṭiya protective chant. By 'causing to recite' (bhaṇāpente) is meant causing another to recite with a prefatory request, saying, 'Recite.' By 'the protective chant rooted in the teaching' (parittaṃ sāsanogadhaṃ) is meant that, without reciting the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta at the very beginning, one should recite the Mettā Sutta, the Dhajagga Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta—these suttas included in the teaching—for seven days, and then, according to the preliminary preparations, one should recite the Āṭānāṭiya protective chant. This is the construction.

280. “Āgantvā sīlaṃ detu, dhammaṃ parittañca bhāsatū”ti kenaci pesito gantvā sīlaṃ vā dātuṃ dhammaṃ parittaṃ vā vattuṃ labbhatīti sambandho.

280. The connection is that if sent by someone with the message, 'Having come, let him give precepts, speak the Dhamma, and recite a protective text,' it is permissible to go and give precepts or speak the Dhamma or recite a protective text.

Bhesajjaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Remedies is concluded.

37. Uggahaniddesavaṇṇanā

37. Commentary on the Exposition of Grasping.

281. Puggala-saddamatte [M 0.0378] payutte attanopi gahaṇasambhavo siyāti byabhicāratthaṃ añña-saddappayogo. Sati sambhave byabhicāre visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ hotīti. Dasabhedampi ratananti “muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ lohitaṅko masāragalla”nti (pāci. 506) evaṃ vuttaṃ dasabhedampi ratanaṃ. Uggaṇhantassāti gaṇhantassa sampaṭicchantassa.

281. When the mere word 'person' is used, there might be the possibility of it being taken for oneself; to avoid this deviation, the word 'another' is used. When there is a possibility of deviation, the qualification is meaningful. 'The tenfold jewel' refers to 'pearl, gem, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's eye'—thus the tenfold jewel is described. 'For one who grasps' means for one who takes, who receives.

282-3. Tesu attatthaṃ uggaṇhantassa dvīsu nissaggīti sambandho. Tesūti tesu dasasu majjhe. Dvīsūti rajatajātarūpasaṅkhātesu dvīsu nissaggiyavatthūsu. Attatthanti iminā navakammādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ atthāya dukkaṭanti dīpeti. Sesesu dukkaṭanti avasesesu aṭṭhasu sabbesampi atthāya uggaṇhantassa dukkaṭanti attho. Gaṇañca saṅghañca puggalañca anāmasitvā “cetyassa navakammassa dammī”ti vutte ca na paṭikkhipeti sambandhanīyaṃ. Na paṭikkhipeti iminā saṅghādiṃ āmasitvā vutte paṭikkhipanaṃ dīpeti. Paṭikkhitte “kappiyakārakānaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, mama purisānaṃ mayhameva vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Catupaccayatthāya ca dinnaṃ yena yena attho hoti, tadatthaṃ upanetabbaṃ. Tesaṃ cīvaratthāya dinnaṃ cīvareyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace cīvarena tādiso attho natthi, piṇḍapātādīhi saṅgho kilamati, saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apaloketvā tadatthāyapi upanetabbaṃ. Esa nayo piṇḍapātagilānapaccayatthāya [V 0.0319] dinnepi. Senāsanatthāya dinnaṃ pana garubhaṇḍattā tattheva upanetabbaṃ, senāsanesu nassantesu jagganatthaṃ mūlacchejjaṃ akatvā avissajjetvā yāpanamattaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

Among these, for one who grasps for personal use, there is relinquishment in two cases; this is the connection. 'Among these' means among these ten. 'Two' refers to the two objects that entail relinquishment, namely silver and gold. By 'for personal use,' it is shown that for the sake of the five purposes beginning with new construction, it is an offense of wrongdoing. 'In the remaining, it is an offense of wrongdoing' means that in the remaining eight cases, for one who grasps for any purpose whatsoever, it is an offense of wrongdoing. If, without consulting the group, the Sangha, or an individual, it is said, 'I give this for the new construction of the shrine,' and one does not refuse it, this is to be connected. By 'does not refuse it,' it is shown that if it is said after consulting the Sangha and others, one should refuse. If, upon refusal, one says, 'It will be in the hands of the stewards, or in the hands of my attendants, or in my own hands—you may simply use the requisites,' it is permissible. What is given for the sake of the four requisites should be applied to whatever purpose is needed. What is given for the sake of robes should be applied to robes alone. If there is no such need for robes, but the Sangha is troubled by a lack of almsfood and other things, having sought permission for the welfare of the Sangha, it may then be applied to that purpose as well. This same method applies when something is given for almsfood or for requisites for the sick. However, what is given for the sake of lodgings, being a heavy item, should be applied to that purpose itself. If lodgings are deteriorating, for the purpose of their upkeep, without depleting the capital or abandoning them, they should be used just for maintenance.

284. Khettādīnaṃ [M 0.0379] kesañci dukkaṭavatthūnaṃ sampaṭicchanūpāyaṃ dassetuṃ “khetta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khettanti pubbaṇṇaviruhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Vatthunti aparaṇṇaucchuphalādīnaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Dāsapasvādikanti dāsapasupupphārāmaphalārāmādikaṃ. Paṭikkhipitvā kappiyena kamena ca gaṇheyyāti sambandho. Kappiyena kamena cāti ettha kama-saddo vohārappaṭipāṭivacano, tasmā paresaṃ attano ca kappiyavohārakkamenevāti attho.

284. To show the method for accepting things like fields, which for some are objects entailing an offense of wrongdoing, the words 'field' and so on are stated. Therein, 'field' is a place where early-ripening grains grow. 'Ground' is a place where late-ripening grains, sugarcane, fruits, and the like grow. 'Servants, livestock, and so on' includes servants, livestock, flower gardens, fruit gardens, and the like. The connection is: 'having refused, one should accept by an allowable method.' Herein, in 'by an allowable method,' the word 'method' refers to the order of customary speech; therefore, the meaning is 'only by the method of allowable customary speech, both that of others and of oneself'.

So ca khettavatthūsu tāva “cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vā “kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe bhavissatī”ti vā “saṅgho kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ bhuñjatū”ti vā “sīmaṃ demā”ti vā parehi vutto, “sādhu, upāsaka migapakkhino ettha nibbhayā sukhena jīvissantī”ti attanā vā taḷāke yathāvutteneva “udakaṃ paribhuñjissanti, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissanti, migapakkhino pivissantī”ti parehi vā “sādhu, upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissatī”tiādinā attanā vā dāse “ārāmikaṃ dammi, veyyāvaccakaraṃ dammi, kappiyakārakaṃ dammī”ti vā pasūsu “pañcagorasaparibhogatthāya dammī”ti ārāme “vanaṃ dammī”ti evamādinā vutto veditabbo. Sace pana koci abyatto akappiyavohārena khettādiṃ paṭiggaṇhāti vā kāreti vā, taṃ bhikkhūhi na paribhuñjitabbaṃ, taṃ nissāya laddhaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍampi akappiyameva. Abyattena pana lajjībhikkhunā kārāpitesu kiñcāpi paṭiggahaṇaṃ kappiyaṃ, bhikkhussa payogapaccayā uppannena missattā visagatapiṇḍapāto viya, akappiyamaṃsabhojanaṃ viya ca dubbinibbhogaṃ hoti, sabbesaṃ akappiyameva.

And this method, concerning fields and grounds, should be understood as follows: when he is spoken to by others, 'Enjoy the four requisites,' or 'It will be in the hands of the stewards,' or 'May the Sangha enjoy allowable goods,' or 'We give a boundary'; or when he himself says, 'Good, lay follower, may the deer and birds live here without fear and in happiness'; or concerning a pond, as mentioned, when he is spoken to by others, 'They will use the water, they will wash their belongings, the deer and birds will drink,' or he himself says, 'Good, lay follower, the Sangha will drink the water,' and so on; or concerning servants, 'I give a monastery attendant, I give a service attendant, I give a steward'; or concerning livestock, 'I give for the use of the five products of the cow'; or concerning a park, 'I give the woodland,' and so on. But if some incompetent person accepts or causes to be accepted a field or the like through unallowable speech, it should not be used by the monks. Even allowable goods obtained on account of that are indeed unallowable. However, in the case of things caused to be done by an incompetent but scrupulous monk, although the acceptance is allowable, because it is mixed with what has arisen from the monk's effort as a condition, it is difficult to partake of, like almsfood mixed with poison or like eating unallowable meat; for all, it is indeed unallowable.

285-6. Nava…pe… kiriyā ca anave mattikuddhāraṇañca bandho ca āḷiyā thirakāro ca anave kedāre atirekabhāgaggahaṇañca nave ca aparicchinnabhāge sasse “ettake [M 0.0380] dethā”ti kahāpaṇuṭṭhāpanañcāti sabbesampi akappiyanti sambandho. Mātikā ca kedāro ca taḷāko cāti dvando mātika…pe… taḷākā. Tesaṃ kiriyāti samāso. Anaveti catupaccayavasena paṭiggahite purāṇataḷāke. Udakavasena paṭiggahite pana suddhacittānaṃ vaṭṭati. Bandhoti [V 0.0320] pāḷiyā bandho. Porāṇakedāre niyamitapakatibhāgattā āha “anave”ti. Aparicchinnabhāgeti “ettake bhūmibhāge ettako bhāgo dātabbo”ti evaṃ aparicchinnabhāge.

New... and so on... actions, and taking clay from an old one, and the binding and strengthening of a dyke, and taking an excess portion in an old field, and in a new, unspecified portion of a crop, demanding payment, saying, 'Give this much'—the connection is that all these are unallowable for everyone. 'Watercourse, field, and pond' is a dvanda compound: 'watercourse...pond.' 'Their actions' is a compound. 'In an old one' refers to an old pond accepted on the basis of the four requisites. If accepted by means of water, however, it is permissible for those of pure mind. 'Binding' means the binding of the embankment. Because the portion is fixed by custom in an old field, it is said 'in an old one'. 'In an unspecified portion' means in a portion where it is not specified thus: 'For such a portion of land, such a portion should be given,' thus in an unspecified portion.

287-9. “Kasa vappa” iccādiṃ avatvā ca “ettakāya bhūmiyā ettako bhāgo deyyo”ti bhūmiṃ vā patiṭṭhāpeti, tassevetamakappiyanti sambandho. Ca-saddo avadhāraṇe. Patiṭṭhāpetīti yo bhikkhu patiṭṭhāpeti. Tassevāti tassa patiṭṭhāpakabhikkhusseva. Etanti patiṭṭhāpitabhūmito laddhadhaññaṃ “ettake bhūmibhāge sassaṃ kataṃ, ettakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ vadante pamāṇagaṇhanatthaṃ daṇḍarajjubhi minane vā khale ṭhatvā rakkhaṇe vā taṃ nīharāpane vā koṭṭhāgārādipaṭisāmane vā etaṃ tasseva akappiyanti sambandhanīyaṃ. Patiṭṭhāpeti cāti so bhikkhu patiṭṭhāpeti ca. Katanti amhehi kataṃ. Vadantevanti evaṃ kassake vadante. Pamāṇanti bhūmippamāṇaṃ. Nīharāpaneti khalato gehassa nīharāpane. Etanti mitaladdharakkhitādikaṃ. Tassevāti mānakarakkhakādino eva. Apubbassa anuppāditattā aññesaṃ kappatīti āha “tassevetamakappiya”nti.

And without saying, 'Plow, sow,' and so on, if he establishes a field, saying, 'For this much land, this much portion should be given,' this is unallowable for him alone—this is the connection. The word 'ca' is for emphasis. 'Establishes' refers to the monk who establishes it. 'For him alone' means for that very monk who establishes it. 'This' refers to the grain obtained from the established land; when they say, 'This much crop was produced on this portion of land, take this much,' the measuring with sticks or ropes for the purpose of taking the amount, or standing guard at the threshing floor, or having it removed, or managing the granary and so on—this is to be understood as unallowable for him alone. 'And establishes' means that monk establishes it. 'Done' means done by us. 'When they say' means when the farmers speak thus. 'Amount' means the measure of the land. 'Having it removed' means having it removed from the threshing floor to the house. 'This' refers to what is measured, obtained, guarded, and so on. 'For him' means for the very one who measures, guards, and so on. Because it was not produced by the others, it is allowable for them; thus it is said, 'this is unallowable for him alone'.

290. Paṭisāmanappasaṅgenāha “paṭisāmeyyā”tiādi. Pitusantakampi gihisantakaṃ yaṃ kiñcīti sambandho. Pitusantakanti pitā ca mātā ca pitaro, tesaṃ santakaṃ. Gihisantakanti iminā [M 0.0381] pañcannaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ santakaṃ yaṃ kiñci parikkhāraṃ paṭisāmetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Yaṃ kiñcīti kappiyaṃ akappiyaṃ vā antamaso mātukaṇṇapiḷandhanatālapaṇṇampi. Bhaṇḍāgārikasīsenāti sīsaṅgamiva padhānaṃ yaṃ kiñci “sīsa”nti idha upacāravasena vuccati, tathā bhaṇḍāgārikasaddopi bhāvappadhāno, bhaṇḍāgāriko bhaṇḍāgārikattaṃ sīsaṃ padhānanti visesanaparapade kammadhārayo, tena, bhaṇḍāgārikattassa padhānakaraṇenāti attho.

290. In connection with managing, it is said, 'He should manage,' and so on. The connection is that he may manage anything belonging to his parents or belonging to a householder. 'Belonging to his parents' means what belongs to his father and mother, who are 'parents.' By 'property of a householder,' it is shown that it is allowable to manage any requisite whatsoever belonging to the five co-religionists. 'Anything' means whether allowable or unallowable, even down to a mother's ear ornament or a palm leaf. By 'Bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena' means that just as the head is the principal limb, so 'head' is used here metaphorically for anything principal. Similarly, the word 'bhaṇḍāgārika' (storeroom-keeper) is primary in its abstract sense. The compound is a karmadhāraya with the qualifying word placed after: 'the storeroom-keeper, that is, the state of being a storeroom-keeper, is the head, the principal thing.' Therefore, the meaning is 'by making the state of being a storeroom-keeper primary'.

291-2. Avassaṃ paṭisāmiyanti avassaṃ saṅgopetabbaṃ. Vuttepīti mātāpitūhi vuttepi.

'I will certainly look after it' means it must certainly be protected. 'Even when told' means even when told by his parents.

293-4. Vaḍḍhakiādayo vā rājavallabhā vā “sakaṃ parikkhāraṃ vā sayanabhaṇḍaṃ vā paṭisāmetvā dehī”ti yadi vadanti, chandatopi bhayāpi na kareyyāti yojanā. Parikkhāranti vāsipharasuādiupakaraṇabhaṇḍaṃ. Chandatopi bhayāpīti vaḍḍhakiādīsu chandena, rājavallabhesu bhayena.

293-4. If carpenters and so on, or royal favorites, say, 'Restore and give your own requisites or bedding,' he should not do so out of desire or fear—this is the connection. 'Requisites' refers to equipment like axes, adzes, and other tools. 'Out of desire or fear' means out of desire for the carpenters and so on, and out of fear of the royal favorites.

295-6. Paṭisāmituṃ [V 0.0321] vaṭṭatīti yojetabbaṃ. Saṅkantīti yādise padese “bhikkhūhi vā sāmaṇerehi vā gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti saṅkaṃ uppādenti, tādise vihārāvasathassantoti yojanīyaṃ. Vihārāvasathassāti vihārassa ca āvasathassa ca. Ratananti dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ. Ratnasammatanti vatthādikaṃ. Nikkhipeyyāti sāmike diṭṭhe niyametvā dātuṃ “ettakā kahāpaṇā”tiādinānurūpena mattikalañchanādinimittena vā saññāṇaṃ katvā nikkhipeyya. Gahetvānāti tādise asati attanāva gahetvā. Tādiseti ratane vā ratanasammate vā sati. Sāmikānāgamaṃ ñatvāti yadi attani āsaṅkanti, maggā okkamma nisīdiya pacchā sāmikānaṃ anāgamanaṃ [M 0.0382] viññāya. Patirūpanti ratanasammate paṃsukūlaggahaṇaṃ ratane nirussukkagamananti evarūpaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anurūpanti.

295-6. 'It is allowable to restore'—this should be construed. 'They suspect'—this should be applied to the interior of such a monastery or lodging in a place where they arouse the suspicion, 'This will be taken by monks or novices.' 'Of the monastery and lodging' means of the monastery and of the lodging. 'Jewel' means the ten kinds of jewels. 'Considered a jewel' means cloth and the like. 'Should deposit' means, having seen the owner, having determined to give it, one should deposit it after making an identification by a suitable mark, such as saying, 'This many coins,' or by a clay seal and the like. 'Having taken' means, when such an owner is not present, having taken it oneself. 'Such' refers to when there is a jewel or something considered a jewel. 'Knowing the owner’s absence' means if they suspect oneself, stepping aside from the path and sitting down, then later, having understood the owner's non-arrival. 'Suitable' means taking rag-robes for things considered jewels, and proceeding without eagerness for actual jewels—such conduct is appropriate for monks.

Uggahaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Grasping is completed.

38. Dūsananiddesavaṇṇanā

38. Commentary on the Exposition of Corruption

297. Dadatoti sasantakaṃ parasantakañca dentassa. Kuladūsanadukkaṭanti attano duppaṭipattiyā kulānaṃ dūsanaṃ pasādavināsanaṃ kuladūsanaṃ, tena dukkaṭaṃ kuladūsanadukkaṭaṃ.

297. ‘He gives’ refers to one who gives what belongs to oneself and what belongs to others. ‘An offense of corrupting families’ (kuladūsanadukkaṭa) means the corruption of families (kuladūsana), which is the destruction of the faith of families due to one’s own bad conduct; by that it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa), thus an offense of corrupting families.

298. Ettha saṅghikaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ issarena dentassa thullaccayanti sambandho. Etthāti etesaṃ pupphādīnaṃ majjhe. Issarenāti taddhitalopena vuttaṃ, issariyena issaravatāyāti attho. Dentassāti kulasaṅgahatthāya issaravatāya dadato. Thullaccayanti kulasaṅgahatthāya dadato “kuladūsanadukkaṭa”nti sāmaññavihitadukkaṭena saddhiṃ “pañcimāni, bhikkhave, avissajjiyāni, na vissajjetabbāni saṅghena vā gaṇena vā puggalena vā, vissajjitānipi avissajjitāni honti. Yo vissajjeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (cūḷava. 321) evaṃ vuttathullaccayanti attho. Aññattha thullaccayameva. Senāsanatthāya niyamitepi eseva nayo. Saṅghassa santakaṃ theyyā dentassa dukkaṭādīnīti sambandhitabbaṃ. Dentassāti vuttanayameva. Dukkaṭādīnīti kulasaṅgahatthāya dadato kuladūsanadukkaṭena saddhiṃ māsake vā ūnamāsake vā dukkaṭaṃ[V 0.0322], atirekamāsake vā ūnapañcamāsake vā thullaccayaṃ, pañcamāsake vā atirekapañcamāsake vā pārājikanti evaṃ dukkaṭādīni hontīti attho. Aññattha dukkaṭādīneva.

298. Here, the connection is that for one giving communal heavy property by authority, there is a grave offense. ‘Here’ means among these flowers and so forth. ‘By authority’ (issarena) is said by elision of the taddhita suffix, meaning by lordship, by acting as a lord (issariyena issaravatāya). ‘For one giving’ (dentassa) means for one giving by acting as a lord for the purpose of gaining favor from families. ‘Grave offense’ (thullaccaya) means the grave offense stated thus: ‘Monks, there are these five things that should not be given away, not to be distributed by the Sangha, or by a group, or by an individual; even if given away, they remain not given away. Whoever gives them away incurs a grave offense’ (Cūḷavagga 321), along with the generally prescribed offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) of ‘corrupting families’ for one giving for the purpose of gaining favor from families. Elsewhere, it is simply a grave offense. The same principle applies even when it is designated for lodging. It should be connected that for one giving what belongs to the Sangha by way of theft, there are offenses of wrongdoing and so forth. ‘For one giving’ (dentassa) is as explained before. ‘Offenses of wrongdoing and so forth’ (dukkaṭādīni) means that for one giving for the purpose of gaining favor from families, along with the offense of corrupting families, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for a māsaka or less than a māsaka, a grave offense (thullaccaya) for more than a māsaka or less than five māsakas, and a pārājika offense for five māsakas or more than five māsakas; thus, there are offenses of wrongdoing and so forth. Elsewhere, it is simply offenses of wrongdoing and so forth.

299-300. Kulasaṅgahatthaṃ [M 0.0383] phalapupphūpagaṃ rukkhaṃ sabbathā ropetuñca ropāpetuñca jaggituñca na vaṭṭatīti sambandhanīyaṃ. Ca-saddo ocinituṃ ocināpetuṃ, ganthituṃ ganthāpetunti ca avuttāni ca samuccinoti. Phalapupphāni sampādanavasena upagacchatīti phalapupphūpagaṃ. Sabbathāti kappiyavohāraakappiyavohārapariyāyaobhāsanimittakammavasena sabbappakāreneva. Tattha kappiyavohāro nāma “imaṃ rukkhaṃ jāna, imaṃ āvāṭaṃ jāna, imaṃ mālāvacchaṃ jāna, ettha udakaṃ jānā”ti vacanaṃ, sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇañca. Tabbipariyāyena akappiyavohāro nāma. Pariyāyo nāma “paṇḍitena mālāvacchādayo ropāpetabbā, na cirasseva upakārāya saṃvattantī”tiādivacanaṃ. Obhāso nāma kuddālakhaṇittādīni ca mālāvacche ca gahetvā ṭhānaṃ. Nimittakammaṃ nāma kuddālaudakabhājanādīnaṃ āharitvā samīpe ṭhapanaṃ. Jaggitunti vadanti udakasecanādīni katvā. Ganthanaganthāpanesu pana sabbāpi cha pupphavikatiyo veditabbā ganthimaṃ gopphimaṃ vedhimaṃ veṭhimaṃ pūrimaṃ vāyimanti. Nāmavaseneva panetesaṃ viseso veditabbo. Taṃ pana kulasaṅgahato aññatrāpi bhikkhussa kātumpi akappiyavacanena kārāpetumpi na vaṭṭati. “Evaṃ jāna, evaṃ kate sobheyya, yathā etāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti, tathā karohī”tiādinā pana kappiyavacanena kārāpetuṃ vinā kulasaṅgahaṃ vaṭṭati. Ropanādīnīti akappiyapathaviyaṃ ropāpanasiñcāpanādīni, aññattha ropanādīni.

299-300. It should be connected that it is not permissible to plant, have planted, or tend a tree that yields fruits and flowers in any way for the purpose of gaining favor from families. The word ‘ca’ (and) also includes what is not stated, namely, to gather, to have gathered, to tie, and to have tied. It is called ‘phalapupphūpagaṃ’ because it yields fruits and flowers by way of producing them. ‘In any way’ (sabbathā) means in every possible way, namely, by proper speech, improper speech, indirect speech, suggestive action, and symbolic act. Here, ‘proper speech’ means saying, ‘Know this tree, know this pit, know this flower bed, know the water here,’ and also straightening a dry watercourse. ‘Improper speech’ is the opposite of that. ‘Indirect speech’ means saying, ‘A wise person should have flower beds planted; they will soon be useful,’ and so on. ‘Suggestive action’ means taking a spade, a digging tool, and so on, and standing at a flower bed. ‘Symbolic act’ means bringing tools like a spade, water pot, etc., and placing them nearby. They say ‘to tend’ (jaggituṃ) means by doing things like watering. Regarding tying and having tied, all six types of flower arrangements should be understood: tied (ganthimaṃ), bundled (gopphimaṃ), strung (vedhimaṃ), wrapped (veṭhimaṃ), filled (pūrimaṃ), or woven (vāyimaṃ). However, the distinction among them should be understood only by name. However, apart from gaining favor from families, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to do these things himself or to have them done through improper speech. But with proper speech—such as saying, ‘Know this, if done this way it would look good, arrange these flowers so they don’t scatter,’ and so on—it is permissible without involving gaining favor from families. ‘Planting, etc.’ refers to having planted or having watered on improper ground, and planting, etc., elsewhere.

301-2. Idāni pupphadānādīsu aṭṭhasu kulasaṅgahavatthūsu avasesāni dve dassetuṃ “vuttāvā”tiādimāha. Vuttāva micchājīvavivajjanāyaṃ vuttā eva. Jaṅghapesane vinicchayo vuccatīti pāṭhaseso. Pitaro bhaṇḍuṃ sakaṃ veyyāvaccakaraṃ ṭhapetvā gihikammesu dūtasāsanaṃ haraṇe padavārena [M 0.0384] dukkaṭanti sambandho. Sahadhammikesu vattabbameva natthīti pitādayova vuttā. Gihikammasūti visayasattamī. Padavārenāti padakkamena, pade padeti adhippāyo. Paṭhamaṃ sāsanaṃ aggahetvāpi puna vadato dukkaṭanti yojetabbaṃ. Punāti pacchā. “Ayaṃ dāni so gāmo, handa naṃ sāsanaṃ ārocemī”ti maggā okkamantassa ca pade pade vadato ca dukkaṭanti adhippāyo. Tassa pana sāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā sayameva kāruññe ṭhitena gantvā attano patirūpaṃ [V 0.0323] sāsanaṃ ārocetuṃ, “mama vacanena bhagavato pāde vandathā”tiādikaṃ gihīnaṃ kappiyasāsanaṃ harituñca vaṭṭati.

301-2. Now, to explain the remaining two of the eight bases for gaining favor from families, beginning with flower offerings and so forth, he says ‘as previously stated’ and so on. It has already been stated in the section on the avoidance of wrong livelihood. The remainder of the text states that the decision regarding being sent on foot is declared. The connection is that when parents make a monk their attendant and have him carry a message on household business, there is an offense of wrongdoing for every step. Among fellow Dhamma practitioners, there is nothing to be said; only parents and the like are mentioned. ‘On household business’ (gihikammesu) is a locative of sphere. ‘For every step’ (padavārena) means by sequence of steps; the intention is at each step. It should be connected that even if the initial instruction is not received, repeating it entails an offense of wrongdoing. ‘Again’ (puna) means afterwards. The intention is that for one who, deviating from the path, speaks, saying, ‘This is now that village—come, let me announce the message,’ there is an offense of wrongdoing for every step. However, having refused that message, it is permissible for him to go himself out of compassion and deliver a suitable message; and it is permissible to convey allowable messages to householders, such as, ‘At my word, pay homage to the Blessed One’s feet,’ and so on.

303. Abhūtārocanarūpiyasaṃvohāruggahādisāti abhūtārocanāya rūpiyasaṃvohāre ca uggahe uppannapaccaye ādisanti kathenti pakāsentīti abhūtā…pe… hādisā, taṃsadisāti vuttaṃ hoti.

303. ‘Abhūtārocanarūpiyasaṃvohāruggahādisā’ means that they point out, state, and reveal opportunities that have arisen from false proclamation, monetary transactions, and seizing; thus it is said to be ‘abhūtā…pe…hādisā’, meaning similar to that.

304. Pitūnaṃ harāpetvā haritvāpi pupphāni vatthupūjatthaṃ dātuṃ, sesañātīnaṃ pattānaṃ vatthupūjatthaṃ dātunti yojanīyaṃ. “Harāpetvā haritvā”ti vutte “pakkositvā pakkosāpetvā vā”ti vuttameva siyāti na vuttaṃ. Pattānanti pakkosakena pattāpi gahitā. Vatthupūjatthanti ratanattayapūjanatthaṃ. Upāsakānampi pana sampattānaṃ vatthupūjatthaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Liṅgādipūjatthanti sivaliṅgagiṇḍubimbādipūjanatthaṃ.

304. It should be construed that it is permissible to give flowers to parents, having had them brought or having brought them oneself, for the purpose of worshiping the object of reverence, and to give to the remaining relatives who have arrived for the purpose of worshiping the object of reverence. The phrase ‘having invited or having caused to be invited’ is not used, because when ‘having had brought or having brought’ is said, that would already be implied. ‘Of those who have arrived’ (pattānaṃ) means that even those who have arrived through an inviter are included. ‘For the purpose of worshiping the object of reverence’ (vatthupūjatthaṃ) means for the purpose of worshiping the Triple Gem. Moreover, it is indeed permissible to give to the lay devotees who have arrived for the purpose of worshiping the object of reverence. ‘For the purpose of worshiping symbols, etc.’ (liṅgādipūjatthaṃ) means for the purpose of worshiping Shiva lingas, ball-shaped images, and the like.

305. Tathā phalanti iminā pupphe vuttaṃ sabbaṃ apadisati. Paribbayavihīnānanti paribbayaṃ pātheyyaṃ vihīnaṃ naṭṭhaṃ yesaṃ āgantukānanti samāso. Saparanti attano vissāsikā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.436-437) pana “attano santakaṃyevā”ti vacanaṃ thullaccayādivibhāgato mocetvā vuttaṃ.

305. Thus, by this word 'fruits', it refers to everything said regarding flowers. ‘Those without provisions’ (paribbayavihīnānaṃ) is a compound meaning those newcomers (āgantukānaṃ) for whom provisions or journey-food are lacking or lost. ‘With their own’ (saparā) means those in whom one trusts. In the commentary (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.436-437), however, the statement ‘only what belongs to oneself’ is said after having been excluded from the classification of grave offenses and so forth.

306. Sammatena [M 0.0385] deyyanti yojanā. Deyyanti catutthabhāgaṃ dātabbaṃ. Itarena tu apaloketvā dātabbanti sambandhitabbaṃ. Itarena tu asammatena pana.

306. The construction is: 'It should be given by agreement.' 'It should be given' means a fourth part should be given. It should be connected that in the other case, however, it should be given after informing. 'In the other case' means, however, when there is no agreement.
