307. Paricchijjāti “ettakāni phalāni dātabbānī”ti evaṃ phalaparicchedena vā “imehi rukkhehi dātabbānī”ti evaṃ rukkhaparicchedena vā paricchinditvā. Tatoti paricchinnaphalato rukkhato vā. Yācamānassa gilānassetarassa vāti sambandhanīyaṃ. Rukkhāva dassiyāti “idha phalāni sundarāni, ito gaṇhathā”ti avatvā “ito gahetuṃ labbhatī”ti rukkhā vā dassetabbā.

307. ‘Having specified’ (paricchijja) means having specified either by a specification of the fruits, saying ‘this much fruit should be given,’ or by a specification of the trees, saying ‘it should be given from these trees.’ ‘From that’ means from the specified fruit or tree. It should be connected with 'for the one who asks, whether sick or another.' ‘The trees should be shown’ means that without saying, ‘Here the fruits are beautiful, take from here,’ the trees should be shown, saying, ‘It is permissible to take from here.’

308. Idāni aṭṭhasu pupphādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vinicchayaṃ dassetvā yathāvuttaphalapupphavinicchayaṃ avasesesu [V 0.0324] catūsu apadisanto “sirīsā”tiādimāha. Sirīsacuṇṇakasavādicuṇṇeti kasāvaṃ yaṃ kiñci ādi yassa, tameva cuṇṇaṃ, sirīsacuṇṇañca kasāvādicuṇṇañcāti samāso. “Sirīsacuṇṇaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kasāva”nti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.436-437) vuttaṃ. “Kasāvādī”ti vattabbe rassena vuttaṃ. Sesesūti veḷuādīsu tīsu. Pāḷiyā avuttassāpi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā āha “paṇṇampettha pavesaye”ti. Etthāti pupphādīsūti.

308. Now, having shown the decision regarding four of the eight categories of flowers and so forth, and referring to the previously mentioned decision regarding fruits and flowers for the remaining four, he says ‘sirīsa’ and so on. ‘Sirīsa powder and powder with an astringent taste, etc.’ (sirīsacuṇṇakasavādicuṇṇa) is a compound of 'sirīsa powder' and 'powder with an astringent taste, etc.', which means any powder that has an astringent substance as its primary component. For it is said in the commentary (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.436-437), ‘Sirīsa powder or any other astringent substance.’ It is said with a short vowel where ‘kasāvādi’ should be said. ‘In the rest’ means among the three, such as bamboo and so on. Although not mentioned in the canonical text, because it is stated in the commentary, he says, ‘Here, one should include the leaf as well.’ ‘Here’ means among flowers and so forth.

Dūsananiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Defilements is concluded.

39. Vassūpanāyikaniddesavaṇṇanā

39. Commentary on the Exposition of Entering the Rains-Residence

309-310. Purimikā pacchimikā iti vassūpanāyikā duveti sambandho. Āsāḷhipuṇṇamāya anantare pāṭipadadivase upagantabbā pacchimikāya pure bhavāti purimā, sā eva purimikā. Tato pacchā bhavā aparāya puṇṇamāya anantare [M 0.0386] pāṭipadadivase upagantabbā pacchimikā. Upanayanaṃ pāpuṇanaṃ upagamanaṃ upanāyikā, vassanti vuṭṭhi, idha pana vassakālaṃ “vassa”nti upacārena gahetvā tattha vāso upacāreneva “vassa”nti vuccati, vassassa vassāvāsassa upanāyikā vacībhedavasena vā ālayakaraṇavasena vā upagamanaṃ vassūpanāyikā. Tattha ālayapariggāho ca vacībhedo cāti purimikā vassūpanāyikā duve, ālayapariggāho ca vacībhedo cāti pacchimikā vassūpanāyikā duvebhi sambandhitabbaṃ. Tatthāti tāsu dvīsu. Tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “ediso”tiādi vuttaṃ. So ālayapariggāho ca vacībhedo ca “imasmiṃ vihāre imaṃ temāsaṃ vassaṃ upemi, idha vassaṃ upemī”ti ediso, etādisoti attho. Ettha ca kamuppattianādarā vacībhedo paṭhamaṃ vutto. Ubhayathā vassaṃ upagantuṃ vaṭṭati. Teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 179; mahāva. aṭṭha. 207) “sacepi ‘idha vassaṃ vasissāmī’ti ālayo atthi, asatiyā pana vassaṃ na upeti, gahitasenāsanaṃ suggahitaṃ, chinnavasso na hoti, pavāretuṃ labhatiyeva, vināpi hi vacībhedaṃ ālayakaraṇamattenapi vassaṃ upagatameva hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Nāvāsatthavajesu pana pariyesitvā senāsanaṃ alabhantena ālayakaraṇamatteneva upagantabbaṃ. Upagacchantena ca vihāraṃ paṭijaggitvā pānīyaṃ [V 0.0325] paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā sabbaṃ cetiyavandanādisāmīcikammaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā upagantabbaṃ. Ālayapariggahe ālayaṃ dassetuṃ “cittuppādettha ālayo”ti āha. Etthāti dvīsu.

309-310. The connection is: the `vassūpanāyikā` (entering of the rains-residence) is twofold: the earlier and the later. The earlier one, `purimikā`, is to be entered on the first day after the full moon of Āsāḷha; because it is before the later one, it is the earlier (`purimā`), and that itself is the `purimikā`. The one that is after that, to be entered on the first day after the next full moon, is the later, `pacchimikā`. `Upanāyikā` means entering, reaching, approaching. `Vassa` means rain, but here the rainy season is figuratively called `vassa`, and dwelling there is also figuratively called `vassa`. Thus, `vassūpanāyikā` is the entering of the `vassa` or rains-residence, which is the approaching either by way of verbal declaration or by way of securing a dwelling. Therein, the earlier `vassūpanāyikā` is twofold: securing a dwelling place and verbal declaration; and it should be connected that the later `vassūpanāyikā` is also twofold: securing a dwelling place and verbal declaration. ‘Therein’ means in those two. To show both of these, ‘of this sort,’ etc., is said. That securing of a dwelling place and verbal declaration is of this sort: ‘I enter upon the rains for these three months in this monastery,’ or ‘I enter upon the rains here.’ This is the meaning. And here, verbal declaration is mentioned first without regard to the order of occurrence. It is proper to enter the rains in either way. Therefore it is said in the commentary (vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 179; mahāva. aṭṭha. 207): ‘Even if there is an intention for a dwelling—“I will dwell for the rains here”—but one does not enter upon the rains due to forgetfulness, the lodging taken is well-taken, one's rains-residence is not broken, and one is allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā. Indeed, even without a verbal declaration, by the mere act of securing a dwelling, the rains-residence is considered entered upon.’ However, in the case of ships, dwellings, and caravans, one who searches for but does not find a lodging should enter by the mere act of securing a dwelling. And one who is entering should do so after having repaired the monastery, having set up drinking water and water for use, and having completed all proper duties such as venerating the cetiya. To show what ‘dwelling’ (`ālaya`) means in the phrase ‘securing a dwelling,’ he says, ‘the dwelling here is the arising of a thought.’ ‘Here’ means in the two methods.

311. Tadahūti tasmiṃ vassūpanāyikadivase. Jānanti “ajja vassūpanāyikā”ti jānanto, anupagacchatotimassa visesanaṃ.

311. ‘On that day’ (Tadahū) means on the day of entering the rains-residence. ‘Knowing’ (Jānaṃ) means knowing, ‘Today is the day for entering the rains-residence’; it is an adjective qualifying ‘one who does not enter’.

312. Dutiyanti [M 0.0387] pacchimikaṃ. Anupagatoti kenaci antarāyena purimikaṃ anupagato. Temāsanti purimaṃ vā temāsaṃ pacchimaṃ vā temāsaṃ. Vassaṃ upagantvā pana aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvāpi tadaheva sattāhakaraṇīyena pakkamantassāpi antosattāhe nivattentassāpi anāpatti.

312. ‘The second’ (dutiyaṃ) refers to the later (pacchimikā) rains-residence. ‘Not having entered’ (anupagato) means one who has not entered the earlier rains-residence due to some obstacle. ‘Three months’ (temāsaṃ) means either the earlier three months or the later three months. However, for one who, having entered the rains-residence, departs on that very day for a seven-day duty even without letting the dawn arise, and for one who returns within the seven days, there is no offense.

313-5. Mātāpitūnaṃ pañcannaṃ sahadhammikānañca atthāya gilānatadupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ osadhañca esissaṃ vā pucchissāmi vā upaṭṭhissaṃ vā gantvā ahaṃ nābhirataṃ vūpakāsessaṃ vā kukkuccaṃ vinodanañca diṭṭhiṃ vivecanañca garukādikaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ vāpi ussukkaṃ vāpi karissaṃ vāpi kāressaṃ vāpīti evamādinā sattāhakiccena pahitepi vā apahitepi vā gantuṃ labbhanti yojanā.

313-5. The construction is that for a seven-day duty such as the following, one is permitted to go, whether sent or not sent: for the benefit of parents and the five categories of co-religionists, 'I will go to seek or ask for food for the sick and their attendants, and medicine, or to attend to them; or I will lead away a fellow practitioner who is discontented, or dispel remorse, or resolve a view, or make an effort for emergence from a serious offense and so on, or cause others to do so.'

Ettha pana labbhamānakavasena yojetvā vakkhamānanayena attho veditabbo. Mātādisutiyā teyeva gilāna-saddena gayhanti, tesaṃ upaṭṭhākā tadupaṭṭhākā, gilānā ca tadupaṭṭhākā ca, tesaṃ bhattanti samāso. Osadhanti tesaṃyeva gilānānaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Esissanti pariyesissāmi. Pucchissāmīti teyeva sattajane gilāne pucchissaṃ. Upaṭṭhissanti teyeva gilāne upaṭṭhahissāmi. Abhiramatīti abhirato, visabhāgarūpādidassanena sāsane na abhirato nābhirato. Abhiramaṇaṃ vā abhirataṃ, natthi abhiratamassāti nābhirato, taṃ. Sahadhammikesu yo nābhirato, taṃ vūpakāsessaṃ vikkhepaharaṇatthaṃ aññattha nayissāmi. Kukkuccanti pañcannaṃyeva uppannaṃ vinayakukkuccaṃ. Kitakayoge vikappena dutiyā. Diṭṭhinti tesaṃyeva micchādiṭṭhiyā. Garukamādikanti garukaṃ ādi yassāti viggaho. Ādi-saddena sāmaṇerānaṃ vassapucchanaṃ, sikkhāsamādayitukāmatā, tajjanīyādikammakaraṇaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti [M 0.0388] bhikkhuno garukāpattiyā parivāsamānattadānādīhi vuṭṭhānaṃ. Ussukkanti vassapucchanādiussukkaṃ. Evamādināti [V 0.0326] ettha ādi-saddena diṭṭhigatādīnaṃ dhammakathākaraṇādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Gantuṃ labbhanti ettha gacchantena antoupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhiteneva “antosattāhe āgacchissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā gantabbaṃ. Sace ābhogaṃ akatvā upacārasīmaṃ atikkamati, chinnavasso hotīti vadanti. Sattāhakiccenāti sattāhassa labbhamānakaṃ vuttaṃ vakkhamānañca saṅghakammādi kiccaṃ sattāhakiccaṃ. Sattamaaruṇamattasseva vihāre uṭṭhāpanīyattā sattāhassa sākallena gahaṇaṃ.

Here, however, the meaning should be understood by applying it according to the method to be explained, in connection with what is permitted. By the hearing of 'parents, etc.', those very ones are understood by the word 'sick.' Their attendants are 'tadupaṭṭhākā'; the compound means 'food for the sick and their attendants.' 'Medicine' means medicine for those very sick people. 'Esissaṃ' means 'I will seek.' 'Pucchissaṃ' means 'I will ask about those very seven sick people.' 'Upaṭṭhissaṃ' means 'I will attend to those very sick people.' 'Abhirato' means 'delighting.' 'Nābhirato' (not delighting) means one who does not delight in the Dispensation due to seeing disagreeable forms and so on. Alternatively, 'abhirataṃ' is 'delight,' and 'nābhirato' means 'one for whom there is no delight,' referring to that person. That one among the co-religionists who is not delighting, 'that one I will lead away' (vūpakāsessaṃ), meaning for the sake of removing distraction, I will lead him elsewhere. 'Kukkuccaṃ' means a disciplinary scruple that has arisen regarding the five categories. In connection with an action, the accusative is used optionally. 'Diṭṭhi' means their wrong view. 'Garukādikaṃ' (serious and so on) is dissolved as: 'that of which serious is the beginning.' By the word 'and so on' is included questioning novices about their years of ordination, the desire to undertake the training, and performing disciplinary acts such as censure. 'Vuṭṭhānaṃ' (emergence) means the emergence of a monk from a serious offense by means of probation, penance, and so on. 'Ussukkaṃ' (effort) means effort regarding questioning about the rains-residence and so on. 'Evamādinā' (thus and so on): here, by the word 'and so on' he includes teaching the Dhamma with regard to wrong views and so on. 'One is permitted to go' (Gantuṃ labbhanti): here, one who is going should go only after making a resolution while standing within the inner boundary: 'I will return within seven days.' If, without making a resolution, one crosses the boundary, they say one's rains-residence is broken. 'By a seven-day duty' (Sattāhakiccena) refers to the duties permitted for seven days, both those mentioned and those to be mentioned, such as formal acts of the Saṅgha. Because the seventh dawn must be made to arise while in the monastery, the seven days are taken as a whole.

316. Saṅghakamme vajeti saṅghassa kicce uposathāgārādīsu senāsanesu vā cetiyachattavedikādīsu vā antamaso puggalikasenāsanesu vāpi kattabbanimitte vajeyyāti attho. Dhammasavanatthaṃ nimantito vāpi vaje, garūhi pesito vāpi vaje, garūnaṃ passituṃ vāpi vajeti yojetabbaṃ. Nimantitoti ettha sace paṭhamaṃyeva katikā katā hoti, “asukadivasaṃ nāma sannipatitabba”nti nimantitoyeva nāma hoti. Garūhīti ācariyupajjhāyehi. Pahitoti bhaṇḍadhovanādiatthāya pesito. Passitunti agilānepi.

316. ‘He may go for an act of the Saṅgha’ means he may go on account of a duty to be done for the Saṅgha, in lodgings such as the Uposatha hall, or at stupas, umbrellas, railings, and so on, or at the very least in individual lodgings. It should be construed that he may also go when invited for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, or when sent by his elders, or to see his elders. Herein, regarding ‘invited,’ if an agreement was made beforehand, such as, ‘We should assemble on such-and-such a day,’ then he is indeed considered invited. ‘By elders’ means by teachers and preceptors. ‘Sent’ means dispatched for the purpose of washing robes and so on. ‘To see’ means even when they are not ill.

317. Bhaṇḍa…pe… dassane na vajeti yojanīyaṃ. Etthāpi nimittatthe sattamī. Bhaṇḍaṃ nāma cīvaraṃ. Ñātī mātāpitūhi aññe. Upaṭṭhākā upāsakā. “Ajjeva āgamissa”nti adūrago na pāpuṇeyya, labbhanti sambandho. Labbhanti imassa apāpuṇanaṃ vuttakammaṃ. Ajjevāgamissanti sāmantavihāraṃ gantvā puna āgacchantassa antarāmagge sace aruṇuggamanaṃ hoti, vassacchedopi na hoti, ratticchedadukkaṭañca natthīti vadanti.

317. It should be construed that one should not go for the seeing of robes... and so on. Here too, the locative case is used in the sense of a reason. ‘Bhaṇḍaṃ’ means a robe. ‘Ñātī’ means relatives other than parents. ‘Upaṭṭhākā’ refers to lay devotees. The connection is: thinking, ‘I will return today,’ one who has not gone far might not arrive; this is permissible. The non-arrival is the stated action that is permitted. Regarding ‘he will come today’: if, for one who has gone to a neighboring monastery and is returning, dawn breaks while on the way, the rains-residence is not broken, and there is no dukkaṭa offense for breaking the night—so they say.

318. Sesañātīhīti [M 0.0389] mātāpitūhi avasesañātīhi. Niddisitvāvāti dānadhammasavanādīni. “Pahite pesite”ti cettha “labbha”nti anuvattanīyaṃ.

318. ‘By other relatives’ means by relatives other than one's parents. ‘Having pointed out’ refers to giving, listening to the Dhamma, and so on. Here, with ‘when sent or dispatched,’ the words ‘it is permissible’ should be carried forward.

319. Attano antarāye satīti corasarīsapavāḷajīvitabrahmacariyantarāye, antamaso bhesajjālābhapatirūpaupaṭṭhākālābhepi. “Vassacchedakāraṇampi sattāhakaraṇīyaṃ siyā”ti keci porāṇā vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati, sabbathā vassacchedena bahi vāsāya anuññātakāraṇaṃ sattāhamattaṃ bahi vītināmetvā antovihāreyeva vāsena vassacchedākāraṇaṃ kathaṃ nāma na siyāti. Chinnavasso no pavārayeti sambandho.

319. ‘When there is a personal danger’ refers to dangers from thieves, snakes, or wild beasts, and dangers to one's life or the holy life, or at the very least, the non-acquisition of medicine or a suitable attendant. Some ancient teachers say, ‘Even a reason that would break the rains-residence could be a matter for the seven-day leave.’ This seems reasonable; for if a reason is permitted for dwelling outside, thereby breaking the rains-residence, how indeed could dwelling within the monastery after spending merely seven days outside not be a reason for the rains-residence to remain unbroken? ‘One whose rains-residence is broken does not invite’ is the connection.

320. “Asenāsanikenā”ti [V 0.0327] imināva viññāyamānatthattepi “ajjhokāse cā”ti vacanaṃ “ahaṃ abbhokāsiko, kiṃ me senāsanenā”ti vāsānivattanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Rukkhassa susireti suddhe rukkhasusire. Mahantassa pana susirassa anto padaracchadanakuṭikaṃ katvā pavisanadvāraṃ yojetvā upagantuṃ vaṭṭati. “Viṭapepi aṭṭakaṃ bandhitvā”tiādi vuttanayameva. Tathā chattacāṭīsupi tadanurūpena veditabbaṃ. Chavakuṭi nāma ṭaṅkitamañcādibhedā kuṭi. Tattha ṭaṅkitamañco nāma dīghe mañcapāde majjhe vijjhitvā aṭaniyo pavesetvā kato, catunnaṃ pāsāṇānaṃ upari pāsāṇaṃ attharitvā katampi ṭaṅkitamañco.

320. Although the meaning is already understood by ‘by one without lodgings,’ the phrase ‘and also in the open air’ is stated to prevent one from refraining from dwelling in a proper lodging with the thought, ‘I am an open-air dweller; what need have I for lodgings?’ ‘In the hollow of a tree’ means in a simple tree hollow. But for a large hollow, it is permissible to enter and dwell after having made a hut with a floor and roof inside and having fitted an entrance. ‘In a fork of a tree, having built a platform,’ etc., is just as was stated. Likewise, it should be understood accordingly for sunshades and large pots. ‘A charnel hut’ means a hut of the type of a ṭaṅkitamañca and so on. Here, a ṭaṅkitamañca is one made by piercing long bed legs in the middle and inserting crossbars; one made by spreading a stone slab on top of four stones is also a ṭaṅkitamañca.

321. Asenāsanikenāti yassa tiṇapaṇṇaiṭṭhakasilāsudhāsaṅkhātānaṃ pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ aññatarena channaṃ yojitadvārabandhanaṃ senāsanaṃ natthi, tena. Idaṃ pana vacībhedaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttanti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ, tathā ca sati nāvādīsu viya visuṃ vidhānena bhavitabbanti. Nāvāsatthavajūpagoti iminā asenāsanikena nāvādīsu vassaṃ upagantuṃ [M 0.0390] vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Tattha ca kuṭikaṃ pariyesitvā labhantena tattha pavisitvā vihārābhāvato “vihāre”ti avatvā “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ, alabhantena ālayo kātabbo. Pavāretuñcāti ca-saddena vassacchedanimittāya āpattiyā abhāvaṃ sampiṇḍeti. “Vaje satthe nāvāyanti tīsu ṭhānesu natthi vassacchede āpatti, pavāretuñca labbhatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 203) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Vassacchedeti ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yena vajo tena gantu”nti (mahāva. 203) vuttattā, satthassa nāvāya ca gamanasabhāveneva ṭhitattā ca vassūpagataṭṭhāne avasitvā aññattha gamanamattaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

321. ‘By one without a lodging’ means by one who does not have a lodging covered by any of the five types of roofing—namely grass, leaves, bricks, stones, or plaster—and fitted with a door and frame. However, some say this is said with reference to a determination made by a verbal expression, but that is not right; for if that were so, there would have to be a separate regulation, as in the case of boats and so on. By ‘one who goes with a boat, a caravan, or a cow-pen,’ it is shown that it is permissible for one without a lodging to enter the rains-residence on boats and so on. And in that case, one who seeks and finds a hut should enter it and, due to the absence of a monastery, without saying ‘in the monastery,’ should say three times, ‘I enter the rains-residence here.’ One who does not find one should make a shelter. By the word ‘and’ in ‘and to perform the Pavāraṇā,’ he includes the absence of an offense that would be a cause for breaking the rains-residence. It is said in the commentary: ‘In a cow-pen, a caravan, and a boat—in these three places there is no offense of breaking the rains-residence, and it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā.’ And regarding ‘breaking the rains-residence,’ it should be understood that this is said with reference to merely going elsewhere after not dwelling in the place where the rains-residence was entered, because it was said, ‘I allow, monks, to go where the cow-pen goes,’ and because it is the nature of a caravan and a boat to travel.

Vassūpanāyikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Rains-Residence is finished.

40. Avebhaṅgiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

40. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Indivisible

322-5. Ārāmā…pe… mattikabhaṇḍānīti ete pañca avibhājiyāti sambandhitabbaṃ[V 0.0328]. Pañcāti “ārāmārāmavatthūni eka”ntiādinā rāsivasena pañca, sarūpavasena panetāni paṇṇaṃ tiṇe pakkhipitvā pañcavīsatividhāni honti. Tathā cāha –

322-5. ‘Monasteries…’ up to ‘…earthenware vessels’—these five should be connected with ‘are indivisible.’ The five are five by way of categories, beginning with ‘monasteries and monastery grounds are one.’ But in terms of their own form, when leaves and grass are included, they become twenty-five kinds. And so it is said:

“Dvisaṅgahāni dve honti, tatiyaṃ catusaṅgahaṃ;

Catutthaṃ navakoṭṭhāsaṃ, pañcamaṃ aṭṭhabhedanaṃ.

Two are collections of two, the third is a collection of four; the fourth has nine parts, the fifth has eight divisions.

“Iti pañcahi rāsīhi, pañcanimmalalocano;

Pañcavīsavidhaṃ nātho, garubhaṇḍaṃ pakāsayī”ti. (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321);

Thus, with five groups, the Lord with stainless eyes revealed the weighty goods in twenty-five ways.

Tattha ārāmo nāma pupphārāmo vā phalārāmo vā. Ārāmavatthu nāma tesaṃyeva patiṭṭhānokāso, vinaṭṭhesu vā tesu porāṇakabhūmibhāgo. Vihāro nāma [M 0.0391] pāsādādi yaṃ kiñci senāsanaṃ. Lohakumbhī nāma kāḷalohena vā tambalohena vā katakumbhī. Kaṭāhādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha bhāṇakanti arañjaro vuccati. Vārakoti ghaṭo. Rāsiṃ apekkhitvā eteti pulliṅganiddeso. Avibhājiyāti mūlacchejjavasena avebhaṅgiyā. Parivattanavasena pana paribhuñjantassa vissajjentassa ca anāpatti. Avissajjiyāni cāti ca-saddena avebhaṅgiyāni cāti avuttaṃ sampiṇḍeti.

Therein, ‘monastery’ means either a flower garden or a fruit garden. ‘Monastery land’ means the site for their establishment, or, if they are ruined, the ancient plot of land. ‘Dwelling’ means any lodging, such as a storied building. ‘Metal pot’ means a pot made of black metal (iron) or red metal (copper). The same principle applies to cauldrons and the like. Here, ‘bhāṇaka’ is called an arañjara. ‘Vāraka’ is a ghaṭa. The masculine designation ‘ete’ is used with reference to the ‘group.’ ‘Not to be divided’ means indivisible in the sense of cutting off at the root. However, by way of exchange, there is no offense for one who uses or disposes of them. By the word ‘and’ in ‘and not to be disposed of,’ he includes the unstated ‘and indivisible.’

326-8. Ekantagarubhaṇḍattā ādito tayo rāsī ṭhapetvā catuttharāsito paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍāgarubhaṇḍe vibhajituṃ “vallī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Aḍḍhabāhumattāpi valli ca aṭṭhaṅgulāyato veḷu ca muṭṭhimattampi tiṇādi ca ekampi paṇṇañca pākatā vā pañcavaṇṇā vā tālapakkappamāṇāpi mattikā ca tālapakkappamāṇāpi sudhā ca tālapakkappamāṇāpi kaṅguṭṭhaādikā ca dinnā vā tatthajātakā vā saṅghikā rakkhitā abhājiyā, rajjuyottādi ca dinnā saṅghikā abhājiyāti yojanā. Veḷu pariṇāhato paṇṇasūcidaṇḍamatto gahetabbo. Tiṇaṃ muñjaṃ pabbajañca ādisaddasaṅgahitaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci tiṇaṃ. Paṇṇo aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇo rittapotthako garubhaṇḍameva. Pākatāti pakatiyā jātā. Pañcavaṇṇāti rattasetādipañcavaṇṇā. Sudhākaṅguṭṭhādayo mattikaggahaṇena gahitā. Kaṅguṭṭhaādikāti ādi-saddena sajjurasajātihiṅgulakādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Dinnāti saṅghassa dinnā. Tatthajātāti saṅghikabhūmiyaṃ jātā. Rajjuyottādīti suttamakacivākanāḷikerahīracammamayā rajju ca yottādi ca. Ādi-saddena [V 0.0329] makacivākādike vaṭṭetvā katā ekavaṭṭā gahitā. Byatirekavasena panettha catuttharāsimhi itare bhājiyāti [M 0.0392] veditabbā. Saṅghike kamme, cetiyassa vā kamme niṭṭhite bhājiyāti yojanīyaṃ.

326-8. Because they are entirely heavy goods, the first three piles were set aside. Starting from the fourth pile, the division into heavy and light goods began with 'vines,' and so on. Even a vine as thick as half an arm, a bamboo eight finger-breadths long, a handful of grass and the like, a single leaf, whether natural or five-colored, a lump of clay the size of a palmyra fruit, a lump of lime the size of a palmyra fruit, and ochre and the like the size of a palmyra fruit—whether given or grown on Saṅgha land—are Saṅgha property, to be protected, and are indivisible. Ropes, cords, and the like given to the Saṅgha are also indivisible—this is the connection. Bamboo should be taken as being the size of the handle of a leaf-sewing needle in circumference. Grass (tiṇa) refers to any remaining grass, excluding muñja, pabbaja, and what is included by the word 'etc.'. A leaf eight finger-breadths in size and an empty book are indeed heavy goods. 'Natural' means naturally grown. 'Five-colored' refers to the five colors such as red, white, and so on. Lime, ochre, and the like are included by the mention of clay. By 'ochre and the like,' the inclusion of items such as sajjurasa, jātihiṅgulaka, and so on is meant by the word 'etc.'. 'Given' means given to the Saṅgha. 'Grown there' means grown on Saṅgha land. 'Ropes, cords, and the like' means a rope made of thread, bark fiber, coconut fiber, deer hide, or leather, and a cord, and so on. By the word 'and the like,' single-stranded ropes made by twisting bark fiber and similar materials are included. By way of contrast, it should be understood that in this fourth pile, the other items are divisible. When the work for the Saṅgha or the work for a cetiya is finished, they are to be divided—this is how it should be construed.

329. Lohabhaṇḍesu bhikkhusāruppaṃ pattādi vā tathā vippakatākataṃ lohabhaṇḍaṃ tathā pādagaṇhakaṃ vārakaṃ bhājiyanti yojanā. Pattādīti ayopatto ayathālakaṃ tambalohathālakaṃ añjanisalākā kaṇṇamalaharaṇī sūci paṇṇasūci khuddako pipphalako khuddakaṃ ārakaṇḍakaṃ kuñcikā tāḷādi. Vippakatanti apariniṭṭhitaṃ. Akatanti sabbaso akataṃ. Pādagaṇhakanti sīhaḷadīpe pādagaṇhanakaṃ. Pādo nāma catutthaṃso, magadhanāḷiyā pañcanāḷimattā. Magadhanāḷi ca nāmesā ūnapañcapasatā veditabbā. Tathā ghaṭako telabhājanañca. Yāya vāsiyā ṭhapetvā dantakaṭṭhacchedanaṃ vā ucchutacchanaṃ vā aññaṃ mahākammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, ayaṃ bhājiyā. Sammuñjanidaṇḍakhaṇanakaṃ pana adaṇḍakaṃ phalamattameva, yaṃ sakkā sipāṭikāya pakkhipitvā pariharituṃ, ayaṃ bhājanīyā. Tipukoṭṭakaupakaraṇesu tipucchedanakasatthakaṃ suvaṇṇakārūpakaraṇesu suvaṇṇacchedanakasatthakaṃ cammakāraupakaraṇesu cammachindanakaṃ khuddakasatthaṃ nahāpitatuṇṇakāraupakaraṇesu ṭhapetvā mahākattariṃ mahāsaṇḍāsañca mahāpipphalakañca sabbāni bhājanīyabhaṇḍāni. Tathā kuñcikā. Vuttavipallāsena pana lohabhaṇḍe abhājiyāti veditabbā.

329. Among metal items, those suitable for a bhikkhu, such as a bowl and the like, as well as unfinished or unworked metal items, and likewise a foot-stand and a pot, are divisible—this is the connection. 'Bowl and the like' refers to an iron bowl, an iron dish, a copper dish, an antimony rod, an ear-pick, a needle, a leaf-sewing needle, a small knife, a small awl, a key, a lock, and so on. 'Unfinished' means not fully completed. 'Unworked' means entirely unmade. 'Foot-stand' refers to what is known in the island of Sri Lanka as a pādagaṇhanaka. A pāda is a quarter, a measure of five Magadhan nāḷis. And this Magadhan nāḷi should be understood as a little less than five pasatas. Likewise, a small pot and an oil container. An adze with which no major work can be done, apart from cutting a tooth-stick or trimming sugarcane, is divisible. As for a digging tool for a broom handle, being just the blade without a handle, which can be put in a sheath and carried about, this is divisible. Among the tools of a tin-worker, a knife for cutting tin; among the tools of a goldsmith, a knife for cutting gold; among the tools of a leather-worker, a small knife for cutting leather; among the tools of barbers and tailors, excluding large scissors, large tongs, and a large knife, all are divisible items. Likewise, a key. However, by way of the opposite of what has been stated, it should be understood that some metal items are indivisible.

330. “Veḷumhī”tiādinā dārubhaṇḍāni dasseti. Dārubhaṇḍena pana saṅgahetvā sabbāpi dāruveḷucammupāhanādivikati veditabbā. Chattadaṇḍo ca salākā cāti dvando. Upāhanāya daṇḍako upāhanadaṇḍako.

330. By 'In bamboo,' etc., it indicates wooden articles. However, under 'wooden articles,' all products of wood, bamboo, leather, sandals, and so forth should be understood. 'Umbrella stick and slat' is a dvandva compound. The stick of a sandal is a 'sandal-stick.'

331. Anuññātavāsidaṇḍoti anuññātavāsiyā daṇḍo. Araṇañjanisiṅgādīti ādi-saddena añjanisalākā chattaṃ [M 0.0393] muṭṭhipaṇṇaṃ upāhanā dhammakaraṇo pādagaṇhanakato anatirittaṃ āmalakatumbaṃ āmalakaghaṭo lābukatumbaṃ lābukaghaṭo visāṇatumbanti idaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

331. "A stick for a permitted adze" means a handle for a permitted adze. "Fire-stick, antimony pot, horn, etc."—by the word "etc.," it includes an antimony rod, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan, sandals, a water-strainer, what does not exceed a foot-stand, a myrobalan gourd, a myrobalan pot, a bottle gourd, a bottle gourd pot, and a horn container—this is included.

332. Yathāvuttato aññaṃ dārubhaṇḍesu garubhaṇḍaṃ. Mattikāmayo pādaghaṭako bhājiyoti yojanā. Pādaghaṭakoti pādassa pahonako ghaṭako. Iminā mattikābhaṇḍaṃ upalakkheti, tasmā patto thālakaṃ kuṇḍikāti imāni bhājanīyāni, vuttāvasesā abhājiyā.

332. Among wooden articles, anything other than what has been mentioned is a heavy item. "A foot-pot made of clay is divisible" is the connection. "Foot-pot" means a small pot sufficient for the feet. This indicates clay articles; therefore, a bowl, a dish, and a water-pot are divisible, while the rest of what has been mentioned are indivisible.

333-4. Garunā [V 0.0330] garubhaṇḍañca thāvarañca parivatteyya, thāvarena ca thāvarampi parivatteyyāti yojetabbaṃ. Garunā mañcapīṭhādinā. Thāvaranti ārāmādi paṭhamarāsidvayaṃ. Tathā katvā ca bhuñjitunti evañca parivattetvā tato ābhataṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ paribhuñjeyyāti attho, vidhimhi ayaṃ tuṃpaccayo. Phātikammena vallādiṃ gaṇheti sambandhanīyaṃ. Phātikammaṃ nāma samakaṃ vā atirekaṃ vā tadagghanakaṃ vā vaḍḍhikammaṃ. Sesanti paṭhamarāsittikanti.

333-4. It should be construed thus: one may exchange heavy goods for other heavy goods or for immovable property, and one may exchange immovable property for other immovable property. 'Heavy goods' refers to items like beds and chairs. 'Immovable property' refers to the first two piles, such as monasteries and the like. 'And having done so, one may consume' means: having exchanged in this way, one may make use of the allowable goods obtained from it; this '-tuṃ' suffix is in the sense of an injunction. It should be connected that one may take vines and the like through a transaction for growth (phātikamma). A transaction for growth is a transaction of increase, being either of equal value, of greater value, or at that price. 'The rest' refers to the first three piles.

Avebhaṅgiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Indivisible is concluded.

41. Pakiṇṇakaniddesavaṇṇanā

41. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Miscellaneous

335. Sadvārabandhane sodukkhalakapāsake ṭhāne divā sayantena parivattakaṃ dvāraṃ bandheyyāti sambandho. Dvārañca dvārabandhanañca dvārabandhanāni majjhepadalopavasena, bandhana-saddeneva vā dvārabāhā vuccanti, saha dvārabandhanehīti sadvārabandhanaṃ, ṭhānaṃ. Heṭṭhā udukkhalakañca upari pāsako ca, saha udukkhalapāsakehīti samāso. Tādise ṭhāne pākārādiparikkhepena bhavitabbanti parikkhitteti viññāyati. So ca uccato sahaseyyappahonake vuttanayoti vadanti[M 0.0394]. Sayantenāti pāde bhūmito mocetvā nipajjantena. Parivattakanti saṃvaraṇavivaraṇavasena ito cito ca parivattanayoggaṃ. Dvāranti antamaso dussasāṇidvārampi. Bandheyyāti sabbantimena vidhinā yāvatā sīsaṃ na pavisati, tāvatāpi bandheyya, saṃvareyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

335. The connection is: 'In a place with a door-fastening and with a socket and bolt, one who is lying down during the day should fasten the revolving door.' 'The door and the door-fastening' becomes dvārabandhanāni by way of elision of the middle term; or by the word 'fastening' alone, the door-posts are meant. 'With the door-fastenings' (sadvārabandhanaṃ) refers to the place. Below is the socket and above is the bolt; 'with the socket and bolt' (sodukkhalapāsakehi) is a compound. In such a place, there should be an enclosure of a wall, etc.; thus it is understood as 'enclosed.' And they say that it is high enough for sleeping with a companion, according to the stated method. 'Lying down' means lying down after lifting the feet from the ground. 'Revolving' refers to what is capable of being turned this way and that for closing and opening. 'Door' means even a door made of cloth or hemp. 'Should fasten' means one should fasten it by the final method, to the extent that the head cannot enter; this means one should secure it.

336. Ābhogo cāpīti “esa jaggissatī”ti ābhogo cāpi. Ca-saddena “dvāraṃ jaggāhī”ti vacanampi samuccinoti. Savase taṃ ākāraṃ vināti sassa attano vase āyatte ṭhāne, yattha pana bahūnaṃ sañcaraṇattā dvāraṃ saṃvutampi saṃvutaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, dvāraṃ alabhantā pākāraṃ abhiruhitvāpi vicaranti, tādise pariveṇe saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ natthi. Atha vā sassa vaso āyatto, na yakkhādīnaṃ tehi gahitakattassa, bandhitvā nipajjāpitattassa ca abhāvenāti [V 0.0331] savaso. Tasmiṃ sati pubbe vuttadvāraṃ saṃvaraṇaābhogakaraṇavacanasaṅkhātaṃ ākāranti attho.

336. 'And also the thought' means also the thought: 'He will be vigilant.' By the word 'ca' (and), it also includes the statement, 'Guard the door.' 'Except for that manner under one's control' means in a place subject to one's own power. However, in a place where, due to many people coming and going, a closed door does not remain closed, and where, unable to find the door, they even climb over the wall and wander about—in such a precinct, there is no duty of closing it. Alternatively, 'under one's own control' means that one's own authority is established, not that of yakkhas and so on, due to the absence of being seized, bound, and made to lie down by them. This being the case, the meaning is the previously mentioned 'manner,' which is designated as the closing of the door, the making of the thought, and the utterance of the words.

337. Ratanānīti muttādīni dasavidhāni. Tattha pana jātiphalikaṃ upādāya sabbopi maṇi veḷuriyopi lohitaṅko masāragallo ca dhotāpi adhotaviddhāpi anāmāsā, kācamaṇi ca pānīyasaṅkho dhoto adhotopi āmāsā, silā dhotaviddhā suvaṇṇena saddhiṃ pacitā muggavaṇṇā ca anāmāsā. Cetiyagharagopakānaṃ suvaṇṇacetiye kacavarameva harituṃ vaṭṭati. Ārakūṭalohampi jātarūpagatikameva. Itthirūpānīti antamaso piṭṭhamayaitthirūpānipi. Dhaññanti antamaso tatthajātakampi magge pasāritampi sattavidhaṃ dhaññaṃ. Kīḷāvasena aparaṇṇāni tālaphalādīnipi anāmāsāni, pasāritampi na maddantena gantabbaṃ, asati magge maggaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gantabbaṃ. Itthipasādhananti antamaso piḷandhanatthāya ṭhapitaṃ nivāsanatālapaṇṇamuddikampi.

337. The ten kinds of precious things include pearls and so forth. Among them, the jātiphalika gem, all other gems, veḷuriya, ruby, and coral, whether washed or unwashed, pierced or unpierced, are not to be touched. Glass gems and pānīyasaṅkha, whether washed or unwashed, are to be touched. Stone, when washed, pierced, and heated together with gold, becomes the color of mung beans and is not to be touched. For the guardians of cetiya houses, only sweepings may be taken from gold cetiyas. Even brass is considered as gold. Female forms—even female forms made of flour—are included. Grains, even if grown there or scattered along the path, include the seven kinds of grains. For the sake of play, pulses, palm fruits, and the like are not to be touched; even if scattered, one should not tread on them. If there is no path, one should determine a path and proceed. Female adornments—even a palm leaf ring placed for adornment—are included.

338. Sitthatelodatelehīti [M 0.0395] madhusitthakaniyyāsādīsu yena kenaci telamissakasilesena ca udakamissakatelena ca. Phaṇahatthaphaṇehīti phaṇamiva phaṇaṃ, aṅgulīhi phaṇakiccakaraṇena hatthoyeva phaṇaṃ hatthaphaṇaṃ, dantamayādi yaṃ kiñci phaṇañceva hatthaphaṇañcāti dvando. Osaṇṭheyyāti olikhitvā sannisīdāpeyya.

338. By 'with beeswax-oil and water-oil' is meant any sticky substance mixed with oil, such as beeswax or resin, and oil mixed with water. By 'with a comb and a hand-comb' is meant: a comb (phaṇa) is so-called because it resembles a snake's hood; the hand itself is a hand-comb (hatthaphaṇa) by performing the function of a comb with the fingers. It is a dvanda compound referring to any kind of comb, such as one made of ivory, and a hand-comb. 'Should level it' means to smooth it down and cause it to settle.

339. Ekapāvuraṇā vā ekattharaṇā vā na tuvaṭṭayuṃ, ekamañce na tuvaṭṭayunti yojanā. Ekaṃ pāvuraṇaṃ ekaṃ attharaṇaṃ etesanti viggaho. Na tuvaṭṭayunti na nipajjeyyuṃ. Ekasmiṃ bhājane vāpi na bhuñjeyyunti yojetabbaṃ.

339. 'With one cover or one spread, they should not lie down together; on one bed, they should not lie down together'—this is the construction. 'They who have one cover, one spread'—this is the analysis. 'Should not lie down together' means they should not lie down. 'Nor should they eat from one bowl'—this should be construed.

340. Manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena aṭṭha aṅgulāni yassa, adhikena sahitaṃ aṭṭhaṅgulanti samāso. Lasuṇaṃ magadhesu jātaṃ āmalakabhaṇḍikaṃ lasuṇaṃ na khādeyyāti sambandho. Na akallakoti agilāno.

340. 'Eight finger-widths' (aṭṭhaṅgula) is a compound meaning that which has eight finger-widths by human measure, or eight finger-widths together with more. 'One should not eat garlic, garlic grown in Magadha, or garlic of the āmalaka-fruit type'—this is the connection. 'Not unfit' (na akallako) means not ill.

341. Hīnukkaṭṭhehi jātiādīhi ukkaṭṭhaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā ujuṃ vā aññāpadesena vā davā vade, dubbhāsitanti sambandho. Jātiādīhīti jātināmagottakammasippaābādhaliṅgakilesaāpattiakkosehi[V 0.0332]. Ukkaṭṭhanti jātyādīhiyeva ukkaṭṭhaṃ upasampannaṃ anupasampannaṃ vā. Davāti keḷihasādhippāyatāya. Ujuṃ vāti “caṇḍālosī”tiādinā nayena. Aññāpadesena vāti “santi idhekacce caṇḍālā”tiādinā nayena.

341. Whether one speaks of someone as superior or inferior with reference to low or high qualities such as birth, either directly, by allusion, or in jest, such speech is 'ill-spoken'—this is the connection. 'With birth, etc.' refers to birth, name, lineage, occupation, craft, sickness, gender, defilements, offense, or abuse. 'Superior' means one who is superior by birth etc., whether ordained or not ordained. 'In jest' (davā) means with playful intent. 'Directly' (ujuṃ vā) means in the manner of saying, 'You are an outcaste,' etc. 'By allusion' (aññāpadesena vā) means in the manner of saying, 'There are some outcastes here,' etc.

342. Dīghe nakheti maṃsappamāṇato. Dīghe keseti dvaṅgulato. Sacepi na dīghā, dumāsato ekadivasampi atikkāmetuṃ na labhati. Dīghe nāsalometi nāsato bahi nikkhante. Vīsatimaṭṭhanti vīsatiyā nakhānaṃ maṭṭhañca. Sambādheti ubhosu upakacchakesu, muttakaraṇe ca lomahāraṇañca [M 0.0396] na labbhāti sambandhanīyaṃ. Na labbhāti ete maṭṭhādayo na labbhantīti attho, nipāto vā labbhāti. Ābādhappaccayā pana sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharituṃ vaṭṭati.

342. 'Long nails' means beyond the measure of the flesh. 'Long hair' means beyond two finger-widths. Even if the hair is not long, one may not let even a single day pass beyond two months. 'Long nose hair' means when it has grown out from the nose. 'The polishing of twenty' means the polishing of the twenty nails. 'In a constricted place' refers to both armpits; and it should be connected that removing hair in both armpits and at the organ of urination is not allowed. 'Not allowed' (na labbhāti) means these polishings, etc., are not allowed; or, 'na' is a particle used with 'labbhati'. However, on account of illness, it is allowable to remove hair in a constricted place.

343. Saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃ vā saṅghikaṃ vā sayanāsanaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ na bādheyyāti yojanā. Saṅghassa uddiṭṭhaṃ saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃ, saṅghaṃ uddissa katanti adhippāyo. Yo yo vuḍḍho yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, vuḍḍhappaṭipāṭiyāti attho. Na bādheyyāti na paṭibāheyya. Allapādā nāma yehi akkantaṭṭhāne udakaṃ paññāyati. Sayanāsananti mañcapīṭhādi, iminā paribhaṇḍakatā bhūmītipi upalakkhitā. Sudhotapādakaṃ vāpi saupāhano tathevāti sambandho. Sudhotapādakanti dhotapādeheva akkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Dhotā pādā yassa akkamanassāti kiriyāvisesanasamāso. Yadi pana tattha nevāsikā adhotapādehipi vaḷañjenti, tatheva vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tathevāti paribhaṇḍakataṃ bhūmiṃ senāsanaṃ vā nakkameti attho.

343. The construction is that one should not hinder access to a bed or seat designated for the Sangha or belonging to the Sangha, according to seniority. 'Designated for the Sangha' (saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃ) means designated of the Sangha; the intention is that it was made for the Sangha. 'According to seniority' (yathāvuḍḍhaṃ) means according to the order of seniority. 'Should not hinder' (na bādheyya) means should not obstruct. 'With wet feet' (allapādā) means when water is visible in the place one has stepped. 'Bed or seat' (sayanāsana) includes beds, benches, etc.; by this, a floor treated as furniture is also indicated. The connection is 'with well-washed feet' or 'with footwear, likewise.' 'A place for well-washed feet' (sudhotapādakaṃ) means a place to be stepped on only with washed feet. 'Whose feet are washed for the stepping' is an adverbial compound. But if the resident monks use the place even with unwashed feet, it is permissible to use it in the same way. 'Likewise' (tatheva) means not stepping on the floor treated as furniture or on the lodging.

344. Saṅghāṭiyāti adhiṭṭhitasaṅghāṭiyā. Pāde pariggahetvā āsanaṃ pallattho, pallatthaṃ karotīti pallatthātidhātussa pallattheti rūpaṃ. Vihārepi antaragharepi pallatthikāya na nisīdeyyāti adhippāyo, parikammakataṃ bhittādinti yojanā. Parikammakatanti setavaṇṇena vā cittakammena vā kataparikammaṃ. Ādi-saddo dvāravātapānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Na apassayeti cīvarādinā appaṭicchādetvā apassayanaṃ na kareyya. No na ācameti neva na ācame, ācameyyāti attho. Dve paṭisedhā pakatiyatthaṃ gamentīti. Santeti iminā udake asante anāpattīti dīpeti.

344. 'With the outer robe' (saṅghāṭiyā) means with the determined outer robe. 'Pallattheti' is a verb form from the root 'pallatth' in the sense of 'to make a cross-legged posture' (pallatthaṃ karoti), which is a sitting posture with the feet gathered. The meaning is that one should not sit with legs crossed in a monastery or inside a house; the connection is to a prepared wall, etc. 'Prepared' (parikammakataṃ) means prepared with whitewash or decorative work. The word 'etc.' includes doors, windows, and so forth. 'Should not lean' (na apassaye) means one should not lean without first covering the surface with a robe or the like. 'Nor not rinse' (no na ācame) means one should indeed rinse; two negations convey the natural meaning. By the word 'being present' (sante), it is shown that there is no offense if water is not present.

345. Akappiyasamādāneti bhikkhūnaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ akappiye samādāne. Davāti nipāto[V 0.0333], kīḷādhippāyenāti attho. Silāpavijjhaneti antamaso hatthayantenapi sakkharikāyapi [M 0.0397] khipane. Sabhāgāya desanāya āvikamme ca dukkaṭanti yojetabbaṃ. Sabhāgāyāti vatthuvasena samāno bhāgo etissā āpattiyāti viggaho. Ca-saddo tādisiyā paṭiggahaṇamattaṃ samuccinoti.

345. 'In taking up what is unsuitable' refers to monks or novices taking up what is unsuitable. 'Davā' is a particle, meaning with the intention of play. 'In throwing stones' includes throwing even a pebble with the hand or with a hand-sling. It should be connected that for a similar confession and for making it known, there is a dukkaṭa offense. 'Similar' (sabhāgāya) is analyzed as: 'this offense has a similar portion (bhāgo) by way of the object (vatthu)'. The word 'and' (ca) also includes the mere acceptance of such a thing.

346. Paṭissavo nāma “ubhopi mayaṃ idha vassaṃ vasissāma, ekato uddisāpemā”tiādipaṭijānanaṃ, tassa visaṃvādo pacchā akaraṇaṃ paṭissavavisaṃvādo, tasmiṃ, nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Suddhacittassāti kathanasamaye “karissāmī”ti evaṃ pavattacittassa. Itarassāti aññassa asuddhacittassa.

346. 'A commitment' (paṭissava) is an agreement such as, 'Both of us will spend the rains here, and we will together recite the Pāṭimokkha.' Breaking that commitment by not fulfilling it afterward is 'breaking a commitment' (paṭissavavisaṃvādo). In that case (tasmiṃ), the locative case has the meaning of cause. 'Of one with a pure mind' (suddhacittassa) refers to one whose mind, at the time of speaking, is set on thinking, 'I will do it.' 'Of another' (itarassa) refers to another whose mind is not pure.

347. Kicceti sukkhakaṭṭhādiggahaṇakicce sati eva porisaṃ purisappamāṇaṃ abhiruheyyāti sambandho. Āpadāsūti vāḷamigadassanādīsu.

347. 'When there is a duty' means when there is a duty such as gathering dry firewood; the connection is that one may climb up to a man's height. 'In emergencies' (āpadāsu) refers to situations such as seeing a beast of prey.

348. Parissāvanaṃ vināti sambandho. Addhānanti heṭṭhimantena addhayojanasaṅkhātaṃ addhānaṃ. Sace na hoti parissāvanaṃ vā dhammakaraṇo vā, saṅghāṭikaṇṇopi adhiṭṭhātabbo. Yācamānassāti parissāvanaṃ yācantassa.

348. The connection is 'without a water strainer' (parissāvanaṃ vinā). 'Journey' (addhānaṃ) means a journey reckoned as half a yojana at a minimum. If there is no water strainer or filter cloth, even a corner of the Saṅghāṭi robe should be determined for use. 'Of one who is asking' (yācamānassa) means of one who asks for a water strainer.

349. Ābādhappaccayā aññatra sesaṅge ca attaghātane ca dukkaṭanti yojanā. Sesaṅgeti aṅgajātato kaṇṇanāsādiavasese avayavacchedane. Attaghātaneti āhārupacchedādinā attano māraṇe.

349. The construction is: except on account of illness, in the case of the remaining limbs and in the case of suicide, there is a dukkaṭa offense. 'In the case of the remaining limbs' refers to the cutting off of the remaining body parts, such as ears, nose, etc., apart from the genital organ. 'In the case of suicide' means killing oneself by cutting off food, etc.

350. Tūlikāya kayiramānaṃ itthipurisādikaṃ cittañca potthakañca kaṭṭhādīsu kayiramānaṃ cittapotthakāni, tāniyeva rūpānīti samāso. Jātakādīni pana parehi kārāpetuṃ labbhanti. Mālākammādīni sayampi kātuṃ labbhanti. Ārāmāraññagehesu bhuñjantaṃ na uṭṭhāpeyyāti yojetabbaṃ. Vihārasaṅkhāto [M 0.0398] ārāmo ca araññañca antaragharasaṅkhātaṃ gehañcāti dvando. “Ārāma…pe… gehesū”ti vattabbe e-kārassa a-kārakaraṇena gāthābandhavasena vuttaṃ. Okāse kate pana “pavisathā”ti vutte ca pavisitabbaṃ upanisīditabbañca.

350. A painting or a model of a man, woman, etc., made with a brush, and paintings and models made on wood, etc., are 'painted images and models' (cittapotthakāni); these themselves are 'forms' (rūpāni)—this is the compound. However, Jātaka stories and the like may be commissioned from others. Garland-making and similar tasks may also be done by oneself. It should be connected with the instruction: ‘One should not make a person get up while they are eating in a monastery, a forest, or a house.’ ‘Monastery, forest, and house’ is a dvanda compound, where ‘ārāma’ is a monastery, ‘arañña’ is a forest, and ‘geha’ is an inner house. Although it should be said ‘ārāmesu…gehesu’ (in monasteries…in houses), it is stated as it is for the sake of the verse meter, by changing the ‘e’ vowel to an ‘a’ vowel. However, when permission is given and one is told, ‘You may enter,’ one should enter and sit down.

351. Pumayuttāni [V 0.0334] yānāni ca sivikañca hatthavaṭṭakañca pāṭaṅkiñca abhiruhituṃ gilānassa kappateti sambandho. Pumayuttānīti assagavādipurisayuttāni, na dhenuyuttāni, sārathi pana itthī vā hotu puriso vā, vaṭṭati. Hatthavaṭṭakepi eseva nayo, yānānīti rathasakaṭādīni, sivikanti pīṭhakasivikaṃ, pīṭhakayānanti attho. Pāṭaṅkīti andolikā. Gilānassāti ettha gilāno nāma na appakenapi sīsābādhādimattena veditabbo, yo pana na sakkoti vinā yānena gantuṃ, evarūpo veditabbo. Tathā hi yānaṃ anujānantena bhagavatā kosalesu janapadesu bhagavantaṃ dassanāya sāvatthiṃ gacchantaṃ aññataraṃ gilānaṃ bhikkhuṃ gantumasakkuṇeyyatāya aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā manussehi taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “ehi, bhante, gamissāmā”ti vutte “nāhaṃ, āvuso, gamissāmi, gilānomhī”ti vuttavatthusmiṃ (mahāva. 253) anuññātaṃ, tathā vadanto ca so bhikkhu gamanupacchedasādhakameva gelaññaṃ sandhāyāhāti viññāyati adhippetatthanipphattiyā upacchinnattā, apica yānena ekaparicchedāya upāhanāya paricchedaṃ ṭhapentena aṭṭhakathācariyena “gilānena bhikkhunā saupāhanenāti ettha gilāno nāma yo na sakkoti anupāhanena gāmaṃ pavisitu”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 256) vuttaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttagilānova gilānoti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

351. It is permissible for a sick bhikkhu to mount vehicles drawn by males, a palanquin, an elephant's howdah, or a litter—this is the connection. ‘Drawn by males’ means drawn by horses, oxen, or men, not by cows; but whether the driver is a woman or a man is acceptable. The same applies to an elephant's howdah. ‘Vehicles’ include chariots and carts. ‘Sivikā’ means a seat-palanquin, that is, a seat-vehicle. ‘Pāṭaṅkī’ means a hammock-litter. Here, ‘sick’ is not to be understood as one with merely a slight ailment like a headache, but rather as one who is unable to go without a vehicle; such a person is to be understood. For instance, when the Blessed One permitted the use of a vehicle, it was in the context of a certain sick bhikkhu in the Kosala country who, being unable to go to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One, was seen sitting at the foot of a certain tree. When people, knowing his situation, said, ‘Come, venerable sir, let us go,’ he replied, ‘I cannot go, friends, I am sick.’ It was in this incident (Mahāvagga 253) that the allowance was made. Thus, it is understood that when that bhikkhu spoke thus, he was referring to an illness that truly prevented walking, because his intended journey had been cut short. Furthermore, when the commentary teachers were establishing the limit for sandals for a single journey by vehicle, they stated in the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 256): ‘Here, a “sick bhikkhu with sandals” means one who cannot enter the village without sandals.’ Therefore, it should be concluded here that ‘sick’ refers only to the sick person as described.

352. Davaṃ [M 0.0399] karaṇeti keḷiyā karaṇe. Aññassāti antamaso dussīlassāpi. Upalāḷaneti “pattaṃ dassāmi, cīvaraṃ dassāmī”tiādinā.

352. ‘Making sport’ means engaging in play. ‘For another’ means even for an immoral person. ‘Cajoling’ means by saying, ‘I will give a bowl, I will give a robe,’ and so on.

353. Vivaritvā na dassayeti sambandhanīyaṃ. Tā bhikkhuniyo.

353. ‘Having opened, one should not show’—this is to be connected. This refers to the bhikkhunīs.

354. Ovādanti bhikkhunīhi terasiyaṃ vā cātuddasiyaṃ vā āgantvā uposathaṃ pucchitvā “cātuddaso”tiādinā bhikkhunā ācikkhite puna tāhi uposathadivase samāgantvā ovādūpasaṅkamanayācanaṃ, taṃ pātimokkhuddesakassa ārocetvā tena katasanniṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā pāṭipade paccāharitabbanti ajānanakaṃ bālañca tathā kātuṃ asamatthaṃ gilānañca pāṭipade gantukāmaṃ gamiyañca vajjetvā aññassa gahaṇapaccāharaṇāni akātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tena vuttaṃ “na gaṇhato”tiādi.

354. The exhortation to the nuns means that when they, having come on the thirteenth or fourteenth day to ask about the Uposatha, are informed by a bhikkhu, saying ‘it is the fourteenth,’ etc., they then gather again on the Uposatha day itself to request the approach for the exhortation. This should be reported to the one reciting the Pātimokkha, and having obtained his decision, it should be delivered back on the first day of the fortnight. Excluding an ignorant person, a fool, one unable to do so, a sick person, one who wishes to go on the first day of the fortnight, or one who is traveling, it is not proper for another to refuse to undertake the receiving and returning. Therefore, it is said: ‘For one not taking up...’ etc.

355. Lokāyatanti [V 0.0335] niratthakakāraṇappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ titthiyasatthaṃ. Tiracchānavijjā ca imināva upalakkhitā. Na vāceyyāti paresaṃ na vāceyya. Imināva attano pariyāpuṇanampi paṭikkhittaṃ lokāyatatiracchānavijjāti ca rāgadosamohavaḍḍhāni buddhādigarahitā saggamokkhānaṃ tiro tiriyato añcitā gatā pavattā kabbanāṭakādikā sabbāpi vijjā anulomavasena vā vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā garuke ṭhātabbanti vinayayuttitopi saṅgahitāti veditabbā. Evañca no garūnamupadeso. Peḷāyapīti yattha pātiṃ ṭhapetvā sukhino bhuñjanti, tambalohena rajatena vā katāya tāya āsittakūpadhānasaṅkhātāya peḷāya ṭhapetvā.

355. ‘Lokāyata’ refers to the doctrines of heretical sects, which are connected with meaningless reasoning. And ‘animal knowledge’ is also characterized by this. ‘One should not teach’ means one should not teach others. By this, even one’s own learning of such things is prohibited. And it should be understood that all such knowledge as Lokāyata and animal knowledge—which increase greed, hatred, and delusion, are condemned by the Buddhas and others, and which, obstructing heaven and liberation, proceed in a crooked way, such as poetry, drama, etc.—is included by the logic of the Vinaya, and even if encountered in a way that seems to conform to the Vinaya, it should be regarded as a serious matter. Thus, this is the instruction of our teachers. ‘In a receptacle’ means having placed the bowl in a receptacle made of bronze or silver, known as a ‘covered support,’ in which one places a bowl to eat comfortably.

356. Pārutañca nivāsanañca, gihīnaṃ hatthisoṇḍādivasena pārutanivāsanaṃ yassa pārupanassa nivāsanassāti kiriyāvisesanasamāso[M 0.0400]. Gihipārutanivāsanaṃ na pārupe na nivāseyyāti sambandho. Saṃvelliyaṃ na nivāseyyāti mallakammakarādayo viya kacchaṃ katvā na nivāseyya. Evaṃ nivāsetuṃ gilānassāpi maggappaṭipannassāpi na vaṭṭati. Yampi maggaṃ gacchantā ekaṃ vā dve vā koṇe ukkhipitvā antaravāsakassa upari lagganti, na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ apārupitvā anivāsetvā ca nibbikāraṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ pārupitabbaṃ timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādentena parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetabbañca, tathā apārupitvā anivāsetvā ca ārāme vā antaraghare vā anādarena yaṃ kiñci vikāraṃ karontassa dukkaṭaṃ. Dāyanti vanaṃ. Nālimpayeyyāti “sabbūpakārāni vinassantū”ti vā khiḍḍādhippāyena vā nālimpayeyya.

356. ‘Upper robe’ and ‘lower robe’ refers to the wearing of the upper and lower garments of laypeople in the ‘elephant’s trunk’ style and so on; this is a compound functioning as an adverbial modifier. The connection is that one should not wear the upper robe or lower robe in the manner of a layperson. ‘One should not wear a tucked-up garment’ means one should not wear it tucked up between the legs like wrestlers, laborers, and so on. It is not proper for even a sick person or one on a journey to wear it in this way. Also, when traveling on a road, it is not proper to lift one or two corners and fasten them over the inner robe. Rather than wearing them in these ways, the upper robe should be worn evenly all around, without alteration, and the lower robe should be worn evenly, concealing the three circles. Similarly, for one who, out of disrespect, wears them improperly in any way in a monastery or within a house, not wearing the upper and lower robes properly, there is a dukkaṭa offense. ‘Dāya’ means a wood. ‘One should not set fire’ means one should not set fire either with the intention, ‘May all useful things be destroyed,’ or with playful intent.

357. Vaḍḍhiṃ no payojaye aññātakappavārite no yāceti yojanā. Aññassāti sahadhammikassāpi. Katipāhaṃ bhutvā vāti yojanīyaṃ. Punoti nipāto.

357. The connection is: ‘One should not engage in usury, nor should one ask for what is forbidden by the conventions of unrelated families.’ ‘For another’ means even for a fellow practitioner. ‘Having eaten for a few days’—this is to be connected. ‘Puna’ is a particle.

358. Daṇḍinaṃ ñatvā vā añatvā vā uddissa rakkhaṃ yācane daṇḍite daṇḍo assa gīvāti yojanā. Daṇḍaṃ gaṇhatīti paccayantassa daṇḍinaṃ daṇḍaggahaṇanti attho. Uddissāti “amhākaṃ vihāre asukena ca asukena ca idaṃ nāma kata”nti, “karissa”nti vā evaṃ atītaṃ vā anāgataṃ vā ārabbha. Yācaneti vohārikesu yācane sati. Daṇḍiteti tehi daṇḍe gahite so daṇḍo assa yācakassa bhikkhuno gīvā, iṇaṃ hotīti attho. Vohārikehi pana “kenā”ti vutte “asukenāti vattuṃ amhākaṃ na vaṭṭati, tumheyeva jānissatha, kevalañhi mayaṃ rakkhaṃ yācāma, taṃ no detha, avahaṭabhaṇḍañca maṃ āharāpethā”ti vattabbaṃ[V 0.0336]. Evaṃ anodissa ācikkhaṇā hoti, sā vaṭṭati. Pārājikādikāti pārājikathullaccayadukkaṭāni.

358. The connection is: when protection is requested by specifying an offender, whether known or unknown, and the offender is punished, that punishment is on the neck of the requester. ‘Taking the punishment’ means the taking of the punishment from the offender who is returning—this is the meaning. ‘By specifying’ means referring to a past or future action, such as saying, ‘In our monastery, such and such was done by so-and-so,’ or ‘will be done.’ ‘Requesting’ applies when there is a request to those concerned with legal matters. ‘Punished’ means that when punishment is imposed by them, that punishment is on the neck of the requesting bhikkhu, meaning it becomes his debt. However, when questioned by those concerned with legal matters, ‘By whom?’ one should reply, ‘It is not proper for us to name anyone; you yourselves will know. We merely request protection—give it to us and have the stolen goods brought back to me.’ In this way, there is an indication without specifying, and that is permissible. ‘Pārājika and so on’ refers to Pārājika, thullaccaya, and dukkaṭa offenses.

359.

359.

“Harantesu [M 0.0401] parikkhāraṃ,

Coro coroti bhāsite;

Anatthāyesaṃ gaṇhante”ti. –

“When requisites are being carried off, when ‘Thief! Thief!’ is said for their ruin, when they are seized.”

Pāṭhehi bhavitabbaṃ. Evañhi sati “harantesū”ti bahuvacanena saha ghaṭate. Parikkhāraṃ harantesu esaṃ anatthāya “coro coro”ti bhāsite daṇḍaṃ gaṇhante tattakaṃ assa gīvāti yojetabbaṃ. Harantesūti coresu gahetvā gacchantesu. Esanti corānaṃ. Gaṇhanteti vohārikajane gaṇhante. Yattakaṃ gahitaṃ, tattakaṃ assa bhikkhuno gīvā, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ hotīti attho.

The reading should be thus. For in this way it accords with the plural ‘harantesu’. The connection is that when requisites are being carried off, and ‘Thief! Thief!’ is said for their ruin, and the authorities seize them, then the monk’s neck is liable for that much. ‘Harantesu’ means when thieves are taking and going. ‘Esaṃ’ refers to the thieves. ‘Gaṇhante’ means when the authorities seize them. Whatever was taken, that much is on the bhikkhu’s neck, meaning the price of the goods must be paid.

360. Pākārakuṭṭānaṃ bahi vaḷañje vāpi vīhādināḷikerādiropime harite vāpi vighāsuccārasaṅkāramuttaṃ nāvalokiya chaḍḍeyya, dukkaṭanti sambandho. Vaḷañje nāvalokiyāti ca iminā oloketvā vā avaḷañje vā vighāsādīni chaḍḍentassa anāpattīti dīpeti. Vīhi ādi yesaṃ sāliādīnaṃ te vīhādayo, nāḷikero ādi yesaṃ ambapanasādīnaṃ te nāḷikerādayo, vīhādayo ca nāḷikerādayo cāti dvando, tesaṃ ropo, tena nibbattaṃ vīhādi…pe… ropimaṃ. Hariteti haritaṭṭhāne. Vighāso nāma ucchiṭṭhodakacalakādi.

360. The connection is that one should not, without looking, discard leftover food, excrement, rubbish, or urine outside the walls or fences, in a cultivated area, or on green vegetation grown from rice, coconut trees, and so on; this is a dukkaṭa offense. And by the phrase ‘without looking in a cultivated area,’ it is shown that there is no offense for one who discards leftover food and so on after looking, or in an uncultivated area. ‘Rice, etc.’ refers to rice, other grains, and so on. ‘Coconut trees, etc.’ refers to mango trees, jackfruit trees, and so on. The compound ‘rice, etc., and coconut trees, etc.’ refers to what is grown from them, hence ‘grown from rice, etc.’ ‘On green vegetation’ means in a green place. ‘Leftover food’ refers to leavings, water, dregs, and the like.

361. Dhammayuttampi naccañca gītañca vāditañca yojāpetuñca payojetuñca payuttāni passituñca “upahāraṃ karomā”ti vutte sampaṭicchituṃ vā na labbhanti sambandho. Dhammayuttampīti ratanattayaguṇūpasaṃhitatāya antamaso dhammena puññena saṃyuttampi. Naccanti antamaso morasukamakkaṭādīnaṃ naccampi. Gītanti antamaso gītassa pubbabhāge kayiramānaṃ dantagītampi. Vāditanti antamaso udakabherivāditampi. Yojāpetunti aññehi kārāpetuṃ. Payojetunti attanā kātuṃ. Āyatakena [M 0.0402] gītassarena dhammampi bhāsituṃ na vaṭṭati. Payuttānīti parehi yehi kehici katāni. Passitunti iminā anolocanadassanampi gahitanti sotuntipi attho viññāyati. Antarārāme ṭhitassa passato anāpatti. Vīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā gīvaṃ parivattetvā passatopi āpattiyeva. Yena kenaci karaṇīyena gataṭṭhāne passati, suṇāti vā, anāpatti. Sampaṭicchitunti [V 0.0337] “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchituṃ. “Upahārakaraṇaṃ nāma sundara”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Vā-saddo samuccaye.

361. The connection is: even if connected with the Dhamma, one is not allowed to arrange or engage in dancing, singing, or playing music, or to watch such performances, or to approve when it is said, “We are making an offering.” ‘Connected with the Dhamma’ means even if associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem, or at least connected with the Dhamma and merit. ‘Dancing’ means even the dancing of peacocks, parrots, monkeys, and so on. ‘Singing’ means even the humming done in the preliminary part of a song. ‘Playing music’ means even the playing of a water-drum. ‘To arrange’ means to have others perform. ‘To engage’ means to perform oneself. It is not allowable to recite the Dhamma with a drawn-out singing tone. ‘Performances’ means those done by any others whatsoever. By ‘to watch,’ even seeing without close inspection is included; it is also understood that the meaning ‘to listen’ is included. There is no offense for one standing within the monastery who sees it. But if one stands in the street and turns one’s neck to watch, it is an offense. If one sees or hears it at a place one has gone to for some necessary business, there is no offense. ‘To approve’ means to approve by saying, ‘Good.’ It is allowable to say, ‘Making an offering is a beautiful thing.’ The word ‘or’ is used in the sense of inclusion.

362. “Kīḷatthaṃ kataṃ rājāgāra”ntiādinā sambandhitabbaṃ. Cittena vicittakaṃ āgāraṃ cittāgārakaṃ.

362. It should be connected with the phrase ‘a royal residence made for the purpose of amusement,’ and so on. A residence made variegated with paintings is a ‘picture gallery’ (cittāgāraka).

363. Āsanena nave na paṭibāheyyāti yojanā. Āsanenāti āsanato. Na paṭibāheyyāti na uṭṭhāpeyya. Uṇhe cīvaraṃ na nidaheyyāti yojanīyaṃ. Na nidaheyyāti adhikaṃ na nidaheyya. Garunāti ācariyupajjhāyena. Paṇāmitoti “mā idha pavisā”tiādinā nikkaḍḍhito.

363. The connection is: ‘One should not displace a junior by means of a seat.’ ‘By a seat’ means from the seat. ‘Should not displace’ means should not make one rise. The connection is: ‘One should not place a robe in the heat.’ ‘Should not place’ means should not place it excessively. ‘By a senior’ means by a teacher or preceptor. ‘Driven away’ means expelled by saying, ‘Do not enter here,’ and so on.

364. Sattahi āpattīhi ca bhikkhuṃ vāpi aññeneva ca upāsakaṃ vāpi parammukhā akkosane dukkaṭanti yojetabbaṃ. Āpattīhi cāti ca-saddo avadhāraṇe. Aññeneva cāti ettha eva cāti nipātasamudāyo, eko eva vā avadhāraṇe, vuttato aññeneva “asaddho”tiādināti attho. Parammukhāti nipāto, tassa asammukheti attho. Sammukhā vadantassa pācittiyaṃ. Pāpagarahaṇavasena pana vadato anāpatti.

364. It should be construed that reviling a bhikkhu or a lay follower in their absence with any of the seven offenses, or in some other way, is a dukkaṭa offense. In ‘with offenses,’ the word ‘ca’ is for emphasis. Here, in ‘aññeneva ca,’ ‘eva ca’ is a collection of particles, or ‘eva’ alone is for emphasis; the meaning is ‘in another way than what has been stated,’ such as by calling them ‘faithless,’ and so on. ‘In their absence’ is a particle; its meaning is ‘not in their presence.’ For one who speaks in their presence, it is a pācittiya offense. However, for one who speaks by way of censuring what is evil, there is no offense.

365. Saddhādeyyaṃ saddhāya dātabbaṃ cīvarañca ca-saddena avasesampi vinipātetuṃ nāsetuṃ na labbhaṃ, pitūnaṃ labbhanti sambandho. Ñātīnampīti pi-saddo sambhāvane.

365. A ‘gift of faith’ is that which is to be given with faith. A robe and, by the word ‘ca,’ also remaining items, should not be squandered or destroyed; the connection is that they may be received by one's parents. In ‘for relatives too,’ the word ‘pi’ is in the sense of possibility.

366. Aññatra [M 0.0403] vassaṃvuttho aññato bhāgaṃ gaṇheyya, dukkaṭanti sambandho. Aññatrāti aññasmiṃ vihāre. Aññatoti aññavihārato. Paṭideyyāti gahitaṭṭhāne dadeyya. Gahite tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ naṭṭhe vā jiṇṇe vā tassa gīvāho tīti sambandho. Codito no dadeyya, tesaṃ dhuranikkhepato bhaṇḍagghakāriyo hotīti yojanā. Coditoti vatthusāmikehi “dehī”ti vutto. Tesanti tasmiṃ vihāre lābhīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ.

366. The connection is: If one who has spent the Rains-residence elsewhere takes a share from another place, it is a dukkaṭa offense. ‘Elsewhere’ means in another monastery. ‘From elsewhere’ means from another monastery. ‘Should return it’ means one should give it back in the place where it was taken. The connection is: if that item taken is lost or worn out, he is liable for it. The explanation is: if, when urged, one does not give it back, since they are released from their responsibility, one becomes liable for the value of the goods. ‘Urged’ means being told by the owners of the item, ‘Give it back.’ ‘Of them’ refers to the bhikkhus who are recipients of gains in that monastery.

367. Santaruttaro vā kallo saupāhano vā gāmaṃ na paviseyya, cāmarīmakasabījaniṃ na dhāreyyāti yojanīyaṃ. Antarañca uttarañca, saha antaruttarena santaruttaro. Aggaḷagutte vihāre [V 0.0338] saṅghāṭiṃ nikkhipitvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Āraññakena pana bhaṇḍukkhalikāya pakkhipitvā pāsāṇarukkhasusirādīsu paṭicchannesu ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Antaruttarānaṃ nikkhepe ayameva nayo. Kalloti agilāno. Makasānaṃ bījanī makasabījanī, camarīnaṃ vāḷehi katā makasabījanīti samāso.

367. The connection is: One should not enter a village wearing both an inner and outer robe, or, if healthy, wearing sandals; nor should one carry a yak-tail whisk or a fly-whisk. ‘With an inner and outer robe’ (santaruttaro) means with both the inner robe and the upper robe. In a monastery with secured gates, it is permissible to leave the outer robe behind and go. A forest-dweller, however, should place it in a cloth bundle and leave it in a concealed place such as a rock crevice or a hollow tree before going. This same principle applies to leaving behind the inner and outer robes. ‘Healthy’ means not ill. ‘Fly-whisk’ (makasabījanī) is a fan for flies; a fly-whisk made with the hairs of a yak (camarī) is the compound.

368. Ārāmato bahīti sambandhanīyaṃ. Ārāmatoti ārāmūpacārato. Na dhāreyyāti agilāno na dhāreyya. Yassa pana kāyadāho vā pittakopo vā hoti, cakkhu vā dubbalaṃ, añño vā koci ābādho vinā chattena uppajjati, tassa gāme vā araññe vā chattaṃ vaṭṭati. Guttiyā labbhatīti vasse cīvaraguttatthaṃ, vāḷamigacorabhayesu attaguttatthampi labbhatīti attho. Ekapaṇṇachattaṃ pana sabbattheva vaṭṭati.

368. It should be connected with ‘outside the monastery.’ ‘From the monastery’ means from the monastery precincts. ‘Should not carry’ means one who is not ill should not carry it. But for one who has a burning sensation in the body, or an affliction of bile, or weak eyes, or any other ailment that arises without an umbrella, it is permissible to carry an umbrella in the village or the forest. ‘It is allowed for protection’ means it is allowed for the protection of the robe in the rainy season, and the meaning is that it is also allowed for self-protection from the dangers of predatory animals and thieves. A single-leaf umbrella, however, is permissible everywhere.

369. Ubhatokājaṃ na gāheyyāti sambandho. Ubhato daṇḍassa ubhayakoṭiyaṃ bhārabandhakājaṃ ubhatokājaṃ, alopatappuriso. Ekantarikakājakanti antarameva [M 0.0404] antarikaṃ, ekañca antarikañcāti dvando, ekantarike bhārabandhakājanti tappuriso ekatokājakaṃ, antarikakājakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Hatthe olambo assa bhārassāti samāso.

369. The connection is: ‘One should not carry a double-ended carrying pole.’ A carrying pole for binding a load at both ends of a staff is ‘ubhatokāja’; it is a tatpurisa compound with elision. As for ‘ekantarikakājaka’ (single-middle carrying pole): the middle itself is ‘antarika’; ‘eka’ (one) and ‘antarika’ (middle) form a dvanda compound; a carrying pole for binding a load at the single middle point is a tatpurisa compound. It is called a single-ended carrying pole or a middle carrying pole. ‘A load which has a loop for the hand’ is the meaning of the compound.

370. Anokāsakatanti “karotu me āyasmā okāsaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo”ti evaṃ codakena okāse kārāpite natthi okāso kato anena cuditakenāti bahubbīhi. Codeyyāti cāvanaakkosakammavuṭṭhānādhippāyena codeyya. Uposathappavāraṇaṭṭhapanaanuvijjadhammakathādhippāyesu okāsakammaṃ natthi. Suddhassāti anāpattikatāya suddhassa. Avatthusminti akāraṇe. Tathāti dukkaṭaṃ atidisati. Karontenāpi “bhūtameva nu kho āpattiṃ vadati, abhūta”nti evaṃ upaparikkhitvā kātabbā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, puggalaṃ tulayitvā okāsaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 153) hi vuttaṃ.

370. ‘Not having been given an opportunity’ (anokāsakata) is a bahubbīhi compound, meaning: when the accuser has requested an opportunity by saying, ‘Venerable, give me an opportunity, I wish to speak to you,’ no opportunity has been given by the one accused. ‘Should accuse’ means to accuse with the intention of dislodging, reviling, or removal from a formal act. There is no act of giving an opportunity for the purposes of Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, establishing a rule, investigation, or Dhamma talks. ‘Of a pure one’ means of one who is pure due to being without offense. ‘Without basis’ means without reason. ‘Thus’ applies the dukkaṭa offense by extension. Even when doing so, one should act only after investigating thus: ‘Is he speaking truthfully about an offense, or falsely?’ For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, I allow one to give an opportunity after evaluating the person.’

371. Sattānaṃ pakataṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulādhikaṃ mañcappaṭipādaṃ vā uccapādakaṃ mañcaṃ vā na dhārayeti yojanā. Pakatiyā aṅgulaṃ pakataṅgulaṃ. Tañca vaḍḍhakiaṅgulaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭha ca tāni aṅgulāni ca, tehi tamadhikaṃ yassāti samāso. Mañcānaṃ paṭipādo, yattha mañcapāde nikkhipanti. Aṭṭhaṅgulato uccā pādā yassāti bahubbīhi.

371. The connection is: one should not use a bed-support exceeding eight standard fingerbreadths, or a bed with high legs. A standard fingerbreadth is a normal fingerbreadth. And it should be understood as the carpenter’s fingerbreadth. The compound means: ‘eight and those fingerbreadths, and that which exceeds them.’ A bed-support (mañcappaṭipāda) is that upon which the legs of the bed are placed. ‘Having legs higher than eight fingerbreadths’ is a bahubbīhi compound.

372. Mūgabbatādinti [V 0.0339] mūgānamiva tuṇhībhāvasaṅkhātaṃ vataṃ ādi yassa govatādino titthiyavatassāti samāso. Khurameva bhaṇḍaṃ khurabhaṇḍaṃ. Pubbe nhāpito nhāpitapubbako, visesanassa paranipāto.

372. ‘The vow of the mute, etc.’ (Mūgabbatādi) is a compound meaning: the vow, known as keeping silent like the mute, which is the beginning of the vows of sectarians such as the cow-practitioners. ‘Razor-requisite’ (Khurabhaṇḍa) means the razor itself is the requisite. ‘Formerly a barber’ (nhāpitapubbako) means one who was formerly a barber; the adjective is placed after.

373. Hatthakammanti hatthena kātabbaṃ vaḍḍhakiādīnaṃ kammaṃ. Anussaraṇaṃ “kappiyattaṃ me yena yācitaṃ, amhehi imassa [M 0.0405] dātabba”nti evaṃ cittappavattianusāro, tassā yācanāya anusāro tadanusāro, tato laddhaṃ yaṃ kiñci gahetunti yojanā. Kammato niggato nikkammo, vighāsādādi. Taṃ ayācitvāpi kāretunti sambandho. Āharāpetunti araññato ānetuṃ. Aparasantakanti dārutiṇapalālādikaṃ aparapariggahitaṃ.

373. ‘Handicraft’ refers to work to be done by hand, such as the work of carpenters, etc. ‘Recollection’ means following the course of thought thus: ‘That by which it was requested of me has been made allowable; it should be given by us to him.’ Following that request is ‘following that recollection’; the connection is to take whatever is obtained from that. ‘Free from work’ (nikkamma) refers to what is left over from work, such as food scraps, etc. The connection is that one may have it done even without being asked. ‘To have it brought’ means to have it brought from the forest. ‘Not belonging to another’ refers to wood, grass, straw, etc., that has not been taken possession of by another.

374. Gihīnaṃ yattakaṃ deti, gopake dente gahetuṃ labbhaṃ, saṅghacetiyasantake yathāparicchedaṃ gahetuṃ labbhanti yojanā. Detīti gopako bhikkhūnaṃ deti. Gahetunti tattakaṃ gahetuṃ. Saṅghacetiyasantaketi vetanagopakehi dīyamāne saṅghassa cetiyassa ca santake. Yathāparicchedanti yaṃ tesaṃ saṅghena anuññātaṃ hoti “divase divase ettakaṃ nāma khādathā”ti, taṃ paricchedaṃ anatikkamma. Saṅghike ca cetiyasantake ca keṇiyā gahetvā ārakkhantasseva hi dāne paricchedo natthi.

374. The explanation is: ‘Whatever he gives to laypeople, when the cowherd gives, it can be taken; what belongs to the Saṅgha or a shrine can be taken according to the limit’. ‘Gives’ means the cowherd gives to the bhikkhus. ‘To be taken’ means that much can be taken. ‘Belonging to the Saṅgha or the shrine’ means that belonging to the Saṅgha and the shrine, when given by hired cowherds. ‘According to the limit’ means not exceeding the limit permitted to them by the Saṅgha, such as, ‘Eat this much each day’. Indeed, for one who guards what belongs to the Saṅgha or the shrine, having taken it on hire, there is no limit in giving.

375. “Kāyavācāhi dvīhi āpattiṃ āpajjeyyā”ti yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ, methunadhamme parūpakkame sati sādiyantassa akiriyasamuṭṭhānabhāvasambhavato. Chahi vāti āpattuppattikāraṇasaṅkhātehi chahi samuṭṭhānehi vā āpattiṃ āpajjeyyāti sambandho. Sabbāpattīnañhi kāyo vācā kāyavācā kāyacittaṃ vācācittaṃ kāyavācācittanti cha samuṭṭhānāni. Tattha purimāni tīṇi acittakāni, pacchimāni sacittakāni.

375. ‘One may incur an offense through two means, body and speech’—this is stated generally, because when there is a sexual assault by another, it is possible for an offense to arise from the non-action of one who consents. The connection is: ‘Or through six’ means one may incur an offense through the six origins, which are reckoned as the causes for the arising of offenses. Indeed, all offenses have six origins: body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind. Among these, the first three are without intention, while the latter three are with intention.

Tidhā ekasamuṭṭhānā, pañcadhā dvisamuṭṭhitā;

Dvidhā ticaturo ṭhānā, ekadhā chasamuṭṭhitā.

Threefold are those of single origin, fivefold are those of double origin; twofold are those of three or four origins, onefold are those of six origins.

Tattha catutthena pañcamena chaṭṭhena ca samuṭṭhānato ekasamuṭṭhānā tidhā. Paṭhamacatutthehi ca dutiyapañcamehi ca tatiyachaṭṭhehi ca catutthachaṭṭhehi ca pañcamachaṭṭhehi ca samuṭṭhānato [M 0.0406] dvisamuṭṭhitā pañcadhā[V 0.0340]. Paṭhamehi ca tīhi pacchimehi ca tīhi samuṭṭhānato tisamuṭṭhānā dvidhā. Paṭhamatatiyacatutthachaṭṭhehi ca dutiyatatiyapañcamachaṭṭhehi ca samuṭṭhānato catusamuṭṭhānā dvidhā. Chahipi samuṭṭhito chasamuṭṭhānā ekadhā. Alajji…pe… saññitāya cāti imehi chahi vā āpattiṃ āpajjeyyāti sambandho. Yo sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjati, āpattiṃ parigūhati, agatigamanañca gacchati, ediso vuccati alajjī puggalo. Alajjī ca aññāṇo ca kukkuccapakato ca kukkuccena abhibhūtoti dvando. Bhāve ttappaccayo.

Therein, arising from the fourth, fifth, and sixth origins, those with a single origin are threefold. Arising from the first and fourth, the second and fifth, the third and sixth, the fourth and sixth, and the fifth and sixth, those with two origins are fivefold. Arising from the first three and from the last three, those with three origins are twofold. Arising from the first, third, fourth, and sixth, and from the second, third, fifth, and sixth, those with four origins are twofold. Arising from all six, those with six origins are onefold. The connection is: one may incur an offense through these six: shamelessness... and perception. Whoever intentionally incurs an offense, conceals the offense, and follows a wrong course—such a person is called a shameless person. ‘Shameless and ignorant and afflicted by scruples and overwhelmed by scruples’—this is a dvandva compound. The suffix '-tta' is in the sense of state.

Tattha yo akappiyabhāvaṃ jānantoyeva madditvā vītikkamaṃ karoti, ayaṃ alajjitā āpajjati. Mando momūho kattabbākattabbaṃ ajānanto akattabbaṃ karoti, kattabbaṃ virādheti, ayaṃ aññāṇattā āpajjati. Kappiyākappiyaṃ nissāya kukkucce uppanne vinayadharaṃ apucchitvā madditvā vītikkamati, ayaṃ kukkuccapakatattā āpajjati. Satiyā plavo sammoho satiplavo, sahaseyyaticīvaravippavāsādīni satiplavā āpajjati. Kappañca akappiyañca kappākappiyaṃ, kappākappiye saññā, sā assa atthīti kappā…pe… saññī, tassa bhāvoti tā-paccayo. Ya-lopena pana “saññitā”ti vuttaṃ, karaṇatthe vā paccattavacanaṃ. Te ca “akappiye”tiādīnaṃ yathākkamena yujjanti. Tattha yo acchamaṃsaṃ “sūkaramaṃsa”nti khādati, vikāle kālasaññitāya bhuñjati, ayaṃ akappiye kappiyasaññitāya āpajjati. Yo pana sūkaramaṃsaṃ “acchamaṃsa”nti khādati, kāle vikālasaññāya bhuñjati, ayaṃ kappiye akappiyasaññitāya āpajjati.

Therein, one who, knowing something to be unfit, disregards it and transgresses, incurs an offense due to shamelessness. A dull and foolish person, not knowing what should or should not be done, does what should not be done and neglects what should be done, incurs an offense due to ignorance. When scruples arise concerning what is fit or unfit, and without consulting a Vinaya expert, one disregards it and transgresses, one incurs an offense due to being afflicted by scruples. A lapse of mindfulness is confusion; this is a lapse of mindfulness. One incurs offenses such as sleeping together with a layperson and being separated from the three robes through a lapse of mindfulness. What is allowable and what is unallowable is the allowable-and-unallowable. Perception of the allowable and unallowable; if one has this, one is called 'one who perceives'. The suffix '-tā' denotes the state of this. By the elision of 'ya', it is called 'saññitā', or it is a singular ending in the instrumental sense. And these apply respectively to the phrases beginning with 'in the unallowable'. Herein, one who eats bear meat thinking it is pork, or eats at the wrong time perceiving it as the right time, incurs an offense due to perceiving the unallowable as allowable. On the other hand, one who eats pork thinking it is bear meat, or eats at the right time perceiving it as the wrong time, incurs an offense due to perceiving the allowable as unallowable.

376. Alajjiaññāṇatāya kāyavācāhi āpattiṃ chādayeti yojanā. Liṅgeti liṅgaparivattananimittaṃ. Liṅge saṅghe [M 0.0407] ca gaṇe ca ekasmiṃ cāti āpattivuṭṭhiti catudhā hotīti seso.

376. The connection is: one conceals an offense by body and speech through shamelessness and ignorance. 'Gender' refers to the cause for the change of gender. The remainder is: rehabilitation from an offense occurs in four ways: in relation to gender, in the Saṅgha, in a group, and with an individual.

377. Paccayadvayeti cīvare piṇḍapāte ca. Parikathobhāsaviññattīti abhilāpamattametaṃ. Sahacaritassa pana nimittakammassāpi ettheva saṅgaho veditabbo. Tattha pariyāyena kathanaṃ parikathā. Ujukameva avatvā yathā adhippāyo vibhūto hoti, evaṃ obhāsanaṃ obhāso. Paccaye uddissa yathā adhippāyo ñāyati, evaṃ viññāpanaṃ viññatti. Nimittakaraṇaṃ nimittakammaṃ. Tatiyeti senāsane. Seseti gilānapaccaye.

377. ‘In the pair of requisites’ means in robes and almsfood. ‘Allusion, intimation, and request’—this is merely a matter of speech. However, the associated act of making a sign should also be understood as included here. Therein, speaking indirectly is an allusion. Making a hint in such a way that the intention is revealed, without speaking directly, is an intimation.
