“The ascetic life, if poorly grasped, drags one down to hell.”

Aparampi [V 0.0360] vuttaṃ –

And further, it was said:

“Sithilo hi paribbajo, bhiyyo ākirate raja”nti. (dha. pa. 313);

“A lax ascetic life stirs up more dust.”

Iccassa bhikkhubhāvo visuddhi nāma na hoti. Yasmā pana gihiādiko hutvā dānasaraṇasīlasaṃvarādīhi saggamaggaṃ vā jhānavimokkhamaggaṃ vā ārādhetuṃ bhabbo hoti, tasmāssa [M 0.0431] gihiādibhāvo visuddhi nāma hoti. Adhiṭṭhānavisiṭṭhena saṃvarena visuddhi saṃvaravisuddhi. Dhammena samena paccayānaṃ eṭṭhiyā suddhi eṭṭhisuddhi. Catūsu paccayesu paccavekkhaṇena suddhi paccavekkhaṇasuddhi. “Catubbidhā pātī”tiādīsu pātimokkhasaṃvarasammatanti “pātimokkhasaṃvaro”ti sammataṃ sīlaṃ.

Thus for him, the state of a bhikkhu is not called purity. But since, having become a layperson or the like, one is able to cultivate the path to heaven or the path to jhāna and liberation through generosity, refuge, virtue, and restraint, their state as a layperson or the like is called purity. Purity through restraint, namely, restraint distinguished by firm resolve, is purity of restraint. Purity through seeking requisites righteously and equitably is purity of seeking. Purity through reflection on the four requisites is purity of reflection. In passages such as “the fourfold downfall,” the virtue agreed upon as Pātimokkha restraint is what is meant by “Pātimokkha restraint.”

456. Cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvarā sujjhatīti indriyasaṃvaro saṃvarasuddhīti vuttoti yojanā.

456. “Because one is purified through restraint founded on the mind, therefore sense-restraint is called purity of restraint.” Such is the construction.

457. Anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena uppādentassa eṭṭhiyā suddhattā ājīvanissitaṃ eṭṭhisuddhīti vuttanti sambandho. Uppādentassāti paccaye uppādentassa.

457. The connection is: “Having abandoned improper seeking, for one who produces by righteous means, due to the purity of seeking, it is called purity of seeking dependent on livelihood.” “Produces” means one who produces the requisites.

458. Paccavekkhaṇasujjhanāti hetumhi pañcamīti.

458. In “because of purification by reflection,” the fifth case (ablative) is used in the sense of cause.

Suddhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Purity is concluded.

48. Santosaniddesavaṇṇanā

48. Commentary on the Exposition of Contentment

459. Paṃsukūlaṃ piṇḍiyālopo rukkhamūlaṃ pūtimuttabhesajjanti ime cattāro paccayā appagghanakatāya appā ceva kassacipi ālayābhāvena anavajjā ca gatagataṭṭhāne labbhamānatāya [V 0.0361] sulabhā cāti vuccanti, tenāha “appenā”tiādi. Mattaññūti pariyesanappaṭiggahaṇaparibhogavissajjanesu catūsu mattaññutāvasena pamāṇaññū.

459. The four requisites—rag-robes, alms-food, the root of a tree for lodging, and fermented urine as medicine—are said to be of little value, being few, blameless due to the absence of attachment for anyone, and easily obtainable wherever one goes. Hence, it is said: “With little” and so on. “Knowing moderation” means knowing the proper measure, with regard to moderation, in four things: seeking, receiving, using, and relinquishing.

460. Kathaṃ santuṭṭhoti āha “atīta”ntiādi. Paccuppannena yāpentoti yathālābhayathābalayathāsāruppavasena paccuppannena yathāvuttacatubbidhapaccayena yāpentoti.

460. How is one content? It is said, “with the past,” and so on. “One sustains oneself with the present” means one sustains oneself with the four kinds of requisites mentioned above which are presently arisen, according to what is obtained, according to one’s strength, and according to what is suitable.

Santosaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Contentment is concluded.

49. Caturārakkhaniddesavaṇṇanā

49. Commentary on the Exposition of the Four Protections

461-2. Buddhānussati [M 0.0432] …pe… maraṇassatīti imā caturārakkhā nāmāti seso. Ārakattādināti ārakabhāvo ārakattaṃ, taṃ ādi yassa “arīnaṃ hatattā”tiādikassa taṃ ārakattādi. Tena tena maggena savāsanānaṃ arānaṃ hatattā ārakā sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhitoti ā-kārassa rassattaṃ, ka-kārassa ha-kāraṃ sānunāsikaṃ katvā “araha”nti padasiddhi veditabbā. “Ārakā”ti ca vutte sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato, visesatthinā ca visesassa anuppayojitabbattā “kilesehī”ti labbhati.

461-2. Recollection of the Buddha [...] mindfulness of death—these are called the four protections; the rest is to be understood. By 'ārakattā' and so on: 'ārakatta' is the state of being distant. This is the beginning of the phrase 'because of the destruction of enemies,' and so on. Because enemies, together with their latent tendencies, have been destroyed by that very path, they are distant (ārakā)—standing very, very far away from all defilements. The shortening of the 'ā' vowel and the change of the 'ka' consonant to a nasalized 'ha' consonant are to be understood as forming the word 'arahant'. When 'ārakā' is said, because it indicates a general meaning and does not stand for a specific one, and because a specific meaning is not supplied by one who desires it, 'from defilements' is understood.

Sammāti aviparītaṃ. Sāmanti sayameva, aparaneyyo hutvāti attho. “Sambuddho”ti hi ettha saṃ-saddo “saya”nti etassa atthassa bodhako daṭṭhabbo. Buddhatoti bhāvappadhānoyaṃ niddeso, buddhattāti attho. “Arahaṃ” iti vā “sammāsambuddho” iti vā bhagavato navabhede guṇe yā punappunaṃ anussati, sā buddhānussatīti yojanā. “Sammāsambuddho itī”ti vattabbe a-kāro sandhivasena āgato. Iti-saddo panettha ādiattho, iccādīti attho. Navabhedeti “anuttaro purisadammasārathī”ti ekato gahetvā. Ettha pana upacāro uppajjati, na appanā, tathā maraṇassatiyaṃ. Itaresu pana ubhayampi uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Buddhānussati.

'Sammā' means not inverted. 'Sāmaṃ' means by oneself, the meaning being that one is not led by others. Here, the prefix 'saṃ-' in 'Sambuddho' should be seen as indicating the meaning of 'by oneself'. 'Buddho ti' is an exposition predominant in the sense of state, meaning 'Buddhatta' (the state of a Buddha). The repeated recollection of the ninefold qualities of the Blessed One, such as 'Arahaṃ' or 'Sammāsambuddho,' is the construction called 'Buddhānussati' (Recollection of the Buddha). When it should be said 'Sammāsambuddho iti,' the letter 'a' has come by way of sandhi. Here, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning,' signifying 'and so on'. The ninefold qualities are arrived at by taking 'the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed' as one. Here, however, only access concentration (upacāra) arises, not full absorption (appanā), just as in mindfulness of death. In the other cases, both can arise—this should be understood. Recollection of the Buddha.

463-4. “Sīmaṭṭhā”tiādinā mettābhāvanaṃ dasseti. Sīmaṭṭhasaṅgheti sīmāyaṃ tiṭṭhatīti sīmaṭṭho[V 0.0362], sova saṅgho. Gocaragāmamhi issare janeti sambandho. Tattha mānuse upādāya sabbasattesūti yojetabbaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ gāme. Sukhitā hontu averāti padacchedo. Ādināti [M 0.0433] “abyāpajjā hontu, anīghā hontu, sukhī attānaṃ pariharantū”ti iminā. Paricchijja paricchijjāti “imasmiṃ vihāre sabbe bhikkhū”tiādinā evampi paricchinditvā paricchinditvā. Mettābhāvanā.

463-4. By 'those in the boundary' and so on, he shows the development of loving-kindness. In 'Sīmaṭṭhasaṅghe': 'Sīmaṭṭha' means one who stands in the boundary; that is the Sangha. The connection is that it generates influential people in the alms-resort village. There, taking humans as a basis, it should be connected to all beings. 'There' means in that village. 'Sukhitā hontu averā'—this is the word division. 'And so on' refers to 'may they be free from oppression, may they be free from distress, may they maintain themselves happily'. 'Delimiting again and again' means delimiting again and again in such ways as 'all the monks in this monastery,' and so on. The development of loving-kindness.

465-6. Idāni asubhaṃ niddisanto sabbapaṭhamaṃ sādhetabbaṃ sattavidhamuggahakosallaṃ “vaṇṇe”ccādinā dasseti. Sattavidhañhi taṃ nayato āgataṃ vācāsajjhāyamanasāsajjhāyehi saddhiṃ. Tattha paṭhamaṃ vācāya sajjhāyantena cattāri tacapañcakādīni paricchinditvā anulomappaṭilomavasena kātabbaṃ. Yathā pana vacasā, tatheva manasāpi sajjhāyo kātabbo. Vacasā sajjhāyo hi manasā sajjhāyassa paccayo. So pana lakkhaṇappaṭivedhassa paccayo. Tattha vaṇṇo nāma kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānaṃ tesaṃyeva saṇṭhānaṃ. Okāso tesaṃyeva patiṭṭhokāso. Disā nābhito uddhaṃ uparimadisā, adho heṭṭhimā. Paricchedo nāma “ayaṃ koṭṭhāso heṭṭhā ca upari ca tiriyañca iminā nāma paricchinno”ti evaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo ceva “kesā na lomā, lomā na kesā”ti evaṃ amissakatāvasena visabhāgaparicchedo ca. Kesādikoṭṭhāse vavatthapetvāti sambandho. Vavatthapetvāti vuttanayena vavatthapetvā.

465-6. Now, in explaining the repulsive, he first shows the sevenfold skill in grasping that must be mastered, beginning with 'color'. For that sevenfold skill is derived by way of method, together with verbal recitation and mental recitation. Here, first, when reciting verbally, one should define the four pentads, such as the skin pentad, and so on, in forward and reverse order. Just as with verbal recitation, so too should mental recitation be done. Verbal recitation is indeed a condition for mental recitation, and that, in turn, is a condition for penetrating the characteristics. Here, 'color' means the color of the hair and so on. 'Shape' is the shape of those very things. 'Location' is the place where those very things are established. 'Direction' means upward from the navel is the upper direction, downward is the lower. 'Delimitation' is both the homogeneous delimitation, as in 'this portion is bounded below, above, and around by such-and-such,' and the heterogeneous delimitation, by way of non-mixture, as in 'hair is not body hair, body hair is not hair'. The connection is: having distinguished them in the portion of hair and so on. 'Having distinguished' means having distinguished in the manner stated.

Evaṃ vavatthapentena yathāvuttaṃ sattavidhaṃ uggahakosallaṃ sampādetvā aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ manasikārakosallaṃ sampādetabbanti dassetuṃ “anupubbato”tiādimāha. Tattha appanāto tayo ca suttantāti ime cattāropi nayatovāgate nātisīghādīsu pakkhipitvā dasavidhatā veditabbā. Anupubbatoti sajjhāyakaraṇato paṭṭhāya anupaṭipāṭiyā. Nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇikaṃ katvāti kiriyāvisesanaṃ. Vikkhepaṃ [M 0.0434] paṭibāhayanti kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cetaso vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhanto. Paṇṇattiṃ samatikkammāti yāyaṃ “kesā lomā”ti paṇṇatti, taṃ atikkamitvā, “paṭikkūla”nti cittaṃ ṭhapetvāti adhippāyo. Anupubbato muñcantassāti yo yo koṭṭhāso na upaṭṭhāti, taṃ taṃ anukkamena muñcato, tassa “bhāvanā”ti iminā sambandho veditabbo.

To show that one who is thus distinguishing should accomplish the eighteenfold skill in attention after accomplishing the sevenfold skill in grasping as stated, it is said, 'gradually,' and so on. Here, the three from absorption and the one from the Suttanta, these four, having come by way of method, are to be included in 'not too fast' and so on, and thus the tenfold nature should be understood. 'Gradually' means in due order, starting from the recitation. 'Having done not too fast, not too slow' is an adverbial qualifier of the action. 'Warding off distraction' means, having given up the meditation subject, warding off the mind's distraction towards various external objects. 'Transcending the concept' means having transcended that concept which is 'hair of the head, hair of the body'; the meaning is establishing the mind on 'repulsiveness.' 'For one gradually releasing' means for one who releases in succession whichever part does not appear; its connection with 'development' should be understood.

467. Evaṃ ubhayakosallaṃ sampādetvā sabbakoṭṭhāse vaṇṇādivasena vavatthapetvā vaṇṇādivaseneva [V 0.0363] pañcadhā paṭikkūlatā vavatthapetabbāti dassetuṃ “vaṇṇā”tiādimāha. Vaṇṇa…pe… okāsehi koṭṭhāse paṭikkūlāti bhāvanā asubhanti yojanā. Tatra kesā tāva pakativaṇṇena kāḷakā addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā, saṇṭhānato dīghavaṭṭatulādaṇḍasaṇṭhānā, disato uparimadisāya jātā, okāsato ubhosu passesu kaṇṇacūḷikāhi, purato naḷāṭantena, pacchato gaḷavāṭakena paricchinnā, sīsakaṭāhaveṭhanaallacammaṃ kesānaṃ okāso. Paricchedato kesā sīsaveṭhanacamme vīhaggamattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena heṭṭhā attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā. Dve kesā ekato natthīti ayaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. “Kesā na lomā, lomā na kesā”ti evaṃ avasesaekatiṃ sakoṭṭhāsehi amissīkatā kesā nāma pāṭiyekko eko koṭṭhāsoti ayaṃ visabhāgaparicchedo. Idaṃ kesānaṃ vaṇṇādito nicchayanaṃ. Idaṃ pana nesaṃ vaṇṇādivasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlato nicchayanaṃ – kesā nāmete vaṇṇatopi paṭikkūlā āsayatopi saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi okāsatopi paṭikkūlāti evaṃ sesakoṭṭhāsānampi yathāyogaṃ veditabbaṃ.

467. Having thus accomplished both skills, and having distinguished all the parts by way of color and so on, in order to show that the fivefold repulsiveness should be distinguished by way of color and so on, he begins with 'color.' The application is: the development of the parts as repulsive by color... and by location is the meditation on the unattractive. Herein, first, the hairs of the head: by their natural color, they are black, the color of jet. By shape, they have the shape of a long, round measuring rod. By direction, they are grown in the upward direction. By location, they are delimited on both sides by the tips of the ears, in front by the forehead's edge, and behind by the nape of the neck; the moist skin covering the skull-pan is the location for the hairs of the head. By delimitation, the hairs of the head are established, having penetrated the skin covering the skull to the extent of a grain of rice, delimited below by their own root-base, above by space, and sideways by one another. 'Two hairs are not together'—this is the delimitation by similar part. 'Hairs of the head are not hairs of the body, hairs of the body are not hairs of the head'—thus, unmixed with the remaining thirty-one parts, the hairs of the head are a single, separate part; this is the delimitation by dissimilar part. This is the determination of the hairs of the head by color and so on. And this is the determination of their fivefold repulsiveness by way of color and so on: these hairs of the head are repulsive by color, repulsive by origin, repulsive by shape, repulsive by smell, and repulsive by location. In the same way, this should be understood as is appropriate for the remaining parts as well.

Uddhumātādivatthūsūti [M 0.0435] uddhumātakavinīlakavipubbakavicchiddakavikkhāyitakavikkhittakahatavi- kkhittakalohitakapuḷavakaaṭṭhikasaṅkhātesu dasesu aviññāṇakaasubhavatthūsu asubhākāraṃ gahetvā pavattā bhāvanā vā asubhanti sambandho. Asubhabhāvanā.

In the objects beginning with the swollen: the development that proceeds by grasping the aspect of foulness in the ten lifeless, foul objects reckoned as the swollen, the livid, the festering, the fissured, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeleton, is the foul [meditation]; this is the connection. The development of the foul.

468. “Maraṇaṃ me bhavissatī”ti vā “jīvitaṃ me uparujjhatī”ti vā “maraṇaṃ maraṇa”nti vā yoniso bhāvayitvānāti yojanā. Jīvitanti rūpajīvitindriyañca arūpajīvitindriyañca. Yonisoti upāyena. Evaṃ pavattayatoyeva hi ekaccassa nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, maraṇārammaṇā sati saṇṭhāti, upacārappattameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti.

468. The connection is: having wisely developed the thought, 'Death will come to me,' or 'My life is being cut off,' or 'Death, death!' 'Life' means both the material life-faculty and the immaterial life-faculty. 'Wisely' means by a proper method. For it is just by proceeding in this way that for a certain person the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness with death as its object is established, and the meditation subject attains access concentration.

469-470. Yassa pana ettāvatā na hoti, tena vadhakapaccūpaṭṭhānādīhi aṭṭhahākārehi maraṇaṃ anussaritabbanti dassetuṃ “vadhakassevā”tiādimāha. Vadhakassa iva upaṭṭhānāti “imassa sīsaṃ chindissāmī”ti asiṃ gahetvā gīvāya sañcārayamānassa vadhakassa viya maraṇassa upaṭṭhānato. Sampattīnaṃ vipattitoti bhogasampattiyā jīvitasampattiyā ca vināsamaraṇasaṅkhātavipattito. Upasaṃharatoti yasamahattato puññamahattato thāmamahattato iddhimahattato paññāmahattato paccekabuddhato sammāsambuddhatoti imehi sattahākārehi attano upasaṃharaṇato[V 0.0364]. Kāyabahusādhāraṇāti asītiyā kimikulānaṃ, anekasatānaṃ rogānaṃ, bāhirānañca ahivicchikādīnaṃ maraṇassa paccayānaṃ sādhāraṇato. Āyudubbalatoti assāsapassāsūpanibaddhattairiyāpathūpanibaddhattādinā āyuno dubbalato. Kālavavatthānassa abhāvatoti “imasmiṃyeva kāle maritabbaṃ, na aññasmi”nti evaṃ kālavavatthānassa abhāvato. Addhānassa paricchedāti “manussānaṃ jīvitassa paricchedo nāma [M 0.0436] etarahi paritto, addhā yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ jīvatī”ti evaṃ addhānassa kālassa paricchedato.

469-470. But for one for whom this does not occur by so much, in order to show that death should be recollected in eight ways, beginning with its appearance as a murderer, he said, 'like a murderer,' etc. From its appearance as a murderer: from the appearance of death like a murderer who, having taken a sword, brings it to the neck, thinking, 'I will cut off this one's head.' From the ruin of success: from the ruin, called death, of the success of wealth and the success of life. From comparison: from comparing oneself in these seven ways: with those of great fame, great merit, great strength, great psychic power, great wisdom, with Paccekabuddhas, and with Sammāsambuddhas. From the body's sharing with many dangers: from its being shared with the eighty families of worms, the many hundreds of diseases, and external causes of death such as snakes and scorpions. From the weakness of the life-span: from the weakness of life due to its dependence on the in-breaths and out-breaths, its dependence on the postures, etc. From the absence of a fixed time: from the absence of a fixed time, such that 'one must die at this very time, not at another.' From the limitation of the duration: from the limitation of the duration of time, thus: 'The limit of the life of human beings is now short; indeed, one who lives long lives for a hundred years.'

Ettha pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā vipassanāya saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pattukāmena buddhaputtena yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ ādikammikassa kulaputtassa vasena ādito paṭṭhāya saṅkhepenopadissāma. Catubbidhaṃ tāva sīlaṃ sodhetabbaṃ. Tattha tividhā visujjhanā anāpajjanaṃ, āpannavuṭṭhānaṃ, kilesehi ca appaṭipīḷanaṃ. Evaṃ visuddhasīlassa hi bhāvanā sampajjati. Yampidaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīnaṃ vasena ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ vuccati, tampi sādhukaṃ paripūretabbaṃ. Tato –

Here, what is to be done by a son of the Buddha who, having developed a meditation subject, wishes to attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges, that we shall briefly set forth from the beginning, by way of the clansman who is a beginner. First, the fourfold virtue must be purified. Therein, the purification is threefold: not falling into an offense, rising from an offense into which one has fallen, and not being oppressed by the defilements. For one of purified virtue, the development succeeds. And that which is called the virtue of good conduct, by way of the duties in a shrine courtyard and so on, that too should be well fulfilled. Then—

“Āvāso ca kulaṃ lābho, gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ;

Addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho, gantho iddhīti te dasā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.41) –

“Dwelling, family, and gain, a following, and work as the fifth; travel, kin, and illness, study, and psychic power—these are the ten.”

Evaṃ vuttesu dasasu palibodhesu yo palibodho, yo upacchinditabbo. Evaṃ upacchinnapalibodhena –

Among these ten impediments thus mentioned, whichever impediment exists, that should be cut off. By one who has thus cut off the impediments—

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no cāṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37) –

“He is endearing, respected, and to be revered, an admonisher and one who patiently accepts advice; a speaker of profound discourse, and one who does not engage you in a wrong place.”

Evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇaṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānañca pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānañca. Tattha sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhikkhusaṅghādīsu mettā, maraṇassati ca, “asubhasaññā”tipi eke. Etaṃ pana tayaṃ sabbattha atthayitabbaṃ icchitabbanti [V 0.0365] katvā, adhippetassa ca yogānuyogakammassa padaṭṭhānattā “sabbatthakakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu pana yaṃ yassa caritānukūlaṃ, taṃ tassa niccaṃ pariharitabbattā yathāvutteneva nayena “pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati, tato –

Having approached a teacher with the aforementioned characteristics, a meditation subject should be learned. It is of two kinds: a meditation subject for all situations and a personal meditation subject. Therein, the meditation subject for all situations is loving-kindness towards the community of bhikkhus and so on, and mindfulness of death; some say also the perception of foulness. Because these three should be sought and wished for everywhere, and because they are a proximate cause for the intended work of devoted practice, it is called the 'meditation subject for all situations.' Then, among the thirty-eight objects, whichever is suitable for one's temperament, because that should be constantly maintained by that person, it is called the 'personal meditation subject.' Then—

“Mahāvāsaṃ [M 0.0437] navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

“A large monastery, a new monastery, a dilapidated one, and one on a main road; a spring, a place with edible leaves, with flowers, or with fruit, and a place that is sought after.

“Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

“A city, a place with timber, a field; a port with unsuitable people; an unsuitable border region, and where a friend is not to be found.

“Aṭṭhārasetāni ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.52) –

“These eighteen places, thus having understood, a wise person should avoid from afar, like a path that is fraught with peril.”

Vuttaaṭṭhārasasenāsanadosavajjitaṃ “idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti naccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasireneva uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammavinayadharā mātikādharā. Te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati ‘idaṃ bhante kathaṃ, imassa ko attho’ti. Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttāniṃ karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭhānīyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11) vuttapañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ senāsanaṃ upagamma tattha vasantena “dīghāni kesalomanakhāni chinditabbāni, jiṇṇacīvaresu aggaḷaanuvātaparibhaṇḍadānādinā daḷhīkammaṃ vā tantacchedādīsu tunnakammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ, kiliṭṭhāni rajitabbāni, sace patte malaṃ hoti, patto pacitabbo, mañcapīṭhādīni sodhetabbānī”ti evaṃ vuttaupacchinnakhuddakapalibodhena katabhattakiccena bhattasammadaṃ vinodetvā ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena cittaṃ sampahaṃsetvā [M 0.0438] ācariyuggahato ekapadampi asammuyhantena manasi kātabbanti.

Having avoided the eighteen faults of a dwelling as stated, and having gone to such a dwelling endowed with the five factors as described, one residing there should cut long hair, body hair, and nails. If the robes are old, they should be reinforced by applying patches or mended where threads have broken; soiled ones should be dyed. If the bowl is dirty, it should be boiled. The bed and bench should be cleansed. Thus, with minor impediments eliminated as stated, having completed the meal duties and dispelled the drowsiness after the meal, one should gladden the mind by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, and then apply the mind without forgetting even a single word received from the teacher.

Caturārakkhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Four Protections is completed.

50. Vipassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

50. The Commentary on the Exposition of Insight

471-2. Nāmarūpanti [V 0.0366] cittacetasikasaṅkhātaṃ nāmañca aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ rūpañca. “Namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, nāmarūpato na añño attādiko koci atthī”ti evaṃ jhānalābhī ce, jhānato vuṭṭhāya jhānagataṃ vā vipassanāyāniko ce, pakiṇṇakabhūtaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā. Pātimokkhasaṃvarādi sīlavisuddhi, caturārakkhavasena dīpitā sopacārasamādhisaṅkhātā cittavisuddhi ca vuttāva nāmāti iminā diṭṭhivisuddhi kathitā. Tato tassa paccayañca pariggahetvāti sambandho. Tassa paccayanti “paṭisandhikkhaṇe nāmarūpadvayameva avijjātaṇhāupādānakammehi uppajjati, na issarādikāraṇenā”tiādinā tassa kāraṇaṃ, iminā kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi dassitā.

‘Name and form’ refers to name, reckoned as consciousness and mental factors, and form, which is of twenty-eight kinds. ‘Name has the characteristic of inclining, form has the characteristic of being afflicted; apart from name and form, there is no other self or the like.’ Thus, one comprehends name and form: if one is an attainer of jhāna, upon emerging from jhāna, one comprehends the name and form pertaining to that jhāna; or if one is a practitioner of insight, one comprehends name and form as scattered phenomena. The purification of virtue, such as restraint according to the Pātimokkha, and the purification of mind, reckoned as access concentration and explained by way of the four protections, have already been stated. By this comprehension of name and form, the purification of view is declared. Then, the connection is ‘and having comprehended its condition.’ ‘Its condition’ refers to its cause: ‘At the moment of rebirth-linking, the pair of name and form arises only from ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma, not from a cause such as a creator.’ By this, the purification by overcoming doubt is shown.

Hutvā abhāvato aniccāti sabbepi nāmarūpasaṅkhārā uppajjitvā abhāvāpajjanato aniccā. Udayabbayapīḷanā dukkhāti uppādanirodhavasena pīḷanato dukkhā. Avasavattittā anattāti attano vase avattanato anattāti evaṃ saṅkhārehi saddhiṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā. Punappunaṃ sammasantoti yathāvuttanayena sammasanto samathayāniko vipassanāyāniko ca yogāvacaro. Iminā maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi ca dassitā. Saṅkhārānameva [M 0.0439] hi udayabbayādinānupassanato udayabbayabhaṅgabhayaādīnavanibbidāmuñcitukamyatāpaṭisaṅkhānupassanāsa- ṅkhārupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhātassa aṭṭhavidhassa ñāṇassa vasena sikhāppattaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma. Anupubbena sabbasaṃyojanakkhayaṃ pāpuṇeyyāti iminā ñāṇadassanavisuddhi dassitā. Sabbasaṃyojanakkhayanti orambhāgiyānaṃ pañcannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ heṭṭhā maggattayena khepitattā, itaresaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khepitattā ca sabbesaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khayante jātaṃ arahattamaggaṃ.

All formations of name and form are impermanent because, having arisen, they cease to be. They are suffering because they are oppressed by arising and ceasing. They are not-self because they do not occur under one's own control. Thus, having attributed the three characteristics to formations, the practitioner, whether one of tranquility or one of insight, contemplates again and again in the way described. By this, the purification of knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice, are shown. For insight knowledge, which has reached its culmination by way of the eight kinds of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of arising and passing away, of dissolution, of fear, of danger, of disenchantment, of desire for deliverance, of reflection, and of equanimity toward formations—through contemplation of the arising and passing away, etc., of formations, is called the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice. ‘Gradually, one may reach the destruction of all fetters’—by this, the purification of knowledge and vision is shown. The destruction of all fetters means the path of arahantship, which arises at the end of the destruction of all fetters, since the five lower fetters are eliminated by the first three paths and the remaining higher fetters are also eliminated.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Conclusion

473. Yasmā [V 0.0367] kāraṇā yā sikkhanā, ayaṃ bhikkhukiccaṃ, ato tasmā kāraṇāti attho.

473. For whatever reason there is this training, this is a monk's duty; therefore, the meaning is 'for that reason'.

474. Niccaso lokavicārinoti niccaṃ loke vicarato. Mālutasseva parissamo na sambhotīti yojanā. Mālutassevāti vātassa iva. Na sambhotīti na hoti.

474. ‘Always wandering in the world’ means constantly moving about in the world. The connection is: ‘No weariness arises, like the wind.’ ‘Like the wind’ means just as the wind. ‘No weariness arises’ means it does not arise.

475-6. Tambapaṇṇi eva tambapaṇṇiyo, ketu viya ketu, tambapaṇṇiye ketūti tappuriso. Tena racitā dhammavinayaññupasaṃsitā ayaṃ khuddasikkhā parimāṇato gāthānaṃ pañcamattehi satehi ettāvatā niṭṭhānamupāgatāti sambandho.

475-6. `Tambapaṇṇiyo` is from `Tambapaṇṇi`; `ketu` is a banner. `Tambapaṇṇiye ketu` ('the banner of Tambapaṇṇi') is a tatpuruṣa compound. The connection is: This Minor Training, praised by those who know the Dhamma and Vinaya, was composed by him. In measure, with about five hundred verses, it has thus reached its conclusion.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concluding Account is finished.

Nigamanakathā

The Conclusion

Kārāpitetirucire [M 0.0440] pavare vihāre;

Mānādhikāripurinā garunā guṇena;

Vassaṃ vasaṃ damiḷaso vidhahaṃ akāsiṃ;

Ākaṅkhaṭīka jinasāsanasampavuddhiṃ.

In a very beautiful and excellent monastery, caused to be built by the noble officer Māna, who is respected for his virtue; dwelling there during the rains, I, a Tamil, composed this, desiring the full flourishing of the Victor's Dispensation.

Puññena sattharacanājanitena tena;

Sambuddhasāsanavarodayakāraṇena;

Lokāmisesu pana me samayaṃ alaggo;

Sambuddhasāsanavarodayamācareyyaṃ.

By that merit born from this composition for the Teacher, a cause for the excellent flourishing of the Buddha's Dispensation, may I, never attached to worldly allurements, practice for the excellent flourishing of the Buddha's Dispensation.

Atthesu [V 0.0368] akkharapadesu vinicchayesu;

Pubbāparesu likhitaṃ khalitaṃ yadatthi;

Ohāya khantumarahanti vadantu santā;

Diṭṭhāparādhamatha vā kimulālanena.

Whatever error has been written, whether preceding or following, in meanings, letters, words, or judgments; may the good people, disregarding it, be pleased to forgive, or may they speak out, having seen the fault. What use is there in flattery?

Yenantatantaratanākaramanthanena;

Manthācalollasitañāṇavarena laddhā;

Sārāmatātisukhitā sukhayanti caññe;

Te me jayanti garavo garavo guṇehi.

By whose churning of the ocean of gems of the endless scriptures, with excellent wisdom obtained that shines forth like Mount Manthara; they, exceedingly happy with the deathless essence, also make others happy. Victorious are those teachers of mine, revered for their virtues.

Paratthasampādanato, puññenādhigatenahaṃ;

Paratthasampādanako, bhaveyyaṃ jātijātiyaṃ.

By the merit I have acquired from accomplishing the good of others, may I be one who accomplishes the good of others, in birth after birth.

Sisso āha –

The disciple said:

Paramappicchatānekasantosopasamesinaṃ;

Sucisallekhavuttīnaṃ, sadāraññanivāsinaṃ.

Of those with supreme fewness of wishes, much contentment, and seeking peace; of those pure in conduct, austere in habits, always dwelling in the forest.

Sāsanujjotakārīnaṃ, ācerattamupāgataṃ;

Udumbaragirikhyātayatīnaṃ yatipuṅgavaṃ.

Of those who illuminate the Dispensation, of the ascetics famed for Udumbara Mountain—him, the chief among ascetics, who has attained the state of a teacher.

Medhaṅkara [M 0.0441] iti khyātanāmadheyyaṃ tapodhanaṃ;

Theraṃ thiradayāmedhānidhānaṃ sādhupūjitaṃ.

The ascetic whose wealth is austerity, known by the name Medhaṅkara; the Elder, a treasure of steadfast compassion and wisdom, venerated by the good.

Sissaṃ sahāyamāgamma, kalyāṇamittamattano;

Sodhetuṃ sāsanaṃ satthu, parakkamamakāsi yo.

Who, having approached his own disciple and good friend, made an effort to purify the Teacher's Dispensation.

Susaddasiddhiṃ [V 0.0369] yo yoganicchayaṃ sabbhi vaṇṇitaṃ;

Akā subodhālaṅkāraṃ, vuttodayamanākulaṃ.

Who composed the Susaddasiddhi and the Yoganicchaya, praised by the good; who composed the clear Subodhālaṅkāra and Vuttodaya.

Saṅgharakkhitanāmena, mahātherena dhīmatā;

Nivāsabhūtenānekaguṇānappicchatādinaṃ.

By the wise great elder named Saṅgharakkhita, who was an abode of many virtues, such as fewness of wishes.

Teneva racitā sādhu, sāsanodayakārinā;

Khuddasikkhāya ṭīkāpi, sumaṅgalappasādanī.

By him, the one who promotes the Dispensation, was well composed also a commentary on the Khuddasikkhā, named Sumaṅgalappasādanī.

Nigamanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Concluding Account is completed.

Iti sumaṅgalappasādanī nāma

Thus ends the Sumaṅgalappasādanī.

Khuddasikkhā-abhinavaṭīkā samattā.

The New Commentary on the Khuddasikkhā is completed.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Mūlasikkhā

The Root Training

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Natvā [M 0.0443][V 0.0371] nāthaṃ pavakkhāmi, mūlasikkhaṃ samāsato;

Bhikkhunā navakenādo, mūlabhāsāya sikkhituṃ.

Having bowed to the Protector, I shall explain the Root Training in brief, for a new monk to train first in the root language.

1. Pārājikaniddeso

1. Exposition of the Offenses of Defeat

1.

1.

Saṃ nimittaṃ pavesanto, bhikkhu maggattaye cuto;

Pavesanaṭṭhituddhāra-paviṭṭhe cepi sādiyaṃ.

A bhikkhu, while inserting the male organ, falls from the three paths; even if he delights in its insertion, abiding, withdrawal, or having been inserted.

2.

2.

Adinnaṃ mānusaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, theyyāyekena ādiyaṃ;

Pañcavīsāvahāresu, garukaṃ ce cuto bhave.

Taking human goods not given, with thievish intent; in the twenty-five types of theft, if the item is of significant value, he is defeated.

3.

3.

Ādiyanto [V 0.0372] harantova-harantopiriyāpathaṃ;

Vikopento tathā ṭhānā, cāventopi parājiko.

By taking, by causing to take, by altering its position, or by moving it from its place, one is defeated.

4.

4.

Tattha nānekabhaṇḍānaṃ, pañcakānaṃ vasā pana;

Avahārā dasañceti, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

Herein, concerning various goods, the thefts are to be understood by the discerning one through pentads, and also as ten.

5.

5.

Sāhatthāṇattiko ceva, nissaggo cātthasādhako;

Dhuranikkhepanañceva, idaṃ sāhatthapañcakaṃ.

By one's own hand and by command, by depositing and by accomplishing the purpose, and by laying down the burden—this is the pentad of theft by one's own hand.

6.

6.

Pubbasahappayogo [M 0.0444] ca, saṃvidhāharaṇampi ca;

Saṅketakammaṃ nimittaṃ, pubbappayogapañcakaṃ.

Prior cooperative effort, taking by arrangement, action by signal, and a hint—this is the pentad of prior effort.

7.

7.

Theyyāpasayhaparikappa-ppaṭicchannakusādikā;

Avahārā ime pañca, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

By stealth, by force, by fraudulent contrivance, by concealment, and by trickery; these five are the types of theft to be understood by the discerning one.

8.

8.

Manussapāṇaṃ pāṇoti, jānaṃ vadhakacetasā;

Jīvitā yo viyojeti, sāsanā so parājito.

Whoever, knowing it to be a human being, with murderous intent deprives them of life, that one is defeated from the teaching.

9.

9.

Jhānādibhedaṃ hadaye asantaṃ,

Aññapadesañca vinādhimānaṃ;

Manussajātissa vadeyya bhikkhu,

Ñātakkhaṇe tena parājiko bhaveti.

Should a bhikkhu declare to a human a distinction such as jhāna that is not present in his heart, or make a baseless claim of superior attainment, at the moment it is understood, he is thereby defeated.

2. Garukāpattiniddeso

2. Exposition of Grave Offenses

10.

10.

Mocetukāmacittena, upakkamma vimocayaṃ;

Sukkamaññatra supinā, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

With a mind desiring emission, having made an effort and emitted semen, except in a dream, an ascetic incurs a grave offense.

11.

11.

Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena[V 0.0373], manussitthiṃ parāmasaṃ;

Itthisaññī upakkamma, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

An ascetic who, with lust for bodily contact, perceiving her as a woman, and making an effort, touches a human woman, incurs a grave offense.

12.

12.

Duṭṭhullavācassādena, maggaṃ vārabbha methunaṃ;

Obhāsanto manussitthiṃ, suṇamānaṃ garuṃ phuse.

With delight in coarse speech, addressing a human woman concerning sexual intercourse or the sexual organs while she is listening, one incurs a grave offense.

13.

13.

Vaṇṇaṃ vatvāttanokāma-pāricariyāya methunaṃ;

Itthiṃ methunarāgena, yācamāno garuṃ phuse.

An ascetic who, with sexual lust, requests a woman for sexual intercourse by praising sensual service to himself, incurs a grave offense.

14.

14.

Sandesaṃ paṭiggaṇhitvā, purisassitthiyāpi vā;

Vīmaṃsitvā haraṃpaccā, samaṇo garukaṃ phuse.

An ascetic who, having undertaken to carry a message for a man to a woman or for a woman to a man, delivers it, incurs a grave offense.

15.

15.

Cāvetukāmo codento, amūlantimavatthunā;

Codāpayaṃ vā samaṇo, suṇamānaṃ garuṃ phuse.

An ascetic who, wishing to dislodge another, accuses him or causes him to be accused of a baseless offense of defeat, incurs a grave offense if the accused one understands.

16.

16.

Lesamattaṃ upādāya, amūlantimavatthunā;

Cāvetukāmo codento, suṇamānaṃ garuṃ phuseti.

Taking up a mere trifle as a pretext, and wishing to dislodge another, one who accuses him of a baseless offense of defeat incurs a grave offense if the accused one understands.

3. Nissaggiyaniddeso

3. Exposition of the Offenses of Forfeiture

17.

17.

Vikappanamadhiṭṭhāna-makatvā [M 0.0445] kālacīvaraṃ;

Dasāhamatimāpeti, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyā.

If, without having made a determination or a formal sharing of a robe, one keeps it for more than ten days, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

18.

18.

Bhikkhusammutiyāññatra, ticīvaramadhiṭṭhitaṃ;

Ekāhamatimāpeti, nissaggi samayaṃ vinā.

Except with the Sangha's permission, if one is separated from one's determined set of three robes for more than one night, it becomes subject to forfeiture, unless there is an allowable circumstance.

19.

19.

Aññātikā bhikkhuniyā, purāṇacīvaraṃ pana;

Dhovāpeti rajāpeti, ākoṭāpeti taṃ siyā.

If one has an old robe washed, dyed, or beaten by an unrelated bhikkhunī, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

20.

20.

Aññātikā [V 0.0374] bhikkhuniyā, hatthato kiñci mūlakaṃ;

Adatvā cīvarādāne, nissaggiyamudīritaṃ.

If one accepts a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī without giving anything in exchange, it is declared subject to forfeiture.

21.

21.

Appavāritamaññātiṃ, viññāpentassa cīvaraṃ;

Aññatra samayā tassa, nissaggiyamudīritaṃ.

For one who requests a robe from an unrelated person who has not made an invitation, it is declared subject to forfeiture, except in an allowable circumstance.

22.

22.

Rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ vā, māsakaṃ vā kahāpaṇaṃ;

Gaṇheyya vā gaṇhāpeyya, nissaggi sādiyeyya vā.

Should one accept or cause to be accepted, or consent to the depositing of, gold or silver, or money, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

23.

23.

Parivatteyya nissaggi, rajatādi catubbidhaṃ;

Kappiyaṃ kappiyenāpi, ṭhapetvā sahadhammike.

Should one engage in various kinds of exchange involving gold and silver, it is an offense of forfeiture.

24.

24.

Vikappanamadhiṭṭhāna-makatvāna pamāṇikaṃ;

Dasāhamatimāpeti, pattaṃ nissaggiyaṃ siyā.

If, without having made a determination or a formal sharing of a bowl of the proper size, one keeps it for more than ten days, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

25.

25.

Pañcabandhanato ūna-patte sati paraṃ pana;

Viññāpeti navaṃ pattaṃ, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyā.

If, while possessing a bowl with fewer than five mends, one should request a new bowl, it becomes subject to forfeiture.

26.

26.

Paṭiggahetvā bhuñjanto, sappitelādikaṃ pana;

Sattāhamatimāpeti, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyā.

If, having received medicines such as ghee, oil, and so on, one stores them for more than seven days, they become subject to forfeiture.

27.

27.

Bhikkhussa cīvaraṃ datvā, acchindantassa taṃ puna;

Sakasaññāya nissaggi, acchindāpayatopi vā.

Having given a robe to a bhikkhu, if one takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense of forfeiture.

28.

28.

Appavāritamaññātiṃ[M 0.0446], suttaṃ yāciya cīvaraṃ;

Vāyāpentassa nissaggi, vinā ñātippavārite.

If one requests thread from an unrelated person by whom one has not been invited and has a robe woven, it is to be forfeited, unless one has been invited by relatives.

29.

29.

Jānanto [V 0.0375] bhikkhu saṅghassa, lābhaṃ pariṇataṃ pana;

Attano pariṇāmeti, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyāti.

If a bhikkhu, knowing it to be so, diverts to himself a gain that has accrued to the Saṅgha, it is to be forfeited.

4. Pācittiyaniddeso

4. The Exposition of Pācittiya Offenses

30.

30.

Sampajānamusāvāde, pācittiyamudīritaṃ;

Bhikkhuñca omasantassa, pesuññaharaṇepi ca.

Intentional false speech is declared a pācittiya offense; likewise, speaking scornfully of a bhikkhu, and also slander.

31.

31.

Ṭhapetvā bhikkhuniṃ bhikkhuṃ, aññena piṭakattayaṃ;

Padasodhammaṃ bhaṇantassa, pācittiyamudīritaṃ.

For one who recites the Dhamma word by word together with an unordained person, a pācittiya offense is declared.

32.

32.

Anupasampanneneva, sayitvāna tirattiyaṃ;

Pācitti sahaseyyāya, catutthatthaṅgate puna.

For lying down together with an unordained person for three nights, a pācittiya offense is incurred; and again at the end of the fourth night.

33.

33.

Itthiyā ekarattampi, seyyaṃ kappayatopi vā;

Desentassa vinā viññuṃ, dhammañca chappaduttariṃ.

For arranging to lie down with a woman even for a single night, or for teaching a woman more than six sentences of Dhamma without a discerning man present, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

34.

34.

Duṭṭhullaṃ bhikkhuno vajjaṃ, bhikkhusammutiyā vinā;

Abhikkhuno vadantassa, pācittiyamudīritaṃ.

For telling an unordained person of a bhikkhu's serious offense, without authorization from the bhikkhus, a pācittiya offense is declared.

35.

35.

Khaṇeyya vā khaṇāpeyya, pathaviñca akappiyaṃ;

Bhūtagāmaṃ vikopeyya, tassa pācittiyaṃ siyā.

If one digs the earth or has it dug, or destroys plant life, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

36.

36.

Ajjhokāse tu mañcādiṃ, katvā santharaṇādikaṃ;

Saṅghikaṃ yāti pācitti, akatvāpucchanādikaṃ.

If, having set out a bed or spread belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air, one departs without putting it away or having it put away, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

37.

37.

Saṅghikāvasathe seyyaṃ, katvā santharaṇādikaṃ;

Akatvāpucchanādiṃ yo, yāti pācitti tassapi.

If, having set out bedding or a spread in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, one departs without putting it away or having it put away, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

38.

38.

Jānaṃ sappāṇakaṃ toyaṃ, pācitti paribhuñjato;

Aññātikā bhikkhuniyā, ṭhapetvā pārivattakaṃ.

A pācittiya is incurred for knowingly using water containing living beings, and for giving a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī, except in an exchange.

39.

39.

Cīvaraṃ [M 0.0447][V 0.0376] deti pācitti, cīvaraṃ sibbatopi ca;

Atirittaṃ akāretvā, pavāretvāna bhuñjato.

Giving a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī is a pācittiya offense, as is sewing a robe for one; also for one who, having indicated he is satisfied, eats food that has not been made a 'left-over'.

40.

40.

Bhikkhuṃ āsādanāpekkho, pavāreti pavāritaṃ;

Anatirittena bhutte tu, pācittiyamudīritaṃ.

If, intending to cause annoyance, one offers food to a bhikkhu who has already indicated he is satisfied, a pācittiya offense is declared; and also for eating food that has not been made a 'left-over'.

41.

41.

Sannidhibhojanaṃ bhuñje, vikāle yāvakālikaṃ;

Bhuñjato vāpi pācitti, agilāno paṇītakaṃ.

If one eats stored food; or eats in the afternoon food that is only permissible in the forenoon; or, when not ill, eats choice food, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

42.

42.

Viññāpetvāna bhuñjeyya, sappibhattādikampi ca;

Appaṭiggahitaṃ bhuñje, dantakaṭṭhodakaṃ vinā.

If one, when not ill, requests and eats choice foods such as ghee-rice; or eats what has not been formally offered—except for a tooth-stick and water—a pācittiya offense is incurred.

43.

43.

Titthiyassa dade kiñci, bhuñjitabbaṃ sahatthato;

Nisajjaṃ vāraho kappe, mātugāmena cekato.

If one gives something edible to a sectarian with one's own hand, or sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

44.

44.

Surāmerayapānepi, pācittiyamudīritaṃ;

Aṅgulipatodake cāpi, hasadhammepi codake.

Drinking intoxicants is declared a pācittiya offense; and also poking with the finger, playing in water, or showing disrespect.

45.

45.

Anādarepi pācitti, bhikkhuṃ bhīsayatopi vā;

Bhayānakaṃ kathaṃ katvā, dassetvā vā bhayānakaṃ.

Disrespect towards a bhikkhu is a pācittiya offense; as is frightening a bhikkhu.

46.

46.

Ṭhapetvā paccayaṃ kiñci, agilāno jaleyya vā;

Jotiṃ jalāpayeyyāpi, tassa pācittiyaṃ siyā.

If a bhikkhu who is not ill, without some other valid reason, lights a fire or has one lit, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

47.

47.

Kappabindumanādāya, navacīvarabhogino;

Hasāpekkhassa pācitti, bhikkhuno cīvarādikaṃ.

For one who uses a new robe without applying a marking spot, a pācittiya is incurred; and for a bhikkhu who hides another's robe or other requisite, even as a joke.

48.

48.

Apanetvā [V 0.0377] nidhentassa, nidhāpentassa vā pana;

Jānaṃ pāṇaṃ mārentassa, tiracchānagatampi ca.

For one who takes away and conceals another's requisite, or has it concealed; and for one who knowingly deprives a living being of life, even an animal, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

49.

49.

Chādetukāmo chādeti, duṭṭhullaṃ bhikkhunopi ca;

Gāmantaragatassāpi, saṃvidhāyitthiyā saha.

If, wishing to conceal it, one conceals another bhikkhu's serious offense; or if one travels on a journey by arrangement with a woman, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

50.

50.

Bhikkhuṃ [M 0.0448] paharato vāpi, talasattikamuggire;

Codeti vā codāpeti, garukāmūlakenapi.

For striking a bhikkhu, or for raising a hand against one; and for accusing a bhikkhu of a groundless serious offense, or causing him to be accused, a pācittiya offense is incurred.

51.

51.

Kukkuccuppādane cāpi, bhaṇḍanatthāyupassutiṃ;

Sotuṃ bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ, yāti pācittiyaṃ siyā.

Causing anxiety to a bhikkhu is a pācittiya offense; as is going to eavesdrop on those who are quarreling for the sake of contention.

52.

52.

Saṅghassa lābhaṃ pariṇāmitaṃ tu,

Nāmeti yo taṃ parapuggalassa;

Pucchaṃ akatvāpi ca santabhikkhuṃ,

Pācitti gāmassa gate vikāleti.

Whoever diverts a gain accrued to the Saṅgha to another person; and whoever enters a village at the wrong time without having asked a resident bhikkhu, incurs a pācittiya offense.

5. Pakiṇṇakaniddeso

5. The Exposition of Miscellaneous Matters

53.

53.

Saṅghikaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ yo, deti aññassa issaro;

Thullaccayaṃ yathāvatthuṃ, theyyā pārājikādipi.

Whoever, being in charge, gives heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha to another, commits a thullaccaya offense or, depending on the circumstances, even a pārājika offense for theft.

54.

54.

Kusādimayacīrāni, kambalaṃ kesavālajaṃ;

Samayaṃ vinā dhārayato, lūkapakkhājinakkhipaṃ.

For one who wears, without a proper reason, robes made of grass and the like, a blanket made of hair, coarse garments, garments of feathers, animal hides, or bark-cloth, it is an offense.

55.

55.

Satthakamme vatthikamme, saṃ nimittañca chindato;

Thullaccayaṃ manussānaṃ, maṃsādibhojanepi vā.

For performing surgery, for administering an enema, or for destroying a boundary marker, a thullaccaya offense is incurred; and also for eating the flesh of humans and the like.

56.

56.

Kadalerakakkadussāni[V 0.0378], potthakaṃ sabbanīlakaṃ;

Sabbapītādikañcāpi, dhārayantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who wears cloths made from plantain fiber, eraka grass, or bark; a cloth that is entirely blue; and also one that is entirely yellow and so on, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

57.

57.

Hatthissuragasoṇānaṃ, sīhabyagghacchadīpinaṃ;

Taracchassa ca maṃsādiṃ, uddissakatakampi ca.

The flesh of elephants, horses, snakes, and dogs; of lions, tigers, bears, and leopards; and the flesh of a hyena and so on; and also that which is specially prepared for one.

58.

58.

Anāpucchitamaṃsañca, bhuñjato dukkaṭaṃ siyā;

Yātānupubbaṃ hitvāna, dakatitthādikaṃ vaje.

For one who eats meat without having asked, it is an offense of wrong-doing; as is abandoning the proper sequence and going to a bathing place or the like.

59.

59.

Sahasā [M 0.0449] vubbhajitvāna, pavise nikkhameyya vā;

Vaccapassāvakuṭikaṃ, vinā ukkāsikaṃ vise.

Rising up suddenly to enter or exit; entering a toilet without clearing one's throat.

60.

60.

Nitthunanto kare vaccaṃ, dantakaṭṭhañca khādayaṃ;

Vaccapassāvadoṇīnaṃ, bahi vaccādikaṃ kare.

Grunting while defecating, and chewing a tooth-stick; relieving oneself outside the toilet or urinal troughs.

61.

61.

Kharena cāvalekheyya, kaṭṭhaṃ pāteyya kūpake;

Ūhatañca na dhoveyya, uklāpañca na sodhaye.

Scraping harshly; dropping the stick into the pit; not washing what is soiled; and not cleaning the filth.

62.

62.

Dakakiccaṃ karontassa, katvā “capucapū”ti ca;

Anajjhiṭṭhova therena, pātimokkhampi uddise.

For one performing a water-duty to make splashing sounds; and for an elder to recite the Pātimokkha without being requested.

63.

63.

Anāpucchāya pañhassa, kathane vissajjanepi ca;

Sajjhāyakaraṇe dīpa-jālane vijjhāpanepi ca.

Speaking about or answering a question without being asked; in performing recitation; and in lighting or extinguishing a lamp.

64.

64.

Vātapānakavāṭāni, vivareyya thakeyya vā;

Vandanādiṃ kare naggo, gamanaṃ bhojanādikaṃ.

Opening or closing windows or doors; performing veneration, going about, eating, and so on, while naked.

65.

65.

Parikammaṃ [V 0.0379] kare kāre, tipaṭicchannakaṃ vinā;

Kāyaṃ nahāyaṃ ghaṃseyya, kuṭṭe thambhe tarumhi vā.

Doing or causing work to be done on a building without a triple covering; while bathing, rubbing one's body against a wall, a pillar, or a tree.

66.

66.

Kuruvindakasuttena, aññamaññassa kāyato;

Agilāno bahārāme, careyya saupāhano.

Using a kuruvindaka-dyed thread; touching one another's body; and, when not ill, walking about the monastery grounds wearing sandals.

67.

67.

Upāhanaṃ yo dhāreti, sabbanīlādikampi ca;

Nimittaṃ itthiyā ratto, mukhaṃ vā bhikkhadāyiyā.

Whoever wears sandals that are entirely blue and so on; being lustfully attached to a woman's sexual organ, or to the face of a female alms-giver.

68.

68.

Ujjhānasaññī aññassa, pattaṃ vā attano mukhaṃ;

Ādāsādimhi passeyya, uccāsanamahāsane.

Being resentful towards another's bowl; looking at one's own face in a mirror or the like; or sitting on high seats or grand seats.

69.

69.

Nisajjādiṃ karontassa, dukkaṭaṃ vandanepi ca;

Ukkhittānupasampanna-nānāsaṃvāsakādinaṃ.

For one who performs sitting and so on, it is an offense of wrong-doing; and also in venerating the suspended, the unordained, those of different communions, and the like.

70.

70.

Ekato paṇḍakitthīhi, ubhatobyañjanena vā;

Dīghāsane nisīdeyya, adīghe āsane pana.

Sitting together with eunuchs, women, or with a hermaphrodite on a long seat, or on a seat that is not long.

71.

71.

Asamānāsanikena, mañcapīṭhe sayeyya vā;

Kulasaṅgahatthaṃ dadato, phalapupphādikampi ca.

Sharing a seat unequally, or lying on a bed or bench with another; and giving fruit, flowers, and the like for the purpose of gaining the support of a family.

72.

72.

Ganthimādiṃ [M 0.0450] kare kāre, jinavāritapaccaye;

Paribhuñjeyya abyatto, anissāya vaseyya vā.

Doing or causing to be done weaving and the like with requisites forbidden by the Conqueror; for an unskilled person to make use of them; or to dwell without dependence.

73.

73.

Anuññātehi aññassa, bhesajjaṃ vā kare vade;

Kare sāpattiko bhikkhu, uposathappavāraṇaṃ.

Preparing or prescribing medicine for another without authorization; for a monk who has an offense to perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā.

74.

74.

Dvārabandhādike [V 0.0380] ṭhāne, parivattakavāṭakaṃ;

Apidhāya vinābhogaṃ, niyogaṃ vā saye divā.

In a place with a door-frame or a revolving door, closing it without due consideration; or sleeping during the day without an order.

75.

75.

Dhaññitthirūparatanaṃ, āvudhitthipasādhanaṃ;

Tūriyabhaṇḍaṃ phalaṃ rukkhe, pubbaṇṇādiñca āmase.

Touching grain, women, images, treasures, weapons, women's ornaments, musical instruments, fruit on a tree, and early crops and the like.

76.

76.

Sasitthodakatelehi, phaṇahatthaphaṇehi vā;

Kesamosaṇṭhanekasmiṃ, bhājane bhojanepi ca.

Arranging the hair with beeswax, water, or oils, or with a hand-comb or other combs; and eating from a single vessel with another.

77.

77.

Ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā, sayeyyuṃ dvekamañcake;

Dantakaṭṭhañca khādeyya, adhikūnaṃ pamāṇato.

For two to sleep on one bed with a single sheet and covering; and to chew a tooth-stick that is longer or shorter than the standard measure.

78.

78.

Yojeti vā yojāpeti, naccaṃ gītañca vāditaṃ;

Dassanaṃ savanaṃ tesaṃ, karontassa ca dukkaṭaṃ.

Engaging in or arranging dancing, singing, or instrumental music; and for one who goes to see or hear them, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

79.

79.

Vīhādiropime cāpi, bahipākārakuṭṭake;

Vaccādichaḍḍanādimhi, dīghakesādidhāraṇe.

Climbing trees and so on, or on outer enclosure walls; in the disposing of excrement and the like; in the keeping of long hair and the like.

80.

80.

Nakhamaṭṭhakaraṇādimhi, sambādhe lomahāraṇe;

Parikammakataṃ bhūmiṃ, akkame saupāhano.

Polishing the nails and so on; removing body hair in a confined space; stepping on prepared ground while wearing sandals.

81.

81.

Adhotaallapādehi, saṅghikaṃ mañcapīṭhakaṃ;

Parikammakataṃ bhittiṃ, āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who, with unwashed and wet feet, touches a bed or seat belonging to the Sangha, or a prepared wall, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

82.

82.

Saṅghāṭiyāpi pallatthe, dupparibhuñjeyya cīvaraṃ;

Akāyabandhano gāmaṃ, vaje katvāna vaccakaṃ.

Wearing the outer robe draped over both shoulders, or using a robe improperly; going into a village without a waistband after having relieved oneself.

83.

83.

Nācameyya [V 0.0381] dake sante, samādeyya akappiye;

Desanārocanādimhi, sabhāgāpattiyāpi ca.

Rinsing the mouth in still water; accepting unallowable things; and confessing or announcing a shared offense.

84.

84.

Na [M 0.0451] vase vassaṃ visaṃvāde, suddhacitte paṭissavaṃ;

Vassaṃ vasitvā gamane, ananuññātakiccato.

Dwelling for the rains retreat in discord; giving a promise with an impure mind; and after dwelling for the rains retreat, departing on unpermitted business.

85.

85.

Vināpadaṃ tarussuddhaṃ, porisamhābhirūhaṇe;

Aparissāvanoddhānaṃ, vaje taṃ yācato na de.

Clearing around a tree where there is no path; climbing higher than a man's height; not using a water-strainer or a fireplace; not giving to one who asks.

86.

86.

Attano ghātane itthi-rūpādiṃ kārayeyya vā;

Hitvā mālādikaṃ cittaṃ, jātakādiṃ sayaṃ kare.

Inciting one's own death; or having an image of a woman and so forth made; abandoning one's duties for a painting of garlands and so forth; or oneself composing Jātaka stories and so forth.

87.

87.

Bhuñjantamuṭṭhape tassa, sālādīsu nisīdato;

Vuḍḍhānaṃ pana okāsaṃ, adatvā vāpi dukkaṭaṃ.

One should not make a person get up who is eating, or who is sitting in halls and so forth; and not giving space to elders is also a wrong-doing.

88.

88.

Yānādimabhirūheyya, kallako ratanattayaṃ;

Ārabbha vade davañña-parisāyopalālane.

Mounting a vehicle and so forth; a rogue speaking in jest concerning the Triple Gem, or for the sake of flattering an assembly.

89.

89.

Kāyādiṃ vivaritvāna, bhikkhunīnaṃ na dassaye;

Vāce lokāyataṃ palitaṃ, gaṇheyya gaṇhāpeyya vā.

One should not expose the body and so forth and show it to nuns; nor should one recite or teach worldly philosophy or `palita` texts, nor learn them or cause others to learn them.

90.

90.

Yattha katthaci peḷāyaṃ, bhuñjato pattahatthako;

Vātapānakavāṭaṃ vā, paṇāme sodakampi ca.

Eating with bowl in hand in any confined space; or shutting a window or a door; or offering water.

91.

91.

Uṇheyya paṭisāmeyya, atiuṇheyya vodakaṃ;

Ṭhapeyya bhūmiyaṃ pattaṃ, aṅke vā mañcapīṭhake.

Warming or putting away requisites improperly; overheating water; placing the bowl on the ground, on the lap, or on a couch or chair.

92.

92.

Miḍḍhante [V 0.0382] paribhaṇḍante, pāde chatte ṭhapeti vā;

Calakādiṃ ṭhape pattaṃ, patte vā hatthadhovane.

One should not place the bowl on a latrine, on utensils, on the feet, or on an umbrella; nor on a moving object and so forth; nor should one wash one's hands over the bowl.

93.

93.

Pattena nīharantassa, ucchiṭṭhamudakampi ca;

Akappiyampi pattaṃ vā, paribhuñjeyya dukkaṭaṃ.

For one who removes leftovers with a bowl, or even leftover water, or who uses an unsuitable bowl, there is a wrong-doing.

94.

94.

Vade “jīvā”ti khipite, na sikkhati anādaro;

Parimaṇḍalakādimhi, sekhiye dukkaṭaṃ siyā.

If, when something is thrown, one says 'Live!', and being disrespectful, does not train, there is a wrong-doing in the Sekhiya rules, such as that concerning wearing the robes evenly all around.

95.

95.

Yo [M 0.0452] bhaṇḍagāre payutova bhaṇḍakaṃ,

Mātūna pācittiyamassa gopaye;

Davāya hīnenapi jātiādinā,

Vadeyya dubbhāsitamuttamampi yoti.

For one appointed in a storeroom who does not guard the goods, it is a Pācittiya offense. Whoever, in jest, speaks ill speech with reference to low birth and so forth, even to a superior person, commits an offense.

6. Vattādikaṇḍaniddeso

6. The Exposition of the Section on Duties and So Forth.

96.

96.

Upajjhācariyavattañca, gamikāgantukampi ca;

Senāsanādivattañca, kātabbaṃ piyasīlinā.

The duties toward preceptors and teachers, and toward those departing and arriving, as well as duties regarding lodgings and so forth, should be performed by one who holds virtue dear.

97.

97.

Hatthapāse ṭhito kiñci, gahitabbaṃ dade tidhā;

Gahetukāmo gaṇheyya, dvidhāyaṃ sampaṭiggaho.

Standing within arm's reach, one should offer something to be taken in three ways. One wishing to take should take; this acceptance is twofold.

98.

98.

Saṅghāṭimuttarāsaṅgaṃ, tathā antaravāsakaṃ;

“Etaṃ imaṃ adhiṭṭhāmi”, tathā “paccuddharāmi”ti.

The double-layered outer robe, the upper robe, and likewise the under-robe: 'I determine this,' and likewise, 'I relinquish it.'

99.

99.

“Imaṃ imāni etāni, etampi cīvara”nti vā;

“Parikkhāracoḷānī”ti, tathā “paccuddharāmi”ti.

Or: 'This,' 'these,' 'those,' or 'this very robe,' or 'accessory cloths,' and likewise, 'I relinquish it.'

100.

100.

“Etaṃ [V 0.0383] imaṃ adhiṭṭhāmi, pattaṃ paccuddharāmi”ti;

Evaṃ paccuddharedhiṭṭhe, cīvarādiṃ yathāvidhi.

'I determine this bowl,' and 'I relinquish the bowl.' Thus should one determine and relinquish robes and so forth, according to the rule.

101.

101.

Sañcarittaṃ vinā sesā, sacittā garukantimā;

Acchinnaṃ pariṇataṃ hitvā, nissaggiyamacittakaṃ.

Except for the offense of messengership, the remaining heavy offenses are with intent and final. Excluding those concerning what is not stolen and what has been dedicated, Nissaggiya offenses are without intent.

102.

102.

Padasodhammaṃ duve seyyā, itthiyā dhammadesanā;

Duve senāsanānīpi, sibbanaṃ cīvarassapi.

Teaching the Dhamma word by word; the two rules on sleeping; teaching the Dhamma to a woman; also the two rules on lodgings; and the sewing of a robe.

103.

103.

Pavāritaṃ surāpānaṃ, pañcasannidhiādikaṃ;

Jotinujjālanañceva, kappabindumanādikaṃ;

Gāmappavesanantete, pācittīsu acittakā.

Eating after being formally satisfied; drinking alcohol; the five kinds of storage and so forth; the kindling of a fire; the determination-mark and so forth; entering a village—these among the Pācittiyas are without intent.

104.

104.

Pakiṇṇakesu uddissa-kataṃ hitvāññamaṃsakaṃ;

Ekattharaṇapāvuraṇaṃ, ekamañce tuvaṭṭanaṃ;

Ekato bhuñjanañcāpi, naccagītādisattapi.

Among the miscellaneous rules: regarding meat prepared for a specific purpose and other meat; a single mat or covering; turning over on a single bed; eating together; and also attachment to dancing, singing, and so forth.

105.

105.

Akāyabandhanañcāpi[M 0.0453], pattahatthakavāṭakaṃ;

Acittakamidaṃ sabbaṃ, sesamettha sacittakaṃ.

Not wearing a belt; and having a bowl in hand at the door-panel; all this is without intent, the rest here is with intent.

106.

106.

Vītikkamanacittena, sacittakamacittakaṃ;

Paññattijānanenāpi, vadantācariyā tathā.

An offense is intentional or unintentional depending on the mind of transgression; and also on the knowledge of the regulation, so say the teachers.

107.

107.

Pubbakaraṇādikaṃ katvā, uposathappavāraṇaṃ;

Navadhā dīpitaṃ sabbaṃ, kātabbaṃ piyasīlinā.

Having performed the preliminary duties and so forth for the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā—all this, which has been explained ninefold, should be done by one who holds virtue dear.

108.

108.

Sammajjanī padīpo ca, udakaṃ āsanena ca;

Uposathassa etāni, pubbakaraṇanti vuccati.

Sweeping, a lamp, water, and a seat—these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.

109.

109.

Chandapārisuddhiutukkhānaṃ[V 0.0384], bhikkhugaṇanā ca ovādo;

Uposathassa etāni, pubbakiccanti vuccati.

Bringing consent and purity, the declaration of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation—these are called the preliminary tasks for the Uposatha.

110.

110.

Uposatho yāvatikā ca bhikkhū kammappattā,

Sabhāgāpattiyo ca na vijjanti;

Vajjanīyā ca puggalā tasmiṃ na honti,

Pattakallanti vuccati.

The Uposatha is called 'timely and fit' when the requisite number of monks fit for the act are present, when there are no common offenses, and when there are no individuals present who should be avoided.

111. Pubbakaraṇapubbakiccāni samāpetvā desitāpattikassa samaggassa bhikkhusaṅghassa anumatiyā pātimokkhaṃ uddisituṃ ārādhanaṃ karoma.

111. Having completed the preliminary duties and tasks, with the consent of the united Saṅgha of bhikkhus who have confessed their offenses, we make the request to recite the Pātimokkha.

112.

112.

Pārisuddhiadhiṭṭhāna-suttuddesavasā tidhā;

Gaṇapuggalasaṅghā ca, taṃ kareyyuṃ yathākkamaṃ.

It is threefold by way of the Uposatha of Purity, of Determination, and of Recitation. A group, an individual, and the Saṅgha, respectively, should perform it.

113.

113.

Cātuddaso pannaraso, sāmaggī dinato tidhā;

Dinapuggalakattabbā-kārato te naveritā.

Threefold by day—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the day of concord. By way of day, individual, and what is to be done, these are declared as nine.

114.

114.

Tayo tayoti katvāna, dinapuggalabhedato;

Tevācīdvekavācīti, nava vuttā pavāraṇā.

By division of day and individual, making it three by three; with three speeches, two speeches, and one speech, nine Pavāraṇās are declared.

115.

115.

Kattikantimapakkhamhā, hemaṃ phaggunapuṇṇamā;

Tassa antimapakkhamhā, gimhaṃ āsāḷhipuṇṇamā;

Vassakālaṃ tato sesaṃ, catuvīsatuposathā.

From the waning half of Kattika, winter lasts until the full moon of Phagguna; from the waning half of that, summer lasts until the full moon of Āsāḷhi; the rest from then is the rainy season, with twenty-four Uposathas.

116.

116.

Cātuddasā [M 0.0454] cha etesu, pakkhā tatiyasattamā;

Ñeyyā pannarasā sesā, aṭṭhārasa uposathā.

Among these, the Uposathas of six fortnights—the third and the seventh—are on the fourteenth day. The remaining eighteen Uposathas are to be known as being on the fifteenth day.

117. “Chandaṃ dammi, chandaṃ me hara, chandaṃ me ārocehī”ti chandaṃ dātabbaṃ.

117. “I give my consent; take my consent; announce my consent”—thus should consent be given.

118. “Pārisuddhiṃ [V 0.0385] dammi, pārisuddhiṃ me hara, pārisuddhiṃ me ārocehī”ti pārisuddhi dātabbā.

118. “I give my purity; take my purity; announce my purity”—thus should purity be given.

119. “Pavāraṇaṃ dammi, pavāraṇaṃ me hara, pavāraṇaṃ me ārocehi, mamatthāya pavārehī”ti pavāraṇā dātabbā.

119. “I give my Pavāraṇā; take my Pavāraṇā; announce my Pavāraṇā; perform the Pavāraṇā on my behalf”—thus should the Pavāraṇā be given.

120. Āpattidesakena “ahaṃ, bhante, sambahulā nānāvatthukā āpattiyo āpajjiṃ, tā tumhamūle paṭidesemī”ti vatvā paṭiggaṇhantena “passasi, āvuso, tā āpattiyo”ti vutte “āma, bhante, passāmī”ti vatvā puna paṭiggaṇhantena “āyatiṃ, āvuso, saṃvareyyāsī”ti vutte “sādhu, suṭṭhu, bhante saṃvarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā desetabbaṃ.

120. The one confessing an offense should say: “Venerable sir, I have committed numerous offenses on various grounds; I confess them in your presence.” When the one receiving the confession says: “Friend, do you see those offenses?” he should reply: “Yes, venerable sir, I see them.” When the one receiving the confession says further: “Friend, in the future you should be restrained,” he should say three times: “Good, very good, venerable sir, I will be restrained.” Thus should the confession be made.

121. Vematiṃ ārocentena “ahaṃ, bhante, sambahulāsu nānāvatthukāsu āpattīsu vematiko, yadā nibbematiko bhavissāmi, tadā tā āpattiyo paṭikarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā ārocetabbaṃ.

121. One announcing a doubt should say three times: “Venerable sir, I am doubtful about numerous offenses on various grounds. When I am free from doubt, then I will atone for those offenses.” Thus should it be announced.

122. “Ajja me uposatho ‘pannaraso, cātuddaso’ti vā adhiṭṭhāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā puggalena adhiṭṭhānuposatho kātabbo.

122. A personal Uposatha of determination should be performed by saying three times: “I determine today to be my Uposatha, the fifteenth,” or “the fourteenth.”

123. Dvīsu pana therena “parisuddho ahaṃ āvuso, ‘parisuddho’ti maṃ dhārehī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ. Navakenapi tatheva vattabbaṃ. “Bhante, dhārethā”ti vacanaṃ viseso.

123. In the case of two, however, the elder should say three times: “Friend, I am pure; hold me as pure.” The junior should also say the same. The difference is the phrase: “Venerable sir, please hold me as pure.”

124. Tīsu [M 0.0455] pana “suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajjuposatho pannaraso, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kareyyāmā”ti ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā paṭipāṭiyā vuttanayena pārisuddhiuposatho kātabbo.

124. In the case of three, however, after presenting the motion—“Venerable sirs, please listen to me. Today is the Uposatha, the fifteenth. If it is timely for the venerable sirs, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purity”—the Uposatha of purity should be performed in due order according to the method described.

125. “Ajja me pavāraṇā ‘cātuddasī, pannarasī’ti vā adhiṭṭhāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā ekena pavāretabbaṃ.

125. The Pavāraṇā should be performed by one person by saying three times: “I determine today to be my Pavāraṇā, the fourteenth,” or “the fifteenth.”

126. Dvīsu [V 0.0386] pana therena “ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmantaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadatu maṃ āyasmā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā pavāretabbaṃ. Navakenāpi tatheva vattabbaṃ. “Bhante”ti vacanaṃ viseso.

126. In the case of two, however, the elder should perform the Pavāraṇā by saying three times: “Friend, I invite the venerable one with respect to what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable one speak to me out of compassion; upon seeing it, I will make amends.” The junior should also speak in the same way, the difference being the word “Venerable Sir”.

127. Tīsu vā catūsu vā pana “suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pavāreyyāmā”ti ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā therena “ahaṃ, āvuso, āyasmante pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmantā anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā pavāretabbaṃ. Navakehipi tatheva paṭipāṭiyā pavāretabbaṃ. “Bhante”tivacanaṃ viseso.

127. In the case of three or four, however, after presenting the motion—“Venerable sirs, today is the Pavāraṇā, the fifteenth. If it is timely for the venerable sirs, let us invite one another”—the elder should perform the Pavāraṇā by saying three times: “Friends, I invite the venerable ones with respect to what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; upon seeing it, I will make amends.” The juniors should also perform the Pavāraṇā in the same way, in due order, the difference being the word “Venerable Sir”.

128. Catūhi adhikesu pana “suṇātu me āvuso saṅgho, ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho pavāreyyā”ti ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā vuḍḍhatarena “saṅghaṃ, āvuso, pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā pavāretabbaṃ. Navakehipi tatheva paṭipāṭiyā “saṅghaṃ, bhante, pavāremi diṭṭhena vā sutena [M 0.0456] vā parisaṅkāya vā, vadantu maṃ āyasmanto anukampaṃ upādāya, passanto paṭikarissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā pavāretabbaṃ.

128. In the case of more than four, however, after presenting the motion—“Friends, may the Sangha listen to me. Today is the Pavāraṇā, the fifteenth. If it is timely for the Sangha, may the Sangha perform the Pavāraṇā”—the most senior monk should perform the Pavāraṇā by saying three times: “Friends, I invite the Sangha with respect to what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; upon seeing it, I will make amends.” The juniors should also perform the Pavāraṇā in the same way, in due order, by saying three times: “Venerable Sir, I invite the Sangha with respect to what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; upon seeing it, I will make amends.”

Mūlasikkhā niṭṭhitā.

The Mūlasikkhā is completed.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Mūlasikkhā-ṭīkā

Mūlasikkhā-Ṭīkā

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Sabbakāmadadaṃ [M 0.0457][V 0.0387] sabbaratane ratanattayaṃ;

Uttamaṃ uttamataraṃ, vanditvā vandanārahaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, worthy of veneration, the giver of all that is desired, the highest among all jewels, the supreme, the most excellent.

Caraṇe brahmacārīnaṃ, ācariyānaṃ siraṃ mama;

Ṭhapetvāna karissāmi, mūlasikkhatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Having placed my head at the feet of the teachers who live the holy life, I shall proceed to explain the meaning of the Mūlasikkhā.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

Tatthādo tāva sabbasakkatassa sabbasattuttamassa satthuno paṇāmaṃ dassento āha “natvā nātha”ntyādi. Nāthaṃ catūhi nāthaṅgehi samannāgataṃ bhagavantaṃ natvā vanditvā ādo ādimhi upasampannato paṭṭhāya navakena bhikkhunā adhunā pabbajitena upasampannena mūlabhāsāya māgadhabhāsāya sikkhituṃ samāsato saṅkhepena mūlasikkhaṃ ahaṃ pavakkhāmīti piṇḍattho.

Herein, at the outset, showing homage to the Teacher, who is honored by all and supreme among all beings, he speaks thus: “Having bowed to the Protector,” and so forth. The summary meaning is: Having bowed to and venerated the Protector, the Blessed One, who is endowed with the four qualities of a protector, I shall declare concisely, in brief, the Mūlasikkhā, the basic training to be learned in the root language, the Māgadha language, by a new monk who has recently gone forth and been fully ordained, starting from the very beginning of his full ordination.

Ayaṃ [V 0.0388] pana avayavattho – natvāti tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāro hutvā kāyavacīmanodvārehi vanditvāti attho. Nāthatīti nātho, veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ mettāyanavasena āsīsati patthetīti attho, atha vā nāthati veneyyagate [M 0.0458] kilese upatāpetīti attho, nāthati vā yācatīti attho. Bhagavā hi “sādhu, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ attasampattiṃ paccavekkheyyā”tiādinā (a. ni. 8.7) sattānaṃ taṃ taṃ hitappaṭipattiṃ yācitvāpi karuṇāya samussāhito te tattha niyojeti. Paramena vā cittissariyena samannāgato sabbasatte īsati abhibhavatīti paramissaro bhagavā “nātho”ti vuccati. Sabbo cāyamattho saddasatthānusārato veditabbo. Pavakkhāmīti pakārena kathessāmi. Mūlasikkhāti adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāvasena tissopi sikkhā, upasampannassa suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanaṭṭhena mūlā ca sā sikkhitabbato sikkhā cāti mūlasikkhā. Ganthavasenettha saṅkhipitvā vuttattā taddīpano gantho “mūlasikkhā”ti vuccati.

This, however, is the explanation of the individual words: Natvā means having venerated with body, speech, and mind, having become inclined, prone, and bent towards that. A nātha is one who protects; this means one who wishes for the welfare and happiness of those to be trained, by way of loving-kindness; or it means one who torments the defilements of those to be trained; or it means one who entreats. For the Blessed One, spurred on by compassion, urges beings towards their respective beneficial practices and establishes them therein, even by entreating them, saying, “Good, monks, a monk should from time to time reflect on his own attainments,” and so on (AN 8.7). Or, endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind, he is master over all beings and surpasses them; hence the Blessed One, the supreme lord, is called nātha. And all this meaning should be understood in accordance with the science of grammar. Pavakkhāmi means: I shall explain in a special manner. Mūlasikkhā refers to the threefold training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom; it is the ‘root’ because it is the foundation for the well-established state of one who is fully ordained, and it is a ‘training’ because it is to be trained in. Here, because it is stated concisely in the form of a treatise, the text that explains it is called ‘Mūlasikkhā’.

Tattha katamaṃ sīlaṃ, katamaṃ adhisīlaṃ, katamaṃ cittaṃ, katamaṃ adhicittaṃ, katamā paññā, katamā adhipaññāti? Vuccate – pañcaṅgaaṭṭhaṅgadasaṅgasīlaṃ tāva sīlameva. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pana “adhisīla”nti vuccati. Tañhi sūriyo viya pajjotānaṃ, sineru viya pabbatānaṃ sabbalokiyasīlānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca. Pātimokkhasaṃvaratopi ca maggaphalasampayuttameva sīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ, taṃ pana idha nādhippetaṃ. Na hi taṃ sikkhanto methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati. Kāmāvacarāni pana aṭṭha kusalacittāni, lokiyaaṭṭhasamāpatticittāni ca ekajjhaṃ katvā cittameva. Vipassanāpādakaṃ aṭṭhasamāpatticittaṃ pana “adhicitta”nti vuccati. Tañhi sabbalokiyacittānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca. Tatopi ca maggaphalacittameva adhicittaṃ, taṃ pana idha nādhippetaṃ. Na hi taṃ sikkhanto methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati. “Atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭha”ntiādinayappavattaṃ kammassakatāñāṇaṃ paññā, tilakkhaṇākāraparicchedakaṃ pana vipassanāñāṇaṃ “adhipaññā”ti [M 0.0459] vuccati. Sā hi sabbalokiyapaññānaṃ adhikā ceva uttamā ca. Tatopi ca maggaphalapaññāva adhipaññā, sā pana idha nādhippetā. Na hi taṃ sikkhanto methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati.

Herein, what is virtue? What is higher virtue? What is mind? What is higher mind? What is wisdom? What is higher wisdom? It is said: First, the fivefold, eightfold, and tenfold virtue is simply virtue. The virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint, however, is called 'higher virtue,' for it is superior and supreme among all worldly virtues, like the sun among luminaries and Mount Sineru among mountains. And even beyond Pātimokkha-restraint, the virtue associated with the path and fruition is higher virtue, but that is not intended here, for one who trains in it does not engage in sexual intercourse. The eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere and the mundane eight attainment-consciousnesses, taken together, are simply mind. The eight attainment-consciousnesses that serve as a basis for insight, however, are called 'higher mind,' for they are superior and supreme among all worldly consciousnesses. And even beyond that, the consciousness associated with the path and fruition is higher mind, but that is not intended here, for one who trains in it does not engage in sexual intercourse. The knowledge of the ownership of kamma, which proceeds in the manner of 'There is what is given, there is what is offered,' and so on, is wisdom. The knowledge of insight that discerns the three characteristics, however, is called 'higher wisdom,' for it is superior and supreme among all worldly wisdoms. And even beyond that, the wisdom associated with the path and fruition is higher wisdom, but that is not intended here, for one who trains in it does not engage in sexual intercourse.

Tāsu tīsu adhisīlasikkhā cārittavārittavasena duvidhampi sīlaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamānena, tappaṭipakkhe kilese tadaṅgappahānavasena pajahantena sikkhitabbā. Adhicittasikkhā [V 0.0389] yathāvuttesu ārammaṇesu abhiyogavasena jhānappaṭipakkhānaṃ nīvaraṇagaṇānaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kurumānena sikkhitabbā. Adhipaññāsikkhā pana yathānurūpaṃ tadaṅgappahānasamucchedavasena sānusaye kilese samucchindantena sikkhitabbā. Tasmā suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanaṭṭhena mūlā ca sā sikkhitabbato sikkhā cāti mūlasikkhā, kammavacanicchāyaṃ “mūlasikkha”nti vuttaṃ.

Among these three, the training in higher virtue should be undertaken by one who practices both kinds of virtue—that of conduct and that of restraint—as instructed, and who abandons the opposing defilements by way of abandonment by substitution. The training in higher mind should be undertaken by one who brings about the abandonment by suppression of the group of hindrances, which are the opponents of jhāna, by means of application to the aforementioned meditation objects. The training in higher wisdom, however, should be undertaken by one who eradicates the defilements along with their underlying tendencies, as is suitable, by means of abandonment by substitution and abandonment by eradication. Therefore, because it is a root in the sense of accomplishing a well-established state, and because it is a training in that it ought to be trained in, it is the 'root training'; in the style of a verbal noun, it is called 'mūlasikkha'.

Samāsīyate saṅkhipīyateti samāso, tato samāsato. Samaggena saṅghena ñatticatutthena kammena akuppena ṭhānārahena upasampannoti bhikkhu. Tattha sabbantimena pariyāyena pañcavaggakaraṇīye kamme yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā, tesaṃ āgatattā, chandārahānaṃ chandassa āhaṭattā, sammukhībhūtānañca appaṭikkosanato ekasmiṃ kamme samaggabhāvaṃ upagatena saṅghena tīhi anussāvanāhi ekāya ñattiyā kātabbakammasaṅkhātena ñatticatutthena dhammikena vinayakammena vatthuñattianussāvanasīmāparisāsampattisampannattā akopetabbataṃ, appaṭikkositabbataṃ upagatena ṭhānārahena kāraṇārahena satthusāsanārahena upasampanno nāma, uparibhāvaṃ samāpanno pattoti attho. Bhikkhubhāvo hi uparibhāvo. Tañcesa yathāvuttena kammena samāpannattā “upasampanno”ti vuccati, tena bhikkhunā. Ūnapañcavassatāya navako, tena navakena [M 0.0460] adhunā pabbajitena, acirapabbajitenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ādoti ādimhiyevāti attho, ādito paṭṭhāyāti vā. Api ca thero “ādo”ti vacanena saddhāpabbajitānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ ālasiyadosena, appaṭipajjantānaṃ aññāṇadosena ca aññathā paṭipajjantānaṃ saṃvegaṃ janeti. Kathaṃ? Atidullabhaṃ khaṇaṃ samavāyaṃ paṭilabhitvā taṅkhaṇaṃ na kusītena vā niratthakakathāpasutena vā vītināmetabbaṃ, kiṃ kātabbaṃ? Ādito paṭṭhāya nirantarameva tīsu sikkhāsu ādaro janetabboti.

A contraction is called 'samāsa' because it is abbreviated or condensed; hence, 'samāsato' (in brief). A bhikkhu is one who has been fully ordained (upasampanno) by a united Sangha through a ñatticatuttha kamma, which is unshakable and worthy of its position.
