Herein, regarding an act to be performed by a chapter of five, all the bhikkhus eligible for the act have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, and those present have not objected. Thus, by a Sangha that has attained unity in a single act, through a lawful Vinaya act designated as a ñatticatuttha kamma—consisting of one motion and three announcements—which has become unassailable and indisputable because it is endowed with the completion of the object, motion, announcements, boundary, and assembly, one is fully ordained. 'Upasampanno' means one who has attained or reached a higher state. The state of a bhikkhu is indeed a higher state. Since he has attained it through the aforementioned act, that bhikkhu is called 'upasampanno'. A 'navaka' (new monk) is one with less than five years' seniority; by this is meant a newly ordained one, one who has recently gone forth. 'Ādo' means 'at the very beginning,' or 'from the outset.' Moreover, with the word 'ādo,' the elder inspires a sense of urgency in sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith but, due to the fault of laziness, do not practice, or, due to the fault of ignorance, practice wrongly. How so? Having obtained this exceedingly rare opportunity and conjunction of conditions, one should not let this moment pass by in laziness or in being devoted to useless talk. What should be done? From the very beginning, one should generate earnestness in the three trainings without interruption.

“Sā māgadhī mūlabhāsā, narā yāyādikappikā;

Brahmāno cassutālāpā, sambuddhā cāpi bhāsare”ti. –

That Māgadhī is the root language, which primeval humans spoke; Brahmās and those who have not heard another tongue, and also the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, speak it.

Vacanato mūlabhāsāyāti māgadhamūlāya bhāsāya, sabhāvaniruttiyā bhāsāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sikkhitunti uggaṇhituṃ.

By the phrase 'in the root language' is meant in the Māgadhī root language; that is to say, in the language of natural expression. 'To be learned' means to be grasped.

1. Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pārājika

1. Idāni [V 0.0390] sabbasikkhānaṃ pana mūlabhūtattā adhisīlasikkhāva paṭhamaṃ vuttā, tatrāpi mahāsāvajjattā, mūlacchejjavasena pavattanato ca sabbapaṭhamaṃ pārājikaṃ jānitabbanti dassento “saṃ nimitta”ntyādimāha. Tattha maggattaye saṃ nimittaṃ pavesanto bhikkhu cutoti attho. Saṃ nimittanti attano aṅgajātaṃ, sabbantimena paricchedena ekatilabījamattampi attano aṅgajātanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhikkhūti anikkhittasikkho. Maggattayeti ettha manussāmanussatiracchānagatānaṃ vasena tisso itthiyo, tayo ubhatobyañjanakā, tayo paṇḍakā, tayo purisāti pārājikavatthubhūtānaṃ nimittānaṃ nissayā dvādasa sattā honti. Tesaṃ vaccapassāvamukhamaggavasena tayo maggā. Tattha manussitthiyā tayo, amanussitthiyā tayo, tiracchānagatitthiyā tayoti nava[M 0.0461], tathā manussubhatobyañjanakādīnaṃ. Manussapaṇḍakādīnaṃ pana vaccamukhamaggavasena dve dveti cha, tathā manussapurisādīnanti sabbesaṃ vasena tiṃsa maggā honti. Te sabbe pariggahetvā idha “maggattaye”ti vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ maggattaye, dvādasannaṃ sattānaṃ tīsu maggesu yattha katthaci maggeti attho. Cutoti sakkattā vā brahmattā vā cutasatto viya sāsanato cuto hoti, pārājiko hotīti attho.

1. Now, since the training in higher virtue is the foundation of all trainings, it is mentioned first. And within that, to show that the pārājika offense should be known first of all, because it is a grave offense and because it proceeds by way of severing the root, the text begins with 'one's own organ,' and so on. Here, the meaning is that a bhikkhu who inserts his own organ into one of the three paths is 'cut off.' 'One's own organ' means one's own genital; by the most ultimate definition, this means even a portion of one's own genital the size of a single sesame seed. 'Bhikkhu' means one who has not relinquished the training. Regarding 'the three paths,' the supports for the organs that are the basis for a pārājika offense are twelve types of beings: three kinds of women (human, non-human, and animal), three kinds of hermaphrodites, three kinds of eunuchs, and three kinds of men. For them, there are three paths: the path of feces, the path of urine, and the path of the mouth. Among these, for a human woman there are three paths, for a non-human woman three, and for an animal woman three, making nine. Likewise for human hermaphrodites and so on. For human eunuchs and so on, however, there are two paths each—the path of feces and the path of the mouth—making six. Likewise for human men and so on. Thus, for all of them, there are thirty paths. Encompassing all of these, it is said here 'in the three paths,' meaning in any one of the paths of the twelve beings. 'Cut off' means that just as a being who has fallen from the state of Sakka or the state of Brahmā is cut off, so too is one cut off from the Dispensation; that is, one commits a pārājika offense.

Idāni pavesanaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ attupakkameneva hoti, parūpakkamenāpi hoti, tatthāpi sevanacitte sati pārājiko hotīti dassanatthaṃ “pavesanā”tyādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – yo bhikkhu pavesanaṭṭhitauddharaṇapaviṭṭhakkhaṇesu aññataraṃ khaṇaṃ cepi sādiyaṃ sādiyanto sacepi tasmiṃ khaṇe sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpento, cuto pārājiko hoti. Yo pana sabbaso asādiyanto āsīvisamukhaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ paviṭṭhaṃ viya ca maññati, so nipparādho hoti. Ettha pana ṭhitaṃ nāma sukkavissaṭṭhisamayappattaṃ. Paṭhamapārājikaṃ.

Now, insertion occurs not only through one's own effort but also through another's effort. To show that even in that case, if there is a mind intent on the act, one commits a pārājika offense, the text states 'insertion,' and so on. The meaning is this: if a bhikkhu, consenting, takes pleasure at any one of the moments—of insertion, of remaining, of withdrawal, or while it is inserted—and if at that moment he arouses a mind intent on the act, he is cut off, he commits a pārājika offense. But one who does not consent at all and regards it as though entering the mouth of a venomous snake or a pit of hot coals is without offense. Here, 'remaining' means reaching the moment of the emission of semen. The first pārājika.

2-7. Idāni dutiyaṃ dassetuṃ “adinnaṃ mānusaṃ bhaṇḍa”ntyādimāha. Tattha yo bhikkhu adinnaṃ mānusaṃ garukaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ pañcavīsāvahāresu yena kenaci avahārena ādiyanto cuto bhaveti sambandho. Adinnanti yaṃ kiñci parapariggahitaṃ sassāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, taṃ tehi sāmikehi kāyena vā vācāya vā na dinnanti adinnaṃ, anissaṭṭhaṃ apariccattaṃ rakkhitaṃ gopitaṃ mamāyitaṃ parapariggahitaṃ. Manussassa idanti mānusaṃ, manussasantakaṃ, “bhaṇḍa”ntiminā tulyādhikaraṇaṃ[V 0.0391]. Theyyāyekenāti theyyāya ekena, ekena avahārenāti attho. Liṅgabhedaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. “Theyyā kenacī”ti vā pāṭho. Tattha thenoti coro, thenassa bhāvo theyyā, karaṇatthe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, tasmā kenaci theyyena [M 0.0462] avahārenāti attho. Ādiyanti ādiyanto gaṇhanto. Pañcavīsāvahāresūti pañcapañcake samodhānetvā pañcavīsati avahārā. Tattha pañcapañcakāni nāma nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ pubbappayogapañcakaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakanti.

Now, to explain the second pārājika, it begins with 'what is not given, human goods,' and so on. Herein, the connection is as follows: a monk who, through any of the twenty-five modes of appropriation, takes what is not given—human goods of significant value—is defeated. 'What is not given' refers to any goods possessed by others, belonging to an owner, which have not been given by those owners through body or speech—what is not relinquished, not abandoned, guarded, protected, cherished, or held by others. 'Human' means belonging to humans, possessed by humans; the term 'goods' is in apposition with this. 'By one act of theft' means by one mode of appropriation. It is stated thus by making a distinction in grammatical gender. Alternatively, the reading may be 'by any act of theft.' Herein, 'thief' means a robber; the state of being a thief is 'theft.' This is a singular noun in the instrumental case, hence the meaning is 'by any mode of appropriation through theft.' 'Taking' means seizing, grasping. 'Twenty-five modes of appropriation' refers to the twenty-five methods which result from combining the sets of five. Herein, the five sets of five are: the fivefold classification of diverse goods, the fivefold classification of a single good, the fivefold classification of personal action, the fivefold classification of prior effort, and the fivefold classification of theft-appropriation.

Tattha saviññāṇakāviññāṇakamissakabhaṇḍavasena nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ, saviññāṇakabhaṇḍavasena ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ. Tattha nānābhaṇḍavasena tāva evaṃ veditabbo – yo ārāmaṃ abhiyuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ bhavissatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, āpatti pārājikassa. Aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto sīse bhāraṃ theyyacitto āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Khandhaṃ oropeti, āpatti pārājikassa. Upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “dehi me bhaṇḍa”nti vuccamāno “nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti bhaṇati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, āpatti pārājikassa. “Sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ nessāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ saṅkāmeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ saṅkāmeti, āpatti pārājikassa. Thalaṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Ṭhānā cāveti, āpatti pārājikassa. Ayamettha nānābhaṇḍavasena yojanā. Ekabhaṇḍavasena pana sassāmikaṃ dāsaṃ vā tiracchānaṃ vā yathāvuttena abhiyogādinā nayena ādiyati vā harati vā avaharati vā iriyāpathaṃ kopeti vā ṭhānā cāveti vāti. Ayamettha ekabhaṇḍavasena yojanā.

Here, the fivefold classification of diverse goods is based on goods with consciousness, without consciousness, and mixed. The fivefold classification of a single good is based on goods with consciousness. First, concerning diverse goods, it should be understood as follows: One who lays claim to a monastery commits an offense of wrong conduct. If he causes doubt in the owner, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If the owner, thinking, 'It will not be mine,' relinquishes his claim, it is an offense entailing expulsion. While carrying another's goods, if one with a thieving intent touches a load on his head, it is an offense of wrong conduct. If he makes it quiver, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If he lowers the load from his shoulder, it is an offense entailing expulsion. When goods have been deposited and one is told, 'Give me the goods,' and he replies, 'I did not take it,' it is an offense of wrong conduct. If he causes doubt in the owner, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If the owner, thinking, 'He will not give it to me,' relinquishes his claim, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If, intending, 'I will take the goods along with the carrier,' he moves the first foot, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If he moves the second foot, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If, with a thieving intent, he touches goods placed on the ground, it is an offense of wrong conduct. If he makes them quiver, it is an offense of grave misconduct. If he moves them from their place, it is an offense entailing expulsion. This is the application here concerning diverse goods. Regarding a single good, however, it is as follows: one takes, carries away, or misappropriates a slave or an animal belonging to an owner, or disturbs its posture or moves it from its place, in the manner described above with laying claim, and so on. This is the application here concerning a single good.

Pañca avahārā sāhatthiko āṇattiko nissaggiyo atthasādhako dhuranikkhepoti. Tattha sāhatthiko nāma [M 0.0463] parassa bhaṇḍaṃ sahatthā avaharati. Āṇattiko nāma “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpeti. Nissaggiyo nāma antosuṅkaghāte ṭhito bahisuṅkaghātaṃ pāteti, āpatti pārājikassa. Atthasādhako nāma “asukaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā avaharā”ti āṇāpeti. Tattha sace paro anantarāyiko hutvā taṃ avaharati, āṇāpako āṇattikkhaṇeyeva [V 0.0392] pārājiko hoti, avahārako pana avahaṭakāle, ayaṃ atthasādhako. Dhuranikkhepo pana upanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena veditabboti idaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ.

The five modes of appropriation are: personal action, command, disposal, accomplishment of a purpose, and relinquishing a claim. Herein, 'personal action' means one misappropriates another's goods with one's own hand. 'Command' means one orders another, 'Misappropriate such-and-such a person's goods.' 'Disposal' means that, while standing inside a customs house, one causes goods to fall outside the customs house; this is an offense entailing expulsion. 'Accomplishment of a purpose' means one orders, 'Misappropriate such-and-such goods when you are able to.' Herein, if the other person, being without obstruction, misappropriates them, the one who commanded becomes subject to expulsion at the moment of commanding, while the one who misappropriated becomes so at the time of the misappropriation; this is 'accomplishment of a purpose.' 'Relinquishing a claim,' however, should be understood in relation to deposited goods. This is the fivefold classification of personal action.

Aparepi pañca avahārā pubbappayogo sahappayogo saṃvidhāvahāro saṅketakammaṃ nimittakammanti. Tattha āṇattivasena pubbappayogo veditabbo, ṭhānācāvanavasena sahappayogo. Saṃvidhāvahāro nāma sambahulā bhikkhū “amukaṃ nāma gehaṃ gantvā, chadanaṃ vā bhinditvā, sandhiṃ vā chinditvā bhaṇḍaṃ harissāmā”ti saṃvidahitvā gacchanti, tesu eko bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Saṅketakammaṃ nāma sañjānanakammaṃ kālaparicchedavasena saññākaraṇaṃ. Ettha ca “purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte ajja vā purebhattaṃ avaharatu, sve vā anāgate saṃvacchare vā, natthi visaṅketo, saṅketakārakassa āṇattikkhaṇe, itarassa ṭhānā cāvaneti evaṃ āpatti ubhinnaṃ pārājikassa. Nimittakammaṃ nāma saññuppādanatthaṃ kassaci nimittassa karaṇaṃ akkhinikhaṇanahatthālaṅghanapāṇippahāraaṅguliphoṭanagīvunnāmanaukkāsanādinā anekappakāraṃ. Avahārako āṇāpakena yaṃ nimittasaññaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, taṃ “eta”nti maññamāno tameva avaharati, ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. Yaṃ “avaharā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ “eta”nti maññamāno aññaṃ tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhapitaṃ avaharati, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpatti. Idaṃ pubbappayogapañcakaṃ.

There are another five modes of appropriation: prior effort, simultaneous effort, concerted misappropriation, action by agreement, and action by signal. Here, prior effort should be understood by way of a command, while simultaneous effort should be understood by way of displacement from a place. Concerted misappropriation means that several monks conspire, saying, 'We will go to such-and-such a house, and having broken through the roof or cut through a wall, we will carry away the goods.' If one of them misappropriates the goods, upon its removal, all are subject to expulsion. Action by agreement is an act of recognition, making a sign by way of a time limit. Here, if it is said, 'Misappropriate it before the meal,' whether one misappropriates it today before the meal, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no misunderstanding of the agreement. The one who made the agreement is subject to expulsion at the moment of commanding, and the other at the moment of moving it from its place; thus, both are subject to expulsion. Action by signal means making some signal to produce an understanding, in various ways, such as by a wink of the eye, passing the hand over, a strike of the hand, a snap of the fingers, a raising of the neck, or a cough. If the one who misappropriates, understanding the signal made by the instigator, misappropriates that very thing, both are subject to expulsion. If, thinking 'this is it' regarding what was instructed to be misappropriated, he misappropriates another thing placed in that same location, there is no offense for the instigator. This is the fivefold classification of prior effort.

Aparepi [M 0.0464] pañca avahārā theyyāvahāro pasayhāvahāro parikappāvahāro paṭicchannāvahāro kusāvahāroti. Tattha yo kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vañcetvā gaṇhāti, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro theyyāvahāro. Yo santajjetvā sayaṃ dassetvā tesaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhāti, yo vā attano pattabalito ca adhikaṃ balakkārena gaṇhāti rājarājamahāmattādayo viya, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro pasayhāvahāro. Parikappetvā gaṇhato panāvahāro parikappāvahāro. So duvidho bhaṇḍokāsaparikappavasena. Tatra yo “sāṭako ce, gaṇhissāmi, suttaṃ ce, na gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappetvā andhakāre pasibbakaṃ gaṇhāti, tatra sāṭako ce, uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ, suttaṃ ce hoti, rakkhati. Ayaṃ bhaṇḍaparikappo nāma. Yo ṭhānaṃ parikappetvā bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāti, tassa taṃ parikappitaparicchedaṃ atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Ayaṃ okāsaparikappo nāma. Evamimesaṃ dvinnaṃ parikappānaṃ vasena parikappetvā gaṇhato avahāro parikappāvahāro. Paṭicchādetvā parassa bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhato avahāro paṭicchannāvahāro nāma. Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā [V 0.0393] avaharaṇaṃ kusāvahāro. Yo kusaṃ pātetvā cīvare bhājiyamāne attano koṭṭhāsassa samīpe ṭhitaṃ appagghataraṃ vā mahagghataraṃ vā samasamaṃ vā parassa koṭṭhāsaṃ disvā sace paṭhamataraṃ parakoṭṭhāsato kusadaṇḍakaṃ uddharati, attano koṭṭhāse pātetukāmatāya uddhāre rakkhati, pātanepi rakkhati, attano koṭṭhāsato pana kusadaṇḍaṃ uddharati, uddhāre rakkhati, taṃ uddharitvā parakoṭṭhāse pātentassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Ayaṃ kusāvahāro nāmāti imesu pañcavīsāvahāresu yena kenaci avahārena gaṇhanto pārājiko bhaveti attho.

Furthermore, there are five other kinds of appropriation: appropriation by stealth, appropriation by force, appropriation by scheming, appropriation by concealment, and appropriation by means of a straw. Herein, when one takes by deceiving with counterfeit measures, counterfeit coins, and so forth, the appropriation of one so taking is appropriation by stealth. When one takes their property by intimidating them and showing oneself, or when one, like kings, royal ministers, and so forth, takes by force more than the tax due to oneself, the appropriation of one so taking is appropriation by force. However, the appropriation of one who takes after scheming is appropriation by scheming. It is of two kinds: by way of scheming regarding goods and scheming regarding location. Herein, if one schemes, thinking, 'If it is a cloak, I will take it; if it is thread, I will not take it,' and then takes a bundle in the dark—if it is a cloak, one incurs a pārājika offense immediately upon lifting it; if it is thread, one is safe. This is called scheming regarding goods. When one schemes regarding a place and then takes goods, one incurs a pārājika offense as soon as one exceeds that schemed-upon boundary. This is called scheming regarding location. Thus, the appropriation of one who takes after scheming by way of these two kinds of scheming is appropriation by scheming. The appropriation of one who takes another's goods after concealing them is called appropriation by concealment. Appropriation by transferring a straw is kusāvahāra. Herein, when robes are being divided by casting straws, one who, seeing another's portion near one's own portion—whether of lesser, greater, or equal value—if one first lifts the straw marker from the other's portion with the intention of dropping it on one's own portion, one is safe in the lifting and also in the dropping. But when one lifts the straw marker from one's own portion, one is safe in the lifting; having lifted it, while dropping it on the other's portion, at the very moment it is released from the hand, one incurs a pārājika offense. This is called appropriation by means of a straw. The meaning is that among these twenty-five kinds of appropriation, one who takes by any of these means becomes a pārājika offender.

Garukanti [M 0.0465] pañcamāsakaṃ. Vīsatimāsako hi kahāpaṇo, kahāpaṇassa catuttho bhāgo pādo nāma, tasmā pañcamāsakaṃ vā pādaṃ vā garukanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha “cattāro vīhayo guñjā, dve guñjā māsako bhave”ti vacanato vīhivasena cattālīsa vīhayo dasa guñjā pañcamāsakoti veditabbo. Yaṃ pana sāmaṇerasikkhāyaṃ “vīsativīhī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ atthi, vīmaṃsitabbametaṃ. Dutiyapārājikaṃ.

'Weighty' means five māsakas. For twenty māsakas make one kahāpaṇa, and a fourth part of a kahāpaṇa is called a pāda. Therefore, five māsakas or a pāda should be understood as 'weighty'. In this regard, according to the statement, 'Four vīhis make one guñjā, and two guñjās make one māsaka,' forty vīhis, or ten guñjās, should be understood as five māsakas. However, what is mentioned in the Sāmaṇera Training as 'twenty vīhis' is not found in the Canon or the commentaries. This should be examined. The Second Pārājika.

8. Idāni tatiyaṃ dassetuṃ “manussapāṇaṃ pāṇo”tyādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo bhikkhu “manussapāṇo” iti jānanto vadhakacittena manussapāṇaṃ jīvitā viyojeti, so bhikkhu sāsanā pārājiko hotīti samudāyattho.

8. Now, to present the Third Pārājika, it is said, 'A human being is a living being,' and so forth. Herein, the collective meaning is that a monk who, knowing 'this is a human being,' with murderous intent deprives a human being of life, that monk is defeated and excluded from the Dispensation.

Manussapāṇanti mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhicittena sahuppannaṃ atiparittaṃ kalalarūpaṃ ādiṃ katvā pakatiyā vīsavassasatāyukassa sattassa yāva maraṇakālā etthantare anupubbena vuddhippatto attabhāvo, eso manussapāṇo nāma, evarūpaṃ manussapāṇanti attho. Pāṇoti jānanti “pāṇo” iti jānanto “taṃ jīvitā voropemī”ti jānanto. Vadhakacetasāti vadhakacittena, itthambhūte karaṇavacanaṃ, vadhakacitto hutvā maraṇādhippāyo hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jīvitāti jīvitindriyato. Yoti aniyamavacanaṃ. Soti etena niyamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Viyojetīti vuttappakāraṃ manussaviggahaṃ kalalakālepi tāpanamaddanehi vā bhesajjasampadānena vā tato vā uddhampi tadanurūpena upakkamena jīvitā viyojetīti attho. Sāsanāti parāpubbajidhātuppayoge nissakkavacanaṃ, tena satthusāsanatoti attho. Parājitoti parājayamāpanno. Hotīti pāṭhaseso. Tatiyapārājikaṃ.

'Human being' (manussapāṇa) means the existence (attabhāva) that has gradually developed, starting from the extremely subtle kalala form that arises together with the rebirth-consciousness in the mother’s womb, up to the time of death for a being with a normal lifespan of one hundred and twenty years. This is what is called a human being; such is the meaning of 'human being.' 'Knowing it as a living being' (pāṇoti jānanto) means knowing 'it is a living being,' and knowing 'I will deprive it of life.' 'With murderous intent' (vadhakacetasā) means with a murderous mind. This is an instrumental expression in the sense of 'being such.' It means being of a murderous mind, having the intention to kill. 'Of life' (jīvitā) means from the life faculty. 'Who' (yo) is an indefinite term. 'He' (so) indicates the definite referent. 'Deprives' (viyojeti) means deprives of life the human form as described, whether by causing pain or by crushing even at the kalala stage, or by administering medicine, or by any other suitable method thereafter—this is the meaning. 'From the Dispensation' (sāsanā) is an ablative expression used with the verb root 'ji' prefixed by 'parā'. Thus, it means 'from the Dispensation of the Teacher.' 'Defeated' (parājito) means one who has met with defeat. 'Is' (hoti) is the remainder of the text. The Third Pārājika.

9. Idāni [M 0.0466][V 0.0394] catutthaṃ dassetuṃ “jhānādibheda”ntyādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo bhikkhu aññāpadesañca adhimānañca vajjetvā hadaye asantaṃ jhānādibhedaṃ dhammaṃ manussajātikassa sattassa vadeyya, tasmiṃ khaṇe ñāte so tato sāsanā pārājiko eva hotīti attho.

9. Now, to present the Fourth Pārājika, it is said, ‘distinctions such as jhāna,’ and so forth. Herein, the meaning is that a monk who, avoiding misrepresentation and arrogance, were to declare to a human being a state, such as jhāna or other distinctions, that does not exist in his heart, at the very moment it is known, he is indeed defeated and excluded from the Dispensation.

Jhānādibhedanti “jhānaṃ vimokkho samādhi samāpatti ñāṇadassanaṃ maggabhāvanā phalasacchikiriyā kilesappahānaṃ vinīvaraṇatā cittassa suññāgāre abhiratī”ti (pārā. 198) evaṃ vuttaṃ jhānādibhedaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ. Hadayeti citte. Asantanti asaṃvijjamānaṃ. Aññāpadesanti “yo te vihāre vasi, so bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī”tiādinā nayena aññāpadesaṃ vajjetvāti attho. Vināti vajjanatthe nipāto, tassa vajjetvāti attho. Adhimānanti “adhigatā mayā”ti evaṃ uppannaṃ mānanti attho. Adhigato mānoti viggaho, taṃ adhimānaṃ vajjetvāti attho. Manussajātissāti manussajātikassa, na devabrahmādīsu aññatarassāti attho. Vadeyyāti āroceyya. Ñātakkhaṇeti ñāte khaṇeti chedo, tasmiṃ tenārocitakkhaṇe manussajātikena ñāteti attho. Tenāti nissakke karaṇavacanaṃ, tato sāsanato pārājikoti attho. Catutthapārājikaṃ.

‘Distinctions such as jhāna’ (jhānādibheda) means the supramundane quality (uttarimanussadhamma) described thus: ‘jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandonment of defilements, the mind being free from hindrances, delight in a solitary dwelling’ (Pārā. 198). ‘In his heart’ (hadaye) means in his mind. ‘Non-existent’ (asanta) means not present. ‘Misrepresentation’ (aññāpadesa) means avoiding misrepresentation by such a method as saying, ‘The monk who stayed in your dwelling has attained the first jhāna,’ and so forth; this is the meaning. ‘Avoiding’ (vinā) is a particle in the sense of avoidance; its meaning is ‘having avoided.’ ‘Arrogance’ (adhimāna) means the conceit that arises thinking, ‘I have attained.’ The analysis is ‘attained conceit.’ The meaning is to avoid that arrogance. ‘To one of human birth’ (manussajātissa) means to one of human birth, not to any of the devas or Brahmās, and so forth. ‘Were to declare’ (vadeyya) means were to announce. ‘At the moment it is known’ (ñātakkhaṇe) is a compound of ‘ñāte khaṇe’ (at the known moment). The meaning is: at the moment it is declared by him, it is known by the human being. The word 'tena' ('by him') is an instrumental with an ablative sense of cause. Thus, the meaning is: on account of that, he is a pārājika from the Dispensation. The Fourth Pārājika.

Pārājikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Pārājikas is concluded.

2. Garukāpattiniddesavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Exposition of Grave Offenses

10. Idāni saṅghādisesaṃ pakāsetuṃ “mocetukāmacittenā”tiādimāraddhaṃ. Tattha mocetuṃ kāmetīti mocetukāmaṃ, mocetukāmañca taṃ cittañcāti mocetukāmacittaṃ[M 0.0467], tena, mocanassādacittenāti attho. Ekādasannañhi rāgānaṃ ekena mocanassādena āpatti hotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

10. Now, to explain the Saṅghādisesa offenses, the passage beginning with 'with a mind desiring to cause emission' is commenced. Herein, 'mocetukāma' is one who desires (kāmeti) to cause emission (mocetuṃ). 'Mocetukāmacitta' is that mind which desires to cause emission. By that phrase, the meaning is 'with a mind delighting in emission.' For it is said that an offense is incurred through the one delight in emission among the eleven kinds of lust.

Tatrime ekādasa assādā mocanassādo muccanassādo muttassādo methunassādo phassassādo kaṇḍūvanassādo dassanassādo nisajjassādo vācassādo gehasitapemaṃ vanabhaṅgiyanti. Tattha mocanassādacetanāya cetento ceva assādento ca upakkamati, muccati, saṅghādiseso[V 0.0395], na muccati ce, thullaccayaṃ. Sace pana sayanakāle rāgapariyuṭṭhito hutvā ūrunā vā muṭṭhinā vā aṅgajātaṃ gāḷhaṃ pīḷetvā mocanatthāya saussāho supati, supantassa cassa asuci muccati, saṅghādiseso. Muccanassāde attano dhammatāya muccamānaṃ assādeti, na upakkamati, muccati, anāpatti. Muttassāde attano dhammatāya mutte ṭhānā cute asucimhi pacchā assādentassa vinā upakkamena muccati, anāpatti. Methunassāde methunarāgena mātugāmaṃ gaṇhāti, tena asuci muccati, anāpatti, dukkaṭaṃ pana āpajjati. Phassassādo duvidho ajjhattiko bāhiro cāti. Tattha attano nimittaṃ “thaddhaṃ, mudukanti jānissāmī”ti vā lolabhāvena vā kīḷāpayato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Bāhiraphassassāde pana kāyasaṃsaggarāgena itthiṃ phusato, āliṅgato ca asuci muccati, anāpatti, kāyasaṃsaggasaṅghādisesaṃ pana āpajjati.

Herein, these are the eleven delights: the delight in causing emission, the delight in emission, the delight in what has been emitted, the delight in sexual intercourse, the delight in contact, the delight in scratching, the delight in seeing, the delight in sitting, the delight in speaking, domestic affection, and forest-breaking. In this case, if one intends with the volition of delight in causing emission, and both wills and delights, and makes an effort, and emission occurs, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense; if it does not occur, it is a thullaccaya. However, if, at bedtime, one is overcome by lust and, pressing the organ firmly with the thigh or fist for the purpose of causing emission, one sleeps with effort, and if semen is emitted while one is sleeping, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In the delight in emission, if one delights in what is being emitted naturally, without making an effort, and emission occurs, there is no offense. In the delight in what has been emitted, if one delights in the semen after it has naturally fallen from its place, without any effort, there is no offense. In the delight in sexual intercourse, if one grasps a woman with lust for sexual intercourse, and semen is emitted thereby, there is no offense, but one commits a dukkaṭa. The delight in contact is twofold: internal and external. Herein, if one causes one's own organ to play, thinking 'I will know whether it is stiff or soft,' or out of frivolity, and semen is emitted, there is no offense. But in the external delight in contact, if one touches or embraces a woman with lust for bodily contact, and semen is emitted, there is no offense, but one commits the Saṅghādisesa offense concerning bodily contact.

Kaṇḍūvanassāde daddukacchupiḷakapāṇakādīnaṃ aññatarena khajjamānaṃ nimittaṃ kaṇḍūvanassādena kaṇḍūvato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Dassanassāde itthiyā anokāsaṃ upanijjhāyato asuci muccati, anāpatti, dukkaṭaṃ pana hoti. Nisajjassāde mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisinnassa muttepi anāpatti[M 0.0468], rahonisajjāpatti pana hoti. Vācassāde mātugāmaṃ methunappaṭisaṃyuttāhi vācāhi obhāsantassa muttepi anāpatti, duṭṭhullavācāsaṅghādisesaṃ pana āpajjati. Gehasitapeme mātādīnaṃ mātādipemena āliṅganādiṃ karontassa muttepi anāpatti. Vanabhaṅgaṃ santhavakaraṇatthāya itthiyā pesitapupphādivanabhaṅgasaññitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ “itthannāmāya imaṃ pesita”nti assādena āmasantassa muttepi anāpattīti. Evametesu mocanassādena āpatti hotīti dassetuṃ “mocetu…pe… nā”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā mocetukāmaṃ cittaṃ yassa soyaṃ mocetukāmacitto, tena, itthambhūte karaṇavacanaṃ, mocetukāmacitto hutvāti attho.

In the delight in scratching, if one scratches the organ which is itching due to ringworm, scabies, pimples, or other such irritations, and semen is emitted due to the delight in scratching, there is no offense. In the delight in seeing, if one gazes at a woman improperly, and semen is emitted, there is no offense, but it is a dukkaṭa. In the delight in sitting, if semen is emitted while one is sitting alone with a woman, there is no offense, but there is an offense concerning sitting in private. In the delight in speaking, if semen is emitted while one is addressing a woman with words connected with sexual intercourse, there is no offense, but one commits a Saṅghādisesa offense concerning lewd speech. In domestic affection, if semen is emitted while one is embracing or doing similar acts with affection for one's mother or others, there is no offense. In forest-breaking, if one touches a gift, such as flowers, that is called 'forest-breaking' and sent by a woman for the purpose of establishing familiarity, thinking, 'This was sent by so-and-so,' and semen is emitted due to the delight, there is no offense. Thus, in these cases, to show that an offense occurs by means of the delight in causing emission, the passage “intending to cause emission…etc.” is stated. Alternatively, “one whose mind desires to cause emission” (mocetukāmacitto) refers to one whose mind is “desiring to cause emission” (mocetukāmaṃ cittaṃ yassa so). By that, it is a statement of the instrumental case in such a state, meaning “having become one whose mind desires to cause emission.”

Upakkammāti hatthādīsu yena kenaci nimitte upakkamitvāti attho. Vimocayanti yaṃ antamaso ekā khuddakamakkhikā piveyya, tattakampi vimocentoti attho. Sukkanti nīlapītalohitodātatakkateladakakhīradadhisappivaṇṇasaṅkhātesu dasavidhesu sukkesu yaṃ kiñci sukkaṃ. Aññatra supināti yā supinante sukkavissaṭṭhi hoti, taṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Samaṇoti yo koci upasampanno. Garukanti saṅghādisesaṃ. Phuseti āpajjeyyāti attho. Cetanā upakkamo muccananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgānīti. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadaṃ.

“Upakkammāti” (makes an effort) means “making an effort on the sexual organ with anything, such as the hand, etc.” “Vimocayanti” (causes to be emitted) means “causing to be emitted even that much which a single tiny fly might drink.” “Sukkanti” (semen) refers to any semen among the ten kinds enumerated by color: blue, yellow, red, white, buttermilk-colored, oil-colored, water-colored, milk-colored, curd-colored, or ghee-colored. “Aññatra supinā” (except in a dream) means “excluding that emission of semen which occurs in a dream.” “Samaṇo” (monk) means “any fully ordained monk whatsoever.” “Garukaṃ” (grave) means “a Saṅghādisesa offense.” “Phuseti” (touches) means “one commits an offense.” “Volition, effort, and emission”—these are the three factors here. This is the training rule concerning the emission of semen.

11. Idāni [V 0.0396] kāyasaṃsaggaṃ dassetuṃ “kāyasaṃsaggarāgenā”tiādimāraddhaṃ. Bhikkhu manussitthiyā manussitthisaññī hutvā kāyasaṃsaggarāgena upakkamitvā manussitthiṃ parāmasanto saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjeyyāti yojanā. Tattha kāyasaṃsaggarāgenāti hatthaggahaṇādikāyasamphassena rāgena kāyamissarāgena. Manussitthinti tadahujātampi jīvamānakamanussitthiṃ. Parāmasanti parāmasanto, itthīti saññā itthisaññā[M 0.0469], sā assa atthīti itthisaññī, itthisaññī hutvāti attho. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā, kāyasaṃsaggarāgo, tena rāgena vāyāmo, hatthaggāhādisamāpajjananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadaṃ.

11. Now, in order to explain bodily contact, the passage beginning with “with lust for bodily contact” is commenced. The construction is: “If a bhikkhu, perceiving a human female as a human female, makes an effort with lust for bodily contact and touches a human female, he commits a Saṅghādisesa offense.” Herein, “with lust for bodily contact” (kāyasaṃsaggarāgena) means “with lust for bodily contact such as holding hands, etc., with lust for mixing bodies.” “Manussitthiṃ” (a human female) refers to “a living human female, even one born on that very day.” “Parāmasanti” (touches) means “touching.” “Perception as a female” (itthīti saññā) is “female perception” (itthisaññā). “One who has that” (sā assa atthīti) is “perceiving as a female” (itthisaññī). The meaning is “having become one perceiving as a female.” A human female, perception of her as female, lust for bodily contact, effort due to that lust, and the act of touching, such as seizing the hand—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule concerning bodily contact.

12. Idāni duṭṭhullaṃ dassetuṃ “duṭṭhullavācassādenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha duṭṭhullavācassādenāti vaccamaggapassāvamaggamethunadhammappaṭisaṃyuttavācassādarāgena. Maggaṃ vārabbha methunanti vaccamaggapassāvamaggānaṃ aññataraṃ maggaṃ vā methunaṃ vā ārabbhāti attho. Obhāsantoti avabhāsanto. Manussitthinti viññuṃ paṭibalaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullaṃ sallakkhaṇasamatthaṃ manussitthiṃ. Suṇamānanti suṇantiṃ. Iminā paṭibalāyapi itthiyā aviññattipathe ṭhitāya dūtena vā paṇṇena vā ārocentassa duṭṭhullavācāpatti na hotīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā, duṭṭhullavācassādarāgo, tena rāgena obhāsanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Duṭṭhullavācassādasikkhāpadaṃ.

12. Now, in order to explain lewd speech, the passage beginning with “with delight in lewd speech” is commenced. Herein, “with delight in lewd speech” (duṭṭhullavācassādena) means “with lustful delight in speech connected with the excrement passage, the urine passage, or sexual intercourse.” “Maggaṃ vārabbha methunaṃ” (referring to a passage or sexual intercourse) means “referring to either one of the excrement passage or the urine passage, or to sexual intercourse.” “Obhāsanto” (addressing) means “speaking to.” “Manussitthiṃ” (a human female) refers to “a human female who is intelligent, capable, and able to discern well-spoken and ill-spoken words, and lewd and non-lewd words.” “Suṇamānaṃ” (listening) means “listening.” By this it is shown that even if one announces it to a capable woman who is in a state of not understanding, through a messenger or a letter, there is no offense of lewd speech. A human female, perception of her as female, lustful delight in lewd speech, addressing her due to that lust, and her understanding at that moment—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule concerning delight in lewd speech.

13. Idāni attakāmapāricariyaṃ dassetuṃ “vaṇṇa”ntyādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo bhikkhu attano kāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ vatvā methunarāgena itthiṃ methunaṃ yācamāno garuṃ phuseti sambandho. Vaṇṇaṃ vatvāti guṇaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsetvā. Attanokāmapāricariyāyāti methunadhammasaṅkhātena kāmena pāricariyā kāmapāricariyā, attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā attanokāmapāricariyā, aluttasamāsoyaṃ. Atha vā attanoti katvatthe sāmivacanaṃ, attano kāmitā icchitāti attanokāmā, sayaṃ methunarāgavasena patthitāti attho, attanokāmā ca sā pāricariyā cāti attanokāmapāricariyā[M 0.0470], tāya attanokāmapāricariyāya, “etadaggaṃ, bhagini, pāricariyānaṃ, yā mādisaṃ sīlavantaṃ kalyāṇadhammaṃ brahmacāriṃ etena dhammena paricareyyā”ti evaṃ vaṇṇaṃ vatvāti attho. Yācadhātuno dvikammikattā “itthiṃ methunaṃ yācamāno”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha itthinti duṭṭhullobhāsane vuttappakāraṃ itthiṃ. Manussitthī, itthisaññitā[V 0.0397], attakāmapāricariyāya rāgo, tena rāgena vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadaṃ.

13. Now, in order to explain “service for one's own sensual pleasure,” the passage beginning with “praise” is stated. Herein, the connection is: “If a bhikkhu, having spoken praise for the sake of service for his own sensual pleasure, solicits a woman for sexual intercourse with lust for sexual intercourse, he commits a grave offense.” “Having spoken praise” (vaṇṇaṃ vatvā) means “having declared the virtue and benefit.” “For the sake of service for one's own sensual pleasure” (attanokāmapāricariyāya) means “service (pāricariyā) by means of sensual pleasure (kāmena) which is sexual intercourse (methunadhammasaṅkhātena) is ‘service for sensual pleasure’ (kāmapāricariyā). ‘Service for sensual pleasure for one's own sake’ (attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā) is ‘service for one's own sensual pleasure’ (attanokāmapāricariyā). This is an unelided compound. Alternatively, “one's own” (attano) is a genitive case in the sense of the agent. “Desired by oneself” (attano kāmitā icchitā) is “one's own desire” (attanokāmā), meaning “desired by oneself by way of lust for sexual intercourse.” And that which is “one's own desire” and “service” is “service for one's own sensual pleasure” (attanokāmapāricariyā). By that “service for one's own sensual pleasure,” the meaning is “having spoken praise thus: ‘Sister, this is the foremost of services, that one should serve a virtuous, good-natured celibate like me with this act’.” Because the root “to solicit” (yācadhātu) takes two objects, it is said, “soliciting a woman for sexual intercourse.” Herein, “a woman” (itthiṃ) refers to a woman of the kind described in the context of lewd speech. A human female, perception of her as female, lust for service for one's own sensual pleasure, speaking praise due to that lust, and her understanding at that moment—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule concerning service for one's own sensual pleasure.

14. Idāni sañcarittaṃ dassetuṃ “sandesa”ntyādimāraddhaṃ. Tattha bhikkhu purisassa vā sandesaṃ, itthiyā vā sandesaṃ paṭiggahetvā vīmaṃsitvā paccāharanto garukaṃ phuseti sambandho. Tattha sandesanti “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ māturakkhitaṃ brūhi ‘hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā”ti (pārā. 305) evaṃ vuttaṃ purisassa sāsanaṃ, “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ purisaṃ brūhi ‘ahaṃ tassa bhariyā bhavissāmī”ti (pārā. 326-327 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) evaṃ vuttaṃ itthiyā sāsanaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhitvāti “sādhu upāsakā”ti vā “hotū”ti vā “ārocessāmī”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena vacībhedaṃ katvā vā sīsakampanādīhi vā paṭiggaṇhitvā sampaṭicchitvāti attho. Vīmaṃsitvāti vuttappakārena sāsanaṃ gahetvā purisassa vā itthiyā vā tesaṃ avassārocanakānaṃ mātāpitābhātābhaginiādīnaṃ vā ārocetvāti attho. Haraṃpaccāti ettha “paccāhara”nti vattabbe chandahānibhayā hara-saddaṃ pubbanipātaṃ katvā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yattha pahitena tattha gantvā tena ārocitā sā itthī “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchatu vā paṭikkhipatu vā lajjāya vā tuṇhī hotu, puna āgantvā tassa purisassa haranto ettāvatā imāya paṭiggahaṇārocanappaccāharaṇasaṅkhātāya tivaṅgasampattiyā [M 0.0471] so bhikkhu saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjeyyāti attho. Tesaṃ manussajātikatā, alaṃvacanīyatā, paṭiggaṇhanavīmaṃsanappaccāharaṇānīti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Sañcarittasikkhāpadaṃ.

14. Now, to explain the act of matchmaking, the section beginning with “message” is commenced. Herein, a monk who receives a message from a man or a woman, informs the recipient, and then reports it back, incurs a grave offense; this is the connection. Here, “message” refers to instructions given by a man, such as: “Go, venerable sir, and tell such-and-such a woman under her mother’s protection, ‘Be the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased with wealth,’” (Pārā. 305). Or instructions given by a woman, such as: “Go, venerable sir, and tell such-and-such a man, ‘I will become his wife,’” (Pārā. 326–327, slightly different). “Receives” means accepting it by saying, “Very well, lay follower,” or “So be it,” or “I will inform them,” or by any verbal response, or by nodding the head, etc.—that is the meaning of receiving. “Informs” means having taken the message in the manner described and having informed the man or woman, or their guardians—such as parents, brothers, sisters, etc.—who must be informed. “Reports back”—here, though “paccāhara” should be used, the word “hara” is placed as a prefix to avoid metrical defect; it should be understood that it is stated thus. Having gone where he was sent and informed her, if that woman accepts by saying, “Good,” or rejects it, or remains silent out of shame, and then the monk returns and reports back to that man—by this much, with the accomplishment of these three factors, namely, receiving, informing, and reporting back, that monk would incur a saṅghādisesa offense. Their being of human nature, their being capable of being addressed, and the acts of receiving, informing, and reporting back—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule on matchmaking.

15. Idāni amūlakaṃ pakāsetuṃ “cāvetukāmo”tiādimāraddhaṃ. Cāvetukāmo bhikkhu amūlantimavatthunā aññaṃ suṇamānaṃ bhikkhuṃ codento vā codāpento vā garuṃ phuseti sambandho. Tattha cāvetukāmoti brahmacariyā cāvetukāmo. Codentoti “tvaṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosi, assamaṇosi, asakyaputtiyosī”tiādīhi vacanehi sayaṃ codentoti attho. Evaṃ codentassa vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso. Amūlantimavatthunāti yaṃ codakena cuditakamhi puggale adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, idaṃ etesaṃ dassanasavanaparisaṅkitasaṅkhātānaṃ mūlānaṃ abhāvato nāssa mūlanti amūlaṃ, antimaṃ vatthu yassa pārājikassa tadidaṃ antimavatthu, amūlañca taṃ antimavatthu ceti amūlantimavatthu, tena amūlantimavatthunā, bhikkhuno anurūpesu ekūnavīsatiyā pārājikesu aññatarenāti attho. Codāpayanti codāpayanto, tassa samīpe ṭhatvā [V 0.0398] aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetvā codāpento tassa āṇattassa vācāya vācāya garuṃ phuseti attho. Suṇamānanti iminā parammukhā dūtena vā paṇṇena vā codentassa na ruhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Parammukhā pana sattahi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Yaṃ codeti, tassa upasampannoti saṅkhyūpagamanaṃ, tasmiṃ suddhasaññitā, yena pārājikena codeti, tassa diṭṭhādivasena amūlakatā, cāvanādhippāyena sammukhā codanā, tassa taṅkhaṇavijānananti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Amūlakasikkhāpadaṃ.

15. Now, to explain the groundless accusation, the section beginning with “wishing to expel” is commenced. A bhikkhu who wishes to expel another, accusing or causing another to accuse a listening bhikkhu with a groundless final offense, incurs a grave offense; this is the connection. Here, “wishing to expel” means desiring to expel him from the holy life. “Accusing” means personally reproaching him with statements such as, “You have committed an offense entailing expulsion, you are no ascetic, no follower of the Sakyan,” and so on. For each utterance made in this way, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. “With a groundless final offense” refers to what the accuser has not seen, heard, or suspected in the person being accused. Because it lacks the roots of those classified as seen, heard, or suspected, it is called groundless. The final offense is the matter of that pārājika. Thus, it is a groundless final offense—meaning, by means of any one of the nineteen pārājika offenses suitable for a bhikkhu. “Causing another to accuse” means standing near and instructing another bhikkhu to accuse. For each utterance made by that instructed one, he incurs a grave offense. “Listening” indicates that it does not apply if the accusation is made through a messenger or a letter sent without facing the accused. However, if one speaks not face-to-face, mentioning the seven classes of offenses, it is a dukkaṭa offense. The five factors here are: 1. The one he accuses is an ordained bhikkhu. 2. There is a perception of purity in him. 3. The groundlessness is due to not having seen, heard, or suspected. 4. The accusation is made face-to-face with the intent to expel. 5. The one accused understands it at that moment. This is the training rule on groundless accusations.

16. Idāni [M 0.0472] aññabhāgiyaṃ dassetuṃ “lesamatta”ntiādimāha. Tattha lesamattamupādāyāti jātināmagottaliṅgāpattipattacīvarūpajjhāyācariyasenāsanalesasaṅkhātesu dasasu lesesu yo tasmiṃ puggale dissati, taṃ lesamattaṃ upādāya nissāya bhikkhuṃ brahmacariyā cāvetukāmo amūlantimavatthunā suṇamānaṃ bhikkhuṃ codento garuṃ phuseti attho. Kathaṃ? Añño khattiyajātiko iminā codakena pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto diṭṭho hoti, so aññaṃ attano veriṃ khattiyajātikaṃ bhikkhuṃ passitvā taṃ khattiyajātilesaṃ gahetvā evaṃ “khattiyo mayā diṭṭho pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto, tvaṃ khattiyo pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosī”ti vā “tvaṃ so khattiyo, nāñño, pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī”ti vā codeti, evaṃ nāmalesādayopi veditabbā. Aṅgāni panettha anantarasadisāni. Aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadaṃ.

16. Now, to show what pertains to an unrelated factor, he says, “based on a mere trifle,” etc. Herein, “based on a mere trifle” means, relying on any of the ten trifles—such as birth, name, clan, gender, offense, bowl, robe, preceptor, teacher, or dwelling—that are seen in that person, one who wishes to make a monk fall away from the holy life by accusing a listening bhikkhu with a groundless final offense, relying on such a trifle, incurs a grave offense. How so? Another person of the warrior caste, for example, was seen by this accuser committing a pārājika offense. Then, seeing another monk of the warrior caste who is his enemy, and taking that trifle of warrior caste, he accuses him thus: “A warrior was seen by me committing a pārājika offense; you are a warrior, you have committed a pārājika offense,” or “You are that warrior, no other, you have committed a pārājika offense.” In this way, the trifles of name and so forth should also be understood. The factors here are similar to the immediately preceding ones. This is the training rule on unrelated factors.

Garukāpattiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of Grave Offenses is concluded.

3. Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Nissaggiya Rules

17. Idāni cīvaravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “vikappana”ntyādimuddhaṭaṃ. Yo bhikkhu akālacīvaraṃ vikappanañca adhiṭṭhānañca akatvā dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, tassa bhikkhuno nissaggiyaṃ siyāti piṇḍattho. Tattha akālacīvaranti akāle cīvaraṃ, khomaṃ kappāsikaṃ koseyyaṃ kambalaṃ sāṇaṃ bhaṅganti jātito cha cīvarāni, dukūlaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ somārapaṭṭaṃ cīnapaṭṭaṃ iddhijaṃ devadinnanti imāni pana cha anulomacīvarāni. Tesu dukūlaṃ sāṇassa anulomaṃ vākamayattā. Paṭṭuṇṇādīni [V 0.0399] tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhijādīni dvayāni khomādīnaṃ anulomāni tesamaññatarabhāvato[M 0.0473]. Imesaṃ channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ akālacīvaraṃ.

17. Now, to explain the rules concerning robes, the passage beginning with “designation” is cited. The gist is: if a bhikkhu keeps an out-of-season robe for more than ten days without making a designation or a determination regarding it, that bhikkhu incurs forfeiture. Here, “out-of-season robe” means a robe acquired out of season. There are six kinds of robes by origin: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and bhaṅga. Moreover, there are these six kinds of conforming robes: dukūla, paṭṭuṇṇa, somāra cloth, Chinese cloth, cloth of psychic power, and divinely-obtained cloth. Among these, dukūla is similar to hemp, because it is made of bark fiber. The three, paṭṭuṇṇa and the others, are similar to silk because they are made of thread produced by insects. The two, cloth of psychic power and divinely-obtained cloth, are similar to linen and the like because of being a type of one of them. An out-of-season robe is any one of these six kinds of robes.

Vikappanamadhiṭṭhānanti ettha pana vikappanūpagaṃ adhiṭṭhānūpagañca evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āyāmena aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena caturaṅgulavitthataṃ pacchimacīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358). Majjhimassa purisassa dīghaso dve vidatthiyo, tiriyaṃ vidatthi. Dve vikappanā sammukhāvikappanā ca parammukhāvikappanā ca. Kathaṃ? “Imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ sammukhāvikappanā. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti, ekassa santike “imaṃ cīvaraṃ tissassa bhikkhuno vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ aparāpi sammukhāvikappanā. Tena bhikkhunā “tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti, “imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti vattabbaṃ, tena vattabbo “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā sambhatto vā”ti, tato itarena “tisso bhikkhū”ti vattabbaṃ, puna tena “ahaṃ tissassa bhikkhuno dammī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ parammukhāvikappanā. “Tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Bahuke “imānī”ti, ahatthapāse “etaṃ, etānī”ti vā. Evaṃ vikappanañca akatvāti attho.

Herein, regarding 'assigning and determining,' what is suitable for assigning and what is suitable for determining should be understood thus. In this regard, the Pāli text states: 'I allow, monks, a patch-robe eight Sugata-fingerbreadths in length and four fingerbreadths in width to be assigned' (Mahāvagga 358). For a man of medium height, this is two spans in length and one span across. There are two kinds of assigning: assigning face-to-face and assigning in absence. How? One should say, 'I assign this robe to you'; this is assigning face-to-face. Or, in the presence of one person, one should say, 'I assign this robe to the monk Tissa,' and the recipient should be told, 'Use what is mine, or give it away, or do with it as you see fit'; this is another kind of assigning face-to-face. For assigning in absence, the owner-monk should say to an intermediary, 'I give this robe to you for the purpose of assigning.' The intermediary should then ask, 'Who is your friend, acquaintance, or intimate?' The other, the owner, should then say, 'The monk Tissa.' Then he, the intermediary, should say, 'I give it to the monk Tissa'; this is assigning in absence. When it is said, 'Use what belongs to the monk Tissa, or give it away, or do with it as you see fit,' this is called a withdrawal. For many items, one should say 'these'; if they are not within hand's reach, 'that' or 'those'. The meaning is 'and without having done assigning in this way'.

Ticīvarassa pana pamāṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena sugatacīvarato ūnakaṃ vaṭṭati, lāmakaparicchedena saṅghāṭiyā, uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghato muṭṭhipañcakaṃ, tiriyaṃ muṭṭhittikaṃ, antaravāsako dīghato muṭṭhipañcako, tiriyaṃ dvihatthopi aḍḍhateyyo vā vaṭṭati. Vuttappamāṇato adhikañca ūnakañca “parikkhāracoḷa”nti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Dve cīvarassa adhiṭṭhānā kāyena vā adhiṭṭheti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭheti. Ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahantena rajitvā [M 0.0474] kappabinduṃ datvā purāṇasaṅghāṭiṃ “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmī”ti paccuddharitvā navaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ hatthena gahetvā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena adhiṭṭhātabbā, idaṃ kāyena adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena aphusantassa na vaṭṭati. Vācāya adhiṭṭhānaṃ pana vacībhedaṃ katvā vācāya adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, sace hatthapāse “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti, sace ahatthapāse ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā[V 0.0400]. Esa nayo uttarāsaṅge, antaravāsake ca. Ticīvarādīni sabbāni ekato katvā “imāni cīvarāni parikkhāracoḷāni adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭatīti. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhānañca akatvāti attho.

Regarding the measurement of the three robes, by the highest limit, it is proper for it to be smaller than the Sugata’s robe. By the lowest limit, for the outer robe and the upper robe, the length is five fists and the width is three fists; for the lower robe, the length is five fists, and the width is two or two and a half cubits. What is larger or smaller than the stated measurement should be determined as 'requisite-cloth.' There are two ways of determining a robe: one determines by body or one determines by speech. When determining the three robes, having dyed it and applied the marking-spot, one should withdraw the old outer robe, saying, 'I withdraw this outer robe.' Then, taking the new outer robe in hand, having made a mental reflection, 'I determine this outer robe,' and making a bodily gesture, it should be determined by body. This is determination by body. It is not valid for one who does not touch it with some part of the body. Determination by speech, however, should be done by making a verbal utterance. If it is within hand's reach, one should utter the words, 'I determine this outer robe.' If it is not within hand's reach, having noted its location, one should utter the words, 'I determine that outer robe.' This is the method for the upper robe and the lower robe as well. It is also proper to determine all the three robes and so on together, saying, 'I determine these robes as requisite-cloths.' The meaning is 'and without having done the determination in this way'.

Dasa ahāni dasāhaṃ. Atimāpetīti atikkāmeti. Tassāti tassa bhikkhuno. Nissaggiyanti nissajjanaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, pubbabhāge kattabbassa vinayakammassetaṃ nāmaṃ, nissaggiyamassa atthīti nissaggiyaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Pācittiyaṃ, taṃ atikkāmayato sahanissaggiyavinayakammaṃ pācittiyaṃ siyā, ayamettha attho. Taṃ panetaṃ cīvaraṃ yaṃ divasaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa yo aruṇo, so uppannadivasanissito, tasmā cīvaruppādadivasena saddhiṃ ekādase aruṇuggamane dasāhātikkamitaṃ hotīti. Cīvarassa attano santakatā, jātippamāṇayuttatā, chinnapalibodhabhāvo, atirekacīvaratā, dasāhātikkamoti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadaṃ.

'Ten days' (dasāhaṃ) means ten days. 'Lets it exceed' (atimāpeti) means goes beyond. 'His' (tassa) means of that monk. 'Entailing forfeiture' (nissaggiyaṃ): relinquishment is nissaggiyaṃ; this is the name for the disciplinary act to be performed in the preliminary stage. That which has forfeiture is nissaggiyaṃ. What is that? A pācittiya offense. For one who lets it go beyond, there would be a pācittiya offense together with the disciplinary act of forfeiture; this is the meaning here. Now, as for that robe, on whatever day it arose, the dawn of that day is connected with the day of arising. Therefore, including the day the robe arose, at the rising of the dawn on the eleventh day, it has exceeded ten days. Herein, these are the five factors: the robe being one's own possession, its being of the proper kind and size, the state of being free from ties, its being an extra robe, and the exceeding of ten days. The first training rule concerning the Kathina.

18. Idāni dutiyaṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhusammutiyā”tyādimāraddhaṃ. Yo bhikkhusammutiṃ vajjetvā kālañca vinā adhiṭṭhitaṃ ticīvaraṃ ekāhaṃ atikkamāpeti, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyāti sambandho. Tattha bhikkhusammutiyāññatrāti yaṃ saṅgho gilānassa bhikkhuno ticīvarena vippavāsasammutiṃ deti[M 0.0475], taṃ ṭhapetvā. Ticīvaramadhiṭṭhitanti karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tena ticīvarādhiṭṭhānanayena adhiṭṭhitesu saṅghāṭiādīsu yena kenaci cīvarena. Ekāhanti ekarattaṃ. Atimāpetīti vippavasati, viyutto vasatīti attho. Tassa aladdhasammutikassa bhikkhuno ekarattampi cīvarena vippavāsato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ siyāti attho. Samayaṃ vināti cīvarakālaṃ vajjetvā. Adhiṭṭhitacīvaratā, anatthatakathinatā, aladdhasammutitā, rattivippavāsoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni. Dutiyakathinasikkhāpadaṃ.

18. Now, to show the second rule, the passage beginning 'except by the consent of the monks' is introduced. The connection is: for a monk who, excluding the consent of the monks and apart from the proper season, is separated for one day from the determined triple robe, there is an offense entailing forfeiture. Therein, 'except by the consent of the monks' means setting aside the consent the Sangha gives to a sick monk to be away from his triple robe. 'The determined triple robe' is a usage in the instrumental sense; thereby it means any robe, such as the outer robe, that has been determined in the manner of determining the triple robe. 'One day' means one night. 'Lets it exceed' (atimāpeti) means is away; the meaning is 'dwells separated.' The meaning is that for a monk who has not received consent, from being away from the robe for even one night, there is a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture. 'Apart from the season' means excluding the robe season. Herein, these are the four factors: its being a determined robe, the Kathina not having been spread, not having received consent, and being away for a night. The second training rule concerning the Kathina.

19. Idāni purāṇacīvaraṃ dassetuṃ “aññātikā”tyādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha aññātikāti aññātikāya “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso”tiādīsu viya, aññātikāya neva mātusambandhena na pitusambandhena sambaddhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhikkhuniyāti aṭṭhavācikakammena upasampannāya. Ākoṭāpetīti paharāpeti. Tanti nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Purāṇacīvaratā, upacāre [V 0.0401] ṭhatvā aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā āṇāpanaṃ, tassā dhovanādīni cāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadaṃ.

19. Now, to show the rule concerning an old robe, the passage beginning 'unrelated' is introduced. Therein, 'unrelated' (aññātikā): just as in 'reflecting wisely' (paṭisaṅkhā yoniso), it is the instrumental case aññātikāya, meaning 'by one who is unrelated,' that is, not connected through the mother's side nor through the father's side. 'A bhikkhunī' means one who has been fully ordained by the act with eight announcements. 'Has it beaten' (ākoṭāpeti) means has it struck. The meaning is that there would be a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture. Herein, these are the three factors: its being an old robe, giving an order to an unrelated bhikkhunī while standing in the vicinity, and her washing it, and so on. The training rule concerning an old robe.

20. Kiñci mūlakanti kiñci pābhataṃ. Cīvarādāneti cīvarassa ādāne cīvarappaṭiggahaṇe. Vikappanūpagacīvaratā, pārivattakābhāvo, aññātikāya hatthato gahaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadaṃ.

20. 'With some price' (kiñci mūlakaṃ) means with some gift. 'In the taking of a robe' (cīvarādāne) means in the taking of a robe, in the acceptance of a robe. Herein, these are the three factors: its being a robe suitable for assigning, the absence of an exchange, and taking it from the hand of an unrelated female. The training rule concerning the acceptance of a robe.

21. Appavāritanti “vadeyyātha, bhante, yena attho”ti icchāpitaṃ icchaṃ ruciṃ uppāditaṃ, na pavāritanti appavāritaṃ. Viññāpentassāti yācantassa. Aññatra samayāti naṭṭhacīvarakālaṃ ṭhapetvā. Vikappanūpagacīvaratā, samayābhāvo, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadaṃ.

21. 'Uninvited' (appavāritaṃ): not having had a wish or liking produced by being invited with the words, 'Speak, venerable sir, what you need'; not invited is appavāritaṃ. 'For one who makes a request' (viññāpentassa) means for one who asks. 'Except on an occasion' (aññatra samayā) means setting aside the time when one's robe has been lost. Herein, these are the four factors: its being a robe suitable for assigning, the absence of a proper occasion, a request made to an unrelated person, and the acquisition through that. The training rule concerning a request to an unrelated person.

22. Rajatanti [M 0.0476] rūpiyaṃ. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Māsakanti tayo māsakā lohamāsako dārumāsako jatumāsakoti. Tattha lohamāsakoti tambalohādīhi katamāsako. Dārumāsakoti sāradārunā vā veḷupesikāya vā antamaso tālapaṇṇenapi rūpaṃ chinditvā katamāsako. Jatumāsakoti lākhāya vā niyyāsena vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā katamāsako. Kahāpaṇanti suvaṇṇamayaṃ vā rūpiyamayaṃ vā pākatikaṃ vā. Gaṇheyyāti attano atthāya dīyamānaṃ vā katthaci ṭhitaṃ vā nippariggahaṃ disvā sayaṃ gaṇheyya. Gaṇhāpeyyāti tadeva aññena gāhāpeyya. Nissaggīti gahaṇādīsu yaṃ kiñci karontassa aghanabaddhesu vatthugaṇanāya nissaggi siyāti attho. Sādiyeyya vāti kāyavācāhi appaṭikkhipitvā cittena adhivāseyya. Jātarūparajatabhāvo, attuddesikatā, gahaṇādīsu aññatarabhāvoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadaṃ.

22. ‘Rajatanti’ means silver. ‘Jātarūpanti’ means gold. ‘Māsakanti’ refers to three kinds of māsakas: a metal māsaka, a wooden māsaka, and a lac māsaka. Among these, a metal māsaka is one made from copper or similar metals. A wooden māsaka is one shaped from hardwood, a bamboo chip, or even just a cut piece of palm leaf. A lac māsaka is one formed by shaping lac or resin. ‘Kahāpaṇanti’ refers to a coin made of gold or silver, or a standard one. ‘Gaṇheyyāti’ means taking for oneself something given or, seeing something ownerless left somewhere, taking it oneself. ‘Gaṇhāpeyyāti’ means having someone else take it. ‘Nissaggīti’ means that for one who performs any act such as taking, it entails forfeiture according to the count of the objects, in the case of those not bound by a fixed price. ‘Sādiyeyya vāti’ means accepting it without verbal or physical refusal, consenting with the mind. Here, the three factors are: the nature of gold or silver, the intention for oneself, and the occurrence of any act such as taking. This is the training rule on the acceptance of money.

23. Rajatādicatubbidhaṃ akappiyaṃ kappiyenāpi parivatteyya sahadhammike ṭhapetvā, nissaggiyaṃ siyāti sambandho. Tattha akappiyanti akappiyavatthuṃ. Kappiyenāti kappiyavatthunā. Sahadhammiketi bhikkhubhikkhunisāmaṇerasāmaṇerisikkhamānasaṅkhāte pañca sahadhammike. Rūpiyabhāvo, parivattanañcāti imānettha dve aṅgāni. Rūpiyaparivattanasikkhāpadaṃ.

23. If one exchanges the four kinds of unallowable things beginning with silver for an allowable item, except with fellow monastics, it entails forfeiture—this is the connection. Here, ‘akappiyanti’ means an unallowable object. ‘Kappiyenāti’ means with an allowable object. ‘Sahadhammiketi’ refers to the five fellow monastics: monks, nuns, male novices, female novices, and probationary nuns. The two factors here are: the nature of money, and the exchange. This is the training rule on exchanging money.

24. “Imaṃ [V 0.0402] pattaṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”tiādinā vikappanañca “imaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādinā adhiṭṭhānañca akatvāti attho. Pamāṇikanti etthāyaṃ vinicchayo – anupahatapurāṇasālitaṇḍulānaṃ sukoṭṭitaparisuddhānaṃ dve magadhanāḷiyo gahetvā tehi taṇḍulehi anuttaṇḍulamakilinnamapiṇḍitaṃ suvisadaṃ kundamakuḷarāsisadisaṃ avassāvitodanaṃ pacitvā niravasesaṃ patte pakkhipitvā tassa odanassa [M 0.0477] catutthabhāgappamāṇo nātighano nātitanuko hatthahāriyo sabbasambhārasaṅkhato muggasūpo pakkhipitabbo, tato ālopassa anurūpaṃ yāvacarimālopappahonakaṃ macchamaṃsādibyañjanaṃ pakkhipitabbaṃ. Sappitelatakkarasakañjikādīni pana agaṇanūpagāni honti. Tāni hi odanagatikāni neva hāpetuṃ, na vaḍḍhetuṃ sakkonti. Evametaṃ sabbampi pakkhittaṃ sace pana pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, suttena vā hīrena vā chindantassa suttassa vā hīrassa vā heṭṭhimantaṃ phusati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti, antogatameva hoti, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho nāma. Ukkaṭṭhato upaḍḍhappamāṇo majjhimo. Majjhimato upaḍḍhappamāṇo omako. Tesampi vuttanayeneva pabhedo veditabbo. Iccetesu ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho ca omakomako cāti dve apattā, sesā satta pattā pamāṇayuttā nāmāti evaṃ pamāṇena yutto pamāṇiko, taṃ pamāṇikaṃ. Pattanti sattasu pattesu aññataraṃ pattaṃ. Pattassa attano santakatā, pamāṇayuttatā, adhiṭṭhānūpagatā, atirekapattatā, dasāhātikkamoti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Paṭhamapattasikkhāpadaṃ.

24. The meaning is: without having performed the designation (vikappana) by saying, ‘I designate this bowl for you,’ etc., and the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) by saying, ‘I determine upon this bowl,’ etc. Regarding ‘of proper size,’ here is the determination: Two Magadhan nāḷis of unblemished, old, well-husked and purified rice grains should be taken. With these grains, rice should be cooked—not watery, not sticky, not lumpy, very clear, resembling a heap of jasmine buds—and the water should be drained off. Having placed all of it into the bowl without remainder, a mung bean soup, neither too thick nor too thin, able to be taken by hand, complete with all ingredients, should be placed into it, in a quantity measuring one-fourth of the rice. After that, relishes such as fish, meat, etc., should be placed into it, in proportion to the mouthful, enough for the last mouthful. However, ghee, oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, and so on, are not counted, for they follow the nature of the rice and can neither decrease nor increase it. If all this has been placed in the bowl and it stands level with the lower line of the bowl's mouth rim, or if when cutting it with a thread or a strand of hair, the lower end of the thread or hair touches it, this is called a ‘superior bowl.’ If it surpasses that line and stands like a mound, this is called a ‘superior-inferior’ (ukkaṭṭhomaka) bowl. If it does not reach that line and remains inside, this is called a ‘superior-superior’ (ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha) bowl. Half the size of the superior bowl is the medium bowl. Half the size of the medium bowl is the inferior bowl. The distinctions among these, too, should be understood in the manner stated. Thus, among these, the ‘superior-superior’ (ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha) and the ‘inferior-inferior’ (omakomaka) are two improper bowls; the remaining seven bowls are said to be endowed with the proper measure. Thus, endowed with the proper measure is ‘of proper size;’ that is the bowl of proper size. A ‘bowl’ refers to one of the seven bowls. Ownership of the bowl, being of proper size, being subject to determination, being an excess bowl, and exceeding ten days—these are the five factors here. This is the first training rule on bowls.

25. Yo bhikkhu pañcabandhanato ūnapatte sati paraṃ pana navaṃ pattaṃ viññāpeti, tassapi bhikkhuno nissaggiyaṃ siyāti sambandho. Tattha paranti aññaṃ, “navaṃ patta”ntiminā tulyādhikaraṇaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānūpagapattassa ūnapañcabandhanatā, attuddesikatā, kataviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadaṃ.

25. If a monk, when his determined bowl has fewer than five mends, then requests another new bowl, it entails forfeiture for that monk—this is the connection. Here, ‘paraṃ’ means another, and it is in apposition with ‘new bowl.’ The four factors here are: the determined bowl having fewer than five mends, its being intended for oneself, the request having been made, and the acquisition through that request. This is the training rule concerning a bowl with fewer than five mends.

26. Yo sappitelādikaṃ pana bhesajjaṃ paṭiggahetvā sattāhaparamaṃ sannidhikārakaṃ bhuñjanto sattāhaṃ atikkāmeti[M 0.0478], tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyāti attho. Tattha sappitelādikanti ettha ādi-saddo navanītamadhuphāṇitaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha sappi nāma gavādīnaṃ sappi, yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappi, tathā navanītaṃ. Telaṃ nāma tilasāsapamadhukaeraṇḍavasādīhi nibbattaṃ. Madhu nāma [V 0.0403] makkhikāmadhumeva. Ucchurasaṃ upādāya pana apakkā vā avatthukapakkā vā sabbāpi ucchuvikati phāṇitanti veditabbaṃ. Bhesajjavidhānasikkhāpadaṃ.

26. If a monk, having received medicine such as ghee and oil, which may be stored for a maximum of seven days, consumes it having stored it beyond seven days, it entails forfeiture—this is the meaning. Herein, in ‘ghee, oil, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes fresh butter, honey, and molasses. Here, ‘ghee’ means the ghee of cows and other animals whose meat is allowable; the ghee of such animals is allowable, as is fresh butter. ‘Oil’ means that which is produced from sesame, mustard, madhuca, castor beans, fat, and so on. ‘Honey’ means only the honey of bees. However, beginning with sugarcane juice, any sugarcane product, whether uncooked or cooked without a base, should be understood as ‘molasses.’ This is the training rule on the procedure for medicines.

27. Bhikkhussa cīvaraṃ datvā puna taṃ cīvaraṃ sakasaññāya acchindantassa vā acchindāpayatopi vā nissaggiyaṃ siyāti yojanā. Tattha datvāti veyyāvaccādīni paccāsīsamāno datvā. Acchindantassāti veyyāvaccādīni akarontaṃ disvā balakkārena gaṇhantassa, tathā acchindāpayatoti. Vikappanūpagacīvaratā, sāmaṃdinnatā, sakasaññitā, upasampannatā, kodhavasena acchindanaṃ vā acchindāpanaṃ vāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Acchindanasikkhāpadaṃ.

27. For a monk who, having given a robe to a monk, then takes that robe back or has it taken back with the perception that it is his own, it entails forfeiture—this is the explanation. Herein, ‘having given’ means giving while expecting services and so on in return. ‘Takes it back’ refers to forcibly seizing it upon seeing that services and so on are not being performed; and similarly for ‘has it taken back.’ The five factors here are: the robe being subject to designation, its having been given by oneself, the perception that it is one’s own, the recipient being fully ordained, and the taking back or having it taken back out of anger. This is the training rule on taking back.

28. Appavāritaṃ aññātiṃ gahapatiṃ suttaṃ yācitvā ñātippavārite vajjetvā tantavāyehi cīvaraṃ vāyāpentassa nissaggiyaṃ siyāti piṇḍattho. Tattha suttanti chabbidhaṃ khomasuttādikaṃ vā tesaṃ anulomaṃ vā. Yāciyāti cīvaratthāya yācitvā. Cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttaṃ, attuddesikatā, akappiyatantavāyena akappiyaviññattiyā vāyāpananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Suttaviññattisikkhāpadaṃ.

28. For a monk who, having asked for thread from an unrelated householder who has not made an invitation, setting aside invited relatives, then has a robe woven by weavers, it entails forfeiture—this is the summary meaning. Here, ‘thread’ refers to the six kinds, such as linen thread, or anything suitable for them. ‘Having asked’ means having asked for the purpose of a robe. The three factors here are: the thread having been requested for the purpose of a robe, its being for one's own purpose, and having it woven by an unsuitable weaver or through an unsuitable request. This is the training rule on requesting thread.

29. Yo bhikkhu saṅghassa pariṇataṃ lābhaṃ jānanto attano pariṇāmeti, tassa nissaggiyaṃ siyāti attho. Tattha jānanti jānanto. Lābhanti labhitabbaṃ cīvarādivatthuṃ. Pariṇatanti saṅghassa ninnaṃ saṅghassa poṇaṃ saṅghassa pabbhāraṃ hutvā [M 0.0479] ṭhitaṃ. Attano pariṇāmetīti “mayhaṃ dethā”tiādīni vadanto attani ninnaṃ karoti. Saṅghe pariṇatabhāvo, taṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmanaṃ, paṭilābhoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni. Pariṇāmanasikkhāpadaṃ.

29. If a monk, knowing that a gain has been dedicated to the Sangha, diverts it to himself, it entails forfeiture for him—this is the meaning. Here, ‘jānanti’ means knowing. ‘Lābhanti’ refers to an item to be obtained, such as a robe. ‘Pariṇatanti’ means it has become inclined towards the Sangha, tending towards the Sangha, or leaning towards the Sangha. ‘Attano pariṇāmetīti’ means that by saying, “Give it to me,” and so on, one inclines it towards oneself. The three factors here are: the item being dedicated to the Sangha, knowing this and diverting it to oneself, and its acquisition. This is the training rule on diversion.

Nissaggiyaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the Nissaggiya rules is concluded.

4. Pācittiyaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Pācittiya Rules

30. Idāni [V 0.0404] pācittiyaṃ dassetuṃ “sampajānamusāvāde”tyādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sampajānamusāvādeti nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tasmā yo bhikkhu sampajānanto musā vadati, tassa tannimittaṃ taṃhetu tappaccayā pācittiyaṃ udīritanti attho. Bhikkhuñca omasantassāti jātināmagottakammasippavayaābādhaliṅgakilesāpattiakkosesu bhūtena vā abhūtena vā yena kenaci mukhasattinā bhikkhuṃ ovijjhantassa bhikkhuno pācittiyaṃ udīritanti attho. Pesuññaharaṇepi cāti bhikkhussa pesuññaharaṇe, jātiādīhi akkosavatthūhi bhikkhuṃ akkosantassa bhikkhuno sutvā bhikkhuno piyakamyatāya vā bhedādhippāyena vā yo akkuddho, tassa bhikkhussa kāyena vā vācāya vā pesuññaharaṇavacane pācittiyaṃ udīritanti attho.

30. Now, to present the Pācittiya, the section beginning with “in intentional false speech” is commenced. Here, “in intentional false speech” is a locative expression indicating the cause. Therefore, the meaning is: for any bhikkhu who knowingly speaks falsely, a Pācittiya offense is declared on account of that, for that reason, for that cause. And for one who reviles a bhikkhu: the meaning is that a Pācittiya offense is declared for a bhikkhu who assails another bhikkhu with any kind of verbal dart, whether true or false, concerning birth, name, lineage, occupation, craft, age, illness, physical characteristics, defilements, offenses, or insults. And also in the case of carrying tales: for a bhikkhu who, having heard another bhikkhu being insulted with grounds such as birth, etc., then, wishing to be agreeable to that bhikkhu or with the intention of causing dissension, conveys these tales to that bhikkhu by body or by speech, even if he is not angry, a Pācittiya offense is declared—this is the meaning.

31. Saṅgītittayamāruḷhaṃ piṭakattayaṃ dhammaṃ bhikkhuñca bhikkhuniñca ṭhapetvā aññena puggalena saddhiṃ ekato padaṃ padaṃ bhaṇantassa bhikkhuno padagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ udīritanti samudāyattho.

31. The overall meaning is this: For a bhikkhu who, excluding another bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, recites word by word together with an unordained person the Dhamma that has been established by the three councils and is contained in the three baskets, a Pācittiya offense is declared for each word.

32. Anupasampannenevāti bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā antamaso pārājikavatthubhūtena tiracchānagatenāpi saha tirattiyaṃ sayitvā catutthadivase atthaṅgate sūriye puna sahaseyyāya [M 0.0480] pācitti siyāti sambandho. Tattha sahaseyyāyāti sabbacchannaparicchinne, yebhuyyenacchannaparicchinne vā senāsane pubbāpariyena vā ekakkhaṇe vā ekato nisajjanāya. Tattha chadanaṃ anāhacca diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhena pākārādinā paricchinnampi sabbaparicchinnamicceva veditabbaṃ.

32. By ‘one not fully ordained’ is meant anyone apart from a bhikkhu, even down to an animal that could be the basis for a Pārājika offense. The connection is that if one lies down together with such a person for three nights, on the fourth day after the sun has set, a Pācittiya offense is incurred by lying down together again. Here, ‘lying down together’ refers to lying down or sitting together, either sequentially or simultaneously, in a dwelling that is completely enclosed or mostly enclosed. In this context, a space enclosed by a wall or similar structure with a height of one and a half cubits, even without a roof, should be understood as completely enclosed.

33. Ekarattampi itthiyā saddhiṃ seyyaṃ kappayato tassa bhikkhunopi pācitti siyāti attho. Tattha itthiyāti antamaso tadahujātāyapi manussitthiyā. Desentassa vinā viññuṃ, dhammañca chappaduttarinti viññuṃ purisaṃ vinā itthiyā chappadato uttariṃ dhammaṃ desentassa bhikkhuno pācitti siyāti attho. Tattha “chappaduttari”nti ettha eko gāthāpādo ekaṃ padanti evaṃ sabbattha padappamāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Cha padāni chappadaṃ, chappadato uttariṃ chappaduttariṃ.

33. The meaning is that even if a bhikkhu arranges to lie down with a woman for a single night, he incurs a Pācittiya offense. Here, ‘a woman’ means a human female, even one born that very day. For a bhikkhu who teaches Dhamma of more than six words to a woman without a knowledgeable man present, a Pācittiya offense is incurred—this is the meaning. Here, regarding ‘more than six words,’ the measure of a word should be understood in all such cases as follows: one line of a verse is one word. Six words are ‘six-word’; more than six words is ‘more-than-six-word’.

34. Bhikkhusammutiṃ [V 0.0405] ṭhapetvā bhikkhuno duṭṭhullaṃ vajjaṃ abhikkhuno vadantassa pācittiyaṃ udīritanti attho. Tattha duṭṭhullanti idha saṅghādisesaṃ adhippetaṃ. Bhikkhusammutiyāti yaṃ saṅgho abhiṇhāpattikassa bhikkhuno āyatiṃ saṃvaratthāya āpattīnañca kulānañca pariyantaṃ katvā vā akatvā vā tikkhattuṃ apaloketvā katikaṃ karoti, taṃ ṭhapetvā. Abhikkhunoti anupasampannassa. Vadantassāti ārocentassa.

34. The meaning is that if a bhikkhu, unless authorized by the Sangha, speaks of another bhikkhu’s grave offense to one who is not a bhikkhu, a Pācittiya offense is declared. Here, ‘grave offense’ refers to a Saṅghādisesa offense. By ‘authorized by the Sangha’ is meant the exclusion of a formal act which the Sangha establishes for a bhikkhu who frequently commits offenses, for the sake of future restraint, either setting or not setting limits regarding offenses and families, after announcing it three times. By ‘one who is not a bhikkhu’ is meant one who is not fully ordained. By ‘speaks’ is meant reports.

35. Yo akappiyaṃ pathaviṃ khaṇeyya vā khaṇāpeyya vā, tassa pācittiyaṃ siyā. Tattha akappiyanti uddhanapacanādivasena vā tathā tathā adaḍḍhā vā jātapathavī vuccati. Sā tividhā suddhamissapuñjavasena. Tattha suddhapathavī nāma pakatiyā suddhapaṃsu vā suddhamattikā vā. Missapathavī nāma yattha paṃsuto vā mattikato vā pāsāṇasakkharakathalamarumbavālukāsu aññatarassa tatiyabhāgo hoti. Puñjapathavī [M 0.0481] nāma atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭho paṃsupuñjo vā mattikāpuñjo vā hoti. Vuttalakkhaṇena pana missakapuñjopi piṭṭhipāsāṇe ṭhitasukhumarajampi ca deve phusayante sakiṃ ce tintaṃ, cātumāsaccayena tintokāso puñjapathavīsaṅkhameva gacchati. Yo bhikkhu bhūtagāmaṃ vikopeyya, tassa pācittiyaṃ siyāti sambandho. Tattha bhūtagāmanti bhavanti, abhavuṃ cāti bhūtā, jāyanti vaḍḍhanti jātā vaḍḍhitā cāti attho, gāmoti rāsi, bhūtānaṃ gāmo, bhūtā eva vā gāmoti bhūtagāmo, patiṭṭhitaharitatiṇarukkhādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ bhūtagāmaṃ. Vikopeyyāti chedanabhedanādīni kareyya.

35. If a bhikkhu digs or causes to dig earth that is not allowable, a Pācittiya offense is incurred. Here, ‘not allowable’ is said of natural earth that is unburnt, unlike that used for ovens, cooking, and so on. It is of three kinds: pure, mixed, or heaped. ‘Pure earth’ means naturally pure dust or clay. ‘Mixed earth’ means where, besides dust or clay, a third part consists of one of these: stones, gravel, potsherds, pebbles, or sand. ‘Heaped earth’ means a heap of dust or clay that has been exposed to rain for more than four months.
